units.la: DIssertatio hæc de Socino & Socinianismo, quæ tui nominis Patrocinium petit, non uno nomine illud à Te postulat. Nam sive ipsam Compositionem, sive Argumentum hujus libelli, sive Authoritatem tuam in Ecclesia, sive præsentem hujus Ecclesiæ nostræ Statum, in qua præsides, confidero, Dignitati tuæ inprimis debita videtur. Etenim primo, non possum non lubens, gratusque fateri, me in hoc Opusculo conficiendo, haud mediocriter instructum, adjutumque fuisse, Suppellectile ista libraria, qua Bibliotheca tua eximie locupletata est. Deinde Dignitas ista Episcopalis, qua superemines in Ecclesia, ut Facultatem dat, sic & obligat, præ cæteris è clero Anglicano,ad suscipiendum veteris Fidei Catholicæ Patrocinium contra cujuscunque generis novatores; istos præsertim, qui ipsius Christianismi fundamenta convellunt. Hujusmodi vero Patrocinium eo magis necessarium est, magisque tempestive poscitur quo novatorum Dogmata perniciofiora sunt, & numero plura; quo periculosius se ingerunt, latiusque se spargunt. Socinianismus autem, ut bene notum est, quædam Hydra multiceps est, sive Compendiū Hæresium, earumque pessimarum, quas proinde Ecclesia Catholica jampridem Synodis frequentibus damnavit earumque Patronos gravissimo Anathemate percussit. Porro, cum Anabaptismus utplurimum rude vulgus infecerit, cui Dogmata de Bonorum Communitate, & Immunitate à Jure atque Dominio magistratuum, valde allube-scunt, Socinianismus è contra eo periculosior est, quia non tam crassos Politici corporis humores corrumpere gessit atque conturbare, quam Spiritus tenuiores atque subtiliores, (cujusmodi sunt animales in cerebro versantes) nimirum Ingenia politiora, & generosiora, quæ cum hujusmodi virus penitus imbiberint, multo validiora sunt ad malum istud, quo sic tincta sunt & penitus imbuta, undiquaque dispergendum, Hæresisque istius Pestem etiam iis affiare[?] satagunt, qui & Ingenio pollent; & Dignitate præstant. Huc accedit valde speciosus rectæ Rationis Prætextus, qui cunctis blandissime arridet, & quasi fascino quodam Homines dementat. Plerique enim innata quadam Philautia laborant, qua sibi præ cæteris sapere videntur; & obstinatione Animi, quæ præfractos reddit, & alieni Arbitrii impatientes, eo quod judicandi libertatem intra certos limites coerceat, Rationem quasi captivam in Triumpho ducat, & Opiniones cujusque privatas Authoritati publicæ vel invitas subdat. Sed quod adhuc propius attingit, & validius urget germanos Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ Filios, unicuique Horum, hodie præsertim, ex Officio incumbet, Matrem suam, tot nominibus sibi venerabilem, ut contra omne genus Adversarios pro viribus defendere, sic & Ipsius famam vindicare à malignantium Calumniis; Romanensium præcipue, qui, præter vim apertam, fraudibus rem agunt, eo periculosius, quo occultius: partim dum sectas nescio quot contra Iosam & excitant, & fovent, quibus ex omni Parte oppugnetur; partim, dum atrocissimis Calumniis eandem defamare nituntur, cunctisque invisam reddere. Præsertim, cum affirmant Ipsam in hoc Socinianismo patrocinari, dum uniuscujusque Privati Rationem S. Scripturæ Interpretem statuit, omniumque Controversiarum in Religionis negotio Judicem, sepositâ Ecclesiæ Authoritate, aliisque mediis ad rite judicandum requisitis. Quasi non aliter Ecclesiæ nostræ Reformationem, Doctrinamque in ipsa stabilitatem tueri possemus, quam ex Socinianorum Principiis; quia sc.[?] infallibili isti Authoritati, quam Ecclesia Romana sibi perperam arrogat, Rationis nostræ Judicium in universum subjicere recusamus. Enimvero, plus satis notum est, quam aversa sit Ecclesia nostra à Socinianismo, seu potius, quam ei adversa; idque non solum ex Seren: Regis nostri Jacobi (veteris Fidei Catholicæ, dum in vivis erat, acerrimi Defensoris) Protestatione Anti.vorstia[?]; sed multo luculentius ex publica Fidei nostræ Consessione Articulis 39. comprehensa; & nuperius in Canone 4*. Synodi Anglicanæ, quæ celebrata est A. D. 1640. quo hæc Hæresium colluvies diserte impugnatur, & gravissima censura damnata est. Tantumque abest, ut Rationem cujusque privatam in Tribunali juridico collocemus, in Ecclesiasticæ Authoritatis opprobrium, ut ex adverso, omnes Concionatores apud nos, legitime ad munus istud exequendum admissi, ex Decreto Ecclesiæ nostræ teneantur —Ne quid unquam doceant pro Concione, quod à Populo religiose teneri & credi velint, nisi quod consentaneum sit Doctrinæ Veteris aut Novi Testamenti; quodque ex illa ipsa Doctrina Catholici Patres, & veteres Episcopi collegerint. lib. Can. 1571. Tit de Concionatoribus. His tamen non obstantibus, Socinianorum libros apud nos passim dispersos habuimus, & à junioribus quoque Scholasticis avidè perlectos in contemptum Canonis supra memorati, 1640. Et quod multo pejus est, quosdam ex his Anglice versos habuimus ut plures etiam è vulgo corrumperent, qui Imperitia juxta, & Inconstantia laborantes, facilius perverti solent, & Catholica Fide deserta, quam nunquam probè didicerunt, in errorum Devia se abduci patiuntur. Imo, neque defuerunt aliqui inter nos Theologi, qui tum in concionibus, tum scriptis in publicum editis, nimis ostenderunt, quantum fav« verint quibusdam Socinianorum Dogmatibus.
units.tr: This dissertation on Socinus and Socinianism, which seeks the protection of your name, has more than one reason to ask it of you. Whether I consider its composition, its subject, your authority in the Church, or the present state of this our Church over which you preside, it seems chiefly owed to your dignity. First, I cannot but gladly and gratefully admit that in composing this little work I was not a little instructed and helped by that stock of books with which your library is so richly furnished. Next, that episcopal dignity by which you stand above others in the Church gives you the power, and also lays on you the obligation, beyond the other clergy of England, to take up the defence of the old Catholic faith against innovators of every kind, and especially those who undermine the very foundations of Christianity. Such a defence is all the more necessary and is all the more urgently called for in proportion as the doctrines of the innovators are more pernicious and more numerous, and as they insinuate themselves more dangerously and spread more widely. Now Socinianism, as is well known, is a sort of many-headed Hydra, or a compendium of heresies, and of the worst of them, which the Catholic Church long ago condemned in crowded synods and struck with the gravest anathema, together with their patrons. Furthermore, since Anabaptism has infected for the most part the common rabble, who are greatly attracted to the doctrines of community of goods and of exemption from the right and dominion of the magistrates, Socinianism on the other hand is the more dangerous, because it sets out to corrupt and disturb not so much the coarse humours of the body politic as the finer and more subtle spirits (such as those that move about in the brain), that is, the more refined and noble minds. Once these have drunk this poison deeply, they are far more powerful in spreading that evil, by which they are so steeped and thoroughly imbued, everywhere; and they strive to breathe the plague of this heresy also upon those who excel in talent and in rank. Added to this is the very specious pretext of right reason, which smiles most winningly upon all and drives men mad as if by some charm. For most men suffer from a certain innate self-love, by which they seem to themselves wiser than others; and from an obstinacy of mind which makes them headstrong and impatient of another's judgment, since it restrains the freedom of judging within certain limits; and which leads reason, as it were, a captive in triumph, and subjects each one's private opinions to public authority even against their will. But what touches us still more closely and presses more strongly on the true sons of the English Church is that it falls to each of them, today especially, as a duty, to defend our Mother, so venerable to us in so many respects, against adversaries of every kind to the best of their powers, and likewise to vindicate her reputation from the calumnies of the malicious, above all of the Romanists, who, besides open force, work by frauds, all the more dangerously because they are more hidden: partly, while they both stir up and foster I know not how many sects against her, by which she may be attacked on every side; partly, while they strive to defame her with the most atrocious calumnies and to make her hateful to all. Especially when they affirm that she patronises this Socinianism, since she makes each private person's reason the interpreter of Holy Scripture and the judge of all controversies in matters of religion, with the authority of the Church set aside and the other means required for judging rightly set aside. As if we could not otherwise defend the Reformation of our Church, and the stability of her doctrine, except from the principles of the Socinians; because we refuse to subject the judgment of our reason entirely to that infallible authority which the Church of Rome wrongly arrogates to itself. Indeed, it is well enough known how far our Church is averse to Socinianism, or rather how opposed to it she is; and this is shown not only by the protestation against Vorstius of our most serene King James (while he lived, the most zealous defender of the old Catholic faith), but far more clearly by the public confession of our faith comprised in the 39 Articles, and more recently by Canon 4 of the English Synod, which was held in the year of our Lord 1640, in which this mass of heresies is expressly attacked and condemned with the gravest censure. And so far is it from our placing each private reason in the seat of judgment, to the reproach of ecclesiastical authority, that on the contrary all the preachers admitted among us lawfully to discharge that office are bound by the decree of our Church: never to teach anything in the pulpit which they wish the people to hold and believe religiously, except what agrees with the doctrine of the Old and New Testament, and what the Catholic Fathers and the ancient bishops have gathered from that very doctrine. (Lib. Can. 1571, Tit. Of Preachers.) Nevertheless, despite these things, we have had Socinian books scattered here and there among us, and eagerly read even by the younger scholars, in contempt of the aforesaid canon of 1640. And what is much worse, we have had some of them translated into English, so that more of the common people might be corrupted; and these, suffering from both want of learning and inconstancy, are more easily perverted, and, having abandoned the Catholic faith which they never learned properly, allow themselves to be led aside into the byways of error. Indeed, there have not been wanting among us some theologians who, both in sermons and in writings published to the public, have shown too plainly how much they favoured certain doctrines of the Socinians.

units.la: His causis permotus[?] hujusmodi Dissertationes neutiquam intempestivas putavi; adeoque fiduciam mihi tandem sumpsi, Humanitate tua toties & tamdiu experta confisus, Tractatum hunc in manus tuas dare, & Patrocinio tam venerabili munitum, in publicum edere; valde fœlicem me existimaturus, si quo modo huic Hæresi perniciosissimæ viam aliquatenus obstruere valeam, erranem[?] aliquem reducere, vacillantem confirmare, rudem & imperitum in Fide melius instruere, Dogmatis Socinianæ fœditatem demonstrare, & speciosum rectæ Rationis Prætextum, de quo tantopere gloriantur hujus Sectæ Homines, & cujus fallaci ostentatione se plerisque commendant, detegere atque è medio tollere. Sed ne tædio ultra sim[?], sola jam vota supersunt, ut Deus Opt. Max. Fidem istam Catholicam, quam hic aut alibi planavit[?], vindicet ac defendat, Ecclesiam suam inter tot Hostes inviolatam conservet, Veritatem & Pacem in ipsa stabiliat, Hæreses eradicet, schismata resarciat, Sectarios cujuscunque generis ad bonam mentem revocet; & (ut hæc omnia melius fiant, sibique constent) Hierarchiam Ecclesiasticam incolumem servet, Authoritate vigentem reddat, & sanctitate venerandam; nominatim vero, Reverentiam tuam in omnibus istis copiose beet[?], quæ ad munus tuum Episcopale, ut oportet, complendum conducunt, & ad laudabilem amplissimæ istius Dioecesèos[?] Gubernationem, cui jam præfectus es. Sic orat
units.tr: Moved by these causes, I have thought that such a dissertation is by no means untimely; and so I at last took courage, trusting in your kindness, which I have so often and so long experienced, to put this treatise into your hands and, fortified by so venerable a patronage, to publish it. I shall count myself very fortunate if in some way I can block the path of this most pernicious heresy, bring back some wanderer, strengthen one who wavers, better instruct the unlearned and ignorant in the faith, demonstrate the foulness of the Socinian doctrine, and expose and remove the specious pretext of right reason, of which these men of the sect boast so greatly and by whose deceptive show they commend themselves to most people. But, lest I weary you further, only prayers remain: that God, the Best and Greatest, may vindicate and defend this Catholic faith, which he has set forth here and elsewhere, preserve his Church unharmed amid so many enemies, establish truth and peace in her, eradicate heresies, repair schisms, and call back sectaries of every kind to a sound mind; and that, so that all these things may be better done and agree with one another, he may preserve the ecclesiastical hierarchy unharmed, make it flourish with authority and revere it for its holiness; and especially that he may abundantly bless your Reverence in all those things which conduce to the proper discharge of your episcopal office, and to the praiseworthy government of that very ample diocese over which you now preside. Thus he prays.

units.la: SCire Te velim, Christiane & Catholice lector, hanc Dissertationem de Socino & Socinianismo, esse Partem Operis multo majoris; cui Titulum dedi, De Judice Controversiarum, & Catholicæ Veritatis Regula. Et in hoc Argumento tractando, singula illa, quæ potui Diligentia, examinavi, quæ Theologi ad alterutrum Caput referre solent; viz. S. Scripturam, Traditionem Catholicam; Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Authoritatem, hujus sæculi præsertim; Concilia, præcipue Oecumenica; Ecclesiæ Romanæ Prærogativam, quam sibi in judicando vendicat; Spiritum privatum; Judicium Ecclesiæ primitivæ, sive Consensum Patrum; denique rectam sive sanam Rationem. In quorum ordine, S. Scriptura ante Omnia pro Fundamento jacta (quæ tamen, ut in quibusdam filet, sic & in Aliis dubia est, atque obscura, variisque Interpretationibus obnoxia,) Reliqua ad Ædificium superstruendum spectant, & sibi vendicant, vel Interpretum munus in Scriptura explicanda; vel Judicum, in Controversiis[?] determinandis; vel potius, utrumque simul. Horum Singulis, pro modulo Tenuitatis meae, quod aequum atque debitum est attribui; & quousque conferant ad Veritatem elucidandam, ad Regulam Fidei firmandam, litesque Theologicas definiendas, pro virili mea demonstravi; quam necessaria item sint qualemve usum habeant, in alterutro munere pergendo. Argumentum sane ex sua natura nobilissimum, Nobisque simul explicatu necessarium, maximi Momenti in se, nec minus Omnibus utile cognitu. Controversiarum omnium Theologicarum, veluti Clavis, quae januam aperit ad divinae veritatis Adytum, qua semel conspecta, sententiamque suam ferente, illico lites conticescunt. Ita ut ex hujus Argumenti explicatione legitima, Illarum omnium Determinatio quam maxime pendeat. Quid autem in eo tractando praestiterim, Aliorum erit judicare, qui me multo melius judicare norunt. Hoc tantum mihi dicere fas sit, quod, in isto opere conficiendo, veritatem sincere quasierim[?], Diligentiam haud mediocrem adhibuerim, & quod Plura de hoc Argumento conatus fuerim in unum & idem volumen compingere, quam uspiam alibi me vidisse memini. At utrum integrum hoc Opus unquam in publicum proditurum sit, plane nescio, cum expensa Praeli certa sint eaque sat gravia, Tempora vero incerta, & Periculo plena; qualia nec Bibliopolæ favent, nec lectori; neque Illi Animum addunt ad Sumptus in Prælium erogandos, neque huic ad libros, ampliores præsertim, coemendos. Interim, hic libellus periculum sui facit, dum Oculis eruditissimi seculi, nec minus Opinionum varietate distractissimi, se visendum exponit; cujus tamen Censuram subire paratus est, quam iniquam fore haud veretur in Plerisque, cum Socinianissimus iste; quam detegit simul & impugnat, ab omnibus per orbem Christianum Ecclesiis communi suffragio damnetur, quæ tamen in Aliis non paucis inter se differunt, ita ut hic communis Christianismi Causam agere videar, quæ cunctis vere Fidelibus non potest non esse chara. Cur vero hanc Operis mei Partem præ Cæteris elegerim, quam in lucem primum emitterem, cum revera omnium ultima sit, ita se Res habet. Dissertationem hanc annexui isti Operis Parti, quæ tractat de recta sive sana Ratione, & Reliquas simul sumptas Magnitudine fere adæquat; ea vero de Causa annexui, quia Sociniani præ omnibus Sectariis, de Istius[?] Patrocinio se maxime jactant, & ad eam semper appellant. Atque hoc est (ut Istud[?] obiter moneam) quod occasionem præbuit excusoris errori, cui in singulis hujus libelli Paginis hic Titulus cernatur, De recta sive sana Ratione
units.tr: I want you to know, Christian and Catholic reader, that this Dissertation on Socinus and Socinianism is part of a much larger work, to which I have given the title: On the Judge of Controversies, and the Catholic Rule of Truth. In treating this subject I have carefully examined each of the heads that theologians are accustomed to refer to it: Holy Scripture; Catholic tradition; the authority of the Catholic Church, especially in this age; councils, chiefly the ecumenical ones; the prerogative which the Roman Church claims for itself in judging; private spirit; the judgment of the primitive Church, or the consensus of the Fathers; and finally right or sound reason. In this series, Holy Scripture is laid first as the foundation (which nevertheless, as some hold, is in certain respects doubtful and obscure, and open to various interpretations). The others pertain to the building to be erected upon it, and claim either the office of interpreting Scripture or the office of judging controversies, or rather both at once. To each of these I have given, as far as my modest ability allows, what is due and fitting, and I have shown, as well as I could, how far each contributes to clarifying the truth, confirming the Rule of Faith and settling theological disputes, and how necessary each is and what use it has in discharging either office. The subject is indeed most noble in its own nature, necessary for us to explain, of the greatest weight in itself, and no less useful for everyone to know. It is like a key to all theological controversies, opening the door to the sanctuary of divine truth; once that is seen and gives its sentence, the disputes at once fall silent. So much so that the settlement of all these disputes depends very largely on a proper explanation of this subject. How well I have handled it, others will judge, who know how to judge far better than I. Let me say only this much: in composing this work I have sincerely sought the truth, applied no small diligence, and tried to gather into one volume more on this subject than I remember seeing anywhere else. But whether this entire work will ever be published, I really do not know, since the costs of printing are certain and quite heavy, while the times are uncertain and full of danger. Such times favour neither booksellers nor readers; they do not encourage the one to spend money on printing, nor the other to buy books, especially larger ones. Meanwhile this little book is making a trial of itself, exposing itself to be looked at by the eyes of a most learned age, and one most divided by variety of opinions. Yet it is ready to undergo its judgment, which it does not fear will be unfair to most readers, since this Socinianism, which it at the same time uncovers and attacks, is condemned by common consent of all the Churches throughout the Christian world, although those Churches differ among themselves on many other points. Thus I seem here to be pleading the common cause of Christianity, which cannot but be dear to all truly faithful. As for why I chose this part of my work, which is really the last of all, to publish first, the matter stands as follows. I have attached this dissertation to that part of the work which treats of right or sound reason, and which nearly equals all the rest taken together in size. I attached it for this reason: the Socinians, above all other sectaries, boast most of its support and always appeal to it. And this is (to mention it in passing) what gave occasion for the printer's error, by which the title On Right or Sound Reason appears on every page of this little book.

units.la: tione ; cum potius ita se habieret , De Socino & Socinianismo. Quem errorem , ut spero , facile condonabis, cum parum aut nihil ad Rem ipsam spectet. Eandem vero ante Caeteras in lucem emisi, tum quia in & ex se completa est, & ab antecedentibus minime dependens; tum, quia Haeresis ista, quam patefacere conatur, & patefactam pessundare ; ut in se perniciosissima est, sic & periculosissime se Hominum mentibus insinuat sub rectae Rationis obtentu, praesertim, in hoc Seculo, ubi tot Homines ubique occurrunt, vago & instabili Ingenio praediti, Principiorum Fidei Christianae vel omnino nescii, vel Eiusdem leviter instructis[?]; Authoritatis Ecclesiasticae superbi Contemptores, Opinionibus malesanis praeoccupati, praefracti & indociles, alieni Consilii impatientes, propriae Rationis admirabundi Cultores, & sibi soli in omnibus placentes. Quantum vero spectat ad Catalogum Dogmatum Socinianorum ( quae ut particulatim recenseo, ita fusius prosequor ) & hoc ultra Tibi notum velim, quod multo majorem locorum citatorum partem, vel Ipse propria Manu exscripserim, vel diligenter exscribendam curaverim. Pauca solum restant, quorum singula fere citavi ex Fide Josuae Stegmanni, in Photinianismo suo, & petita sunt ut plurimum e libro Smalcii contra Frantzium ; quem licet sollicite[?] quaesitum,
units.tr: ...rather it stood thus: concerning Socinus and Socinianism. This error, as I hope, you will readily pardon, since it bears little or nothing on the matter itself. I have published this work before the others, both because it is complete in itself and depends in no way on what goes before; and because this heresy, which it tries to expose and, once exposed, to overthrow, is as ruinous in itself as it insinuates itself most dangerously into men's minds under the pretext of right reason. This is especially so in this age, when so many men everywhere meet us, endowed with a wandering and unstable wit, either wholly ignorant of the principles of the Christian faith or only slightly instructed in them; proud despisers of ecclesiastical authority, preoccupied with mad opinions, obstinate and unteachable, impatient of counsel, admiring cultivators of their own reason, and pleased with themselves alone in everything. As for the catalogue of the Socinian dogmas (which I both list one by one and pursue at greater length), I would also have you know this beyond what you have been told: I either copied out with my own hand, or carefully had copied out, by far the greater part of the cited passages. Only a few remain, nearly each of which I have cited from the faith of Josua Stegmann in his Photinianism, and which have been taken for the most part from Smalcius's book against Francius; which, though I sought it diligently...

units.la: adhuc tamen comparare non potui , adeoque nec consulere. Interim Spiro[?] ,Stegmannum ista Smalcii loca mala Fide non citasse , cum in aliis Citationibus ipsum satis æquum ac diligentem reperierim. Hoc autem idcirco monui, Ne quis me iniquiorem existimet in Opinionibus Illorum recensendis, Eisque videar errores aliquos imputasse , qui in ipsorum Scriptis non extant visendi. Quod certe neutiquam facerem sciens lubensque , in Illorum , vel Aliorum quorumcunque , præjudicium. Hoc unum habeo quod adjiciam ; quod si Dissertatio hæc Doctis, Bonisque fuerit accepta , Animum Mihi fortasse dabit reliquum Opus Prælo mandare, si minus simul & integre , saltem divisim & per partes. Interea , libellum hunc , pro Candore tuo, æqui bonique consule, & Conatibus Illius esto propitius , qui nihil magis in votis habet , quam Fidei Catholicæ Veritatem , & Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Pacem. Vale , Meique, inter precandum , ne sis Immemor.
units.tr: I have not yet been able to obtain it, and so could not consult it. Meanwhile, I hope that Stegmann did not cite those passages of Smalcius in bad faith, since in his other citations I have found him quite fair and diligent. I have given this warning so that no one may think me unfair in setting out their opinions, or think that I have imputed to them errors that are not to be found in their writings. I would certainly never do that knowingly and willingly, to their prejudice or to anyone else's. I have one more thing to add: if this dissertation is well received by learned and good men, it may perhaps give me the heart to publish the rest of the work, if not all at once and in full, then at least separately and part by part. Meanwhile, take this little book in good part, in your candour, and be favourable to the efforts of one who has no greater wish than for the truth of the Catholic faith and the peace of the Catholic Church. Farewell, and do not forget me in your prayers.

units.la: DE SOCINO ET SOCINIANISMO Dissertatio.
units.tr: On Socinus and Socinianism: A Dissertation.

units.la: ARGUMENTUM.
units.tr: Argument.

units.la: Origo Sectæ Sociniane, à Lalio Socino; & Fausto illius ex fratre nepote; quorum Historia brevi percurritur. Utriusque ingenium, eruditio, & mores, præsertim Fausti. Quomodo, & unde hic Faustus Hæresium & Hæreticorum farraginem in unum compegerit, novamque sectam de suo instituerit. Artes quibus usus est, in Dogmatibus suis uniusque ingenio commendandis, Discipulisque sibi colligendis. Opportunitates item, quas sedulo Idem arripuit, ad Hæreses suas disseminandas, præsertim in Polonia. Ejusdem superbia summa, & arrogantia, dum suo ipsius ingenio in omnibus fidit; & Amicorum Judicia vilipendit; neque hoc contentus, Catholicam Ecclesiam contemnit; eamque non suæ solius ætatis, sed & seculi Primitivi, cum Patribus, Conciliis, & unanimi consensu Doctorum[?] illius, totaque corpore Ecclesiae suis Pastoribus adhaerentis. Adversarii Socini, iique non solum e Pontificiis, sed & ex Ecclesiis Reformatis, imo, & ex Anti-Trinitariis, qui ipsius Principiis imitantes. Invocationem & Adorationem Christi prorsus abnegabant. Inter Hos praecipui, Franciscus Davidis in Transylvania, & Christianus Franken in Polonia; quorum Disputationes de hoc Argumento cum Socino extant inter Illius opera, ut & alia Disputatio ejusdem Socini cum Erasmo Johannis, Ariano. Postulata Socinianorum paulo aequiora, allata a Joachimo Stegmanno, Postulata eorundem plane iniqua & absurda, de Judice Controversiarum, Interpretatione S. Scripturae, viribus Rationis naturalis in Religionis negotio, Haereticis non coercendis, Ecclesia, Aliisque quibusdam. Catalogus Haeresium a Socinianis assertarum, cum perniciosis illarum effectibus. Socini, & Socinianorum Concessa, Postulata Socinianis proposita quae vel infiis Concessis Postulata Socinianis proposita quae vel in istis Concessis fundantur, vel alias sanae Rationi & Aequitati consona sunt.
units.tr: The origin of the Socinian sect, from Lelius Socinus and from his nephew Faustus, the son of his brother; their history is briefly run through. The character, learning and manners of each, especially of Faustus. How and from where this Faustus gathered a hodgepodge of heresies and heretics into one body and founded a new sect of his own. The arts he used to commend his doctrines and his own genius, and to gather disciples to himself. The opportunities, too, which he eagerly seized to spread his heresies, especially in Poland. His great pride and arrogance, since he trusts his own genius in all things and despises the judgments of his friends; and, not content with this, he scorns the Catholic Church, and that not only of his own age but also of the primitive age, together with the Fathers, the Councils, the unanimous consent of its teachers, and the whole body of the Church, which clings to its ministers. The opponents of Socinus, and those not only among the Papists but also among the Reformed Churches, and even among the Anti-Trinitarians, who imitate his principles. They utterly rejected the invocation and worship of Christ. Among these the most prominent were Francis David in Transylvania and Christian Franken in Poland; their disputations with Socinus on this subject exist among his works, as does another disputation of Socinus himself with Erasmus Johannis, the Arian. The demands of the Socinians, somewhat more fair, put forward by Joachim Stegmann; the demands of the same men which are plainly unjust and absurd, concerning the judge of controversies, the interpretation of Holy Scripture, the powers of natural reason in the matter of religion, the non-coercion of heretics, the Church, and some others. A catalogue of the heresies asserted by the Socinians, with their pernicious effects. The concessions of Socinus and the Socinians, and the demands made of the Socinians, which are either founded on these concessions or are otherwise consonant with sound reason and fairness.

units.la: SOcinianorum Secta a duobus Socinis nomen & originem accepit, Laelio sc.[?] & Fausto ipsius ex fratre nepote, utroque ex nobili familia Senis in Italia oriundo, Juris prudentiae studio imprimis dedita, cujusque peritia quamplures ex ea celebres evaserunt: Marianus Socinus, tantopere ab Aenea Sylvio (Ejus concive & postea Papa Romano, nomine Pii 2.) laudatus, fuit hujus Fausti Abavus. Pater autem Fausti, ob summum ingenii acumen, dictus est Pater subtilitatum. Neque sane filium habuit ex hac parte ullatenus degenerem. Mortuus autem dicitur, cum nondum excesserat Annum 31. Meminerant haec ab ipso Fausto in Epistola sua ad virum Excellentissimum, N. N. paulo ante mortem conscripta. Faustus vero natus est; ut ibidem ipse narrat, quinto die Decembris, juxta vetus Calendarium. A.C. 1539. duabus Horis & tribus fere quadrantibus, ante ortum Solis.
units.tr: The Socinian sect received its name and origin from two Socini, Lelius, namely, and Faustus, his nephew through his brother, both of them born in Siena in Italy, of a noble family, devoted above all to the study of law, in which many became famous through their skill. Marianus Socinus, so highly praised by Aeneas Sylvius (a fellow citizen of his and afterwards Roman Pope, under the name of Pius II), was the great-grandfather of this Faustus. The father of Faustus, on account of the great keenness of his intellect, was called the Father of Subtleties. Nor indeed did he have a son in this respect at all degenerate. He is said to have died before he had reached his thirty-first year. Faustus himself recalls these facts in his letter to the most excellent man, N. N., written shortly before his death. Faustus was born, as he himself relates in the same place, on the fifth day of December, according to the old calendar, in the year of Christ 1539, two hours and nearly three quarters before sunrise.

units.la: §. 2. Sed ut ad Lælium revertamur. Is dicitur ab Equite Polono, qui vitam Fausti conscripsit, Juri Civili, sicut & Antecessores ejus, operam primo dedisse. Postea vero, dissidiis circa Religionem exortis, per Lutherum & Alios, qui varias corruptelas in Ecclesia Romana palam arguebant, & Reformationem acriter urgebant, sese ad Theologiæ studium applicuisse, ut hujus ope errores receptos detegeret atque adeo Ecclesiæ morbos, quibus tunc Temporis laboravit, sanaret. Hoc autem ut melius præstaret, Scripturam imprimis consuluisse fertur, ad cujus sensus felicius eruendos præter excellentis Ingenii altitudinem, & Judicii acrimoniam, dicitur attentisse[?] scientiam haud mediocrem linguæ Græcæ & Hebraicæ & aliquantulam Arabicæ. Quibus instructus, ut studia sua promoveret, & se in veritatis perquisitione securius dirigeret, Patriam suam reliquit; & cum primariis illius ætatis Theologis, qui opus reformandæ Ecclesiæ aggressi sunt, familiarius conversabatur; sc. Bullingero, Brentio, Munstero, Musculo, Petro Martyre, Zanchio, Beza, præcipue autem, cum Melanchthone & Calvino, ut ex eorum Epistolis liquet. His solitus est identidem nova sua Dogmata inter colloquendum proponere; non tamen audacter ea asserendo & propugnando, sed fere Dubitantis more veritatemque sincere quærentis. Qua sua in speciem modestia hoc saltem effecit, ut ab eorum colloquio atque consortio non in totum rejiceretur. Tandem tamen, eo usque urgebat Calvinum istiusmodi quaestionibus, ut eum serio monere cogeretur, ne sibi posthac ista portenta Quaestionum proponeret, sed quaerendi pruritum mature corrigeret, Si Tibi inquit, per aereas illas Speculationes volitare lubet, sine me, quaeso, humilem Christi Discipulum ea meditari, quae ad fidei mea aedificationem faciunt. Ac ego quidem silentio meo id, quod cupio, consequar, ne Tu mihi postea sis molestus. Cum vero ultra pergendo, Serveti Blasphemias, alias que insana Dogmata, apertius in se tuenda suscepisset, una & altera Epistola, ab eodem Calvino gravius increpitus est. Non longe post, Servetus ob Haeresin Genevae combustus est. Laelium vero exemisse dicitur a supplicio, incredibilis modestia, morumque Dexteritas, quae Adversarios Illius ita exarmaunt, ut cujus libertatem ferre non poterant; Personam tamen odisse non sustinerent.
units.tr: §. 2. But let us return to Lelius. He is said, by the Polish knight who wrote the life of Faustus, to have first devoted himself to civil law, as did his forebears. Afterwards, however, when disputes about religion had arisen through Luther and others, who openly exposed the various corruptions in the Roman Church and urgently pressed for reformation, he applied himself to the study of theology, so that by its means he might detect the received errors and thus heal the diseases of the Church, by which it was then afflicted. In order to do this the better, he is said to have consulted Scripture above all, and, to bring out its meaning more successfully, he is said to have applied, besides the great height of his excellent intellect and the keenness of his judgment, no small knowledge of Greek and Hebrew and some slight knowledge of Arabic. Equipped with these, that he might advance his studies and direct himself more securely in the search for truth, he left his homeland; and he associated more intimately with the leading theologians of that age who had undertaken the work of reforming the Church, namely Bullinger, Brenz, Münster, Musculus, Peter Martyr, Zanchius, Beza, and especially Melanchthon and Calvin, as is clear from their letters. With these he was accustomed from time to time to propose his new doctrines in conversation; yet he did not assert and defend them boldly, but for the most part in the manner of one who doubts and sincerely seeks the truth. By this show of modesty he at least achieved this much, that he was not altogether shut out from their company and fellowship. At length, however, he pressed Calvin with questions of this kind to such a degree that Calvin was forced to warn him seriously not to put these monstrous questions to him any more, but to correct his itch for inquiry in good time: If you, he said, delight to flit about among those airy speculations, I beg you to leave me, a humble disciple of Christ, to meditate on those things which serve the building up of my faith. And indeed I shall attain what I desire by my silence, so that you may not afterwards be troublesome to me. But when he went further and undertook to defend more openly the blasphemies of Servetus and other insane doctrines, he was rebuked more severely by Calvin in one or two letters. Not long afterwards, Servetus was burned at Geneva for heresy. Lelius, however, is said to have escaped the punishment by his incredible modesty and the adroitness of his manners, which so disarmed his opponents that they could not bear his freedom, yet could not bring themselves to hate the man.

units.la: §. 3. Quod vero ad Peregrinationes ejus attinet; dicitur Patriam suam reliquisse, cum natus esset Annos 21. A. C. 1547 proximo quadriennio peregravit Galliam, Britanniam, Belgium, Germaniam totam, & Poloniam, quam primum ingressus est, A. C. 1551. quo tempore conversatus est cum plerisque e nobilitate Polonica. Persuasit Franc: Lismanino Patria Corcyraeo, & Bonae Sfortiae Reginae, a Confessionibus, cucullum suum monachalem abjicere, & Papismo deserto, in suas partes transfire. In Poloniam rediit post mortem Patris Mariani, qui Bononiae obiit, A. C. 1556. Quando impetravit literas Regum Poloniae atque Bohemiae, quibus munitus, secum ius in urbe Veneta, cum Amicis de Patrimonio suo agere posset. Tunc maxime apparuit, quantum petuerit apud Nobilitatem Polonicam Ionicam atque Germanicam ; summis enim studiis tunc certatum est in ejus causa apud Lud. Priulam Venetiarum, & Cosmum Etruriæ Ducem, &c. Annis 1558. & 1559. Non longe post, obiit Tiguri, ubi sedem per aliquot Annos fixerat, &c. mense Maio, A. C. 1562. Anno autem ætatis suæ 37º. Cum autem adhuc in vivis esset, absens, & per litteras, in Sententiam suam traxerat fratres suos, & familiares, eorumque uxores; ex quo factum est, ut Socinorum familia huc illuc dispersa fuerit, atque dissipata. Tunc Faustus quoq; Italia derelicta, Lugdunū in Gallia se contulit; ex his[?] quantum ingenio suo sideret Lælius in Rebus[?] Theologicis, qui veteris Ecclesiæ Doctoribus aut neglectis aut contemptis, & præcipuis ætatis suæ Theologis, qui Ecclesiæ reformandæ operam navarunt, posthabitis, ex suo ipsius sensu scripturas interpretabatur, & nova Dogmata condebat; quæ tamen, ut sibi divinitus revelata, quibus visum est, clam impertivit. Justo sane Dei judicio, ut qui spreverat Duces à Deo sibi datos ad veritatem investigandam, & sibi soli saperet, à Deo desertus, & Diaboli sub Angelica specie, Delitescentis Illusionibus expositus, in gravissimos errores abduceretur. Hic præ cæte[?] is, fuit viæ Dux, & Auctor novi Dogmatis, Fausto nepoti, per avia & abrupta Hæresium vaganti. Hic ista errorum semina sparsit, quæ, sub Lilius[?] cultura, non longe post in amplissimam messem excreverunt. Hic demum lapides istos sedulo collegit, quibus, aliquanto post Tempore, fundamenti loco jactis à Fausto, insana illa Socinianismi moles ab eodem paulatim superstructa est.
units.tr: §. 3. As for his travels: he is said to have left his homeland when he was twenty-one years old, in the year of Christ 1547. Over the following four years he travelled through France, Britain, Belgium and the whole of Germany, and then Poland, which he first entered in the year of Christ 1551, and at that time he associated with many of the Polish nobility. He persuaded Francis Lismanino of Corfu, confessor to Queen Bona Sforza, to cast off his monastic cowl, to abandon Popery and to pass over to their side. He returned to Poland after the death of his father Marian, who died at Bologna in the year of Christ 1556, when he obtained letters from the Kings of Poland and Bohemia, by which, armed, he could deal with his friends in the Venetian city about his patrimony. Then especially it became clear how much influence he had with the Polish, Hungarian and German nobility; for the greatest efforts were then made on his behalf with Lodovico Priuli, Doge of Venice, and Cosimo, Duke of Etruria, and others, in the years 1558 and 1559. Not long afterwards he died at Zurich, where he had fixed his seat for some years, in the month of May, in the year of Christ 1562, in the thirty-seventh year of his age. Yet while he was still alive, though absent, and by letters, he had drawn his brothers and his family, and their wives, into his opinion; as a result the Socini family was scattered here and there and dissipated. Then Faustus, too, abandoned Italy and betook himself to Lyon in France. From this it may be seen how much Lelius trusted his own genius in theological matters: he, neglecting or despising the teachers of the ancient Church, and setting aside the chief theologians of his age who had undertaken the work of reforming the Church, interpreted the Scriptures according to his own sense and devised new doctrines, which, however, as though divinely revealed to him, he communicated secretly to whom he saw fit. With just judgment of God, since he had spurned the guides given him by God for investigating the truth, and was wise only for himself, he was deserted by God and, exposed to the illusions of the devil lurking under an angelic appearance, was led into the gravest errors. He was, among the others, the guide of the way and the author of the new doctrine for his nephew Faustus, who was wandering through the byways and precipices of heresy. He scattered these seeds of error, which, under the cultivation of Lelius, grew not long afterwards into a very ample harvest. Finally, he diligently gathered those stones with which, some time afterwards, the mad mass of Socinianism was gradually built up by Faustus, who had laid them as the foundation.

units.la: §. 5. Cum autem Lælius supremum Diem obiit, Faustus erat Lugduni in Gallia, ubi per Triennium commoratus fuerat, post fugam suam ex Italia. Tunc temporis erat Juvenis 23. circiter Annorum. Audita vero Patrui morte, accelerato itinere Tigurum Pervenit ut Chartas sibi legatas arriperet, & in tuto poneret; qua sellinatione sua, structas iis Patrui lucubrationibus insidias aegre antevertisse fertur. Lalius enim moriens, scripta sua huic suo nepoti legaverat, opportuno tempore propalam edenda. Quippe perhibetur, eum, dum in vivis esset, inter Amicos gloriari solitum, Faustum posse se omnia felicius explicaturum, atque perfecturum. Ita, post obitum Patrui, Faustus hac literaria supellectile instructus, in Italiam discessit, & in Aula Magni Ducis Hetruriae per duodecim Annos commoratus est. Hac tandem relicta, Basileam venit, A. C. 1574. aetatis suae 35. Illic Theologiae operam navavit, per tres Annos, & amplius, sacris praecipue voluminibus intentus. Ibi quoque primum suum librum edidit, De Christo Servatore. Postea, à celebri Medico Georgio Blandrata in Transylvaniam evocatus fuit, ut Franciscum Davidis à suis erroribus liberaret, quocum frustra disputavit. Non longe post in Poloniam recessit, jam quadragenarius, A. C. 1579. & Anti-Trinitariis se statim adjunxit. Cum autem accusatus esset, apud Stephanum Bathoreum Poloniae Regem, de seditioso quodam scripto contra Magistratum civilem (sc. de libello contra Palaeologum) Cracovia discedens, ubi quartum jam Annum degebat, confugit ad Christophori Morstinii Domum, Paulikonii Domini, paucis passuum millibus à Cracovia distantem; ubi non tam latebris & obscuritate istius secessus, quam nobilitatis in Gente Polonica, Privilegiis, sese tutatus est. Illud Rus suburbanum, per Triennium & ultra, fovit hunc Hof[?] pitem ubi non longe post, Filia ejusdem Morstinii in uxorem ducta, nomine Elizabetha, Patroni sui Gener factus est, unde securitatem suam in illis locis, affinitatibus & amicitiis stabilivisse visus est. Ibi librum suum conscripsit contra Gabr [?] Eutropium Canonicum Posnaniensis Collegii. Ibidem quoque Filiam suscepit ex modo nominata uxore, Agnetem dictam, circa Pentecosten Anni 1587. Eodem Anno, mense Septembri, uxor decessit; & Ipse non longe post tum mo[?]rbo diutino conflictatus [?] est, tum Patrimonium in Italia amisit post obitum Ducis Francisci. Filia Socini, post mortem sui Patris, nupta fuit Stanislao Wiszowakio equiti Polono, ex quo Filiorum, Filiarumque mater facta est.
units.tr: §. 5. When Laelius died, Faustus was at Lyon in France, where he had stayed for three years after fleeing from Italy. He was then a young man of about twenty-three. On hearing of his uncle's death, he hastened to Zürich to seize the papers left to him and put them in safe keeping. By this haste he is said to have narrowly forestalled the plots laid against his uncle's writings. Laelius, dying, had left these writings to this nephew, to be published openly at a suitable time. It is reported that while he was alive he used to boast among his friends that Faustus would be able to explain and complete everything more happily. So, after his uncle's death, Faustus, equipped with this literary stock, went to Italy and stayed for twelve years at the court of the Grand Duke of Tuscany. Finally leaving it, he came to Basel in 1574, in the thirty-fifth year of his age. There he devoted himself to theology for three years and more, chiefly occupied with the sacred books. There too he first published his book, On Christ the Saviour. Afterwards the famous physician Giorgio Blandrata summoned him to Transylvania to free Francis David from his errors, and with him he disputed in vain. Not long after, already forty years old, he withdrew to Poland in 1579 and at once joined the Anti-Trinitarians. When he was accused before Stephen Báthory, King of Poland, of a seditious writing against the civil magistrate (namely the booklet against Palaeologus), he left Kraków, where he had now spent a fourth year, and took refuge in the house of Christopher Morstin, lord of Pawlikowice, a few miles from Kraków. There he protected himself less by the hiding-places and obscurity of this retreat than by the privileges of nobility among the Polish people. That country estate sheltered him for three years and more. There, not long after, Morstin's daughter, named Elizabeth, was taken as his wife, and he became the son-in-law of his patron, by which he seems to have secured his safety in those parts through family ties and friendships. There he wrote his book against Gabriel Eutropius, canon of the college at Poznań. Also there, around Pentecost of 1587, he had a daughter, called Agnes, by the wife just named. In September of the same year the wife died; and he himself, not long after, was worn down by a lingering illness, and lost his patrimony in Italy after the death of Duke Francis. Socinus's daughter, after her father's death, was married to Stanislaus Wiszowaty, a Polish knight, and became the mother of sons and daughters.

units.la: §. 6. Quod vero ad Socinum ipsum; Omnium fere odia in se concitavit, post librum de Christo Servatore Typis evulgatum; propter quem, aliaque Scripta blasphema, quae in vulgi Aures simul, manusque venerant, cum jam Cracoviam rediisset (ubi ut plurimum degebat) commoto per Scholasticos Tumultu, aeger tunc, et forte curandae valetudini intentus, e cubiculo extrahitur seminudus et per forum ac celeberrimas plateas, deposcentibus ad Supplicium plerisque, contumeliose raptatur; tandem vero, cum pessime multatus fuisset, a Martino Vadovita Professo e Cracoviensi, aegre furenti multitudini eripitur. Cum autem adhuc ei minas intenderent, inde discessit, non multis ante Obitum Annis, et se Luclavicias contulit, Pagum novem circiter milliaribus Cracovia dissitum; usus mensa & Aedibus viri nobilis Abrahami Blonscii. Ibi post aliquot Annos supremum diem obiit, sc. A. C. 1604, ineunte; aetatis item suae 65°. pariter ineunte.
units.tr: §. 6. As for Socinus himself, after his book On Christ the Saviour was published in print, he stirred up almost everyone's hatred against himself, on account of it and other blasphemous writings which had reached the ears and hands of the common people. When he had returned to Kraków (where he mostly lived), a tumult was raised by the scholars. He was then sick and perhaps intent on restoring his health when he was dragged from his bedroom, half-naked, and insultingly hauled through the marketplace and the most crowded streets, most of the crowd demanding his execution. At last, having been very badly mauled, he was snatched with difficulty from the raging mob by Martin Wadowita, a professor at Kraków. Since they still threatened him, he left there not many years before his death and betook himself to Luclavice, a village about nine miles from Kraków, using the table and house of the noble Abraham Blonski. There, after some years, he died, in early 1604, also at the beginning of his sixty-fifth year.

units.la: §. 7. Ita vixit, ita mortuus est Faustus Socinus, præcipuus hujus Sectæ Auctor; qui dum in vivis erat, huic uni operam sedulo dedisse visus est, ut Patrui sui Lælii Dictata, quæ Chartis mandata sibi legaverat, penitius digereret, & perfectius excoleret. Huic studio cum satis, ut putavit, incubuisset, illico libros conscribere coepit [?] & ubique Gentium evulgare, in Germania, Transylvania, Polonia, ipsaque Italia. Fertur scripisse [?] ab Anno 1570. nec à scribendo cessavit, donec vivere desiit.
units.tr: §. 7. Thus lived and thus died Faustus Socinus, the chief author of this sect. While he was alive, he seems to have devoted himself diligently to this one task: to arrange more thoroughly and polish more perfectly the teachings of his uncle Laelius, which had been left to him in writing. When he had, as he thought, applied himself enough to this study, he at once began to write books and to publish them everywhere among the nations: in Germany, Transylvania, Poland, and Italy itself. He is said to have begun writing in the year 1570, and he did not stop writing until he ceased to live.

units.la: Enimvero in hisce libris suis novum plane Religionis Systema molitus est. Siquidem haud satis habuit, hunc aut illum Fidei Christianæ Articulum convellere, sensum orthodoxum & à majoribus receptum pervertere, aut Fundamento antiquitus jacto, cum plerisque antehac Hæreticis, malefana Dogmata superstruere, nisi & ab ipsis Fundamentis, quæ loco antiquæ Fidei Ipse de novo jecerat, integrum & ex suo Ipsius ingenio efformatum, e igeret [?] Ædificium.
units.tr: Indeed, in these books he laboured to build a wholly new system of religion. For he was not content to overthrow this or that article of the Christian faith, to pervert the orthodox sense received from our forebears, or to erect pernicious doctrines on the old foundation, which he shared with many earlier heretics. Unless he also laid new foundations in place of the ancient faith and raised from them an entire edifice, shaped by his own genius, he would not have been satisfied.

units.la: Hic enim, ut arbitror, primus omnium, inter cunctos hucusque Sectarios, ex proprio Ingenio, Patrui sui Chartis quodammodo adjuto, per singula Theologiæ Capita, aliam novamque sibi [?] formam Religionis introduxit; nimirum in Fidei Dogmatibus, in Politia atque Disciplina Ecclesiæ, in Sacramentis item & Sacramentalibus, inq; Forma cultus Divini, sacrisque Ritibus ad eum spectantibus, quos Ecclesia Catholica, à majoribus olim acceptos, adhuc retinet & solenniter observat.
units.tr: For here, as I think, he was the first of all the sectaries so far to introduce, out of his own genius and with his uncle's papers somewhat helping him, another new form of religion, running through each head of theology. Namely, he did this in the dogmas of faith, in the polity and discipline of the Church, likewise in the sacraments and sacramentals, and in the form of divine worship and the sacred rites belonging to it, which the Catholic Church, having received them long ago from its forebears, still retains and solemnly observes.

units.la: Etenim his omnibus, aut in totum abolitis, aut sædissime depravatis, practicam solum Theologiæ partem excoluisse videtur, quæ de moribus & officiis tractat.
units.tr: For in all these matters, either wholly abolished or most foully corrupted, he seems to have cultivated only the practical part of theology, which deals with morals and duties.

units.la: Huc Socinus refert totam ferè de Deo notitiam, viz. [?] ad Promissa, & præcepta Evangelica, quæ sunt
units.tr: To this part Socinus refers almost the whole knowledge of God, namely as far as it concerns the evangelical promises and precepts, which are

units.la: objecta fidei practicæ, & Obedientiæ Deo præstandæ ex fide promissorum; parum solicitus de cognitione Naturæ Divinæ, & Attributorum illuc pertinentium, modo observantia mandatorum divinorum integre exhibeatur. Quasi Christiani parum aut nihil interfit, scire quid Deus sit, modo constet, quid velit. Propter hanc quoque Crellius illius Discipulus, non parum celebratur in Ethicis suis. Adeo ut Philosophiæ moralis Professores potius censendi sint, quam fidei Christianæ. Imo, ne hanc quoque in quibusdam, nobis integram & inviolatam tradiderunt, cum aliqua lege Christi vera permiserint, & multo plura eadem lege permissa vetuerint. Quid? quod multo pejus est; duo ista Socinianorum Dogmata de Anima humana omnis sensus expers, post egressum e corpore donec ad Christi Adventum e Somno expergefiat; & totalis Interitus, sive Abolitio Impiorum, post Judicium a Christo peractum, omnem plane virtutem e mundo tollunt & omnimodæ morum licentiæ latam portam aperiunt. Cum enim multo major Pars Hominum, a malo abstineat, & in officio contineatur, supplicii metu potius quam amore virtutis; quid non audebunt ambitiosi, avari, luxuriosi, omniqué nequitiæ dediti quotiescunque ad fraudibus & dolis, aut aperta vi, cupiditates suas explere datum est, si modo persuadere sibi possint, nullas omnino restare pœnas post hanc vitam à se subeundas, quotcunque aut qualiacunque flagitia sua in hac vita fuerint? Idcirco, ne jactent sese Socinicni de morum præceptis, & honestioris vitæ Regulis. Nam & Epicurus has tradidit; qui etiam libros conscripsit de Sanctitate & Pietate adversus Deos, ut Cicero memorat lib. I. de nat. Deorum; cum tamen satis notum sit, quomodo illius placita omnem Religionem funditus è mundo sustulerint, & cum Religione virtutem; dum Providentiam divinam negavit, & statum futuri seculi.
units.tr: the objects of practical faith, and the obedience to be rendered to God from faith in the promises. He cares little for knowledge of the divine nature and of the attributes pertaining to it, provided that obedience to the divine commands is fully rendered. As if it mattered little or nothing to a Christian to know what God is, provided it is clear what he wills. On this account, too, Crellius, his disciple, is much praised in his Ethics, so that the professors of moral philosophy are rather to be counted as teachers of the Christian faith. Indeed, they have not even handed this down to us whole and inviolate in some respects, since they have permitted, by some law of Christ, things that are true, and forbidden by the same law much that was permitted. What is more, and much worse: these two Socinian doctrines, that the human soul, devoid of all sensation after leaving the body, sleeps until Christ's coming, and that the wicked are totally destroyed or annihilated after the judgment carried out by Christ, entirely remove all virtue from the world and open a broad gate to every licence in morals. For since a much greater part of mankind abstains from evil and keeps to its duty out of fear of punishment rather than love of virtue, what will the ambitious, the greedy, the lustful, and those given over to every wickedness not dare, whenever they have the chance to fulfil their desires by fraud and trickery or by open force, if only they can persuade themselves that no punishments at all remain for them to undergo after this life, however many or whatever sins they have committed in it? Therefore let the Socinians not boast of the precepts of morals and the rules of a more honourable life. For Epicurus too handed these down, and he also wrote books On Holiness and Piety against the gods, as Cicero records in book I of On the Nature of the Gods. Yet it is well enough known how his tenets removed every religion from the world, and with religion virtue, since he denied divine providence and the state of the future age.

units.la: §. 8. Sed redeamus ad ipsum Socinum. Cum Illius Dogmata in variis Tractatibus ab eo scriptis sparsim extarent, & paulo fusius atque liberius ibi traderentur, visum est nonnullis ejus Discipulis, eadem in summam redigere, & systematice componere.
units.tr: §. 8. But let us return to Socinus himself. Since his doctrines lay scattered in various treatises he had written, where they were set out somewhat more fully and freely, some of his disciples thought it fitting to reduce them to a summary and to arrange them systematically.

units.la: Quod tentarunt Moscorovius in Catechismo Racoviensi, Oftorodus in Institutionibus suis, Smalcius contra Franzium, & Volkelius imprimis, in libro, cui Titulum dedit De vera Religione; eodem plane Jure, quo Lucianus monstrosissimæ Fabulæ nomen tribuit, veræ Historiæ. Alii autem, parum aut nihil Illius Doctrinæ addiderunt, sed cum, vel Argumentis ulterius confirmarunt, vel Commentariis suis in aliquot S. Scripturæ partes verius illustrarunt. Eniedinus enim, Aliique quidam in hoc operam posuerunt, ut loca quædam S. Scripturæ in sensum alienum perverterent, dum vel sua Dogmata astruere, vel sensus orthodoxos, à nostris Theologis alienatos, destruere conati sunt. Alii vero Polemice scripserunt in defensionem Doctrinæ Socinianæ. At si Aliqui fortasse ei quidpiam superstruxerint, nemo tamen, quantum videre mihi contigit, Principia ab illo, posita mutavit, vel iisdem nova quædam & aliena adjecit. Itaque Eques ille Polonus, qui Socini vitam conscripsit, cum hoc præcipue nomine laudat, quod in animo semper habuerit nobilioris Fidei Doctrinam tradere. Unde in fine istius Historiolæ, cum non inepte comparare videtur cum Ignatio Loyola, Jesuitici ordinis fundatore. Ignatium quoque, ait, ut alios taceam, majorum nostrorum memorja Patriam, Agnatos, Opes, Honores, aliasque illece-
units.tr: What Moscorovius attempted in the Racovian Catechism, Ostorodt in his Institutions, Smalcius against Franz, and above all Volkelius in the book he titled On the True Religion, he did with the same right as Lucian, who gave the name True History to a most monstrous fable. Others, however, added little or nothing to his doctrine. They either confirmed it further with arguments or more truly illustrated some parts of Holy Scripture in their commentaries. Enjedinus and certain others laboured to twist certain passages of Holy Scripture into an alien sense, trying either to establish their own doctrines or to overthrow the orthodox senses held by our theologians. Others wrote polemically in defence of the Socinian doctrine. But if some have perhaps built something upon it, no one, as far as I have been able to see, has changed the principles laid down by him, or added to them any new and foreign matter. Thus that Polish knight who wrote the life of Socinus praises him chiefly on this account, that he always intended to set forth the doctrine of a nobler faith. Hence, at the end of that little history, when he seems not inaptly to compare him with Ignatius Loyola, founder of the Jesuit order, he says: Ignatius too, not to mention others, in the memory of our elders, had despised country, kinsfolk, wealth, honours and other

Nequis autem miretur aut scandalum ex eo patiatur, quod hujus Sectae Dogmata in tantum apud quamplures invaluerint, mecum advertat si lubet, quasdam hujus Incrementi Causas. Nam praeter Novitatis studium, qua Omnium fere mentes gratissime afficici solent & a consuetis facile abripi alia non pauca, tum in persona Socini, tum in Doctrina ab Ipso propositâ tum in Modo Proponendi, tum in Hominibus, quibus Eandem proposuit tum in Statu Aetatis simul illius, atque Gentis apud quam potissimum praevaluit, infeliciter una concurrerunt, quae plurimos nec Ignobiles, nec Insulsos, nec literarum imperitos, ad favorem sibi, suoque Dogmati conciliandum, valide sollicitarunt. Siquidem,
units.tr: but also sought the patronage of kings and other princes and great men. Among them Moscorovius, not long after the death of Socinus, dared to send his Racovian Catechism, which contains the sum of Socinianism, to our most serene King James, with a dedicatory letter in which these words occur: Our Church has had this catechism translated into Latin, and has charged me to inscribe and dedicate it to the august name of Your Sacred Royal Majesty; just as I too, on their behalf, inscribe it to Your Sacred Royal Majesty and humbly dedicate it. In the following year, 1610, Conrad Vorstius, a disciple of Socinus, dedicated his Theological Treatise on God to Maurice, Landgrave of Hesse. The same man dedicated his Apologetic Exegesis on the same book to the Dutch states, in 1614. Both books, by order of this King of ours, were publicly burned in St Paul's churchyard and in both universities. Lest anyone wonder at this or take offence that the doctrines of this sect have prevailed so widely among so many, let him consider with me, if he pleases, some causes of this growth. For besides the love of novelty, by which almost everyone's minds are most gladly stirred and easily carried away from the customary, many other things came unhappily together: in the person of Socinus, in the doctrine he proposed, in the manner of proposing it, in the men to whom he proposed it, and in the state of the age and of the nation in which it chiefly prevailed. These strongly drew very many, not ignoble, not foolish and not unlettered, to favour themselves and their doctrine. Namely,

units.la: §. 10. Primo, Multa in ipsius Socini persona spectanda occurrebant, quibus & venerationem Sibi conciliavit apud Omnes quibus innotuit, et Amorem, Ingenium ei sublime, & acutum et ad omnia idoneum buscunque[?] Illud intendere voluit, & applicare. Memoria tenax nec minus prompta ad reddendum quæcunque exceperat. Eloquentia quoque in promtu ad Animi sui Sensum expedite efferendum. Ratiocinandi facultas ad disputandum parata, sive Aliena impugnare vellet, sive Sua defendere. Hæc omnia apparuerunt in Disputationibus iis, quas crebro cum Dogmatum suorum Adversariis habuit. In Tractatibus, quos composuit; imo, & in quotidianis Colloquiis, quæ Occasione data, cum suis familiaribus iniit. Inprimis, Memoriæ felicissimæ insigne Specimen edidit; in Disputatione quadam cum Christiano Franken quam cum eo habuisse narratur, in Consessu Synodi Chmelnicensis; ubi ( sine ope alicuius Scripti quo Sibi tunc uti non dabatur, ad Capita Argumentorum brevi consignanda ) ordine repetiisse dicitur 5o Illius Argumenta contra Invocationem Christi, quæ præmeditata secum adduxerat, & continenter efferebat; & Unicuique Responsum suum sigillatim aptasse, ita ut Adversarius abierit confusus. Neque solis Naturæ Dotibus excelluit; quin & has adauxit & expolivit & ad summam perfectionis Gradum perduxit partim frequentibus Exercitiis, partim Artium liberalium Auxiliis. Cum enim inter Illius Opera extet Tractatus de Sophisticis Elenchis, certum est Eum logicæ technis atque fallaciis probe instructum fuisse, & Earum omnium bene gnarum quascunque Ars illa suppeditat. Nec minus constat vel Historiam Illius vel Epistolas perlegenti, quam cunctis persuadendi Artibus longe multumque prætaret. Itaque cum hæ duæ Artes insuper accedere naturali isti facundiæ & ratiocinandi facultati quibus antea pollebat, necesse est ut Eas, quamplurimum adiuverint si, mul, & adornaverint. At simul notum est logicam ut & Rhetoricam, instar Gladii accipitis sese habere & in malum æque ac bonum adhiberi nec minus ad falsi quam ad Veri partes tuendas usurpati & posse & solere. Unde est quod logicam Tullianus non inepte appellet, Artem [?]struendi ac destruendi versipellem[?]. Quomodo autem & quanto studio his Artibus usus fuerit Socinus cum Discipulis Illius in sequentibus apparebit.
units.tr: §. 10. First, many things in the person of Socinus himself were worthy of note, by which he won veneration from all who knew him, and love. He had a lofty and sharp intellect, fit for everything to which he chose to direct and apply it. His memory was tenacious and no less ready to give back whatever it had taken in. His eloquence was at hand to express his feeling readily, and his faculty of reasoning was ready for disputation, whether he wished to attack the views of others or to defend his own. All these appeared in the disputations he often held with adversaries of his doctrines, in the treatises he composed, and even in the daily conversations he entered into with his intimates when occasion offered. Above all, he gave a remarkable proof of his most happy memory in a certain disputation with Christian Franken, which he is said to have held in the assembly of the Synod of Chmielnik. There, without the aid of any written notes, which he was not then allowed to use for jotting down the heads of the arguments, he is said to have repeated in order the 50 arguments of his own against the invocation of Christ, which he had prepared beforehand and brought with him, and delivered them continuously. He also fitted to each one his own answer, point by point, so that his opponent went away confused. Nor did he excel only in natural gifts. He also increased and polished these and brought them to the highest degree of perfection, partly by frequent exercise and partly by the aids of the liberal arts. For since among his works there exists a treatise On Sophistical Refutations, it is certain that he was well instructed in the rules of logic and well acquainted with all the fallacies that that art supplies. Nor is it less evident to anyone who reads his History or his Letters that he far surpassed all the arts of persuasion. Thus, since these two arts were added to the natural eloquence and faculty of reasoning he already possessed, they must have greatly helped and adorned them. At the same time it is well known that logic and rhetoric are like a hawk's sword: they can be applied to evil as well as good, and can and do serve to defend the cause of the false no less than of the true. Hence Cicero not inaptly calls logic an art of building up and tearing down, of a versatile kind. How and with what zeal Socinus made use of these arts will appear in what follows, with his disciples.

units.la: §. 11. His Animi Doribus accessit justa Corporis Statura, procera vicinior & plane virilis; congrua & elegans membrorum proportio, in corpore aliquanto graciliori, intra modum tamen, frons læta & porrecta, & Oculorum masculus vigor; vultus placidus ac decorus, ita tamen ut Oris gratia ac venustas de Illius vigore atque majestate nihil imminueret; Habitus demum Gestusque totius Corporis ad summam Elegantiam compositus. Hæc item omnia decorabat & multo gratiora reddebat, Educatio ingenua, & consuetudo vitæ sermonisque cum Viris primariis Ordinis, quibuscum Conversari solebat. Nam ut erat vir genere Nobilis, ita & aulicis moribus insignite excultus; comis erga Omnes & humanus, accessu & alloquio facilis, officiosus in Amicos, erga cumctos affabilis. Imo, Honorem Cuique ultra modum exhibuisse dicitur, adeo ut Illi crimini daretur ab Amicis, tantus Sui Contemptus, & Aliorum Cultus. His accessit modestus Corporis Cultus comptus tamen, ac decorus, nam [?]etsi à fastu, luxuque longe aberat, faciles tamen, & in promptu habendas, non aspernabatur Munditias.
units.tr: §. 11. To these gifts of mind was added a fair bodily stature, rather tall and thoroughly manly; a fitting and graceful proportion of the limbs, in a body somewhat slender yet within measure; a cheerful and open brow, and a manly vigour in the eyes; a calm and dignified countenance, yet such that the charm and grace of his face did not diminish its vigour and majesty; and finally his bearing and the gestures of his whole body arranged with the greatest elegance. His liberal upbringing and the habit of life and conversation with the leading men of the order with whom he was accustomed to associate also adorned and made all this far more pleasing. For as he was a man of noble birth, so he was also finely cultivated with courtly manners: courteous and humane towards all, easy of access and conversation, obliging to friends, affable to everyone. Indeed he is said to have shown honour to each person beyond measure, so that his friends charged him with the fault of having such a great contempt for himself and such great respect for others. To this was added a modest yet neat and becoming care of his person; for though he was far from pride and luxury, he did not disdain cleanliness, which was easy and readily at hand.

units.la: §. 12. Indolem quoque dicitur habere ad omne Genus Honesti pronam atque paratam, quam et variis Virtutibus excoluisse fertur. Diligentia, Modestia et Humilitate, Mansuetudine atque Patientia, Liberalitate in Amicos, et Misericordia in Pauperes, simplicitate et Integritate Morum, et ardentissimo Veritatis divinæ promovendæ Zelo. Neminem unquam contempsisse visus est. Neque unquam otiosus apparuit, sed vel legendo, vel scribendo, vel differendo occupatus est. Nullam rem, nisi consulto et circumspecte, aggressus est; Nihilque scribere auspicatus est, nisi longa et matura Meditatione concoctum. Cum primum ingressus est Poloniam, et Anti-Trinitariis Se adjunxisset, in Multos incidit, quorum Dogmata cum suis minime congruebant. Cum autem Dissensum suum haudquaquam reticeret, satis aspere atque diu Repulsam passus est. Qua tamen Ignominia Se minime affectum ostendit, cum neque in Iram prorumperet aut hostile odium foveret, aut Ullum alienati Animi Indicium proderet. Candor, et inaffectata Simplicitas in Moribus Illius apparuit, quibus ita Gravitas inerat, ut omnino Fastus atque Supercilium abesset; et Hominem facilius revereri velles, quam posses timere. Cum autem natura ad Bilem pronus fuerit, seu potius præceps, ita tamen fregit hanc vesanam[?] Animi Rabiem, ut Mansuetudo illa, quæ in Eo post eluxit et Plerisque admirationi fuit, visa fuerit potius Naturæ Dos, quam fructus Virtutis. Patientiæ quoque, in Malis omne genus tolerandis, eximia Documenta dedit. Cum enim natura, ut modo diximus, irritabilis Ingenii esset, et Sensus valde delicati, Nihil mali Ei accidere potuit, quod Eum non penitius afficeret, et acerrimo Dolore Cor Illius transfigeret. Attamen, et in his quoque Certaminibus, quæ multa et gravia pertulit, Naturæ suæ victor & Triumphator apparuit, fertur enim calamitates ab Alienis, Injurias à suis, Pericula ab Hostibus, Ingratitudinem ab Amicis, Invidiam à Doctis, odium ab imperitis, Infamiam ab omnibus, Pauperiem à fortuna, denique ab ipsis Anti-Trinitariorum cætibus, quibus instruendis, & in unum coagmentandis tantum operæ impendisset, jugem nec sine ignominia Repulsam, summa Animi magnitudine, perpessum fuisse. Ad hæc, de eo narratur quam alienus fuerit ab avaritia, quam promptus ad opera Charitatis, & omnia Humanitatis officia. Nam quamdiu, post Patrimonium sibi in Italia obreptum, vel tenuissimo sumptu conditionem suam tolerare potuit, adduci nequiit, ut munere[?] a ultro sibi oblata caperet. Quinetiam, ultro in egenos facultates suas erogabat. Neque cleemosynis[?] tantum erogandis studium adhibuit, sed & omne liberalitatis Genus lubenter exercuit. Præterea, zelum ardentissimum Divinæ veritatis promovendæ præ se tulit. Siquidem, non solum suis ipsius sumptibus nonnullos libros in lucem edidisse fertur, sed & Doctrinam suam (quam ut verbo Divino per omnia consentaneam, cunctis persuasissimam esse voluit) omnibus, quia potuit, modis propagare nunquam destitit, scriptis integris sive Tractatibus, epistolis huc illuc missis, privatis publicisque Disputationibus, Informationibus eorum quos mentis suæ habuit Interpretes; longis item itineribus, quorum pleraque ab extrema Silefiæ ora, in intimam usque Lituaniam suscepta sunt; valetudinis, famæ, fortunarum dispendio; sui denique capitis Periculo. Tam acrem, tam indefessum zelum in Dogmate ipso passim evulgando demonstravit, quod pro veritate Divina, aut revera habuit, aut saltem haberi voluit.
units.tr: §. 12. He is also said to have had a nature inclined and ready for every kind of what is honourable, and he is reported to have cultivated it with various virtues: diligence, modesty and humility, gentleness and patience, generosity to friends, compassion for the poor, simplicity and integrity of life, and a most ardent zeal for promoting divine truth. He never appeared to despise anyone. Nor did he ever seem idle; he was always occupied either with reading, writing or disputing. He undertook nothing except after careful and deliberate thought, and he began to write nothing that had not been ripened by long and mature meditation. When he first came to Poland and joined the Anti-Trinitarians, he fell in with many people whose doctrines did not at all agree with his own. Since he did not conceal his dissent, he suffered a rebuff that was fairly harsh and long-lasting. Yet he showed no sign of being affected by this disgrace: he did not burst out in anger, nor did he nurse hostile hatred, nor did he give any sign of an estranged mind. Candour and unaffected simplicity appeared in his manners, and there was in them such gravity that there was no pride or haughtiness at all; one would sooner revere the man than fear him. Although by nature he was prone, or rather headlong, to bile, he so curbed this wild rage of spirit that the gentleness which later shone forth in him, and which was a matter of wonder to most people, seemed to be a gift of nature rather than the fruit of virtue. He also gave outstanding examples of patience in bearing every kind of misfortune. For since, as we have just said, he had a irritable temperament and very delicate feelings, no evil could befall him without affecting him more deeply and piercing his heart with the sharpest pain. Yet even in those struggles, which he endured in great number and severity, he appeared the conqueror and triumphant over his own nature. For it is reported that he bore with the greatest greatness of spirit calamities at the hands of strangers, injuries from his own people, dangers from enemies, ingratitude from friends, envy from the learned, hatred from the unlearned, infamy from all, poverty from fortune, and finally, from the very congregations of the Anti-Trinitarians, for whose instruction and union he had expended so much effort, a constant rebuff, not without disgrace. Besides this, it is related how far removed he was from avarice, how ready for works of charity and all the duties of humanity. For as long as he could bear his condition with the very slightest expense, after the patrimony that had slipped from him in Italy, he could not be brought to accept any post that was offered to him unsolicited. Moreover, he spent his resources on the needy of his own accord. Nor did he apply himself only to distributing alms, but he also willingly practised every kind of liberality. Furthermore, he displayed a most ardent zeal for promoting divine truth. For not only is he reported to have published several books at his own expense, but he also never ceased, by every means he could, to spread his doctrine, which he wished to be persuaded to all as wholly consonant with the divine Word: by written works, whole treatises or letters sent here and there, private and public disputations, instruction of those whom he regarded as interpreters of his mind; likewise by long journeys, most of which he undertook from the far edge of Silesia into the innermost parts of Lithuania; at the cost of his health, reputation and fortunes, and finally at the risk of his own life. He showed such a keen and tireless zeal in spreading this doctrine everywhere that he either truly possessed, or at least wished to be thought to possess, it for the sake of divine truth.

units.la: §. 13. Postremo modestiam insignem atque Humilitatem, ut in caetera conversatione ostendit; ita praecipue in eo, quod Delicta sua reprehendi facile passus fit, & severiora quaedam Amicorum monita, ad redargutionem criminum spectantia, non solum patienti ac tranquillo, sed & grato Animo exceperit. Documento fit, inter alia, Responsum illud ad Epistolam Marcelli Squarcialupi, concivis (ut puto) fui, & in exilio socii; qui cum Socinum, inter Alia quaedam, redarguisset de nimio calore inter disputandum, quum[?] etiam ait non raro in clamores inconditos erupisse; ita reponit Socinus, ut culpam suam ingenue fateatur, & Gratias ei reddat pro amica atque tempestiva monitione; ut & aliis quibusdam Amicis, qui fe de eadem culpa antea monuissent; Illi autem, prae caeteris. Sic enim pergit, --Quamquam plus Tibi, quam illis, me debere agnosco, quod ipsi, nec tam aperte istud meum vitium mihi significarunt, neque Id quod Tu deinde addis, addiderunt; sed illud prorsus me celarunt. Nec enim unquam me inter disputandum furere mihi ne leviter quidem indicarunt, qui vix me aliquando irascci, aut sunt dicere. At Tu me ab Ira ad furorem devenire, idque de levi causa asseveras. Hoc profecto non leve est vitium, & me summa ope niti decet, ut eo prorsus liberer. Illud, quicquid Tibi visum fuerit, constanter affirmare possum, me inter disputandum, commoveri quidem sapissime aliqua ratione; id tamen dolore fieri, quod Adversarius veritatem, ut mihi videtur, agnoscere & amplecti nolit. Aliter autem, animo me turbari, aut irasci; vel perraro, vel fortasse nunquam contingere. Utcunque sit, Tibi immortales pro Admonitione tua Gratias ago. Namque ea, ut spero, fiet, ut posthac [?] me in disputando moderatum[?] non esse merito affirmare possit. Sic ille, Epist. ad Marc: Squarc: dat: Cracoviæ. Nov: 20. 1581. extat autem, Tomo 1. pag. 367. col. 1.
units.tr: §. 13. Lastly, he showed remarkable modesty and humility, as he did in the rest of his conduct; and this especially in that he readily allowed his faults to be rebuked, and received with a not only patient and calm but even grateful mind certain rather severe admonitions of friends that bore on the correction of his failings. An example of this is, among other things, that reply to the letter of Marcello Squarcialupi, a fellow citizen (I think) of mine and a companion in exile, who, while rebuking Socinus, among other things, for excessive heat in disputing, also said that he not infrequently broke out into disorderly shouting. Socinus replied in such a way that he openly confesses his fault and gives thanks to him for his friendly and timely warning, as he also did to certain other friends who had earlier warned him of the same fault, but to him above the rest. For he goes on thus: --Although I acknowledge that I owe more to you than to them, because they did not point out this fault of mine so openly, nor did they add what you then add, but kept it entirely hidden from me. For they never even faintly indicated to me that I rage in disputing, they who scarcely say that I am ever angry at all. But you assert that I pass from anger to fury, and that for a slight cause. Certainly this is no slight fault, and I ought to strive with all my power to be wholly freed from it. As for the rest, whatever it may have seemed to you, I can firmly affirm that in disputing I am indeed quite often moved in some way, but that this happens from grief that my opponent, as it seems to me, is unwilling to acknowledge and embrace the truth. But that I should be troubled or angry in mind otherwise is either very rarely or perhaps never the case. Be that as it may, I give you immortal thanks for your admonition. For I hope it will come about that from now on I may rightly be able to affirm that I am not immoderate in disputing. Thus he writes, in the letter to Marcello Squarcialupi, dated at Kraków, 20 November 1581; it is found in Tome 1, page 367, column 1.

units.la: §. 14. Tantus ac talis erat hujus Sectæ Auctor ac Patronus in quo omnia, quibus Homines eximie affici, & quasi extra se rapi solent, ita concurrerunt, ut omnes, quibuscum conversabatur, quasi fascino quodam dementaverit, & non exiguam Admirationem sui, cum Amore conjunctam, cunctorum animis imprimeret.
