Cum autem Ingenio excelso, bonaq; indole ita excelluerit; cum ratiocinatione simul & eloquio admodum polleret; cum insignia virtutum specimina apud omnes offenderet, quas vel egregias habuit, vel egregie simulavit; cum natura simul & moribus ita comparatus esset, ut ad omne Genus humanum demerendum quasi factus videretur; minime mirum est, si quamplurimos fefellit [?], & in suas Partes attraxerit. Ita, quod Augustinus olim de Fausto Manichæo, nec incommode, nec immerito dici potest de Fausto Socino, Eum magnum Diaboli laqueum fuisse.
units.tr: §. 14. So great and such was the author and patron of this sect, in whom all the qualities by which men are wont to be singularly moved and as it were carried out of themselves so came together that he bewitched all those with whom he associated, as if by some charm, and impressed upon the minds of all a considerable admiration of himself joined with affection. Since he excelled in a lofty intellect and good disposition; since he was very strong both in reasoning and in eloquence; since he presented outstanding specimens of virtue to all, which he either truly possessed or skilfully feigned; since by nature and manners he was so constituted that he seemed made, as it were, to win over the whole human race, it is by no means surprising that he deceived very many and drew them to his side. So what Augustine once said of Faustus the Manichaean can, not inappropriately and not undeservedly, be said of Faustus Socinus, that he was a great snare of the Devil.

units.la: §. 15. Secundo, ut patientissime tulit quosvis Oppugnantes, eorumque studium laudavit in veritate perquirenda; & gratulatus est iisdem, quod secum in quibusdam saltem convenirent; ita nova sua Dogmata non imperiose ac minaciter Discipulis suis imposuit, sed ea leniter ac modeste proposuit amplectenda. Cum enim mos fuisset, non solum Pontificiis, sed & aliis quarumcunque fere partium Doctoribus, sub terribili Damnationis interminatione, & æternæ salutis jactura, Placita sua cunctis obtrudere, Ille nihil credendum injunxit, ut absolute necessarium, nisi quod verbis dilertis in Scriptura extaret, aut saltem ex eis clare deduci posset. Imo, nihil ad salutem absolute necessarium esse voluit, nisi Scientiam promissorum atque Praeceptorum, à Christo traditorum; & quæ istam scientiam consequuntur, exque ea dependent, fidem illis Christi Promissis, & Obedientiam ejus Præceptis, constanter atque sincere præstandam. Alia, quæ minoris momenti putabat, aut obscurius in S. literis tradita, ac proinde disceptationibus obnoxia, licet ipse de iis sententiam suam in hanc, illamve partem tulerit, haud tamen suam istam sententiam cunctis obtrusit, ut omnino necefsariam ad salutem adsequendam. Quod ad me attinet nullam mihi, inquit, est Dubium, quin omnes Illi, sive Calviniani, sive Lutherani, sive Anabaptistae, sive Ariani, qui se ad Prescriptum Christi gesserint; (nec e-nim dubito ex singulis istorum Ordinibus Tales esse non Paucos, aut saltem esse posse) cælestis vitæ Haereditatem adituri sint. Papistas solos excipit, quos omnes hodie Idololatras esse statuit. Deinde addit— Quantum ad Res Salutis non necessarias idem in S. literarum, quod in Aliorum cujuscunque generis librorum explicatione, usu veniet, in quo mihil, argui potest inconveniens. Ut enim suo quisque modo illos interpretatur, absque eo ut vel Aliorum se subjiciat Judicio, vel de vero illorum sensu ita quicquam habeat exploratum, ut error subesse nequeat: Sic etiam, in Rebus Salutis nostra non necessariis, S. literæ explicabuntur. Quanquam Ille[?] quidem id insuper habent præ Aliis eximium, quod cum Res sint Divinæ, ac proinde sibi ipsis contrariæ, aut inter se dissentanea esse nequeant, ubique per seipsa tuto explicari possint. Hæc Ille, Epist: 3* ad Andr: Dudithium. pag. 502. col. 2. in fine Tom. 1. Idem alibi— Ad salutem per Christum consequendam, ea tantum sunt necessaria, sine quibus Fides in ipsum Christum, seu in Deum per Christum (sc. Fides in promissis, ut non semel se explicat) ejusque Praeceptorum Obedientia consistere nequit. Epist: 4. ad Jo: Volkelium.pag. 454. Col. 1. Ita laxus ac lenis est Socinus, sive Res, sive Personas spectes [?], quoties necessaria ad salutem definit. Quinetiam, in omnibus suis Dogmatibus, quae palam asseruit, & ab omnibus recipi voluit, ut in o aculis Divinis fundata, non tamen ea, ut Doctoris irrefragabilis Dictata Discipulis suis tenenda injungit, & sine mora aut mansitatione deglutienda; sed molliter ac sobrie, verbisque tam Affectu plenis, quam sanam Rationem prae se ferentibus, ea commendat Animis cunctorum. Amice monet; Pathetice hortatur, orat [?], obsecrat, & obtestatur, ut suos errores agnoscant & abjiciant; solam veritatem a se quaeri religiose profitetur; pro convitiis, sana [?] consilia, & Supplicationes refert, humilitate simul, & Amore pio, in speciem refertas; errantium miseretur; obstinatos emollit; Repugnantes non rejicit & a se longe pellit, sed ad se leniter attrahit; ratiocinatur, & persuadet, & ad illorum Rationem appellat, ita ut ipsos totidem Judices statuere videatur ad sententiam de cunctis suis Dogmatibus, prout sibi aequum visum fuerit, ferendam. Denique quod ipse conferre non potuit, a Deo petit, ut ille Spiritum Illuminationis impertiret Doctrinae suae oppugnatoribus qui veritatem demonstraret, eosque dirigeret in via quae recta ducit ad vitam aeternam.
units.tr: §. 15. Secondly, just as he bore very patiently any who opposed him, and praised their zeal in seeking after truth, and rejoiced with them that they agreed with him at least in some points, so he did not imperiously or threateningly impose his new doctrines on his disciples, but proposed them gently and modestly to be embraced. For although it had been the custom not only among the Papists but also among the teachers of almost every other party to force their opinions upon everyone under the dreadful threat of damnation and at the peril of eternal salvation, he enjoined nothing to be believed as absolutely necessary except what stood in express words in Scripture or could at least be clearly deduced from it. Indeed, he wished that nothing was absolutely necessary to salvation except knowledge of the promises and precepts delivered by Christ, and what follows from that knowledge and depends upon it: faith in those promises of Christ, and obedience to his precepts, to be rendered constantly and sincerely. Other matters, which he thought of lesser importance, or which were delivered more obscurely in the Holy Scriptures and therefore open to dispute, he did not impose on everyone as wholly necessary to attaining salvation, even though he himself had taken his own view of them on this side or that. As far as I am concerned, he says, I have no doubt that all those, whether Calvinists, or Lutherans, or Anabaptists, or Arians, who have conducted themselves according to the prescription of Christ (for I do not doubt that there are not a few of each of these bodies, or at least that there can be), will attain the inheritance of the heavenly life. He excepts only the Papists, whom he now judges all to be idolaters. Then he adds: As far as things not necessary to salvation are concerned, the same will happen in the explanation of the Holy Scriptures as in the explanation of books of any other kind, in which I can see no inconvenience to be charged. For just as each person interprets them in his own way, without either submitting himself to the judgment of others or having anything so certain about their true sense that error cannot lie in it, so also in matters not necessary to our salvation the Holy Scriptures will be explained. Although these writings have this outstanding advantage over others, that since they are divine matters, and therefore cannot be contrary to themselves or disagree among themselves, they can everywhere be safely explained by themselves. Thus he; Letter 3 to Andreas Dudithius, page 502, column 2, near the end of Tome 1. Elsewhere again: For obtaining salvation through Christ, only those things are necessary without which faith in Christ himself, or in God through Christ (namely faith in the promises, as he explains more than once), and obedience to his precepts, cannot subsist. Letter 4 to Johannes Volkelius, page 454, column 1. So lax and gentle is Socinus, whether one looks at the matters or at the persons, whenever he defines what is necessary to salvation. Moreover, in all his doctrines, which he openly asserted and wished to be received by all as founded on the divine oracles, he does not enjoin them on his disciples to be held as the irrefutable dictates of a teacher and swallowed without delay or hesitation; rather, he commends them to the minds of all gently and soberly, in words as full of feeling as they are displaying sound reasoning. He warns in a friendly way, exhorts with emotion, pleads, beseeches and entreats them to recognise and cast off their errors; he solemnly professes that he seeks only the truth; in reply to insults he offers sound counsel and entreaties, combining humility and devoted love in a show of abundance; he has pity on those who err; he softens the obstinate; he does not reject or drive far from himself those who resist, but gently draws them to himself; he reasons, persuades, and appeals to their reason, so that he seems to make them so many judges to pass sentence on all his doctrines as he thinks fitting. Finally, what he himself could not accomplish by argument, he asks of God, that God would grant the Spirit of illumination to the opponents of his teaching, to show them the truth and to direct them in the way that leads to eternal life.

units.la: §. 16. Has persuasorias Artes, variasque Affectuum Illecebras, quibus tot Discipulos sibi conciliavit, passim videre est in Epistolis illius. Non abs re erit, ex iis unam & alteram Pericopam in exemplum adhibere. Matthaeus Radecius, Secretarius Gedanensis, multum dubitavit de Invocatione & Adoratione Christo praestanda, qui secundum Socini Dogma, nudus Homo erat. Socinus in sua ad eum Epistola, post Ratiocinationem satis prolixam, quasi ei per se sumptae dissideret, ad veteris Ecclesiae Authoritatem confugit; qua in medium allata, ad preces se convertit—Noli igitur, rogo atque obsecro Te Veritati manifestissima quidquam repugnare, & summum ac praestantissimum Christianae Pietatis mysterium, ac Fundamentum agnosce; supremam sc. in nos omnes Jesu Nazareno datam a Deo in perpetuum praesentem Potestatem & Gubernationem. Niemoievius, vir magnae Authoritatis apud Polonos, ei multum restiterat. Quid autem Socinus refert? Vincat, inquit, ut Tu in ipso tuo Scripto concludis, veritas. Quod ut in nobis, potissimum eveniat, id caveamus diligentissime, quod Tu me mones, ne praejudicata opiniones, nobis noceant; neve nos pudeat, ut ais, a minori aliquando admoneri, ab eoque discere. Sic ille Resp: ad Epist: secundam Jo: Niemoievii. pag. 423. Tom. 1. Jacobus Covetus Parisiensis, minister Evangelicus, misit ad Socinum, librum a se conscriptum contra Thesis illius de Jesu Christo Servatore, quem hisce verbis concludit, Ex his omnibus satis liquet, Christum ideo vere Servatorem nostrum esse, quod morte sua Deo pro nobis Peccatoribus plene satisfecerit, Nosque ex dono Dei credentes satisfactionis & justitiae suae perfectissima gratuita Imputatione servaverit. Et haec quidem ex Dei verbo depromta, tanta, ut spero, apud Te Authoritatis erunt, ut posthac malis cum Scriptura credere ac sentire quam absque Scriptura ex tuo sensu per devia aberrare. Tu, propterea Boni consules &c. pag. 246. Tom. 2. Quid ad haec Socinus? In hac tua Conclusione, ait, nihil est ad quod respondendum mihi sit, nisi ut Tibi gratias agam, qui cum crederes me sententiam de Christo Servatore nostro, veritati contrariam, & a S. literis abhorrentem sequi, reducere me conatus su[?] in viam reIam, Testimoniis Scripturæ, variisque Rationibus, & sane pro hac non vulgari Humanitate, & propensi in me Animi significatione, me Tibi plurimum debere, & nunc confiteor, & perpetuo agnoscam. Non pauci enim ex iis, qui tecum sentirent, fuissent, qui longe aliter, quam Tu feceris, mecum egissent, & tanquam pestilentem Hominem, me penitus aversati essent. Quare, si unquam parem Tibi Gratiam referendi Occasio ipse mihi obtulerit, non committam, ut ingrati Animi abs Te, vel a quovis Alio, merito accusari possim. —Sed & tui ad me scribendi, & mei Tibi Respondendi sine dubio Finis erit, si veritati, & Dei Gloria, simulque tua & Aliorum salúti omnia posthabueris. Deum vero precatus fueris (ut quidem ego ex Animo precor) ut si imprudens hactenus in eum, & in Ejus filium in Evangelio ministrando continumeliosus fuisti, populumque Tibi commissi, dum salutem curare credis, Damnationem, procurasti, Tibi benigne veniam dare, & Spiritu suo mentem tuam perfundere, ac sui cognitionis luce collustrare velit.
units.tr: §. 16. Such persuasive arts and varied enticements of the emotions, by which he won over so many disciples, can be seen everywhere in his letters. It will not be out of place to cite one or two passages from them as examples. Matthaeus Radecius, the Danzig secretary, had many doubts about whether Christ should be invoked and worshipped, since by Socinus's doctrine Christ was a mere man. In his letter to him, after a rather lengthy argument, Socinus, as if he disagreed with the argument on its own terms, had recourse to the authority of the ancient Church. Having brought this forward, he turned to prayer: Therefore, I beg and entreat you, do not set yourself against the most manifest truth, but acknowledge the highest and most excellent mystery and foundation of Christian piety, namely, the supreme and everlasting power and government over all of us, given by God to Jesus of Nazareth. Niemoievius, a man of great authority among the Poles, had strongly resisted him. What then does Socinus reply? Let truth prevail, he says, as you yourself conclude in your writing. So that this may happen especially among us, let us take the greatest care with what you warn me of, that preconceived opinions do us harm, and that we should not be ashamed, as you say, to be admonished at times by a lesser person and to learn from him. So he replies in his second answer to the letter of John Niemoievius, p. 423, vol. 1. James Covetus of Paris, an evangelical minister, sent Socinus a book written by himself against his thesis concerning Jesus Christ the Saviour, which he concludes with these words: From all these things it is clear enough that Christ is truly our Saviour because by his death he fully satisfied God for us sinners, and because he has saved us who believe, by the gift of God, through the most perfect gratuitous imputation of his satisfaction and righteousness. These things, drawn from the word of God, will, I hope, carry such authority with you that from now on you will prefer to believe and think with Scripture rather than to go astray by your own sense apart from Scripture. Therefore, you will kindly take this in good part, etc. p. 246, vol. 2. What does Socinus say to this? In your conclusion, he says, there is nothing to which I need to reply, except to thank you, who, when you believed that I was following an opinion about Christ our Saviour that was contrary to truth and abhorrent to the Holy Scriptures, tried to bring me back into the right way by testimonies of Scripture, by various arguments; and certainly, for this not common kindness and the disposition of good will towards me that you show, I both acknowledge and will always acknowledge that I owe you very much. For not a few of those who thought as you do would have dealt with me quite differently from how you have, and would have shunned me completely as a plague-carrier. Therefore, if ever an occasion to repay you in kind should offer itself, I will not allow myself to be justly accused by you, or by anyone else, of an ungrateful mind. But there will undoubtedly be an end both to your writing to me and to my answering you, if you put everything second to truth and the glory of God, and also to your own salvation and that of others. But if you pray to God (as indeed I pray sincerely) that, if you have hitherto been insolent against him and against his Son in preaching the gospel, and in believing that you were caring for the salvation of the people committed to you, have procured their damnation, he may graciously grant you pardon, and be willing to fill your mind with his Spirit and illuminate it with the light of his knowledge.

units.la: Andr: Dudithius ei dubia quædam solvenda proposuerat. Quod cum fecisset in Epistola responsoria, hæc tandem adjicit; Credas mihi velim, mea me Tenuitatis probe mihi conscium; Idque satis habere perspectum, me neque ad disputandum cum Hominibus tuæ fortis, nec ad tibi de Quæstionibus tam sublimibus satisfaciendum, aptum esse. Quinimo novi, aut tenendum mihi silentium, aut saltem veniam a Te petendam, quod ita libere Tibi respondeam, Tecumque sermonem conferam.
units.tr: Andreas Dudithius had proposed certain doubts to him to be resolved. When he had done this in a reply letter, he finally adds these words: Believe me, I am well aware of my own slightness, and I know that it is sufficiently clear that I am suited neither to disputing with men of your strength nor to satisfying you on such lofty questions. Indeed, I know that I ought either to keep silent, or at least to ask your pardon, for answering you so freely and conferring with you in discussion.

units.la: Epist: 3. ad Andr: Dudithium pag. 508. Col. 1. Tom. 1. Franc: Puccius, nobilis Florentinus, Epistolam miserat ad Socinum in qua 110 Argumenta adduxerat pro immortalitate Rerum, præsertim[?] vero Hominis in prima Creatione. Hæc Socinus refutanda da in fe susceperat, Defendit fe Puccius altero Scripto, & paulo acrius, verbisque asperioribus Socinum redarguit. Videamus jam, quomodo se gerat Socinus in Replicatione sua ad hujusmodi Antagoniftam. Cavi, inquit, quantum potui nè Te Convitio aliquo aut Maledicto laederem quamvis à Te graviter & frequenter lacessitus fuerim. Siquid tamen Mihi imprudenti exciderit, quod Animum tuum, praeter Id, quod par est, offendat, ut benigne Mihi Id ignoscas vehementer & summis precibus à Te peto atque contendo. Sed Illud vehementius multo pro tua Salutis desiderio, Te rogo, seu potius moneo, ut posthac, si fieri potest aut mecum, aut cum quovis Alio, sive coram sive ex Scripto disputans, à Convitiis abstineas. Nam praeterquam, quod virum Nobilem ac literatum, qualis Tu es, minime decent, & Adversarii Causam juvant, à regno Dei, eum, qui Ipsis deditus est, excludunt, ut Paulus aperte testatur; qui etiam praecipit, ne cum ejusmodi Hominibus, qui inter Christianos se esse profitentur, vel cibum quidem sumamus. Quod si à Convitiis, ut divino regno non judicemur indigni, abstinendum Nobis est; à Calumniis multo magis abstinere debemus; quibus tamen Tu, in tuo Scripto adversum Me, delectatus quodammodo fuisse videris. Quare quid Tibi faciendum sit vides. Hac [?]praescriptis, & praeterea Vita absolutiori Innocentia & Christiana Sanctitati studueris, quicquid in hac Controversia nostra unquam sensurus [?]fis, Ego & Te semper meum in Christo fratrem esse agnoscam, & Tibi mecum satis convenire putabo. & quod Tu Mihi perhumaniter facturum Te polliceris, si Tecum de veritate conveniam, hoc est ut Ego interpretor, si tuam Sententiam veram esse assensus fuero, Id Ego reipsa praestabo. Ex Te enim, & multa addiscere curabo, quae Me docere potes, & quantum in Me fuerit Tecum cum in Studiis, tum in Conatibus tuis omnibus, adjumento ero. Sin autem Te non multum curare animadvertere potero, ut vetere Homine deposito novum imbuas; etiamsi non in hac quaestione tantum sed in omnibus Christianae Religionis Placitis, quin & in singulis divinarum literarum sententiis, atque adeo verbis & syllabis interpretandis, mecum prorsus sentires, nou[?] tamen Te, vel fratrem agnovero, vel Tibi mecum convenire existimavero. Spero, Te omnino, non factis minus quam lingua verum Christianum plane Nobis expressurum. Neque enim ignoras, quam gravia divina Supplicia impendeant iis, quibus caelestis illa Veritas patefacta est, nec dignam tanta Cognitione vitam instituunt. Deus Opt. Max: pro sua clementia, Te nunquam deserat, & Studia ac labores tuos ad Ecclesiae suae utilitatem dirigat atque convertat.
units.tr: Letter 3 to Andreas Dudithius, p. 508, col. 1, vol. 1. Franciscus Puccius, a Florentine nobleman, had sent a letter to Socinus in which he had adduced 110 arguments for the immortality of things, especially of man in his first creation. Socinus had undertaken to refute these. Puccius defended himself in a second writing, and rebuked Socinus somewhat more sharply, with harsher words. Let us now see how Socinus conducts himself in his reply to such an antagonist. I was careful, he says, as far as I could, not to hurt you with any insult or abuse, although you have been gravely and frequently attacking me. If, however, something has slipped from me unawares that offends your mind beyond what is fitting, I earnestly and most urgently ask and beg you to pardon me kindly. But much more strongly, for the sake of your desire for salvation, I ask, or rather advise, you that from now on, if it can be done, whether disputing with me or with anyone else, whether in person or in writing, you abstain from insults. For, apart from the fact that such conduct is hardly becoming to a noble and learned man such as you are, and helps the cause of the adversary, it excludes from the kingdom of God the one who is devoted to it, as Paul clearly testifies; who also commands that we not so much as eat with such men, who profess to be Christians. But if we must abstain from insults so that we are not judged unworthy of the divine kingdom, we must abstain from slanders much more; yet you seem somehow to have taken delight in these in your writing against me. Therefore you see what you must do. If you strive after these prescribed things, and besides, after a more complete life of innocence and Christian holiness, whatever you may in the end think in this controversy of ours, I will always acknowledge you as my brother in Christ, and I will think that we agree well enough together. And what you promise you will do for me most courteously, if I come to agreement with you about the truth, that is, as I interpret it, if I assent that your opinion is true, I will indeed do this in fact. For I will take care to learn many things from you, which you can teach me, and as far as lies in me I will be a help to you both in your studies and in all your endeavours. But if I can perceive that you are not much concerned to put off the old man and put on the new, then, even if you agreed with me entirely not only on this question but on all the tenets of the Christian religion, and even on the individual sayings of the divine letters, and even on the interpretation of words and syllables, I still would not acknowledge you as a brother, nor think that you agree with me. I hope that you will show yourself plainly to us as a true Christian, not less in deeds than in speech. For you know well how grave the divine punishments are that hang over those to whom that heavenly truth has been revealed, and who do not order their lives worthily of such knowledge. May God, most good and most great, in his mercy never forsake you, and direct and turn your studies and labours to the usefulness of his Church.

units.la: §. 17. Haec autem ea de Causa aliquanto fusius citavi ut eo luculentius appareret, quantam Humilitatis atque Modestiae, Charitatis & pii Zeli, virtutis Morumque probitatis speciem prae se ferat in Scriptis suis; praesertim in Epistolis, quas partim ad apertos sjuorum Dogmatum Impugnato. es conscripsit. partim ad Dubios atque Haesitantes; quorum Plerosque his Artibus tandem Sibi conciliavit & in suam Scholam illectos Disciplinae suae ita paulatim assuefecit, ut Cunctorum Dogmatum suorum strenui Assertores paulo post evaserint.
units.tr: §. 17. I have quoted these passages somewhat more fully for this reason: so that it may appear more clearly what a semblance of humility and modesty, of charity and pious zeal, of virtue and integrity of morals he displays in his writings, especially in those letters which he wrote partly to open opponents of his doctrines, partly to doubtful and hesitant persons. Most of these he at last won over by such arts, and, having enticed them into his school, so gradually accustomed them to his discipline that, a little later, they became zealous champions of all his doctrines.

units.la: §. 18. A[?]tibus vero iisdem fere olim usi sunt Encratitae & Euchitae, atque Pelagiani, aliique quidam veteris aevi Haeretici, qui sub nomine Christiano vitae severioris[?] zelum simulabant. Ita & Pseudapostoli, Paulo testante, se in Ministros Justitiae transfo.mabant; sicut ipse satanas, Illorum Magister, sub specie Angeli lucis apparere solet, ut expeditius, & sine suspicione fallat incautos. Et hic ipse Socinus, in ilta Epistola sua ad Puccium, quam in hac ipsa Replicatione sua defendit, Anima humana mortalitatem asserue. at; quo Errore Nihil magis officit Pietati in Deum & Probitati morum; licet hic videri velit adeo studiosus piae probæque vitæ Vindex, ut illius respectu Opinionum suarum approbationem pro nihilo habere videatur. Ita molliter, adeo leni tacitoque Passu, se paulatim insinuavit Serpens hic lubricus atque versicolor; suaque Dogmata lethali veneno imbuta, latenter infudit in mentes Auditorum. Nimirum, optime novit, quod natura duci velimus, non cogi; Fidem impetrari, non exigi; quodque non solum æquum putemus, sed & pro Iure nost[?] o poscamus, ut mens nostra liberrima sit, præsertim in Religionis negotio. Hinc est quod Ecclesiae Authoritatem, quamvis ab ipso Deo derivatam, firmissimeque munitam, plerumque reverearmur potius, quam amemus; quodque illius decreta quæ Assensum & Obsequium à nobis exigunt, quamvis summa Ratione confirmata sint, minus tamen grata habeamus. Independentes esse volumus, nostrique ipsorum Domini; ideoque leges omnes, quasi tot vincula & Compedes, libertatisque nativæ Impedimenta abrumpere studemus à nobis ac rejicere. At hinc simul fit, quod hoc pasto in Prædam non raro cedimus subdolis, hujusmodi Impostoribus; qui, ut jampridem monuit Apostolus διὰ χρηστολογίας[?] καὶ εὐλογίας, per Blandiloquentiam & verba speciosa, corda ἀκάκων, hoc est, simplicium, & minime malorum decipiunt ac seducunt. Etenim mirari subit ( quod tamen experientia frequens fieri docet ) quam propensi sint Homines, ac veluti parati ad incidendum in has fraudes; adeo ut etiam contra sanæ Rationis Dicta, malint probabilibus Argumentis, & suo Arbitrio permissis, utrum admittantur, vel non, persuaderi, quam irrefragabilibus ad Assensum cogi. Valida Argumentorum Tela, quasi tot Hostium infensorum Arma, refo[?] midare[?] solemus, & a nobis repellere; at speciosas verorum Hostium fallacias sponte admittimus, & sub Colloquii obtentu in Insidias cadimus. Sic Aviculæ incidunt in Retia dolosa, dum Aucupis fistulæ incautius auscultant. Sic molles lenesque adblandientis solis Radii, viatorem illum paulatim denudant, quem ventus asperrimus atque validissimus, omni vi sua, vestibus spoliare non potuit. Sic Retiarius Myrmillonem vincit, ducitque captivum. Sic demum, hostis infensissimus humani Generis, sagis & veneficis obsequium suum promptissime exhibere videtur, dum ad eorum nutum simul appareet, et voluntati paret, adque illorum arbitrium se in speciem accommodat, cum interim iisdem revera imperet, eosque suæ Potestati subditos habeat. Iftiusmodi artificia Socinus hic usu pavit, qui contradicentes patientissime ferre solitus est, & placidissime tractare, donec hoc tandem effecerit, ut speciosa Humilitatis ac modestiæ ostentatione, cum ementito veritatis tuendæ atque propagandæ studio conjuncta, Adversarium in suas partes pertraxerit, atque hoc sæpenumero effecit, non tam speciosis Rationum momentis, quam simulatione modestiæ. Exemplo sit illud Socini Responsum, quo asseruit, nullam esse necessitatem ordinationis in Ecclesia, quæ facultatem det exercendi Ministerium Evangelicum, à Præpositis ipsius conferendam. Non video, inquit, quare non liceat Homini in Scripturis perito, ac probe, illud officium assumere. Quid vero, aut in se infirmius & ineptius, aut tam celebri Rationis sanæ Patrono indignius, proferri potuit? Ille non videt, seu potius videre non vult, ergo Alii omnes delusi sunt, qui se videre putant, & unanimi suffragio necessitatem istius ordinationis se videre testantur. Ergo tota Christi Ecclesia ante Socinum, instar Sodomiticæ Gentis, quæ ante ostium Loti cæcitate percussa est, Januam istam, qua pastoribus omnibus bonis ac legitimis introeundum est in Christi Ovile, discernere non potuit; ita ut hoc pacto, furibus exclusis, latronibusque abactis, qui vel aliunde scandere solent, vel in Caulam vi irrumpere conantur, legitimos duntaxat Pastores sequatur Christi Grex, vocique illo um[?] sedulo & secure auscultet. Ergo Traditione Ecclesiæ sepositæ, praxique Traditioni isti consona, quam ab Apostolis usque derivatam per tot Annorum Centurias ipsa retinuit, derelictis, & procul ablegatis, unius privati Hominis ductui & arbitrio, clausis oculis, obsequendum est. Ergo demum, ipsa S. Scriptura, quæ sobriis ingenuisque lectoribus hanc necessitatem & praxin satis clare ostendit, & cunctis hactenus Christianis, ex antiqua & non interrupta Catholicorum Doctorum Interpretatione, hunc sensum dictavit, non nisi difficilioribus, distortisque Fausti Socini Conspiciliis perlegenda est. Quid autem Religioni, quid Æquitati, quid sanæ Rationi magis adversum, vel esse[?] potest, vel excogitari? Nihilominus, istiusmodi Responsa, etiam in Aliis quamplurimis non exigui momenti Dogmatibus apud perplures illius Discipulos valuere, qui & in Conjecturas illius, dubiaque Problemata ab ipso obiter definita, & Opiniones nullo fundamento subnixas pro indubiis oraculis accipere parati fuerunt. Ita, quos validioribus solidæ Rationis armis superare non potuit, sub specie amici Colloquii, & pacifici Fæderis ineundi, emollivit, ac decepit, & in suam sententiam pertraxit non invitos. Quos Argumentorum robore frangere nequiit, obsequio flexit; & Affectibus eorum, in partes suas, orationis suaviloquio pellectis, Judicii vires enervavit; aciemque mentis aut occæcavit, aut obtudit. Ita callidus Hostis, cui Robur deest, fraudibus rem agit; & Adversarium multo fortiorem, nunc moras nectendo, nunc insidias tendendo, nunc Pacis ostentatione facta, & Fæderis ineundi simulatione; nunc demum proditione hostilium Copiarum, in sui ipsius partes pertraxerat, eum paulatim fatigat atque attrit, & tandem in suam potestatem redigit non obnitentem: Equidem lenem Jacobi vocem hic audio, at hirsutas Esau manus sentio. Aut Apocalypticam illam Bestiam videre mihi videor, Agni mansueti cornibus, at sævi Draconis lingua trisulca instructam & armatam, qua Homines in Terra degentes decepisse dicitur, & decipiendo occidisse. Ita Serpens leni sibilo Evam olim aggressus est, & blandiloquio suo persuasit, ut ambitiosa Scientiæ sublimiores affectatione delinita, vetitum à Deo fructum degustare auderet.
units.tr: §. 18. The Encratites and Euchites, the Pelagians, and certain other heretics of old, who under the Christian name pretended zeal for a stricter life, used nearly the same arts. So too the false apostles, as Paul testifies, transformed themselves into ministers of righteousness; just as Satan himself, their master, is wont to appear in the guise of an angel of light, so that he may deceive the unwary more readily and without suspicion. And this same Socinus, in that letter of his to Puccius, which he defends in this very Reply, asserts that the human soul is mortal. Nothing does more harm to piety toward God and to integrity of morals than this error, although he wishes to appear such an eager champion of a godly and upright life that he seems to count the approval of his own opinions as nothing in comparison. So gently, with so soft and silent a step, this slippery, many-coloured serpent insinuated himself, and secretly poured his doctrines, steeped in deadly poison, into the minds of his hearers. He knew well, no doubt, that we wish to be led by reason, not compelled; that faith is to be won, not exacted; and that we think it not only fair but also our right to demand that our mind be wholly free, especially in matters of religion. Hence it is that we revere rather than love the authority of the Church, although it is derived from God himself and most firmly fortified; and its decrees, which demand our assent and obedience, though confirmed by the highest reason, we nevertheless hold less welcome. We want to be independent and our own masters; and so we strive to break off and cast away from ourselves all laws, as so many chains and fetters and hindrances to our native liberty. But at the same time it follows that in this way we often fall as prey to deceitful impostors of this kind, who, as the Apostle long ago warned, deceive and seduce by smooth talk and fair speech [διὰ χρηστολογίας καὶ εὐλογίας] the hearts of the guileless [ἀκάκων], that is, of the simple and not at all wicked. Indeed, it is astonishing (though frequent experience shows it to be so) how prone men are, and how ready, as it were, to fall into these snares; so that even against the dictates of sound reason they prefer to be persuaded by probable arguments, left to their own judgement as to whether they are accepted or not, rather than be compelled to assent by irrefutable ones. We are accustomed to repel and throw back from ourselves the strong weapons of argument, like so many arms of hostile enemies; but we willingly admit the specious deceits of true enemies, and under the pretext of conversation we fall into their ambushes. So birds fall into deceitful nets while they listen too carelessly to the fowler's pipe. So the soft and gentle rays of the flattering sun strip that traveller of his cloak, which the fiercest and most powerful wind, with all its force, could not strip off him. So the net-fighter (retiarius) conquers the Myrmillo and leads him away captive. So, finally, the most hostile enemy of the human race seems most readily to offer his service to sorcerers and witches, while he appears at their nod, obeys their will, and outwardly accommodates himself to their judgement, although in reality he commands them and holds them subject to his own power. Socinus practised such artifices here, he who was wont to bear with opponents most patiently and to handle them most calmly, until at last he achieved this: by a specious display of humility and modesty, joined with a pretended zeal for defending and spreading the truth, he drew his adversary over to his side; and he did this very often, not so much by the weighty force of his arguments as by his pretence of modesty. Let that reply of Socinus serve as an example, in which he asserted that there is no necessity for ordination in the Church, conferred by its presiding officers, to give the power of exercising the Evangelical ministry. I do not see, he says, why a man skilled in the Scriptures, and sound in them, may not take up that office. But what could be put forward that is weaker and more foolish in itself, or more unworthy of so famous a patron of sound reason? He does not see, or rather does not wish to see; therefore all the others who think they see are deceived, and by unanimous consent testify that they see the necessity of that ordination. Therefore the whole Church of Christ before Socinus, like the Sodomite people who were struck with blindness before the door of Lot, could not discern that gate through which all good and lawful pastors must enter into Christ's fold; so that in this way, with thieves shut out and robbers driven away (those who usually climb in from elsewhere or try to force their way into the sheepfold), the flock of Christ should follow only its lawful pastors and listen to their voice diligently and without fear. Therefore the tradition of the Church must be set aside, and the practice consonant with that tradition, which it has kept from the Apostles down through so many centuries of years; these must be abandoned and cast far away, and with eyes shut we must obey the guidance and judgement of one private man. Lastly, Holy Scripture itself, which shows this necessity and practice quite clearly to sober and sincere readers, and which until now has dictated this sense to all Christians from the ancient and unbroken interpretation of the Catholic teachers, is to be read only through the more difficult and distorted spectacles of Faustus Socinus. And what can be, or be imagined, more opposed to religion, to fairness, or to sound reason? Nevertheless, such responses also carried weight with very many of his disciples in very many other doctrines of no small importance; they were ready to accept as undoubted oracles his conjectures and doubtful problems, which he had defined only in passing, and opinions resting on no foundation. Thus those whom he could not overcome with the stronger weapons of solid reason, he softened and deceived under the appearance of a friendly conversation and of entering into a peaceful covenant, and drew them, not unwilling, into his own opinion. Those whom he could not break by the force of argument, he bent by compliance; and having enticed their affections to his own side by the sweet-speaking of his discourse, he weakened the powers of their judgement, and either blinded or dulled the edge of their mind. So the crafty enemy, lacking strength, carries on his affairs by deceit; and by now delaying, now laying ambushes, now making a show of peace and a pretence of entering into a covenant, now at last by treachery of his hostile forces, he draws into his own party an adversary far stronger than himself, wears him down and gradually exhausts him, and at last reduces him to his power, though he does not resist. Indeed, I hear here the gentle voice of Jacob, but I feel the hairy hands of Esau. Or I seem to see that Apocalyptic Beast, furnished and armed with the horns of the meek Lamb, but with the forked tongue of a fierce dragon, by which it is said to have deceived the men dwelling on the earth, and by deceiving to have slain them. So the serpent long ago approached Eve with a gentle hiss, and by his smooth speech persuaded her, lured by the ambitious desire of a higher knowledge, to dare to taste the fruit forbidden by God.

units.la: §. 20. Eisdem quoque Artibus usi sunt & Alii Heterodoxi, qui licet se Socino totos non dederint, neque illius Doctrinam palam professi fuerint, vestigiis tamen ejus in hoc insistunt, quod fide antiqua, & veteris Ecclesiæ Praxi, una posthabitis nova & contraria docuerint; & sub prætextu fallibilitatis istius, cui Patres (ut Homines) fuerunt obnoxii, Interterpretationem S. Scripturæ, licet antiquitus ad Illos derivatam & nnanimiter ab iisdem afiertam, rejicere ausi sint; quodque insuper Opinionem propriam Istius loco substituerint; & Rationem privatam publicis veterum Decretis, communibusque sententiis, haudquaquam veriti sint opponere. Sic, inter Alia non pauca, Hierarchiam Ecclesiasticam tollere conantur, Clericique ac Plebis Christianæ discrimen. Neque enim ad hanc innovati Dogmatis assertionem, aliqua evidenti Demonstratione, aut Argumento irrefragabili vel ipsi se compelli profitentur, vel Alios adigere; quin suam duntaxat Opinionem atque Conjecturam ad hoc sufficere putant, ut ab omnibus admittatur. Non video, inquit unus Horum, quo minus hoc per Scripturas liceat. Atque iterum. Videtur hoc nobis verbo Divino contrarium. Cum ipsis in locis ea doceant, quæ Fidei, Praxique veterum adversantur. Novi sc. Pythagoræ exorti sunt, aut fatidici Phœbi Sacerdotes, quorum nudæ opiniones, seu Divinationes, pro totidem oraculis habendæ sunt. Ex his vero, & similibus Recentiorum Dictis, patet, quod omnem Authoritatem idcirco detrahant Antiquis, ut eam in se transferant. Patres, aiunt, Homines fuerunt, adeoque & fallibiles & fallaces. Ergo eis fidendum non est; præsertim in Re tanti momenti, qualis est æterna salus Animarum; ne Cæci cæcos Duces sequantur, cumque iis simul in foveam cadamus. Atque hoc modo simplicibus & Incautis imponere solent, quasi & ipsi quoque, qui sic a gnuut contra majores, eoque vilipendunt præse, non essent Homines, æque ac illi, iisdem erroribus lapsibusque obnoxii. Seipsos tamen Populo in Duces offerre, imo & imponere, æquum putant, quasi ipsi errare nec possent, nec vellent, aut sui sequaces in Devia abducere.
units.tr: §. 20. Other heterodox men have also used the same arts; although they have not given themselves wholly to Socinus, nor openly professed his doctrine, yet in this they follow his footsteps: that, setting aside the ancient faith and the practice of the early Church, they have taught new and contrary things; and under the pretext of that fallibility to which the Fathers, being men, were subject, they have dared to reject the interpretation of Holy Scripture, although it was handed down to them from antiquity and unanimously affirmed by them; and moreover they have substituted their own opinion for it; and they have not feared to set private reason against the public decrees of the ancients and the common opinions. Thus, among many other things, they try to abolish the ecclesiastical hierarchy, and the distinction between clergy and the Christian people. For they do not profess that they are compelled by any clear demonstration or irrefutable argument to assert this novel doctrine, nor do they compel others to accept it; rather they think that their opinion and conjecture alone is enough for it to be admitted by all. I do not see, says one of these men, why this should not be allowed by the Scriptures. And again: This seems to us contrary to the divine Word. Yet in those very passages they teach things which are opposed to the faith and the practice of the ancients. They are like new Pythagoreans who have arisen, or the prophetic priests of Phoebus, whose bare opinions or divinations are to be held as so many oracles. From these and similar sayings of the more recent writers it is plain that they strip the ancients of all authority precisely so that they may transfer it to themselves. The Fathers, they say, were men, and therefore both fallible and deceivers. Therefore they are not to be trusted; especially in a matter of such moment as the eternal salvation of souls; lest the blind should follow the blind, and we should fall with them into the pit. And in this way they are wont to impose upon simple and incautious people, as if they themselves, who thus scorn their elders and so despise them, were not men, subject to the same errors and falls as the others. Yet they think it fair to offer themselves, and even to impose themselves, as leaders of the people, as though they could neither err nor wish to, or lead their followers astray into byways.

units.la: §. 21. Tertio, Aliud quoque fuit, huic simulatæ modestiæ & Humilitati annexum, quo Socinus apud multos prævaluit. Nimirum, quod non solum unicuique Doctrinæ à se propositæ Arbitrium constituere visus sit, sed etiam quod latam Fenestram aperuerit unicuique novatori, ut quodcunque sibi visum fuerit, ex suo Ingenio procuderet, & ad Arbitrium promulgaret. Enimvero ut natura nobis insitum est, nolle lubenter ad Aliorum judicium & sententiam astringi, (quod Servitutis Genus quoddam putamus, & infirmæ Rationis Argumentum) sed potius Judicum Partes in nos assumere, quoties alienum quidpiam Nobis proponitur examinandum, ut Illud pro Arbitrio, vel approbemus vel damnemus; ita nihil fere Naturæ nostræ magis allubescit [?], quam Curiositatis studium, & Innovandi libido. Ingeniosiores præsertim, agiles esse solent & inquieti; ita ut neque norint ubi Pedem sistant aut sistere ament. Sedem quamcunque fixam, certamque, præcipue ab Alio quovis Sibi assignatam, pro Carcere habent; & in Aliorum quorumcunque Verba, legesque jurare, Captivitatis Genus autumant minime ferendum. Ita Nomades plerumque sunt, qui nulibi [?] fixum Domicilium habent, neque sub ullius Dominio constanter degunt, sed huc illuc pro libitu vagantur. Itaque Socinus huic Epidemio morbo favens, quem probe noverat se longe, lateque propagasse, & Hominum plerosque corripuisse, eandem licentiam, quam Sibi ipsi assumpsit, Aliis facile concessit. Neque sane mirum est Socinum quamplures Discipulos, hac Efca gratissima delinitos, ad se, suamque Sectam allexisse. Facillimum enim Cuique est, volentem ad se accedere, & , qua Natura ducit attrahere. & in hoc non minus perniciose libidini humani Ingenii visus est indulsisse, quam Epicurus olim libidini Carnis indulsit. Quid quod superbiæ quoque isti & Ignaviæ, quibus Genus humanum plus obnoxium est, in hac Re faverit, gratumque fecerit. Quid enim superbius, quam Nulli subiici velle aut Alterius Cujuscunque sententiæ astringi in Religionis negotio; quin è contra, nova Fidei Principia ex suo Ingenio cudere, & Doctrinæ hactenus ab Ecclesia receptæ, pro suo Arbitrio, aut admittendæ, aut ablegandæ, se Judicem constituere? quid item Ignaviæ magis gratificatur, quam lectione Veterum omnino neglecta, (in quorum Scriptis diligentius versandum est Ei, qui Veritatem istam invenire desiderat, quam hodie inter tot Polemicos Theologos, Sectasque Multiplices fere perdidimus ) se solum consulere, proprioque Ingenio fidere, in Doc-trina Christiana dignoscenda „deque Ea sententiam in singulis Articulis ferenda? Quid autem ipse Socinus in hac Re fecerit, satis aperte testatur in Epistola sua ad Squarcialupum, qui cum pro Jure Amicitiæ(erat enim intimus Socino ) eum reprehendisset de libro quodam, quem scripserat contra Jac: Palæo-logum celebrem fama & e uditione Græcum, nemine Amicorum in Consilium adhibito, qui Eum indicio suo regere, & Censuram de libro isto ferre, tum optime possent, tum promptissime vellent, hoc Responsum ab Eo tulit. Quod addis, Me nihil emittere debere, nisi bene & sæpe à libero judicio Magistrorum excussum & examinatum, qui sint Magistri isti, non satis intelligo. Neminem enim Ego in iis Rebus, de quibus in Responsione illa mea (sc: ad Palæologum de Magistratu) disseritur, ex iis qui hodie vivunt, illa ex parte Magistrum agnosco, sed sed Deum tantummodo Præceptorem habui, sacrasque literas. Quinetiam in universa ipsa divinarum Rerum scientia, quacunque tandem illa in Me sit, præter unum Lalium Patruum meum qui jam diu mortuus est; vel potius, præter quædam Paucula ab Ipso conscripta, & multa annotata, nullum prorsus Magistrum Me habere contigit. Sed fortasse Magistros appellas Eos, qui & Alios, ut Tibi videtur, & me docere possint. Ego ut ingenue fatear, in iis quæ in Responsione illa Mihi tractare necesse fuit, ne unum quidem hactenus novi ejusmodi Magistrum tametsi multa adhuc in iisdem Rebus Me doceri posse, plane persuasum habeam. Utinam unum aliquem invenerem. Tu si Eum Te reperisse existimas, indicato tantum, & Me Judicium tuum magnifacere statim videbis, & quin docear, prorsus non recusare; Epist. ad Squarc: P. 362. col: 1. Tom:
units.tr: §. 21. Thirdly, there was another thing, attached to this feigned modesty and humility, by which Socinus prevailed with many. Namely, he seemed not only to set up his own judgment as the arbiter of each doctrine he proposed, but also to have thrown open a wide window to every innovator, so that each could coin whatever seemed good to him from his own wit and publish it at his own discretion. Indeed, just as it is natural for us to be unwilling to be bound to the judgment and opinion of others (which we regard as a kind of servitude and a sign of weak reason), but rather to take on the role of judges ourselves whenever something foreign is put before us to examine, so that we may approve or condemn it at our pleasure, so scarcely anything is more agreeable to our nature than the desire for curiosity and the lust for innovation. The more gifted especially tend to be restless and nimble, so that they neither know where to plant their feet nor wish to. Any fixed and settled seat, especially one assigned to them by someone else, they regard as a prison; and they think that swearing to the words and laws of any others is a kind of captivity that is by no means to be endured. So they are for the most part nomads, who have no fixed home anywhere and do not live constantly under anyone's rule, but wander hither and thither at will. Therefore Socinus, favouring this epidemic disease, which he well knew had spread far and wide and seized most people, readily granted to others the same licence he had claimed for himself. Nor is it surprising that Socinus attracted many disciples to himself and his sect, charmed by this most welcome bait. For it is very easy for anyone who wishes to come to him, and to be drawn where nature leads; and in this he seems to have indulged the lust of the human mind no less perniciously than Epicurus once indulged the lust of the flesh. And what of the fact that he also favoured and made pleasing to people that pride and sloth to which the human race is more prone? For what is more proud than to wish to be subject to no one, or to be bound by the opinion of any other person in matters of religion; or rather, to coin new principles of faith from one's own wit, and to constitute oneself the judge, deciding at one's pleasure whether the doctrines hitherto received by the Church are to be admitted or rejected? What again gratifies sloth more than, having entirely neglected the reading of the ancients (in whose writings he who desires to find that truth must diligently labour, a truth which today, amid so many polemical theologians and manifold sects, we have almost lost), to consult only oneself, trust one's own wit in discerning Christian doctrine, and pass judgment on each article? What Socinus himself did in this matter he testifies quite plainly in his letter to Squarcialupus. Since Squarcialupus was an intimate friend of Socinus, he reproached him, out of the right of friendship, about a certain book Socinus had written against Jacob Palaeologus, a Greek famous for his reputation and learning. Socinus gave him this reply, although no friend had been called in to counsel him, who could well and most readily have guided him by their judgment and given their censure of that book. As for your addition that I ought to put nothing forth unless it has been well and often sifted and examined by the free judgment of the masters, I do not quite understand who these masters are. For in those matters which are discussed in that answer of mine (namely, to Palaeologus on the magistracy) I acknowledge no master among those now living, but I have had God alone as teacher, and the sacred letters. Moreover, in the whole science of divine things, whatever it may be in me, I have had no master at all, except my uncle Lalius, who has been dead a long time; or rather, except a few small things written by him and many notes. But perhaps you call masters those who can teach both others, as it seems to you, and me. To be frank, in those matters which I had to treat in that answer I have not yet known a single such master, although I am thoroughly persuaded that I could still be taught much in those same matters. Would that I might find one. If you think you have found him, only point him out, and you will soon see how highly I value your judgment, and that I by no means refuse to be taught. Epist. ad Squarc: P. 362. col: 1. Tom:

units.la: 1. Quibus in verbis ut summam Arrogantiam ostendit, (licet aliquantulum Modestiæ in Clausula, simulet) ita fiduciam [?] quoque summam ponit in suo solius Ingenio; adeoque palam testatur, se Veteris Ecclesiæ Monumenta haud consuluisse, in novo suæ Theologiæ Systemate conficiendo; sed ex proprio Cerebro deprompsisse quodcunque Sibi placuit, illudque sub nomine Veritatis divinæ Omnibus expoluisse. Equidem Deum Præceptorem in speciem agnoscit, at Seipsum solummodo constituit divinæ legis Interpretem. Vetustiorem autem Eruditionem prorsus ignoravit, quæ Eum instrueret ac dirige et in S. Scriptura rite interpretanda; quippe quæ nec opus se habere putavit, nec in Ea se exercere voluit, propter ingratum legendi Tædium, & Patrum sententias inter se conferendi laborem. Maluit itaque vir aulicus, & Theologiæ studiis paulo serius se dans Itinere isto prolixo ac molesto, per remota, obscura, ac salebrosa Antiquitatis Monumenta, praetermisso, Domi se continere, suum Ipsius Ingenium confulere, & intra microcosmi sui Confinia otiose spatiari. Taedii fuga partim, partim Philautia, atque Superbia, & inanis Gloriæ Aucupium una suaserunt: tum ne Veterum Scripta perlegeret, tum ut Novitates suas Scripto propalaret. Maluit, cum multis Aliis Doctor esse, quam Discipulus; & novam Sectam ducere, quam in veteris Ecclesiæ agmine inter novissimos procedere.
units.tr: 1. In these words, as he shows great arrogance (although he pretends some modesty in the closing clause), he likewise places the highest confidence in his own wit alone. He thus openly testifies that in constructing the new system of his theology he did not consult the monuments of the ancient Church, but drew from his own brain whatever pleased him and presented it to everyone under the name of divine truth. Indeed, he acknowledges God as teacher in appearance, but he has made himself alone the interpreter of the divine law. He was utterly ignorant of older learning, which might have instructed and guided him in the proper interpretation of Holy Scripture; for he thought it unnecessary, nor did he wish to exercise himself in it, on account of the unpleasant tedium of reading and the labour of comparing the opinions of the Fathers with one another. So this courtier, who turned to theological studies rather late, preferred to pass by that long and troublesome journey through the remote, obscure and rough monuments of antiquity, to stay at home, consult his own wit, and stroll idly within the confines of his own microcosm. Partly flight from tedium, partly self-love, pride and the hunt for empty glory together persuaded him, both not to read through the writings of the ancients and to publish his novelties in print. He preferred, along with many others, to be a teacher rather than a disciple, and to lead a new sect rather than to march among the last in the column of the ancient Church.

units.la: §. 23. Quantum vero nativis Ingenii sui Dotibus sidebat in Rebus Theologicis, & quam parum instructus accesserit ad scribendum, si Artium & Disciplinæ Scholasticæ Adjumenta spectemus, ab Ipso audiamus in Epistola ad Virum excell: N. N. non longe ante mortem conscripta, Quid exquisiti Iudicii, ait, in ejusmodi Philosophicis, & Theologicis, iisque difficillimis Disputationibus expectari à Me poterit, Homine, qui nec Philosophiam unquam didicit, nec scholasticam, quam vocant, Theologiam unquam attigit, & ipsius Logicæ Artis nihil nisi Rudimenta quædam, idque valde sero degustavit. Nolo enim Te ignorare plerasque Disputationes meas, quarum quædam non sunt editæ, scriptas à me fuisse, cum nondum Dialecticæ Arti ullam operam dedissem. Cujusmodi sunt, ista disputatio de Servatore; adversus Puccium, Palæologum, & Francisci Davidis, de Baptismo aquæ, de loco 7ma [?] Cap. ad Romanos, de Authoritate S. Scripturæ, Responsio ad paranesin Volani, Animadversiones in Thesès, de Trino & uno Deo, Collegii Posnaniensis & alia quaedam imperfecta; ut posthac non mireris, si in meis Scriptis multa deprehenderis. minus rectè tradita & conclusa. Sed inquies, cur igitur eas scripsisti, cum tam male instructus ad eas scribendas esses? Nimirum, quia vel Iussu eorum, quibus parendum mihi erat, vel Adversariorum Provocatione, sui ad id faciendum compulsus. pag. 490. Col. 1. Tom. 1. Ubi, ut Causas scribendi affeit[?] minime justas & idoneas (satis enim constat, quosdam libros à se editos, nec Amicorum Iussu, nec Adversariorum Provocatione, sed sponte sua, & Amicis renitentibus) ita clare demonstrat, tum, quam imperitus fuerit, & expers Artium istarum, quæ ad Theologiam perdiscendam apprime conducunt; tum, quantum nativis ingenii sui viribus niteretur. Quod & Eques Polonus, qui vitam ejus conscripsit rectè observat quando narrat, quomodo Socinus impressionem variorum Hostium, à quibus satis acerbe ac diu Repulsam passus est, suo sibi ingenio senserit[?] propulsandam; cum primum sc. venerit in Poloniam.
units.tr: §. 23. How far he trusted in the natural gifts of his own wit in theological matters, and how poorly equipped he came to writing if we consider the aids of the arts and scholastic learning, let us hear from himself in a letter to the most excellent N. N., written not long before his death: What refined judgment, he says, can be expected from me in such philosophical and theological, and most difficult, disputations? I am a man who never learned philosophy, never touched what is called scholastic theology, and have tasted only some rudiments of the art of logic itself, and that very late. For I do not want you to be unaware that most of my disputations, some of which have not been published, were written by me before I had devoted any effort to the art of dialectic. Such are that disputation on the Saviour against Pucci, Palaeologus, and Francis David, on the baptism of water, on the seventh chapter of Romans, on the authority of Holy Scripture, the response to Volanus's exhortation, the animadversions on the Theses concerning the Triune and one God, the College of Posen, and certain other imperfect things; so that hereafter you should not be surprised if you find much in my writings less rightly handed down and concluded. But you will say, why then did you write them, since you were so poorly instructed for writing them? Clearly because I was compelled to do so, either by the command of those to whom I had to obey, or by the challenge of adversaries. p. 490, col. 1, Tom. 1. Here, while he states reasons for writing that are by no means just or fitting (for it is quite clear that he published some books on his own accord, not at the command of friends or the challenge of adversaries, but against the wishes of his friends), he clearly shows both how unskilled he was and how destitute of those arts which are most useful for learning theology, and how far he relied on the strength of his natural wit. The Polish knight who wrote his life also rightly observes this, when he relates how Socinus, as soon as he came to Poland, perceived that he must repel by his own wit the attacks of various enemies, by whom he had suffered rather bitter and long-lasting rebuff.

units.la: §. 24. Attamen in hoc saltem speciem æquitatis præ se tulit, quod eandem sententiandi, judicandique libertatem, quam sibi vendicavit, cæteris omnibus indulserit. Sic enim in tractatu suo de Ecclesia, unumquemque ipsius judicio dirigendum reliquit, sive in sensu S. Scripturæ eruendo, sive Censuram ferendo de Aliorum Doctrina; quia sic tuto inniti non possumus Aliorum quorumvis judicio, sive hodie viventium sive veterum Ecclesiæ Doctorum. -- Non ausendendum est[?], ait, quid Homines docuerint, sentiantve, vel antehac docuerint aut senserint, quicunque illi tandem, aut quotcunque sint aut fuerint. pag. 344. Tom.
units.tr: §. 24. Yet in this at least he showed a semblance of fairness: he granted to everyone else the same freedom of thinking and judging that he claimed for himself. In his treatise on the Church he left each person to be guided by his own judgement, whether in drawing out the sense of Holy Scripture or in passing censure on the teaching of others, because we cannot safely rest on the judgement of any others, whether living today or of the ancient teachers of the Church. It is not to be listened to, he says, what men have taught or think, or have taught or thought before, whoever they are and however many they have been or are. p. 344, Tom.

units.la: 1. Idem, Epist. 3. ad Andr. Dudithium. -- Quod quæris, quis Controversiarum in rebus sacris aboriendarum[?], Judex sit futurus? Ego vero respondeo, extra vos Ipsos Alio nobis Judice opus non esse, quam Deo & Christo, qui sua Sententia beabit, quotquot Nostrum imbuti deprehendentur Doctrina ad salutem consequendum necessaria, si modo eam vita expresserimus; Cateros vero Illa destitutos condemnabit, tanquam eos, qui, quod non eadem par erat, Probitate ißent praediti, ipsi in Causa fuerint: Aliud Judicium expectandum non est. Sibi quoque advigilare par est, Idque pro vero admittere ac spondere (licet universus Terrarum orbis in Alia omnia iret) quod Ipsemet totus ad Dei obsequium conversus, de genuino S. literarum sensu arbitratur & intelligit. pag. 502 Col. 1. Tom. 1. Paulo antea vero asseverat, Scientiam Promissorum atque Praeceptorum unum esse illud necessarium ad salutem requisitum, obedientia sc. accedente, quae scientiae isti correspondeat. In reliquis, inquit, si quis occurrat error nemo ob illum Caelo excludetur. Unde consequitur, sine jactura Salutis aeternae, credi aliquid in S. literis praeceptum aut vetitum esse, quod revera illic non sit praeceptum aut vetitum. Sic Ille. p. 501, Col. 2. Hanc insanam licentiam, & sibi sumpsit Socinus, & Aliis persuasit. At utrum illud Vincentii Lirinensis serio perpendisset: Religio Christiana est Depositum secundum Apostolum. Depositum, inquit, custodi. Quid autem est Depositum? Quod Tibi creditum est, non quod à Te inventum; quod accepisti, non quod excogitasti; Rem non Ingenii, sed Doctrinae, non Usurpationis privatae, sed publicae Traditionis; Rem ad Te perductam, non à Te prolatam; in qua non Auctor debes esse, sed Custos; non Institutor, sed Sectator; non Ducens, sed Sequens. Haec ille, Cap. 29. Quae si Socinus, ejusque Socii ac Discipuli, ut oportuit, & legissent & serio considerassent, nunquam aurei [?] hujus Depositi loco, quod ab Apostolis Ecclesia Christi receperat, & Filiis suis per unumquodque Saeculum in manus tradidit: at, Æs virorum, numerosque reprobos Dei effigie fraudulenter insculptos, nobis ausi fuissent obtrudere.
units.tr: 1. The same, Epistle 3 to Andreas Dudith. As to your question, who will be the judge of controversies that arise in sacred matters? I answer that, apart from yourselves, we need no other judge than God and Christ, who will approve those of our people who are found imbued with the teaching necessary for obtaining salvation, provided we have expressed it in our lives; and who will condemn the rest, who lack it, as those who, since they were not endowed with the same uprightness, were themselves at fault in the matter. No other judgement is to be expected. It is also right to keep watch over oneself, and to admit and affirm as true (even if the whole world went in another direction) whatever one, wholly turned to the obedience of God, judges and understands to be the genuine sense of the sacred letters. p. 502, col. 1, Tom. 1. A little earlier, however, he asserts that knowledge of the promises and precepts is the one thing necessary for salvation, together with the obedience that corresponds to that knowledge. In other matters, he says, if any error occurs, no one will be excluded from heaven on account of it. Hence it follows that, without loss of eternal salvation, something may be believed to be commanded or forbidden in the Scriptures which in fact is neither commanded nor forbidden there. Thus he, p. 501, col. 2. This mad licence Socinus assumed for himself and persuaded others of. But did he seriously weigh that saying of Vincent of Lerins: The Christian religion is a deposit, according to the Apostle. Guard the deposit, he says. But what is the deposit? What has been entrusted to you, not what you have discovered; what you have received, not what you have devised; a matter not of wit but of teaching, not of private usurpation but of public tradition; a thing brought to you, not put forward by you; in which you ought to be not the author but the guardian; not the founder but the follower; not the leader but the one who follows. Thus he, chapter 29. If Socinus and his associates and disciples had, as they ought, both read and seriously considered these things, they would never have dared to foist upon us, in place of this golden deposit which the Church of Christ received from the Apostles and handed down to her sons from hand to hand through every age, bronze coins of men, and reprobate coins fraudulently stamped with the image of God.

units.la: §. 25. Quarto, Neque hic substitit Socinus. At sicui unumquemque & suae, & Alterius cujuscunque Doctrinae Judicem constituit; inque hoc superbiae simul innatae, & Ignaviae Generis humani favit; ita quoque ejusmodi Dogmata proponere studuit, quae & sibimetipsi & inter se, quamplurimos conciliarent. Etenim Ecclesiae occidentis, per multos jam Annos, sub tyrannico Ecclesiae Romanae jugo laboraverant, quae sua Dictata, pro totidem indubitatae Fidei Articulis, caeteris omnibus imposuisset. E contra, Socinus omnia fere vituperabat, & erroris arguebat, quaecunque Ecclesia Romana tenuit, & in usu habuit; quasi illa Religionem pristinam non solum corrupisset, sed & in universum perdidisset. Porro, haud mirum est, Hoc valde gratum fuisse quamplurimis qui ex illius Tyrannidis odio, & superstitionis horrore, quas gravissime detestabantur, in adversam Partem plus juito[?] propensiores erant. Difficillimum enim est iis, qui extremitatem invisam fugere nituntur, ita moderari sibimetipsis, Cursumque à se institutum regere, ut in medio Gradum sistant. Hinc factum est, ut Complures, quicquid Ecclesiae Romanae Fidei, Politiae, Cultui, & Consuetudinibus ab ea receptis, contrarium fuit, pro vero & Bono parati essent accipere. Praesertim, cum ubique fere, & ex ore omnium suorum Doctorum audirent, Papam Romanum esse illum Anti-Christum, ab Apostolo Paulo praedictum, qui in Templo Dei sessurus esset; & Ecclesiam ei subditam, esse illam meretricem Babylonicam, Joanni Apostolo in Visione praemonstratam. Unde hanc veri, falsique Regulam praeparatiores erant admittere, quandocunque sibi proponeretur, nempe; Quicquid Ecclesia Romana tenet, & in usu habet, non potest non esse falsum & improbandum, ergo, Quicquid ei ex adverso repugnat, pro vero, Bonoque habendum est. Neutiquam vero mirandum est, si Homines, quos hoc modo paratos ac dispositos invenit, Socinus ad se allexerit, suorumque Dogmatum Fautores essecerit, quæ in singulis fere Capitibus, è diametro oppositæ sunt Ecclesiæ Romanæ Dictatis, etiā ubi antiquam fidem, praximque retinuit. Hinc aliquis non inepte Ecclesiam Romanam sub magnifici cujusdam Templi forma depinxit, cujus Tectum Lutherus, Sociisque ejus submoverunt; parietes autem, Calvinus, & illius coadjutores demoliti sunt; Anti-Trinitarii vero, quales erant Socinus, & ejusdem farinæ Sectarii, eam ab ipsis fundamentis, rutris suis, ligonibusque adhibitis, atque id genus Ferramentis, penitus diruerunt.
units.tr: §. 25. Fourthly, Socinus did not stop here either. He made each person the judge of his own doctrine and that of anyone else, and in this he indulged both the pride innate in us and the sloth of the human race. He also strove to propose such dogmas as would win over very many, both to himself and to one another. For the churches of the West had for many years laboured under the tyrannical yoke of the Roman Church, which had imposed its own dictates on everyone else as so many articles of indubitable faith. Socinus, on the contrary, disparaged almost everything the Roman Church held and practised and charged it with error, as if she had not only corrupted the ancient religion but utterly destroyed it. Moreover, it is no wonder this was very welcome to many who, out of hatred of that tyranny and horror of the superstition, which they detested most heartily, were more inclined than was right to the opposite side. For it is very hard for those who strive to flee a hated extreme to moderate themselves in such a way, and to steer the course they have set, that they stop at the middle ground. Hence it came about that many were ready to accept as true and good whatever was contrary to the faith, polity, worship and customs received from the Roman Church. Especially since they heard almost everywhere, and from the mouths of all their teachers, that the Roman Pope is that Antichrist foretold by the Apostle Paul, who would sit in the temple of God, and that the Church subject to him is that Babylonian harlot shown beforehand to the Apostle John in vision. Hence they were more ready to admit this rule of truth and falsehood whenever it was put before them: whatever the Roman Church holds and practises cannot but be false and to be rejected; therefore whatever opposes it must be held as true and good. It is by no means surprising that Socinus drew to himself men whom he found so prepared and disposed, and made them supporters of his own doctrines, which in almost every chapter are diametrically opposed to the Roman dictates, even where he retained the ancient faith and practice. Hence someone not inaptly pictured the Roman Church as a magnificent temple, whose roof Luther and his fellows removed, whose walls Calvin and his helpers pulled down; but the Anti-Trinitarians, such as Socinus and sectaries of the same kind, utterly overthrew it from its very foundations, with their spades, mattocks and tools of that sort.

units.la: §.26. Et certe multo facilius est Homines in eandem sententiam adducere, et sibi mutuo coadunare, in negativis, quam in positivis Dogmatibus. Nam vel odium, vel metus Hostis publici, eos frequenter in unum cogit, & vires Illorum invicem sociat, qui sese mutuo oppugnare parati sunt, quoties propria Res agitur, aut unus Aliquis Fæderatorum leges Cæteris præscribere conatur. Ita Græciæ urbes, Gentesque variæ, contra Xerxem; Cretenses item, contra quemvis Hostem externum, inter se fæderabantur (unde Adagium, Syncretismus) qui tamen, Hoste communi sublato, sese mutuo quam acerrime impetere solebant. Veteres pariter Hæretici, sat bene inter se convenerunt in oppugnanda Ecclesia Catholica. At quoties Aliqui ex eis dogmatiza[?]e cæperunt, propriosque Fidei Articulos condere, quibus cæteri constringerentur, illico in Partes abiere. Sic enim contigit Arianis, imperante Constantio, cum maxime dominarentur, & Catholicos gravissime premerent.
units.tr: §. 26. And certainly it is much easier to bring men into the same opinion and join them together in negative doctrines than in positive ones. For either hatred or fear of a public enemy often gathers them into one and unites the strength of those who are ready to attack one another whenever their own affairs are at stake, or whenever one of the confederates tries to prescribe laws to the rest. So the cities of Greece and various peoples banded together against Xerxes; the Cretans likewise against any foreign enemy (whence the proverb "syncretism"), who nevertheless, once the common enemy was removed, were wont to attack one another most fiercely. Likewise the ancient heretics agreed well enough among themselves in attacking the Catholic Church. But whenever some of them began to dogmatize and frame their own articles of faith, by which the rest were to be bound, they at once broke into parties. So it happened to the Arians under Constantius, when they were most powerful and oppressed the Catholics most severely.

units.la: §. 27 Cæterum[?] Paucissima fuerunt, quæ Socinus vel credenda, vel obseruanda Suis præscripsit; neque Alia fere quam quæ, si recepta non forent, Christianismi plane abnegati Recusantes arguerent, eosdemque in numerum infidelium redigerent. Attamen cum Hoc tantum asserere auderet, Christum invocandum esse atque adorandum, Contradictores habuit nec paucos, nec parvi nominis inter Anti-Trinitarios. Adeo facile & expeditum est, Socios Nobis ascisceres[?], in destruendo potius, quam in construendo. Et enim non agre reperiuntur, qui veterem Structuram conjunctis studiis, Conatibusque impetant, & frustulatim convellant, eo quod Ille hoc, Iste aliud in ea mendosum[?], & inconcinne dispositum, aut cernat, aut se cernere putet.
units.tr: §. 27. Moreover, Socinus prescribed very few things for his followers to believe or observe, and hardly any except those which, if they were not received, would convict those who refused them of having wholly renounced Christianity and would reduce them to the number of unbelievers. Yet when he dared to assert only this, that Christ is to be invoked and adored, he had opponents, and not few or of no great name, among the Anti-Trinitarians. So easy and expeditious is it to gain companions for us in destroying rather than in building. For there are not hard to find people who, with united zeal and effort, attack the old structure and tear it down piece by piece, because one sees, or thinks he sees, that this flaw is in it, and another that one, and that it is badly and unevenly arranged.

units.la: At quam primum novum Ædificium, Veteris jam diruti loco construi cæperit, tunc statim videre est, quot Capita, tot sententias ædificatorum. Tunc inter se divisi cernuntur. Tunc inter eos convenire nequit vel de Materia vel de Magnitudine, vel de Forma Ædificii construendi ejusque Partium variarum. Singuli item in sua Sententia pertinacius hærent, neque aut ab ea se divelli patiuntur, aut alienæ cedere. Pro diversitate Imaginationum & Affectuum diversa sentiunt. Consule item loquuntur instar Ædificatorum Babelis, adeoque cessat Opus, Operariis à se discedentibus, aut se mutuo impugnantibus.
units.tr: But as soon as the new building begins to be erected in place of the old one now demolished, one sees at once how many builders, so many opinions. Then they are seen to be divided among themselves. Then they cannot agree either about the material, or the size, or the form of the building to be constructed and its various parts. Each also clings more stubbornly to his own opinion and suffers himself neither to be torn away from it nor to yield to another's. According to the diversity of their imaginations and emotions they think differently. They speak in confusion, like the builders of Babel, and so the work stops, the workmen departing from one another or attacking one another.

units.la: § .28 Socinus quidem palam professus est, se Papismum velle destruere, & ex Ecclesia Christi radicitus extirpare; sed adeo temere, & imperite Opus hoc agg essus est ut omne fere Triticum una cum zizaniis, infælici Opera eradicaverit. Cum enim Tyrannidem Papalem tollere vellet, eadem Opera Hierarchiam Ecclesiasticam è medio sustulit. Non aliter missæ Sacrificium propitiatorium, & Transubstantiationem destruere voluit, quam omnem Eucharistiæ necessitatem, & efficaciam penitus tollendo, & qualemcunque Christi præsentiam in Eadem Purgatorium item & Sanctorum Invocationem, quam optime aboleri putavit, negando vitam omnem, sensumque Animarum humanarum in statu Separationis, & definiendo Psychopannychiam. Ita Medici imperiti, & immites non aliter morbos è Corpore humano tollere solent, quam simul evacuando succos, humoresque salutares, Spi-tusque vitales penitus exhauriendo.
units.tr: Socinus indeed openly professed that he wanted to destroy Popery and root it out from the Church of Christ. But he undertook this work so rashly and unskilfully that, in his unhappy labour, he uprooted almost all the wheat along with the tares. When he wanted to remove the Papal tyranny, he at the same time removed the ecclesiastical hierarchy. Likewise, he wanted to destroy the propitiatory sacrifice of the Mass and transubstantiation, by abolishing entirely all necessity and efficacy of the Eucharist, and whatever presence of Christ there is in it. He also thought that purgatory and the invocation of the saints could best be abolished, by denying all life and sensation of human souls in the state of separation, and by defining psychopannychy. Thus unskilled and cruel doctors do not usually remove diseases from the human body except by draining away the wholesome juices and humours too, and by exhausting the vital spirits completely.

units.la: §. 29. Equidem Socinus Ejusque socii ( si modo Ipsis Fides adhibenda sit ) hoc pacto reconciliare studuerunt, non modo Christianos inter dissentientes, (Controversiis omnibus, cum materia sua, abscissis & Dogmatibus Fidei ad Paucissima redactis) sed Mahometanos quoque, & Judaos Gentilesque Idololatras, qui omnes à Trinitatis Dogmate, aliisque Pluribus, quæ Sociniani e medio sublata volunt, quam maxime abhorruerunt. His ergo scandalis, ut Ipsis appellare visum est, amotis, & Pariete intergerrino[?] plane diruto, viam bene paratam existimarunt, qua Infideles in Caulam Ecclesiæ introirent. Sed quo successu hoc tentarunt? Isti Infideles non sunt conversi, at hi boni Reconciliatores facti sunt Apostatæ. Siquidem haud ignotum est, quamplures ex Anti-Trinitariorum Schola prodiisse[?], qui partim in Judaismum, partim in Mahometanismum, partim in Epicureismum & Libertinismum, & partim in apertum Atheismum prolapsi sunt. Hæc enim neque semel, neque ab uno solo socino olim objecta sunt; quæ nec diffiteri aulus est, etsi excusationes quasdam afferre conetur, at minime justas & idoneas. Inter opera Socini recensentur 30 Scrupuli ab excellenti quodam viro propositi, et Ipsius solutiones singulis appositæ. Quorum decimus tertius objicit Socini Sociis atq; discipulis. Quod eorum plerique nulla Pietatis commendatione, nullo laudato prioris vitæ exemplo commendati fuerint. Imo, inquit, ut plerumque videmus, hæc Doctrina de Christo, per vagabundos, & contentionum zeli carnalis plenos Homines, Alios, ex lustris, Aulis, Ganeis, prolata est. Scrupulus 18us objicit iisdem. Quod cum præfervidus ipsorum zelus deferbuit, in propagandâ Regno Christi, ut ipsi pra se ferebant, in quendam Atheismum prolapsi fuerint, ita ut Alii aperte Christum, alii vero etiam Deum, & Inferos negent. Cui Socinus nihil habet quod reponat, nisi illud Joannis. 1. Epist. 2. 19. ex nobis prodierunt sed non erant ex Nobis. Idem, solut: scrupuli 27mi, fatetur Judaizantes, qui partim ex se prodierunt, multum impedivisse suæ Doctrinæ progressum. Neque audet aliquid pro certo affirmare de Pietatis Incremento, vel Decremento, inter suæ sectæ Professores, Decrementum potius fateri cogitur; cujus ignominiam ex hoc elevare conatur --Quod hoc perpetuum sit in omni Religionis mutatione, quantumvis bona, ut major sit ab initio Hominum Pietas, quam postea. Hæc Ille, Tom. 1. pag. 327. Idem ad Synodum Wægroviensem scribens, in qua suæ ipsius Sectæ Homines convenerant, sic eos compellat --Visum est mihi vos hortari, ut de Adoratione & Invocatione Christi in Ecclesiis nostris conservanda, imprimis laboretis. Hæc enim retenta, perfacile omnes Judaici errores, convelluntur, ea vero vel abjecta, vel spreta, nulla ratione fieri potest, ne ubique Judaismus vigeat, vel potius turpis Epicureismus, atque Atheismus. —Quod fi unquam Temporum & Personarum ratio tulit, ut id fieret (viz. ut in publicis Precibus, statutis quibusdam Diebus, Christus Jesus Dei Filius nominatim invocaretur) nunc maxime inter nos fert, cum & nos tanquam Jesu Christi contemptores, pessime apud Alios Christiani nominis Homines audiamus; & eorum, qui Christi nomen profitentes, ipsum tamen nec adorant, nec adorandum censent; & nihilominus, quia Trinitatis opinionem abjecerunt, ex noftro Catu[?] esse existimantur: aliquis omnino fit numerus.
units.tr: §. 29. Indeed Socinus and his associates (if their word is to be trusted) strove to reconcile in this way not only Christians who disagreed among themselves (all controversies being cut away along with their subject matter, and the articles of faith reduced to very few), but also Mohammedans, Jews and Gentile idolaters, all of whom shrank with the greatest abhorrence from the dogma of the Trinity and the many other things which the Socinians want removed.
