Having therefore removed these stumbling-blocks, as they chose to call them, and having utterly thrown down the dividing wall, they thought they had prepared a well-made way by which unbelievers might enter the fold of the Church. But with what success did they attempt this? Those unbelievers were not converted, but these good reconcilers became apostates. For it is well known that many have come out of the school of the Anti-Trinitarians, and some of them have fallen partly into Judaism, partly into Mohammedanism, partly into Epicureanism and libertinism, and partly into open atheism. These charges have been made not once, nor by one man alone, and Socinus has not dared to deny them, although he tries to offer some excuses, which are very far from just and adequate. Among the works of Socinus are listed thirty scruples proposed by a certain excellent man, with Socinus's solutions appended to each. The thirteenth of these objects to Socinus's associates and disciples: "That most of them were recommended by no commendation of piety, by no praised example of former life. Indeed, as we very often see, this doctrine about Christ has been put forward by vagabonds and men full of contentious carnal zeal, and others from brothels, courts and taverns." The eighteenth scruple objects to the same people: "That when their fervent zeal cooled in propagating the kingdom of Christ, as they themselves professed, they fell into a certain atheism, so that some openly deny Christ, and others even God and the lower world." To this Socinus has nothing to reply except that saying of John, "They went out from us, but they were not of us," 1 John 2. 19. The same man, in his solution to the twenty-seventh scruple, admits that the Judaizers, who partly came out from among themselves, greatly hindered the progress of his doctrine. Nor does he dare to affirm anything for certain about an increase or decrease of piety among the professors of his sect; he is rather forced to admit a decrease, and tries to lift the shame of it by saying: "That this is perpetual in every change of religion, however good, so that the piety of men is greater at the beginning than afterwards." So he writes, vol. 1, p. 327. The same man, writing to the Synod of Wągrowiec, in which men of his own sect had gathered, addresses them thus: "It seemed to me right to exhort you to labour above all to keep the adoration and invocation of Christ in our churches. For if this is retained, all Jewish errors are easily uprooted; but if it is cast off or despised, it can in no way be prevented that Judaism, or rather foul Epicureanism and atheism, should flourish everywhere. But if ever the reason of the times and of persons required that this should be done (namely, that in public prayers on certain set days Jesus Christ, the Son of God, should be invoked by name), now most of all it bears upon us, since we are heard by others, among men of the Christian name, as despisers of Jesus Christ, and very badly so; and of those who profess the name of Christ, yet neither adore him nor think him to be adored; and nevertheless, because they have cast off the opinion of the Trinity, they are thought to be of our sect: some number of this kind must certainly exist."

units.la: §.30. Ex Horum numero erat Franciscus Davidis, qui Socini Principiis insistens, affirmantis Chriftū esse nudumHominem, eum censuit nec adorandum, nec invocandum esse, & ad hoc probandum, inter Alia, Argumentum affert ex Mahometis Alcorano. Sic enim arguit: Ut non perperam in Alcorano fingitur, Christum suis Cultoribus opem ferre non posse, quia contra ejus Doctrinam & manifestas Assertiones ipsum Deum esse fassi sint, cum tamen Ipse fe Dei Filium esse professus fit; ita merito reprehenduntur, qui Christum adorandum & invocandum esse docent, cum Ipse Patrem invocandum esse praeceperit.vid.op. Socini, Tom. 2. p. 751. Col. 2. ex quo liquet, unde ille ejusque similes, blasphemias suas hauferint contra Jesum Christum, nempe, ex Alcorano, librisque Talmudicis; quod Socinus ibidem ei regerit; At interim fateri non vult, suam ipsius Doctrinam, de Jesu Christo nudo Homine hisce Blasphemiis, non solum occasionem idoneam, sed & justam nimis Causam praebuisse. Veruntamen idem Socinus in Difput: cum Christiano Franken, (quae extat Op. Tom. 2. pag. 767.) qui iisdem Principiis insistens, eadem docuit cum Francisco Davidis, arguit eos qui Christum ado andum esse negabant, lapsus in Atheismum; quod se observasse dicit quamplurimis evenisse; ideoque monet eundem Franken, ne cum iis pariter in Atheismum labatur. Eques item ille Polonus, qui Socini vitam conscripsit, meminit insignis cujusdam contra Atheos laboris, quem refellendis ingeniosis magni cujusdam viri commentis susceperat; eum vero periisse dicit, cum aliis Socini Scriptis, in Tumultu Cracoviensi, cujus antea meminimus. Apparet quoque ex ejusdem operibus, quamplures vel denegasse, vel saltem in dubium vocasse Authoritatem S. Canonis; & Martinum quendam Seidelium, Olaviensem Silesium negasse Jesum esse Messiam illum promissum, Davidis Filium, & in Regno successorem, quia non accepit Regnum mundanum. Hic item dicitur, tres Epistolas misisse de hoc Argumento ad Coetum Cracoviensem, dictum minorem; qui ex Anti-Trinitariis sine dubio constabat. Socinus enim, illius Coetus nomine, Responsa dedit ad illas tres Epistolas. Vid. Soc. Op. Tom. 2. pag. 804.
units.tr: §.30. Among this number was Francis David, who, following the principles of Socinus and asserting that Christ is a mere man, held that he is neither to be adored nor to be invoked. To prove this, among other arguments, he brings one from Mohammed's Koran. For he argues thus: "Just as it is falsely feigned in the Koran that Christ cannot bring help to his worshippers, because they have confessed him to be God, against his doctrine and plain assertions, although he himself professed to be the Son of God; so those are rightly reproved who teach that Christ is to be adored and invoked, since he himself commanded that the Father be invoked." See the works of Socinus, vol. 2, p. 751, col. 2. From this it is clear where he and men like him drew their blasphemies against Jesus Christ, namely from the Koran and the Talmudic books; and Socinus throws this back at him in the same place. Yet meanwhile he is unwilling to admit that his own doctrine, that Jesus Christ is a mere man, provided not only a suitable occasion but a far too just cause for these blasphemies. Moreover, the same Socinus, in his disputation with the Christian Franken (which is extant in his Works, vol. 2, p. 767), argues against those who had denied that Christ is to be adored. Franken, following the same principles, taught the same things as Francis David, and Socinus argues that such men had fallen into atheism; he says he has observed this to have happened to very many, and therefore warns Franken not to slip into atheism along with them. That Polish knight, too, who wrote the life of Socinus, mentions a certain notable work against the atheists which Socinus had undertaken, to refute the ingenious inventions of a certain great man; but he says it perished along with other writings of Socinus in the Cracow tumult, which we mentioned before. It appears also from his works that many either denied, or at least called into doubt, the authority of the sacred canon; and that a certain Martin Seidel, a Silesian from Oława, denied that Jesus is that promised Messiah, son of David, and successor in the kingdom, because he did not receive a worldly kingdom. He is also said to have sent three letters on this subject to the Cracow congregation, the smaller one, which without doubt consisted of Anti-Trinitarians. For Socinus, in the name of that congregation, gave replies to those three letters. See Socinus, Op. vol. 2, p. 804.

units.la: §. 31. Hi sc. erant genuini fructus istius Reformationis (ut iis vocare libuit) quam AntiTrinitarii, (quorum Socinus tandem Princeps evasit) in Transylvaniam, Poloniam, Silesiam, Hungariam, Partesque vicinas introduxerunt. Hi fructus, sponte enati sunt ex enormi ista licentia, quam & Socinus sibi arrogavit, Aliisque indulsit, in Religionis Dogmatibus de novo cudendis. Hi denique fructus Doctrinæ Socinianæ, ut in aliis Articulis, ita præcipue in iis, ubi asserunt Jesum Christum esse nudum Hominem, & omnimodam Infensationem Animæ humanæ separatæ, cum totali Abositione[?] Impiorum in die Iudicii. Itaque Franc: Puccius non immerito videtur exprobrare Socino, Quod sibi finxerit Pietatem quandam novam, in qua bene sentire facile negligitur, & summa licentia detorquendi S. literas ad libitum, & quidlibet ex quolibet colligendi, usurpatur. Et quod de ejus sanitate omnino desperandum sit, si non moveatur Divinis Oraculis, imo ea depravare non vereatur suis frigidissimis Commentis, unde hortatur eum, Ne amplius resistere veritati & in Divinum numen contumeliosus esse velit - & postea Non me latet, Te etiam negare immortalitatem Animarum, nisi Christianorum in Resurrectione. Confugis ad impium Dogma Epicureorum, qui existimarunt cum corporibus Animas interire, & omnia simul morte deleri.
units.tr: §. 31. These, namely, were the genuine fruits of that Reformation (as they chose to call it) which the Anti-Trinitarians, of whom Socinus at last became the leader, introduced into Transylvania, Poland, Silesia, Hungary, and the neighbouring regions. These fruits sprang up spontaneously from that enormous licence which Socinus claimed for himself and granted to others, of coining new dogmas of religion. These, finally, are the fruits of the Socinian doctrine, as in other articles, so especially in those where they assert that Jesus Christ is a mere man, and teach a total insensibility of the separated human soul, together with the total abolition of the wicked on the day of judgment. Therefore Francis Pucci does not seem unjustly to reproach Socinus, because he has invented for himself a new kind of piety, in which thinking rightly is easily neglected, and the greatest licence of twisting the Holy Scriptures at will and gathering anything from anything is employed. He says that there must be utter despair of Socinus's sanity, unless he is moved by the divine oracles, and indeed does not shrink from corrupting them with his most frigid inventions; whence he urges him: "Not to wish to resist the truth any longer, nor to be insolent against the divine majesty." And afterwards: "It is not hidden from me that you also deny the immortality of souls, except that of Christians at the resurrection. You take refuge in the impious dogma of the Epicureans, who thought that souls perish along with bodies, and that all things are destroyed together at death."

units.la: Dicis tamen eos, quamvis ita sentirem, existimasse tamen se posse jolidus[?] voluptates experiri & ideo summum Bonum in voluptate potuisse. Num igitur existimas Epicureos bene sensisse? Si bene senserunt, quid Nos solliciti de futuris & aeternis summus[?]? Edamus, & Bibamus, cras enim[?] moriemur. Sin pessime, quomodo vis errore eorum Tuum tegere? Def. Fr. Puccii ad Resp. Socinii. Op. Sec.[?] Tom. 2. pag. 264. & 267. (ol.[?] 2.
units.tr: You say, however, that although they thought as I do, the Epicureans still supposed they could enjoy abundant pleasures, and so could place the highest good in pleasure. Do you then think the Epicureans were right? If they were right, why should we be anxious about future and eternal things? "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." But if they were badly wrong, how can you hope to cover your own error with theirs? Fr. Puccius, in reply to Socinus. Opera Socini, vol. 2, pp. 264 and 267.

units.la: §. 32. Quinto. Ad haec, Socini successum, in Dogmatibus suis propagandis, plurimum adjuvit status Provinciarum Polonicarum, quando ipse ad eas primum accessit. Erenim tunc Temporis, miser imo inter se discissi erant in Religionis negotio, Aliis Alios accerrime impetentibus. Poloniam tunc dixeris cum Africa sedes permutasse, Regione ista monstrorum ferace, ubi omne Genus Ferarum generatur, atque alitur; de quibus fertur, quod cum ad Aquas convenerunt bibendi causa, pro Ingenio quaeque suo, & Affectu, cum caeteris, aut Marte aut venere commiscentur ex quo congressu Aliae occidunt, & Aliae nascunturtur. Sic & in Polonia factum est, ubi nulla Opinio tam monstrosa excogitari potuit, quin Prædicatorem nacta fuerit, Aliosque sui Fautores. Hinc autem Dissidia necessario exorta sunt, inter tot Opinionum, Sectarumque Authores simul atque Asseclas, qui non mitius inter se, quam cum Catholicis & Orthodoxis digladiabantur. Diversimodi errores, non minus sibi invicem, quam veritati adversi, Patronos suos, Pugilisque adepti sunt Photiniani, Ariani, Anabaptistæ, Davidiani, Budneistæ, Judaizantes, Anti-Scripturistæ, Libertini, & Atheismi fautores, sua Dogmata impune divulgabant. Anti-Trinitatorium Principes erant, Geo: Blandrata, & Fr. Davidis, Jo. Paulus Alciatus, Matthæus Gribaldus, Petrus Statorius, Franciscus Lismaninus, Gregorius Schomanus, Krovicius, Grego ius Paulus, & Erasmus Joannis Arianus. Geo. Blandrata, & Fr: Davidis, inter primos, libris Latine editis, Doctrinam suam propaga unt, ut Andr: Dudithius testatur in Epistola ad Bezam conscripta. A. C. 1571. Op. Soc. Tom. 1. p. 524. His accedens F. Socinus, primo in Transylvaniam, deinde in Poloniam se contulit. Cum autem illos, Aliosque plures, inter se conflictantes invenerat, & multo validiores in refellendis Adversariorum Dogmatibus, quam in suis ipsorum defendendis, delassatos tandem mutuisque confractos Dimicationibus, & plane nescientes quo se verterent, aut ubi Pedem figerent, ad externum sibi conciliavit, & in sua Castra pellexit, ut sub ipsius vexillo militarent. Sic olim Philippus Macedonum Rex (ut Civilia cum Sacris aliquatenus conferamus) varios Graciæ Populos, urbesque inter se prius diffidentes, diffidiisque suis labefactatas, non ægre subegit. Et Cæsar Augustus, ut Tacitus observat, Romanos civilibus Discordiis fessos[?], nomine Principis sub Imperium accepit. Et (ut exemplum paulo congruentius asseram) sic Mahometes varias Arabiæ Gentes, non minus Religionibus quam Tribubus discrepantes, in unum composuit, suoque Dominio subdidit, tam in sacris, quam in Civilibus, & successores illius, cum Schismata & Hæreses inter Christianos passim invalescerent in oriente, Mahometanismum longe, late-que disseminarunt.
units.tr: §. 32. Fifthly, Socinus's success in spreading his doctrines was greatly helped by the condition of the Polish provinces when he first came among them. At that time they were wretchedly divided among themselves in matters of religion, each side attacking the others most fiercely. You would have said that Poland had exchanged its seat with Africa, that land fertile in monsters, where every kind of wild beast is bred and reared. It is said of those beasts that when they gather at the waters to drink, each one, according to its nature and disposition, mingles with the rest either in war or in love, and from this encounter some die and others are born. So it happened in Poland, where no opinion was so monstrous that it could not find a preacher and others to support it. From this, of necessity, quarrels arose among so many authors and followers of opinions and sects, who fought among themselves no less bitterly than against Catholics and Orthodox. The Photinians, Arians, Anabaptists, Davidians, Budnaeans, Judaizers, Anti-Scripturists, Libertines and promoters of atheism, each with its own errors, no less hostile to one another than to the truth, found their champions and fighters, and spread their doctrines with impunity. The leaders of the anti-Trinitarians were Georgius Blandrata, Franciscus David, Johannes Paulus Alciatus, Matthaeus Gribaldus, Petrus Statorius, Franciscus Lismaninus, Gregorius Schomanus, Krovicius, Gregorius Paulus, and Erasmus Johannis Arianus. Georgius Blandrata and Franciscus David, among the first, spread their doctrine through books published in Latin, as Andreas Dudithius testifies in a letter written to Beza in the year 1571 (Op. Soc. Tom. 1, p. 524). F. Socinus, joining them, first went to Transylvania and then to Poland. But when he found those and many others fighting among themselves, and far stronger in refuting the doctrines of their opponents than in defending their own, and at last worn out and broken by their mutual conflicts, and quite uncertain where to turn or where to plant their feet, he won them over to himself from outside and enticed them into his own camp, so that they might serve under his banner. Thus of old Philip, King of the Macedonians (to compare civil affairs with sacred ones to some degree), without difficulty subdued the various peoples and cities of Greece, which had been at odds with one another and weakened by their own dissensions. And Caesar Augustus, as Tacitus observes, received the Romans, weary of civil discords, under his empire in the name of Prince. And (to assert a rather more fitting example) so Mahomet united the various Arabian peoples, who differed in their religions no less than in their tribes, into one, and subjected them to his dominion, both in sacred and in civil matters; and his successors, when schisms and heresies everywhere grew strong among Christians in the East, spread Mahometanism far and wide.

units.la: §. 33. Sed & Aliud quoque fuit, quod Socinum non parum adjuvit in hoc suo Conatu perficiendo; nempe Doctrinæ suæ Compages, quam ita callide formavit, & in unum composuit, ut nihil omnino novum, & inter Sectarios inauditum, prædicaret, sed quod prius inter eos innotuerat, & ab hac vel illa Secta antea divulgatum esset atque defensum. Ita Partes systematis sui Theologici undique collegit, diversaque Sectariorum sententias in unum quasi volumen compegit, partim hinc, partim illinc deceptas, ut singulis placeret, quorum singulis de suo aliquid proposuit. Hoc & ipse testatur, in Apologetica sua Epistola ad Mart: Vadovitam – Nullum Dogma in meis Scriptis in lucem editis asserui, quod non modo alibi, sed in hoc ipso Regno, ubi ea sunt edita, ab Aliis ante me, & meum hoc Adventum, partim publice, & voce & Scripto assertum; partim jam affirmatum, & discutiendum propositum non fuisse. Et speciatim, quod ad Doctrinam suam contra Christi satisfactionem, affirmat, eam desumptam fuisse e Dialogis Bernardini Ochini, lingua Polonica editis, Annis 35 ante hanc suam Epistolam conscriptam[?]. Hæc autem data est Jun. 14. 1598. Op. Soc. Tom. 1. pag. 475. Sic & in Hoc quoque Mahometem imitatus est, in Alcorano suo consarcinando; in quo reperiuntur aliqui Gentilium Ritus, à Majoribus accepti; non paucæ è Talmude Judæorum Fabulæ, Ritusque ab iisdem traditi; quædam item Christiano um[?] Dogmata & Instituta, partim laudabilia Catholicorum, partim ab Hæreticis mutuo impta[?]. Sic utrique quamplurimis placere studuit, ut e diversis variorum Dogmatum Professoribus quamplurimos Discipulos sibi colligeret. Quod & utrque effecit apud eos, qui in Fide vacillantes, & inter varias Opiniones huc illuc distracti, in illo unam[?] Sententiam tandem concesserunt. Ita Nautæ profugi aut imperiti, in Mari ignoto aberrantes, & huc illuc à quovis vento jactati, potentiori cuivis Piratæ se in manus dedunt. Ita quoque Viatores incerti, qui patrio Solo vertiginose deserto, in Solitudine invia vagantur, cum bene defelli sunt, & de optato Itineris exitu plane desperant, se cuivis viæ Duci, qui se ultro offerit, & speciosa pollicetur, dirigendos permittunt.
units.tr: §. 33. But there was also another thing that helped Socinus not a little in carrying out this undertaking: the structure of his doctrine, which he shaped and put together so cleverly that he proclaimed nothing new at all, nothing unheard of among the sectaries, but what had already become known among them and had been previously spread and defended by this or that sect. Thus he gathered the parts of his theological system from every side and put together the differing opinions of the sectaries into one volume, as it were, borrowed partly from here and partly from there, so that it would please each of them, and he offered each something of his own. He himself testifies to this in his Apologetic letter to Martin Wadowita: I have asserted no doctrine in my published writings which had not been asserted before me, not only elsewhere but in this very kingdom where these writings were published, by others, partly publicly, by voice and by writing, and partly already affirmed and proposed for discussion. And in particular, as to his doctrine against the satisfaction of Christ, he affirms that he took it from the Dialogues of Bernardino Ochino, published in the Polish language, thirty-five years before this letter of his was written. This letter is dated June 14, 1598. Opera Socini, vol. 1, p. 475. So too in this he imitated Mahomet, in patching together his Koran; in which are found some rites of the Gentiles, received from their ancestors; not a few fables from the Talmud of the Jews, and rites handed down by them; and certain doctrines and institutions of the Christians, partly praiseworthy ones of the Catholics, partly ones borrowed from heretics. Thus each of them took pains to please very many, so as to gather very many disciples to himself from the various professors of diverse doctrines. And both succeeded in this among those who, wavering in faith and pulled hither and thither among various opinions, at last yielded to one opinion. So fugitive or inexperienced sailors, wandering in an unknown sea and tossed hither and thither by every wind, surrender themselves to any more powerful pirate. So too uncertain travelers, who, having dizzily abandoned their native soil, wander in a trackless wilderness, when they have been well and truly lost and have quite despaired of reaching their intended destination, allow themselves to be directed by any guide of the road who offers himself freely and promises fine things.

units.la: §. 34. Sexto; Huc adde, quod Socinus in hoc suo Conatu, non solum adjutus fuerit Temporis illius Opportunitate, in quo Factiones ubique glisceba nt[?]; sed & ipsius Regni Polonici Statu atque Politia, in quo latis notum est quanta Authoritate pollent Palatini, & Castellani, cæterique Nobiles, in suo quisque Gradu, qui in Præfecturis suis atque Districtibus, fere sui Juris sunt; ut qui amplissimis Privilegiis fruantur, & propemodum, quicquid volunt, possint. Quid mirum est igitur, si Socinus, Ipse Nobilis, natura item Comis & Affabilis, & super hæc, Artibus aulicis, apprime eruditus, sese in Nobilium Polonorum favorem insinuaverit, quorum Amicitia & Authoritate fretus suam Doctrinam longe, disseminare valuit, & Difcipulos Sibi passim colligere? Præsertim, cum ad hæc externa Adjumenta accesserint istæ Virtutes, aut saltem Species Virtutum, quarum antea memini, Candor &c: & Modestia summa, Mansuetudo, atque Patientia, zelus pro veritate divina, & pla- cidissima Morum urbanitas inter conversandum cum Hominibus; quarum ut specimina præ se tulit in quotidiana Vitæ Consuetudine, sic & in Epistolis suis ad Amicos conscriptis, Eadem ubique demonstrat. Siquidem Hoc pro certissimo Axiomate jamdudum apud Me obtinuit, (utpote quod creb.is experimentis hucusque probatum suit, ac proinde fidem indubiam meretur) Neminem multum Mali posse in Ecclesia Dei, nec in Genere humano seducendo admodum proficere, nisi qui eximium aliquid Boni in se habet, & su- pra Vulgi mores, aut saltem prætendit. Satanas itaque nunquam magis cavendus est, quam cum in Angelum lucis se transfigurat. Tunc enim Pios & Veritatis amantes decipit, si minus attentos, vigilesque deprehenderit. Sic & Ministri Illius studiosissimæ evitandi sunt cum ovinis[?] pellibus induti, simplicitatis & innocentiæ speciem præ se ferunt; intus autem lupinam rabiem fovent, quam opportunitate data, exerere & exercere solent in perniciem Gregis Christiani: Nam minime aut illum, aut Hos latet, Vitium simul atque Falsitatem, si nude proponantur, & prout in se sunt, apparebant, Plerisque horrori fore. Proinde, Fuco, pulchrisque Coloribus ut plurimum delibuta sunt, ut sub mentita[?] Veritatis, Virtutisque specie, incautis placeant & imponant.
units.tr: §. 34. Sixthly; Add to this that Socinus, in this undertaking of his, was helped not only by the opportunity of that time, when factions were flourishing everywhere, but also by the state and constitution of the Polish kingdom itself, in which it is well known how much authority the palatines, the castellans, and the other nobles, each in his own rank, possess; who, in their own districts and jurisdictions, are almost their own masters, since they enjoy very ample privileges and can do almost whatever they wish. What wonder, then, if Socinus, himself a nobleman, by nature also courteous and affable, and besides this, thoroughly trained in courtly arts, insinuated himself into the favor of the Polish nobles, relying on whose friendship and authority he was able to spread his doctrine far and wide and gather disciples to himself everywhere? Especially since to these external aids were added those virtues, or at least the appearance of virtues, which I mentioned before: candor and great modesty, gentleness and patience, zeal for divine truth, and a most pleasant courtesy of manners in dealing with men. As he showed specimens of these in his daily life, so he displays them everywhere in his letters written to friends. For this has long held as a most certain axiom with me (as it has been proved by frequent experience up to now, and therefore deserves undoubted belief): that no one can do much harm in the Church of God, or accomplish much in seducing mankind, unless he has some outstanding good in himself, and rises above the ordinary manners of the crowd, or at least pretends to. Satan therefore is never more to be guarded against than when he transforms himself into an angel of light. For then he deceives the pious and the lovers of truth, if he finds them less attentive and watchful. So too his most zealous ministers are to be avoided: clothed in sheep's skins, they show the appearance of simplicity and innocence, but inwardly they nourish wolfish rage, which, when opportunity is given, they are wont to bring out and exercise to the ruin of the Christian flock. For it is not hidden from either that vice and falsehood, if they are set forth naked and as they are in themselves, would be an object of horror to most people. Therefore they are for the most part smeared with paint and fair colors, so that under the feigned appearance of truth and virtue they may please and deceive the unwary.

units.la: §. 35. Nihilominus Socinus, licet his Artibus & & Opportunitatibus insigniter adjutus, non tamen adeo prævalere potuit in Hæresi sua disseminanda, ut non multos Adversarios invenerit, qui palam atque constanter Illius Conatibus se oppo-suerant, atque impia Dogmata ab eo divulgata conjunctis Suffragiis damnarunt. Extra Regnum Poloniæ, Adversarium nactus est Jacobum Covetum Parisiensem, Ministrum Evangelicum, qui scripsit, contra Theses Ejus de Jesu Christo Servatore, quas Socinus emiserat, cum adhuc Basileæ commoraretur; librumque suum misit ad Socinum ex Francofurto ad Mænum. Cal. Aprilis, 1577. & cum inter 30 Scrupulos, ab excellenti quodam Viro propositos Socino, Hoc inter Alia perplura objicetu, Angliam & Scotiam Illius Dogmata penitus aversari; fatetur Ille quod sic objectum est, sed eum contemptu summo rejicit, inquiens, Quid attinebat Angliæ, Scotiæque Regna hoc loco commemorare, quæ Doctrinam nostrorum Hominum propriam, tanquam pestilentissimam aversantur? Resp: ad Scrup: 24. At intra Regnum Poloniæ, ubi diutius vixit, quamplurima scripsit, Discipulos undique collegit, & in Cætus tandem formavit, multo plures habuit, qui sibi adversarentur; atque Hos, non solum è numero Pontificiorum (quod mirum erat, cum se Illius omnibus ex professo Hostem statuerit) sed & Ecclesiarum Reformatarum Theologis, tum Bohemicæ, tum Augustanæ, tum Helveticæ Confessionis, qui per amplissimum illud Regnum magno numero dispersi erant, & Cætus suos habebant legitime stabilitos. Nam præter Assertiones Collegii Posnaniensis de Trino & uno Deo, quas Gabriel Eutropius illius Collegii Canonicus edidit; Andreas Volanus Minist[?]e: in Lituania, contra cum scripsit, de Christi natura, & Peccatorum per Ipsum expiatione. Gregorius item Zarnovecius, Minister Evangelicus, scripsit contra librum illius de Jesu Christo Servatore, Polonice, ut Socinus ipse memorat in Epistola ad Mart: Vadovitani. Quinimo, & Eques ille Polonus, qui Socini vitam conscripsit, ultro fatetur, quod cum Socinus in Poloniam veniret, & AntiTrinitariis se statim adjunxisset, satis acerbe atque diu Repulsam passus sit, cum Dissensionem in quibusdam Dogmatibus non premeret; quod plerique è Ministris natu majoribus, Niemoievius item & Czechovicius viri maximae Authoritatis apud Polonos, ei refragarentur; denique quod & ipse, & Laelius illius Patruus, cum suo aevo jugiter spreti & inglorii fuerint, & solis odiis Nobiles, ne morituri quidem secundioris Famae auspicium delibaverint.
units.tr: §. 35. Nevertheless Socinus, although he was remarkably aided by these arts and opportunities, could not prevail so far in spreading his heresy that he did not find many opponents who openly and steadily resisted his efforts and condemned, by united votes, the impious doctrines he had published. Outside the Kingdom of Poland he found an opponent in Jacob Covet of Paris, an Evangelical minister, who wrote against his theses concerning Jesus Christ the Saviour, which Socinus had put forth while he was still staying at Basel. Covet sent his book to Socinus from Frankfurt am Main on 1 April 1577. Among the thirty scruples that a certain distinguished man put to Socinus, this was one of many objections: that England and Scotland utterly abhor his doctrines. Socinus admits what was objected, but rejects it with the greatest contempt, saying: "What was the point of mentioning here the kingdoms of England and Scotland, which abhor the doctrine peculiar to our people as most pestilential?" Reply to Scruple 24. But within the Kingdom of Poland, where he lived for a long time, wrote a great deal, gathered disciples from every side and at last formed them into congregations, he had far more who opposed him. These were drawn not only from the Papists (which was no surprise, since he had declared himself their open enemy in everything), but also from the theologians of the Reformed Churches, of the Bohemian, the Augsburg and the Helvetic Confession, who were scattered in large numbers through that very wide kingdom and had their congregations lawfully established. For besides the assertions of the college of Posen concerning the Triune and one God, which Gabriel Eutropius, a canon of that college, published, Andreas Volanus, minister in Lithuania, wrote against him concerning the nature of Christ and the expiation of sins through him. Likewise Gregory Zarnovecius, an Evangelical minister, wrote in Polish against Socinus's book on Jesus Christ the Saviour, as Socinus himself mentions in his letter to Martin of Wadowice. Moreover, that Polish nobleman who wrote the life of Socinus freely admits that when Socinus came to Poland and had at once attached himself to the Antitrinitarians, he suffered a fairly bitter and long rejection, because he did not press his dissent in certain doctrines; that most of the older ministers, and Niemojewski and Czechowicz, men of the greatest authority among the Poles, opposed him; and finally that both he and his uncle Laelius, though they were always despised and inglorious during their lifetime, and were honoured only by the hatred of the nobles, did not even taste the omen of a better fame at their death.

units.la: §.. 36. Sed quod mihi, inter Socini Adversarios, maximi momenti videtur ad Hærefin illius damnandam, quae eadem fuit cum illa Anti-Trinitariorum, quorum secta adhaesit. Hoc est, quod omnes Theologi, virique Principes in Polonia, triplicis Confessionis, modo memoratae, sc: Bohemicae, Augustanae, & Helveticae, tandem in unum convenerint, Synodisque frequentibus coactis, Consensum in Doctrina unanimiter statuerint, triplici Confessione à singulis approbata, omnique contraria Doctrina, sive Pontificiorum, sive Sectariorum, pariter damnata. Præcipue vero se opponunt AntiTrinitariis, quos ut publicos & professos Evangelicae Doctrinae Hostes junctis suffragiis anathematizant, & è sua Communione pellunt. Atque hoc fecerunt partim ante Socini adventum in Poloniam, partim post. In synodo Sendomir: sic, quæ celebrata est. A.D. 1570. Apr. 14. —Postea quam dia, multumque cum Sectariis Tritheitis, Ebionitis, Anabaptistis, conflictatum esset, ac tandem Divino favore ex tot tamisque certaminibus, & deplorandis contentionibus emersimus; visum est iisdem Ecclesiis Polonicis reformatis & Orthodoxis, quæ in quibusdam Capitibus & Formulis Doctrina, Hostibus veritatis & Evangelii minime consentire videbantur, Pacis & Concordiæ studio Synodum convocare, atque Confessionem mutuam restari. Quare habita amica & Christiana collatione sic junctis compositisque animis consensimus in hæc Capita. Primum, triplici Ecclesiarum nostrarum Confessione mutuo ap-probata, sancte invicem pollicisi sumus, unanimiter, se-cundum Regulam verbi Dei, nos defensuros Consensum hunc mutuum in vera & pura Christi Religione, contra Pontificios, contra Sectarios, denique omnes Hostes Evangelii & veritatis. Synodus Generalis Cracoviensis celebrata A.D. 1573. Anti-Trinitarios, sub nomine Arianabaptistarum[?], insuper hac gravissima censura ferit, Actu 4ᵖ[?] cum ex his, inquiunt, aliquot Concionatores, & Auditores, suapte sponte ad Synodum nostram venissent, & de suo Dogmate ibidem differere vellent, Synodus post gravem de iis Deliberationem, denegavit eis colloquium & disputationem, & talem Decretum fecit: Significant Arianabaptistæ, è Nobis egressi, non mirum in Doctrina Christi, ac Fide de vero Deo Patre & Filio, cum Spiritu Sancto, adeoque Deum non habent, & jam à nobis sæpissime Colloquiis ac Scriptis admoniti, pertinaciter in errore manent, nullum jam amplius cum Ipsis Commercium, quamdiu Sententiam suam tuentur, habeamus, nullas Disputationes ipsorum admittamus, sed eos, librosque illorum blasphemos secundum Præceptum Spiritus S. vitemus, ne alias Fundamentum Religionis Christiana (fidem firmissimam de Deo, in cujus nomine sumus baptizati) [?]subinde nos commovere, ac in Dubium vocare videamur; & ne operibus eorum malis, Doctrinis venenatis, atque Blasphemiis, Gloriam Domini oppugnantibus communicemus. Imo, non solum se illorum Doctrinae adversos, sed & ab eorundem ceremoniis alienos ostendunt, ne in minimo cum eis communicent: sic enim decernunt Actu 6°. ejusdem Synodi -- De Ceremoniis, praesertim in usu Coenae Domini, mota quaestione, An ea in omnibus Ecclesiis nostris uniformes esse possent? Conclusum est, ut secundum morem primitivae Ecclesiae, libertati Christi-ana Ceremonia inter nos permittantur. Monitis tamen fratribus, siqui sessione in Sacra Coena utuntur, ut eam Ceremoniam [?]Ariambaptistis propriam relinquant. Atq; iterum in Synodo Petricoviensi Generali A.D. 1578. me-se Junio, idem decernunt -- Ceremonias libertati Christianae donamus ac permittimus, ut Stantes, vel Genua flectentes, Pii Sacramentum Corporis & Sanguinis Christi sumant, sessionis vero ad mensam Domini, quia praeter Ritus in omnibus per Europam Evangelicis Ecclesiis vulgo consuetos, illi inter nos primi Authores extiterunt, qui omnia temere in Ecclesia immutantes, & sine scientia Christum quasi imitantes a nobis ad Arianismum perfidi Transfuga facti sunt; quare hanc propriam Ipsis (ut Christum, ita & Sacra ejus irreverenter tractantibus) & tanquam minus honestam ac religiosam, [?]limplicioribusque admodum scandalosam, Ceremoniam rejicimus. Posthac in Synodo Gen: Wlodislaviensi, A.D. 1583. Jun: 19. cum Socinus jam per 4. Annos in Polonia mansisset, Harmonia trium Istarum Confessionum de novo confirmata est, Actu 4. Prohibitum quoque est, libros aliquos proprio arbitrio publicare, sed eos solos qui a superioribus in Ecclesia examinati fuerint & approbati. Act. 5. Repetitum item Decretum contra sessionem ad mensam Domini, ne in usu sit in ullis sui Consensus Ecclesiis Poloniae, & Lituaniae &c. Nam hac Caeremonia, aiunt, (licet cum caeteris, libera) Ecclesiis Christianis, & caeteris Evangelicis, non usitata, tantumque infidelibus Arianis, cum Domino pari folio sese collocantibus, propria. Cum itaque sessio putissimum occasione, & malo auspicio Illorum, qui miserrime ex nobis exciderunt, & Dominum, qui nos redemit, abnegarunt, in consuetudinem irrepsit aliquot nostris Ecclesiis, rogamus & hortamur omnes istos Coetus, & Fratres nostros in Domino, ut sessionem commutent in Ceremonias nobis in Ecclesiis Evangelicis per Europam consuetas, &c. Act. 6. Denique in Synodo Gen: Torunensi, quae habita est A.D. 1592. Aug. 21. Acta priorum Synodorum Generalium denuo confirmantur, & tres Fidei Confessiones unanimi Consensu approbantur, quarum primaria Capita distincte enumerantur; & praecipue faciunt contra Socinianos ut ex Titulis apparet. Unde concludunt, Se per hunc consensum in Doctrina, & se invicem mutuo conglutinare, & ab omnibus Haereticis, Sectariis, & blasphemis Idololatris, Apostolicam & Orthodoxam Fidem adulterantibus, sejungere. Ibidem etiam actum est de conservanda ac tuenda puritate Doctrinae de Deo, ejus essentia, & Personis propter eos qui a voce Trinitatis abhorrent; & decretum, ut qui ea voce uti nolent tanquam de fide suspecti, ex Coetu Evangelico excluderentur. Decretum autem de hoc consensu in haec verba formatum est --Consensum nostrum Evangelicum Sendomiria[?]. A. D. 1570. institutum, & eodem Anno Consignatione[?] Posnaniensi[?] illustratum, ac postea Generalibus Synodis, Cracoviensi, Petricoviensi, & Wlodislaviensi auctum, stabilitumque, prout ista in Exemplari Torunii, Latine & Polonice A. D. 1592. excuso continentur; universi hac nostra Generali Torunienfi Synodo comprobamus, atque confirmamus, & contra Adversarios, qui tam verbis, quam Scriptis haktenus, Discordiam, & fictum consensum nobis Evangelicis obiectare ausi sunt, hunc verum Consensum sincere nos amplexi & fovere, atque secundum eum in sancta concordia vere conjunctos esse profitemur. Deinde sequitur — Quilibet minister Evangelicus in Regno Poloniae, & magno Ducatu Lituaniae, ac caeteris Provinciis adjunctis, tenebitur hunc consensum (cui hos quoque Synodi Torunienfis Canones incorporamus) non tantum habere & legere, sed etiam ex Praescripto illius, & Canonum in eo expressorum, tum ipse agere, tum Coetum sibi commissum gubernare. Et paulo post —Quicunque in Doctrina Evangelii Dei nobiscum non consentit, & qui Idololatriam aut Haeresin amplectitur; denique qui concordiam nostram dirimit, neque consensum Nobiscum retinere vult, Poenam superius descriptam, sine ulla dilatione, reipsa sustineat; viz. ut minister & munere ministerii, & loco privetur: Patronus vero, ut ministro multetur, & contra ejusmodi excommunicatio vibretur. Et in Praefatione ad Acta harum Synodorum, profitentur hoc modo —Addicti Sanctae Concordiae, & operam dantes aedificationi Ecclesiae atque extirpationi Scandalorum, nos qui in Poloniae Regno idololatriam, Antichristi rejecimus, & omnes Haereses Christianae Fidei, Symbolo Apostolorum, Niceno, & Athanasiano &c. adeoque Authoritati Scripturarum repugnantes, vitamus, ac puram Evangelii Doctrinam sincere profitentes, & exequi studentes, Evangelici vocamur.
units.tr: §. 36. But what seems to me of the greatest weight, among Socinus's opponents, for condemning his heresy, which was the same as that of the Antitrinitarians to whose sect he adhered, is this: that all the theologians and leading men in Poland of the threefold Confession just mentioned, namely the Bohemian, the Augsburg and the Helvetic, at last came together into one body, and, by holding frequent synods, unanimously settled a consensus in doctrine, the threefold Confession being approved by each, and every contrary doctrine, whether of the Papists or of the sectaries, being equally condemned. Above all, they set themselves against the Antitrinitarians, whom they unitedly anathematized as open and professed enemies of the Evangelical doctrine, and expelled from their communion. And they did this partly before Socinus's arrival in Poland, partly after. In the synod of Sandomierz, which was held on 14 April 1570: "After our country had long and much struggled with the sectaries, the Tritheists, the Ebionites and the Anabaptists, and at last by God's favour had emerged from so many and such grave conflicts and deplorable contentions, it seemed good to the Polish Churches, Reformed and Orthodox, which seemed not fully to agree with the enemies of truth and the Gospel in certain heads and formulas of doctrine, to convene a synod in the zeal for peace and concord, and to restore a mutual Confession. Wherefore, after a friendly and Christian conference, our minds being thus joined and settled, we agreed on these heads. First, the threefold Confession of our Churches having been mutually approved, we solemnly promised one another, unanimously, that according to the rule of the Word of God we would defend this mutual consensus in the true and pure religion of Christ against the Papists, against the sectaries, and finally against all enemies of the Gospel and of truth."* The General Synod of Cracow, held in 1573, also struck the Antitrinitarians, under the name of Arian-Anabaptists, with this most grave censure. When some of their preachers and hearers, they say, had of their own accord come to our synod and wished to debate their doctrine there, the synod, after serious deliberation about them, refused them a colloquy and disputation, and made this decree: "The Arian-Anabaptists, who have gone out from us, show no wonder in the doctrine of Christ and in the faith concerning the true God the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit, and so they have no God; and since they have been often admonished by us in conferences and writings, they remain obstinately in error. We will have no further fellowship with them so long as they hold their opinion; we will admit no disputations of theirs, but we will avoid them and their blasphemous books according to the precept of the Holy Spirit, lest we seem to be shaken and to call into doubt from time to time the foundation of the Christian religion (the most firm faith concerning God in whose name we were baptized); and lest we share in their evil works, their poisonous doctrines and blasphemies, which assail the glory of the Lord." Nay, they show themselves not only opposed to their doctrine but also alien to their ceremonies, so as not to share with them even in the smallest thing. For so this same synod decrees, Act 6: "When the question was raised concerning ceremonies, especially in the use of the Lord's Supper, whether they could be uniform in all our Churches, it was concluded that, according to the custom of the primitive Church, the ceremonies should be left among us to Christian liberty. Yet the brethren who use sitting at the Holy Supper are to be admonished to abandon that ceremony, which belongs to the Arian-Anabaptists." And again at the General Synod of Pinczów, in June 1578, they decree the same: "We grant and permit to Christian liberty the ceremonies, so that the pious may receive the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of Christ standing or kneeling; but as for sitting at the table of the Lord, since besides the rites commonly in use in all the Evangelical Churches throughout Europe, those among us were the first authors who, rashly changing everything in the Church and, lacking knowledge, as it were imitating Christ, became perfidious deserters from us to Arianism; therefore we reject this peculiar ceremony of theirs, which treats Christ and his sacred things irreverently, as less honourable and religious, and very scandalous to the simpler sort." Afterwards, at the General Synod of Włodzisław, on 19 June 1583, when Socinus had already stayed in Poland for four years, the harmony of these three Confessions was confirmed anew. Act 4. It was also forbidden that anyone publish books on his own authority, but only those that had been examined and approved by the superiors in the Church. Act 5. The decree against sitting at the Lord's table was likewise repeated, that it should not be in use in any of the Churches of the consensus in Poland, Lithuania, and so on. "For this ceremony, they say, though free like the others, is not used by the other Christian and Evangelical Churches, and belongs only to the unbelieving Arians, who set themselves down at the table with the Lord on equal footing. Since, then, sitting has crept into custom in some of our Churches, chiefly through the occasion and evil example of those who most wretchedly fell away from us and denied the Lord who redeemed us, we ask and exhort all those congregations and our brethren in the Lord to change the sitting into the ceremonies customary among us in the Evangelical Churches throughout Europe, etc." Act 6. Finally, at the General Synod of Toruń, held on 21 August 1592, the Acts of the earlier General Synods were confirmed again, and the three Confessions of faith were approved by unanimous consent, their principal heads being listed distinctly; and it is clear from the titles that these measures were especially directed against the Socinians. Whence they conclude that by this consensus in doctrine they bind themselves to one another and separate themselves from all heretics, sectaries and blasphemous idolaters who corrupt the Apostolic and Orthodox faith. In the same place it was also decided to preserve and defend the purity of doctrine concerning God, his essence and the Persons, against those who shrink from the word Trinity; and it was decreed that those who did not wish to use that word, as suspect in the faith, should be excluded from the Evangelical congregation. The decree concerning this consensus is worded thus: "Our Evangelical consensus, instituted at Sandomierz in 1570, and in the same year illustrated by the Poznań agreement, and afterwards increased and established by the General Synods of Cracow, Pinczów and Włodzisław, as those things are contained in the copy printed at Toruń in Latin and Polish in 1592; we all, in this our General Synod of Toruń, approve and confirm, and against the adversaries who until now have dared to object to us Evangelicals discord and a feigned consensus, both in word and in writing, we profess that we have sincerely embraced and cherished this true consensus, and that we are truly united in holy concord according to it." Then follows: "Every Evangelical minister in the Kingdom of Poland, the great Duchy of Lithuania, and the other provinces joined to them, shall be bound not only to have and read this consensus (into which we also incorporate these canons of the Synod of Toruń), but also, according to its prescription and the canons expressed in it, both himself to act accordingly and to govern the congregation committed to him." And a little later: "Whoever does not agree with us in the doctrine of the Gospel of God, and whoever embraces idolatry or heresy, and finally whoever breaks our concord and is unwilling to keep the consensus with us, let him at once undergo the penalty described above, namely that a minister be deprived of his ministry and of his place; and the patron, moreover, be fined as the minister is, and excommunication be hurled against such persons." And in the Preface to the Acts of these Synods they profess in this manner: "Devoted to holy concord, and labouring for the edification of the Church and the removal of scandals, we, who in the Kingdom of Poland have rejected the idolatry of Antichrist, and avoid all heresies that oppose the Christian faith, the Apostles' Creed, the Nicene and the Athanasian, and so on, and therefore the authority of the Scriptures, and who sincerely profess and strive to practise the pure doctrine of the Gospel, are called Evangelicals."

units.la: §. 37. Tot, tantosque Adversarios expertus est Socinus, cum ipse Catholicae Fidei, & Ecclesiae Authoritati adversaretur. At quod adhuc magis mirum est, & notatu dignum, ex horum munie o erant, non solum Orthodoxi, qui reformationem errorum legitimè instituerant, sed & ipsi Sectarii, qui una cum ipso à Catholica Fide desciverant, Anabaptistæ, Mennonitæ, Judaizantes, Chiliastæ, imò, & ipsi Principes Anti-Trinitariorum, qui primùm [?] libris Latinè editis suam Hærefin disseminaverant, & viam Socino straverant. Tales erant Iac: Palæologus, & Franciscus Davidis in Transylvania, quibus postea accessit Christianus Franken in Polonia. Atque his jure addi potest Erasmus Johannis Arianus[?]. Erasmus hic Scholæ Rector aliquandiu fuerat Antuerpiæ, ubi cum Hæresis suæ libros clam emisisset, Gulielmus Princeps Auriacus, re cognita, conatus ejus tempestive repressit, ne error exitialis se latius diffunderet; illumque aufugere coegit in Transylvaniam, ubi Arianismum palam docuit in cœtu Claudiopolitano, cujus Minister erat. Hic autem, utcunque Anti-Trinitarius, Sententiam tamen ab illa Socini diversam tenuit. Ajebat enim, Christum fuisse Substantiam spiritualem à Deo ante reliqua omnia creatam, quæ postea carnem nostram induit, conceptus ex Spiritu Sancto in utero Beatæ Virginis: Socinus autem asseruit, Christum fuisse nudum Hominem, neque ullatenus extitisse, antequam natus esset ex Maria Virgine. Hoc enim cum Paulo Samosateno, ac Photino tenuit; cum Ebione item ac Cerintho. Cum hoc Erasmo Socinus Disputationem iniit Cracoviæ, quæ finita est Novembris 30. 1584. Eamque postea edidit Socinus, & Moscorovio dedicavit, &c[?]: Junii 16. 1595. Atque extat inter Illius Opera.
units.tr: §. 37. Socinus met with so many and such great opponents, since he himself set himself against the authority of the Catholic Faith and the Church. What is still more remarkable and worth noting is that among these opponents were not only the Orthodox, who had lawfully undertaken the reform of errors, but also the sectaries themselves, who had revolted from the Catholic Faith together with him: Anabaptists, Mennonites, Judaizers, Chiliasts, and even the leaders of the Anti-Trinitarians, who first spread their heresy in books published in Latin and paved the way for Socinus. Such were Jacob Paleologus and Francis David in Transylvania, to whom later Christian Francken in Poland was added. To these may rightly be added Erasmus Johannis the Arian. This Erasmus had for some time been Rector of a school at Antwerp, where, after secretly putting out books of his heresy, William Prince of Orange, when the matter became known, promptly tried to suppress his efforts, so that the deadly error might not spread more widely; and he forced him to flee into Transylvania, where he openly taught Arianism in the congregation at Cluj, of which he was minister. Yet although he was an Anti-Trinitarian, he held an opinion different from that of Socinus. For he said that Christ was a spiritual substance, created by God before all other things, who afterwards put on our flesh, having been conceived of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Blessed Virgin. Socinus, however, asserted that Christ was a mere man, and had in no way existed before he was born of the Virgin Mary. For in this he agreed with Paul of Samosata and Photinus, and likewise with Ebion and Cerinthus. Socinus held a disputation with this Erasmus at Cracow, which was finished on 30 November 1584. Socinus afterwards published it and dedicated it to Moscorovius, on 16 June 1595. It is extant among his works.

units.la: §. 38. Quod autem spectat ad Alios Tres, qui jure dici pofpossunt Triumviri Anti-Trinitariorum[?], illi ulterius extenderunt Dogma Socini de natura Christi; & Principiis iisdem cum Illo insistentes, qui Christum nudum Hominem ex natura sua Deumque solummodo factum affirmavit, Adorationem Deo soli debitam, atque Invocationem, Eidem denegarunt. De Jac: Palaeologo ita queritur Socinus in Epistola ad Marc: Squarcialupum——Annon primus Omnium in Transylvania Sententiam illam maxime impiam & detestandam de non adorando, neque invocando Christo, docuit, & scriptam reliquit? Nomine ejus Doctrina hodie, quae à quibusdam Francisci Davidis esse creditur, integra eaque non pauca Ecclesiae in Hungaria fadissime sunt corruptae? Nonne is in Lituania alterum quendam Franciscum Davidis, quantum in se fuit, jam excitavit, & Provincia illius Ecclesias suo veneno infecit, ab ipsisque Polania Ecclesiis jam fere divulsit ac separavit? Tom: 1. p. 365. col: 2. Franc: Davidis successit Jac: Palaeologo, & eandem Haeresin docuit in Transylvania. A qua ut Geo: Blandrata eum averteret, Basilea Socinum accersivit. Quod ut commodius efficeret, utrumque in eadem Domo hospitari fecit per quatuor Menses, ut familiarius inter se conversarentur, & habitis mutuo Colloquiis in eamdem Sententiam de Christo convenirent. At Franc: Davidis suae Opinioni firmiter addictus & Famae tuendae avidus, quam apud Discipulos suos jampridem comparaverat, Eadem apud Eosdem publice praedicare denuo coepit; propter quod, à Principe Transylvaniae in Carcerem conjectus est, ubi non longe post, Diem supremum obiit. Hujus Incarcerationis, Mortisque sequentis invidiam sustinuit Socinus, ex opinione Quorundam, licet eam[?] à se amovere studiosissimè niteretur. Christianus Franken utrique succedens, idem Dogma acerrime defendit, & summo studio propagavit in Polonia. Cum Hoc ergo solennem Disputationem instituit Socinus, quam & habuit, in Aula Christophori Paulicovii, mense Martio A. D. 1584. Extat haec Disputatio de Honore Christi inter op: Socini. Tom: 2. P. 767. & quamvis ei adjectae sint Notae non paucae, & Responsiones ad ea quae Franken dixit; ut & Correctiones quaedam Eorum, quae Ipse Socinum dicentem facit, (sive a Socino, sive potius ab aliquo Illius Discipulo superadditae) attamen, quantum Mihi videtur, potiores Partes tulit Chr: Franken in ista Disputatione, prout isthic refertur.
units.tr: §. 38. As for the other three, who may rightly be called the triumvirs of the Anti-Trinitarians, they went further in extending the doctrine of Socinus concerning the nature of Christ. Proceeding on the same principles as he did, they affirmed that Christ was a mere man, who had become God only by his own nature, and they denied to him alone the adoration and invocation due to God alone. Socinus complains of Jacob Paleologus thus, in a letter to Marcus Squarcialupus: Was he not the first of all in Transylvania to teach, and to leave in writing, that most impious and detestable opinion, that Christ is not to be adored or invoked? Under his name, is not the doctrine, which is today believed by some to be that of Francis David, whole and not a few, have been most foully corrupted in the churches of Hungary? Did he not in Lithuania already stir up, as far as he could, another Francis David, and infect the churches of that province with his poison, and almost tear them away and separate them from the Polish churches themselves? Vol. 1, p. 365, col. 2. Francis David succeeded Jacob Paleologus and taught the same heresy in Transylvania. George Blandrata sent for Socinus from Basel to turn him away from it. To make this more convenient, he had the two lodge in the same house for four months, so that they might converse more familiarly and, after mutual discussions, come to agree in the same opinion about Christ. But Francis David, firmly attached to his own opinion and eager to protect the reputation he had long since won among his disciples, began again to preach publicly the same things among them. On account of this, he was cast into prison by the Prince of Transylvania, where, not long afterwards, he died. Socinus bore the odium of this imprisonment and of the death that followed, in the opinion of some, although he most earnestly strove to clear himself of it. Christian Francken, succeeding both, defended the same doctrine most vigorously and spread it with great zeal in Poland. With him Socinus therefore arranged a formal disputation, which he also held in the hall of Christopher Paulicovius, in March 1584. This disputation on the honour of Christ is extant among the works of Socinus, vol. 2, p. 767. And although a good number of notes have been added to it, and replies to what Francken said, as well as certain corrections of those things which he makes Socinus say (whether added by Socinus or rather by some disciple of his), nevertheless, as it seems to me, Christian Francken had the better of the argument in that disputation, as it is reported there.

units.la: §. 39. Hi Tres Anti-Trinitariorum Antesignani, Socini conatus praecipue impediebant in Doctrina sua propaganda, & Coetibus colligendis. Neque ulli ex omnibus iis, quos expertus est, Antagonistis, ei adeo molesti erant; ac Hi; neque in quibus refellendis solicitius elaboravit. Siquidem suis Ipsius armis Illum petebant, cum in iisdem castris educati fuissent, & Militiae Socinianae Artes probe edocti. Quibus, eorumque Discipulis, dum os obstruere conatus est, Argumentis undiquaque petitis; cum tandem loca S. Scripturae à se contra eos allata eludi videret, & in alienum sensum perverti, prout & Ipse multoties fecerat, tum in novis suis Dogmatibus exinde astruendis, tum in Telis Antagonistarum repellendis, necesse habuit acerrimus hic Ecclesiasticae Traditionis Hostis Veterumque Ecclesiae Patrum Contemptor, ad Asylum, tandem confugere. Ut patet, inter Alia quaedam, ex Epistola 3:, quam ad Matthaeum RadeRadecium scripsit, quem non longe à fine illius ita compellat, & cum eo verecunde expostulat de Adoratione & Invocatione Christi, de quibus ille plurimum dubitavit, an debitæ fuerint vel non, ac proinde licitæ.—Etsi verissimum est, inquit, quod ais, hic de Re omnium maxima agi, nihil est tamen quod Nos suspensos sive ancipites, qualem Te esse confiteris, hac in Re tenere debeat. Imo, quia de Re omnium maxima in Religione nostra agitur, nihil prorsus est cunctandum, sed apertissima Veritas statim amplectenda, & mordicus retinenda. Nam unde factum esse existimas, ut ab ipso ferme nascentis Ecclesiæ Christi Initio, usque ad nostra Tem-pora, tot viri, adeo ut nullus sit Numerus, non minus Pietate quam Doctrina clarissimi, tot ipsius Christi Sanctissimi Martyres, eum alioqui gravissimum errorem secuti fuerint, quod Christus sit unus ille Deus, qui omnia creavit, aut certe ex Illius substantia propria genitus; nisi quia nimis aperte insanctis[?] literiis ea illi tribui animadverterunt, quæ soli Deo tribui consueverunt; & inter Cetera, potissimum Adorationem & Invocationem; Eave[?] à quibus Adoratio & Invocatio; illa, ut prorsus debita; Hæc, ut plane conveniens, nullo pacto sejungi possunt. Nolisigitur, rogo & obsecro Te, Veritati manifestissimæ quicquam repugnare, & summum ac præstantissimum Christianæ Pietatis Mysterium at Fundamentum agnosce, supremam sc. in nos omnes datam à Deo in perpetuum præsentem Potestatem & Gubernationem. Hæc Epistola data est die 8. Jan: A.D. 1586. Cracoviæ. Extat autem, Op.: Soc: Tom: 1. p. 391. col: 2. Atque eadem Clausula repetitur in Tract: de Ecclesia, prope finem. Quæ verba Socini, ut Mihi videtur, observatu dignissima sunt; idque non solum, quod in his coactus sit fateri, Christum esse unum illum Deum, qui omnia creavit; aut certe ex illius propria substantia genitum; atque adeo non esse Creaturam, nudumque Hominem, qui non extitit, antequam ex B. V. Maria natus esset; (quod alibi toties affirmat, variisque Argumentis, quantum in se est, propugnat) sed etiam, & multo magis, quod hoc afferere cogatur ex Authoritate veterum Ecclesiae Doctorum, qui (ut verissime inquit) nimis aperte in S. Scriptura ea Christo tribui animadverterunt, quae soli Deo tribui consueverunt; &, inter caetera, potissimum Adorationem & Invocationem. Unde & Eum obnixe rogat, ne manifestissimae Veritati quicquam repugnare velit. Porro, constet modo sibi Socinus Illiusque Discipuli Magistri sui Dictatis auscultare velint, ut ad eandem Regulam caetera sua Dogmata examinari patiantur, riteque sic examinata ad Illam conformentur, neque aliud, neque amplius quidquam ab eis petimus. Sed quis non videt, ex hoc Concessio[?], totum Socinianismum illico ruiturum, & abolitum iri ex Ecclesia; nimirum si Interpretatio S. Scripturae ab antiquis Patribus allata, qui Fidem Christianam Pietate simul ac Doctrina adornarunt, & Martyrio insuper confirmarunt, pro vera & Authentica accipienda sit; & si Omnes Interpretationem eam oppugnantes, in manifestissima Veritate oculos claudant.
units.tr: §. 39. These three forerunners of the Anti-Trinitarians especially hindered Socinus's efforts to propagate his doctrine and to gather assemblies. Of all the opponents he encountered, none was so troublesome to him, nor did he labour more anxiously to refute any others. For they attacked him with his own weapons, since they had been brought up in the same camp and were thoroughly taught the arts of the Socinian soldiery. When he tried to silence them and their disciples, using arguments drawn from every quarter, and at last saw that the passages of Holy Scripture he had brought against them were being explained away and twisted into another sense, as he himself had often done, then this most bitter enemy of ecclesiastical tradition and despiser of the ancient Fathers of the Church was obliged at last to take refuge in a sanctuary, both to establish his new doctrines and to repel the darts of his opponents. This is clear, among other things, from the letter which he wrote to Matthew Radecius, which he addresses near its end, and with which he reproachfully expostulates concerning the adoration and invocation of Christ, about which Radecius had greatly doubted whether they were due or not, and therefore lawful. Although it is most true, he says, that, as you say, a matter of the greatest importance is at stake here, there is nothing that ought to keep us, or you, who confess yourself to be such, in suspense or wavering on this point. Indeed, because a matter of the greatest importance in our religion is at issue, nothing at all is to be delayed, but the most manifest truth is to be embraced at once and held fast with tooth and nail. For from what cause do you think it has come about that, from almost the very beginning of the nascent Church of Christ down to our own times, so many men, so countless in number, no less distinguished by piety than by learning, so many most holy martyrs of Christ himself, followed that otherwise most grave error, that Christ is that one God who created all things, or at least was begotten of his very substance; unless because they noticed that in the holy writings those things were too plainly ascribed to him which are wont to be ascribed to God alone; and among the rest, above all, adoration and invocation, which cannot in any way be separated from one another: the former as wholly due, the latter as plainly fitting. I beg and entreat you, therefore, not to be unwilling to oppose anything to the most manifest truth, but to acknowledge as the highest and most excellent mystery and foundation of Christian piety that supreme and present power and government, given by God to us all for ever. This letter was dated 8 January 1586, at Cracow. It is extant in the works of Socinus, vol. 1, p. 391, col. 2. The same clause is repeated in the treatise on the Church, near the end. These words of Socinus seem to me most worthy of observation; and not only because in them he was compelled to confess that Christ is that one God who created all things, or at least was begotten of his own substance, and so is not a creature, nor a mere man who did not exist before he was born of the Blessed Virgin Mary (which he elsewhere so often affirms and, as far as he can, defends with various arguments), but much more because he is forced to assert this by the authority of the ancient teachers of the Church, who (as he most truly says) noticed that in Holy Scripture those things were too plainly ascribed to Christ which are wont to be ascribed to God alone, and among the rest, above all, adoration and invocation. Hence he earnestly begs him not to wish to oppose anything to the most manifest truth. Furthermore, let Socinus and his disciples only agree to listen to the dictates of their master, so as to allow their other doctrines to be examined by the same rule, and, once so examined, to be brought into conformity with it; we ask nothing else and nothing more of them. But who does not see that, from this concession, the whole of Socinianism will at once collapse and be abolished from the Church; namely, if the interpretation of Holy Scripture offered by the ancient Fathers, who adorned the Christian faith with piety as well as doctrine and confirmed it moreover by martyrdom, is to be accepted as true and authentic, and if all who oppose that interpretation shut their eyes to the most manifest truth.

units.la: §. 4o.[?] Inter hic advertere lubet, ad quas astru-angustias redactus fuerit Socinus, cum ad Scripturam solam appellaret in Dogmatibus suis astruendis; nempe, ad Scripturam suo Ipsius sensu expositam, seu potius, in Eum detortam. Quippe nihil mirum erat, si Discipuli Illius, Aliique cujufcunque Generis Sectarii,Interpretationes ejus non illico, & fine examine admiserint, sed in suo quisque sensu abundaret. Liberum enim erat cuicunque alteri, æque ac Socino, sentire quicquid sibi visum fuerit, suisque Placitis afferendis Scripturam adaptare. Nam sic merito poterant arguere. Cur Alios suum ad sensum admittendum astringeret, qui sensum antiquitus receptum in tot Fidei Articulis saltidiose rejecerat? Cur Authoritatem aliquam in Socino agnoscerent, qui Ecclesiæ Catholicæ veterumque illius Doctorum Authoritatem omnino sustulerat? Quo jure Socinus Illud improbaret in Aliis, cujus ipse toties Exemplum dederat? Hinc factum est, ut Socinus cum videret parilem & dogmatizandi, & interpretandi licentiam, quam ipse sibi arrogaverat, ab Aliis itidem usurpatam, necessarium sibi tandem putaret, Veterum Authoritate, tanquam Ajacis clypeo, se defendere, quam prius admodum vilipenderat, & a se contemptim abjecerat.
units.tr: Here it is worth noting how narrow the straits were into which Socinus was driven when he appealed to Scripture alone to establish his doctrines, namely Scripture expounded in his own sense, or rather twisted to suit it. Indeed it was no wonder that his disciples and other sectaries of every kind did not readily and without examination accept his interpretations, but each abounded in his own sense. For it was as free for anyone else as for Socinus to think whatever seemed good to him and to adapt Scripture to his own opinions. They could rightly argue thus: Why should he bind others to his sense, when he had frivolously rejected the sense received from antiquity in so many articles of faith? Why should they acknowledge any authority in Socinus, who had utterly abolished the authority of the Catholic Church and of its ancient teachers? By what right would Socinus disapprove in others what he himself had so often exemplified? Hence it came about that Socinus, seeing that the same licence to teach doctrine and to interpret which he had claimed for himself was likewise usurped by others, at last thought it necessary to defend himself by the authority of the Ancients, as with the shield of Ajax, which he had previously held in great contempt and cast aside with scorn.

units.la: §. 41 Atqbe [?] idem fere feuferunt [?] uniuscujusque ætatis Hæresiarchæ, nuperius autem in Anglia nostra primarii Schismatum hic glisceentibus Authores atque Patroni. Hi etenim, cum, spreta Ecclesiæ Authoritate atque conculcata, Hierarchiam, Cultum Dei publicum, Consuetudines antiquitus receptas, Ceremoniasque decoras ac laudabiles, incautius oppugnassent, istiusmodi Argumentis temere usi, quæ omne Regimen Ecclesiasticum, Ordinem totum atque decorum publici Cultus, Consuetudines omnes Ecclesiasticas, etiam ex vetustissima traditione derivatas, Praxique Catholica stabilitas, ritus demum quoscunque, etsi in se laudabiles, si modo Authoritate humana præscriberentur, pro illicitis damnarunt; paulo post experti sunt quamplurimos suorum Discipulorum & iisdem Argumentis armatos, & iisdem Magistrorum suorum vestigiis insistentes, Omnia illa impetere, & certatim demoliri, quæcunque hi novi Ædificatores, in veteris Ecclesiæ à se prius demolitæ loco, erexissent. Hinc Omnia statim peffundata sunt, Politia Ecclesiastica, Ordo Cultus divini, lectio S. Scripturæ, cum Precibus & Hymnis ei connexis, Recitatio Symboli, usus ipsius Orationis Dominicæ, Pædobaptismus, sacra Synaxis, & Cætera fere cuncta antiquitus recepta, & universaliter in Ecclesia antehac observata; Schismatis Authoribus fero tandem sapientibus, & velint, nolint, ad Ecclesiæ primitivæ Doctrinam Praxinque (at frustra) appellantibus, quas in Matre Ecclesia, à se diruta atque destructa, cum Tempus esset, agnoscere noluerunt. Adeo temere & imprudenter, ne quid durius dicam, agunt omnes ii, qui ex Ignorantia vel Incuria; multo magis, qui ex Superbia, vel Invidia & Malitia Ecclesiæ Primitivæ Scita & Instituta, quæ ad Posteros derivata sunt, & ab Eisdem universaliter accepta convellere amant; cum facillime prævidere possent, si modo Mentis oculos aperire, animumque, vellent advertere, Eos omnes, qui Veterum Authoritati detrahere student, Eadem Opera suam omnino destruere.
units.tr: The same almost happened with every heresiarch of every age, and more recently in our own England, where the chief authors and patrons of the schisms that spread here were of this kind. For these men, having rashly attacked, with contempt for and trampling upon the authority of the Church, the hierarchy, the public worship of God, customs received from antiquity and decent and laudable ceremonies, and having used arguments of such a sort that they condemned all ecclesiastical government, the whole order and decency of public worship, all ecclesiastical customs even those derived from the most ancient tradition, and the established Catholic practice, and finally any rites whatever, even if laudable in themselves, provided they were prescribed by human authority, soon found that very many of their disciples, armed with the same arguments and following the very footsteps of their masters, assailed all those things and eagerly tore down whatever those new builders had erected in place of the old Church which they themselves had first demolished. Hence everything was at once overthrown: ecclesiastical polity, the order of divine worship, the reading of Scripture with the prayers and hymns joined to it, the recitation of the Creed, the use of the Lord's Prayer itself, infant baptism, the holy Synaxis, and almost all the other things received from antiquity and universally observed in the Church until then. The authors of the schism, wise at last too late, and willy-nilly appealing (in vain) to the doctrine and practice of the primitive Church, were unwilling to recognise in the Mother Church what they had pulled down and destroyed when there was still time. So rashly and imprudently, not to say more harshly, act all who, from ignorance or carelessness, and much more those who from pride, envy or malice, love to overturn the decrees and institutions of the primitive Church that have been handed down to posterity and universally accepted by them. Yet they could very easily foresee, if only they would open the eyes of their mind and attend, that all who strive to detract from the authority of the Ancients are by that very effort utterly destroying their own.

units.la: §. 42. Hæc habui, quæ dicerem de Socino Ejusque Sociis ac Discipulis; deque Artibus iis atque Opportunitatibus, quibus uti solebant in Hæresi sua disseminanda. Restat, ut quædam Illorum Postulata recenseam[?], quæ non parum faciunt ad illius Argumenti elucidationem, quod præ manibus habemus ; ut & ulteriorem Eorum Confirmationem, quæ prius asseruimus. His adjiciemus Catalogum istorum Dogmatum, quæ in Socinianorum Scriptis occurrunt, cum perniciosissimis eorundem Consequentiis ; Hypocrisin item, & miserrima subterfugia Socini ; reliquorumque Anti-Trinitariorum ; Denique Postulata quædam ex nostra Parte proponemus, quæ ab iis concedi & æquum, & necesse est, nisi rectæ Rationi simul renunciare velint, suisque Ipsorum Concessis, quæ hisce postulatis præfiximus. Postulata autem Socinianorum triplicis Generis atque Gradus sunt ; quædam sic; satis æqua ; quædam, prorsus iniqua ; quædam item in medio quasi Ordine constituta, quæ non nisi Sensu restricto, & limitatione adhibita, concedi par est.
units.tr: I have said these things about Socinus and his associates and disciples, and about the arts and opportunities they were accustomed to use in spreading their heresy. It remains that I should review some of their demands, which contribute not a little to the elucidation of the subject before us and to the further confirmation of what we asserted earlier. To these we shall add a catalogue of the doctrines that occur in the writings of the Socinians, together with their most pernicious consequences, and likewise the hypocrisy and most wretched subterfuges of Socinus and of the other Anti-Trinitarians. Finally, we shall propose certain demands on our side, which it is both fair and necessary that they concede, unless they wish to renounce right reason and their own concessions, which they have prefixed to these demands. The demands of the Socinians are of three kinds and grades: some are fairly equitable, some are wholly unfair, and some are, as it were, placed in a middle order, which ought to be conceded only in a restricted sense and with the limitation applied.

units.la: §. 43. Primo, quædam Illorum Postulata æquitatem quandam præ se ferunt, si commode accipiantur. Quod vero ex æquo petunt, æquum est ut obtineant. Hæc autem fere sunt ; quæ ut plurimum excerpsi ex libello Joachimi Stegmanni de Judice & Norma Controversiarum Fidei. Viz: 1. Quod Intellectus humanus Divinorum æque ac Humanorum rationem postulet. 2. Quod Spiritus Sanctus non tollat Rationem, sed extollat. 3. Quod Ratio humana æque indeterminata, sive indifferens sit ad Divina, ac ad Humana ; licet non æque apta & idonea. 4. Quod Authoritas omnis, quoad Agnitionem, à Rationis Judicio pendeat. 5. Quod Fides præsupponat & sequatur Judicium, tum Rationis, tum Sensus. 6. Quod Religio Rationem exigat, & ad Eam appellet. 7. Quod Veritas S. Scripturæ, non nisi Rationis Judicio examinetur atque dignoscatur. 8. Quod omnia Certamina olim exorta, non solum inter Ethnicos Philosophos de Rebus naturæ inter se mutuo pugnantes, sed etiam inter eoidem[?] Paganos, Judæos & Hæreticos cum Christianis Catholicis (quæ olim & acerrima, & innumera fuerunt) quæcunque tandem consopita sunt, ex Infidelium & Heterodoxorum Convictione, non nisi Ratione Judice determinata sint atque composita. 9. Quod non omnino necesse sit omnes lites, etiam minoris Momenti, à publica Authoritate in Ecclesia definiri. Satis est quod Opinionum sibi adversantium Patroni eo usque in officio continentur ut neque prædicando, neque scribendo Pacem Ecclesiæ perturbent & Hæresi aut Schismati viam adaperiant. 10. Quod Nihil reperiatur in S. Scriptura Fidei nostræ propositum, quod Logicæ Regulis minime congruat. Logica vero est Ars Ratione bene utendi. 11. Quod in singulis Controversiis inter Doctos hodie agitatis, Rationis nostræ Judicio innitamur, quoties alteruri Parti Assensum præbemus. Cur enim Quispiam è Nobis hujus potius quam diversum aut contrarium sentientis Opinionem sequitur, nisi quod Eam Cæteris meliorem judicat? Quo autem Judice hoc censet nisi sua Ipsius Ratione? 12. Quod in Absurda quam plurima necesse sit incidere, qui Rationis Judicium abnegat. Vel enim, inquit Stegmannus, agnoscis Me Rationes tuas, sive Argumenta posse dijudicare, vel non? Si Illud, Rationem agnoscis Judicem: sin Illud, Cur non tantum surdo narras fabulam, sed & eadem opera multis Mihi verbis persuadere conaris, Me surdum esse? Deinde, vel intelligit Adversarius, qua Ipse contra Rationis Judicium profert, vel minime. Si Hoc, Nihil agit: Sin Illud, Rationis ipsius, cujus ope intelligit, Judicio, aut vera censet, aut falsa. Si vera censet, cur Rationis Judicium damnat? sin falsa, quomodo pugnat, mecumque contendit? An Me creditum[?] existimat Ipsi ea dicenti, qua Ipse falsa esse Judicat? Sin Rationem sanam in Judicio suo adhibet, cur contra Rationis Judicium disputat? 13. Quod Satanæ in hac Re versutia potissimum appareat, dum sacrarum literarum acerrimos Patronos atque Assertores, omni Rationis Judicio in iisdem exponendis privare nititur; idque sub ipsius Religionis Prætextu. Unde fit, ut S. Scriptura, Reformatorum pia Industria quasi restituta, parum aut nihil piis lectoribus & Auditoribus prosit, tum nihil Ipsorum Hostibus obsit. Siquidem hoc pacto, quantum in se est, verbum Dei suo Fructu privant, & absurdissimis quibusque Absurdis latam fenestram aperiunt; tandemque in Prædam cedunt, aut Pontificiis, aut Fanaticis: nimirum aut Illis, Fidem implicitam postulantibus: aut His, peculiarem Spiritus S. Illuminationem prætendentibus. 14. Quod Fides præsupponat Intelligentiam, usumque proinde Rationis; atque adeo, quod Homo maxime spiritualis Ratione uti cogatur. 15. Quod Ratio de Nihilo sententiam suam ferre possit, nisi Judicium illius Principiis certis & idoneis nitatur.Hæc autem sunt,vel communia Rebus naturalibus ac divinis, vel propria S. Scripturæ. Quicquid vero Ratio rite colligit, vel ex His, vel ex Illis, neutiquam potest S. Scripturæ contradicere. 16. Quod non pauca Theologica sint, quæ è Principiis philosophicis, & è consideratione Rerum naturalium atque humanarum cognosci queunt. Reliqua autem, quæ sine S. Scriptura cognosci nequeunt, potius supra Naturam vel Philofophiam, quam supra Rationem esse dicenda sunt. At hoc Postulatum non est admittendum, fi intelligatur de Ratione mere naturali. Concedi autem potest de Facultate Rationis in sese absolute spectata. Hæc enim in vere Fidelibus cælitus illuminata est, & Spiritus Sti auxilio supra vires nativas elevatur. 17. Quod Ratio sufficiat ad Cognitionem eorum omnium quæ sunt ad Salutem necessaria. Hoc etiam Postulatum admitti bene potest, fi modo intelligatur de Ratione è S. literis probe edoƈta, quæ ista Omnia fatis aperte proponunt cuicunque lectori Rationis sanæ compoti, & quæ inibi legit, ferio consideranti. 18. Quod Deus, atque Res omnes divinæ, ad nostram Salutem spectantes, quarumque cognitionem Deus à Nobis requirit, à Ratione humana vere percipi possint, etsi non perfecte, & Conceptu Rei perceptæ adæquato. Nam ut Universalia intelligantur à Nobis, etsi non per Species a rebus sensibilibus desumptas; sic & Spiritus resque spirituales. Ad cognitionem autem Dei, triplici via pervenitur, fc: Causalitatis, perfectionis, & Remotionis omnis Imperfecti. Primo, via Causalitatis; quæcunque enim in hoc Mundo cernimus, vel non cernimus, à Deo creata fuisse intelligimus; & ex his Operibus intelligere datur, quis & qualis & quantus fit Opifex universorum. Deinde ex Facultatibus & Operibus cæterisque Creaturarum Perfectionibus, quibus Ahæ Alias excellunt, & quæ hic illi maxima tum Specierum, tum Graduum varietate, inter Easdem disperguntur, colligimus perfectionem Dei Creatoris, à quo singulæ processerunt ac tanta varietate distributæ sunt. Necesse est enim, ut hæc summe sit in se & eminentissimo Gradu universas Perfectiones in singulis Creaturis spectabiles comprehendat & exuperet, ut sol radios luminis per Aerem, & Oceanus aquas Fluviorum & lacuum, per Tetram dispersas. Denique, quicquid Imperfecti discernimus inter Creaturas, ideo removere discimus; quippe qui est ens in se omni Modo, Graduque perfectum, sicut est Fons omnis Perfectionis inter Creaturas distributae. Hinc est, quod dicimus, Deum esse increatum, infinitum, immaterialem, immobilem, invisibilem, incomprehensibilem, immensum, immortalem.
