Enimvero, hujusmodi Rationis nostrae Perceptio, etsi in sua natura imperfecta sit, nequaquam tamen sperneda est, cum neque nulla Cognitio sit, neque salsa. Nam Adaequatio nostri Intellectus cum re intellecta non eo extendi debet, ut in se comprehendat omnimodam Rei intellectae perfectionem, & ex adverso, omnem imperfectionem ex parte sui prorsus excludat. Tum enim paucissima, etiam ex Rebus naturalibus, à nobis vere cognoscerentur. Sufficit autem ad veritatem Cognitionis, Conceptuum nostrorum cum re ipsa Convenientia, ejusmodi sc: qua Nihil Intellectui nostro repraesentetur, quod in re ipsa non sit; nihilque, quod in re insit, negetur. At si Plura sint in re ista, quam per speciem intelligibilem Rationi nostrae offeruntur, Species illa imperfecta quidem dici potest, sed non falsa. Imo ob id ipsum Conceptus imperfectus est verus, quia perfectus esset verus; cum Imperfectus sit Pars Perfecti. Si ergo Totum tale est, partem esse talem minime dubitandum est E.C. Siquis Equum toto Corpore album, pedibus album, diceret, quod Illos solos videret, aut meminerit esse albos, Conceptus esset imperfectus sed in se verus. At Siquis Conceptum imperfectum pro perfecto venditet, & hoc tandem quod concipit, Rei conceptae inesse pronunciet; negans interim, Alia plura inesse, quae tamen revera insunt, vel etiam contrarium ponens, Conceptus Illius non dicendus est imperfectus, sed plane alterius Generis ac proinde falsus; idque ob hoc Ipsum, quod perfectior Conceptus verus efset[?]. Pars enim non est Integrum. E. C. Siquis Equum toto Corpore album, Pedibus solis album esse diceret aut ex aliqua parte Corporis nigrum. Ita quoque, siquis porcum pro Ove aut Ægrotum pro Sano conciperet. 19.[?] Quod neque Sensus, neque Ratio nostra, fallatur circa propria Objecta, debito modo disposita[?]; cum sint ipsae facultates nostrae sanae sunt, atque Organa illarum illaesa. Quomodo enim errare possumus in exercitio nostrarum Facultatum, Causis omnibus Erroris remotis? Imo, plerumque in nostra Potestate est, si modo hoc Ipsum ageremus, usumque diligentem Mediorum a Deo & Natura nobis concessorum adhiberemus omnem Erroris Causam in Rebus majoris momenti, non solum advertere, sed & amovere; adeoque Errorem inde enascentem, aut praevertere, aut corrigere. Certe, haud credendum est, Omnes Homines, in re eadem, eodem plane Modo, simul errare 20.[?] Quod Certitudo ibi poni debeat, ubi Dubitatio locum non habet; & quod hujusmodi Certitudo suos Gradus habeat. Dubitatio enim ibi dicitur esse, ubi in utramque Partem, vel reipsa sunt, vel esse videntur. Rationes aeque validae; ita ut, quo Te vertas inter has duas, vel non omnino, vel non aeque saltem appareat; ut cum Statera in aequilibrio se sistit, ex aequalitate Ponderum in utraque lance positorum. Quamprimum autem majus, aliquod pondus alterutri lanci impo-nitur illico tollitur hoc Æquilibrium, altera lance depressa, & altera elevata. At sicut multi sunt Gradus præponderationis in Statera, seu [?] quod idem est, elevandæ hujus lancis, & alterius deprimendæ; ita quoque Se[?] Res habet in Assensu mentis nostræ. Quamprimum enim alterius Partis Rationes præponderant, certitudo fit, Animo extra Dubitationem collocato; cum Assensus noster subsistere[?] possit, quasi in spatiis intermediis. Hoc vero fit, cum hujus Partis Rationes, licet alicujus sint Ponderis, non tamen æquipollent adversæ Partis Rationibus, sed eis locum cedunt. Certitudo quippe oritur ex majori quasi gravitate Argumentorum unius Partis præ Altera, quæ infert Concludendi necessitatem. Etsi enim multitudo quoque Argumentorum non parum valeat, per se tamen summa haud quicquam efficit, nisi singulis Argumentis aliqua Gravitas, seu vis probandi insit. Tunc demum, ut in exercitu --quæ non prosunt[?] Singula, Juncta juvant. Cæteroquin, vel una Ratio firmiter concludens, longe plus valet, quam ingens futilium & leviuscularum numerus. Quanto magis, si Singulæ adeo fortes sint, ut per se etiam, sine Aliarum auxilio, sufficere possint? 21 Quod nihil Deo imputandum sit, quod Justitiæ & Æquitati palam repugnat. Itaque aliquid[?] occurrit in S. Scriptura, quo prima fronte Tale quidpiam consequi videatur. Cuivis pio & cordato in Illud sedulo elaborandum est, ut commoda Interpretatione adhibita ita explicetur, ne Iniquitatis minimam Particulam Deo omnis Æquitatis, & Rectitudinis Fonti imputari necesse sit. Hoc vero postulatum admitti sine dubio debet, prout verba sonant, ac non in sensu Socinianorum, qui illud statuunt in Deo iniquum esse, quod revera Tale non est, cum S. Scriptura Illud Deo diserte attribuat, & Ecclesia Christi Catholica idem semper asseruerit. E. C. Imputatio peccati primorum Parentum toti humano Generi; Mors Christi innocentis pro redemptione nocentium, cum satisfactione pro Peccatis & imputatione Justitiæ Illius, per fidem applicatæ cunctis salvandis; Æternitas item poenarum in Gehenna pro peccatis in Tempore admissis. 22. Quod Fides neque cogatur, neque ex voluntatis imperio dependeat. Equidem Homo exterior cogi potest vel ad fidem istam abnegandam, quam intus & in corde amplectitur; vel ad Fidem istam, sive Religionem aperte profitendam, quam intus & in corde negat; sed interior Homo, sive Animus, immunis est ab omni externa vi quæ ad Cor penetrare nullo modo potest. Quicquid ergo Homo credit, sponte credit, non coactus. Imo, (quod ultra demonstrandum est.) nemo aliquid credit, quia vult credere, sed quia ejus Intellectus, idoneo aliquo Argumento, de Rei propositæ veritate convincitur. Hoc autem à Pico Mirandulano quinque Argumentis probatur, viz Primo, non est in potestate nostra judicare, hoc vel illud esse aut non esse, ex solo voluntatis arbitrio. Siquidem comperimus, quoties aliqua Res dubia proponitur, de qua mens nostra nihil determinavit in hanc illamve partem, quod in neutram propendeamus, priusquam accedat aliqua Ratio convincens, aut experimentum proprii sensus, aut Testimonium Alicujus fide digni, quod faciat alterutram præponderare. Secundo, nemo potest alicui Propositioni assentiri, aut veram esse concludere, nisi sibi vera appareat. At hæc veri apparentia, non dependet, aut procedit ex Actu solius voluntatis, sed ex Rei ipsius evidentia, aut ex Testimonio Alterius. Tertio, etsi Actio Intellectus, quoad exercitium, pendeat à voluntate, nimirum, in cogitando de Re proposita, vel ab ea se avertendo; non tamen quoad Specificationem, hoc est, quoad Assensum, vel Dissensum. Nam hi mentis Actus, qui sibi mutuo contrarii sunt, fundantur in, & procedunt a diversa atque contraria Rerum ipsarum Apparentia, cum respectu ad lumen istud mentis nostræ, quæ juxta istam Apparentiam de Re proposita judicat. Quarto, solum voluntatis mandatum non potest efficere, ut Homo credat illud, de quo Rationem idoneam reddere paratus esse debet, quoties Hoc ab eo serio postulatur. Sic autem se Res habet in Fidei Christianæ Dogmatibus, ex Petri præcepto. 1 Pet. 2. 15. ut & ex consona sententia atque Praxi omnium Theologorum: Inter cæteros autem, Scotus Proleg. in Sent. qu. 2. octo Argumenta adducit huc tendentia, viz. lumen Prophetiæ, Harmoniam sive Consensum librorum S. Scripturæ, diligentem Inquisitionem eorum qui Evangelium primo receperunt, Authoritatem atque Gravitatem Sacrorum Scriptorum, rationabilem veritatem Rerum Scriptarum, cum absurditate contrariorum errorum; perpetuam stabilitatem atque Constantiam Ecclesiæ, tum in Duratione, tum in fide; & Miracula Fidem confirmantia. Quinto, si dentur Duo, quorum Hic diserte credit, quia vult; ille autem diserte recusat eandem Rem credere, quia non vult; neutrius Actus est Alterius Actu rationabilior; sed è contra, uterque in hoc se gerit Tyranni instar, aut Hominis pervicaci Ingenio prædıti, cui solum Arbitrium pro lege est --Sic volo, sic jubeo, stat pro Ratione voluntas. Quis autem tam impius est, ut dicat,
units.tr: §. 43. First, some of their demands carry a certain fairness on their face, if they are taken in a reasonable sense. What they ask for on the ground of fairness is fair, and they ought to obtain it. Most of these I have excerpted, for the most part, from the little book of Joachim Stegmann, On the Judge and Norm of Controversies of Faith. They are as follows: 1. That the human intellect demands a reason for divine things just as for human things. 2. That the Holy Spirit does not abolish reason but raises it up. 3. That human reason is as indeterminate, or indifferent, with regard to divine things as to human things, although it is not equally fit and suited to them. 4. That all authority, as far as our knowledge of it goes, depends on the judgment of reason. 5. That faith presupposes and follows judgment, both of reason and of sense. 6. That religion requires reason and appeals to it. 7. That the truth of Holy Scripture is examined and recognised only by the judgment of reason. 8. That all the disputes that arose in former times, not only among the heathen philosophers, who fought with one another over the things of nature, but also between the same pagans, Jews and heretics and the Catholic Christians (which were once both very bitter and innumerable), however they have at last been quieted, have been settled and composed only by reason as judge, through the conviction of unbelievers and heterodox persons. 9. That it is not at all necessary for all disputes, even those of minor importance, to be settled by public authority in the Church. It is enough that the defenders of opinions opposed to one another are kept within their duty, so that by preaching or writing they do not disturb the peace of the Church or open the way to heresy or schism. 10. That nothing is found in Holy Scripture proposed as our faith that does not agree with the rules of logic. Logic, however, is the art of using reason rightly. 11. That in the individual controversies debated today among the learned we rely on the judgment of our reason whenever we give our assent to either side. For why does any one of us follow the opinion of this man rather than of one who thinks otherwise or contrary, unless he judges it better than the rest? And by what judge does he judge this, if not by his own reason? 12. That whoever rejects the judgment of reason must necessarily fall into very many absurdities. For either, says Stegmann, do you acknowledge that I can judge your reasons or arguments, or not? If the former, you acknowledge reason as judge; but if the latter, why do you not merely tell a tale to a deaf man, but also, by the same labour, try to persuade me with many words that I am deaf? Next, either your opponent understands what he brings forward against the judgment of reason, or not at all. If not at all, he accomplishes nothing; but if he understands, then by the judgment of that very reason by whose help he understands, he holds it either true or false. If he holds it true, why does he condemn the judgment of reason? But if false, how does he fight and contend with me? Or does he think that I believe him when he says what he himself judges to be false? But if he uses sound reason in his judgment, why does he dispute against the judgment of reason? 13. That Satan shows his cunning in this matter especially, while he tries to deprive the keenest defenders and champions of the sacred letters of all judgment of reason in expounding them, and that under the very pretext of religion. Hence it comes about that Holy Scripture, as if restored by the pious industry of the Reformers, is of little or no use to pious readers and hearers, and does no harm to their enemies. For in this way, as far as in them lies, they deprive the Word of God of its fruit and open a wide window to all manner of absurdities; and at last they fall as prey either to the Papists or to the fanatics: that is, either to those who demand implicit faith, or to those who pretend to a peculiar illumination of the Holy Spirit. 14. That faith presupposes understanding, and therefore the use of reason; and so, that the most spiritual man is compelled to use reason. 15. That reason can pronounce its opinion on nothing unless its judgment rests on certain and suitable principles. These principles are either common to natural and divine things, or proper to Holy Scripture. Whatever reason rightly infers from either of them can by no means contradict Holy Scripture. 16. That there are not a few theological matters which can be known from philosophical principles and from the consideration of natural and human things. The remaining things, which cannot be known without Holy Scripture, are to be called above nature or philosophy rather than above reason. This postulate, however, is not to be admitted if it is understood of reason merely natural. It may be granted, though, concerning the faculty of reason considered absolutely in itself; for this is illuminated from heaven in true believers, and is raised by the aid of the Holy Spirit above its native powers. 17. That reason suffices for the knowledge of all those things which are necessary to salvation. This postulate too may well be admitted, if it is understood of reason properly instructed from the sacred letters, which set forth all these things quite plainly to any reader who is of sound reason, and who considers seriously what he reads there. 18. That God and all divine things that pertain to our salvation, and whose knowledge God requires of us, can be truly perceived by human reason, even if not perfectly, and with a concept of the thing perceived that is adequate. For just as universals are understood by us, even if not through species taken from sensible things, so too are spirits and spiritual things. Now the knowledge of God is reached in a threefold way, namely: by causality, by perfection, and by the removal of all imperfection. First, by the way of causality: for whatever we see in this world, or do not see, we understand to have been created by God; and from these works it is given to understand what sort and how great the Maker of all things is. Next, from the faculties and works and the other perfections of creatures, by which some excel others, and which are scattered among them here and there with the greatest variety of both kinds and degrees, we gather the perfection of God the Creator, from whom each has proceeded and by whom they have been distributed with such variety. For it is necessary that this perfection, being supremely in itself and at the most eminent degree, should comprehend and surpass all the perfections observable in individual creatures, just as the sun's rays of light through the air, and the ocean the waters of rivers and lakes scattered through the dark. Finally, whatever imperfection we discern among creatures we learn therefore to remove from God; since he is a being perfect in every mode and degree, just as he is the fount of all perfection distributed among creatures. Hence we say that God is uncreated, infinite, immaterial, immutable, invisible, incomprehensible, immense, immortal. Indeed, such a perception of our reason, although in its own nature it is imperfect, is by no means to be despised, since it is neither no knowledge nor false knowledge. For the adequation of our intellect with the thing understood ought not to extend so far that it comprehends in itself all the perfection of the thing understood, and on the other hand excludes from its own side every imperfection entirely. For then very few things, even among natural things, would be truly known by us. It is enough for the truth of knowledge, however, that our concepts agree with the thing itself, in such a way that nothing is represented to our intellect which is not in the thing, and nothing is denied of it which is in the thing. But if there are more things in the thing than are offered to our reason through the intelligible species, that species may indeed be called imperfect, but not false. Indeed, for this very reason the concept is imperfect and yet true, because it would be true if it were perfect, since the imperfect is a part of the perfect. If then the whole is such, it is by no means to be doubted that the part is such, therefore. If anyone should say that a horse is white in its whole body, white in its feet, and that he sees only these, or remembers that they are white, his concept would be imperfect but in itself true. But if anyone puts forward an imperfect concept as perfect, and pronounces that what he conceives is inherent in the conceived thing, while denying meanwhile that many other things are in it which nevertheless really are in it, or even asserting the contrary, that concept of his is not to be called imperfect but plainly of another kind, and therefore false; and this for the very reason that a more perfect concept would be true, since a part is not the whole. Therefore, if anyone should say that a horse is white in its whole body, and white only in its feet, or black in some part of its body. So too, if anyone should conceive a pig for a sheep, or a sick man for a healthy one. 19. That neither sense nor our reason is deceived about their proper objects, when these are rightly disposed, since the faculties themselves are sound in us, and their organs unharmed. For how can we err in the exercise of our faculties, when all the causes of error are removed? Indeed, it is for the most part within our power, if only we were to take this in hand and apply a diligent use of the means granted us by God and nature, not only to notice but also to remove every cause of error in matters of greater moment, and so either to forestall or to correct the error arising from them. Certainly, it is not to be believed that all men, in the same matter, err together in exactly the same way. 20. That certainty ought to be placed where doubt has no place, and that such certainty has its degrees. For doubt is said to exist where there are reasons of equal weight on both sides, either really or apparently, so that, whichever way you turn between these two, either not at all or at least not equally does it appear; as a balance comes to rest in equilibrium from the equality of the weights placed on either pan. As soon as some greater weight is laid on one of the pans, this equilibrium is at once destroyed, one pan depressed and the other raised. But just as there are many degrees of preponderance in a balance, or, what is the same, of raising one pan and lowering the other, so the matter stands also in the assent of our mind. For as soon as the reasons of one side preponderate, certainty comes about, the mind being placed beyond doubt, since our assent can rest as it were in the intermediate spaces. This happens when the reasons of this side, although they have some weight, nevertheless are not equal to the reasons of the opposing side, but give way to them. For certainty arises from a kind of greater weight of the arguments of one side over the other, which brings about the necessity of concluding. For although the multitude of arguments also counts for not a little, yet the sum by itself achieves nothing, unless each single argument has some weight or force of proving. Then at last, as in an army: single men who do not avail, joined together do help. Otherwise, one reason that concludes firmly is worth far more than a huge number of trifling and rather light ones. How much more so, if each of them is so strong that it can suffice even by itself, without the aid of the others? 21. That nothing is to be imputed to God which plainly contradicts justice and equity. Therefore, something occurs in Holy Scripture which at first sight seems to imply some such thing. Every pious and discerning person must labour carefully at this, that by applying a suitable interpretation it be so explained that it is necessary to impute not even the smallest particle of injustice to God, the fount of all equity and rectitude. This postulate ought undoubtedly to be admitted, as the words sound, and not in the sense of the Socinians, who maintain that God is unjust in what is in truth not such, since Holy Scripture expressly attributes it to God, and the Catholic Church of Christ has always asserted the same. Therefore: the imputation of the sin of the first parents to the whole human race; the death of Christ, innocent, for the redemption of the guilty, with satisfaction for sins and the imputation of his righteousness, applied by faith to all who are to be saved; likewise the eternity of punishments in Gehenna for sins committed in time. 22. That faith is neither compelled nor depends on the command of the will. Indeed, the outward man may be compelled either to deny that faith which he embraces inwardly and in his heart, or to openly profess that faith or religion which he inwardly and in his heart denies; but the inner man, or the mind, is immune from all external force, which can in no way penetrate to the heart. Whatever a man believes, therefore, he believes of his own accord, not under compulsion. Indeed, (which must be shown further on) no one believes anything because he wants to believe, but because his intellect is convinced of the truth of the proposed thing by some suitable argument. This is proved by Pico of Mirandola with five arguments, namely: first, it is not in our power to judge that this or that is or is not, from the mere decision of the will. For we find that whenever some doubtful matter is proposed, about which our mind has determined nothing in this or that direction, we do not lean to either side before some convincing reason, or the experience of our own sense, or the testimony of some trustworthy person, comes in and makes one side preponderate. Second, no one can assent to any proposition, or conclude that it is true, unless it appears true to him. But this appearance of truth does not depend on or proceed from an act of the will alone, but from the evidence of the thing itself, or from the testimony of another. Third, although the act of the intellect, as to its exercise, depends on the will, namely in thinking about the proposed matter or turning away from it, it does not so depend as to its specification, that is, as to assent or dissent. For these acts of the mind, which are contrary to one another, are founded on and proceed from a different and contrary appearance of the things themselves, in relation to that light of our mind which judges the proposed matter according to that appearance. Fourth, the mere command of the will cannot bring it about that a man believes that of which he ought to be ready to give a suitable reason, whenever this is seriously demanded of him. Yet this is how matters stand with the doctrines of the Christian faith, by the precept of Peter: 1 Pet. 2. 15. and also by the agreeing opinion and practice of all theologians. Among the rest, Scotus, Proleg. in Sent. qu. 2, adduces eight arguments tending to this: the light of prophecy, the harmony or agreement of the books of Holy Scripture, the careful inquiry of those who first received the Gospel, the authority and gravity of the sacred writers, the reasonable truth of the things written, together with the absurdity of the contrary errors; the perpetual stability and constancy of the Church, both in its duration and in its faith; and the miracles confirming the faith. Fifth, if there are two, of whom the one expressly believes a thing because he wants to, while the other expressly refuses to believe the same thing because he does not want to; neither's act is more reasonable than the other's; but on the contrary, each behaves in this like a tyrant, or like a man endowed with a stubborn temper, for whom mere will is law: Thus I will, thus I command; let will stand in place of reason. Who, however, is so impious as to say that

units.la: Christianos non majore Ratione credere Evangelio, quam Infideles recusant? Pico assentit Card: Cameracensis, Sent. qu. 1. Art. 2. Sicut impossibile est, inquit, assentiri sine Ratione, ita videtur Impossibile assentiri plus, quam Ratio probat vel probare videtur. Durandus pariter in 3ªm Sent. Dist. 24. qu. 3. Num. 7, 8. Ratio non totaliter dimittitur a Credente. Imo, non est possibile aliter Credere, saltem meritorie. Cum enim Credere sit quoddam Assentire, Assentire autem Nemo potest, nisi ei quod apparet verum; ergo oportet ut Illud quod creditur, appareat verum Rationi, vel in se, vel ratione medii, per quod assentitur. Et si non in se, sed tantum ratione medii, Illud medium apparebit verum, vel in se, vel per aliud medium. Et si non est Processus in Infinitum, oportet quod deveniatur ad Primum, quod apparet Rationi esse verum in se, & secundum se.
units.tr: Do Christians not believe the Gospel on any better ground than the unbelievers refuse it? Pico agrees with Cardinal Cameracensis, Sent. qu. 1, art. 2: "Just as it is impossible to assent without reason, so it seems impossible to assent to more than reason proves or seems to prove." Durandus likewise, in 3 Sent., dist. 24, qu. 3, nn. 7, 8: "The believer does not altogether dismiss reason. Indeed, it is not possible to believe otherwise, at least meritoriously. For since to believe is a kind of assenting, and no one can assent except to what appears true, it is necessary that what is believed should appear true to reason, either in itself or by means of a medium through which one assents. And if it appears true not in itself but only by means of a medium, that medium will appear true either in itself or through another medium. And since there cannot be an infinite regress, we must arrive at a first principle which appears true to reason in itself and by itself."

units.la: §. 44. Hæc sunt ista Socinianorum Postulata, quæ æquitatem aliquam præ se ferunt, adeoque concedi ex æquo postulant. Restant Alia, quæ vel prima specie iniqua sunt, vel fraudulenter & simulatorie proposita, vel saltem non nisi sensu limitato concedenda. Extant autem apud eundem Stegmannum, in libello Ejus paulo ante memorato, viz: de Judice & Norma Controversiarum Fidei Primo, Hoc modo Quæstionis statum ponit de Judice Controversiarum, inter Pontificios ac Socinianos, p. 36. &c: Publicum illi Judicem volunt, Isti Privato contenti sunt. Illi ad Unum istud [?] munus restringunt, isti Omnibus judicandi libertatem relinquunt. Illi Talem requirunt, qui Aliis Sententiam dicat; Istis sufficit, si Quisque sibi ipsi quid verum, rectumque sit dijudicet. Illi, Suum Judicem perpetuo ex Spiritus Sancti Afflatu pronunciantem faciunt; Isti suum sanae Rationis Dictamen sequi affirmant. Illi, Judici suo omnes alios Homines obligatos esse volunt, sibi suo Neminem, nisi ipsum Judicantem, subiicium; eo quod sibi, non aliis judicet. Necesse enim est, ut ait Becanus, ut sit aliquis Judex publicus, qui cum Authoritate, decernendi ac definiendi inter Partes litigantes, Potestatem habeat. Comp: 1. 1. c: 5. Hæc ille. Quæ Verba Stegmanni satis ostendunt, qualem Judicem Sociniani velint, qualemque solum agnoscant. Equidem nos, Pontificem Romanum Controversiarum omnium in Ecclesia Judicem, minime agnoscimus, cujus Sententiæ definitivæ omnes obsequi teneantur; multo minus Infallibilem, & ex Spiritus Sti Instinctu semper pronunciantem. Interim, visibilem & publicum Judicem, seu potius Judicum Consessum, in Ecclesia agnoscimus, & ad lites in ea terminandas necessarium ducimus; ut sine quo, nec Veritas, nec Pax, in Ecclesia conservari possit. Hoc enim & experientia, & ipsa Ratio demonstrat. Atque eadem Ratio luculenter ostendit, quam irrationale & absurdum sit, suam judicandi libertatem unicuique Privato relinquere, ab omni humana Authoritate Solutam atque independentem; quasi Nemine omnino indigeret, qui eum dirigat, Eique præscribat, in Rebus ad Fidem spectantibus; cum tamen, vel ipsis fatentibus, Omnes neutiquam esse possint Judices idonei, ad Sententiam de hujusmodi Rebus commode ferendam. Siquidem idem Stegmannus, p. 73. Ad sanitatem Rationis, ac proinde ad rite judicandum vires Naturæ integras, vegetasque requirit; singularem Judicii acrimoniam Animique probitatem; immunitatem à Vitiis, pravisque Opinionibus, quæ Judicium corrumpant; necnon ab omni pertinacia. Insuper, ad perficiendam eam, requirit Institutionem & Exercitationem; Educationem itcm liberalem, in Disciplinis tum philosophicis, tum sacris. Deinde, p. 77. ostendit, qualis Exercitatio requiratur. Principiis divinis inquit, adiungi debet Exercitatio, qua ea, qua docti sumus, ad Usum accommodamus, variis de Rebus, tum privatim tum publice, lapsus[?] differendo, sive cum Adversariis ipsis sive cum Aliis, qui Adversariorum defendunt Sententias, disputando. Quinetiam, quaecunque vel pro Adversarii Sententia vel pro nostra Sententia contra Adversarios afferri possunt inquirendo & examinando. Sic naturalis illa vis Rationis, ait non conservatur tantum & excitatur, sed & ad exactum ac sincerum de rebus oblatis iudicium promta redditur & expedita. Accedat libertas a Praejudicio, & sincerus Amor Veritatis; imprimis autem Illustratio Spiritus Sti, Cujus ductum Ratio sequatur in judicando. Ita Stegmannus.
units.tr: §. 44. These are the Socinians' demands, which carry a certain appearance of fairness, and so they ask that they be granted as fair. There remain others which are either unfair at first sight, or put forward deceptively and insincerely, or which may be granted only in a limited sense. These are found in the same Stegmann, in the booklet mentioned a little earlier, namely de Judice & Norma Controversiarum Fidei Primo ("On the First Judge and Norm of the Controversies of Faith"). There he states the question de Judice ("concerning the judge") of the controversies between the Papists and the Socinians, p. 36 etc.: "The former want a public judge, the latter are content with a private one. The former restrict this office to one person; the latter leave to everyone the freedom to judge. The former require such a judge as will pronounce the sentence for others; for the latter it is enough that each person judge for himself what is true and right. The former make their judge one who always pronounces by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit; the latter affirm that they follow the dictate of sound reason. The former want all other men bound to their judge, and subject no one to themselves except the one judging, because he judges for himself and not for others. For, as Becanus says, it is necessary that there be some public judge who has the authority to decide and to define between litigating parties." Comp. 1. 1. c. 5. So far Stegmann. These words of Stegmann sufficiently show what kind of judge the Socinians want, and what kind alone they acknowledge. As for us, we by no means acknowledge the Roman pontiff as the judge of all controversies in the Church, whose definitive sentence everyone is bound to obey, much less one who is infallible and always pronounces by the prompting of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, we do acknowledge a visible and public judge, or rather a council of judges, in the Church, and we hold it necessary for ending disputes within it, since without it neither truth nor peace can be preserved in the Church. Both experience and reason itself demonstrate this. And that same reason clearly shows how irrational and absurd it is to leave to each private person the freedom to judge, free and independent of all human authority, as if no one at all needed someone to direct him and prescribe for him in matters pertaining to faith; when yet, as they themselves admit, not everyone can be a suitable judge for pronouncing a sentence fittingly on such matters. Indeed, the same Stegmann, p. 73, requires for the soundness of reason, and therefore for judging rightly, a vigorous and whole natural strength; a singular keenness of judgment and integrity of mind; freedom from vices and from depraved opinions which corrupt judgment; and also freedom from all obstinacy. Moreover, to perfect this, he requires instruction and practice, and a liberal education too, in both philosophical and sacred disciplines. Then, p. 77, he shows what kind of practice is required. "To the divine principles," he says, "there must be added practice, by which we apply what we have been taught to use, in various matters, both privately and publicly, by debating with our adversaries themselves or with others who defend the opinions of our adversaries. Moreover, by inquiring and examining whatever can be brought forward either for the opinion of our adversary or for our own opinion against our adversaries." Thus that natural power of reason, he says, "is not only preserved and stirred up, but is also made ready and prepared for an exact and sincere judgment of the things presented." "Let there be added freedom from prejudice, and a sincere love of truth; above all, the illumination of the Holy Spirit, whose guidance reason should follow in judging." So Stegmann.

units.la: At num Aliquis sana Ratione praeditus existimare potest, haec Omnia ad recte judicandum requisita, in singulis quibusque Hominibus reperiri posse, quos tamen pro se Judices faciunt in rebus Fidei? Nonne Plerique sunt Carnales; vel Animales; Ineruditi vel ignavi; Opinionibus pravis imbuti, vel Partibus addicti; Stupidi aut scelerati; Caeci aut Pertinaces; Mundani demum, & Spiritu Sancto destituti: Certe hujusmodi Homines, vel ipsis Socinianis Judicibus, in judicando errabunt, si modo Judicium suum sequi velint. Sin visum sit Illis, aliam quempiam Judicem eligere (ut certe necesse est, in hoc Casu) quomodo in hujusmodi electione sua sese securos reddent, quod judex sic ab iis electus, praefatis Dotibus probe instructus fit, cum ipsi in hac re ignari sint, ac proinde ad eligendum prorsus inepti? Quomodo caeci idoneum eligent Itineris Ducem, qui eos certo dirigat in via? Sine dubio, quemcunque sic eligunt, temere ac fortuito eligere necesse est. Se tamen illi moderandos dant, suumque Judicium, prout illi libet, efformandum concedunt. Cur itaque Securitati suae multo melius consulere nolunt, Judices illos admittendo, quos Deus iis dedit, & Ipsius Ecclesia semper approbavit, frequentibus experimentis edocta? Cur etiam absolute & indefinite recusant unumquemque Judicem, ex Spiritus Sancti Afflatu pronunciantem; & contraponunt ei judicem qui sanae Rationis Dictamen sequitur; quasi Haec duo sint sibi mutuo contradictoria? Siquidem Nemo sanae mentis Enthusiasmis fidit in hoc Negotio vel in se, vel in Aliis. Neque ipsi Pontificii statuunt Papam Romanum Caulas ad se delatas ex afflatu Spiritus extraordinario determinare; sed hoc solum asserunt, istum dei Spiritum illi assistere in legitimo usu Mediorum. Imo, quid obstat, quo minus dicamus Spiritum Sanctum, certo modo & gradu, adesse & assistere unicuique Judici, probe se Gerenti, in Rebus Theologicis definiendis; sive sit Concilium, sive Episcopus, sive Arbiter quivis idoneus, a Partibus inter se disceptantibus electus; sive Privatus quispiam pro se judicans, Judicio Discretionis? Praesertim, cum ipse Stegmannus inprimis exigat Illustrationem Spiritus Sancti ad recte judicandum, ut modo ostendimus. Attamen, Hic ipse pag: 57. ejusdem libelli, asserit, suum Cuique Judicium sufficere, qui sana Ratione utitur; ut si omnes Homines Spiritu Sancto essent praediti, suum Cuique Judicium omnino sufficeret. Ubi rursus inter se opponit sanam Rationem, & Spiritum Sanctum. Sed interim, quo certo Judicio sana ratio ab insana dignoscetur; aut Spiritus Dei verax à Fallace & Illusorio? Quam multi enim sunt, qui in utroque dignoscendo, & sibi & Aliis imponunt? Num Socinciani soli rectae Rationis proprii, idoneique Judices sunt; cum tamen se opponere audeant non solum Ecclesiae Catholicae huius aevi, sed & omnium retro Seculorum; & Haereses resuscitent[?] ab ea semper damnatas? Nonne fateri coguntur, Plurimos apprime Doctos ac pios, & insignibus Ingenii Dotibus praeditos, ab eorum Dogmatibus plane abhorrere, & semper abhorruisse? Quomodo autem fit, ut veritas tot, tamque eximios Ecclesiae Doctores hactenus latuerit? Imo, (quod multo plus facit ad errores Illorum damnandos) quid in Causa fuit, ut cum primum innotuerint haec nova Socinianorum Dogmata, suis item Argumentis, quaecunque excogitari potuerunt, ab acutissimis, & ingeniosissimis eorum Patronis, suffulta & munita, tantum abstinerit[?], ut apud Illos valerent, ut è contra odio & horrore summo fuerint statim excepta? Num recta Ratio apud Socinianos solos Sedem suam obtinet, atque Dignitatem, cum interim apud Caeteros omnes, qui Christi nomen per totum Terrarum Orbem profitentur, aut plane exulet aut nihili aestimetur. Quis vero hoc putet, qui sana Ratione praeditus est, & qui sibi soli non sapit, atque adeo à Caeteris omnibus pro Insano meritissime habendus sit? At si eo usque ingenui ac modesti sint, ut Aliis omnibus, qui se putant recta Ratione uti, suum Ipsorum Judicium sufficere velint, Contradictoria probant, & simul valere aequum putant; quippe qui neque Socinianis, neque inter se consentiunt. Hoc autem, quam Rationi absonum sit, Nemo non videt. Quid? quod & ipsi prae Caeteris damnant Fanaticos, qui nil nisi Spiritum Sanctum crepant; quodque nos velint Spiritus probare rectae Rationis judicio. Quod argumento est, Uniuscujusque Judicium, qui Spiritum Sanctum se habere putat, aut quem ab Alio haberi censet, non ei sufficere ad sententiam rite ferendam; cum in Hoc facile decipi possit, ut & certum est, quamplures in eo fuisse olim deceptos, & etiamnum decipi. Equidem Stegmannus, p. 39, 40. Judici publico aliquid concedere videtur, sed ironice tantum atque deluforie. Sic enim ait: — Non tam Judici alicui publico sententiam ferendi libertatem adimimus quam Alios ut ipsius sequantur sententiam, cogendi ac puniendi Authoritatem, id est, Jus ac Potestatem, derogamus. Nos, aliosque Homines, ab illa Obligatione, qua Judici isti astricti esse dicuntur, liberatum imus. Sed hoc pacto Praevaricatorem agit dum Judicem simul admittit, & rejicit. Quomodo enim quispiam esse potest judex publicus, sine Authoritate obligandi, & cogendi quoscunque suae Jurisdictioni subditos, ut vel sententiae ab eo latae sese submittant, vel Contumaciae suae Poenam subeant? Certe potestas obligandi judici essentialis est. Alioquin, pro judice publico ludibrium publicum haberemus. Nec minus ridiculi erunt, qui Talem sibi efformant & constituunt, Titulo tenus judicem, phantasticum, precarium, scenicum; judicem sine omni Imperio, aut Potestate coactiva, quam ei expresse denegat Stegmannus; cum suo judici attribuit istiusmodi duntaxat Authoritatem, quam habent quivis viri honesti & graves erga Alios quosvis; cum primis autem Doctores erga Discentes, & Seniores erga Juniores. Paulo post item, &c. pag. 50. Arbitrum Controversiarum nobis concedit quidem; sed Qualem? Non hic disputatur, inquit, Annon in Dubiis duo litigantes Tertium aliquem, (seu totam Ecclesiam, seu quaedam ejus Membra) adire possint ut utra pars verum, utra falsum defendat, explicetur. Id enim omnes facile concedunt —modo intra Arbitrorum, seu Doctorum Terminos se contineant, id est, ut cuique si ipsi eorum Argumenta minus probentur, dissentiendi libertatem relinquant; neque ulli necessitatem quicquam Credendi, vel faciendi, sua tantum Authoritate imponant. Sic ille. At quid tum Arbiter? Cui Bono, aut in quem finem eligitur, si modo sententia illius pro mero arbitrio eligentis, aut recipi potest, aut rejici? Arbiter enim est Judex à privatis electus, sicut Judex ordinarius est publica Authoritate constitutus. Uterque autem constituitur ad finem certum litibus imponendum, adeoque necessario instrui debet Authoritate in hunc finem requisita. Certe Arbitri Authoritas in Rebus ad vitam civilem pertinentibus obligatoria est ex Consensu litigantium, ad faciendum aut dandum, ad dimittendum aut reddendum hoc vel illud. Cur non pariter in Theologicis? si minus ad Credendum, vel faciendum; saltem, ad cohibendum linguam & manum; illam, à Praedicando; Hanc, à scribendo. Quid? quod non solum quaedam membra Ecclesiae (per quas intelligere videtur illius Praepositos, vel singulos, vel in Synodo aliqua particulari congregatos) sed etiam totam Ecclesiam, sive diffusive sumptam, sive in Concilio Oecumenico coactam pariter vilipendit, dum hanc istiusmodi Arbitram facit, tum quae à privato quoquam, pro arbitrio eligi possit, vel non, ad Dubia terminanda; tum cujus sententia definitiva pro libitu item eligentis, admitti possit vel ablega-ri. Ex quo patet, quam nihili habeat Authoritatem Ecclesiae Catholicae, quae omnium vere fidelium Mater est, quam ex ipsius Christi praescripto summe revereri debemus, ejusque legibus obtemperare: quam latam quoque fenestram[?] aperiat cunctis Haereticis & Schismaticis, ad novitates suas, cum Ecclesiae Contemptu, propagandas; praecipue autem, quam adversa sint Socinianorum Dogmata Ecclesiae Christi Catholicae Doctrinae atque Decretis, cum ad illius Tribunal ea nullatenus deferri velint, aut ex ejus sententia definiri. Quo nullum certius & luculentius Documentum afferre potuit, quod nova sint, & aliena à Fide Catholica, ac proinde Haeretica.
units.tr: But can anyone endowed with sound reason think that all these qualities required for judging rightly are to be found in each and every man, whom nevertheless they make their judges in matters of faith? Are not most men carnal or merely natural, unlearned or lazy, steeped in perverse opinions or devoted to parties, stupid or wicked, blind or obstinate, worldly in the end and destitute of the Holy Spirit? Certainly men of this sort, even in the judgment of the Socinians themselves, will go wrong in judging, if they insist on following their own judgment. But if it seems good to them to choose some other judge (as in this case they certainly must), how will they make themselves secure in such a choice, since they are ignorant of this matter and therefore wholly unfit to choose? How will the blind choose a suitable guide for a journey, one who will surely direct them on the way? Without doubt, whomever they choose in this way they must choose rashly and by chance. Yet they hand themselves over to be governed and allow their judgment to be shaped as one pleases. Why then are they unwilling to look much better to their own safety, by admitting those judges whom God has given them and whom the Church itself has always approved, taught by frequent experience? Why also do they absolutely and indefinitely refuse every judge who pronounces by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and set against him a judge who follows the dictate of sound reason, as if these two were mutually contradictory? For no one of sound mind trusts enthusiasms in this business, either in himself or in others. Nor do the Papists themselves hold that the Roman Pope determines the causes brought before him by an extraordinary inspiration of the Spirit; they only assert that the Spirit of God assists him in the lawful use of the means. Indeed, what prevents us from saying that the Holy Spirit, in a certain manner and degree, is present with and assists every judge who conducts himself well in defining theological questions, whether he be a council, a bishop, or any suitable arbiter chosen by parties disputing among themselves, or some private person judging for himself by the judgment of discretion? Especially since Stegmannus himself above all requires the illumination of the Holy Spirit for judging rightly, as we have just shown. Yet on page 57 of the same little book he asserts that each man's own judgment is sufficient, provided he uses sound reason; as if all men were endowed with the Holy Spirit, each man's own judgment would be entirely sufficient. Here again he sets sound reason against the Holy Spirit. But meanwhile, by what sure judgment will sound reason be distinguished from unsound, or the true Spirit of God from the false and illusory? For how many are there who deceive both themselves and others in distinguishing either? Are the Socinians alone the proper and fit judges of right reason, when they dare to oppose not only the Catholic Church of this age but all the Church of past ages, and revive heresies always condemned by it? Are they not forced to confess that very many men, most learned and pious and endowed with remarkable gifts of mind, utterly abhor and have always abhorred their dogmas? And how does it happen that the truth has lain hidden so long from so many and such distinguished teachers of the Church? Indeed (which does far more to condemn their errors) what was the cause that, as soon as these new Socinian dogmas became known, they were at once received with the greatest hatred and horror, and did not prevail with anyone, although their most acute and ingenious patrons supported and fortified them with every argument that could be devised? Does right reason have its seat and dignity among the Socinians alone, while among all others who profess the name of Christ throughout the whole world it either wholly lies exiled or is held of no account? And who would think this, being endowed with sound reason, and who is not wise only to himself, and so must be rightly held mad by all others? But if they are so self-satisfied and immodest as to wish their own judgment to suffice for all others who think they use right reason, they prove contradictory things and at the same time think both can stand, since they agree neither with the Socinians nor with one another. How absurd this is to reason, everyone sees. Moreover, they themselves condemn above all others the Fanatics, who do nothing but boast of the Holy Spirit, and yet they wish us to test the Spirit by the judgment of right reason. This is evidence that the judgment of anyone who thinks he has the Holy Spirit, or who is thought by another to have him, does not suffice for pronouncing a sentence rightly; since in this one may easily be deceived, as is certain, for many have been deceived in it in former times and are still deceived. Indeed Stegmannus, pages 39 and 40, seems to concede something to a public judge, but only ironically and deceptively. For he says: "We do not so much take away from some public judge the freedom to pronounce sentence as we derogate from his authority to compel and punish others to follow his sentence, that is, the right and power. We free ourselves and other men from that obligation by which they are said to be bound to that judge." But in this way he acts the prevaricator, since he at the same time admits and rejects a judge. For how can anyone be a public judge without the authority to bind and compel all who are subject to his jurisdiction, either to submit to the sentence passed by him or to undergo the penalty of their contumacy? Certainly the power to bind is essential to a judge. Otherwise we would have a public laughingstock in place of a public judge. Nor less ridiculous will be those who form and set up for themselves such a judge, a judge in name only, fantastic, precarious, theatrical, a judge without any command or coercive power, which Stegmannus expressly denies him; since he attributes to his judge only that authority which any honest and serious men have over any others, and especially teachers over learners and elders over younger men. A little later also, page 50 and following, he does concede to us an arbiter of controversies; but what sort? "It is not disputed here," he says, "whether in doubtful matters two litigants may approach some third party (whether the whole Church or certain of its members) so that it may be explained which side defends the truth and which falsehood. For all readily concede this, provided they keep within the limits of arbiters or teachers, that is, that each man, if the arguments of these men seem less convincing to him, be left free to dissent, and that they impose on no one any necessity of believing or doing anything by their authority alone." Thus he. But what then of the arbiter? For what good, or to what end, is he chosen, if his sentence may be either accepted or rejected at the mere whim of the one who chose him? For an arbiter is a judge chosen by private persons, just as an ordinary judge is constituted by public authority. Yet both are appointed to put an end to disputes by a certain decision, and so must necessarily be furnished with the authority required for this end. Surely the authority of an arbiter in matters pertaining to civil life is binding by the consent of the litigants, to do or give, to let go or restore this or that. Why not equally in theological matters, if not to believe or to do, at least to restrain tongue and hand: the one from preaching, the other from writing? What is more, he not only holds cheap certain members of the Church (by which he seems to mean its prelates, either singly or gathered in some particular synod) but equally holds cheap the whole Church, whether taken diffusely or assembled in an ecumenical council, when he makes it such an arbiter that it may or may not be chosen by any private person at will to end doubts, and its definitive sentence may likewise be admitted or rejected at the pleasure of the one who chose it. From this it is plain how little authority he gives the Catholic Church, which is the mother of all truly faithful, whom we ought to revere above all by Christ's own command and obey her laws; how wide a window he opens to all heretics and schismatics for spreading their novelties with contempt for the Church; and above all how adverse the dogmas of the Socinians are to the doctrine and decrees of the Catholic Church of Christ, since they will not in any way have them brought before her tribunal or defined by her sentence. No more certain and clearer proof could be offered that they are new, alien to the Catholic faith, and therefore heretical.

units.la: §. 45. Secundo, Sociniani ipsi soli judices esse volunt, quid sit iniquum & Injustum, Inhonestum item in se, ac Naturae Divinae incongruum. Unde Quicquid hujus Generis sibi apparet in S. Scriptura Deo attributum, Illud omne commoda, ut vocant, Interpretatione, in alium sensum convertunt. At revera, hanc licentiam sibi assumunt, non tam ut Deo suum Honorem integrum servent, quam ut Hypothesi suae serviant, & praeconceptae alicui O-pinioni astipulentur; ad quam confirmandam at-que tutandam, verba illius Dei, cujus Honorem prae se ferunt, in sensum à vero alienum detorquent. Nam si veritati tuendae consulerent, verba Dei ita interpretari debuerunt, ut nihil afferrent in Praejudicium seu violationem aut illius Sensus, quem verba Contextus sacri aperte prae se ferunt, & qui in aliis Scripturae locis pro genuino agnoscitur; aut sensus Ecclesiae Catholicae, sive Doctrinae eidem ab Origine traditae, quam semper & ubique apud se retinuit. Neque satis putant S. Scripturam in hac re pervertere ad suam Sententiam confirmandam. Similem quoque licentiam sibi sumunt, in aliis S. Paginæ locis ad suam mentem interpretandis, sive quæ Dogmatibus suis favere videntur, sive adversari. E. G. Ante quam Abraham erat, ego sum. Jo: 8. 58. id est, inquiunt illi, Antequam factus fuerit Abraham, sc. Pater spiritualis multarum Gentium, per prædicationem Evangelii in toto Orbe, & fidem ei datam, ego sum lux mundi, sive veni lux in mundum. Verba illa Thomæ ad Christum, Dominus meus, & Deus meus. Jo: 20. 28. Exponit Eniedinus, non de Christo, quasi ad eum dirigerentur, sed per modum Exclamationis ad Deum Patrem directa, quali mi solemus, cum mirum quiddam & inopinatum Nobis ex improviso occurrit. Verba Christi ad latronem, Amen dico tibi, Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso Luc: 23. 43. ita peruertunt, ponendo comma post Hodie. Dico tibi hodie, mecum eris in Paradiso, viz: Tunc, cum ad Judicium venero. Illud Evangelistæ Joannis, In principio erat Verbum. Jo: 1. 1. Exponunt de Principio Evangelii prædicati. Illud item Psalmistæ, Tu in principio, Domine, Terram fundasti, & Cœli sunt opera manuum tuarum, Psal: 102. 25. quod Apostolus diserte applicat Christo Dei Filio. Hebr. 1. 10. vel Deo Patri tribuunt contra Textus istius cohærentiam cum præcedentibus, vel interpretantur de Mundo, non primitus creato, sed per Christum renovato sub Evangelio. Adde huc Illud Franc: Davidis, qui Socini Dogmati insistens de Christo solo Homine, negavit eum Precibus ad se directis invocandum. Hic enim eam Stephani Proto-martyris orationem, ad Christum hisce verbis directam, Domine Jesu, suscipe Animam meam. Act: 7.
units.tr: §. 45. Secondly, the Socinians want to be the sole judges of what is unjust and iniquitous, and likewise of what is dishonourable in itself and incongruous with the divine nature. So whatever of this kind appears to them to be attributed to God in Holy Scripture, they turn into another sense by what they call commoda Interpretatione, a convenient interpretation. In truth, they assume this licence not so much to keep God's honour intact as to serve their own hypothesis and to support some preconceived opinion. To confirm and defend it, they twist the words of that God whose honour they profess, into a sense foreign to the truth. For if they were concerned to defend the truth, they ought to interpret the words of God so that they did nothing to prejudice or violate either the sense which the words of the sacred context plainly display, and which is acknowledged as the genuine one in other passages of Scripture, or the sense of the Catholic Church, that is, the doctrine handed down to it from the beginning, which it has always and everywhere retained. Nor do they think it enough to pervert Scripture in this matter in order to confirm their own opinion. They take a similar licence in interpreting other passages of the sacred page to suit their own mind, whether they seem to favour their dogmas or to oppose them. For example: "Before Abraham was, I am" (Jn 8:58). That is, they say, before Abraham was made, namely the spiritual father of many nations, through the preaching of the Gospel in the whole world and the faith given to him, I am the light of the world, or I came as the light into the world. The words of Thomas to Christ, My Lord and my God (Jn 20:28), Enedinus explains not as addressed to Christ, but as an exclamation directed to God the Father, such as we are wont to make when something strange and unexpected suddenly meets us. The words of Christ to the thief, "Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise" (Lk 23:43), they pervert by placing the comma after "today": I say to you today, you will be with me in Paradise, namely then, when I come to judgement. The saying of the Evangelist John, "In the beginning was the Word" (Jn 1:1), they explain as referring to the beginning of the Gospel as preached. Likewise the words of the Psalmist, "You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands" (Ps 102:25), which the Apostle expressly applies to Christ the Son of God (Heb. 1:10), they either attribute to God the Father, against the coherence of that text with what precedes, or interpret as referring to the world, not first created, but renewed through Christ under the Gospel. Add to these the case of Francis David, who, following the Socinian dogma that Christ was only a man, denied that he was to be invoked with prayers addressed to him. For he rendered that prayer of Stephen the protomartyr, addressed to Christ in these words, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (Acts 7:59), as follows: O God the Father, who art the Lord of Jesus, receive my spirit. There are almost countless other passages of Scripture in whose exposition they play impiously and absurdly, and try to mock their readers, while they most wretchedly twist them, to establish their own dogmas or to evade the arguments of the orthodox. Moreover, in this, as in very many other matters, they pay no heed at all to the dictate of right reason. For reason bids us accept that sense of the words of Scripture which is much more common and is acknowledged elsewhere where the same matter is treated, and which agrees better with the purpose of the sacred writer, the coherence of the words, the circumstances of the cited passage, and the subject under discussion there. These people, however, demand that preference be given to a sense that is new and unheard of in the Church of God; indeed, one that is contrary to its judgement, distorted and monstrous, and plainly opposed to the analogy of faith, once received and retained through so many centuries. This is especially so if, to bring about this interpretation, words, letters, clauses and other points are changed and transposed, with the strokes of the letters altered, so that the context is transformed and made capable of a new and alien sense, the old and orthodox one being excluded. And this is made all the more blameworthy because such alteration is made not only without the authority of the manuscripts, but even against the testimony of those readings which are held to be the most ancient and best and are everywhere received in the Church, and also against the witness of the most ancient versions, which the primitive Church received and handed down to posterity. Indeed, whoever demands that a new sense of Scripture be admitted, against the judgement of the Church at present and the doctrine commonly received among Christians, must, in order to win credence for this sense, bring forward very strong reasons, both to overturn the commonly received sense and to establish that new one and put it in the place of the old. Otherwise, by no right at all and with no semblance of fairness, can he demand our assent.

units.la: Sic exponit, O Deus Pater, qui es Dominus Iesu, suscipe animam meam. Innumera fere alia sunt S. Scripturæ loca, in quibus exponendis impie & absurde ludunt, suisque lectoribus illudere conantur, dum ad Dogmata sua astruendæ, vel Argumenta Orthodoxorum declinanda, illa miserrime detorquent. Cæterum in hoc, ut in Aliis quamplurimis, rectæ Rationis Dictamini minime obsequuntur. Hæc enim jubet ut iste sensus Verborum S. Scripturæ recipiatur, & præ Cæteris omnibus valeat, qui multo usitatior est & alibi agnitus, ubi de eadem materia tractatur; qui etiam scopo S. Scriptoris, Cohærentiæ verborum, Circumstantiis loci allegati, & Subjecto, de quo isthic disseritur, melius aptiusque convenit. Hic sane postulat, ut præferatur illi sensui qui novus & inauditus est in Ecclesia Dei; imo contrarius illius Judicio, detortus atque monstrosus, Fideique Analogiæ, olim receptæ, & per tot secula retentæ, plane adversus. Præsertim, si ad vim huic Expositioni parandam, Verba, literæ, Commata, aliaque Puncta, cum literarum apicibus mutentur atque transferantur, quæ S. Contextus Metamorphosin faciant; eumque ita transformant, ut novi & alieni sensus capacem reddant, exclusò Vetere & Orthodoxo. Atque hoc eo culpabilius redditur, quod hujusmodi Mutatio fiat, non solum sine Authoritate exemplarium, sed & contra fidem eorum, quæ vetustissima & optima habentur, & passim in Ecclesia recepta sunt; necnon, contra fidem Versionum antiquissimarum, quas Ecclesia primitiva recepit, & ad Posteros transmisit. Enimvero quicunque postulat, ut novus S. Scripturæ sensus admittatur, contra Judicium præsentis Ecclesiæ, & Doctrinam vulgo inter Christianos receptam; necesse habet ad fidem huic sensui conciliandam, Rationes validissimas afferre, tum quae sensum communiter receptum subvertant, tum quae novum istud stabiliant, veterisque loco substituant. Alioquin, nullo omnino Jure, nulla prorsus Æquitatis specie, Assensum nostrum potest exigere.
units.tr: He expounds it thus: O God the Father, who art the Lord Jesus, receive my soul. There are almost countless other passages of Holy Scripture which they handle impiously and absurdly, and which they try to mock their readers with, twisting them most wretchedly in order to establish their own doctrines or to evade the arguments of the Orthodox. In this, as in very many other cases, they also fail to comply with the dictate of right reason. For reason bids that this sense of the words of Holy Scripture be accepted and prevail over all others: the one which is much more common and is acknowledged elsewhere where the same matter is treated, and which also agrees better and more fittingly with the purpose of the Holy Writer, the coherence of the words, the circumstances of the passage cited, and the subject under discussion there. Here, however, they demand that preference be given to a sense which is new and unheard of in the Church of God; indeed, one which is contrary to its judgment, distorted and monstrous, and plainly opposed to the analogy of the faith, once received and retained through so many ages. This holds especially if, to bring about this interpretation, words, letters, clauses and other points are altered and shifted, along with the marks over the letters, so that they transform the holy context and make it capable of a new and foreign sense, the old and orthodox one being excluded. And this is made all the more blameworthy because such a change is made not only without the authority of manuscripts, but also against the witness of those which are held to be the most ancient and best, and are generally received in the Church; and likewise against the witness of the most ancient versions, which the primitive Church received and handed down to posterity. Indeed, whoever demands that a new sense of Holy Scripture be admitted, against the judgment of the Church present and the doctrine commonly received among Christians, is bound to bring very strong reasons to win assent to that sense: both reasons which overturn the commonly received sense, and reasons which establish that new one and put it in the place of the old. Otherwise, by no right at all and with no semblance of fairness, can he demand our assent.

units.la: §. 46. Tertio, Ratio sana sufficit, inquit, ad ejusmodi Cognitionem, quae ad Salutem, vel nostram, vel Aliorum promovendam sufficit. p. 159. Si quidem hoc intelligatur de Ratione humana non illuminata, S. Scriptura palam contradicit, quae interiorem Spiritus S. illuminationem multoties requirit ad Doctrinam salutis rite intelligendam, ut antehac ostendimus; necnon, ad fidem ingenerandam, sine qua nuda cognitio non est salutaris. Idem tamen, p. 138. inter Satanae Artificia ponit Theologorum nostrorum Sententiam, qui prohibent; quo minus Scripturae humano subjiciantur Judicio; neque quisquam immensos Religionis agros Rationis Decempeda metiri ausit. Cum vero Apostolus diserte affirmet, Hominem psychicum sive animalem non capere ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei, neque posse cognoscere, quia spiritualiter discernuntur; stultitiam autem ei esse.
units.tr: §. 46. Thirdly, he says, sound reason is sufficient for that kind of knowledge which suffices to promote salvation, either our own or that of others. p. 159. If this is understood of unenlightened human reason, Holy Scripture plainly contradicts it, since it many times requires the inner illumination of the Holy Spirit for the doctrine of salvation to be rightly understood, as we have shown above; and also for faith to be produced, without which bare knowledge is not saving. Yet the same author, p. 138, counts among Satan's devices the opinion of our theologians who forbid Scripture to be subjected to human judgment, and who say that no one dares to measure the immense fields of religion with the rod of reason. But the Apostle plainly affirms that the psychic or natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned; and that they are foolishness to him.

units.la: 1 Cor. 2. 14. sic interpretatur haec verba idem Stegmannus, sc. p. 145. Postquam Homo psychicus Dei verbum audivit, Talis esse definit. Deinde pergit. Hoc inde tantum sequitur; quod ejus Hominis Ratio, qui verbum Dei nunquam audivit, id ipsum, antequam audiat, cognoscere & dijudicare nequeat, cum non nisi Principia naturalia, Ipsi perspecta sint. Sic Ille. At satis constat unicuique locum istum serio inspicienti quod Apostolus ibi loquatur de tali Psychico, cui verbum Dei in Evangelio jam propositum est. Quomodo enim spiritualia illic memorata ei stultitia videri possunt, priusquam mentis suae Oculis objecta sint, & Illorum stultitiam prout ipsi tunc apparet, habeat sibi expositam? Etenim antequam hoc fiat, nullum omnino Iudicium de iis ferre potest, cum ea prorsus ignoret. De ignotis autem nemo judicare potest, aut Censuram ferre. Apostolus insuper affirmat, ea quae sunt spiritus Dei non posse ab eo sciri, quia spiritualiter discernuntur; Spiritualis autem judicat omnia. Ex quo apparet, hujus scientiae Impedimentum, sive Ignorantiae Causam, non esse positam in defectu Objecti proponendi, sed in defectu luminis spiritualis, quod Mentis Oculos illustret ad Objectum propositum rite discernendum. Paulo supra quoque dixit Apostolus-se [?] loqui Sapientiam in mysterio, quam nemo Principum hujus seculi novit; si enim novissent, Dominum Gloriae non crucifixissent. v. 7,8. Certum autem est ex Evangelica Historia, Verbum externum Evangelii auribus eorum insonuisse & tum Judaeorum, tum Gentilium Principibus satis clare propositum fuisse. At hanc Sapientiam dei mysticam, per Christum in Evangelio revelatam, Neutri interim sciverunt, eo quod non essent Illuminati, Spirituales, Perfecti. Unde idem Apostolus ibidem ait v. 6. Sapientiam loquimur inter, seu, apud Perfectos. Pergit autem Stegmanus in Sententia sua confirmanda dum sic exponit, non capere. v. 14. Non enim inquit, habet sensum quasi si non possit homo animalis percipere seu intelligere mentem Spiritus dei, & quid sibi velit. Hoc enim illi repugnat quod stultum esse judicet. Ergo, ut cognoverit [?] necesse est. Non Capere ergo est, non Admittere, Approbare, Accipere. Sic ille. At ut hoc el [?] concedamus. Hoc non Admittere, seu non Approbare, ex eo procedit, quod non recte intelligat quæ sint Spiritus Dei. Aliud enim est, literalem verborum sensum intelligere; aliud autem, mentem Dicentis scopumque perspicere, cum Authoritate ejusdem, qua Auditores obligat ad fidem Dictis suis adhibendam; præstantiam item atque utilitatem summam Rerum ab Ipso dictarum, cum necessitate easdem admittendi, quæ omnibus incumbit, qui salutem æternam consequi volunt. Illud quidem Homini animali competit, hoc non item. Nam si bene intelligeret, quis loqueretur, nempe Spiritus Dei; Quid item sibi velit in eo quod loquatur; Præstantiam quoque Dictorum rite perpenderet, cum fide & obedientia, quas iisdem præstare tenetur, Illud minime ei Stultum videretur, quod hoc modo proponitur.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2. 14. Stegmann interprets these words thus, p. 145: After the psychic man has heard the word of God, he defines him as such. Then he goes on: From this only it follows that the reason of that man who has never heard the word of God cannot know and judge that very thing before he hears it, since only natural principles are known to him. Thus he. But it is quite clear to anyone who examines that passage carefully that the Apostle there speaks of such a psychic man, to whom the word of God has already been set forth in the Gospel. For how can the things spoken of there seem foolish to him before they have been placed before the eyes of his mind, and before their foolishness, as it then appears to him, has been set out for him? Indeed, before this happens he can form no judgment about them at all, since he is wholly ignorant of them. But no one can judge or pass censure on what is unknown. The Apostle further affirms that the things of the Spirit of God cannot be known by him, because they are spiritually discerned, whereas the spiritual man judges all things. From this it appears that the hindrance to this knowledge, or the cause of the ignorance, lies not in a lack of the object proposed but in a lack of spiritual light, which should illumine the eyes of the mind to discern rightly the object set before it. A little above, the Apostle also said that he speaks wisdom in a mystery, which none of the princes of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. vv. 7, 8. It is certain, however, from the Gospel history that the external word of the Gospel had sounded in their ears and had been set clearly before both the rulers of the Jews and those of the Gentiles. Yet neither of them knew this mystical wisdom of God, revealed in the Gospel through Christ, because they were not enlightened, spiritual, or perfect. Whence the same Apostle says in the same place, v. 6: We speak wisdom among the perfect. Stegmann goes on to confirm his opinion by expounding the words not to receive, v. 14: For he does not have sense, as if the psychic man could not perceive or understand the mind of the Spirit of God and what it means. For this is repugnant to him, since he judges it foolish. Therefore it is necessary for him to know. Not to receive, therefore, is not to admit, approve, accept. Thus he. But even granting this, not admitting or not approving follows from the fact that he does not rightly understand what the things of the Spirit of God are. For it is one thing to understand the literal sense of the words, and another to perceive the mind and aim of the speaker, together with the authority by which he binds his hearers to give faith to his words; likewise the excellence and supreme usefulness of the things he has said, together with the necessity of admitting them, which lies upon all who wish to obtain eternal salvation. The former indeed belongs to the animal man, the latter does not. For if he understood rightly who speaks, namely the Spirit of God; and what he means by what he says; and weighed rightly the excellence of his words, together with the faith and obedience which he is bound to render to them, then what is proposed in this way would not seem foolish to him.

units.la: §. 47. Quarto, Idem Stegmannus de Cognitione Dei Patris, & Christi loquens, hæc habet: Etsi id omnino à nobis requiritur, ut Deum, ejusque Filium cognoscamus, non est tamen cognitio Essentiæ aut Naturæ Divinæ, sed voluntatis, id est, Promissorum & Præceptorum. Sic ille, p. 153, eadem habet Socinus in folio Scrup. 30. ab excellenti quodam viro propositorum, viz. Resp. ad primum p. 327. Tom. 1. At è contra, sine dubio requiritur à nobis, ut cognoscamus, non solum voluntatem, sed & naturam utriusque, quæ & qualis sit, quousque[?] & in quantum Deus eam revelare dignatus est. Nam ex vera hujus notitia, quam maxime pendet Honor & cultus utriusque debitus. Unde enim fluxit omnis illa Idololatria atq; superstitio, quæ olim apud omnes fere Gentes regnabant, atque hodie in plerisque regnant, nisi ex ignorantia veri Dei, Christique Filii ejus? Si enim probe nossent Homines, Deum verum esse unicum & supremum, substantiam spiritualem, invisibilem, & incomprehensibilem, cæterisque attributis ornatam, quibus naturam suam nobis in verbo suo manifestare visum est, nunquam ad tot Idola se convertissent, aut cultum numinis tot superstitionibus corrupissent, quæ Impietatem summam, sævitiam, nefandasque libidines in mores Hominum passim invexerunt. Hinc enim factum est, ut numen Divinum, ejusque cultus, aliis ludibrio & Contemptui foret; Aliis autem, odio & Horrori. Et si eadem Gentes cum Judæis, pro certo nollent, quis & qualis fuerit Jesus ille Nazarenus, quem nos pro Filio Dei unigenito, & Messia illo, Patribus olim promisso habemus atque veneramur, nunquam Evangelium illius repudiassent, nonnenque[?] Christianum prorsus abolere studuissent. Imo si ipsi Sociniani Naturam Divinam, ut oportet, cognovissent, neque unquam ei detraxissent perfectiones ei connatas, Omniscientiam &c. & Omnipræsentiam, quas sapientiores Ethnici in eo lubenter agnoverunt; neque Affectus humanos, Consiliorum mutationem, variasque voluntatis commotiones eidem tribuissent, quæ Imperfectionis Indicia sunt. Idem dici potest de Ignorantia Christi Filii, & Spiritus Sancti, quorum naturas si Sociniani, aliique Sectarii rite perspexissent, nunquam in tot impias & monstrosas Hæreses incidissent.
units.tr: §. 47. Fourthly, the same Stegmann, speaking of the knowledge of God the Father and of Christ, says this: Although it is entirely required of us that we know God and his Son, it is not a knowledge of the Essence or Nature of God, but of his will, that is, of the promises and precepts. So he writes, p. 153. Socinus has the same thing in folio, Scrup. 30, proposed by a certain excellent man, namely in his Reply to the first, p. 327, Tom. 1. On the contrary, however, it is without doubt required of us that we know not only the will but also the nature of each of them, what and of what kind it is, and how far God has deigned to reveal it. For true knowledge of this is what chiefly determines the honour and worship due to each. Whence else did all that idolatry and superstition arise, which once reigned among almost all the Gentiles and today reigns among most of them, if not from ignorance of the true God and of Christ his Son? For if men had properly known that God is one and supreme, a spiritual, invisible and incomprehensible substance, adorned with the other attributes by which it has pleased him to make his nature manifest to us in his Word, they would never have turned to so many idols, nor corrupted the worship of the deity with so many superstitions, which have everywhere introduced the greatest impiety, savagery and unspeakable lusts into human morals. For from this it came about that the divine majesty and its worship were an object of mockery and contempt to some, and of hatred and horror to others. And if the same Gentiles, together with the Jews, had not been certain of who and what kind of man that Jesus of Nazareth was, whom we hold and venerate as the only begotten Son of God and as that Messiah promised of old to the Fathers, they would never have rejected his Gospel, nor sought utterly to abolish even the very name of Christian. Indeed, if the Socinians themselves had known the divine nature as they ought, they would never have taken from it the perfections innate to it, omniscience and so on, and omnipresence, which the wiser Gentiles gladly acknowledged in it; nor would they have ascribed to it human affections, changes of counsel and varying movements of the will, which are signs of imperfection. The same can be said of their ignorance of the Son of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, whose natures, if the Socinians and other sectaries had properly examined, they would never have fallen into so many impious and monstrous heresies.

units.la: §. 48. Quinto, Idem p. 201. &c. prolixe disputans contra corruptionem Rationis humanæ ex lapsu Adami, quam Theologi nostri, cum veteribus, asserunt, eam his verbis denegat, & à nobis pariter denegari vult: --Ratio, inquit, post lapsum, Officium suum facere potest, ut aliæ facultates. Nunc etiam post lapsum in omnibus Hominibus, non magis ad naturalia, quam ad Spiritualia determinata est; neque minus ad Divina, quam ad Humana percipienda & dijudicanda per se accommodatur: Differentia, non nisi in Principiis, ac Revelationis modo, ac Tractationis raritate aut frequentia consistit. Id. p. 206. Quaedam concupiscentia mali, ut Seminis Parentum, transfunditur in Posteros --sed hac fuit in Adamo, Evaque ante lapsum. Concupiverunt enim fructum vetitum, antequam comederunt ---Hac concupiscentia, in quibus inest, in aliis major, in Aliis minor est. Praterea, honesta Educatione & studio corrigi, ac plane tolli potest --Illud ab omni aequitate & justitia remotissimum est, adeoque Deo sine Blasphemia attribui nequit, quod propter primum illud Adami Peccatum, omnes Posteros puniverit, cum innocentes illi hactenus fuerint. Neque enim consentire, neque quicquam ad factum illud conferre, cum nondum essent, potuerunt. Sic ille. At haec illius Postulata contraria sunt verbis S. Scripturae, prout hactenus expolita fuerunt à cunctis Ecclesiae Doctoribus; ac proinde jampridem damnata sunt in Pelagianis, ejusdem Ecclesiae sententia; idque synodis quampluribus, per totum orbem Christianum exinde receptis, & approbatis. Et sane, si S. Scripturas oculo simplici consulere velimus, quam ubique fere reperiemus statum Gentilium ante conversionem ad fidem Christi, veramque veri Dei notitiam, dici statum Ignorantiae atq; Tenebrarum, Evangelio nondum eis illucescente. Imo, ipsi Gentilium philosophi, qui acutissimo Ingenio, & multiplici eruditione pollebant, non solum cum vulgo desipuerunt, sed & ei praeiverunt in superstitiocio cultu fingendo, Morumque corruptela. Cum profiterentur se esse Sapientes, ait Apostolus, stulti facti sunt Rom: 1. 22. Et mutarunt Gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in similitudinem Imaginis corruptibilis Hominis, volucrum, & quadrupedum, & reptilium. v. 23. Propterea tradidit etiam Illos Deus cupiditatibus Cordium Ipsorum, in immunditiam. v. 24. Sed, veleo tacente, experientia crebra hoc idem plus satis evinceret, cum unicuique lectori vulgo notum sit, quam variis Opinionibus fuerint inter se difcisli, quae non minus cum veritate, quam secum pugnarunt. Atque haec opinionum Repugnantia cernebatur, non solum in levioribus quibusdam Dogmatibus, (quod facilius ferri potuit) sed in Rebus maximi Momenti, viz: de natura Dei, & Animae humanae, de origine Mundi, de Providentia, de summo item Hominis bono, & Mediis ad illud assequendum conducentibus. Ex his autem satis liquet, Rationem humanam, in Divinis praesertim ac spiritualibus, infirmatam esse atque corruptam; ita ut ea non adeo certo atque clare perspicere possit, deque iis suum Judicium ferre, ac perspicit atque dijudicat naturalia & humana, quae sibi multo p[?]opiora sunt magisque familiaria. Atque hoc, ex parte saltem, prius agnoverat ipse Stegmannus --Non negamus, inquit, Naturalia Ratione humana familiariora[?], & perfectiora, esse Divina. Ea enim ex Rerum ipsa natura Ratio ipsa observavit, collegit, & constituit. Divina vero Dei intellectu jam constituta accipit. Illa crassiora sunt, & circa ea, ab ineunte statim aetate, ac sine Intermissione, versatur Ratio. Hac vero subtiliora sunt, & vel tarda, vel raro, vel segniter intellectui offeruntur; ut mirum non sit, non aeque promptam esse Rationem &c. Hæc Ille, p. 99.
units.tr: §. 48. Fifthly, the same author, at length, p. 201 and following, disputing against the corruption of human reason from the fall of Adam, which our theologians, with the ancients, affirm, denies it in these words, and wants us likewise to deny it: --Reason, he says, after the fall can perform its office, as other faculties can. Now also after the fall in all men, it is determined no more to natural things than to spiritual ones; nor is it by itself less suited to perceive and judge divine things than human ones: the difference consists only in the principles, in the mode of revelation, and in the rarity or frequency of its exercise. The same, p. 206: A certain concupiscence of evil, like that of the parents' seed, is transmitted to the posterity --but this was in Adam and Eve before the fall. For they desired the forbidden fruit before they ate it --This concupiscence, in those in whom it is present, is greater in some and smaller in others. Moreover, it can be corrected and altogether removed by honest upbringing and effort --It is most remote from all equity and justice, and therefore cannot be attributed to God without blasphemy, that on account of that first sin of Adam he should have punished all the posterity, who until then had been innocent. For they could neither consent to it nor contribute anything to that deed, since they did not yet exist. Thus he. But these assertions of his are contrary to the words of Holy Scripture, as they have hitherto been set forth by all the teachers of the Church; and therefore they have long since been condemned in the Pelagians by the judgment of the same Church, and this by many synods received and approved through the whole Christian world since then. And indeed, if we wish to consult the Holy Scriptures with a simple eye, we shall find almost everywhere that the state of the Gentiles before their conversion to the faith of Christ and the true knowledge of the true God is called a state of ignorance and darkness, the Gospel not yet having shone upon them.
