Indeed, the Gentile philosophers themselves, who excelled in the keenest intellect and manifold learning, not only went astray with the common people, but even led the way for them in devising superstitious worship and corruption of morals. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, says the Apostle, Rom. 1. 22. And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things. v. 23. Therefore God also gave them up to the lusts of their own hearts, to uncleanness. v. 24. But even if I were silent, frequent experience would prove this same thing more than enough, since it is commonly known to every reader how greatly they were divided among themselves by their various opinions, which contended no less with truth than with one another. And this discord of opinions was seen not only in some lesser dogmas (which could be borne more easily), but in matters of the greatest weight: concerning the nature of God and of the human soul, concerning the origin of the world, concerning providence, likewise concerning the chief good of man and the means leading to its attainment. From these things it is sufficiently clear that human reason, especially in divine and spiritual matters, is weakened and corrupted, so that it cannot see so certainly and clearly, nor form and pass its judgment on these, as it sees and judges natural and human things, which are much closer and more familiar to it. And this, at least in part, Stegmann himself had earlier acknowledged: --We do not deny, he says, that divine things are more familiar and perfect to human reason than natural ones. For reason itself has observed, gathered and constituted these from the very nature of things. But divine things it receives already constituted by the understanding of God. The former are coarser, and reason is occupied with them from the very beginning of life, and without interruption. The latter are more subtle, and are offered to the understanding either slowly, or rarely, or sluggishly; so it is no wonder that reason is not equally ready &c. So he, p. 99.

units.la: §. 42. Sexto, Idem Stegmannus Cap. 8. cui Titulum facit, De Abusu Rationis, non vult Hoc ad Respondentem omnino spectare, ut Thelin suam confirmet. Postulat autem hunc Respondendi modum probari, quo dicitur, posse verba ab opponente adducta, alio, ac ille voluit, modo, intelligi. Sunt, inquit, qui acerbiore Sarcasmo hoc Responsum solent accipere, egregia Ratio. Verba alio modo accipi possunt, ergo absunt[?], ergo hoc modo non possunt. At, inquit, Opponentis Consequentia statuitur necessaria, cujus mi-nimum Contradictoria falsa sit. Necessarium autem est, quod aliter esse non potest. Ergo, quod aliter esse potest, non est necessarium. Ostenso autem, Opponentis consequentiam non esse necessariam, Illius conclusionem exinde non vere[?] colligi, sequitur. Sic ille. Hac vero, Ratione recta minime suffragante, concedi sibi postulat. Nam primo, Ad Respondentem spectat, Thesin quam defendit idoneis Argumentis confirmare, æque ac Opponentis Argumenta enervare, quæ in contrarium afferri solent. Hoc enim usu venit in solennioribus Disputationibus, ut status Quæstionis ad discutiendum propositæ rite ponatur, Termini elucidentur, certæ demum Theses di-stincte exhibeantur, & Rationibus appositis sigillatim confirmentur. Deinde, Quicunque vult novas Theses asserere, contra receptam Ecclesiæ Doctrinam, ex æquo & bono tenetur, eædem validis Argumentis firmare quæ eo usque præpolleant, ut evertendis istius Doctrinæ Fundamentis sufficiant. Aliter, nemo sanus illis permovebitur ad deferendum Fidei Dogmata, olim tradita, & communi-ter approbata. Hæc enim quodam Præscriptionis jure, sedem quam nacta sunt, tenent, donec vi aliqua majore extrudantur, sc: vel Rationis ex re-rum ipsarum natura petitæ, vel Authoritatis extrinsecus accedentis. Notum quoque est illud, & vulgo receptum in Scholis, Affirmantis est Probare. Sociniani autem in Thesium suarum Defensione, non se teneri putant, ut demonstrent alteram Praemis-[?]sarum ab opponente allatarum esse falsam, aut Illius Contradictoriam esse veram. Sed hoc satis esse existimant, ut ostendant, eam non esse necessario ac demonstrative veram. Denique, miserrimum sane est, & maximè ridiculum Socinianorum effugium, (quicquid è contra videtur Stegmanno) cum Argumento aliquo premuntur è S. literis deprompto, dicere, verba ab Opponente adducta, posse alio modo accipi, ideoque suo ipsorum sensu accipi debere, non autem in sensu Opponentis. Siquidem Conclusio bene sequitur ex valde Probabilibus, (ut saepissime fit) non autem ex solis Necessariis. Tum enim omnis Syllogismus esset Demonstrativus. Idcirco iure valere debet Conclusio ista, quæ ex probabilibus Præmissis infertur, quamdiu alia Propositio, vel magis, vel saltem æque probabilis, non asseritur ut contrarium. Etenim, si Argumentum æque probabile ex adverso asseratur, neutri Argumento dabitur assensus, sed mens pendebit quasi in æquilibrio. Sin magis Probabile asseratur, eo vergét assensus, & Dubitatio animi Fluctuantis tolletur. Neque enim Certitudo in Puncto consistit, sed latitudinem suam habet, Gradusque distinctos: multi enim sunt Præponderationis Gradus. Unde fit, ut, quam primum alterutrius partis Rationes præponderant, certitudo fiat, & Animus extra Dubitationem ponatur. Quod & ipse Stegmannus alibi sua sponte fatetur; nec tacetur solum, sed & demonstrare conatur ex collatione Bilancis, ut paulo supra ex eo ostendimus.
units.tr: §. 42. Sixthly, the same Stegmann, in chapter 8, which he entitles On the Abuse of Reason, does not want this to apply at all to the Respondent, so that he should confirm his thesis. He demands, however, that this method of replying be approved, by which it is said that the words adduced by the opponent can be understood in another way than he intended. There are, he says, those who take this reply with bitter sarcasm, as an admirable argument. The words can be taken in another way, therefore they are absurd, therefore they cannot be taken in this way. But, he says, the opponent's consequence is held to be necessary, whose contradictory minimum would be false. Now that is necessary which cannot be otherwise. Therefore what can be otherwise is not necessary. But once it is shown that the opponent's consequence is not necessary, it follows that his conclusion is not rightly drawn from it. Thus he. But this method, since right reason does not support it at all, he demands be granted to him. For first, it is for the Respondent to confirm the thesis he defends with suitable arguments, just as to weaken the opponent's arguments, which are usually brought against it. For it happens in more solemn disputations that the state of the question proposed for discussion is properly laid down, the terms are explained, the definite theses are finally set forth distinctly, and confirmed one by one with the arguments applied. Next, whoever wishes to assert new theses against the received doctrine of the Church is bound, in fairness and justice, to confirm them with strong arguments, such as are powerful enough to overthrow the foundations of that doctrine. Otherwise, no sane man will be moved by them to abandon the dogmas of the faith, handed down of old and commonly approved. For these hold their place by a certain right of prescription, which they have gained, until they are thrust out by some greater force, namely either by reason drawn from the nature of things themselves, or by authority coming from outside. It is also well known, and commonly received in the schools, that the one who affirms must prove. The Socinians, however, in defending their theses, do not think they are bound to demonstrate either that one of the premises adduced by the opponent is false, or that its contradictory is true. They think it is enough to show that it is not necessarily and demonstrably true. Finally, it is truly most wretched, and most ridiculous, a Socinian evasion (whatever Stegmann may think to the contrary), when they are pressed with some argument drawn from Holy Scripture, to say that the words adduced by the opponent can be taken in another way, and therefore must be taken in their own sense and not in the sense of the opponent. For a conclusion follows well from very probable premises (as very often happens), not only from necessary ones. Otherwise every syllogism would be demonstrative. Therefore that conclusion which is inferred from probable premises ought rightly to stand, as long as another proposition, either more or at least equally probable, is not asserted as the contrary. For if an argument equally probable is put forward on the other side, assent will be given to neither argument, but the mind will hang as if in equilibrium. But if a more probable one is put forward, assent will incline to it, and the doubt of the wavering mind will be removed. For certainty does not consist in a point, but has its breadth and distinct degrees: for there are many degrees of preponderance. Whence it comes about that as soon as the reasons of one side preponderate, certainty arises and the mind is placed beyond doubt. This Stegmann himself elsewhere admits of his own accord; and not only admits it, but also tries to demonstrate it from a comparison of the balance, as we showed a little above from him.

units.la: §. 50. Septimo, Idem media violenta, nullo omnino casu adhiberi vult, in Religionis negotio. Sic enim ille disserit. Siquis Argumentorum robore, vi Conscientiā[?], amore alterius &c: ad aliquid faciendum cogi dicitur, voluntatis Libertas relinquitur; quod repudiare si vellet, posset. At siquis neget Religionem, evitandæ causa Carceris, exilii, Infamiæ, proscriptionis, Bonorum, Mortisve ipsius potuisset quidem non abnegare, sed potius mala illa perpeti, & propterea excusandus non est. Quia tamen illa Media violenta sunt, ob id ipsum eorum adhibendorum jus nullis Judici in Religionis negotio conceditur. p. 42, 43. At bona pace Stegmanni, hæc Illius Assertio, neque in Omnibus valet, neque erga omnes. Equidem Infidelium Conversio, qui adhuc sunt[?] extra Ecclesiam, non est violentis mediis attentanda.
units.tr: §. 50. Seventhly, the same author wants violent means to be used in no case whatever in matters of religion. He argues thus: "If anyone is said to be compelled to do something by the strength of arguments, by the force of conscience, by love of another, and so on, freedom of the will is left to him, since he could refuse. But if anyone, to avoid prison, exile, infamy, outlawry, loss of goods, or death itself, denies his religion, he could indeed have refused to deny it, but would rather have endured those evils, and therefore is not to be excused. Yet because those are violent means, for that very reason no judge is granted the right to use them in matters of religion." Stegmann, pp. 42, 43. But with all respect to Stegmann, this assertion of his holds neither in all cases nor against all people. Certainly the conversion of unbelievers, who are still outside the Church, is not to be attempted by violent means.

units.la: At Res paulo aliter se habet in iis, qui Fidem Christi jam suscepterunt, & per Baptismum in illius Ecclesiam cooptati sunt. Æquum enim est, ut tunc se submittant legibus tum Ecclesiæ istius, tum Rei-publicæ Christianæ, cujus membra facta sunt, Cujusque Patrocinio fruuntur. Sin è contra obstinate se gerant & cum Aliorum Scandalo leges utriusque violent, æquum pariter est, ut Pœnas istas dent, quæ à legibus sancitæ sunt contra ref[?] actarios Transgressores; cum sc. Admonitiones, aliaque mitiora Remedia comperta fuerint inefficacia, in iis ad Ossicium reducendis. His itaque mediis olim usi sunt piissimi Imperatores, aliique Principes Christiani, contra sui temporis Hæreticos; idque non sine consensu Episcoporum suorum, imo, cum eorum voto, plausuque & licet Augustinus aliquando minus probaverit illam legum severitatem, fatetur tamen se postea, experientia magistra certius edoctum, mutasse sententiam; quippe quæ salutaris severitatis illius fructus sibi quotidie demonstrabat, in Hæreticis ad Ecclesiam reducendis; qui & ipsi deista Conversione sua sibi gratulabantur, Deoque gratias agebant. Siquidem Aliud est, conscientiam violari; Aliud, obstinationem Animi frangi. Equidem raro procedebatur ad mortem infligendam (licet & hanc quoque irrogatam legimus Manichæis, & Priscil-lianistis, necnon & Montanistis, cum Receptoribus suis & Occultatoribus)frequentissime autem ad Carcerem, & exilium, & Bonorum publicationem; ne quid dicam de excommunicatione Hæreticorum, & extrusione Cleri excommunicati ab Ecclesiis quas antea possederant; quæ certe non exiguam infamiæ notam iisdem inusserunt. At fortasse, hic dicent Socinianí [?] nihil tale sub Apostolis factum suisse, nec in aliquot seculis sequentibus, quando Fidei puritas, morum sanctitas, & Charitas, cum Pace, maxime inter Christianos vigebant. Nec sane mirum est, jus gladii tunc Temporis haud exercitum fuisse in coercendis Hæreticis, cum neque Apostoli, neque Episcopi ipsorum successores, Potestate Gladii armati fuerint; neque aliam aliquam Jurisdictionem civilem a Christo acceptam habuerint, qua contumaces Ecclesiæ Filios reprimerent. Interea tamen habuerunt Potestatem ei parilem & æquipollentem, ab ipso Christo sibi datam; quam & exercuerunt, prout occasio se obtulit, & necessitas exegit, in quosdam insignioris notæ Transgressores. Ita legimus, Petrum Mortis sententiam tulisse in Ananiam & Sapphiram; quam & statim inflixit. Paulus item, Elymam magum cæcitate percussit; Idemque Corinthium istum, Incestus reum, Satanæ tradidit, ad interitum Carnis, ut Spiritus salvus fieret in die Domini. 1. Cor. 5. 5. viz. ut Satanas eum morbis quibusdam atque Tormentis affligeret, quibus acrius
units.tr: Matters stand somewhat differently, however, with those who have already embraced the faith of Christ and have been admitted into that Church through baptism. For it is right that they then submit both to the laws of that Church and to those of the Christian commonwealth of which they have become members and from whose protection they benefit. But if, on the contrary, they behave obstinately and, to the scandal of others, violate the laws of both, it is equally right that they undergo those penalties which the laws have enacted against such transgressors, since admonitions and other milder remedies have been found ineffective in bringing them back to their duty. Thus the most pious emperors and other Christian princes have in the past used these means against the heretics of their own times, and not without the consent of their bishops, indeed with their wish and approval. And although Augustine at one time did not greatly approve that severity of the laws, he confesses nevertheless that he later changed his opinion, having been taught more surely by experience; for he saw daily the fruits of that salutary severity in bringing heretics back to the Church, who themselves rejoiced at their conversion and gave thanks to God. For it is one thing for conscience to be violated, another for obstinacy of mind to be broken. Indeed, they rarely proceeded to inflict death (although we read that this too was imposed on the Manichaeans, the Priscillianists, and the Montanists, together with their receivers and concealers), but very frequently to imprisonment, exile, and confiscation of goods; not to mention the excommunication of heretics and the expulsion of excommunicated clergy from the churches they had previously held, which certainly brought no small mark of infamy upon them. But perhaps the Socinians will here say that nothing of the kind was done under the Apostles, nor in the several centuries that followed, when the purity of the faith, the holiness of morals, and charity, together with peace, flourished above all among Christians. Nor is it indeed surprising that the right of the sword was not exercised at that time in restraining heretics, since neither the Apostles nor their successors the bishops were armed with the power of the sword, nor had they received from Christ any other civil jurisdiction by which to restrain the stubborn sons of the Church. Meanwhile, however, they had a power similar and equivalent to it, given to them by Christ himself; and they exercised it, as occasion offered and necessity required, against certain transgressors of more notable note. Thus we read that Peter pronounced a sentence of death against Ananias and Sapphira, and immediately inflicted it. Paul likewise struck the magician Elymas with blindness; and he delivered that Corinthian, guilty of incest, to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord (1 Cor. 5:5), namely, that Satan might afflict him with certain diseases and torments, by which, more sharply

units.la: admonitus atque correptus, ex sensu Pœnarum Corpori inflictarum, tandem excitaretur ad Animæ Pœnitentiam exercendam, quæ ei in die Domini verteret in salutem. Eandem quoque Censuram alibi se inflixisse dicit in Hymenæum & Alexandrum, quos in hunc finem tradidit Satanæ, ut castigati discerent non Blasphemare. 1 Tim. 1. ult: Similem item Pœnam minatur cæteris Corinthiis, variorum Criminum reis, nisi mature resipiscerent, & Adventum suum ad eos morum emendatione prævenirent. 1, Cor. 4. 18. 21. 2, Cor. 10. 4. 11. & 12. 20, 21. & 13. 2. 10.
units.tr: admonished and corrected, through the sense of the punishments inflicted on his body, he might at last be roused to exercise repentance of soul, which would turn to his salvation in the day of the Lord. He says that he had inflicted the same censure elsewhere, on Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom he delivered to Satan to this end, that being chastised they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim. 1 at the end). He likewise threatens the rest of the Corinthians, guilty of various crimes, with a similar punishment, unless they repented in time and anticipated his coming to them by amendment of life (1 Cor. 4:18, 21; 2 Cor. 10:4, 11; 12:20, 21; 13:2, 10).

units.la: §. 51. Et sicut ipsi Apostoli, cum Episcopis illorum successoribus, Jurisdictione aliqua civili sive coerciva non fuerunt armati, ita nec Magistratus aliquos Civiles isto ævo habuerunt ad quos in hoc negotio provocarent. Cum enim illi, qui Judæis simul ac Gentibus tunc Temporis præerant, Infideles essent, & Religionis Christianæ Hostes professi, Hæreticorum causas, si modo ad ipsorum Tribunal delatæ fuissent ab Ecclesiæ præpositis, determinare nec scivissent, nec voluissent. Eusebius tamen refert de Paulo Samosateno, Socinianorum Antecessore, quod, cum damnatus esset in Synodo Antiochena, & Episcopatu depulsus, nec tamen ædibus Episcopalibus cedere vellet; Episcopi, qui eum suffragiis suis damnassent, de hoc Aurelianum Imperatorem interpellare æquum putarunt, & illius auxilium contra Hæresiarcham implorare, quod & obtinuerunt; atque ita, Paulo ejecto, Domnum, à se illius loco electum introduxerunt. Eusebius. Hist. l. 7. c. 24. Quid ergo vetat, quo minus idem hodie fiat in Fidei Christianæ Perduelles, & Ecclesiæ Perturbatores; præsertim sub principibus Christianis, qui pro officio suo Fidei Catholicæ Defensores sunt & utriusque Ta-bulæ Custodes? Deinde, quid si Hæretici (ut semper fere fieri solet) sub Religionis Prætextu, incautos & instabiles ab Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Fide abducant, e-jusque legibus inobsequentes reddant, Schismata creent, Disciplinam conturbent, atque hoc pacto Seditiones excitent, pacemque publicam violent? neq;enim Ecclesia turbata, Respublica diu potest esse tranquilla. Num & Hi abibunt impune & quicquid sibi libet, tum eloquentur. tum agent, sine pudore aut metu cujusquam? num impia & Blasphemia Dogmata ubique spargent & Schismaticorum conventus, sibi pro libitu undiquaque colligent, Magistratu Christiano interim silente, ac cessante? Num Ecclesiæ præpositos, eorumque censuras superbe contemnent, contra leges Politicas æque ac Ecclesias-ticas, nemine conatibus Ipsorum obstante, contemptumque legum vindicante? At Christus, ejus-que Apostoli, & Ecclesiæ veteris Episcopi hæc nun-quam fecisse leguntur[?], ne quidem sub Politia Judaica sibi adversante, aut sub imperio Principum Ethnicorum. Christus ipse adeo Turbas non ciebat, ut non semel à Turbis recessit, partim, ut Inimicorum violentiæ cederet, qui jurgia, rixasque quæ-rebant; partim, ut nimium ac præposterum vulgi studium ac favorem declinaret, cum ipsum pro Rege peterent Doctrinam quoque suam non seditionibus ac tumultibus excitatis p; opagare[?] studuit, sed leniter ac pacifice, & Argumentis ad Conscientiam cujusq; convincendam accommodatis, veritatem illius, & cœlestem originem ostendit Testimonio Joannis Baptistæ, quem Judæi pro Propheta habebant; Prophetarum veterum adimpletione, vocibus Dei patris de Cœlo latis, & innumerabilibus fere miraculis, quibus Ifaias olim Meffiam venturum denotaverat; præcipue, Resurrectionis suæ signo miraculoso, quod ut Judæis non semel dederat, ita Tempore à se præstituto exhibuit. Doctrinam item suam minime novam esse probavit, eo quod Testimonium haberet à Mose & Prophetis, ad quorum proinde Scripta consulenda Auditores suos obnixe hortatur. Quin & suos Discipulos serio monet, ut observarent ac facerent quæcunque Scribæ & Pharisæi eis observanda mandarent, eo quod in Mosis Cathedra sederant. Matt: 23. 2, 3. Sic & Paulus, cum de Seditione concitata à Judæis accusaretur, coram Præside Felice, hac Apologia se purgat, Quod Judæi ejus Accusatores non invenerint eum in Templo cum aliquo disputantem, aut Concursum Turbæ facientem. Act: 24. 12. Et paulo post Invenerunt me, inquit, in Templo quidam ex Asia Judæi, neque cum turba, neque cum Tumultu. v 18. Idem coram Festo, eodem modo se purgat—Si quenquam injuria affeci, aut aliquid Morte dignum feci, non recuso mori. Act: 25. 11. Et paulo prius—Ad Tribunal Cæsaris sto, ubi me oportet judicari. Judæos injuria non affeci, ut Tu probe nosti. v. 10. Deinde, coram eodem Festo Præside, & Rege Agrippa, cum se, suamque Doctrinam defendit, quam Illius Adversarii Novitatis & Hæreseos insimulabant, ostendit se testatum fuisse Evangelium Parvo & Magno, nec quicquam extra ea dicentem, quæ Prophetæ & Mases futura prædixerunt. Act: 26. 22.
units.tr: §. 51. And just as the Apostles themselves, together with their successors the bishops, were not armed with any civil or coercive jurisdiction, so in that age there were no civil magistrates to whom they could appeal in this matter. For since those who then presided over both Jews and Gentiles were unbelievers and professed enemies of the Christian religion, they neither knew how nor wished to decide the causes of heretics, even if these had been brought before their tribunal by the leaders of the Church. Eusebius nevertheless relates of Paul of Samosata, the forerunner of the Socinians, that when he had been condemned in the Synod of Antioch and deposed from the episcopate, yet was unwilling to yield the episcopal house, the bishops who had condemned him by their votes thought it right to appeal on this matter to the Emperor Aurelian and to implore his aid against the heresiarch; which they obtained, and so, Paul having been ejected, they introduced Domnus, chosen by them in his place. Eusebius, Hist. bk. 7, ch. 24. What then prevents the same thing from being done today against the enemies of the Christian faith and the disturbers of the Church, especially under Christian princes, who by their office are defenders of the Catholic faith and guardians of both tables of the law? Further, what if heretics (as almost always happens) under the pretext of religion lead astray the unwary and unsteady from the Catholic faith of the Church, render them disobedient to its laws, create schisms, throw discipline into confusion, and by this means stir up seditions and violate the public peace? For when the Church is troubled, the commonwealth cannot long remain tranquil. Will these people too depart unpunished, and say and do whatever pleases them, without shame or fear of anyone? Will they everywhere spread impious and blasphemous doctrines, and gather for themselves assemblies of schismatics wherever they please, while the Christian magistrate remains silent and inactive? Will they proudly scorn the leaders of the Church and their censures, against the political laws no less than the ecclesiastical ones, with no one opposing their attempts and avenging the contempt of the laws? But Christ and his Apostles and the bishops of the early Church are never read to have done these things, not even under the Jewish polity which opposed them, or under the rule of heathen princes. Christ himself did not so stir up crowds that he did not more than once withdraw from the crowds: partly to yield to the violence of enemies who sought quarrels and brawls, partly to avoid the excessive and unseemly zeal and favour of the common people, when they wished to make him king. Nor did he seek to spread his doctrine by stirring up seditions and tumults, but gently and peacefully, with arguments adapted to convince each man's conscience. He showed its truth and heavenly origin by the testimony of John the Baptist, whom the Jews held to be a prophet; by the fulfilment of the ancient prophets; by the voices of God the Father uttered from heaven; and by the almost countless miracles by which Isaiah had long before foretold that the Messiah would come; above all, by the miraculous sign of his resurrection, which, as he had more than once given it to the Jews, so he exhibited at the time he had appointed. He likewise proved that his doctrine was by no means new, because it had the testimony of Moses and the Prophets, to whose writings accordingly he earnestly urges his hearers to turn. Indeed he also seriously warns his disciples to observe and do whatever the scribes and Pharisees commanded them to observe, because they sat in Moses' seat (Matt. 23:2, 3). So too Paul, when accused of sedition stirred up by the Jews, clears himself before the governor Felix with this defence: that his Jewish accusers had not found him disputing with anyone in the Temple, or causing a gathering of a crowd (Acts 24:12). And a little later: "Certain Jews from Asia found me in the Temple, neither with a crowd nor with a tumult" (v. 18). He clears himself in the same way before Festus: "If I have done wrong to anyone, or committed anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die" (Acts 25:11). And a little before: "I stand at Caesar's tribunal, where I ought to be judged. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you know very well" (v. 10). Then, before the same governor Festus and King Agrippa, when he defends himself and his doctrine, which his adversaries charged as novelty and heresy, he shows that he had borne witness to the Gospel to small and great, saying nothing beyond those things which the prophets and Moses foretold would come (Acts 26:22).

units.la: § 52. Ita se gesserunt Christus, ejusque Apostoli, tum quoad Doctrinam, tum quoad Mores. At novatores hodierni, qui His maxime contraria loquuntur, & agunt, aegre ferre non debent, quod os iis obstruatur; manusque simul & Pedes eo usque coerceantur ut huc illuc vagari non liceat, quocunque malesanus Impetus rapit; perpetrentque quicquid mali in animo habent, ad seductionem Fidelium, perniciem Ecclesiæ, & perturbationem Reipublicæ; quod item asperiora quaedam Remedia usurpentur ad eos in ordinem cogendos, quos leniora adeo non revocarunt ad Officium, ut potius foverint in errore vel etiam irritent ad plura & pejora perpetranda. Idcirco in his Casibus, & erga sic delinquentes, Moses Aaroni opem praestare tenetur, Magistratus civilis Ministerio Evangelico ut qui gladio Spiritus non absterrentur a malo, gladio Magistratus Politici (quem etiam in Fide Christiana defendenda frustra non gerit) ab ea violanda cohibeantur.
units.tr: § 52. Christ and his apostles conducted themselves thus, both in doctrine and in morals. But the novelists of today, who speak and act most contrary to them, ought not to take it ill if their mouths are stopped and their hands and feet restrained, so that they may not wander hither and thither wherever their mad impulse carries them, and may not carry out whatever evil they have in mind, to the seduction of the faithful, the ruin of the Church and the disturbance of the commonwealth. Likewise, harsher remedies are used to bring to order those whom milder ones have not so much recalled to their duty as rather fostered in their error, or even provoked to commit more and worse offences. Therefore, in such cases and towards such offenders, Moses is bound to lend help to Aaron: the civil magistrate, since they are not restrained from evil by the sword of the Spirit, that is, by the evangelical ministry, should be restrained from violating the faith by the sword of the political magistrate (which he does not bear in vain in defending the Christian faith).

units.la: § 53. Quid? quod his pejora quandoque tentantur in Religionis negotio. Surrexerunt enim in Ecclesia, non solum qui fidem Catholicam in quibusdam Articulis, vel prorsus abrogarunt, vel pessime adulteraverunt, sed etiam qui se Prophetas extra ordinem à Deo missos palam professi sunt; imo, qui palam ac procaciter Deum illum blasphemarunt; quem Ecclesia Christiana semper coluit, & agnovit. Etenim Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Filii uniuscujusque saeculi ubique & unanimiter & ore professi sunt, & publice adoraverunt Deum essentia unum in Trinitate Personarum, in cujus nomen & Fidem baptizati fuerunt. Non tamen defuerunt inter Socinianos, eorumque socios, qui Sacro-Sanctum hoc Trinitatis Mysterium ore petulanti atque blasphemo incesserint, Monstrum appellantes, Commentum humanum, novum Idolum, Deum fictitium & Sophisticum, fabulosam chimaram, Turrim Babelis, diabolicam Ideam, tricipitem Cerberum, tricorporem Geryonem; imo, Blasphemum Dogma ex imo Orco per Filium perditionis, virtute Satana, Gentium Ecclesias obtrusum. Haec nempe sunt insignia illa elogia quibus Servetus, Dudithius, ipsèque Socinus, cum reliquis Anti-Trinitariis, ipsius vel Discipulis, vel Sociis, Christianorum Deum, & ab omnibus vere fidelibus summo Honore cultum, adornaverunt: Nam itaque cum huiusmodi Impostores, qui se Prophetas jactant, Deique supremi nuncios coelitus in Terras missos; tum Rabulae hi blasphemi, qui Deuni super omnia Benedictum fœdissimis conviciis incessere non cessant, in sua impietate sine Censura pergent, & impunes abibunt in Republica Christiana? At Apostoli pro sua modestia simul atque prudentia, nec ipsa Gentium idola contumeliis & opprobriis insectari solebant, si modo scribae Ephesio fides danda sit. Hic enim ex eo nomine Paulum ejusque Socios excusat, quod neque sacrilegi fuerint, neque in Dianam blasphemi, quam Ephesii, cum aliis Asiaticis, pro Dea coluerunt. Act; 19,37. Quid ergo merentur illi, qui cum inter Christianos non solum vivant, sed & in numero Illorum censeri volunt, Deum tamen à Christianis communiter agnitum, Deum verum, & ab omnibus vere Fidelibus summa veneratione cultum fœdissimis contumeliis atque conviciis profcindere non verentur? Certe Deus olim sub Lege, mortis poenam statuit, tam in Blasphemos, qui in divinum Numen contumeliosi erant, quam in Pseudo-Prophetas, qui cum à deo mihi non essent, tamen Illius nomine ad Populum locuti sunt; præsertim, si à Fide, Cultuque veri Dei populum abducerent. Similes quoque leges sancitas legimus ab Imperatoribus, aliisque Principibus Christianis. Imo, & ante Christianismi exortum, ab Ethnicis Idololatris idem factum accepimus, qui contemptum Divini numinis, & Religionis injurias, gravissimis suppliciis vindicare soliti sunt; idque non solum in plebeiis, sed in viris Principibus, eximiisque nominis Philosophis. Siquidem hac de causa Alcibiades in exilium pulsus est & per omnium sacerdotum religiones Diis devotus, quod solemnia Cereris mysteria per ludibrium enunciasset. Hinc Anaxagoras, licet a Pericle discipulo studiosissime defensus, quinque tamen Talentis multatus est, atque insuper exilio damnatus, quia Solem ab Atheniensibus pro Deo cultum μύδρον[?] διάπυρον[?] h. e. Ferrum ignitum, sive Globum candentem, asseruerit. Hinc Protagoras ab iisdem Atheniensibus in exilium pulsus est, librique illius diligenter conquisiti, in foro, sub praeconis voce publice cremabantur, quod in principio cujusdam libri, se dubitare, dixerit, an Dii fuerint, necne? Hinc iidem Athenienses Diagoram Melium, Atheum dictum, morte damnarunt; & tum voce praeconis promulgarunt, tum in aerea columna insculpi curarunt, se Interfectori ipsius Talentum daturos; duo autem Talenta illi, quicunque vivum adduceret, ut refert Suidas. Deinde, Socrates ab iisdem, quamvis immerito, & per calumniam, eandem tamen ob causam mortis sententiam in se latam sensit, quam & reipsa subiit. Tanto horrori fuit tantoque in odio, hoc Blasphemiae crimen apud ipsos etiam Gentiles Idololatras, qui verum Deum ignorabant, & Illius Honorem mille Diis fictitiis impertiebantur ut nihilosecius, vel solo Naturae lumine edocti, contumelias cujusque numinis publice culti, & pro vero Deo habiti severissime vindicarent.
units.tr: § 53. What is more, in matters of religion they sometimes attempt things worse than these. For there have arisen in the Church not only men who have either wholly abrogated or grievously corrupted certain articles of the Catholic faith, but also men who have openly professed themselves prophets sent by God outside the ordinary way; indeed, men who have openly and insolently blasphemed that God whom the Christian Church has always worshipped and acknowledged. For the sons of the Catholic Church in every age have everywhere, unanimously and with one voice, professed and publicly adored God, one in essence in a Trinity of Persons, into whose name and faith they were baptized. Nevertheless, there have not been lacking among the Socinians and their associates those who have assailed this most sacred mystery of the Trinity with a wanton and blasphemous tongue, calling it a monster, a human invention, a new idol, a fictitious and sophistical God, a fabulous chimaera, the Tower of Babel, a diabolical idea, a three-headed Cerberus, a three-bodied Geryon; indeed, a blasphemous dogma sent up from the depths of hell through the son of perdition, by the power of Satan, and thrust upon the churches of the Gentiles. These, of course, are the notable epithets with which Servetus, Dudith, Socinus himself, and the rest of the Anti-Trinitarians, whether his disciples or his companions, have adorned the God of the Christians, the God who is worshipped with the highest honour by all truly faithful people. Shall such impostors, who boast that they are prophets and messengers of the supreme God sent from heaven to earth, and such blasphemous wranglers, who do not cease to assail with the foulest abuse the God who is blessed above all things, go on in their impiety without censure, and depart unpunished in the Christian commonwealth? But the apostles, with their modesty and prudence, were not accustomed to assail even the idols of the Gentiles with insults and reproaches, if indeed the Ephesian town clerk is to be believed. For he there excuses Paul and his companions on the ground that they were neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of Diana, whom the Ephesians, together with other Asiatics, worshipped as a goddess. Acts 19.37. What then do those deserve who not only live among Christians but also wish to be counted among them, and yet do not hesitate to tear with the foulest contumely and abuse that God who is commonly acknowledged by Christians, the true God, and who is worshipped with the highest veneration by all truly faithful people? Certainly God, under the Law, appointed the penalty of death both for blasphemers, who were insolent against the divine majesty, and for false prophets, who, though not sent by God, nevertheless spoke in his name to the people; especially if they were leading the people away from the faith and worship of the true God. We read that similar laws were also enacted by the Christian emperors and other Christian princes. Indeed, before the rise of Christianity, we are told that the heathen idolaters did the same, who were accustomed to avenge contempt of the divine majesty and injuries to religion with the most severe punishments; and this was done not only against the common people but also against men of rank and philosophers of outstanding name. For instance, for this cause Alcibiades was driven into exile and devoted to the gods by the rites of all the priests, because he had mocked the solemn mysteries of Ceres. Hence Anaxagoras, although most zealously defended by his pupil Pericles, was nevertheless fined five talents and moreover condemned to exile, because he had asserted that the sun, which the Athenians worshipped as a god, was a red-hot iron (μύδρον διάπυρον), or a glowing globe. Hence Protagoras was driven into exile by the same Athenians, and his books, carefully sought out, were publicly burned in the forum at the herald's proclamation, because at the beginning of a certain book he had said that he doubted whether there were gods or not. Hence the same Athenians condemned Diagoras of Melos, called an atheist, to death; and they both proclaimed by the herald's voice and had inscribed on a bronze column that they would give a talent to whoever killed him, and two talents to whoever brought him in alive, as Suidas relates. Then Socrates, by the same people, though undeservedly and through calumny, incurred a sentence of death for the same cause, which he indeed underwent. So great was the horror and so great the hatred of this crime of blasphemy among the very Gentile idolaters, who did not know the true God and bestowed his honour upon a thousand fictitious gods, that nevertheless, taught by the light of nature alone, they severely avenged insults offered to any divinity publicly worshipped and held to be a true god.

units.la: § 54 Non diffiteor quidem, Stegmannum verbo tenus agnoscere Reverentiam Ecclesiæ ac Reipublicæ debitam; & velle fartam tectam manere Magistratus Politici potestatem pag. 52 Dei quoque, & Domini Jesu Judicium agnoscit, cui Omnes subjectos esse oportet. Sed quid verbis agnoscit, quod factis abnegat? Cur Fidem ab Ecclesia Catholica profefsam rejicit? Cur Politiam Ecclesiæ, cultum Dei publicum, Disciplinam, atque Sacramenta, ab ea, ex Christi Instituto, administrata, conculcat[?]? Cur ex Religione innovata reipublicæ pacem conturbat? Cur Potestates civiles, una cum Ecclesiasticis, a Deo ejusque Christo institutas, Regulasque judicandi ab eisdem præscriptas, ad veritatem simul & pacem in Ecclesia conservandam, pro nihilo ducit? Satis enim notum est, quomodo in his omnibus sese gesserint Socinus, ejusque socii ac discipuli, quorum Patronum ac vindicem Stegmannus in ifthoc libello fe constituit.
units.tr: § 54. I do not deny indeed that Stegmann, in words, acknowledges the reverence due to the Church and the commonwealth, and wishes the power of the political magistrate to remain whole and unimpaired (p. 52). He also acknowledges the judgment of God and of the Lord Jesus, to which all must be subject. But why does he deny in deeds what he acknowledges in words? Why does he reject the faith professed by the Catholic Church? Why does he trample upon the polity of the Church, the public worship of God, the discipline, and the sacraments administered by her according to Christ's institution? Why by his innovated religion does he disturb the peace of the commonwealth? Why does he count for nothing the civil powers, instituted by God and his Christ together with the ecclesiastical ones, and the rules for judging prescribed by them, which are to be preserved for the sake of truth and peace in the Church? For it is well enough known how Socinus, and his associates and disciples, have conducted themselves in all these matters, and whose patron and champion Stegmann has made himself in this little book.

units.la: §.55. Octavo, idem Ib: pag: 155. hanc Objectionem sibi solvendam proponit. Si Illud sibi velint, quod Rationis Judicium, seu Sententia a Ratione lata, repugnet sive contradicat Sententiis sacris seu Theologicis; ut Ratio concludit, unum esse Deum, tum Personas, tum essentia ratione, quia Persona nihil est Aliud, quam essentia una sive individua intelligens; at Theologia dicit, Tres esse Personas in una essentia. Sic in Incarnatione, hypostatica unione, miraculis &c. Dicimus, inquit, Aliud esse, Rationem; Aliud, Judicium sive sententiam Rationis: Illa enim, causa; Hæc, effectum est. Potest autem Aliquid contrarium esse effectui, quod causa tamen non repugnat. Ratio enim nihil judicare potest, nisi Principia habeat, ex quibus judicet &c. Sic Ille. At quomodo potest Aliquid esse contrarium sententiæ, sive Judicio Rationis, quod non est contrarium ipsi Rationi? Quippe si Ratio judicet secundum vera, congruaque Principia, sive propria S. Scripturæ sive communia rebus sacris & naturalibus, & ex iisdem rite concludat, non potest non elicere veram sententiam: sin aliter, falsam elicit. Certe recta Ratio semper recte judicat, quia judicat prout ipsa se habet, ac prout dirigitur juxta normam Principiorum istorum, quibus ipsa utitur in judicando. Quicquid ergo contrarium est Judicio Rationis, Rationi sic judicanti pariter adversatur.
units.tr: §. 55. Eighthly, the same author, at p. 155 of the same work, proposes to himself this objection to be solved: If they mean this, that the judgment of reason, or the opinion formed by reason, is opposed to or contradicts the sacred or theological opinions; as reason concludes that God is one, and that the persons, as to the essence, are one, since a person is nothing other than one individual intelligent essence; but theology says that there are three persons in one essence. So in the Incarnation, the hypostatic union, miracles, and so on. We say, he says, that reason is one thing, and the judgment or opinion of reason another: for the former is the cause, the latter the effect. Now something can be contrary to the effect which nevertheless does not contradict the cause. For reason can pass no judgment unless it has principles from which to judge, and so on. Thus he. But how can something be contrary to the opinion or judgment of reason which is not contrary to reason itself? For if reason judges according to true and congruous principles, whether those proper to Holy Scripture or those common to sacred and natural things, and rightly concludes from them, it cannot but elicit a true opinion; but if otherwise, it elicits a false one. Certainly right reason always judges rightly, because it judges as things really are, and as it is directed by the rule of those principles which it uses in judging. Whatever therefore is contrary to the judgment of reason is equally opposed to reason so judging.

units.la: §. 16. Nono, Idem quoque postulat ( sicut & alii Sociniani ; cum ipso Socino ) ut in Theologicis Controversiis determinandis, sufficiat consensus in iis, quæ sunt ad salutem necessaria. At e contra; licet neque necessarium, nec revera possibile sit, prout Hominum Ingenia, moresque se habent, ut singulæ Controverfiæ etiam minutioris momenti, definiantur, (tanta obscuritas est in quibusdam, tanta levitas in Aliis, tamque ampla occasio Turbarum inde oblata, inter mentium humanarum opinionumque diversitatem, quæ intra Cancellos adeo angustos concludi nolunt) necesse tamen est, ad veritatem simul atque Pacem in Ecclesia conservandam, ut conveniat inter Christianos, tum de Regula judicandi, tum de Judice sententiam laturo. Nisi enim de Regula constet, omne Judicium fallax erit & incertum; & nisi Tribunal quoddam in Ecclesia constituatur, ad quod lites quæcunque, quas oriri contingit, deferantur, & in cujus sententia decretoria acquiescatur, mille Hæresibus veritas catholica opprimetur, mille Schismatibus Pax Ecclesiæ violabitur. Multa enim in se levia, Turbas valde graves sæpe excitarunt; & ex parvis initiis Discordiæ maximæ enatæ sunt. Certe Ecclesia, tum primitiva, tum hodierna, hæc mala frequenter experta est, & cum summo Doloris sensu animadvertit, cum Filios suos inter se acerrime conflictantes viderit, non solum de Fidei Dogmatibus, sed etiam de Ceremoniis, & consuetudinibus, de multis[?] Disciplinæ, & Ecclesiastici Regiminis limitibus, quæ in sua natura Adiaphora sunt. Sed, quod multo plus est, & gravioris momenti, haud convenit inter multos, Quæ sint illa ad salutem necessaria.
units.tr: Ninth, he (as do the other Socinians, along with Socinus himself) also demands that in determining theological controversies, agreement on those things which are necessary to salvation be enough. On the contrary, although it is neither necessary nor really possible, given the nature of human minds and dispositions, to settle every controversy, even those of minor importance (there is such obscurity in some, such triviality in others, and so ample an occasion for disturbance is offered by the diversity of human minds and opinions, which will not be confined within such narrow limits), it is nonetheless necessary, in order to preserve truth and at the same time peace in the Church, that Christians agree both on the rule of judging and on the judge who is to pronounce sentence. For unless there is agreement about the rule, every judgment will be fallacious and uncertain; and unless some tribunal is established in the Church to which whatever disputes arise may be referred, and whose decisive sentence is accepted, Catholic truth will be overwhelmed by a thousand heresies and the peace of the Church violated by a thousand schisms. For many things that are slight in themselves have often stirred up very grave disturbances, and very great discords have sprung from small beginnings. Certainly the Church, both primitive and present, has often experienced these evils, and with the deepest sorrow has seen her sons fighting most bitterly among themselves, not only over the dogmas of faith but also over ceremonies and customs, over many points of discipline, and over the limits of ecclesiastical government, which in their own nature are adiaphora. But, what is much more, and of graver importance, it is not agreed among many which those things are that are necessary to salvation.

units.la: Non pauci enim reperti sunt qui necessaria quædam repudiarunt, quasi omnino reprobanda, aut saltem dubia atque problematica, adeoque nullius Christiani Fidei obtrudenda. Alii ex adverso surrexerunt, qui cerebri sui Commenta, & humana Instituta, pro omnino necessariis obtruserunt, & à cunctis Fidelibus, qui salvi esse cuperent, acceptanda Socinus necessaria restringit ad Præcepta ac Promissa. Pontificii Symbolo Apostolico nescio quot Fidei Articulos adjecerunt. Et omnes fere Hæretici fidem antiquitus receptam, vel decurtarunt, vel Additamentis suis depravarunt. Ita, vel mutilam reddiderunt, vel monstrosam. Itaque imprimis necesse est, ut de hisce fundamentalibus sive necessariis inter Christianos conveniat, quot & quænam sint. Hoc autem nemo sobrius fieri posse putat, quamdiu Ingenia Hominum adeo varia sunt; & Judicium de singulis controversiis cuicunque Privato relinquitur, pro illius opinione & Arbitrio ferendum.
units.tr: For not a few have been found who have rejected certain necessary things, as though they were wholly to be disowned, or at least doubtful and questionable, and therefore not to be imposed on any Christian's faith. Others on the contrary have arisen, who have imposed the figments of their own brains and human institutions as wholly necessary, and demanded that they be accepted by all the faithful who wish to be saved. Socinus restricts the necessary things to the precepts and promises. The Papists have added I know not how many articles of faith to the Apostles' Creed. And nearly all heretics have either shortened the faith received from antiquity or corrupted it with their additions. Thus they have made it either mutilated or monstrous. Therefore it is above all necessary that Christians agree on these fundamental or necessary matters, both how many and which they are. But no sober person thinks this can be done as long as men's minds are so varied, and the judgment on each controversy is left to any private person, to be pronounced according to his own opinion and will.

units.la: §. 57. Decimo; Adjici huc potest illud Smalcii, aliorumque quorundam Socinianorum Postulatum viz. Quod omnes Articuli Fidei literaliter & expressè in S. literis extent, ita ut non sit Opus aliquos exinde per consequentiam deduci. Nam illum in finem, ait Smalcius, potissimum conscriptæ sunt sacræ literæ, ut quid necessarium sit ad salutem, omnibus & singulis expresse constaret. Atq; iterum Omnes simplices tenentur ea intelligere quae ad salutem scitu necessaria sunt; consequentias autem capere, omnibus datum non est. Sic ille, in Refut. disp. Graveri de Sp. S. citante Iosua Stegmanno, in Photinianismo suo. Andr. Dudithius item, Epist. ad Bezam. A. C. 1571. Op. Soc. p 524. Tom. 1. in eandem sententiam ita scribit --Prima sit haec Regula, ut summa S. literae authoritas tribuatur, ita quidem, ut quod ibi expresse non docetur, id, ratiocinationibus humanis adducti, pro Dogmate, ac Fidei nostrae Capite, assumere ac proponere nefarium esse existimemus. Hoc autem ab illis, aliisque Socinianis postulatur, ne cogantur assentiri iis Fidei Articulis, quos impugnare solent, cum tamen valide clareque illorum veritas evincatur per consequentias è S. Pagina deductas. At utique recta Ratio docet, Conclusionem virtute contineri in Præmissis neque consequentiam falsam esse posse, quae ex Principiis in se verissimis rite deducitur. Equidem lubenter agnoscimus, S. Scripturam in Rebus ad salutem necessariis, ut plenam esse, ita & planam; non tamen asserimus, illam adeo diserte & expresse de singulis Dogmatibus loqui, etiam quae majoris momenti sunt, ut nullis sit opus consequentiis. Hae vero Consequentiae ejusmodi sunt, ut vel fieri possint etiam a Simplicioribus, vel saltem ab iis apprehendi, & pro veris agnosci, quamprimum ab Ecclesiae Praepositis atque Doctoribus proponuntur, quibus ex officio praecipue incumbit, illas deducere, plebique Christianae ob oculos ponere. Neque ad hoc astruendum desunt exempla Christi & Apostolorum. Siquidem ipse Christus probavit mortuorum Resurrectionem per consequentiam ex libro Mosis deductam, Matt. 22. 31, 32. cum Exod. 3. 6. Deitatem item suam & æqualitatem cum Patre, per aliam consequentiam probavit, è libro Psalmorum. Jo. 10. 30, 36. cum Psal. 82. 6. necnon è Psalmo 110. 1. ubi David appellat Messiam sibi promissum, Dominum suum. Sic enim arguit Christus. Matt 22. 44, 45. Paulus eandem Christi Deitatem probat ex eo, quod nomen præstantius sortitus fuerit, quam Angeli; quod Thronum, sceptrumque regale dederit ipsi Deus, et unxerit oleo lætitiæ supra Socios; quod Creatio Cœli & Terræ ipsi attributa sit; quod denique Deus Pater eum ad dextram suum sedere fecerit, donec posuerit Inimicos scabellum pedum suorum. Heb. 1. 4. 13. perplures ejusdem generis Argumentationes passim occurrunt in ista ad Hebræos epistola ut & in reliquis Paulinis. deinde, quædam Consequentiæ adeo faciles sunt, ut etiam a vulgaris ingenii Lectoribus fieri possint. Alioquin Christus non hortatus fuisset Judæos in genere ad scrutandum Scripturas, quia de ipso Testimonium ferebant. Hoc enim Testimonium intelligi non poterat, sine diligenti Collatione veterum prophetiarum atque Typorum, cum rebus a Christo gestis, ex qua rite facta concludere possent, eum esse Christum olim prædictum, præsignificatum, & promissum sub lege. Hoc ulterius liquet exemplo Berceënsium, de quibus fertur illos ex collatione Scripturarum, cum iis quæ a Paulo prædicata sunt, ad Fidem Christi addu-ctos fuisse. Act: 27. 11, 12. comp: Jo. 5. 39, 40.
units.tr: §. 57. Tenth, there may be added the postulate of Smalcius and some other Socinians, namely that all articles of faith stand literally and expressly in the Holy Letters, so that there is no need for any of them to be deduced from them by consequence. For to this end, says Smalcius, the Holy Letters were chiefly written, so that what is necessary to salvation should be expressly plain to all and each. And again: All simple folk are bound to understand those things which must be known for salvation; but to grasp consequences is not given to all. Thus he, in his Refutation of Graverus's disputation on the Holy Spirit, citing Joshua Stegmann in his Photinianism. Andreas Dudith likewise, in his letter to Beza of 1571, Opera Socin. p. 524, vol. 1, writes to the same effect: Let this be the first rule, that the highest authority be given to Holy Scripture, in such a way that we judge it impious to take up and propose as a dogma and article of our faith, on the strength of human reasoning, whatever is not expressly taught there. But this is demanded by them and other Socinians so that they need not assent to those articles of faith which they are accustomed to attack, although their truth is clearly and validly proved by consequences drawn from the Holy Page. Yet right reason teaches that a conclusion is contained virtually in its premises, and that a consequence rightly drawn from principles that are in themselves most true cannot be false. Indeed we gladly acknowledge that Holy Scripture, in matters necessary to salvation, is as plain as it is full; yet we do not assert that it speaks so distinctly and expressly of each dogma, even those of greater moment, that no consequences are needed. Such consequences are of a kind that can be made even by the simpler sort, or at least grasped by them and acknowledged as true, as soon as they are set forth by the leaders and teachers of the Church, to whom it belongs chiefly by office to draw them out and place them before the Christian people. Nor are examples of Christ and the Apostles lacking to establish this. For Christ himself proved the resurrection of the dead by a consequence drawn from the book of Moses, Matt. 22. 31, 32, with Exod. 3. 6. He likewise proved his own deity and equality with the Father by another consequence, drawn from the book of Psalms: Jo. 10. 30, 36, with Psal. 82. 6; and also from Psalm 110. 1, where David calls the Messiah promised to him his Lord. For Christ argues thus: Matt. 22. 44, 45. Paul proves the same deity of Christ from the fact that he obtained a more excellent name than the angels; that God gave him a throne and royal sceptre and anointed him with the oil of gladness above his fellows; that the creation of heaven and earth is attributed to him; and finally that God the Father made him sit at his right hand until he should put his enemies as a footstool for his feet. Heb. 1. 4, 13. Very many arguments of the same kind occur everywhere in that Epistle to the Hebrews, as also in the other Pauline letters. Moreover, some consequences are so easy that they can be made even by readers of ordinary ability. Otherwise Christ would not have urged the Jews in general to search the Scriptures, because they bore witness to him. For this testimony could not be understood without a careful comparison of the ancient prophecies and types with the things done by Christ, from which, rightly made, they could conclude that he was the one foretold, foreshadowed, and promised under the law. This is further clear from the example of the Bereans, of whom it is said that, by comparing the Scriptures with what Paul preached, they were brought to faith in Christ. Act. 27. 11, 12; comp. Jo. 5. 39, 40.

units.la: § 58: Hæc dixisse satis sit de Socinianorum postulatis, quæ contra Rationem & Æquum admitti petunt. Restat, ut Illorum Dogmata, in unam quasi Fasciculum collecta, simul exhibeamus Oculis lectorum, quo facilius appareat summa hujus monstrofissimæ[?] Hæresis deformitas, enim gravissima pernicie conjuncta, instar Hydræ Lernæ, quæ & Capite multiplici horrorem incussit, & Veneno mortem intulit. Siquidem ex hoc Catalogo facile patebit, Socinum cum sociis, Discipulisque suis, dissertis verbis pleraque sustulisse, quæ ab Ecclesia Christi primitus accepta sunt, tum quæ ad fidem, tum quæ ad praxin spectant; quæque per tot secula in eadem retenta fuerunt, atque observata. Nam præcipuos Fidei Articulos, vel in universum sustulerunt, vel saepissime corruperunt. Veterum Politiam atque disciplinam Ecclesiasticam, una cum Sacramentis & Sacramentalibus liturgiis, cultusque divini Ritibus antiquitus usurpatis, à se procul amandarunt, aut saltem mutilarunt. Non iis sufficit, Centonem quendam veterum Hæresium nobis exhibuisse, instar Mendicantium Tunicæ, ex diversis, iisque attritis lacerisque panniculis confusæ, ut cum Theodoreto loquar, nisi & novis quibuscunque Commentis viam latam aperirent, dum Cujusque Privati Rationem S. Scripturæ Interpretem constituunt, & Judicem omnium Controversiarum ad Religionem pertinentium. Revelationem Divinam, quæ Religionis omnis origo est, & immota Fidei Basis, etsi non palam tollant, negentque (ne pro Infidelibus plane habeantur) & à Christianismo prorsus alieni, eam tamen clam subruunt, inutilemque reddunt in quamplurimis; partim, dum seipsos solos Divinæ mentis Interpretes faciunt; partim, dum omnia Fidei mysteria, à Deo per Revelationem istam nobis communicata, ad Rationis humanæ Tribunal adducunt, vel approbanda, vel abjicienda, prout illa inter examinandum, principiis illis, quæ sibi perperam assumpsit in judi-
units.tr: § 58. Let it suffice to have said this about the Socinians' demands, which they ask to be admitted against reason and fairness. It remains that we set before the readers' eyes their doctrines, gathered as it were into one bundle, so that the sum of the deformity of this most monstrous heresy may more easily appear, since it is joined with the gravest ruin, like the Lernaean Hydra, which struck horror with its many heads and brought death with its poison. For from this catalogue it will readily be seen that Socinus, with his associates and disciples, has in plain words done away with very many things that were received from the Church of Christ from the beginning, both those that pertain to faith and those that pertain to practice, and that were retained and observed in her through so many ages. For they have either abolished the principal articles of faith altogether or most often corrupted them. The ancient polity and ecclesiastical discipline, together with the sacraments, the sacramental liturgies, and the rites of divine worship used from antiquity, they have banished far from themselves or at least mutilated. It is not enough for them to have presented us with a patchwork of ancient heresies, like the tunic of beggars, stitched together from various threadbare and torn scraps, to use Theodoret's words, unless they also opened a broad way for new inventions of every kind, while they make each private person's reason the interpreter of Holy Scripture and the judge of all controversies pertaining to religion. The divine revelation, which is the origin of all religion and the immovable basis of faith, they do not openly remove; indeed they deny it (lest they be regarded as altogether unbelievers), and being utterly alien to Christianity, they secretly undermine it and render it useless in very many respects: partly by making themselves the sole interpreters of the divine mind, and partly by bringing all the mysteries of faith, communicated to us by God through that revelation, before the tribunal of human reason, to be approved or rejected, according as, when examined by those principles which they have wrongly assumed as the rules of judging, they find them fitting or unfitting.

units.la: Note: the first word "fissimæ" is a line-start fragment continuing from the previous page; its exact letters are doubtful. candi Regulas, congrua vel incongrua deprehenderit. Imo, licentiam sibi sumunt, non solum pervertendi sensum vel bonum S. Scripturæ, sed & mutandi commata, Periodos, literarum apices, literasque ipsas, quoties suis Dogmatibus adversari videntur. Ita ut non immerito, eos potius audaces Criticos dixeris, qui[?] quam humiles, & bonæ fidei Christianos. Sed exhibeamus Catalogum, ex quo hæc omnia luculentius patebunt.
units.tr: candi rules, finds them congruous or incongruous. Indeed, they take the liberty not only of perverting the sense or the good of Holy Scripture, but also of changing clauses, periods, letter-marks, and even letters themselves, whenever these seem to oppose their doctrines. So one might fairly call them bold critics rather than humble Christians of good faith. But let us set out a catalogue, from which all this will be more clearly seen.

units.la: §. 59. Primo, Quod ad S. Scripturam, ejusque interpretationem, & judicium de controversiis Theologicis ferendum, sibi, suisque Discipulis totum tribuunt, cum summo totius Antiquitatis, & Ecclesiæ Catholicæ contemptu. Constat, ait, Socinus, Justinum & Irenæum aliter de Christi Persona sensisse, quam nos sentimus. Sol. 30. Scrup. Ad 5tum[?], p. 327. Tom. 1. Idem de Ecclesia, p. 344. unumquemque relinquit suo ipsius judicio in sensu S. Scripturæ erudendo, & censura ferenda de Aliorum quorumcunque Doctrina; nullorumque sententiæ innitendum esse vult, sive hodie viventium, sive veteris Ecclesiæ Doctorum —Non attendendum est, inquit, quid Homines docuerint, fecerintve vel antehac docuerint, aut senserint, quicunque illi tandem, vel quotcunque sint aut fuerint. Imo, nullam Divinam Patefactionem requiri tam esse vult, præter literam S. Scripturæ. Idem, Epist. 3. ad Matt. Radecium Secretarium Gedanensem. pag. 387. sub specioso prætextu solius S. Scripturæ honorandæ, & ipsius Authoritatem agnoscendi, veterem Ecclesiam Catholicam, cum Doctoribus suis, & Conciliis vilipendit. Inde, inquit, potissimum Dissensiones oriri quilibet facile perspicere poterit, quod soli Dei verbo plerique revera tum adhærent. Nam adhuc, præter S. literas, nescio quæ Concilia, Patres, Antiquitas, maxima sunt in veneratione; adeo ut Divinis oraculis propemodum æquentur, cum tamen ista omnia & siquæ sunt alia ejusmodi, nullas vires præterea apud cordatos Homines habere debeant, quam ut sensus Ecclesiæ illorum Temporum fidem faciant; vel etiam non temere recedendum moneant ab iis Dogmatis, quæ ipsi approbant. Sed S. literis licet aperte reclamantibus, quadam tamen mordicus retinere velle, quia sic ab iis approbantur, hoc nihil aliud est, quam Divinam veritatem consulto pessundare, & ad Antichristiani Regni confirmationem ingentem fenestram patefacere. Legantur modo Pontificiorum scripta adversus Lutheranos & Calvinianos, & satis intelligetur, si præter S. literas Ipsorum Auctoritati sit standum[?], nobis omnibus causa cadendum esse. Quibus in verbis Socinus partim calumniatorem agit, partim Tergiversatorem, & sese manifestissimæ veritati opponit. Siquidem ignorare non potuit, creberrimas, gravissimasque lites oriri solere, suaque ætate ortas, inter Anti-Trinitarios, Anabaptistas, aliosque Sectarios, qui tamen S. Scripturæ literæ unice adhærebant; ideoque ortas, neque adhuc terminatas, quia Authoritate Patrum, Concilio tum, veteribusque Ecclesiæ, contempta & ablegata, sibi solis arrogabant Interpretandi munus. Eum quoque non latuit, quamplurimas Dissensiones in Ecclesia olim consopitas fuisse, ope Conciliorum, & Authoritate Patrum, qui partim propriis suffragiis ex sensu Ecclesiæ sui temporis latis, & partim ex Majorum Testimoniis, qui in Fide Catholica decesserant, litibus sic exortis finem exoptatum imposuerunt. Calumniatur item Orthodoxos, cum asserit Illorum dicta ab iis propemodum exæquari divinis Oraculis. Etenim apud eos in Honore sunt, non ut infallibiles Dogmatum sacrorum Authores, sed ut optimi ac fidelissimi Oraculorum divinorum Interpretes, idque non ex suo Ipsorum Ingenio, sed ex Traditione Apostolica, quæ, priscis istis seculis, è sacro Divinæ veritatis fonte, multo purius fluxit atque defæcatius in Canali suo, quam nunc Diorum. Sin veterum Authoritas huic soli Rei serviret, ut certos nos faceret de Doctrina, quam Ecclesia Catholica sui temporis tenuit ac docuit, & exinde moneret posteros, ne ab ea temere recederent; abunde satis esset ad Socinum innovati Dogmatis, & audaciæ non ferendæ arguendum; qui Doctrinam istam non solum temere abdicavit, sed & conviciis atque contumeliis facillime [?]p [?]oscidit. At pace Socini, illis curæ erat, non tantum sensum atque sententiam Ecclesiæ sui ævi nobis exhibere, sed & Ætatum præcedentium, usque ad primos Evangelii Præcones; ut hoc pacto Fidei suæ Antiquitatem ostenderent, & Consensum Ecclesiæ Catholicæ in unoquoque seculo. Itaque quam fœda macula, quantum in se est, & veteris Ecclesiæ & hodiernæ, quæ vestigiis illius insistit, fidem famamque aspergit Socinus, cum plus satis innuit, veteres Dogmata quædam approbasse, & ad Posteros derivasse, contra Scripturas aperte reclamantes; & hodiernas Ecclesias adeo stupidas fuisse, atque vecordes, ut ea pro veris admitterent sine examine, sub lumine Evangelii tam clare effulgente; atque adeo, si minus ex malitia, saltem ex summa Inscitia vel Socordia, veritatem Divinam pessumdederint, & Antichristi Regno stabiliendo viam latissimam adaperuerint. Sugillat etiam, & novitatis incusat Ecclesiarum reformatarum Theologos, quos Lutheranos & Calvinianos appellat, cum temere affirmat, illis omni-bus causa cadendum esse, si præter S. literas, veterum Authoritati standum sit; cum nescire haud potuerit, eruditissimos ex illis quamplurimum Antiquitati deferto; Novitatem solam Dogmatum & Rituum[?] in ecclesia Romana damnare; & veterum Testimoniis, ut Adversariorum causam refellere, ita & suam stabilire. Sin Anti-Trinitarios solos intelligat, ut suos arguit Apostasiae a fide antiqua, ita probe novit, Theologos iltos, quos nominat, Catholicae Eidei causam contra iltos defendere, tam veterum Testimoniis, quam Authoritate S. Scripturae. Sed quod multo plus est, & Socinum Tergiversationis in hac Re manifestum reddit; in hac ipsa Epistola Authoritatem istam, quam adeo contemptim rejicit, cogitur agnoscere, ne sua ipsius causa cadat, quam in se tuendam suscipit contra eos, qui Invocationem & Adorationem Christo deberi negarunt. Cum enim multa Argumenta e S. literis attulisset, ad sententiam suam confirmandam, quae probe noverat, & posse, & solere ab Adversariis eludi, mole hujus Authoritatis tandem premit Radecium, ut contra qham[?] niti, nec audeat, nec possit Unde factum esse existimas, ut ab ipso quasi nascentis Ecclesiae Christi Initio, usque ad nostra Tempora toties varie[?], adeo ut nullus sit numerus &c. quibus in verbis (uti ea paulo antea citavi) suam de hac Re sententiam validissime confirmat Testimonio veterum, quorum Judicio innitendum esse vult, in sensibus S. Scripturae rite eruendis atque explicandis, ne alias veritati manifestissimae repugnemus. Idem Epist. 3. Andr. Dudithio — extra nos ipsos, Alio nobis Judice opus non est, quam Deo & Christo, controversiarum in rebus sacris obortarum — Sibi quemque advigilare par est, idque pro vero admittere ac tenere (licet universus Terrarum orbis in alia omnia iret) quod ipsemet, totus ad obsequium Dei conversus, de genuino & literarum sensu arbitratur & intelligit. Tom. 1. pag. 502. At quomodo Deo obsequitur, qui media rite intelligendi à Deo sibi data negligit, Fidei Duces aversatur, propriosque sensus, Judicio totius orbis Christiani, anteponit simul & opponit? Idem, Animadv. in Assert. Theol. Coll. Posnan. ad 1. p. 424. Tom. 2. De origine istius Dogmatis (viz. de Trinitate) non adeo summus solicitus. Nam etiamsi ad ipsum mundi initium ea referenda est, id ejus falsitatem evidentissimam nihil minuere poterit. Cum item Andreas Volanus his verbis Socinum urgeret: Magna profecto Impudentia vestra, Ebionita, & inaudita quaedam in contemnendo perpetuo universo Ecclesia Christi Judicio arrogantia, ut quod illa semper de Christo credidit, & quam fidem diversis Haereticis, tanquam Achillis clypeum opposuit, illam vos falsi & erroris insimulare non pudeat. Sic reponit Socinus: Perpetuum illud Christi Ecclesiae Judicium nunquam probabit Volanus. Imo contrarium à nobis manifeste probatur, quotiescunque Testimonia Christi Apostolorum in medium afferimus &c. Quo nihil futilius replicari potuit.
units.tr: §. 59. First, as to Scripture, its interpretation, and the judgment to be passed on theological controversies, they assign all of this to themselves and their disciples, with the greatest contempt for all antiquity and the Catholic Church. It is established, says Socinus, that Justin and Irenaeus thought differently about the Person of Christ than we do. Sol. 30. Scrup. On the 5th [?], p. 327, Tom. 1. The same on the Church, p. 344: he leaves each person to his own judgment in working out the sense of Scripture, and in passing censure on the teaching of anyone else; he wills that no one's opinion be relied upon, whether of those living today or of the teachers of the ancient Church. It is not to be attended to, he says, what men have taught or done, or taught or thought before, whoever they are, or however many they have been or are. Indeed, he wills that no divine revelation be required beyond the letter of Scripture. The same, Epist. 3 to Matthias Radecius, secretary of Danzig, p. 387, under the specious pretext of honouring Scripture alone and acknowledging its authority, he belittles the ancient Catholic Church, with its teachers and councils. From this, he says, the chief dissensions arise, which anyone can easily see, because most people in fact cling to the Word of God alone. For, besides the Holy Scriptures, I know not what councils, fathers, and antiquity are held in the greatest veneration, so that they are almost equated with the divine oracles; yet all these things, and whatever others there are of this sort, ought to have no further force among sensible people than to show the sense of the Church of those times; or at least to advise that one should not lightly depart from the doctrines which they approve. But to hold stubbornly to certain things, though the Holy Writings clearly object, simply because they are approved by these, is nothing else than deliberately to overthrow divine truth and to open a huge window for the strengthening of the Antichristian kingdom. Let the writings of the Papists against the Lutherans and Calvinists be read, and it will be sufficiently understood that, if we must abide by their authority beyond the Holy Writings, the cause of us all must fall. In these words Socinus acts partly as a slanderer, partly as an evader, and sets himself against the plainest truth. For he could not be unaware that very frequent and very grave disputes arise, and arose in his own day, among the Anti-Trinitarians, the Anabaptists, and other sectaries, who nevertheless clung solely to the letter of Scripture; and that these disputes have arisen and are not yet ended, because they have scorned and dismissed the authority of the Fathers, of the councils of that time, and of the ancient Church, and claim for themselves alone the office of interpreting. Nor was it hidden from him that very many dissensions in the Church were formerly quieted, by the help of councils and the authority of the Fathers, who, partly by their own votes given according to the sense of the Church of their time, and partly by the testimonies of predecessors who had died in the Catholic faith, put the desired end to disputes thus arising. He likewise slanders the Orthodox when he asserts that their sayings are almost equated by them with divine oracles. For among them these writings are held in honour, not as infallible authors of sacred doctrines, but as the best and most faithful interpreters of the divine oracles, and this not from their own wit but from apostolic tradition, which in those early ages flowed from the sacred fountain of divine truth far more purely and clearly in its channel than now. But if the authority of the ancients served only this purpose, to assure us of the doctrine which the Catholic Church of its time held and taught, and thereby to warn posterity not to depart from it lightly, it would be quite enough to refute Socinus for his reckless and intolerable novelty and audacity, who not only rashly rejected that doctrine but also very easily tore it apart with reproaches and insults. But with all respect to Socinus, they took care not only to show us the sense and opinion of the Church of their own age, but also of the preceding ages, back to the first heralds of the Gospel, so that in this way they might demonstrate the antiquity of their faith and the consensus of the Catholic Church in every century. Thus what a foul stain Socinus, as far as in him lies, casts on both the faith and the reputation of the ancient Church, and of the present Church which follows her footsteps, when he more than sufficiently implies that the ancients approved certain doctrines and handed them down to posterity, clearly contrary to the Scriptures; and that the present Churches were so dull and mad as to accept these as true without examination, under the light of the Gospel shining so clearly; and so, if not from malice, at least from the greatest ignorance or carelessness, they have overthrown divine truth and opened the broadest road for establishing the kingdom of Antichrist. He also sneers at and accuses of novelty the theologians of the Reformed Churches, whom he calls Lutherans and Calvinists, when he rashly affirms that the cause of all of them must fall, if we must abide by the authority of the ancients beyond the Holy Writings; although he could not have been ignorant that the most learned of them have greatly deferred to antiquity, and that they condemn only the novelty of the doctrines and rites in the Roman Church, and that they confute their adversaries' cause, and establish their own, by the testimonies of the ancients. But if he means the Anti-Trinitarians alone, whom he accuses of apostasy from the ancient faith, he knows well that those theologians whom he names defend the cause of the Catholic faith against them, both by the testimonies of the ancients and by the authority of Holy Scripture. But what is much more, and makes Socinus's evasion in this matter plain: in this very letter he is forced to acknowledge that authority which he so contemptuously rejects, lest his own cause fall, which he undertakes to defend against those who have denied that invocation and adoration are due to Christ. For when he had brought many arguments from the Holy Writings to confirm his opinion, which he well knew could be, and usually was, evaded by his adversaries, he finally presses Radecius with the weight of this authority, so that he neither dares nor is able to strive against it. Hence you think it came about, he says, that from the very beginning of the Church of Christ, as it were, down to our own times, so many variously [?], so that there is no number, etc. In these words (as I cited them a little above) he very strongly confirms his opinion on this matter by the testimony of the ancients, whose judgment he wishes us to rely on in rightly drawing out and explaining the senses of Holy Scripture, lest otherwise we oppose the plainest truth. The same, Epist. 3 to Andreas Dudith: Outside ourselves we need no other judge than God and Christ in controversies arising about sacred things. Each person must watch over himself and hold as true, and maintain, (though the whole world should go otherwise) what he himself, wholly turned to the obedience of God, judges and understands about the genuine sense of the letter. Tom. 1, p. 502. But how does he obey God who neglects the means of right understanding given him by God, despises the leaders of the faith, and sets and opposes his own senses above the judgment of the whole Christian world? The same, Animadversions on the Assertion of the Theologians of the Posnan Colloquy, on 1, p. 424, Tom. 2: About the origin of that doctrine (namely of the Trinity) he is not very concerned. For even if it is referred back to the very beginning of the world, that will not in the least lessen its most evident falsity. Likewise, when Andreas Volanus pressed Socinus with these words: Truly great is your impudence, Ebionite, and an unheard-of arrogance in constantly despising the judgment of the whole Church of Christ, so that you are not ashamed to charge with falsehood and error what she has always believed about Christ, and what faith she has opposed to various heretics as a shield of Achilles. Socinus replies thus: Volanus will never prove that perpetual judgment of the Church of Christ. Indeed the contrary is clearly proved by us whenever we bring forward the testimonies of Christ and the Apostles, etc. Nothing more trifling could be replied to this.

units.la: Quam misera enim petitio Principii est, cum Sociniani veteris Ecclesiae Judicio erronei Dogmatis convincuntur, ab illius sententia ad Scripturam appellare in suo ipsorum sensu intellectum, contra sensum Ecclesiae Catholicae uniuscujusque aevi, quem acceptum retulit ipsis Apostolis, S. Scriptur & Authoribus. Cum Socino idem in hac Re sentiunt illius Discipuli, Andreas Dudithius, & Oftorodus. Dudithius sic in Epist. ad Petrum Carolinum Concionatorem Varadiensem, data Cracoviae Cal. Sextil. 1572. Op. Soc. Tom. 1. p. 533. Col. 2. ubi cum contra Dogma Trinitatis arguisset, haec subdit: Cave Tu, Consensum veteris Ecclesiae nobis opponas; quod etsi facias, nihil proficies. Veritas enim quaerenda est ex verbo Dei, non Hominum qualiumcunque tanta de Re Conspiratio. Ubi, ut modo vidimus in Socino, satis absurde sibi concedi petit, quod in quaestione ponitur, dum ipsum verbi Divini Interpretem facit, & Aliorum quorumcunque sententiam in adversum latam, quasi Conspirationem contra veritatem Divinam temere rejicit. Atque hoc observatu haud indignum est, quas ob causas hic Dudithius, Communione Ecclesiarum Reformatarum deserta, sese tandem ad Socinum, & coetus ab eo collectos, contulerit. Duas autem affert; unam, quod Theologi illarum sese subjicere nollent Authoritati veterum Patrum atque Synodorum ut neque Judicio praesentis Ecclesiae Catholicae: Alteram, quod inter se dissentirent, atque alii alios variorum errorum damnarent. Hinc factum est, ut sese tandem conferret ad Partem Socini, qui cuncta retulit ad diserta S. Scripturae verba, & interpretandi munus unicuique permisit, pro suo Arbitrio exequendum. vid. Epist. Dudithii ad Bezam, datam A. C. 1571. Op. Soc. Tom. 1. pag. 524. Oftorodus autem in hoc aliquanto pejus sentit, quod teneat S. Scripturam posse intelligi, & credi, & obsequium ejus mandatis praeberi, sine interna & speciali S. Spiritus illuminatione & Auxilio. Sic enim Ille — Censemus graviter errare eos, qui putant Sacram Scripturam sine praecedente interna Illuminatione, & singulari Revelatione Spiritus Sancti, nulla ratione Fidem & Obedientiam in Hominibus operari posse. Instit. cap. 1.
units.tr: How wretched a petitio principii it is, when the Socinians are refuted by the judgement of the ancient Church on an erroneous doctrine, to appeal from that judgement to Scripture, understood in their own sense, against the sense of the Catholic Church of every age, which it received from the Apostles themselves, the authors of Holy Scripture. Socinus's disciples, Andreas Dudithius and Ostorodus, think the same on this point. Dudithius writes thus in a letter to Peter Carolinus, preacher at Varad, dated at Cracow, 1 August 1572, Op. Soc. Tom. 1, p. 533, col. 2, where, having argued against the doctrine of the Trinity, he adds: Beware that you do not set against us the consensus of the ancient Church; for even if you do, you will gain nothing. Truth is to be sought from the Word of God, not from the conspiracy of men of whatever kind on such a matter. Here, as we have just seen in Socinus, he absurdly asks to be granted the very point in question, while he makes himself the interpreter of the divine Word and rashly rejects, as a conspiracy against divine truth, the opinion of everyone else delivered against it.
