This observation is not unworthy of note: for what reasons Dudithius, having abandoned communion with the Reformed Churches, at last joined himself to Socinus and the assemblies gathered by him. He gives two. The first is that the theologians of those Churches were unwilling to submit themselves to the authority of the ancient Fathers and Synods, nor to the judgement of the present Catholic Church. The second is that they disagreed among themselves, and some condemned others for various errors. Hence it came about that he at last betook himself to the party of Socinus, who referred everything to the plain words of Holy Scripture and left the office of interpretation to each individual, to be exercised at his own discretion. See Dudithius's letter to Beza, dated A.D. 1571, Op. Soc. Tom. 1, p. 524. Ostorodus, however, thinks in this matter somewhat worse, in holding that Holy Scripture can be understood and believed, and obedience to its commands rendered, without the inner and special illumination and help of the Holy Spirit. For he says: We judge that those err gravely who think that without a preceding inner illumination and singular revelation of the Holy Spirit, Scripture can in no way produce faith and obedience in men. Instit. cap. 1.

units.la: §. 60. Secundo; Huic autem Hypothesi, fundamenti loco substratae, reliqua Dogmata superstruunt, quibus primarios Religionis Christianae Articulos, licet in S. Scriptura fundatos, & Fidei Symbolo comprehensos, pertinaciter impugnant, & funditus subruere conantur. Quod ex sequentibus luculentius apparebit. Nam
units.tr: §. 60. Secondly: upon this hypothesis, laid as the foundation, they build the remaining doctrines, by which they stubbornly attack the primary articles of the Christian religion, though these are founded in Holy Scripture and comprised in the creed, and they try to overthrow them utterly. This will appear more clearly from what follows. For

units.la: §. 61. 1. Quod ad Dei naturam & Attributa, Opusque Creationis attinet; Naturae Divinae quaedam attribuunt, ei prorsus incongrua, dictuque indigna, qualia sunt Passiones humanae, quibus Animus revera commovetur ac perturbatur, & male afficitur, ut Ira, Dolor, metus, ac desperatio; simulque tollunt Perfectiones ei debitas, ut Omniscientiam, Omnipraesentiam sive Immensitatem, Infinitatem, Simplicitatem sive Spiritualitatem, & voluntatis Immutabilitatem. Negant item, Deum ex nihilo, mundum creasse. negat Deum ubique esse, seu latere in medio Rerum impurissimarum ac sordium; sed in coelo esse; Coelum esse ejus Habitaculum; exinde Homines respicere, exaudire. Eum lucem inaccessam habitare, & siqua sunt His similia, quibus Habitaculi, & loci distantia significatur, qua Deus ab Hominibus distinguatur: Barbari, inquit, oramtes, in Coelum manus aut oculos attollunt. Ergo ipsa quodammodo natura omnes Terrarum Populos monere videtur ut in Coelo Deum quaerant, aut esse intelligant. Adjicere potuit, omnes Christianos, juxta ipsius Christi Praeceptum, orantes, ita compellare Deum; Pater noster qui es in Coelis; cum tamen simul credant, eundem in Terris sibi adesse; Christumque ipsum, juxta suum ipsius Promissum, in medio illorum esse, ubicunque congregatorum in nomine ejus. Matt. 18. 20. Idem affirmat. Affectus Deo attributos in S. Scriptura, esse Commotiones quasdam divinae Voluntatis; ita tamen, ut quoties dicitur poenitere, dolere, irasci, indignari, Res ingratæ extra Ipsum non eo usque eum afficiant atque conturbent quin absorbeantur in perenni ista ac interna voluptate, qua semper in se fruitur; & ex eo, quod ea convertat ad quoddam Gaudium suum, disponendo illa ad Nominis sui Gloriam. In eum sensum disserit. Cap: 31, p. 321, 323. Et de Pœnitentia sive dolore Dei, hæc speciatim adiicit—Est Affectio in Deo ingrata, orta ex eo quod Facta sua optima indignissimum, ob alienam nempe Culpam, Eventum sortiri cernat. Volkelius de Creatione, sic—Ideo Deus ex nihilo omnia fecisse dicitur, quia ea creavit ex Materia informi, H. E. Ejusmodi, quæ nec actu, nec naturali aliqua Potentia seu Inclinatione Id fuerit, quod postea ex ea fuit formatum; ita ut nisi vis quædam infinita accessisset, nunquam quicquam ex ea fuisset extiturum. At non extendit hanc vim infinitam ad Creationem hujus materiæ informis ex Nihilo, sed accedit potius ad Illorum sententiam qui eam increatam affirmant, cum Scriptura nihil omnino dicat de Creatione illius. Moscorovius item, de Bapt.: cont: Smigl. c: 3. p. 78,79. Negat, Creationem oportere esse Productionem Rerum ex Nihilo. Atque asserit, quosdam statuere Materiam primam fuisse æternam, non levibus Rationibus impulsos, nec quibus divinæ literæ uspiam contradicant, & refutare conatur omnia Smiglecii Argumenta in contrarium ab eo producta, sc numero 5. Ita limitat Omnipotentiam Dei, ut Crellius modo dictus Omniscientiam divinam certis quibusdam Terminis circumscribit; quando asserit, eam non extendi ad illa, quæ non sunt natura sua Scibilia; Talia autem, inquit, sunt futura Contingentia determinate sumpta. Alioquin, humana voluntatis libertas neganda erit, & omnia erunt necessaria. Cap: 14. pag: 202. Socinus quidem agnoscit prædictionem quorundam Futurorum à Deo, quæ nunquam fallit; eam tamen præposterè dependere vult, non ex Præscientia divina, quæ ad omnia se extendere dicitur, sed ex solo Decreto divino. Sic enim ille: Mirum esse non debet, si Deus Populi sui Afflictionem ab Ægyptiis, tanquam certissime futuram prædicere potuit, non quidem ex prænotione quadam inexplicabili & incomprehensibili omnium quæ fiunt, sed ex Decreto. Sic ille, Prælect: Theol: p. 547. Col:
units.tr: §. 61. 1. As regards the nature and attributes of God, and the work of creation, they ascribe to the divine nature certain things wholly unfitting to it and unworthy to be spoken, such as human passions, by which the mind is truly moved and disturbed and ill affected, as anger, grief, fear and despair; and at the same time they take away the perfections due to him, such as omniscience, omnipresence or immensity, infinity, simplicity or spirituality, and immutability of will. They likewise deny that God created the world out of nothing; they deny that God is everywhere, or that he lies hidden in the midst of the most impure and filthy things, but say that he is in heaven, that heaven is his dwelling, and that from there he looks upon men and hears them, and that he dwells in unapproachable light, and whatever else is similar, by which the distance of dwelling and place is signified, by which God is distinguished from men. The barbarians, he says, all lift their hands or eyes to heaven in prayer. Therefore nature herself seems in some way to warn all the peoples of the earth to seek God, or to understand that he is in heaven. He might have added that all Christians, following Christ's own precept, when they pray address God in this way: Our Father who art in heaven; although at the same time they believe that he is present with them on earth, and that Christ himself, according to his own promise, is in the midst of those gathered in his name. Matt. 18. 20. He likewise affirms that the affections ascribed to God in Holy Scripture are certain movements of the divine will; yet so that whenever it is said that he repents, grieves, is angry, or is indignant, unwelcome things outside himself do not so far affect and disturb him that he is not absorbed in that eternal and inner joy in which he always delights in himself, and from the fact that he turns those things to a certain joy of his own, by disposing them to the glory of his name. He argues to this effect. Cap. 31, pp. 321, 323. And concerning the repentance or grief of God he specifically adds these words: It is an affection in God, unwelcome, arising from the fact that he sees his very best works meet with an outcome most unworthy of them, namely on account of another's fault. Volkelius, on creation, says thus: Therefore God is said to have made all things out of nothing, because he created them out of formless matter, that is, matter which of itself, and by no natural power or inclination, was able to become what was afterwards formed from it; so that unless some infinite power had intervened, nothing would ever have come forth from it. But he does not extend this infinite power to the creation of this formless matter out of nothing; he rather inclines to the opinion of those who affirm that it is uncreated, since Scripture says nothing at all about its creation. Moscorovius likewise, in De Baptismo against Smiglecius, ch. 3, pp. 78, 79, denies that creation must be the production of things out of nothing. He asserts that some hold the first matter to have been eternal, not moved by slight reasons, nor such as the divine letters anywhere contradict, and he tries to refute all the arguments of Smiglecius brought against this, namely in number 5. Crellius, just mentioned, so limits the omnipotence of God, and circumscribes the divine omniscience within certain fixed bounds, when he asserts that it does not extend to those things which are not by their nature knowable. Such, he says, are future contingents taken as determinate. Otherwise human freedom of will must be denied, and all things will be necessary. Ch. 14, p. 202. Socinus indeed acknowledges that God foretold certain future events, which never fail; yet he wants this foreknowledge to depend, absurdly, not on the divine foreknowledge, which is said to extend to all things, but on the divine decree alone. For he says: It ought not to be wondered at, if God could foretell the affliction of his people by the Egyptians as most certainly future, not indeed from some inexplicable and incomprehensible foreknowledge of all things that happen, but from a decree. Thus he, Prælect. Theol. p. 547, col.

units.la: 2. Resp: ad Gen: c: 15. v. 13, 14. Tom: 1. Idem Ib: p. 548. Col: 2. Resp: ad Marc: 14. 30. Petrus propter Temeritatem suam meritus fuerat, ut in ejusmodi scelus laberetur, & divina Gratia, qua ab ipso abstinere potuisset, prorsus destituretur; ex cujus Gratiæ subtractione, jam à Deo in Petri Temeritatis & Arrogantiæ pœnam decreta, unde necessario Negatio illa, occasione oblata, consecutura erat, prædixit Illam Christus; non autem ex alia aliqua Dei Prænotione. Nec alia præterea re opus fuit, nisi ut Occasio Christum negandi Petro daretur. Id quod ipsum Deum curasse, i. e. effecisse, ut ab Ancilla ista aliisque interrogaretur, & ex numero Discipulorum & Comitam Christi esse diceretur, nihil ad rem attinet. Atque Ib: lic[?].—Deus solet falsos Prophetas excitare, ut tentet atque exploret suos Deut: 13. 3. Thess: 2. 10, 11, 12. Igitur potuit Deus per divinos Viros, perque ipsum Christum, falsorum Prophetarum Adventum prædicere; non quia id prævidentia inexplicabili prænosset, sed quia sic futurum decreverat; prædictum simul fuit multos futuros, qui falsis illis prophetis fidem adhibeant; non quia Deus, Ratione quadam prorsus incomprehensibili, multos futuros antea noverit, qui digni sint quibus efficacia illa erroris mittatur; verum, quia cum ejusmodi Homines ii sint, qui Veritati non obediunt, ut ibidem Paulus ait; ii vero, qui veritati non obedient, aut pessimi quidam & perversi sunt Homines, aut ejusmodi qui nimis negligentes in Rebus divinis sunt, quorum semper ingens fuit, & futurus est Numerus; certum est, non defuturos unquam, qui ea Punitione Dei sint digni.
units.tr: 2. Answer to Gen. ch. 15, vv. 13, 14, Tom. 1. The same, ibid., p. 548, col. 2. Answer to Mark 14. 30. Peter, on account of his rashness, had deserved to fall into such a crime, and to be left wholly destitute of the divine grace by which he could have abstained from it; once that grace was withdrawn, God had already decreed the punishment of Peter's rashness and arrogance, whence that denial, given the opportunity, would necessarily follow; Christ foretold it on this ground, and not from any other foreknowledge of God. Nor was anything else needed, except that an opportunity to deny Christ should be given to Peter. That God himself took care, that is, brought it about, that he should be questioned by this maidservant and others, and should be said to be one of the disciples and companions of Christ, is of no concern to the matter. And again, ibid., he says: God is accustomed to raise up false prophets, to test and try his own. Deut. 13. 3. Thess. 2. 10, 11, 12. Therefore God could, through holy men and through Christ himself, foretell the coming of false prophets; not because he foreknew this by an inexplicable foresight, but because he had so decreed it to be. It was foretold at the same time that many would come who would give credit to those false prophets; not because God, by some wholly incomprehensible reasoning, knew beforehand that many would come who were worthy to be sent that effective delusion; but because, since such men are those who do not obey the truth, as Paul says in the same place, and those who do not obey the truth are either very wicked and perverse men, or men who are too negligent in divine things, and their number always has been and will be great, it is certain that there will never be lacking those who are worthy of that punishment of God.

units.la: §. 62. Hæc Socinus. At Inter illius Discipulos, nemo audacius Naturæ divinæ Perfectiones violavit, tum subtrahendo quæ ei debita erant, tum affingendo quæ ei maxime incongrua erant, & eo profusius indigna, quàm Conradus Vorstius, Professor olim Theologiæ in Academia Leidensi, cujus libros proinde, qui blasphema ista Dogmata continebant, Seren. Rex noster Jacobus publice cremari jussit in Cæmeterio Paulino & in utraque Academia. Intercessit quoque, per legatum suum, cum fœderatis Belgii Ordinibus, ut Illum, non solum Munere prosessorio privarent, sed etiam è finibus suæ ditionis pellerent. Et, ut palam ostenderet, quanto zelo tueretur fidem antiquam & Apostolicam, cujus ipse defensor erat, contra insana & impia Vorstii Dogmata, edidit libellum, cui Titulum dedit, Protestatio Antivorstia, in quo Illorum præcipua & maxime perniciosa notavit, excerpta è variis Ipsius Tractatibus, quorum Titulos & paginas in margine citat. Hæc autem fere sunt. Nihil vetat Deo etiam Corpus ascribere, si vocabulum Corporis in Significatione latiore sumamus. Non satis circumspecte loquuntur, qui Deum, ut essentia, sic etiam voluntate, prorsus immutabilem esse affirmant. Nusquam Scriptum legimus, Dei substantiam simpliciter immensam esse; imo non pauca sunt, quæ contrarium sensum habere videntur. Magnitudo nulla actu[?] infinita est. Ergo nec Deus pater peculiarem quandam emitatem[?], seu quasi limitatam & restrictam essentiam habere putandum est. Nusquam diserte Scriptum est, Substantiam Dei simpliciter, seu quovis modo, immensam & infinitam esse; & non pauca in S. literis occurrunt, quae contrarium, non dico clare asserunt, sed tamen asserere videntur. Est in Deo quantitas, sed non physica, verum hyperphysica; attamen nobis plane imperceptibilis & mere spiritualis. Deus quolibet sensu recte Infinitus dici non potest, quum Infinitudo illa, quae Definitioni certa opponitur, in Deum revera non cadat. Deus est in aliquo loco, sed non Physico, verum in Spatio abstractissime sumpto, quod Deus suo divino modo adimplet. Deus compositus est ex Materia & Forma, in sensu quodam improprio, vel, si mavis, per Catachresin quandam, per quam vocabulum Corporis, item quasi Materia & forma, seu quasi compositionis ex Genere & Differentia, aliquando eidem attribui posse non immerito alicui videatur. Deus non est immutabilis, ut essentia, sic Voluntate, unde porro non difficulter efficitur, etiam interna quaedam Accidentia in Deo, hoc est in ipsa (ut sic dicere liceat) proaretica[?] Dei mente & Voluntate, revera existere. Quod alibi sic emollit, seu potius fuco illinit. Deus non quidem subjectum est ullis veris Accidentibus; tametsi per liberam voluntatem quandam Accidentia latissime sic dicta, tum ad se, tum in se recipit Deus. Si omnia, & singula Rerum Eventa praecise & ab aeterno definita fuissent, nihil opus esset continua Rerum Inspectione & Procuratione, quae tamen Deo passim tribuitur. Plenius tamen respondere videntur, qui certam quidem in Genere universalem Dei scientiam esse docent, sed ita tamen, ut plures Certitudinis Causas in visione Praesentium ac Praeteritorum, quam in visione futurorum contingentium agnoscant. Omnia etiam decreta, quae semel apud se praecise definivit, uno modo & actu, post factam Definit[?]onem, accuratissime novit; sed de aliis omnibus & singulis, quaecunque sunt aut fiunt, seorsim & per se considerati, hoc affirmari non potest; quippe quae, non modo successive in Tempore, verumetiam contingenter, & saepe conditionaliter exstiterunt. Futura contingentia, comparative loquendo, etiam coram Deo dici possunt minus certa, quam Praeterita & Praesentia. Quod suum Dogma de limitata & incerta Dei Praescientia à Socino magistro suo, una cum caeteris, didicit; qui, cum negare non aude et praedictionem quorundam contingentium à viris divinitus illuminatis, quae in unam partem certo determinata erant ex decreto Dei, satis tamen absurde, ut mihi videtur, eorundem Praescientiam in Deo negat, ( quam inexplicabilem vocat, & incomprehensibilem ) qua Deus quicquam pro certo determinare possit, quod non certissime futurum praevidit; seu de quo ipse dubius esset; & conjectando solum assequeretur, illud eventurum esse; cum eventus interim revera in & ex se incertus sit, ut qui dependeat ex dubia & incerta voluntatis humanae determinatione, aliisque causis contingenter operantibus. At S. Scriptura scientiam Divinam praedicat omnino infinitam, Praescientiam decretis antecedentem ponit, ut natura sua priorem, futura omnia ut Deo praesentia repraesentat, & Dei consilia imperveftigabilia affirmat, nec Ingenii humani modulo dimetienda. Intelligentiae illius non est numerus, neque In-vestigatio. Psal. 147. 5. Isa. 40. 28. Cogitationes & viae meae, inquit Deus, non sunt sicut vestrae, sed exaltatae prae his, sicut Coeli supra Terras. Isa. 55. 8, 9. Intellexisti cogitationes meas de longe. Ps. 139. 2. omnes vias meas [illegible, ~6 letters]; prævidisti. Ita Sept. v. 3. non est verbum in lingua mea (nondum ore prolatum) quin Tu illud totum, seu omnino noveris. v. 4. Hæc scientia tua est mirabilis supra me; sublimius est, non possum ad eam pertingere. v. 6. O altitudo divitiarum & sapientiæ & Scientiæ Dei! quam inscrutabilia sunt Judicia ejus, & impervestigabiles viæ ejus! Rom. 11. 33. Quos præscivit, prædestinavit. Rom. 8. 29. Electis secundum præscientiam Dei Patris. 1 Pet. 1, 2. A seculo nota sunt Deo omnia opera ejus. Act. 15. 18. Ubi loquitur Jacobus de Operibus Dei, ab eo per Prophetas ante-dictis Deus operatur omnia secundum consilium sive decretum [τὴν βουλὴν]? voluntatis suæ. Eph. 1. 11. Christus de mortuis loquens, qui resurrecturi erant, dicit; omnes Deo vivunt. Luc. 20. 38. quasi jam viverent, & actu surrexerint. Deus mortuos vivificat, & vocat ea quæ non sunt, tanquam essent, seu actu existerent. Rom. 4. 17. Ita suam Deo Gloriam derogat Vorstius certam ei futurorum omnium Præscientiam denegando, cum (ut alibi loquitur) vult Deum per discussum quendam consideratæ[?] de futuris, quasi de Incertis. Nec minus ei injurius est, cum Affectus humanos Deo tribuit, idque vere, & suo modo proprie, hoc est, pro divinæ, licet non pro naturæ nostræ proprietate sc. Affectus Amoris, odii, iræ &c. imo metus atque Desperationis, ut idem Rex noster illi merito exprobrat; licet turpiter negare cogatur, quod turpius asseruisse deprehensus est. Sic & in Reliquis fere, ne plane Blasphemo habeatur, & Dogmata à se asserta, Christianis lectoribus horrori essent ad primam intuitum, illa levit & expolit, & limitationibus quibusdam sophisticis virus lethiferum abscondere nituntur, cuiusmodi sunt, Quodammomodo. Quadamtenus, in mea sensu, Aliquando, improprie loquendo & metaphorice, videtur, nihil absurdi erit si hac Deo ascribamus, & similia; quibus passim utitur tum ut modestiam simulet, tum ut Placitorum suorum venenum placidius & occultius instillet in animos lectorum. Sic enim, ut cum eodem Rege nostro loquar, hic Anti-Johannes in Coelos, & Dei Solium, profano Altarum[?] remigio sublatus, sacram illius et ineffabilem essentiam, quae miranda erat, non rimanda, sacrilegis quaestionibus solicitat, & Infinitatem, unam ex Attributis divinis, cum Immensitate, quae nonnunquam Creaturis tribuitur, commiscet, essentiam & substantiam, cum Hypostasi confundit, primas & secundas Creationes invehit, mediatas & immediatas; Deum quantum facit, & qualem, Aeternitatem e seculorum Periodis componit, & cum Aeviternitate confundit; Deum inficiatur Actum purum, & Qualitatum expertem, utpote qui Aliquid in seipso diversitatis aut multiplicitatis habeat; & (horresco referens) Principium cujusdam mutabilitatis, quasi Bellum non Theologiae solum, sed humanis omnibus scientiis indixit. Denique sic concludit. Neminem hic recusaJudicem, an justius de causis videar commovere, ut vel maxime Reformatae Religionis Professor non ferrem, sed latiore vocis usu Christianus, aut, si velis e Schola Platonis Theologus, naturali saltem numinis Cognitione praeditus.
units.tr: §. 62. So far Socinus. But among his disciples, no one violated the divine perfections more boldly than Conradus Vorstius, once Professor of Theology in the Academy of Leiden. Our most serene King James therefore ordered his books, which contained these blasphemous doctrines, to be publicly burned in St Paul's Churchyard and in both universities. He also interceded, through his envoy, with the United Provinces of the Netherlands, asking that they remove Vorstius not only from his professorship but also from their territories. To show plainly how zealously he defended the ancient and apostolic faith, of which he himself was the champion, against Vorstius's mad and impious doctrines, he published a pamphlet entitled Protestatio Antivorstiana, in which he noted the principal and most pernicious of those doctrines, excerpted from various treatises of Vorstius whose titles and pages he cites in the margin. These are roughly the following. Nothing prevents us from ascribing a body to God as well, if we take the word "body" in a wider sense. They do not speak with sufficient circumspection who affirm that God is wholly immutable, both in his essence and in his will. Nowhere do we read in Scripture that the substance of God is simply immense; indeed there are not a few passages which seem to have the contrary sense. No magnitude is actually infinite. Therefore neither is God the Father to be thought to have some peculiar [limited] quality, or as it were a restricted and confined essence. Nowhere is it expressly written that the substance of God is simply, or in any way, immense and infinite; and not a few places in the holy letters occur which, I do not say clearly assert the contrary, but nevertheless seem to assert it. There is quantity in God, but not physical quantity; rather hyperphysical, yet to us altogether imperceptible and purely spiritual. God cannot rightly be called infinite in any sense, since that infinity which is opposed to a fixed definition does not in fact apply to God. God is in some place, but not a physical place; rather in space taken in the most abstract sense, which God fills in his own divine manner. God is composed of matter and form, in a certain improper sense, or, if you prefer, by a certain catachresis, by which the word "body," and likewise as it were matter and form, or as it were a composition of genus and difference, may sometimes not unreasonably seem to be attributed to him. God is not immutable, either in essence or in will, whence it follows without difficulty that certain internal accidents also really exist in God, that is, in the very (if we may so speak) deliberative mind and will of God. Elsewhere he softens this, or rather smears it over with paint: God is not indeed the subject of any true accidents, although by a free will God receives, both toward himself and in himself, accidents so called in the broadest sense. If all and each of the events of things had been precisely and from eternity defined, there would be no need of a continual overseeing and care of things, which nevertheless is everywhere attributed to God. Yet those seem to answer more fully who teach that God indeed has a certain universal knowledge in general, but acknowledge more causes of certainty in the vision of present and past things than in the vision of future contingent things. God also knows most exactly, in one manner and by a single act after the definition has been made, all the decrees which he has precisely determined within himself; but this cannot be affirmed of all the others, of whatever kind, considered separately and in themselves, since these not only exist successively in time but also contingently, and often conditionally. Future contingent things, speaking comparatively, may even in the sight of God be called less certain than past and present things. In this doctrine of a limited and uncertain foreknowledge of God he learned from his teacher Socinus, together with the rest; who, since he does not dare to deny the prediction of certain contingent things by men divinely enlightened, which were fixed with certainty to one side by the decree of God, yet quite absurdly, as it seems to me, denies the foreknowledge of these things in God (which he calls inexplicable and incomprehensible), by which God could determine anything for certain that he had not foreseen with the utmost certainty as going to be; or about which he himself would be in doubt; and by conjecture alone would he attain that it was going to happen; whereas the event in the meantime is in itself and from itself really uncertain, as depending on the doubtful and uncertain determination of the human will and on other causes operating contingently. But Holy Scripture proclaims a divine knowledge that is wholly infinite, places foreknowledge as preceding decrees, as prior in its nature, represents all future things as present to God, and affirms the counsels of God to be unsearchable, and not to be measured by the measure of the human mind. "Of his understanding there is no number, nor any searching out." Ps. 147. 5. Isa. 40. 28. "My thoughts," says God, "and my ways are not as yours, but are exalted above them, as the heavens are above the earth." Isa. 55. 8, 9. "Thou hast understood my thoughts afar off." Ps. 139. 2. "All my ways [illegible]; thou hast foreseen them." So the Septuagint, v. 3: "There is not a word in my tongue (not yet uttered by the mouth) but thou knowest it wholly, or altogether." v. 4. "This knowledge of thine is wonderful above me; it is too high, I cannot attain to it." v. 6. "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!" Rom. 11. 33. "Whom he foreknew, he also predestinated." Rom. 8. 29. "Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father." 1 Pet. 1. 2. "Known unto God are all his works from the beginning." Acts 15. 18. Where James speaks of the works of God, spoken of beforehand by the prophets, "God does all things according to the counsel [τὴν βουλὴν] or decree of his will." Eph. 1. 11. Christ, speaking of the dead who were to rise again, says: "All live unto God." Luke 20. 38. as though they already lived, and had actually risen. "God quickens the dead, and calls those things which are not as though they were, or actually existed." Rom. 4. 17. Thus Vorstius detracts from the glory of God by denying him a certain foreknowledge of all future things, since (as he says elsewhere) he wishes God to proceed by a certain considered discussion of future things, as if they were uncertain. He is no less injurious to God when he attributes human affections to him, and that truly, and in his own manner properly, that is, according to the property of the divine nature, though not of ours: namely the affections of love, hatred, anger, and so on, even fear and despair, as our same King justly reproaches him for; although he is compelled to deny shamefully what he has been caught asserting more shamefully. So too in almost all the rest, lest he be considered plainly blasphemous, and lest the doctrines he asserts be a horror to Christian readers at first sight, he lightly smooths and polishes them, and strives to hide the deadly poison under certain sophistical limitations, such as these: in a way, to some extent, in my opinion, sometimes, speaking improperly and metaphorically, it seems that nothing absurd will follow if we ascribe these things to God, and the like; which he uses everywhere, both to feign modesty and to instil the poison of his opinions more gently and secretly into the minds of readers. For thus, to speak with the same King of ours, this Anti-John, raised by a profane rowing to the heavens and the throne of God, vexes with sacrilegious questions that sacred and ineffable essence of his, which was to be wondered at, not probed; he mixes infinity, one of the divine attributes, with immensity, which is sometimes ascribed to creatures; he confuses essence and substance with hypostasis; he introduces first and second creations, mediate and immediate; he makes God quantitative, and of what kind, and he composes eternity out of periods of ages and confuses it with aeviternity; he denies that God is pure act and free of qualities, as one who has in himself some diversity or multiplicity; and (I shudder to say it) he declares the principle of a certain mutability, as if he had declared war not only on theology but on all human sciences. Finally he concludes thus: I here refuse no judge whether I seem to stir up these matters with more justice, so that I, though a professor of the Reformed religion, would not bear it, but by a broader use of the word am a Christian, or, if you like, a theologian from the School of Plato, at least endowed with the natural knowledge of the deity.

units.la: § 63. Haec de Vorstio, ejusque impiis Dogmatibus, circa Dei naturam & Attributa, quibus censoriam notam inussit Seren: R. noster Jacobus. Fas sit, pauca quaedam his praefatis adjicere ex R. Davenantii[?] nostri Differt[?], de Praedest. Quibus Vorstius impugnat universalem Dei Praescientiam propriae voluntatis Immutabilitatem, & Dominium in voluntatem humanam. Sic etenim Vorstius. Infallibilis illa, & prorsus universalis omnium futurorum Praescientia nulli usui est in Deo. Not. ad disp. de Deo. pag. 329. Admissa hac Praescientia universali, & prorsus infallibili, necesse est, multa Scriptura loca mirabilibus Glossis torquere. Ib. p. 330. Absit, ut Deo vel Hypocrisin, vel Temeritatem atque Imprudentiam[?] ejusmodi attribuamus, cujusmodi per infallibilem illam omnium futurorum praenotionem, induci omnino videtur. Ib. p. 331. Voluntas Dei ad extra, non minus in Deo, quam in Angelis & Hominibus, ad opposita vertibilis est. Ib. 371. Nihil absurdi ex eo sequitur, quod Deus in Tempore quadam praecise ac definite velle aut nolle dicitur, quae fortassis antea non ita praecise, vel voluit, vel noluit. & crassius, p. 486. Poenitentia recte Deo convenit, quatenus ipsa opera sua, propter supervenientem aliquam causam insperatam, vere improbat, deserit aut mutat. Postremo, de Dominio Dei in nostras voluntates sic statuit. Virtutes & bona Opera libere prorsus & contingenter in nobis esse, aut a nobis fieri, vult Deus; eoque, potentius aut efficacius ea ipsa, quam per modum voti & desiderii velle non potest. Amica Duplic. ad Jo. Piscat. p. 55. Hinc illius Discipuli affirmant, Deum numquam absolute velle, aut praecise intendere, cujuscunque Hominis Conversionem; sed e contra, quod positis omnibus Gratia divinae operationibus, quibus Deus utitur ad Conversionem humanam, ita tamen maneat ipsa conversio in Hominis Potestate, ut converti possit, vel non possit. Haec Ille.
units.tr: § 63. These things concerning Vorstius and his impious doctrines about the nature and attributes of God, on which our most serene King James branded him with a mark of censure. It is permitted to add a few things to these preliminary remarks from our Davenant's Disputation on Predestination. In these Vorstius attacks God's universal foreknowledge, the immutability of his own will, and his dominion over the human will. For thus Vorstius: That infallible and entirely universal foreknowledge of all future things is of no use in God. Notes on the disputation concerning God, p. 329. If this universal and wholly infallible foreknowledge is admitted, it is necessary to twist many passages of Scripture with strange glosses. Ibid., p. 330. Far be it from us to ascribe to God hypocrisy or rashness and imprudence of the kind which seems wholly to follow from that infallible foreknowledge of all future things. Ibid., p. 331. The will of God toward things outside himself is no less changeable in God than in angels and men, toward opposites. Ibid., p. 371. Nothing absurd follows from the fact that God is said to will or not will certain things at a precise and definite time, which perhaps he did not previously will or not will in that precise way. And more crudely, p. 486: Repentance fitly belongs to God, insofar as he truly disapproves, abandons or changes his own works because of some unforeseen cause that supervenes. Finally, on God's dominion over our wills, he lays down this: God wills that virtues and good works should be in us, or done by us, wholly freely and contingently; and he cannot will them by way of a wish and desire, which is more powerful and more effective. Friendly Second Reply to John Piscator, p. 55. Hence his disciples affirm: God never absolutely wills or directly intends the conversion of any man; but on the contrary, although all the operations of divine grace by which God works human conversion are in place, the conversion itself remains in man's power, so that he may be converted or may not be converted. So far he.

units.la: §. 64. S.S. Trinitatis mysterium, quod Ecclesia Catholica non modo semper agnovit, sed & pro primario Fidei Christianae Articulo Filiis suis credendum injunxit, haud satis putarunt disertis verbis abnegare, nisi & impie quoque blasphement. Deum Patrem negant fuisse talem ab aeterno. cum negant eum habuisse Filium ab aeterno. Christum Dei Filium pro nudo Homine habent; ut Paulus Samosatenus olim, & Photinus; & ante eos, Ebion atque Cerinthus; ad quorum Haeresin debellandam Joannes dicitur Evangelium suum scripsisse; ideoque in ipso Principio Illius, Christi Deitatem asseruisse. Necnon Spiritus S. Deitatem omnino tollunt, cum affirmant, eum esse duntaxat virtutem Dei Patris, non autem substantiam aut Personam. Catechismus Racoviensis asserit, Sententiam eorum, qui Christo divinam naturam tribuunt, esse non solum sanae Rationi, verumetiam divinis literis repugnantem; & graviter errare eos, qui statuunt non solum Patrem, verumetiam Filium & Spiritum S. Personas esse in una Deitate. Idem quoque Catechismus, & Schlichtingius in Symbolum, multum laborant, ut Argumenta ab Orthodoxis e S. Scriptura adduci solita pro Deitate utriusque, irrita reddant, dum ea in Haereticum sensum detorquent. Hanc pariter censuram de istiusmodi Argumentis tulit Conr: Vorstius, Argumenta, inquit, quae adferuntur a Patribus, vel a recentioribus Theologis, pro aeterna Christi Generatione, aut fallacia sunt, aut frivola. Smalcius item sic—Substantiam Dei esse simplicissimam, & numero unam, & tamen ex ea generari Alium, contradictionem implicat; & Ratiunculae Adversariorum in contrarium allatae, Deum sc. de Substantia sua Filium generasse, nugatoriae sunt. Resp. ad nova Monst. part. 2dam. c. 22. p. 198. Cum autem Smiglecius objecisset, Christum sibi quamplurima in Evangelio attribuere; quae ipsius aequalitatem cum Deo Patre evincunt, qualis nulli Creaturæ competit Smalcius respondet, Hujusmodi Prærogativam non parum conducere ad augmentum Gloriæ Divinæ, & generis humani Solatium, quæ sunt Duo præcipui fines, ad quos Deus collimat. hæc insuper adiicjens--Dico non posse quidem Creaturam per Omnia prorsus esse æqualem Deo, sed potest esse in quibusdam Rebus Ib. c. 24. p. 216. Paulo post tamen allerit; Christum filii divinam naturam arrogasse, plane controversum est ima omnino falsum, p. 220. Idem, in exam. 100. Errorum, hæc de Christo habet. Christus, ante Resurrectionem, non fuit perfecte, aut Christus, aut Dei filius, aut Deus. Err. 26. Christus dici non potest natura Deus sine Gloriæ patris imminutione. Err. 28. Christus non habet Potestatem rem ullam creandi, &c. ex Nihilo. Creationi Rerum aliquarum nullus hodie est locus. Err. 31. Ergo nec Animarum humanarum, juxta Illum. Christi Potestas non absolute æterna natura est, sc. respectu Fidelium. Err. 32. Idem in exam. 157. Errorum reliquorum, quos Smiglecius ei objecerat, in Resp. ad nova Monst. Christus ante Mundum non extitit. Per eum Mundus non est conditus, Err. 45. Christus Angelos creavit, per reformationem Politiæ Ipsorum; sc. ut nunc ipsi subderentur, sicut trius Deo Patri soli. Err. 36. Pariter, de Dæmonibus--Dæmones per Christum dici possunt creari, quatenus Illorum Potestatem ita reformavit, ut nunc ei subditi sint, & pareant, qui antea soli Deo subdebantur, & parebant. Err. 123. Id. Resp. ad nova Monst. part. 2dm. c. 17. p. 153. Illa verba Apostoli de Melchisedeco sine patre, & matre; non habens Initium dierum, nec finem vitæ. Hebr. 7. 3. Quæ de Melchisedeco typice, de Christo proprie & juxta literam intellexit Ecclesia Catholica; vult Melchisedeco congruere, respectu Sacerdotii; neutiquam vero Christo, absolute atque simpliciter. Ostorodus[?] autem, dum eadem verba explicat, hoc modo satis procaciter Catholicos insectatur, quando ait, derelicta[?]-bilem esse ruditatem[?], & negligentiam summam illorum, qui verba illa ad essentiam, sive naturam Christi referunt, quasi Ille in coelo matrem nullam, ut in Terris patrem nullum, haberet; cum hoc in Melchisedeco locum habere non possit, qui tamen filio Dei assimilatur. Inst. cap. 41. Idem Smalcius in exam. 102[?]. Err. haec habet de Trinitate. Persona est natura individua. Natura est Genus respectu personae. Subsistentia a Natura non distinguitur. Repugnat Rationi, unam numero Essentiam esse in pluribus. Err. 65-98[?].
units.tr: §. 64. The mystery of the Most Holy Trinity, which the Catholic Church has not only always acknowledged but has also enjoined on her children to believe as the primary article of the Christian faith, they have thought it not enough to deny in plain words, unless they also blaspheme impiously. They deny that God the Father was such from eternity, when they deny that he had a Son from eternity. They hold Christ the Son of God to be a mere man, as Paul of Samosata once did, and Photinus; and before them Ebion and Cerinthus, to whose heresy's refutation John is said to have written his Gospel, and who therefore in its very beginning asserted the deity of Christ. Likewise they utterly abolish the deity of the Holy Spirit, when they affirm that he is merely the power of God the Father, and not a substance or a Person. The Racovian Catechism asserts that the opinion of those who attribute the divine nature to Christ is not only repugnant to sound reason but also to the divine writings; and that those err gravely who hold that not only the Father but also the Son and the Holy Spirit are Persons in one Deity. The same Catechism, and Schlichting in his commentary on the Creed, labour greatly to render void the arguments usually brought by the Orthodox from Holy Scripture for the deity of both, by twisting them into a heretical sense. Conrad Vorstius likewise passed this judgement on such arguments: The arguments which are adduced by the Fathers, or by more recent theologians, for the eternal generation of Christ are either fallacious or frivolous. Smalcius likewise says: That the substance of God is most simple and one in number, and yet that another is generated from it, implies a contradiction; and the little reasonings of the adversaries brought to the contrary, namely that God generated a Son from his own substance, are trifling. Reply to the New Monstrosities, part 2, ch. 22, p. 198. When Smiglecius objected that Christ attributes to himself very many things in the Gospel which prove his equality with God the Father, such as no creature can have, Smalcius replies: Such a prerogative contributes not a little to the increase of the glory of God and the comfort of the human race, which are the two chief ends at which God aims. Adding these words: I say that a creature cannot indeed be altogether equal to God in all things, but it can be in some things. Ibid., ch. 24, p. 216. Shortly afterwards, however, he asserts: That Christ arrogated to himself the divine nature of the Son is plainly a controversial matter, indeed altogether false. p. 220. In his examination of the hundred errors, he has this to say about Christ: Christ, before the Resurrection, was not perfectly either Christ, or the Son of God, or God. Error 26. Christ cannot be called God by nature without diminishing the glory of the Father. Error 28. Christ does not have the power to create anything at all out of nothing, etc. There is today no place for the creation of certain things. Error 31. Therefore, according to him, neither of human souls. The power of Christ is not absolutely eternal in nature, namely with respect to believers. Error 32. The same, in the examination of the remaining 157 errors which Smiglecius had charged him with, in his Reply to the New Monstrosities: Christ did not exist before the world. Through him the world was not made, Error 45. Christ created the angels by reforming their polity, namely so that they should now be subject to him, as they were formerly subject to God the Father alone. Error 36. Likewise, concerning demons: Demons may be said to be created through Christ, insofar as he so reformed their power that they are now subject to him and obey him, who were formerly subject and obedient to God alone. Error 123. The same, Reply to the New Monstrosities, part 2, ch. 17, p. 153. As for the apostle's words about Melchizedek, without father or mother, having neither beginning of days nor end of life (Heb. 7:3), which the Catholic Church has understood of Melchizedek figuratively and of Christ properly and according to the letter, Socinus wants them to fit Melchizedek with respect to the priesthood, but by no means Christ absolutely and simply. Ostorodt, however, while explaining the same words, attacks the Catholics rather insolently in this way, when he says: There is a lamentable crudity and extreme negligence in those who refer those words to the essence or nature of Christ, as if he had no mother in heaven, just as on earth he had no father; since this cannot apply to Melchizedek, who nevertheless is likened to the Son of God. Institutes, ch. 41. The same Smalcius, in his examination (102), has these things about the Trinity: A person is an individual nature. Nature is a genus with respect to the person. Subsistence is not distinguished from nature. It is contrary to reason that one numerically identical essence should be in several. Errors 65–98.

units.la: Sed audiamus ipsum Socinum de Trinitate sic differentem usque Tempora Concilii Niceni & aliquanto post, (ut ex omnium, qui tunc extitere, Scriptis liquet) Ille unus verus Deus, quem passim sacra Testimonia praedicant, solus pater Jesu Christi est creditus; & qui contrarium sentiebant ut Sabelliani, & eorum similes, pro Hæreticis plane sunt habiti. Sic Ille, de Ecclesia. p. 345. Quo nihil salsius, aut insulsius dici potuit; cum nemini ignotum esse quaerat[?] Veterum Scripta consulenti, quid senserit Eccle-sia illius aevi de Ebione & Cerintho, & Paulo Samosateno qui Deitatem Christi, ac proinde Trinitatem, negabant; & quod Sabelliani pro Hæreticis ab eadem Ecclesia haberentur, quia Catholicam Fidem de eadem Dogmate, quam ipsa semper tenuerat, violabant; licet alia prorsus Ratione; dum asserebant Trinitatem, non Personarum, sed Nominum solorum; sicut & Praxeas ante eos, qui Deum patrem cum Christo omnino confudit, & crucifixum fuisse asseruit; unde Patripassianus dicebatur, & istius sectæ Princeps. Noetus item Sabelii antecessor, qui docebat[?] Christum eundem, Ipsum esse Patrem & Spiritum Sanctum. Attamen verbis immediate sequentibus, non erubescit Ecclesiam Catholicam suæ ætatis, quæ hanc Sententiam de Trinitate Personarum in una Dei essentia defendit, Antichristianimi[?] rea m ea[?] de Causa peragere. Idem, Animady[?] in Assert. Theol. Col. Posnan. De trino & uno Deo, quarum prima hæc erat .Impia & blasphema secta, [sc. novorum Samosatenorum] Dogma de trino & uno Deo, Commentum Antichristi, tempore S. Justini Martyris inventum, afferit. In quam sic animadvertit Socinus Imo contra Fidem de uno Deo, nullum gravior in Christi Ecclesiam ab Antichristi Spiritu error invectus est, quam in Deo, inque illius simplicissima essentia, plures esse Personas inter se distinctas, quarum qualibet sit verus Deus, & non patrem tantum domini Nostri Jesu Christi, esse illum unum verum Deum, sed Filium quoque ipsum, & Spiritum Sanctum. Quo nihil vel absurdius, vel, ut ita dicam, impossibilius, vel divinis Oraculis magis contrarium, excogitari potest. p. 423. Tom. 2. Hæc Socinus. At Andr. Dudithius, illius Discipulus, aliquanto petulantius incessit hoc S. S. Trinitatis dogma. Sic enim ille in epist. ad Joan. Lacisium equitem Polonum— Non sum jocatus, Lacisi, sed serio admodum professus sum, Confessionis illius Formulam, quæ Athanasii nomine circumfertur (quam non ab Athanasio, sed ab otioso potius aliquo Monacho, fuisse Scriptam, Camerarius noster opinatur) itemque Nicenum illud Symbolum, non esse S. Literis, & Christiana Pietati consentaneum, sed ex humano sensu, & spinosis quibusdam frigidorum Sophistarum argutiis depromptum. Abhorrent illa prorsus, & valde quidem abhorrent à simplici illa & minime fucata Fide, quam Christus ipse, Magister & Servator noster, quamque ejus Discipuli docuerunt, literarumque monumentis consignatam nobis reliquerunt. Op. Soc. p. 500. col. 2. Tom.ii & postea, Audi Augustinum tuum, Trinitatis istius vestra Architectum. Ib. p. 512. col. 2. Idem in Epist ad Bezam --Tuum tibi, Augustinum proferam, cujus tantam Doctrina & Sanctitatis Opinionem in animas Hominum Satanas inservuit[?], ut major ejus, quam Christi Doctrina, fides passim habeatur. Nam, cum alia multa plane ab Evangelio abhorrentia, tum hanc de triplici Deo ecstaticam phantasiam, ex ipsius potissimum facundo Commentorum penu deprompserunt, qui Scholastici Theologi nominantur. Ex hoc nimirum vino biberunt Illi primi. Deinde, reliquas quoque Gentes Temulenti ipsi inebriarunt; ita quidem, ut jam, quod ebriis accidere solet, pro uno Tres, aut etiam plures perturbata visione, aspiciant. Sic ille p. 525. col. 1. Idem, in Epist. ad Petrum Carolinum --Tricipitem, Tergeminum hunc Deum ignorarint Apostoli, & tota illa orthodoxa Ecclesia. p. 533. col. 2.
units.tr: But let us hear Socinus himself differing about the Trinity thus: Up to the time of the Council of Nicaea and somewhat after (as is clear from the writings of all who then existed), that one true God whom the sacred testimonies everywhere proclaim was believed to be the Father of Jesus Christ alone; and those who thought otherwise, such as the Sabellians and their like, were plainly regarded as heretics. Thus he, concerning the Church, p. 345. Nothing could be said more foolish or insipid; since it is unknown to no one who consults the writings of the ancients what the Church of that age thought of Ebion, Cerinthus and Paul of Samosata, who denied the deity of Christ and therefore the Trinity; and that the Sabellians were regarded as heretics by that same Church because they violated the Catholic faith on this doctrine which it had always held, though by a quite different reasoning, since they asserted a Trinity not of Persons but of names only. So too Praxeas before them, who utterly confused God the Father with Christ and asserted that the Father was crucified, whence he was called a Patripassian and was the leader of that sect. Noetus likewise, Sabellius's forerunner, taught that Christ was the same as the Father and the Holy Spirit. Yet in the words immediately following, he does not blush to say that the Catholic Church of his own age, which defends this doctrine of the Trinity of Persons in the one essence of God, acts as an accomplice of Antichrist for this reason. The same, in his Animadversions on the Assertion of the Posen theologians concerning the triune and one God, of which the first was this: An impious and blasphemous sect [namely the new Samosatenes] asserts the dogma of the triune and one God, an invention of Antichrist, devised in the time of St Justin Martyr. On this Socinus remarks: Indeed, against the faith in one God, no more serious error has been introduced into the Church of Christ by the spirit of Antichrist than that in God, and in his most simple essence, there are several Persons distinct from one another, each of whom is the true God, and that not only the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is that one true God, but the Son also and the Holy Spirit. Nothing more absurd, or, so to speak, more impossible, or more contrary to the divine oracles, can be imagined. p. 423, vol. 2. Thus Socinus. But Andreas Dudith, his disciple, attacked this dogma of the Most Holy Trinity somewhat more petulantly. For thus he writes in a letter to John Lasicki, a Polish knight: I have not been joking, Lasicki, but have declared quite seriously that the formula of that Confession which goes around under the name of Athanasius (which our Camerarius thinks was written not by Athanasius but rather by some idle monk), and likewise that Nicene Creed, are not consistent with Holy Scripture or Christian piety, but are drawn from human sense and from the thorny subtleties of cold sophists. Those things are utterly repugnant, and very much repugnant, to that simple and in no way adulterated faith which Christ himself, our Master and Saviour, and his disciples taught, and which they left to us committed to the written record. Works of Socinus, p. 500, col. 2, vol. 2. And afterwards: Listen to your Augustine, the architect of that Trinity of yours. Ibid., p. 512, col. 2. The same, in his letter to Beza: I will bring forward for you your own Augustine, whose opinion of doctrine and sanctity Satan has so insinuated into the souls of men that his faith is held everywhere above the teaching of Christ. For, along with many other things utterly alien to the Gospel, they drew this ecstatic fancy of a threefold God from the very rich storehouse of his commentaries, those who are called scholastic theologians. Those first ones drank from this wine. Then they drunkenly intoxicated the other nations too, so that now, as usually happens to the drunk, they see three, or even more, through a disordered vision, where there is one. Thus he, p. 525, col. 1. The same, in his letter to Peter Carolus: The apostles and that whole orthodox Church did not know this three-headed, triple-natured God. p. 533, col. 2.

units.la: §. 65. Quod ad Christi Incarnationem attinet, non unam Haeresin divulgarunt. Nam aeterni Filii Dei, Dei ex Deo ante saecula geniti, Incarnationem (quam ut summum Salutis nostrae mysterium, atque Fundamentum, venerantur omnes vere Christiani) procacissimis profanisque dictis excipiunt. Ostorodus vocat illam, purum putum Hominum superstitiosorum Figmentum. Instit. c. 17. p. 96. Smalcius, Dogma in Christiana Religione fere monstrosissimum. Item, Opinionem indignam, qua in vera Christi, Ecclesia locum habeat; nedum, ut fundamentum Saltis cum confeamus[?]. Sic ille in Refut. Tho. Graveri de Incarnat. Idem in Exam. 100. Err. hæc habet. Verbum non est Caro factum, & oppositum dicere, error est. Err. 49. Christus a nativitate sua non fuit plenus gratia & veritate. Err. 50. Christus in morte desiit esse Filius Dei. Idem in exam. 154. errorum, hæc asserit eodem spectantia.--Tanta est fabula, ista duarum in Christo naturarum unio, ut vix Alia sit Illi par. Filii Dei cum humana natura unio, est Somnium simile. Christus secundum Carnem, id est, respectu conceptionis, dici potest Dei Filius, & Filius naturalis, quia natus Dei Filius. Christus Infans Deus vere non fuit, nec Christus perfecte nec Salvator nec Dominus. Nec ab infantia Spiritu Sancto repletus fuit, nec Rationis usum habuit, nec veram familiaritatem; quod postea aliquantulum emollit, interpretando de operibus Sanctis. Hæc ille, ab err. 6. ad err. 17. inclusive. Pergit vero sic in suo hoc Dogmate explicando. Christus propter similitudinem cum Deo, accidentaria ratione dicitur Dei Filius. Non enim est, nec esse potest Dei Filius propter generationem ex substantia Dei. Hoc enim ex impossibilibus unum est, Deum ex substantia sua generare. Err. 22. & paulo post. --Christus non est naturalis Dei Imago, sed nostri respectu, sc. ratione Doctrina. Err. 26, 27. Docent quoque, Christum incarnandum fuisse, & in mundum venturum, etiamsi Homo non peccasset; hæc Ratione addita, Quod etiam Homo integer ex hac temporali vita ad aliam transferendus fuisset, si maxime in statu primævo perfectus fuisset[?]; cujus Rei præconem & Perfectorem Deus Christum voluerit. Hoc tenent Sociniani, cum Andrea Osiandro, & Scholasticis nonnullis, vid. Jof. Stegm. Difp. 15. Dicunt item, Christum conceptum ac natum fuisse, non ex solo Maria femine & sanguine, sed ex carnea aliqua substantia, quam Dei virtus in B. Virginis uterum immisit, vel ibi creavit; seu, ex femine a-liquo purissimo, quod hoc pacto immissum est, aut illic creatum. Sic enim loquitur Smalcius, Resp. ad 2.part. Refut. Smiglecii. p. 156, 157, &c. Id. in exam. 157. err. in eundem sensum: Nos tam ex Sanguine Maria, quam ex materia, a Deo ad Christi Corpus gignendum aptata, Christum genitum esse dicimus. Err.
units.tr: §. 65. As for the Incarnation of Christ, they have spread not one heresy but several. They receive with the most insolent and profane words the Incarnation of the eternal Son of God, God from God, begotten before the ages (which all who are truly Christian revere as the chief mystery and foundation of our salvation). Ostorodus calls it nothing but a pure fiction of superstitious men. Institutes, ch. 17, p. 96. Smalcius: a dogma almost monstrous in the Christian religion. Likewise, an opinion unworthy to have a place in the true Church of Christ, much less that we should confess it as the foundation of salvation. Thus he writes in his Refutation of Thomas Grauer on the Incarnation. The same, in Examination, error 100: This error holds: The Word was not made flesh, and to say the opposite is an error. Error 49: Christ from his birth was not full of grace and truth. Error 50: Christ ceased in death to be the Son of God. The same, in Examination of errors 154, he asserts the following, pertaining to the same point: --This union of the two natures in Christ is such a fable that scarcely anything is its equal. The union of the Son of God with human nature is a dream-like thing. Christ, according to the flesh, that is, with respect to his conception, can be called the Son of God and a natural Son, because he was born the Son of God. Christ as an infant was not truly God, nor Christ perfectly, nor Saviour, nor Lord. Nor was he filled with the Holy Spirit from infancy, nor did he have the use of reason, nor true familiarity; which he afterwards somewhat softened by interpreting it of holy works. Thus he writes, from error 6 to error 17 inclusive. But he goes on in explaining this doctrine of his thus: Christ, because of his likeness to God, is called the Son of God in an accidental sense. For he is not, nor can he be, the Son of God by generation from the substance of God. For this is one of the impossibilities, that God should beget from his own substance. Error 22, and a little later: --Christ is not the natural image of God, but with respect to us, that is, by reason of his teaching. Errors 26 and 27. They also teach that Christ would have had to be incarnate and come into the world even if man had not sinned; adding this reason: that even man, if he had been perfect in the first state, would have had to be transferred from this temporal life to another; and God willed Christ to be the herald and perfecter of this matter. The Socinians hold this together with Andreas Osiander and some of the Scholastics; see Joseph Stegmann, Disputation 15. They also say that Christ was conceived and born not from the seed and blood of Mary alone, but from some fleshly substance which the power of God introduced into the womb of the blessed Virgin, or created there; or from some most pure seed, which was introduced or created there in this way. For so Smalcius speaks, in his Reply to the second part of the Refutation of Smiglecius, p. 156, 157, etc. The same, in Examination 157, error to the same effect: We say that Christ was begotten both from the blood of Mary and from matter fitted by God for generating the body of Christ.

units.la: 18. Denique Christum Davidis Filium dictum esse volunt, non quod B. Virgo, ipsius Mater, ex Davidis familia originem duxerit, sed quod fuerit Josepho desponsata ex illa Familia oriundo. Sic etenim idem Smalcius: Satis est, ut Christus dicatur ex semine Davidis factus, si Virginis Maria, quae uxor jam fuit Josephi, semen vel sanguis ad Christi generationem attexit. Jam enim Virgo Maria in Davidis familiam transferat. Resp. ad 2dam part. Refut. Smiglecii. p. 158. & Schlicht. in Symb. p. 47. Jesus Christus Davidis Filius est, secundum Prophetarum Oracula, quatenus in utero Matris suae, non prius, nec alii Alicui, quam Gentis Davidicae viro, desponsatae, sic illius Interventu conceptus, & ex ea genitus fuit.
units.tr: 18. Finally, they want Christ to be called the son of David, not because the blessed Virgin, his mother, derived her origin from the family of David, but because he was betrothed to Joseph, who was descended from that family. For so the same Smalcius: It is enough that Christ is said to be made from the seed of David, if the Virgin Mary, who was already the wife of Joseph, contributed seed or blood to the generation of Christ. For the Virgin Mary is then transferred into the family of David. Reply to the second part of the Refutation of Smiglecius, p. 158; and Schlichting, in the Symbol, p. 47: Jesus Christ is the Son of David according to the oracles of the prophets, in that he was conceived and born of his mother in her womb through the intervention of a man of the Davidic line, to whom she was betrothed, and not before, nor to anyone else.

units.la: §. 66. Quantum ad Christi Invocationem, & Adorationem spectat; Socinus quidem non semel utramque asserit, ut ipsi debitam, & earum observationem acriter urget contra Francisco-Davidianos. Etenim in Epistola sua ad Synodum Wægrovien-sem, Antitrinitarios inibi congregatos, vehementissime hortatur, ut de Adoratione & Invocatione Christi in Ecclesiis suis conservanda, inprimis laborent; eo quod, illa spreta, vel abjecta, nulla ratione fieri possit, quin ubique Judaismus vigeret, vel potius turpis Epicureismus atque Atheismus. Non vult item cum istis amplius in Rebus sacris commercium haberi, qui administrationem Regni Christi, & divinam Potestatem, hoc modo non agnoscunt. Consulit insuper, ut Omnibus Verbi Dei Ministris injungeretur, ut in publicis precibus, statutis quibusdam diebus, Christum Jesum Dei Filium nominatim invocarent Tom. 1. p. 491. Catechismus item Racoviensis de iis Hominibus, qui Christum non invocant, nec adorandum censent, ita sentit; eos prorsus non esse Christianos, cum reipsa Christum non habeant; & licet verbis id negare non audeant, reipsa negent tamen. p. 115. Attamen idem Socinus, cum alibi probasset Adorationem divinam esse Christo debitam, ut Particula [Sicut] qua ipse Christus utitur, — ut omnes honorificent Filium, sicut Patrem honorificant. Jo. 5. 22, 23. Statuit nihilominus haud minimam differentiam inter Honorem istum, qui Deo Patri, & qui Christo ipsius Filio, debetur. De Ecclesia. p. 353. Quam Differentiam explicat in Disput. sua cum Christiano Franken. Dico, inquit, Deum adorari, tanquam Authorem Rerum omnium; Christum autem, ut quoddam medium, per quod ejusmodi Adoratio tendit in Deum. Tom. 2. p. 772. Atque hoc ulterius sic illustrat. Quemadmodum liber iste protrusus per mediam mensam, non dicitur esse eorum, quos in cursu pertransiit, sed ejus tantum ad quem pervenit; ita Christi Adoratio, cum non permaneat in ipsa, sed ulterius pergat in Deum, dicitur esse ipsius Dei. p. 777. Imo alibi, Invocationem Christi, quam (ubi Res ipsius postulabant) ut summe necessariam urgebat, cunctisque suis usurpandam imponi voluit, adeo neglectim habet, ut inter Adiaphora recenseat, qualia sc. a Deo in verbo suo, nec jussa sunt, nec vetita; adeoque ut ibidem recte infert, non omnino necessariam. Sic enim ille, Epist. ad Geo. Eniedinum. p. 485. Col. 2. Tom. 1. Smalcius quoque in hoc, ut in aliis, Magistri sui sententiam tuetur. Cum enim pro nudo Homine Christum habeat, eum tamen invocari vult, & divinis Honoribus affici, ut Deum factum sive Hominem deificatum, & numen secundarii ordinis, Deo supremo subordinatum: Verum, cum ignorare non potuit, Deum unicum celebrari à Mose & Prophetis, sc numen illud suprenum[?], cui soli debetur Invocatio, atque Adoratio Divina; veteres item passim affirmare, Christum olim apparuisse Patriarchis, dixumque Jehovam, & divinis Honoribus affectum suisse (adeo passim & constanter, ut Tertullianus inter caeteros Articulos & hunc ponat, in sua regula Fidei. De praesc: adv: Haeret. cap. 13.) quem tamen ipse, cum suae Sectae Hominibus, pro mera Creatura habet, neque prius existente, quam ex Spiritu Sancto incarnatus fuerit, in utero B. Virginis; ut hunc geminum Honorem Christo afferat, cogitur, tum vilipendere Doctrinam Mosis atque Prophetarum in hac re ut Christianorum Fidei haud correspondentem; tum affirmare, cultum divinum merae Creaturae legitime exhiberi posse, & Angelis creatis olim actu exhibitum fuisse, ex concessione Dei. Sic enim ille, in Exam. 100. errorum—Non est certum, Deum ob naturam divinam practise colendum esse. Err. 8. Unum tantum Deum colere, qui sc. est Deus summus natura, & Independens, est Judaicum quid, & quodammodo Abnegatio Christianae Religionis. Err. 15. Parum curandum est Christianis, quid Prophetae dicant de cultu Dei unius. Err. 16. Potest Deus praecipere, ut quicunque vel Angelorum pro Deo colatur. Err. 17. Angelis, qui sunt Dii caelestes, divinum cultum tribui posse, & revipsa tributum fuisse in vetere Foedere, nemo inficiari potest—Sempen nos obligat Dei præceptum, quamuis etiam cap-tum nostrum superet; & facile est, de Triplo dubi-tare, an recte rem intelligas, quam dubitare, an De-liquid præcipienti sit obtemperandum. Fermisit Deus ut tunc Illud fieret, cum nondum exaltatus esset Iesus Christus, & Mediator Dei atque Hominum con-stitutus. Nunc autem, postquam inter Deum & Homi-nes medius constitit Dominus Iesus, ita sunt reformati Angelorum Throni & Dominationes, ut divinum Honorem Ipsi ab Hominibus exhiberi, nec Deus voluit, nec illi permitterentur. Eph. 1. 20.[?] Interim, hunc honorem divinum, quem ut Christo debitum asserit, non vult esse illi parem qui Patri sive Deo summo debetur. Hæc enim adjicit Christus pari absolute cultu cum Deo non est colendus. Ib. Err. 75. Idem in Resp. ad nov. monst. part. 2. cap. 8. p. 80. ita disserit. Si Antiquitas[?], quæ consecuta est Apostolorum Temporum[?], & hactenus durat, pro Deo non habet eum, qui est subordinatus; quid mirum, si consideretur, quod S. litera restantur, Defectionem à Fide venturam; & futuros eos, qui non sunt confessuri Iesum Christum qui in carne venit, & ipsum qui eos redemit; & eo prolapsuros nomine tenus Christianos, justa Dei Judicio adductos, ut mendacia credant. §. 67. De Redemptione nostra per Christum, sive liberatione à Peccato & morte; de illius Sacrificio propitiatorio, Sacerdotio, merito, morte, officio Prophetico, descensu ad Inferos, Resurrectione, Glorificatione, sessione ad dextram Patris, & Intercessione pro Ecclesia, pariter sentiunt contra Fidem Catholicam. Redemptionem proprie dictam negant, & Metaphoricam duntaxat esse volunt. Pretium item Redemptionis abnegant, sive persolutionem Poenarum nostris peccatis debitarum. Sacrificium Christi propitiatorium pro peccatis, & ejusdem intercessionem pro nobis apud Patrem in Coelis, in quibus munus illius Sacerdotale praecipue consistit, pariter destruunt,aut depravant.[?] Sacerdotium nempe illius figuratum esse volunt, ut & Intercessionem apud Patrem; & mortem Christi solummodo Praeparationem quandam ad sacerdotium suum obeundum. Negant quoque Christum esse Redemptorem, Mediatorem, aut Servatorem proprie sic dictum, viz. respectu liberationis à peccato & morte, sed figurate tantum, & aequivoce; nimirum, quod viam salutis nobis verbo annunciaverit; miraculis, effusione sanguinis, & Resurrectione confirmarit; vitae exemplo, & resurgendo à mortuis, viam salutis ostenderit; quod vitam aeternam nobis daturus sit, ut minister seu Instrumentum conferendi illam; quod sit Mediator solum sub ratione Internuncii, instar Mosis, cujus officium fuit, non Deum Hominibus placare, sed de voluntate Dei Homines admonere. Denique, quod nos Deo reconciliaverit, per simplicem in Gratiam receptionem; non autem Deum Nobis, per alicujus pretii solutionem, & acceptationem. De his enim ita Smalcius: Pontifex legalis ad oblationes proprie dictas constituebatur; at Christus noster Pontifex ad Oblationem improprie dictam constitutus est, & improprie, ac omnino metaphorice, & allegorice nomine sacerdotii insignitur. Resp. ad nova Monst. part 2. cap. 13. p. 129. Idem in exam. 100. Errorum, asserit, Christum metaphorice & improprie appellari Sacerdotem; neque abrulisse verum Sacrificium, sed metaphoricum. Voces Sacrificii, Oblationis, & Interpellationis, quibus mituntur Apostoli, in Epist. ad Hebraeos, improprie & figurate accipi vocibus & phrasibus allegoricis è lege Mosaiea translatis. Christum in Cruce non seipsum sacrificasse, nec obtulisse Deo pro Nobis. Falsum esse, Christum in Terris purgationem Peccatorum fecisse. Christum in Caelis primum, factum esse Pontificem, & ibi Sacrificium suum primum obtulisse. In Christi sacrificio nullum (proprie loquendo) locum esse voluntati Christi, ut in aliis Actionibus. In liberatione nostra per Christum, Nemini quicquam pro nobis solutum, ita ut improprie dicatur Redemtio. Christum non esse sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchisedech, quoad ritum sacrificandi. Christum passione sua & morte, non proprie meruisse suam Exaltationem, quia sc. Apud Deum nullus Merito lo[?]tus est, cum nullum debitum sit ex parte Dei. Deus ἐχαρίσατο, id est gratis donavit Christo exaltationem.
units.tr: §. 66. As for the invocation and adoration of Christ, Socinus indeed asserts both more than once, as due to him, and he presses their observance vigorously against the Francisco-Davidians. In his letter to the synod of Wægrov, where the Antitrinitarians had gathered, he most urgently exhorts them to labour above all to preserve the adoration and invocation of Christ in their churches, because if these are despised or cast aside, it can in no way happen that Judaism, or rather foul Epicureanism and atheism, does not flourish everywhere. He likewise does not want any further dealings in sacred matters with those who do not acknowledge in this way the administration of Christ's kingdom and his divine power. He further advises that all ministers of the Word of God be enjoined to name Jesus Christ, the Son of God, by name in public prayers on certain set days (vol. 1, p. 491). The Racovian Catechism likewise, concerning those men who do not invoke Christ and do not judge him to be worthy of adoration, holds that they are altogether not Christians, since in fact they do not have Christ; and although they do not dare to deny it in words, they nevertheless deny it in fact (p. 115). Yet the same Socinus, after proving elsewhere that divine adoration is due to Christ, from the particle [as] which Christ himself uses, — that all should honour the Son, as they honour the Father (John 5:22, 23), nevertheless lays down that there is no small difference between that honour which is due to God the Father and that which is due to Christ his Son (On the Church, p. 353). He explains this difference in his disputation with the Christian Franken: I say, he says, that God is adored as the author of all things; but Christ, as a certain mediator, through whom such adoration tends to God (vol. 2, p. 772). And he illustrates this further thus: Just as that book, pushed across the middle of the table, is not said to belong to those whom it passes in its course, but only to him at whom it arrives; so the adoration of Christ, since it does not remain in him but goes on further to God, is said to belong to God himself (p. 777). Indeed, elsewhere, he so neglects the invocation of Christ, which he urged as most necessary (where the matter itself demanded it) and wished to be imposed for all to use, that he reckons it among things indifferent, that is, such things as God has neither commanded nor forbidden in his Word; and therefore, as he rightly infers there, not altogether necessary. For thus he writes in his letter to Georg Enyedi (p. 485, col. 2, vol. 1). Smalcius too, in this as in other things, defends the opinion of his master. For while he holds Christ to be a mere man, he nevertheless wishes him to be invoked and honoured with divine honours, as a God made, or a man deified, and a deity of secondary rank, subordinate to the supreme God. But since he could not be ignorant that the one God is celebrated by Moses and the Prophets, namely that supreme deity to whom alone invocation and divine adoration are due; and since the ancients also everywhere affirm that Christ once appeared to the patriarchs, and was called Jehovah and was honoured with divine honours (so widely and constantly that Tertullian, among his other articles, places this one too in his rule of faith, On Prescription against Heretics, ch. 13), whom yet he himself, with the men of his sect, regards as a mere creature, not existing before he was incarnate of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the blessed Virgin: in order to ascribe this twofold honour to Christ, he is compelled both to disparage the teaching of Moses and the Prophets on this matter as not corresponding to the faith of Christians, and to affirm that divine worship can lawfully be offered to a mere creature, and that it was actually once offered to created angels by the concession of God. For thus he writes in his Examination of 100 Errors: It is not certain that God is to be worshipped with divine worship on account of the divine nature (Err. 8). To worship only one God, who is, namely, God supreme by nature and independent, is something Jewish, and in some measure a denial of the Christian religion (Err. 15). Christians should care little what the Prophets say about the worship of the one God (Err. 16). God can command that whoever, even one of the angels, be worshipped as God (Err. 17). That divine worship can be given to angels, who are heavenly gods, and that it was in fact given in the Old Covenant, no one can deny. The command of God always binds us, even though it surpasses our capacity; and it is easier to doubt three times over whether you understand the matter rightly than to doubt whether one must obey the one who commands. God permitted that this should happen at a time when Jesus Christ had not yet been exalted and appointed Mediator between God and men. But now, after the Lord Jesus has stood as mediator between God and men, the thrones and dominions of the angels have been so reformed that neither did God will, nor were they permitted, that divine honour be given to him by men (Eph. 1:20). Meanwhile, this divine honour, which he asserts is due to Christ, he does not wish to be equal to that which is due to the Father or to the supreme God. For he adds: Christ is not to be worshipped with absolutely equal worship with God (ibid., Err. 75). The same man, in his Reply to the New Monstrosities, part 2, ch. 8, p. 80, argues thus: If antiquity, which followed upon the times of the Apostles and has endured until now, does not hold as God him who is subordinate; what wonder is it, if one considers that the Scriptures testify that a defection from the faith will come, and that there will be those who will not confess Jesus Christ who came in the flesh, nor him who redeemed them; and who will fall away, Christians in name only, led by the just judgment of God to believe lies. §. 67. Concerning our redemption through Christ, that is, liberation from sin and death; concerning his propitiatory sacrifice, priesthood, merit, death, prophetic office, descent into hell, resurrection, glorification, sitting at the right hand of the Father, and intercession for the Church, they likewise think contrary to the Catholic faith. They deny redemption properly so called, and wish it to be merely metaphorical. They also deny the price of redemption, that is, the payment of the punishments owed to our sins. They likewise either destroy or corrupt Christ's propitiatory sacrifice for sins, and his intercession for us before the Father in heaven, in which his priestly office chiefly consists. Indeed, they wish his priesthood to be only a figure, as also his intercession before the Father; and they hold that the death of Christ was merely a certain preparation for his carrying out his priesthood. They also deny that Christ is a redeemer, mediator, or saviour properly so called, namely with respect to liberation from sin and death, but only figuratively and equivocally; that is, that he announced to us the way of salvation by the Word, confirmed it by miracles, the shedding of blood and resurrection; showed the way of salvation by the example of his life and by rising from the dead; that he is to give us eternal life as a minister or instrument for conferring it; that he is mediator only in the sense of a go-between, like Moses, whose office was not to appease God for men, but to admonish men about the will of God. Finally, that he reconciled us to God only through simple reception into grace, and not by any payment and acceptance of a price, so as to make God favourable to us. For Smalcius speaks thus about these matters: The legal high priest was appointed for oblations properly so called; but our Christ is appointed as high priest for an oblation improperly so called, and he is marked with the name of priesthood improperly and altogether metaphorically and allegorically. (Reply to the New Monstrosities, part 2, ch. 13, p. 129). The same man, in his Examination of 100 Errors, asserts that Christ is called priest metaphorically and improperly; and he did not abolish the true sacrifice, but a metaphorical one. The words sacrifice, oblation and intercession, which the Apostles use in the Epistle to the Hebrews, are to be taken improperly and figuratively, by allegorical words and phrases transferred from the Mosaic law. Christ did not sacrifice himself on the Cross, nor offer himself to God for us. It is false that Christ made purgation of sins on earth. Christ was first made priest in heaven, and there first offered his sacrifice. In Christ's sacrifice there is no place (properly speaking) for the will of Christ, as there is in other actions. In our liberation through Christ, nothing has been paid for us by anyone, so that it is improperly called redemption. Christ is not a priest according to the order of Melchizedek as regards the rite of sacrificing. Christ did not properly merit his exaltation by his suffering and death, because, namely, with God no merit can be earned, since there is no debt on God's side. God graciously gave [ἐχαρίσατο], that is, freely bestowed on Christ his exaltation.

units.la: Haec ille Err. 57-67. Hinc est, quod Meritum mortis Christi omnino negent. Sic itaque Catechismus Racovien-sis. p. 177.—Etsi nunc vulgo Christiani sentiunt, Christum morte sua nobis salutem meruisse, & pro Peccatis nostris plenarie satisfecisse, tamen ista Sententia est fallax & erronea, & admodum perniciosa. Smalcius quoque Meritum Christi penitus tollit, tam Sui-Ipsius respectu, quam humani Generis. Non promeruit passione sua Christus, ut nomen haberet supra omne Nomen, sed propter passionem, hoc est non sine Passione, ex divina Gratia consecutus est suam summam Dignitatem. Resp. ad nova Monst. part 2. p. 114. & postea—Falso asserit Smiglecius, Christum in Terris purgationem Peccatorum fecisse. Ib. c. 13. p. 132. Meritum infert coactionem in Deo ad mercedem reddendam. Err. 130. Ex dignitate persona non junguntur valor Actionis. Err. 140. Haec item ibidem habet contra Meritum Christi quod veniam Peccatorum, reconciliationem cum Deo, & vitam aeternam nobis acquisivit, sc. in Exam. 157. Errorum. Ubi asserit, Christum nobis Deum non reconciliasse nec ex offenso placatum reddidisse. Deum ex se, & sua sponte propitium fuisse Hominibus, absque Cujusquam reconciliatione. Modum, quo sanguine Christi dicimur redempti, eum esse duntaxat, quod sanguine Christi sit novum Foedus confirmatum, & eodem sanguine nos commoveamur ad spem Gratiae di-vinae, Christusque mediante sanguine suo consecutus sit potestatem nos salvandi seu a morte liberandi. Deo non esse ullum Pretium datum pro nobis. Deum Patrem dici bene posse, nos acquisivisse Sanguine suo; quia sanguis Christi sanguis Dei dici potest. Sanguinem Christi non esse, proprie dicendo, efficientem causam remissionis peccatorum, sed causam administram, vel sine qua non; Dei vero Gratiam esse causam effectri-cem remissionis Peccatorum. Christum Peccatorum nostrorum poenas in se luendas suscepisse. Nusquam in Scrip-tura legi de oblatione Corporis & sanguinis Christi. Non remitti nobis Peccata propter sanguinem Christi, nec sanguinem hunc commovere Deum ad remittenda nobis peccata. Christum vitam aeternam nobis non comparasse, sed paratam a Deo annunciasse; neque effecisse, ut nos Illam a Deo sponte oblatam amplecteremur, & conse-queremur. Christum non habuisse ullum sanguinem, cum per Spiritum aeternum sese obtulit Deo. Sanguinem Christi dici in Scriptura pretiosum, non quod aliquem valorem pretii habeat, sed quod sit sanguis aeterni Foederis. Sola Christi morte peccata non esse expiata, sed & Resurrectione, & sessione ad dextram patris, & Intercessione. Denique Christum sanguine suo pro nobis fuso, veniam peccatorum non impetrasse. Haec ille, Err.[?] 47-72. Tenent insuper Patres in Vetere Testamento, per Christum ut Mediatorem, adeoque per Ipsius Passionem & mortem, justificatos & salvatos non suille ; aut per Fidem in Illius meritum; necnon, eos, qui ante Christum fuerant, sub eodem vetere Testamento, dicunt habuisse tantum Promissiones temporales;Doctrinam vero de remissione Peccatorum per Messiam venturum, non fuisse iis notam ; neque vitam æternam illis promissam, aut Spiritum Sanctum. Sic enim Smalcius in Exam. 157. errorum. Hæc dogmata statuit. Christum non omnibus esse promissum, sed Abrahamo primum, & ejus posteris. Christum in lege veteri non fuisse necessarium Hominibus ad Salutem. Ab initio mundi, fideles in Messiam fidem non habuisse ; atque adeo, fidem in Christum ad Justificationem non fuisse requisitam. Fidem implicitam, seu confusam in Christum ( quam aliqui dicunt, Homines sub vetere Fœdere habuisse ), nihil conferre ad remissionem Peccatorum. Fideles in lege veteri nihil de fructu mortis Christi scivisse. Ante Christi Adventum, Peccata non esse Hominibus remissa propter Christum. Err. 38. 46. & paulo post, Christus non est mortuus pro illis, qui ante ipsum fuerunt, Err. 74. Deinde, hæc adjicit contra meritum & satisfactionem Christi, quibus semper innixa est Ecclesia Catholica, ut unico salutis nostræ Fundamento, & Spei Christianæ fulcro firmissimo, quæ tamen à Smalcio cum summa audacia & petulantia rejiciuntur, ut ex infra-dictis patet.
