Ista per satisfactionem Christi, & meritum Redemptio, tum S. literis, tum sanæ Rationi, contraria est. Gratuita peccatorum Remissio cum satisfactione pugnat. Error crassus est dicere, aliquid nobis per Christum proprie comparatum esse, sc. vitam æternam quam apud Deum paratam, procuravit nobis, & procurat. Christus non solum non satisfecit, sed nec satisfacere po-tuit. Sanguinis Christi valor non est infinitus. Dogma de satisfactione Christi, monstrosum est. Deus pro peccatis satisfacere non potest, nisi & natura divina patiatur. Err. 79. 86. & paulo prius. Deus potest per Christum peccata transmittere, & salutem tribuere ei, qui in Christum non credit, modo in Deum credat. Err. 77. Haec ille ibidem, quae ad superiora referri possunt.
units.tr: So far that writer (Errors 57–67). Hence they deny outright that Christ's death has any merit. Thus the Racovian Catechism, p. 177: Although Christians now commonly think that Christ by his death merited salvation for us and fully satisfied for our sins, this opinion is false, erroneous and very pernicious. Smalcius also removes Christ's merit completely, both with respect to himself and with respect to the human race. Christ did not merit by his passion that he should have a name above every name; rather, because of his passion, that is, not without suffering, he attained his supreme dignity by divine grace. Reply to the New Monstrosities, part 2, p. 114, and afterwards: Smiglecius falsely asserts that Christ made purgation of sins on earth. Ib., ch. 13, p. 132. Merit implies a compulsion on God to render a reward. Errors 130. The value of an action is not joined to the dignity of the person. Errors 140. He likewise says the same there against Christ's merit, that Christ did not acquire for us forgiveness of sins, reconciliation with God and eternal life; namely in the Examination of the 157 Errors, where he asserts that Christ did not reconcile us to God, nor render God, who had been offended, placated. That God was of himself and of his own accord favourable to men, without anyone's reconciliation. The manner in which we are said to be redeemed by the blood of Christ is only this: that the new covenant is confirmed by his blood, and by the same blood we are moved to hope for divine grace, and Christ, by means of his blood, has obtained the power of saving us or freeing us from death. That no price has been given to God for us. That God the Father can well be said to have acquired us by his own blood, because the blood of Christ can be called the blood of God. That the blood of Christ is not, properly speaking, the efficient cause of the remission of sins, but a ministering cause, or a cause without which nothing happens; while the grace of God is the effecting cause of the remission of sins. That Christ took upon himself the punishments of our sins to be paid in himself. That nowhere in Scripture is it read of the offering of the body and blood of Christ. That sins are not forgiven us on account of the blood of Christ, nor does this blood move God to forgive us our sins. That Christ did not procure eternal life for us, but announced it as prepared by God; nor did he bring it about that we should embrace and obtain it when it was freely offered by God. That Christ had no blood when he offered himself to God through the eternal Spirit. That the blood of Christ is called precious in Scripture not because it has any value of price, but because it is the blood of the eternal covenant. That sins were expiated not by the death of Christ alone, but also by his resurrection, his session at the right hand of the Father, and his intercession. Finally, that Christ, having shed his blood for us, did not obtain forgiveness of sins. Thus he (Errors 47–72). Moreover the Fathers under the Old Testament are held not to have been justified and saved through Christ as Mediator, and so not through his passion and death, nor through faith in his merit; and they say that those who lived before Christ under that same Old Testament had only temporal promises; but that the doctrine of the remission of sins through the coming Messiah was unknown to them, nor was eternal life promised to them, or the Holy Spirit. For so Smalcius, in the Examination of the 157 errors, lays down these doctrines: Christ was not promised to all, but first to Abraham and his posterity. Christ was not necessary for men to salvation under the old law. From the beginning of the world the faithful did not have faith in the Messiah; and so faith in Christ was not required for justification. Implicit or confused faith in Christ (which some say men had under the old covenant) contributes nothing to the remission of sins. The faithful under the law knew nothing of the fruit of the death of Christ. Before the coming of Christ, sins were not remitted to men on account of Christ. Errors 38, 46. And a little later: Christ did not die for those who were before him, Errors 74. Then he adds these things against the merit and satisfaction of Christ, on which the Catholic Church has always relied, as the sole foundation of our salvation and the most firm prop of Christian hope; yet these are rejected by Smalcius with the greatest audacity and impudence, as is clear from what follows. That redemption through the satisfaction and merit of Christ is contrary both to Holy Scripture and to sound reason. Gratuitous remission of sins is at odds with satisfaction. It is a gross error to say that anything has been properly procured for us through Christ, namely eternal life, which he has procured and procures for us, being prepared with God. Christ not only did not satisfy, but could not satisfy. The value of Christ's blood is not infinite. The doctrine of Christ's satisfaction is monstrous. God cannot satisfy for sins unless the divine nature itself suffers. Errors 79, 86; and a little earlier: God can through Christ pass over sins, and grant salvation to one who does not believe in Christ, provided he believes in God. Errors 77. These are his words there, which can be referred to the points above.

units.la: Quod spectat ad officium Christi propheticum, negant eum instructum fuisse omniscientia ad illius executionem requisita, ab ipsa Nativitate, & virtute hypostaticae unionis; sed quod aliquanto Tempore ante initium Ministerii, in Coelum ascenderit, ubi cum Deum Patrem viderit, & ab eodem edoctus fuerit, rursus ad homines docendos descenderit. Ita Smalcius affirmat, Christum bis ascendisse in Coelum, semel in vita, secundo post mortem. Err. 75.
units.tr: As regards the prophetic office of Christ, they deny that he was furnished from his very birth, and by virtue of the hypostatic union, with the omniscience required for its discharge; rather, some time before the beginning of his ministry he ascended into heaven, where, having seen God the Father and been taught by him, he came down again to teach men. So Smalcius asserts: that Christ ascended into heaven twice, once during his life, and a second time after death. Errors 75.

units.la: Quod item tempus somniat esse illud, quod in deserto jejunus consumpsit post Baptismum, & Descensum S. Spiritus super eum in specie Columbae; sicut Moses totidem Dies, noctesque jejunans in monte Sina, legem a Deo recepit, Israelitis communicandam. Sic ille, De Divin. Christi cap. 4. p. 13.
units.tr: Likewise, he dreams that the time is that which he spent fasting in the desert after his baptism and the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him in the form of a dove, just as Moses, fasting for as many days and nights on Mount Sinai, received the law from God to be communicated to the Israelites. Thus he, On the Divinity of Christ, ch. 4, p. 13.

units.la: Per Descensum Christi ad Inferos, nihil aliud significari volunt, quam eum verissime mortuum fuisse, & propriissime, ut quivis alius Homo moritur. Ita Smalcius ibidem. cap. 33. vel permansurem in statu mortis, a quo nulla humana ope, nullis naturae viribus, ad superos, Terramque viventium, id est, ad vitam, vitaeque Actionem praeterquam sola insuperabili Dei Potentia, redire quisquam valeat. Ita Schlicht. in Symb. p. 73.
units.tr: By the descent of Christ into Hell they wish nothing else to be signified than that he died most truly, and in the most proper sense, just as any other man dies. So Smalcius in the same place, ch. 33; or that he would remain in the state of death, from which no one by any human help, by no powers of nature, could return to the upper world and the land of the living, that is, to life and the activity of life, except by the unconquerable power of God alone. So Schlichting, on the Creed, p. 73.

units.la: At, pace illorum, Descensus hic significat motum ad locum, non permansionem aut quietem, quae motui opponitur. Apostolus item affirmat, Christum descendisse in Inferiora Terrae, & in Abyssum, Eph. 4. 9. Rom. 10. 7. Quae verba haud intelligi possunt de sepultura Corporis Christi. Veteres item uno fere ore interpretantur hunc Descensum de Anima Christi in statu Separationis, quando ivit εἰς ᾅδου [?], sive in Domum Inferni, nimirum in Habitaculum Animarum separatarum, ubi & permansit usque ad horam Resurrectionis, cum Corpori suo denuo unita est. Atque hoc ex eo patet, quod sient [?] inde reduxerit Animas quamplurimum Sanctorum, qui paulo post illum, e Monumentis suis resurgentes Hierosolyma ingressi sunt, & a multis manifeste conspecti Mat. 27. 52, 53.
units.tr: But, with respect to them, this descent signifies a movement to a place, not a remaining or rest, which is opposed to movement. The Apostle likewise affirms that Christ descended into the lower parts of the earth, and into the abyss, Eph. 4:9; Rom. 10:7. These words cannot be understood of the burial of Christ's body. The ancients also almost unanimously interpret this descent as concerning the soul of Christ in the state of separation, when he went into Hades [εἰς ᾅδου], that is, into the house of Hell, namely the dwelling place of separated souls, where he also remained until the hour of resurrection, when he was again united to his body. And this is clear from the fact that, as he thence led up very many of the saints, who, rising from their tombs shortly after him, entered Jerusalem and were plainly seen by many, Matt. 27:52, 53.

units.la: Christum propria virtute è mortuis resurrexisse, non solum negant, sed & cum risu atque indignatione rejiciunt. Quid enim magis, vel risu dignum, ait Socinus, vel a veritate alienum, aut videri, aut ipse potest, quam eum, qui mortuus sit, seipsum in vitam revocare? Sic ille, Disp. de unius Filii exsistentia: Smalcius item hoc Dogma sic irridet —— Fabula est, Christum aliquam virtutem in Resurrectione declarasse; quae, ut falsa est; ita seipsam etiam destruit. Falsa est, quia Dei Patris virtuti diserte hoc tribuitur in S. Literis, quod Christus ex mortuis resurrexit. Seipsum destruit; nam si Christus mortuus fuit, quomodo omnipotens fuit, vel quomodo aliquid in Resurrectione declarare potuit? cum mortui, ut non sunt, sic etiam nihil agere possint; & si aliquid agant, jam hoc ipso mortui non sunt. Resp. ad nova monst. part. 2. cap. 21. pag. 190. Catechismus quoque Racoviensis dicit, Illos falli vehementer, qui dicunt Christum excitasse Seipsum a mortuis. p. 216. Attamen si Christo ipsi Fides, ut potestatem habuit ponendi vitam, ita & eam denuo assumendi. Jo. 10. 18. Neque dubium est, quin praedixerit Promissum Judaeis factum, solvite Templum hoc (de corpore suo loquens) & in tribus Diebus suscitabo Illud. Ib. cap. 2. 20, 21.
units.tr: That Christ rose from the dead by his own power they not only deny, but also reject with laughter and indignation. For what, says Socinus, can either be more worthy of laughter, or more alien to the truth, either to seem or to be, than that one who is dead should revive himself to life? Thus he, Disputation on the existence of the one Son. Smalcius likewise mocks this doctrine thus: It is a fable that Christ displayed some power in the resurrection; which, as it is false, so also destroys itself. It is false, because Scripture expressly ascribes this to the power of God the Father, that Christ rose from the dead. It destroys itself; for if Christ was dead, how was he almighty, or how could he display anything in the resurrection? since the dead, as they are not, so also can do nothing; and if they do anything, by that very fact they are not dead. Reply to the New Monstrosities, part 2, ch. 21, p. 190. The Racovian Catechism also says: Those are greatly mistaken who say that Christ raised himself from the dead. p. 216. Yet if Christ himself had faith, he had power to lay down his life and to take it up again. John 10:18. Nor is there doubt that he foretold the promise made to the Jews: Destroy this temple (speaking of his body) and in three days I will raise it up. Ib., ch. 2, 20, 21.

units.la: Dicunt etiam, Christum non habuisse corpus immortale statim à Resurrectione, sed tunc demum, cum in Cœlum translatus est. Sic Oftor. Inftit. cap. 41. & Socinus —Non est Christus Jesus, quamvis, ut non amplius mororetur, à mortuis excitatus, immortalitatem sui Corporis, & Gloriam adeptus, nisi cum in cœlum translatus est. Sic ille, de statu primi Hom. c. 8. p. 236. Smalcius Socini Dogma confirmat, quando ait, Christum post Resurrectionem Immortalitatem veram non habuisse, quamdiu in Terris commoratus est. Asserit autem, Christum factum esse immortalem per & post Ascensionem in Cœlum. Resp. ad nova Monst. part. 2. c. 21. p. 193. & paulo post, negat Corpus immortale oculis corporeis videri posse, aut Manibus tangi, cum Immortales Deo similes sint, qui nec videri potest nec tangi. Sic ille Ib. p. 195. Proinde, negat Stephanum & Paulum Corpus Christi immortale oculis humanis aspexisse. Ib. p. 194. At si hæc sententia aliquid virium habeat, aut Ratio à Smalcio allata, S. Scripturæ renunciandum est, quæ non semel satis diserte asserit, Sanctos post Resurrectionem in Corporibus glorificatos, & Christum Dominum in Gloria sua visuros & se invicem. Negat, insuper, omnem Potestatem in Cœlo & in Terra reipsa datam fuisse Christo cum hanc sibi asseruit. Matt. 28. 18. Paulo post vero dandam fuisse contendit. Ib. p. 195. Atque alibi, negat Christum, cum post Resurrectionem dicaret, Accipite Spiritum Sanctum, dediisse illum reipsa, sed tantum prædixisse, quod dandus esset, sc. per Afflatum in die Pentecostes. Exam. 157. Err. 24. Ibidem quoque eadem Dogmata repetit, ne ab eo temere prolata existimaremus —Christus cum Corpore mortali resurrexit, & Filius Dei factus est. Err. 31, 32. Corpus immortale oculis mortalibus videri non potest. Err. 116. Paulus vere Christum non vidit, neque Stephanus. Err. 117. Corpora immortalia tangi non possunt. Err 121. At S. Scriptura è contra affirmat, Christum in Corpore suo glorioso, tum à Stephano, tum à Paulo confpectum fuisse, non inane Phantasma, non Angelum in forma Christi, non ipsam Christi Deitatem, quæ priorsus invisibilis est. Stephanus dicitur intentis in Cœlum oculis vidisse Cœlos apertos & Filium Hominis stantem à dextris Dei. Act. 7. 55. eundem certe quem jam expiraturus sic inter orandum allocutus est, Domine Jesu, suscipe Spiritum meum. v. 59. Ille quoque qui Paulo apparuit eumque in via prope Damascum allocutus est se Jesum Nazarenum vocat, Hb.[?] cap. 9. 5. & 22. 8. Ananias item, ab eodem Jesu præmonitus, & ad Paulum missus, ut illum baptizaret, oculosque illius aperiret, satis clare idem affirmat. Deus, inquit, Te designavit, sive præordinavit, ut videres Justum illum, & audires vocem ex ore ejus. Hb.[?] v. 14. Ipse quoque Paulus ad Corinthios suos scribens, cum recensuisset varias Christi Apparitiones, quibus se visendum exhibuit oculis Discipulorum post Resurrectionem, viz. Cephæ, Jacobi, undecim Apostolorum, Fratrumque quingentorum una congregatorum, tandem hæc adjicit de seipso. Novissime autem omnium, tanquam Abortivo, visus est mihi. 1 Cor. 15. 8. Quod autem Christus, statim à Resurrectione, corporis sui Immortalitatem consecutus sit, ex eo liquet, non solum quod, pro libitu suo evanuerit ex oculis Discipulorum. Luc. 24. 31. clausisque januis ad eos non semel introiverit. Jo. 20.[?] 19, 26. (quæ Corporis sui naturam atque conditionem plane mutatam offendunt,) sed ex diversis ejusdem Apostoli verbis, ubi inquit --Christus resurgens (seu potius, excitatus, ἐγερθεὶς[?] ex mortuis, non amplius moritur; mors ei non ultra (vel amplius) dominatur. Rom. 6. 9. Quinimo, si Christus in Corpore mortali resurrexerit, Corpus illius in statu minus perfecto fuisset per quadraginta Dies, quam corpora Sanctorum post Resurrectionem, cum illa statim immortalitatem induitura sint, & mors illico absorbenda sit in victoriam. Seminatur, inquit, Corpus in corruptione, surget in incorruptione. Seminatur in Ignobilitate, surget in Gloria. Seminatur in Infirmitate, surget in virtute. Seminatur Corpus Animale, surget Corpus Spiritale. 1 Cor. 15. 42, 43, 44. & paulo post -Cum mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, tunc fiet sermo qui scriptus est, Absorpta est mors in victoria. Ib. v. 54. Equidem, de Christo memoratur in Evangelio, quod non solum Corpus suum Discipulis tangendum praebuerit, sed etiam quod cum eis ederit ac biberit post Resurrectionem. Hoc autem sine dubio fecit, non quod victu indigeret ad mortale corpus sustentandum, sed ut veritatem Corporis ostenderet, ejusdem Corporis quod in Sepulchro conditum est. Unde & vestigia vulnerum simul ostendit, idque non oculis duntaxat visenda, sed & manibus palpanda. Alioquin concludere possemus, etiam Angelos illos, qui Abrahamum & Lotum visebant, & cum eisdem comedisse memorantur, fuisse mortales & cibo indiguisse ad vitam sustentandam.
units.tr: They also say that Christ did not have an immortal body immediately from the Resurrection, but only when he was taken up into heaven. So Ostorodt, Institutes ch. 41, and Socinus: "Christ Jesus, although he was raised from the dead so that he would not die again, did not obtain immortality and glory for his body until he was taken up into heaven." So he writes in the work on the first man, ch. 8, p. 236. Smalcius confirms the doctrine of Socinus when he says that Christ did not have true immortality after the Resurrection, as long as he lived on earth. He asserts, however, that Christ became immortal through and after his ascension into heaven (Response to the New Monsters, part 2, ch. 21, p. 193). Shortly after, he denies that an immortal body can be seen with bodily eyes or touched by hands, since immortals are like God, who can be neither seen nor touched (ibid., p. 195). Accordingly, he denies that Stephen and Paul saw the immortal body of Christ with human eyes (ibid., p. 194). But if this opinion or the reason Smalcius advances for it has any force, we must renounce Holy Scripture, which more than once states quite plainly that the saints, glorified in their bodies after the Resurrection, will see Christ the Lord in his glory, and see one another. Moreover, he denies that all power in heaven and on earth was actually given to Christ when he claimed it for himself (Matt. 28. 18), yet he afterwards contends that it was to be given (ibid., p. 195). And elsewhere he denies that Christ, when after the Resurrection he said, "Receive the Holy Spirit," actually gave it, but only foretold that it was to be given, namely by the breathing upon them on the day of Pentecost (Examen, 157; Error 24). In the same place he repeats the same doctrines, lest we think he has put them forward rashly: "Christ rose with a mortal body and was made the Son of God" (Errors 31, 32); "an immortal body cannot be seen with mortal eyes" (Error 116); "Paul did not truly see Christ, nor did Stephen" (Error 117); "immortal bodies cannot be touched" (Error 121). But Scripture, on the contrary, affirms that Christ was seen in his glorious body both by Stephen and by Paul, not as an empty phantom, not as an angel in the form of Christ, nor as the Deity of Christ itself, which is wholly invisible. Stephen is said to have seen, with eyes fixed on heaven, the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7. 55). This was certainly the same one to whom, as he was about to expire, he spoke while praying: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (v. 59). He who appeared to Paul and spoke to him on the road near Damascus also calls himself Jesus of Nazareth (Acts 9. 5; 22. 8). Ananias likewise, forewarned by the same Jesus and sent to Paul to baptize him and open his eyes, affirms the same quite clearly: "God, he says, has appointed you to see that Just One and to hear the voice from his mouth" (Acts 22. 14). Paul himself, too, writing to his Corinthians, after he had recounted the various appearances of Christ by which he showed himself to be seen by the eyes of the disciples after the Resurrection, namely to Cephas, to James, to the eleven apostles, and to five hundred brethren gathered together, at last adds this about himself: "And last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared to me" (1 Cor. 15. 8). That Christ obtained the immortality of his body immediately after the Resurrection is clear not only from the fact that, at his own pleasure, he vanished from the disciples' sight (Luke 24. 31) and more than once entered to them with the doors shut (John 20. 19, 26), which show that the nature and condition of his body was entirely changed, but also from the words of the same apostle, where he says: "Christ, having been raised (or rather, roused, ἐγερθεὶς, from the dead), dies no more; death no longer (or any more) has dominion over him" (Rom. 6. 9). Indeed, if Christ had risen in a mortal body, his body would have been in a less perfect state for forty days than the bodies of the saints after the Resurrection, since theirs are to put on immortality at once, and death is at once to be swallowed up in victory. "It is sown," he says, "a body in corruption; it is raised in incorruption. It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Cor. 15. 42, 43, 44); and shortly after: "When this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory" (ibid., v. 54). Indeed, the Gospel records of Christ that he not only offered his body to the disciples to be touched, but also ate and drank with them after the Resurrection. He certainly did this not because he needed food to sustain a mortal body, but to show the reality of the same body which had been laid in the tomb. Hence he also showed the traces of his wounds, to be seen not only by the eyes but also to be handled by the hands. Otherwise we could conclude that those angels who visited Abraham and Lot, and are recorded to have eaten with them, were mortal and needed food to sustain life.

units.la: Negant etiam Christum, post sui glorificationem in Coelo, amplius habere carnem & sanguinem ita Smalcius cum aliis in exam. 157. errorum - Christus in Coelo imperfectus & maculatus esset, si sanguinem haberet. Err. 155. Corpus Christi non habet vestigia vulnerum. Err. 119. Christus ratione Corporis gloriosi post ascensionem suam in Cœlum,est Spiritus vivificans,sicut primus Homo ratione Corporis, factus est in Animam viventem. Err.
units.tr: They also deny that Christ, after his glorification in heaven, any longer has flesh and blood. So Smalcius, with others, in the Examen of errors 157: "Christ would be imperfect and defiled in heaven if he had blood" (Error 155). "The body of Christ does not have the traces of wounds" (Error 119). "Christ, in respect of his glorious body after his ascension into heaven, is a life-giving Spirit, just as the first man, in respect of his body, was made a living soul" (Error

units.la: 25. Equidem dicimus cum Apostolo, Carnem & Sanguinem Dei Regnum possidere non posse. Sed cum eodem Apostolo inte pretamur ipsius verba de Carne & Sanguine, quales nunc habemus in mortali statu. Immediate enim hæc subdit --Neque corruptio possidebit Incorruptionem. At ceteri, si Christus in Cœlum ascenderit cum eodem corpore quod e sepulchro resurrexit, & si resurrexit in eodem Corpore quod in Sepulchro reconditum est, (ut Evangelium diserte testatur) Corpus ipsius jam in Cœlo glorificatum, habet eandem substantiam carnis & sanguinis, quam antea in Terris habuit, etsi qualitatibus mutatis. Idem enim qui se exinaniv it usque ad mortem Crucis, à Deo fuit in Cœlos exaltatus, Phil. 2.7. 11. Christi Glorificatio non peremit corpus ipsius, sed perfecit; neque aliquid de eo abstulit, sed totum extulit. Alioquin Christus non retineret naturæ humanæ Integritatem, nec Appellationis humanæ veritatem præstaret; cum tamen post Ascensionem quoque suam in Cœlos, imo, cum in summa Gloria venturus est ad judicandum vivos & mortuos, vocetur Homo, & Filius Hominis, Mat. 16.27. & 19. 28. & 24. 27, 30, 37, 44. & 25.31. comp: Act. 7. 56.
units.tr: 25). "We agree with the Apostle that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God." But with the same Apostle we interpret his words about flesh and blood as they now are in our mortal state. For he immediately adds: "Neither does corruption inherit incorruption." But the others say: if Christ ascended into heaven with the same body that rose from the tomb, and if he rose in the same body that was laid in the sepulchre (as the Gospel plainly testifies), then his body, now glorified in heaven, has the same substance of flesh and blood which it had before on earth, though with its qualities changed. For he who humbled himself even to the death of the cross was exalted by God into the heavens (Phil. 2. 7, 11). The glorification of Christ did not destroy his body but perfected it; it took nothing from him but raised all of him up. Otherwise Christ would not keep the integrity of human nature, nor would he make good the truth of the human name, although after his ascension into the heavens, and indeed when he is to come in highest glory to judge the living and the dead, he is called Man and Son of Man (Matt. 16. 27; 19. 28; 24. 27, 30, 37, 44; 25. 31; compare Acts 7. 56).

units.la: De Sessione Christi ad dextram Patris, qua significatur, Dignitas[?] Deo Patri proxima, & potestas ipsi concessa super omnes Creaturas,in ordine ad Ecclesiæ suæ Gubernationem in hoc sæculo, & æternam salutem in futuro; non unum Heterodoxon tenet Smalcius, quo partim Rem totam mala interpretatione corrumpit, partim eam, plusquam oportet, tum adauget, tum diminuit. Sic enim ille. Sessio Christi ad dextram Dei, est Christi Divinitas. In Exam. 100. errorum. Err. 71. Christus in usu suæ Potestatis, quam à Patre accepit, à Deo non dependet. & paulo post— Per sessionem Christi ad dextram Dei affirmari videtur, Deum Christo, in salute Hominum procurandâ, locum quodammodo honoratiorem ad Tempus concessisse— Deus ad certum Tempus Jesu Christo cessit suum Imperium super Homines, quod ad salutem eorum attinet. Ib. Err. 34. Quasi Rex summus exuat se Imperio, cum vices suas ad Tempus alicui Præfecto demandat; ut Pharao quondam Josepho. Quasi Regnum cœleste, quod nunc exercetur in Ecclesia, non appelletur Regnum Dei Patris, æque ac Christi. Eph. 55. Apoc. 12. 10. Quasi demum mater Filiorum Zebedæi, cum supplex petierit à Christo, ut unus illorum ipsi ad dextram assideret in Regno suo, hoc voluerit, ut honoratiorem locum illi cederet. Sed ut in hoc nimius est, ita non longe post Christi regiam Potestatem nimis restringit, dum ait—Christi Providentia, proprie loquendo, ad neminem spectat, nisi qui ejus sit—curam[?] sui tantum populi, proprie loquendo, gerit. Err. 42. At Scriptura non semel affirmat, & Smalcius alibi concedit Christum, post exaltationem suam ad dextram Dei in Cœlis, non solum Dignitate superiorem esse omni Creatura, sed & Potestate, quam & exercet in Angelos, tam Bonos, tam Malos, & licet peculiarem curam Ecclesiæ suæ gerat, quæ ipsius fidem profitetur, & leges observat, neutiquam tamen Providentia sua destituit reliquum Genus humanum, quod totum redemit, & cujus salutem, tum ferio optat, tum sedulo procurat. Alioquin nunquam misisset Apostolos suos, miraculorum virtute armatos, & linguarum Dono instructos, non solum ad incredulos Judæos, sed & ad omnes mundi Gentes ubique dispersas, ut eas per Evangelium invitarent ad fidem amplectendum, qua veniam omnium peccatorum, vitamque simul æternam, omnibus obtulit, quicunque pœnitentiam agere, sincere in ipsum credere, ipsius mandatis obtemperare, & cum in hac fide, tum in Obedientia legibus suis præstanda, ad finem usque vitæ perseverare voluerunt. Neque adhuc cessat, aut unquam cessabit hæc Christi Cura atque Providentia, usquedum Electorum numerum compleverit, & ad judicandum Genus humanum in fine Mundi advenerit. Siquidem Apostolorum Successores sub Christi auspiciis, huic sacræ Militiæ sedulo incubuerunt, ut crucis vexillum ubique circumferrent, Evangelium apud exteras gentes clara voce divulgarent; &, subactis Erroribus atque vitiis, quibus sub Satanæ Tyrannide devincti jacebant, cunctos ita liberatos in Christi Regnum transferrent, Ipsiusque salutari jugo subderent.
units.tr: Concerning the sitting of Christ at the right hand of the Father, by which is signified a dignity next to God the Father and a power granted to him over all creatures, for the governing of his Church in this age and for eternal salvation in the age to come, Smalcius holds not one heterodox view, by which he partly corrupts the whole matter through a bad interpretation, and partly both enlarges and diminishes it more than is right. For he says: "The sitting of Christ at the right hand of God is the divinity of Christ" (Examen of errors, 100, Error 71). "Christ, in the exercise of his power, which he received from the Father, does not depend on God." And a little later: "By the sitting of Christ at the right hand of God it seems to be affirmed that God has granted to Christ, for the procuring of men's salvation, a somewhat more honourable place for a time. God ceded to Jesus Christ, for a certain time, his rule over men, so far as it concerns their salvation" (ibid., Error 34). As if a supreme king were to divest himself of his rule when he entrusts his office for a time to some prefect, as Pharaoh once did with Joseph. As if the heavenly kingdom, which is now exercised in the Church, were not called the kingdom of God the Father as well as of Christ (Eph. 5. 5; Rev. 12. 10). As if, finally, the mother of the sons of Zebedee, when she humbly asked Christ that one of them might sit at his right hand in his kingdom, meant only that he should yield a more honourable place to him. But as he is excessive in this, so not long after he restricts Christ's kingly power too much, when he says: "Christ's providence, properly speaking, belongs to no one except those who are his; properly speaking, he takes care only of his own people" (Error 42). But Scripture affirms more than once, and Smalcius elsewhere concedes, that Christ, after his exaltation to the right hand of God in the heavens, is superior not only in dignity to every creature, but also in power, which he exercises over angels, both good and evil; and although he takes special care of his Church, which professes his faith and observes his laws, he nevertheless by no means withdraws his providence from the rest of the human race, which he has wholly redeemed and whose salvation he both earnestly desires and diligently promotes. Otherwise he would never have sent his apostles, armed with the power of miracles and endowed with the gift of tongues, not only to the unbelieving Jews but also to all the nations of the world dispersed everywhere, to invite them through the Gospel to embrace the faith, by which he offers pardon of all sins and eternal life at the same time to all who are willing to repent, sincerely believe in him, obey his commands, and persevere to the end of their lives both in this faith and in the obedience due to his laws. Nor does this care and providence of Christ cease, or ever will cease, until he has completed the number of the elect and has come at the end of the world to judge the human race. For the successors of the apostles, under Christ's auspices, have diligently applied themselves to this sacred warfare: to carry the banner of the cross everywhere, to spread the Gospel with a clear voice among foreign nations, and, having subdued the errors and vices by which they lay bound under the tyranny of Satan, to transfer all so freed into the kingdom of Christ and place them under his saving yoke.

units.la: Denique negant Christum jam glorificatum vere pro nobis interpellare, seu intercedere apud Patrem in Cœlo; ex eo nempe, quod hoc repugnet potentiæ divinæ Christo concessæ; cum is, qui proprie orat, Potestatem omnia faciendi non habeat. Idcirco, Interpellationem hanc dicunt esse plane figuratam, qua nihil aliud significatur, quam totam illam Potestatem, Christo divina Benignitate contigisse; quo sensu, Interpellare erit, potentia à patre acceptâ, Nostri curam gerere. Christum in cœlo, inquit Smalcius, non nisi improprie interpellare pro Nobis. Exam. 100. Err. 72. Et Catech. Racov: Cum Scriptura testatur, Christum pro nobis interpellare, non sit propterea, ac si ille pro nobis preces ad Deum proprie funderet. Hæc enim simul non consi-
units.tr: Finally, they deny that Christ, now glorified, truly intercedes for us or makes intercession before the Father in heaven. Their reason is that this would conflict with the divine power granted to Christ, since one who properly prays does not have the power to do all things. Therefore they say this intercession is wholly figurative, signifying nothing more than that whole power which Christ received by divine kindness; in this sense, to intercede would be to take care of us with the power received from the Father. Christ in heaven, says Smalcius, intercedes for us only improperly. Exam. 100, Err. 72. The Racovian Catechism says: When Scripture testifies that Christ intercedes for us, it does not follow that he properly pours out prayers to God on our behalf. For these things do not agree at the same time with his perfect power, which God has given him and by which he is our King. Christ's intercession would be the means by which the Holy Spirit should work in our members

units.la: [The last word of the text, "sit", appears at lower right as the catchword.] sit cum perfecta Ipsius potestate, quam Deus ei ipsa concessit, & ob quam ipse Rex noster est. Verum eo sit, ut in Membris nostris insigatur [?] protersus [?] Potestatem omnem, quam Christus habet, non ex sese habere, verum Dei patris Dono; & ita omnia Opera efficere, ac si ad ea efficienda virtutem & Precibus intervenientibus, subinde obtineret. Id vero Spiritus Sanctus propterea facit, ut Patris Prærogativa & Eminentia integra & inviolabilis persistat. Pag. 231. Socinus praeterea hoc mire torquet illa Christi verba: Jo. 14. 13, 14. Collata cum. 15. 16. Quicquid petieritis patrem in Nomine meo, dabo vobis. Cum Christus, ait, se facturum dicit, quicquid patrem Deum in ipsius nomine rogarent, satis significat, Rogare patrem in Christi nomine nihil aliud esse quam patrem rogare, ad ipsum Christum preces dirigendo. Sic ille, Epist. de Invoc. Christi, p. 355. Tom. 1. Sed e contra. Licet non existimemus, Christum in statu Gloriae collocatum, pro nobis apud patrem nunc intercedere, quemadmodum olim in Terris, nempe more supplicis, flexis genibus, intentis in coelum oculis, clamore valido, & lachrymis manantibus; credimus tamen, cum Scriptura & Ecclesia Catholica, Christum satis proprie dici posse pro nobis intercedere, & Preces nostras Deo Patri offerre, ut apud illum acceptae sint, & effectum suum consequantur in gratiam precantium. Modum quidem nescimus quo Preces Nostras sic offert, & pro nobis intercedit, sed Rem ipsam satis testatam habemus in S. Literis, quae affirmant Christum in Coelos exaltatum ad Patris dextram sedere atque illic pro nobis intercedere; Corpus suum, quod olim crucifixum est ad humanum Genus Patri reconciliandum, & ad comparandum dum ea omnia quæ ad Ecclesiæ Salutem conducunt, ejusdem Patris oculis continenter offerre; quæ conferunt Christum cum Moïse & Aarone, qui pro Dei populo intercessisse memorantur; & cum Sacerdotibus Aaronis Posteris, qui cum suffitu ad Altare Incensi, Preces illius Populi Deo offerebant quæ Christum appellant Mediatorem inter Deum Patrem, & Homines quemadmodum Moses olim inter Deum & Israelem; quæ demum jubent nos preces nostras Deo Patri offerre in nomine Christi, id est, illius Meritis, Mediationi, & summæ apud Patrem Gratiæ confisos. —Quis est qui condemnet? Christus is est qui mortuus est, imo vero qui suscitatus est, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, qui etiam interpellat pro nobis. Rom. 8. 34. Idem conferetur cum Moïse Mediatore. Lex per Angelos ordinata est, in manu Mediatoris. Gal. 4. 19. Mediator autem non est unius, Deus vero unus est. Ib. v. 20. Adhortor ante omnia, ut fiant Deprecationes, preces. Pro omnibus Hominibus. Hoc enim bonum & acceptum est coram Servatore nostro Deo, qui vult omnes Homines salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Unus enim est Deus, unus & Mediator Dei & Hominum, Homo Christus Jesus. 1. Tim. 2. 1-5. Nemo sibi ipsi sumit honorem [Pontificatus,] sed qui vocatur à Deo, sicut & Aaron. Ita & Christus non ipse sibi hunc Honorem tribuit, ut fieret pontifex, sed is qui dixit ei, Filius meus es Tu, ego hodie genui te. Heb. 5. 4,5. Christus, propterea quod manet in æternum, habet perpetuum Sacerdotium. Unde & salvare in perpetuum potest eos qui per ipsum accedunt ad Deum utpote semper vivens ad interpellandum pro eis. Ibid. Cap. 7. [?]24, 25. Denique conferantur[?] confer Actionem Zachariæ cum Angelo Apocalyptico. Legimus enim, quod secundum Ritum Functionis Sacerdotalis Zacharias sortitus sit munus suffitus faciendi ingrediendo in Templum Domini. Tota vero multitudo Populi foris precabatur tempore suffitus. Luc. 1. 9, 10. Tum alius Angelus venit, & stetit apud Altare habens Thuribulum aureum, & dati sunt ei suffitus multi, ut offerret cum precibus Sanctorum omnium super Altare aureum, quod est ante Thronum. Ascendit autem fumus suffituum cum precibus Sanctorum, è manu Angeli, in conspectu Dei. Apoc. 8. v. 3, 4. Hic autem Angelus repræsentatur in visione, instar Sacerdotis suffitum adolentis in Templo, nostrique pontificis vividam Imaginem gerit, qui nostras Preces Deo patri offert, Eaque sua ipsius Intercessione comitatas, quasi suffitu suaveolenti, purissimoque[?] acceptissimas illi reddit.
units.tr: [The last word of the text, "sit", appears at lower right as the catchword.] is with his perfect power, which God himself granted to him and on account of which he is our King. The result, however, is that there is impressed upon our members that all the power which Christ has he does not have from himself but by the gift of God the Father, and so he brings about all his works as if, by his intercession and prayers, he obtained the power to accomplish them from time to time. The Holy Spirit does this so that the prerogative and eminence of the Father remain whole and inviolable. Page 231. Moreover, Socinus twists those words of Christ in a remarkable way: John 14:13, 14, compared with 15:16: "Whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do for you." Since Christ says, he says, that he will do whatever they ask God the Father in his name, he sufficiently signifies that to ask the Father in Christ's name is nothing other than to ask the Father, directing the prayers to Christ himself. So he writes in his letter on the invocation of Christ, page 355, volume 1. But on the contrary: although we do not think that Christ, placed in the state of glory, now intercedes for us with the Father as he once did on earth, namely in the manner of a suppliant, with knees bent, eyes fixed on heaven, with a loud cry and streaming tears, we nevertheless believe, with Scripture and the Catholic Church, that Christ can be said quite properly to intercede for us and to offer our prayers to God the Father, so that they may be accepted by him and obtain their effect for the sake of those who pray. Indeed we do not know the manner in which he offers our prayers and intercedes for us, but we have the thing itself sufficiently attested in the Holy Scriptures, which affirm that Christ, exalted into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father and there intercedes for us, continually offering to the eyes of the same Father his body, which was once crucified to reconcile the human race to the Father, and to procure all those things which serve the salvation of the Church. They compare Christ with Moses and Aaron, who are recorded to have interceded for the people of God, and with the sons of Aaron, the priests, who with incense at the altar of incense offered the prayers of that people to God. They call Christ the Mediator between God the Father and men, as Moses once was between God and Israel. Finally, they bid us offer our prayers to God the Father in the name of Christ, that is, trusting in his merits, his mediation, and his supreme grace with the Father. "Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, yes rather who was raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us." Rom. 8:34. The same is to be compared with Moses the mediator: "The law was ordained through angels, in the hand of a mediator." Gal. 3:19. "Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one." Ibid. v. 20. "I exhort, above all, that supplications and prayers be made for all men. For this is good and acceptable before our Saviour God, who wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." 1 Tim. 2:1–5. "No one takes the honour [of the high priesthood] to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was. So also Christ did not himself assume this honour to become high priest, but he who said to him, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'" Heb. 5:4, 5. "Christ, because he remains for ever, has a perpetual priesthood. Whence he is also able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them." Ibid., ch. 7, vv. 24, 25. Finally, let us compare the action of Zechariah with the angel of the Apocalypse. For we read that, according to the rite of the priestly office, Zechariah was chosen by lot to perform the duty of burning incense, entering the temple of the Lord. And the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the time of the incense. Luke 1:9, 10. Then another angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer, and there was given to him much incense, that he should offer it with the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the throne. And the smoke of the incense ascended with the prayers of the saints, from the angel's hand, before God. Apoc. 8:3, 4. Now this angel is represented in the vision in the likeness of a priest burning incense in the temple, and bears a living image of our High Priest, who offers our prayers to God the Father and, accompanied by his own intercession, renders them most acceptable to him, as a fragrant incense of the purest kind.

units.la: §. 68. Spiritum Sanctum nolunt esse Personam, Deo Patri & Filio coæqualem, sed virtutem istam duntaxat, & efficaciam utriusque, per quam operantur, quicquid Supernaturaliter operantur. Smalcius in Exam. 157. Errorum allerit — Spiritum Sanctum in Deo, esse Proprietatem seu Attributum, sicut Sapientiam, atque Justitiam. Err. 132. & Paulo post — Spiritum Sanctum non esse unum, sed Plures, eosque dignitate inæquales, &c. pro diversitate Donorum. Err. 137. Cur autem non pari Ratione, sapientias quoque & Bonitates multiplicat in Deo pro diversitate effectuum, & imparitate Graduum Sapientiæ atque Bonitatis qui in diversis Creaturis spectantur, Ipsis à Deo summa varietate communicati? Schlichtingius quoque in Symbolum. p. 99. vocat Spiritum Sanctum, Virtutem illam, qua Homines sibi sibi charos peculiariter sanctificat; Dei Afflatum, maxima virtutis & efficacie; imo, ipsam Dei virtutem & efficaciam, per quam Deus & Christus omnia quae velint in iis vel per eos, qui illo afflantur, peragunt; & vicissim, qui illo afflantur, omnia quae Natura viris non possunt, per eundem efficiunt. propterea, tum id, quod Ipse Deus & Christus, per Spiritum suum, vel agunt, vel loquuntur; tum id, quod ipso affiati, per eundem Spiritum Sanctum, similiter vel faciunt, vel loquuntur Spiritui Sancto ascribitur. Sic Spiritus Sanctus nobis dat, quid & quomodo loquamur; nos sanctificat, docet, illuminat, mysteria Dei nobis revelat; nos ducit, regit, consolatur, roborat, ipsam in nobis effici[?]; nempe quia haec Omnia Deus & Christus per eum faciunt. Idem in nostris Cordibus clamat, Abba Pater; scrutatur Profunda Dei, & novit ea quae sunt Dei niminum, quia nos per illum clamamus, scrutamur, novimus. Similiter in nobis & pro nobis loquitur, futura praedicit, de Evangelio testatur. Miracula patrat, Mundum arguit, Episcopos constituit, legatos mittit, decernit, cum haec Omnia Deus & Christus, accedente nostra [?] in omnibus opera ac Ministeria, per Spiritum Sanctum peragant. Propterea, haec omnia, atque His similia, & Deo, & Christo, & Spiritui Sancto & Illis, qui eo afflati, Talium sunt Administri, adscribi solent — Cum unus & idem Spiritus dicitur dividere unicuique seorsim, prout vult, divisio Donorum, & porro voluntas, ei tribuitur ad similitudinem eorum quae voluntate & propterea, diversimode agunt; & quatenus divisionis Donorum medium est, seu Instrumentum Divinum quod a divina voluntate regitur. Haec Ille. At ex Adverso, etsi minime diffiteamur Spiritum Sanctum quandoque accipi in S. Scriptura pro Dei Potentia, sive efficacia inter inter operandum, & quandoque pro Donis Spiri-tus Sancti in Hominies [?] collatis (quæ figuratæ huiusce vocis Acceptiones sunt,) quoties tamen proprie accipitur, personam designat, Personam divinæ essentiæ participem, eamque ordine tertiam in S. S. Triade. Siquidem expresse appellatur Deus. Act. 5. 34. [?] & Adiungitur Deo Patri, & Filio (quos omnes pro personis habent) ut ejusdem Naturæ, parisque Dignitatis, particeps, in formula Baptismi, Benedictione Apostolica, & officio Testis de Coelo. Matt. 28. 19. 2. Cor. 13. ult.
units.tr: §. 68. They are unwilling for the Holy Spirit to be a Person co-equal with God the Father and the Son, but only that power and efficacy of both by which they work whatever they work supernaturally. Smalcius, in Exam. 157 of the Errors, asserts: The Holy Spirit in God is a property or attribute, like wisdom and justice. Err. 132. And a little later: The Holy Spirit is not one but many, and unequal in dignity, etc., according to the diversity of gifts. Err. 137. But why, by the same reasoning, do they not also multiply wisdoms and goodnesses in God, according to the diversity of effects and the unequal degrees of wisdom and goodness seen in diverse creatures, which God communicates to them in great variety? Schlichting too, in Symbolum, p. 99, calls the Holy Spirit that power by which he peculiarly sanctifies the men dear to him; the breath of God, of the greatest virtue and efficacy; indeed the very power and efficacy of God, through which God and Christ accomplish all that they will in them, or through those who are inspired by it; and conversely, those who are inspired by it accomplish through the same all the things which nature cannot give to men. Hence both what God himself and Christ do or say through their Spirit, and what men inspired by it do or say through the same Holy Spirit, is ascribed to the Holy Spirit. Thus the Holy Spirit gives us what and how we should speak; he sanctifies us, teaches, illuminates, and reveals the mysteries of God to us; he leads, rules, comforts, and strengthens us, himself being brought about in us, namely because God and Christ do all these things through him. The same Spirit cries in our hearts, Abba, Father; he searches the depths of God and knows the things of God, because we cry, search and know through him. Similarly he speaks in us and for us, foretells the future, and bears witness to the Gospel. He works miracles, convicts the world, appoints bishops, sends legates, and decides, since God and Christ, with our cooperation in all works and ministries, accomplish all these things through the Holy Spirit. Therefore all these things, and things like them, are wont to be ascribed both to God and to Christ and to the Holy Spirit, and to those who are inspired by him as ministers of such things. Since one and the same Spirit is said to divide to each one separately as he wills, the division of gifts, and further will is attributed to him by likeness to those things which act by will and therefore act in diverse ways; and insofar as he is the means of the division of gifts, a divine instrument which is ruled by the divine will. Thus he. But on the other side, although we by no means deny that the Holy Spirit is sometimes taken in Holy Scripture for the power or efficacy of God in working, and sometimes for the gifts of the Holy Spirit conferred on men (which are figurative uses of this word), nevertheless whenever it is taken properly, it designates a Person, a Person sharing the divine essence, and third in order in the Holy Trinity. For he is expressly called God, Act. 5. 34, and is joined to God the Father and the Son (all of whom they regard as persons) as a partaker of the same nature and equal dignity, in the baptismal formula, in the apostolic benediction, and in the office of witness from heaven. Matt. 28. 19; 2 Cor. 13, last verse.

units.la: 1. Jo. 5. 7. Nos dicimus Dei Templa, eo quod sumus Templa Spiritus Sancti, 1. Cor. 3. 16. 17. & 6. 19, 20. & 2. Cor. 6, 16. Talia illi tribuunt in S. Literis, quæ Personæ soli proprie convenient, eique divinæ, ut voluntas, & Distributio Donorum supernaturalium. 1. Cor. 12. 4, 11. Creatio. Psal. 104. 30. & 33. 6. Job 26. 13. Regeneratio. Jo. 3. 5, 6. Tit. 3. 5. Sanctificatio. Rom. 15. 16. 1. Cor. 6. 11. Unctio Christi. Luc. 4. 18. Testificatio de Christo. Jo. 15. 26. Institutio Apostolorum. Jo. 16. 13. Missio Prophetarum sub lege. Isa. 48. v. 16. Vocatio Apostolorum, & Constitutio Episcoporum sub Evangelio. Act. 13. 2. & 20. 28. Immensitas seu ubiquitas. Psal. 139. 7. Omniscientia. 1. Cor. 2. 10. Omnipotentia, demum illius, & Æternitas, apparent ex Operibus Creationis; necnon ex eo, quod vocetur virtus Altissimi, & Digitus Dei; sic Luc. 1. 35. & 11. 20. Cum Matt. 12. 28. Dicitur item Jehova. Isa. 6. 7, 8, 9. Cum Act. 28. 25. Et Deus Israelis. 2. Sam. 23. 2, 3. Equidem, non inviti concedimus, Deum Patrem, & Christum, istos affectus à Schlichtingio supra memoratos per Spiritum Sanctum opera i qui Spiritui S^o. vulgo tribuuntur in Scriptura. Sed quomodo inde concluditur, Spiritum hunc non esse Perso-nam ab utroque distinctam? non magis iane, quam Filium Dei non esse Personam à Patre distinctam, quia Pater per illum dicitur secula fecisse. Heb. 1. 2. omnia creasse, tam in Coelis, quam super Terram. Col. 1. 16. eumque misisse ut redimeret eos, qui sub lege erant. Gal. 4. 4, 5. aut quod nosipsi non simus Personae ab eodem Spiritu Sancto distinctae, quoniam ii effectus ipsi pariter attribuuntur, quos ipsius Afflatu & Adjumento praestamus; ut Schlichtingius fatetur in Instantiis modo allatis. Dicitur quidem virtus Altissimi. Luc: 1. 35. & virtus ex Alto. Ib. cap. 24. 49. Sed haec virtus, non est qualitas aliqua in Deo, ab illius essentia differens, illique superaddita (haec enim, cum simplicissima sit, nullam omi-nino compositionem admittit) sed substantialis, eademque cum ipla Dei Natura. Unde idem Spiritus alibi, non semel, Deus appellatur. Cujus Rei veritas adeo manifesta est, ut coegerit Eniedinum[?], insignem Socinianismi vindicem, disertis verbis agnoscere, Spiritum Sanctum, non accidentalem quandam, sed substantialem Dei virtutem esse, idque, quia quicquid est in Deo, substantia est. Atque hoc insuper addit; Quando Socinians docent, Spiritum Sanctum esse Dei virtutem, eos hoc tantum velle, Quod Deus sit illa virtus & Potentia; & vicissim, quod Potentia illa sit ipse Deus. Sic ille, Explic: loc: Vet: & N. Test: p. 288, 289. Cum autem subjungit, negare se cum suis, Spiritum Sanctum esse Personam substantialem, à Patre & Filio distinctam; manifeste redargui ab ipso Christo ubi affirmat, Paracletum, sive Spiritum Sanctum, mitti à Patre, & à Patre procedere; mitti item in nomine suo, & à seipso mitti. Ego rogabo Patrem, & alterum Paracletum dabit vobis. Jo. 14. 16. Paracletum, qui est Spiritus Sanctus, mittet Pater in nomine meo. Ib. 26. Cum venerit Paracletus, quem ego mittam vobis a Patre, (Spiritus ille veritatis, qui a Patre procedit) ille testabitur de me. c. 15. 26. ex quibus patet, hos Tres esse personas inter se distinctas. Inter se enim necessario discriminantur mittens, & missus, & ille, cujus nomine Aliquis mittitur. Quod vero adjicit Schlichtingius in loco supra citato, Voluntatem & Arbitrium, tam in vulgi sermone, quam in S. literis, variis Rebus per similitudinem tribui, cum earum Actiones effectaque variant & modo sic, modo aliter se habent. Sic ventus dicitur flare, quo vult. Jo. 3. 8. quia, modo in hanc, modo in illam Partem flat. & naves circumagi dicuntur a minimo Gubernaculo, quocunque Impetu Gubernatoris voluerit. Jac. 3. 4. Nec minus Instrumentis ipsis, eorum, qui per illa libere agunt, voluntatem tribui solere; ut cum dicimus, oculos aspicere quo velint, Aures audire quae velint, manum largientis dare quae velit, & quantum velit, & cui velit. Vera quidem haec sunt, sed admodum infirma sui Dogmatis praesidia contra Fidem Catholicam de Spiritu Sancto. Quis enim nescit, per ea metonymiam non raro Accidentibus adscribi, quae sunt istorum subjectorum propria, quibus Accidentia inhaerent? necnon Actiones & effectus animantium proprios, Rebus inanimatis per Prosopopoeiam attribui? Sed quam infirmum, imo quam absurdum est, hinc inferre, Spiritum Sanctum non esse Personam, cui omnes notae, quae veram Personam, proprieque sic dictam designant, non per Metonymiam, neque per Prosopopoeiam, aliumve quemvis Tropum, sed vere & proprie conveniunt, eique in S. Scriptura assignantur? Hoc igitur Dogma, cum cæteris, in Socinianis damnetur, quod S. literis palam adversum est, & ab Ecclesia Catholica jam dudum in Pneumatomachis, & Sabellianis damnatum est
units.tr: 1. Jo. 5. 7. We call them temples of God, because we are temples of the Holy Spirit, 1. Cor. 3. 16. 17. & 6. 19, 20. & 2. Cor. 6, 16. Scripture ascribes to him things that belong properly to a person alone and are divine, such as his will and the distribution of supernatural gifts, 1. Cor. 12. 4, 11. Creation, Psal. 104. 30. & 33. 6. Job 26. 13. Regeneration, Jo. 3. 5, 6. Tit. 3. 5. Sanctification, Rom. 15. 16. 1. Cor. 6. 11. The anointing of Christ, Luc. 4. 18. The testimony concerning Christ, Jo. 15. 26. The instruction of the Apostles, Jo. 16. 13. The sending of the Prophets under the law, Isa. 48. v. 16. The calling of the Apostles and the appointment of bishops under the Gospel, Act. 13. 2. & 20. 28. Immensity or ubiquity, Psal. 139. 7. Omniscience, 1. Cor. 2. 10. Finally, his omnipotence and eternity appear from the works of creation, and also from the fact that he is called the power of the Most High and the finger of God; so Luc. 1. 35. & 11. 20. with Matt. 12. 28. He is also called Jehovah, Isa. 6. 7, 8, 9. with Act. 28. 25. and the God of Israel, 2. Sam. 23. 2, 3. Indeed, we willingly grant that God the Father and Christ perform, through the Holy Spirit, those affections which Schlichting mentioned above and which are commonly attributed to the Spirit in Scripture. But how does it follow from this that this Spirit is not a Person distinct from both? No more than the Son of God is not a Person distinct from the Father, because the Father is said to have made the ages through him, Heb. 1. 2., to have created all things, both in heaven and on earth, Col. 1. 16., and to have sent him to redeem those who were under the law, Gal. 4. 4, 5. Nor does it follow that we ourselves are not persons distinct from the same Holy Spirit, because the same effects are attributed to us which we accomplish by his breath and help, as Schlichting admits in the instances just cited. It is true that he is called the power of the Most High, Luc. 1. 35., and power from on high, ibid. cap. 24. 49. But this power is not some quality in God, differing from his essence and added to it (for since he is most simple, he admits of no composition at all), but is substantial and the same as the very nature of God. Hence the same Spirit is elsewhere, and not once, called God. The truth of this is so manifest that it compelled Enyedinus, the notable champion of Socinianism, to acknowledge in plain words: that the Holy Spirit is not some accidental virtue of God but a substantial one, and this because whatever is in God is substance. And he adds this besides: When the Socinians teach that the Holy Spirit is the virtue of God, they mean only this, that God is that virtue and power; and conversely, that this power is God himself. Thus he, Explic. loc. Vet. & N. Test., pp. 288, 289. But when he goes on to say that he and his followers deny that the Holy Spirit is a substantial Person distinct from the Father and the Son, he is plainly refuted by Christ himself, where he affirms that the Paraclete, or Holy Spirit, is sent by the Father and proceeds from the Father; that he is also sent in the name of Christ and is sent by himself. I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete. Jo. 14. 16. The Paraclete, who is the Holy Spirit, the Father will send in my name. Ib. 26. When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father (that Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father), he will bear witness of me. c. 15. 26. From these passages it is clear that these three are distinct persons from one another. For the one who sends, the one who is sent, and the one in whose name someone is sent are necessarily distinguished from each other. As for what Schlichting adds in the passage cited above: Will and choice are attributed, both in common speech and in the Holy Scriptures, to various things by way of likeness, since their actions and effects vary, and they sometimes behave in one way and sometimes in another. Thus the wind is said to blow where it wills, Jo. 3. 8. because it blows now in this direction, now in that. And ships are said to be steered by the smallest rudder wherever the impulse of the helmsman wills, Jac. 3. 4. Nor is will less commonly ascribed to the instruments themselves by which people act freely, as when we say that eyes look where they wish, ears hear what they wish, and the hand of the giver gives what it wishes, and as much as it wishes, and to whom it wishes. These things are true, but they are very weak supports for his doctrine against the Catholic faith concerning the Holy Spirit. For who does not know that by such means accidents are often ascribed by metonymy to the subjects of which they are the proper properties and in which they inhere, and that the actions and effects proper to living things are attributed by prosopopoeia to inanimate things? But how weak, indeed how absurd, is it to infer from this that the Holy Spirit is not a Person, when all the marks which designate a true Person, properly so called, belong to him truly and properly, not by metonymy, nor by prosopopoeia, nor by any other trope, and are assigned to him in Holy Scripture? This doctrine, then, together with the others, is condemned in the Socinians, because it is openly opposed to the Holy Scriptures and was long ago condemned by the Catholic Church in the Pneumatomachi and the Sabellians.

units.la: §. 69. Negant solum Spiritum Sanctum esse causam nostræ Conversionis, atque Regenerationis. Sic enim disserit Smalcius contra Frantzium, lc. Disp. 8. Quod ait Frantzius, unum & solum Spiritum Sanctum efficere ista omnia virtute & operatione sua, (viz. internum Assensum verbi Divini, Conversionem ad Deum, Agnitionem Christi, & Fidem in illum) hoc est falsum. Certum est, Spiritum Sanctum nihil operari in eo, qui se aptum & obsequentem non præbet. Idem asserit, in nobis quoque situm esse, ut credamus Evangelio prædicato. Sic enim ille — Si hoc falsum est, quod, ma affirmantem facit Smiglecius, cur præcipitur iis, qui audiunt Evangelium, ut credant Evangelio? nam si naturaliter, & absque alia Gratia, credere non possint, frustra id illis præcipitur, & Deus multarum absurdissimarum accusari potest, qui se id tentas, quod ipse novit impossibile esse. Exam. Err. 157. Err. 105. Idem alibi affirmat, Regenerationem nostram nullo modo solius Dei Opus dici posse, sed requiri ad eam, Hominis voluntatem, & Actionem. Resp. ad nova Monst. cap. 2. Asserit item, Regenerationem spiritualem non effici per Spiritum Sanctum, sed illum dari jam Regeneratis dari. Sic ille, lb. cap. 20. Hinc, grande discrimen instituit Moscorovius inter Generationem naturalem, & Regenerationem spiritualem; referente Smiglecio. lib. de Bapt. cont. Mosc. p. 75. Id. de Bapt. cont. Smigl. c. 6. p. 114. affirmat, Prædicationem Evangelii, vi sua nulla modo conferre Fidem, verbi autem auditi opera & ministerio Animum solicitari duntaxat ad credendum. Quare, ex eadem verbi virtute, fidem in Animo confirgere, si modo probus existat. Etiam Socinus in eo multum est ut probet in Homine convertendo aliquam Dei noticiam praerequiri, Animi probitatem, studiumque ea faciendi, quae Deo probantur. Comm: in 1am Epist. Joan. Ibidem quoque ait — Apostolum indicaret, in nobis aliquam rationem fieri esse, ut nos ipsos puros faciamus, &c. cum Peccatorum sordibus inquinati simus. In cap. 3. v. 3. Denique affirmant, Adultos solos, non autem Infantes, esse subjectum Regenerationis & sanctitatis capax. Socinus enim affirmat, Infantem non posse dici Sanctum, cum nihil agat, aut intelligat. Err. 111. Moscorovius vero ulterius procedens, excludit illos à salute, & Redemptione per Christum humano Generi parta, sic inquiens— Cum voluntas Dei de nobis servandis, & Redemptio Christi, ad eos tantum respiciat, qui propositas à Deo & Christo conditiones amplectuntur, & in iis persistunt: & Infantes per aetatem illas Conditiones admittere non possint; apparet, hanc Dei voluntatem, & Christi Redemptionem, in Divinis literis contestatam, ad Infantes non pertinere. De Bapt: cout: Smigl. c. 7. p. 119. 8.
units.tr: §. 69. They deny only that the Holy Spirit is the cause of our conversion and regeneration. Thus Smalcius argues against Frantzius, loc. Disp. 8. What Frantzius says, that the Holy Spirit alone effects all these things by his power and operation (namely, inward assent to the Divine Word, conversion to God, knowledge of Christ, and faith in him), is false. It is certain that the Holy Spirit works nothing in one who does not present himself as fit and compliant. He likewise asserts that it lies in us also to believe the Gospel when it is preached. For he says: — If this is false, which Smiglecius makes out to be affirmed, why are those who hear the Gospel commanded to believe the Gospel? For if they cannot believe naturally and without other grace, it is in vain that this is commanded them, and God may be accused of many most absurd things, if he tries to bring about what he himself knows to be impossible. Exam. Err. 157. Err. 105. He affirms elsewhere that our regeneration can in no way be called the work of God alone, but the will and action of man are required for it. Resp. ad nova Monst. cap. 2. He also asserts that spiritual regeneration is not effected by the Holy Spirit, but that he is given to those already regenerated. Thus he, ib. cap. 20. Hence Moscorovius draws a great distinction between natural generation and spiritual regeneration, as reported by Smiglecius, lib. de Bapt. cont. Mosc. p. 75. In de Bapt. cont. Smigl. c. 6. p. 114. he affirms that the preaching of the Gospel does not by its own power bring about faith in any way, but that by the work and ministry of the heard word the mind is only stirred to believe. Hence, by the same power of the word, faith is strengthened in the mind, provided the man is upright. Socinus too, in his commentary on the First Epistle of John, labours much to prove that in the man to be converted some knowledge of God is required beforehand, together with uprightness of mind and zeal for doing those things that are pleasing to God. Ibidem he also says: The Apostle would indicate that in us there is some reason why we should make ourselves pure, etc., since we are defiled by the filth of sins. On cap. 3. v. 3. Finally, they affirm that adults alone, and not infants, are capable of being the subject of regeneration and sanctity. For Socinus affirms that an infant cannot be called holy, since it does nothing and understands nothing. Err. 111. Moscorovius, going further still, excludes them from salvation and from the redemption through Christ won for the human race, saying: Since God's will concerning our preservation, and Christ's redemption, look only to those who embrace the conditions proposed by God and Christ and persist in them, and infants by reason of their age cannot meet those conditions, it is evident that this will of God and the redemption of Christ, attested in the divine writings, do not pertain to infants. De Bapt. cont. Smigl. c. 7. p. 119. 8.

units.la: §. 70. De libero Arbitrio, & legis Divinae Imple-tione[?], sic opinantur. Catech: Rac: ita de his statuit. p. 161. Ubi novum foedus satis à Deo confirmatum visum est (sc. per miracula, & extraordinaria Spiritus Sancti Dona) iis, qui ad credendum Evangelio apti fuere, ex eo quod ad confirmationem Foederis factum erat, satis in posterum, quod crederent, habuerunt. Hi vero sunt, qui vel Animi probitate praediti sunt, vel ab ea non alieni. & postea. p. 197. Communiter in Hominibus, natura exiguae admodum sunt vires ad ea, quae Deus ab illis requirit, perficiendum, at voluntas ad perficiendum ea, omnibus adest natura. Nihilominus tamen ea vires non ita prorsus exigua sunt, ut Homo, si vim sibi facere velit, divino Auxilio accedente, non possit voluntati divinæ obsecundare. Auxilium vero suum nemini prorsus Deus denegat ex iis, quibus voluntatem suam patefecit. Alioquin Deus neque castigare, neque punire juste Contumaces posset; quod tamen utrumque facit. Et paulo post p. 205. De Prædestinatis ait Paulus, eos vocatos esse secundum Propositum, ut demonstret, eos demum juxta Propositum Dei Evangelio credidisse, & ad salutem prædestinatos esse, qui Deum diligunt. Id vero in Potestate Hominis situm esse, superius expositum est. Ita quoque Smalcius de Perfectione Justitiæ. Perfectio absolutissima est, quando quis nunquam, ne semel quidem, peccavit. Et etiamsi difficillimum sit, propter Carnis Infirmitatem, ut Homo ad istam Perfectionem reipsa pervenias, non est tamen Impossibile prorsus. Difp: 6. cont: Frantz: Sect: 4. Atque alibi, Ersi[?] Christo Joli[?] concessum fuerit, nunquam peccasse; at nec S. litera, nec sana Ratio, nec Quicquam denique prorsus prohibet, ut qui antea peccavit, eo perfectionis postea perveniat, ut nunquam peccet. Nam si omnia possibili Credenti, quomodo etiam possibile non sit, ut nunquam post agnitam veritatem peccet. Resp: ad Frantz: disp. 6. de Bonis Oper: Thef: 43. Idem ib: Thef: 48. Cum hoc Argumento urgeretur, ex oratione Dominica, Sanctos opus habere ut quotidie orent, Dimitte nobis Debita, nostra duplici hoc effugio elabi nititur, at utroque miserrimo. Eorum primum est, Sanctos teneri orare pro delictis ante Cognitionem Christi atque Conversionem perpetratis, & sic, pro addum præteritis, non pro peccatis post commissis. Secundum vero est, quod, cum Peccata non remittantur perfecte, nisi tunc, quando eorum poena sc. Mors aeterna remittitur; ideo precationem illam prorogandam esse usque ad plenam vitae aeternae donationem. At è contra apparet, non solum ex vetere, sed & ex novo Testamento, viros piissimos, post Fidem acceptam, tum deliquisse, tum Delicta sua agnovisse; imo, Cunctis Fidelibus agnoscenda praecepisse: necnon, mortem aeternam, sive Poenas futuri seculi, remitti omnibus Justificatis, etiam in hac vita. Caro concupiscit adversus Spiritum, inquit Apostolus, Illique adversatur, ita ut non quaecunque vultis, illa faciatis. Gal. 5. 17. In multis offendimus omnes. Jac. 3. 2. Si in luce ambulamus, sicut & ipse [Deus] est in luce, sanguis Jesu Christi emundat Nos ab omni Peccato. 1. Jo. 1. 7. Emundat, ait, non emundavit. Unde inferimus, etiam eos qui ambulant in luce, quamdiu sic ambulant, indigere emundatione à peccato. Et paulo post-Si dixerimus, quoniam peccatum non habemus, ipsi nos seducimus, & veritas in nobis non est. Si confiteamur Peccata nostra fidelis est & justus, ut remittat nobis peccata nostra, & emundet nos ab omni iniquitate. v. 8, 9. Deinde quod ad secundum. Justificati ex fide, inquit Paulus, pacem habemus apud Deum, per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum. Per quem & Accessum habemus [ἔχομεν? habuimus] per Fidem, in Gratiam istam, in qua stamus & gloriamur in spe Gloriae Dei. Rom. 5. 1, 2. Quis intentabit crimina adversus Electos Dei? Deus est, qui justificat. Quis est qui condemnat? Christus is est, qui mortuus est, imo potius, qui resurrexit, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, qui etiam interpellat pro nobis. Rom. 8. 33, 34. In Christum nunc, etsi non cernatis eum, tamen credentes, exultatis Gaudio ineffabili & glorioso, reportantes mercedem Fidei vestrae, salutem Animarum. 1, Pet. 18. 9. Nos scimus, quod translati simus de morte ad vitam, quia diligimus Fratres.
units.tr: §. 70. On free will and the fulfilment of the divine law, they hold as follows. The Racovian Catechism decides these matters thus, p. 161: Where the new covenant has seemed sufficiently confirmed by God (namely through miracles and the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit), those who were fit to believe the Gospel had, from what was done to confirm the covenant, enough reason thereafter to believe. These are the ones who are endowed with, or not far removed from, integrity of mind. And later, p. 197: Commonly in men, the natural powers are very small for performing what God requires of them, but the will to perform it is present in all by nature. Nevertheless those powers are not so utterly small that a man, if he is willing to exert himself, with divine help coming to him, cannot obey the will of God. God in no way denies his help to any of those to whom he has made his will known. Otherwise God could not justly rebuke or punish the stubborn, yet he does both. And a little after, p. 205, speaking of the predestined, Paul says that they were called according to purpose, to show that those who love God are at last those who, according to God's purpose, believed the Gospel and were predestined to salvation. That this lies in man's power has been explained above. So too Smalcius, on the perfection of righteousness: Perfection is most absolute when someone has never sinned, not even once. And although it is very difficult, because of the weakness of the flesh, for a man to actually attain that perfection, it is not altogether impossible. Disp. 6, against Frantz, Sect. 4. And elsewhere: Even if it has been granted to Christ alone never to have sinned, neither Holy Scripture, nor sound reason, nor anything at all prohibits that one who sinned before should afterwards attain such perfection that he never sins. For if all things are possible to the believer, why should it not also be possible that he never sins after the truth has been recognised? Reply to Frantz, disp. 6, on Good Works, thesis 43. The same author, ibid., thesis 48. When this argument was pressed against them from the Lord's Prayer, that the saints need to pray daily, Forgive us our debts, they try to escape by a twofold route, and both are most wretched. The first is that the saints are bound to pray for the sins committed before their knowledge of Christ and their conversion, and so for past offences, not for sins committed after. The second is that, since sins are not remitted perfectly until their punishment, namely eternal death, is remitted, that prayer must therefore be deferred until the full gift of eternal life. But on the contrary it appears, not only from the Old but also from the New Testament, that most pious men, after receiving faith, both sinned and acknowledged their sins; indeed, that all believers were taught to acknowledge them; and that eternal death, or the punishments of the age to come, are remitted to all the justified, even in this life. The flesh lusts against the Spirit, says the Apostle, and opposes it, so that you do not do whatever you wish. Gal. 5. 17. In many things we all offend. Jas. 3. 2. If we walk in the light, as he [God] is in the light, the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin. 1 John 1. 7. Note he says cleanses, not has cleansed. Hence we infer that even those who walk in the light, as long as they so walk, need cleansing from sin. And a little after: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. vv. 8, 9. Next, as to the second point. Being justified by faith, says Paul, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have [ἔχομεν? we had] access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Rom. 5. 1, 2. Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns? It is Christ Jesus who died, or rather who was raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us. Rom. 8. 33, 34. On Christ, though you do not now see him, yet believing, you rejoice with joy unspeakable and glorious, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls. 1 Pet. 1. 8, 9. We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers.

units.la: 1. Jo. 3. 14. Qui edit carnem meam & bibit sanguinem meum habet vitam æternam. Sic ipse Christus ad Judæos. Jo, 6. 54. Atque alibi certos nos reddit de remissione peccatorum, per ministerium potestatis Clavium Apostolis primo concessæ, & per istos ad successores suos in Ecclesia derivatæ, cum sc. illos afflavit, & dixit eis, Accipite Spiritum Sanctum; si quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis. Jo. 20. 22, 23.
units.tr: 1 John 3. 14. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life. So Christ himself to the Jews, John 6. 54. And elsewhere he assures us of the forgiveness of sins through the ministry of the power of the keys, first granted to the Apostles, and by them passed on to their successors in the Church, when he breathed on them and said, Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them. John 20. 22, 23.

units.la: §. 71. 9. Quantum ad fidem de Ecclesia Catholica, Triumphantem omnino negant, & Militantem contemnunt. Sacramenta ab ipsa usurpata vel demunt, vel depravant. Cultum Ipsius defamant quasi idolo exhibitum. Communionem ejusdem rejiciunt; perpetuitatem quoque ipsius inficiantur, ut & Spiritum veritatis ipsi à Christo in sæcula futura promissum. Signa sive notas, quibus Ipsa ab aliis cœtibus discriminatur atque dignoscitur, pro nihilo habent, ut inutiles & ineptas. Denique, tum veteris Fidei integritatem, tum veræ Christi Ecclesiæ Nomen atque Prærogativam, ut sibi peculiares, Cœtibus suis arrogant. Quæ singula ex sequentibus apparebunt. Siquidem Ecclesiam nunc Temporis Triumphantem diserte negant dum Sanctos defunctos nolunt secundum Animam vivere & sentire ante diem Resurrectionis; quando demum, & non prius, una cum Corporibus suis Animæ revivi scent[?], & quasi ex somno quodam profundissimo expergesient. Sic & Ecclesiam Christi in hisce Terris militantem pariter vilipen-dunt. dunt, licet ejusdem Christi sponsam dilectam, & omnium verè Fidelium Matrem jure venerabilem; dum & ipsius Doctrinæ fidem derogant, & ipsius legibus obsequium denegant. Necessitatem & efficaciam Sacramentorum & Sacramentalium à Christo, in usum suæ Ecclesiæ institutorum, vel omnino tollunt, vel admodum diminuunt. Et cum Deum, quem in Trinitate Personarum semper agnovit, atque adhuc adorat, Ecclesia Catholica, pro cerebri humani Idolo habeant, necesse est ut hac ratione eandem Ecclesiam, ut Idololatriæ ream, condemnent. Socinus itaque vult suos se segregare ab Ecclesiis Evangelicorum, ob certos quoldam Abusus apud eos, licet à Pastoribus ipsarum minime probatos.—De multis rebus, inquit, quas sibi Evangelici permittunt, contrarias Dei Christique præceptis, quæ interim à præcipuis ipsorum Magistris minimè approbantur, nec cum ipsius Religionis Evangelicæ Doctrina consentiunt (qualia sunt, commubia[?] cum Idololatriis, luxus & Splendor in victu & vestitu, ludicra multa & vana in vita Actiones) mihi de ipsius Doctrina Evangelicorum erroribus agenti, nihil dicendum censui. Tametsi dubium non est, quin hæc quoque justa censeri debeant causa unicuique Pietatis studioso, sese ab illorum Cœtibus segregandi (præsertim, ubi alii sunt cœtus Hominum Christum Jesum colentium, qui sibi ista non permittunt) & iis aliis adhærendi. Sic ille, lib: Quod Regn. Pol. p. 705 Ostorodus item hanc Secessionem heri vult, ob neglectum Disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ, quam ipso judice, reddit Ecclesiam nomine Christi indignam. Instit. Cap. 26. Deinde, perpetuitatem Ecclesiæ visibilis & in Terra militantis perperam asseri dicunt. Sic enim Soci-nus—Non est necesse, aliquam extitisse isto Tempore Sæculo sc. primitivo, post obitum Apostolorum) Veram Ecclesiam faciem. Neque enim eam perpetuo extituram, usquam revera prædictum, aut absolute promissum est. Sol: Scrip: 30. ad 5. Et Paulo post— Illa Christi verba, dic Ecclesia, tum locum habere censenda sunt, cum is, de quo loquitur, fuerit in aliqua visibili Ecclesia. Christi voluntas erat, ut aliqua Ecclesia foret, usque per Apostolos colligeretur; non tamen sequitur, quin pro Hominum malitia fieri potuerit, ut aliquando, idque per longissimum Tempus, nulla visibilis Ecclesia extiterit. ib: ad 7. Idem quoque in Præf: ad has Iplut:— Hanc Propositionem plane damnat, viz. Quod necesse sit semper extare visibilem aliquam Ecclesiam, quæ puram Doctrinam de Deo filiuque ejus retineat. Atque alibi— Ego non nego, sub Antichristo plenam Defectionem fuisse. Antichristum vero illum magnum Hominem illum perditum à Paulo prædictum, non ante extitisse judico, quam Romani Pontifices primatus extitit. De Ecclesia p. 345. Imo, non veretur afferre, hunc desectum Ecclesiæ contigisse ab antiquissimis usque Temporibus, nempe, quam primum Dogma Trinitatis apud eam valuit; quod nunquam non ab eadem assertum est, ut omnes norunt, quibus Historia Ecclesiastica veteris ævi non est porsus ignota. Sic tamen ille disserit contra Ecclesiam Catholicam; & ipsius existentiam, una cum Fide Catholica, destruere molitur; sc. Animadv. 10. In Assert: Theol. Coll. Posnan. Deum quidem unum esse (ait) agnoscit Universa Dei Ecclesia. Sed ita ut Unitatem in Trinitate & Trinitatem in Unitate veneretur, id vel nulla Dei Ecclesia vel certe non quatenus est Dei Ecclesia, ullo modo potest agnoscere; cum Ifud humanum prorsus commentum sit, cui divina veritas am-nibus[?] nibus modis apertissime refragantur. Hæc ille. Cui sufragatur Oftorodus. Inst. Cap. 42. Et Smalcius, Disp. 8. De Ecclesia. Sect. 9. Et paulo post, ad thesin 75, 76. Negant pariter ( quod huic suo Dogmati affine est, illique viam præstruit ) Spiritum Sanctum, à Christo Ecclesiæ suæ promissum, cum ea semper permansisse. Sic enim Socinus--Neque vero Spiritus Sanctus, qui omnem veritatem docere debebat, Ecclesia fuit promissus, sed Illis qui Fundamentum ejus jecerunt; Quorumque & Sermones & Scripta pro divinis, ac de quibus nemini dubium ullum restaret, haberi debuerunt, ut ita semper in promptu nobis situm esset, quod ad cognoscendam divini numinis voluntatem, recurreremus.
