Taceo, quod & ista verba [omnis Veritas] Aliud nihil significent quam omnem veritatem, quæ ad jaciendum Ecclesiæ Fundamentum, Munusque Apostolorum probe obeundum, pertinebat. --De singulari quadam veritate sermo fit μόνῳ [?], idem valet, quoad ὅλῳ [?] Omnem, quod totam. Sic ille, epist. 3 ad Andr. Dudith: p. 501. Col.
units.tr: §. 71. 9. As to the faith concerning the Catholic Church, they altogether deny the Church Triumphant and despise the Church Militant. They either remove or corrupt the sacraments used by her. They defame her worship as if it were offered to an idol. They reject her communion; they also deny her perpetuity, as well as the Spirit of truth promised to her by Christ for the ages to come. They regard as nothing the signs or marks by which she is distinguished and recognised from other assemblies, as useless and unfit. Finally, they claim for their own assemblies the integrity of the old faith, and the name and prerogative of the true Church of Christ, as if these were peculiarly their own. Each of these points will appear from what follows. For they plainly deny that the Church Triumphant exists at the present time, since they will not have the departed saints live and feel in soul before the day of resurrection; only then, and not before, will souls be revived together with their bodies, and they will awake as if from some deepest sleep. In the same way they likewise hold cheap the Church of Christ militant on earth, though she is the beloved bride of Christ and rightly to be revered as the mother of all true believers; for they both undermine the faith of her doctrine and deny obedience to her laws. They either altogether remove or greatly diminish the necessity and efficacy of the sacraments and sacramentals instituted by Christ for the use of his Church. And since they regard as a figment of the human brain the God whom the Catholic Church has always acknowledged in the Trinity of Persons and still adores, they must, on this ground, condemn that same Church as guilty of idolatry. Socinus therefore wishes his followers to separate themselves from the churches of the Evangelicals, on account of certain abuses among them, although these have by no means been approved by their ministers. Of the many things, he says, which the Evangelicals permit themselves, contrary to the precepts of God and Christ, and which meanwhile are by no means approved by their chief teachers, nor agree with the doctrine of that Evangelical religion (such as communion with idolaters, luxury and show in food and clothing, many frivolous and vain activities in life), I, treating of the errors of their doctrine, have thought nothing need be said. Yet there is no doubt that these also ought to be deemed a just cause for anyone zealous for piety to separate himself from their assemblies (especially where there are other assemblies of men who worship Christ Jesus and do not permit themselves these things), and to join those others. So he, in the book Quod Regnum Polonicum, p. 705. Ostorodus likewise wishes this secession to be made on account of the neglect of ecclesiastical discipline, which, in his judgement, renders the Church unworthy of the name of Christ. Institutes, ch. 26. Next, they say that the perpetuity of the visible Church, militant on earth, is wrongly asserted. For thus Socinus: It is not necessary that a true Church should have existed at that time (namely the primitive age, after the death of the Apostles). For it has nowhere been truly foretold, or absolutely promised, that it would exist perpetually. Sol. Script. 30, reply to 5. And a little after: Those words of Christ, tell it to the Church, are to be regarded as applying only when the person spoken of is in some visible Church. It was Christ's will that some Church should be gathered through the Apostles; yet it does not follow that, through the wickedness of men, it could not happen that at some time, and that for a very long time, no visible Church existed. Ibid., reply to 7. The same in the preface to these Iplut.: he plainly condemns this proposition, namely that it is necessary that some visible Church always exist, retaining pure doctrine concerning God and his Son. And elsewhere: I do not deny that under Antichrist there was a complete apostasy. But I judge that that great, lost man, foretold by Paul as Antichrist, did not exist until the primacy of the Roman Pontiffs came into being. On the Church, p. 345. Indeed, he does not hesitate to assert that this defection of the Church occurred from the most ancient times, namely as soon as the doctrine of the Trinity prevailed among her, which has always been affirmed by her, as all know who are not wholly unacquainted with the ecclesiastical history of the early age. Yet he argues thus against the Catholic Church, and labours to destroy her existence together with the Catholic faith: Animadv. 10, on the Assertion of the Theology of the Posnan Colloquy. That God is one, he says, the whole Church of God acknowledges. But that it should venerate unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity, this no Church of God, or certainly not insofar as it is a Church of God, can in any way acknowledge; since that is a purely human invention, which divine truth in every way most plainly opposes. So he. Ostorodus supports him, Inst. ch. 42; and Smalcius, Disp. 8, On the Church, Sect. 9. And a little after, on theses 75 and 76, they likewise deny (which is akin to this dogma of theirs and paves the way for it) that the Holy Spirit, promised by Christ to his Church, has always remained with her. For thus Socinus: Nor was the Holy Spirit, who was to teach all truth, promised to the Church, but to those who laid its foundation; and their sermons and writings were to be held as divine, and about which no one should have any doubt, so that we might always have at hand that to which we could turn to know the will of the divine majesty. I pass over the fact that these words, all truth, signify nothing other than all the truth which pertained to laying the foundation of the Church and to the Apostles' office, which they were to discharge well. Concerning a certain singular truth the discourse is made in the Greek [μόνῳ]; the same holds for the Greek [ὅλῳ] meaning "whole" or "all", that is, the whole. So he, in epistle 3 to Andreas Dudith, p. 501, col.

units.la: 2. Postremo, Socinus, ejusque socii ac Discipuli, neminem solicitum esse volunt de quaerenda vera Christi Ecclesia & de examine notarum, quibus ab Hæreticis & Schismaticis discriminatur; satis autem habent, quod Scripturas ad manum habeant, è quibus instruatur unusquisque in via Salutis. Atque insuper, veritatem Dei, veramque Christi Ecclesiam, ut sibi proprias, vendicare amant. Sic etenim Catech. Rac. p. 234. Non multum juvat signa vera Christi Ecclesiæ inquirere, cum Tibi exposuerim quid veram Ecclesiam constituat; nimirum, salutaris Doctrina, quam quicunque Cœtus habet & profitetur, est vera Christi Ecclesia. Qui vero Cœtus Doctrinam salutarem non habet, nec profitetur, etiamsi nescio quae signa proferat atque pratendat, pro vera Christi Ecclesia haberi non potest. At tenere salutarem Doctrinam, cum Ecclesia Christi sit natura, Signum Illius, si proprie loquaris, esse non potest, cum Signum ipsum a re, cujus Signum est, differre oportet. Ergo, ad cognoscendum quae sit vera Christi Ecclesia, satis est cognovisse salutarem Doctrinam. Etenim, qui hanc amplectitur, jam est in ipsa Ecclesia vera. Quare nihil est cur de notis Ecclesiae quaeras a quibus Ecclesia agnoscatur. Salutaris porro Doctrina quae sit, e nostro sermone, atque colloquutione discere potuisti.
units.tr: 2. Finally, Socinus and his associates and disciples want no one to be anxious about seeking the true Church of Christ or about examining the marks by which it is distinguished from heretics and schismatics. They think it enough that people have the Scriptures at hand, from which each person may be instructed on the way of salvation. Moreover, they like to claim the truth of God and the true Church of Christ as their own. Thus the Racovian Catechism, p. 234: It does not help much to inquire into the true signs of the Church of Christ, since I have explained to you what constitutes the true Church, namely, the saving doctrine. Any assembly that holds and professes the saving doctrine is the true Church of Christ. But an assembly that does not hold or profess the saving doctrine cannot be regarded as the true Church of Christ, however many signs it may put forward and pretend to have. Now, to hold the saving doctrine, since it belongs to the nature of the Church of Christ, cannot be a sign of it, if we speak properly, since a sign must differ from the thing of which it is a sign. Therefore, to know what the true Church of Christ is, it is enough to have learned the saving doctrine. For whoever embraces this doctrine is already in the true Church itself. Hence there is no reason for you to seek the marks of the Church by which the Church is recognised. You could learn what the saving doctrine is from our discussion and conversation.

units.la: Praeclarum sane Argumentum, quod nos securos reddat de vera Christi Ecclesia rite dignoscenda; quodque nos vera Ipsius membra simus; nempe, quod vera Ecclesia sit, quae salutarem Christi Doctrinam tenet atque profitetur; ista autem salutaris Doctrina, non Alia sit quam Sociniana, quae in isto Catechismo proponitur & explicatur. Sehlichtingius pariter in Confessione Fidei, cum Symbolum Apostolicum explicuisset ex Socini sententia, haec adjicit — Credimus Ecclesiam Catholicam non esse Doctrina & Fide variam, sed ubique & omni Tempore, Initio ab Apostolis facto, unius ejusdemque Doctrinae & Fidei; Istius nempe, quae Symbolo hoc comprehensa est, ut qui hanc retineat, vere sit Catholicus; qui vero contrarii aut Alieni quidpiam admisceat, haetenus Catholicus esse non possit. In hanc igitur Sanctam Ecclesiam Catholicam credimus, quia, haec omnia quae Christiani Sanctis moribus dediti, semper & ubique professi sunt, pro veris & indubitatis agnoscimus. Sic ille, p. 114. Rectissime quidem si hoc Fidei antiquae Symbolum expositset juxta sensum antiquae Ecclesiae; sed pessime in eo quod illud in multis depravet, ac detorqueat, ad Haeresin Socini astruendam[?] cumque Fidem simul & Ecclesiam, ejusdem sectæ proprias reddit. Smalcius demum diserte negat, sincerum Verbi Prædicationem, & legitimum Sacramentorum usum, esse veras notas Ecclesiæ veræ; quia sc. vera & salutaris Doctrina est forma Ecclesiæ, utpote quæ dat esse illi; & quod usus Sacramentorum maxime legitimus esse possit inter aliquos, qui tamen non sunt Christi Populus; nimirum, si in Aliis Rebus ad Salutem pertinentibus errent, & impie vivant. Disp. de Ecclesia. Sect. 6.
units.tr: This is certainly a splendid argument, one that makes us secure in rightly recognising the true Church of Christ, and that makes us its true members: namely, that the true Church is the one that holds and professes the saving doctrine of Christ, and that this saving doctrine is none other than the Socinian doctrine, which is set out and explained in that Catechism. Schlichting likewise, in his Confession of Faith, after explaining the Apostles' Creed according to Socinus's opinion, adds these words: We believe that the Catholic Church is not varied in doctrine and faith, but is everywhere and at all times, from its beginning made by the Apostles, of one and the same doctrine and faith, namely of that which is comprehended in this Creed, so that whoever holds to it is truly Catholic, but whoever mixes in anything contrary or foreign cannot be Catholic so far. We therefore believe in this holy Catholic Church, because we acknowledge as true and indubitable all those things which Christians devoted to holy morals have always and everywhere professed. Thus he, p. 114. He would be quite right if he had expounded this ancient Creed according to the sense of the ancient Church; but he does it very badly, in that he corrupts and distorts it in many places in order to establish the heresy of Socinus, and thereby makes both the faith and the Church the peculiar property of his own sect. Smalcius finally denies outright that the sincere preaching of the Word and the lawful use of the sacraments are the true marks of the true Church; because the true and saving doctrine is the form of the Church, since it gives it being; and because the most lawful use of the sacraments can exist among some who nevertheless are not the people of Christ, namely, if they err in other matters pertaining to salvation and live impiously. Disp. de Ecclesia, sect. 6.

units.la: §. 72. 10. Ordinationem Cleri, sive Ministrorum Evangelicorum solennem vocationem atque missionem nullo modo necessariam esse volunt; sed unicuique, è contra, liberam relinquunt munia Ecclesiastica exequendi facultatem, qui se idoneum putat, & à populo pro Tali habetur. Ita nempe Socinus. Cuivis Christiano Homini licet, etiam sine speciali ullo sibi legitime demandato ejus rei munere, Charitatem erga Proximum exercere. Hanc autem Charitatem, in quo consistat sic explicat. Cohortari Alios ad viam æternæ Salutis ingrediendam & insistendam, divinaque Oracula, quæ omnibus sunt proposita, illis explicare. Atque insuper, ut hoc fiat publice, perpetuo peculiarique munere. Ad illud, inquit, munus comprobandum, satis superque est, quod illi ipsi ita volunt, qui Cohortationes istas & exhortationes audiunt; & eorum Suffragiis, qui tale munus habet, vel deligitur ad illud, vel approbatur. Atque hoc extendit etiam ad Sacramentorum Administrationem; hac sc. Ratione motus —— Quia quicquid aut virtutis, aut etiam (si ita placet) mutationis Signis istis accedit, vel Sanctitatis in rota Actione inest, id ab Instituto divino prorsus pendet, non autem ulla ex parte ex persona Administrantis; qui ut tali muvere[?] merito fungatur, satis simpliciter, superque est, ut ab iis, quibus, & inter quos ista Sacramenta admi-nistrat, vel ad Illud deligatur, vel in eo confirmetur. Hæc Ille in Brevi Demonst. p. 325. Idem quoque in Tract. De Ecclesia ita disserit.--Verbi Dei Ministris, qui cum Ecclesia Græca aut Romana non consentiunt, controversia non est movenda, neque ab eis contendendum, ut suæ vocationis aut muneris legitimum Authorem offendant; cum non gerant se pro novis quibusdam Christi Apostolis, aut divinis Prophetis; nec inauditam primum[?] Doctrinam, aut Religionem mundo se annunciare profiteantur, neque ex novis Principiis, prius incognitis Testimoniis quicquam doceant, sed tantum ex iis Principiis, iisque Testimoniis, quæ apud omnes Christiani Nominis certissima sunt ex ipsis sc. Evangelistarum, & Apostolorum, Scriptis. Sententiam eandem tuetur Catech. Racov. p. 240, 241.-Qui docent[?] in Ecclesia & ordini tuendo atque conservando invigilant nullo modo opus habent, ut singulari aliqua Ratione mittantur. Etenim illi nunc nullam novam, nec antea inauditam Doctrinam afferunt, sed Apostolicam, ab Omnibus antiquitus exceptam tantum proponunt, inculcant, utque secundum eam Homines vitam instituant, hortantur.
units.tr: §. 72. 10. They want the ordination of the clergy, or the solemn calling and sending of evangelical ministers, to be in no way necessary; on the contrary, they leave to each person the freedom to exercise ecclesiastical functions if he thinks himself fit and is regarded as such by the people. So Socinus: Any Christian man may, even without any special commission lawfully given to him for that task, exercise charity towards his neighbour. He explains what this charity consists in: to exhort others to enter upon and persevere in the way of eternal salvation, and to explain to them the divine oracles, which are set before all. And further, that this be done publicly, as a perpetual and special office. To approve that office, he says, it is quite enough that those very people who hear these exhortations wish it so, and that he who holds such an office is either chosen for it or approved by their votes. He extends this also to the administration of the sacraments, for this reason: Because whatever virtue, or even (if you like) change, belongs to these signs, or whatever holiness is in the action itself, depends entirely on the divine institution and not in any way on the person of the administrator; and for him to discharge such a function rightly, it is quite enough and more than enough that he be chosen for it, or confirmed in it, by those to whom and among whom he administers these sacraments. Thus he, in the Brief Demonstration, p. 325. He also argues the same in his tract On the Church: No controversy is to be stirred up against the ministers of the Word of God who do not agree with the Greek or Roman Church, nor are they to be pressed to show the lawful author of their calling or office; since they do not pose as new apostles of Christ or divine prophets, nor do they profess to announce to the world a doctrine or religion never heard before, nor do they teach anything from new principles or previously unknown testimonies, but only from those principles and those testimonies which are most certain to all who bear the Christian name, namely from the writings of the evangelists and apostles themselves. The Racovian Catechism, pp. 240–241, defends the same view: Those who teach in the Church and keep watch over maintaining and preserving order have no need to be sent in any special manner. For they now bring forward no new doctrine, nor one never heard before, but merely set forth, inculcate, and exhort people to shape their lives according to the apostolic doctrine that has been received by all from antiquity.

units.la: §. 73. 11. De Iustificatione seu Remissione Peccatorum per Christi Meritum, sic tenent. Primo, Quod Patres sub vetere Testamento per Christum, ut Mediatorem, adeoque per Ipsius passionem & mortem, iustificati & salvati non sint, aut per Fidem in Illius Meritum. Quod scribit Frantzius, ait Smalcius, veteres in Jesum venturum credidisse, & ea Fide iustificatos, inter crassos Errores iure recenseri debet. Disp. 4. cont. Frantz. ad Thesin octavam. Hæc quoque ibidem habet.--Justificatio per Fidem nunquam nunquam fuit hominibus proposita ante Christum vel Fœdere inclusa, nec unquam promissum fuit, Hominem fide justificatum iri; sed nude tantum Hominibus Præcepta, pro ratione Temporis diversa, à Deo tradita fuere, quibus obedirent, nulla etiam Promissione aperta primitus addita Justificationis alicujus. Catech. Rac. idem asserit. p. 212. Sine Fide in Christum nemo prorsus justificatur. Verum id de eo Tempore intelligendum est, quo Christus patefactus est. De quo etiam illa Petri verba accipienda sunt, non esse nomen sub Cœlo datum Hominibus, per quod nos servari oporteat, nisi nomen hoc, Jesus. Act. 3. 12. Nam quod attinet ad Tempus, quod antecessit Christi Patefactionem, de eo id affirmari non potest. Etsi enim omnes, qui unquam in Deum crediderunt, ob fidem justificabuntur (ut ex 11. Cap. ad Hebræos aperte colligi potest) nihilominus ea Justificandi Ratio Fœdere per Mosen dato non fuit comprehensa, verum ab ipsa Dei Gratia mere dependet. At nunc ea Justificandi Ratio per Fidem in Christum, in ipso Fœdere continetur. Unde illorum Fides in Christum non includebat, eoque Apostolus ait, fidem venisse per Evangelium. Atque ad eum modum illi non propter Fidem in Dei Filium, sed in ipsum Deum, sunt justificati. Secundo, Quod Homo non prius justificetur, quam se Christi Præceptis obedientem præstiterit, & omnibus virtutibus probe ornatum. Sic etenim Smalcius --Regeneratio, & reliqua bona Opera, Dilectio, Invocatio, Obedientia, Spes, Charitas &c. tantum abest, ut sint effecta Justificationis, ut absque illis Justificatio nullo modo reipsa existere possit. Neminem enim Deus justificat, nisi illis omnibus virtutibus ornatissimum. Offertur quidem Justificatio Homini etiam absque his, sed reipsa Justificatio nostri nulla esse potest, sine his operibus. Disp. 4, cont. Frantz. Socinus quoque hæc habet in eandem Sensum.—Obedientia præceptorum Christi, quæ est executio, & perfectio, & tanquam forma Fidei, coram Deo nos justificat. De Justif. p. 65. Tertio, Quod Satis-factio seu obedientia Christi passiva, nobis minime imputetur. Hanc enim Sententiam Socinus vocat absurdam & impiam, & commentitiam, & quandam à S. literis, ipsoque cum humano, tum Divino sensu penitus abhorrentem, salutis nostræ Rationem. Imo, non veretur hanc censuram de illa ferre, quod adeo fœda & execrabilis sit, ut pestilentiorem errorem, post Homines natos, in Dei populo extitisse non credat. Plura in hunc sensum reperire est apud eum, lib. 4. De Servatore, Smalcius magistro suo suffragatur, cum hanc Doctrinam vocat, Satanæ Imposturam. Quarto, negant satisfactionem Christi per Fidem nobis imputari, id est, applicari seu impertiri. Hæc enim Doctrina, eodem Socino Judice, vel seipsam destruit, vel sententiam perquam absurdam continet. Proinde pro mero Commento habet, Justitiam Christi nobis imputari. Et ibidem ulterius affirmat, Quod per hanc Doctrinam omnis vera Sanctitas convellatur; quodque hæc Persuasio ab hoste verissimo Generis humani Imprudentium animis propterea fuerit ingesta, ad Sanctimoniam vitæ Christianæ prorsus tollendam. De his consulatur idem lib. 4. De Servat. Quinto, Quod Homo, propter Obedientiam, & Justitiam propriam, à Deo Justus pronuncietur. Asserit enim hoc Socinus, cum ait, Justificari à Deo nihil aliud esse, quam à Deo Justum pronunciari. Id quod certe fieri necesse est, cum legis quam dedit, Præcepta servantur, qualiacunque tandem fuerint. De Justif. p. 77. Idem quoque part. 4 de Servat. cap. 4. hæc habet-Cum Fidem Abrahamo pro Justitia, sive ad Justitiam, imputatam suipse[?] legimus, nulla causa est, cur aliena Justitia mantionem fieri suspicemur, cum manifeste de propria agatur, pro, id est, cujus loco; sive ad quam, id est, ad quam nobis adscribendam, exemplo Abrahami, Fides nobis imputetur. Sexto, Quod solus Deus Fidei Causa non fit, cum Homo, vi liberi Arbitrii, verum Fidei Propositum acceptare possit. Sic enim Socinus, de Justific. ——
units.tr: §. 73. 11. Concerning justification, or the remission of sins through the merit of Christ, they hold as follows. First, that the Fathers under the Old Testament were not justified and saved through Christ as Mediator, and so not through his passion and death, nor through faith in his merit. Smalcius says: That the ancients believed that Jesus would come and were justified by that faith, as Frantz writes, must rightly be counted among gross errors. Disp. 4 against Frantz, on his eighth thesis. He also says there: Justification through faith was never set before men before Christ, nor included in a covenant, nor was it ever promised that man would be justified by faith; but only precepts, different according to the times, were given by God to men to obey, with no open promise of any justification being added at first. The Racovian Catechism asserts the same, p. 212: No one is justified at all without faith in Christ. But this must be understood of the time in which Christ was made known. To this time also those words of Peter apply: there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved, except this name, Jesus. Acts 3:12. As for the time that preceded the revelation of Christ, nothing of this kind can be affirmed. For although all who ever believed in God will be justified because of faith (as can be clearly gathered from Hebrews chapter 11), nevertheless that manner of justification was not included in the covenant given through Moses, but depends purely on the grace of God itself. But now that manner of justification through faith in Christ is contained in the covenant itself. Hence their faith did not include faith in Christ, and so the Apostle says that faith came through the Gospel. And in that way they were justified, not because of faith in the Son of God, but in God himself. Second, that a man is not justified before he has shown himself obedient to the precepts of Christ and adorned with all the virtues. Thus Smalcius: Regeneration and the other good works, love, invocation, obedience, hope, charity, and so on, are so far from being effects of justification that without them justification can in no way actually exist. For God justifies no one unless he is most richly adorned with all these virtues. Justification is indeed offered to man even without these, but actual justification of ours cannot exist without these works. Disp. 4 against Frantz. Socinus also has this to the same effect: The obedience to the precepts of Christ, which is the execution and perfection of faith, and as it were its form, justifies us before God. On Justification, p. 65. Third, that the satisfaction, or the passive obedience of Christ, is in no way imputed to us. Socinus calls this opinion absurd, impious, fabricated, and a scheme of salvation utterly alien to the Scriptures and to both human and divine sense. Indeed he does not hesitate to pass this judgement on it, that it is so foul and detestable that he does not believe a more pestilential error has arisen among the people of God since men were born. More to this effect can be found in him, book 4 On the Saviour. Smalcius supports his master, calling this doctrine a fraud of Satan. Fourth, they deny that the satisfaction of Christ is imputed to us through faith, that is, applied or bestowed. For this doctrine, by Socinus's judgement, either destroys itself or contains a most absurd opinion. Therefore he counts it a mere invention that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us. And in the same place he further asserts that through this doctrine all true holiness is overthrown, and that this persuasion was thrust by the most true enemy of the human race into the minds of the unwary, precisely in order to destroy utterly the holiness of Christian life. On these matters consult the same book 4 On the Saviour. Fifth, that man, on account of obedience and his own righteousness, is pronounced just by God. Socinus asserts this when he says: To be justified by God is nothing other than to be pronounced just by God. This must certainly happen whenever the precepts of the law which he gave are kept, whatever they may be. On Justification, p. 77. He also says the same in part 4 of On the Saviour, ch. 4: When we read that faith was imputed to Abraham for righteousness, or unto righteousness, there is no reason for us to suspect any mention of another's righteousness, since it is clearly about his own, "for" (that is, "in place of which"), or "unto which" (that is, unto which faith is imputed to us to be credited to us, after the example of Abraham). Sixth, that God alone is not the cause of faith, since man, by the power of free will, can accept the proposal of faith. Thus Socinus, On Justification: ——

units.la: Quoniam perfuasione ista & Obedientia Fides in Deum continentur, quae S. Litera Hominem coram Deo justificari testantur; jam satis ex Praeditis constare potest, quaenam in ipso Homine hujus Fidei sit causa & Fundamentum; nempe, recta faciendi, & prava vitandi Amor ac Studium. Idem, de Servat. part. 4. cap. 12. Ex his, inquit, Christi verbis (sc. Jo. 3. 19) Hominis probitatem & malitiam, hanc rejectionis, Illam Receptionis Evangelii, causam esse constat. Haec item ibidem habet—Fides Dei donum est, quia nemo, cui Facultas in Christum credendi datur (datur autem generatim Omnibus, quibus Christus annuntiatur) ut ea Facultas sibi daretur, commeritus antea fuerat; non autem quia Quicunque in Christum credit, id ex singulari Spiritus Sancti Dono habuerit, quo caruerint Illi, qui non credunt; adeo ut in potestate eorum, qui non credunt, positum non fuerit, ut crederent. Septimo; Quod verbum Evangelii praedicatum nullo modo conferat Fidem, aut illius effectiva Causa sit, ne quidem per modum Instrumenti. Ita Moscorovius, de Bapt. cont. Smigl. cap. 6. p. 114. ubi affirmat, Praedicationem Evangelii, ut simpliciter modo Fidem conferre; illius opera & ministerio solicitari duntaxat Animum ad credendum; in quo, si modo probus exstitit, ex eadem verbi virtute, Fidem consurgere. At e contra, Scriptura simul & experientia testantur, Probitatem hanc de qua loquitur Moscorovius, us , ( in quamplurimis saltem ) Evangelio prædicato non præsuppono, sed ab illo effici, cum permulti improbi ad verbi auditi sonum converti legantur, Gratia Christi, quæ Prædicationem istam comitata est, corda ipsorum emolliente, ut fertur de Zacchæo, deque tribus Judæorum millibus, qui ad Petri concionem corde compuncti sunt, ob Christi Crucifixionem à se procuratam, Aliisque pluribus in Historia Evangelica memoratis. Scriptura item multoties hanc verbi prædicati virtutem magnifice extollit. Paulus enim diserte asserit, Evangelium Christi à se prædicatum, esse Potentiam Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Rom. 1. 16. Potentiam item sive virtutem Dei, iis qui salvi sunt. 1. Cor. 1. 18. assimilatur malleo Petræ conterenti. Jer. 23. 29. gladio ancipiti, & penetranti. Hebr. 4. 12. Sagittæ electæ, seu politæ. Isa. 49. 2. Nivi & Pluviæ, quæ Terram fecundant. Isa. 55. 10, 11. & seminii fructifero. Luc. 18. 11. Illi quoque attribuitur spiritualis Nativitas, Jac. 1. 18. 1 Pet. 1. 23. vita spiritualis. Jo. 6. 63.Illuminatio spiritualis. Psal. 119. 105. 2 Pet. 1. 19. sanctificatio spiritualis Jo. 17. v. 17. & vita æterna. Jo. 6. 68. & 20. 31. Octavo, Culpam Peccati in Justificatis manere, quando Reatus tollitur; quia sc. in Justificatione Peccata teguntur, & non imputantur. Smalcius, Err. 157. Nono, Quod in Christo confidendum sit (cum sit nudus Homo) non ut in objecto primario nostræ salutis, sed tantum ut in objecto intermedio, seu causa instrumentali. Ita Socinus contra Wiekum. cap. 4. Hæc sunt ipsius verba — Atqui, nec in Christo Homine ita confidendum est nobis, ut in nostra Felicitatis Auctore, id est, sola & prima causa — Nec unquam probabunt Adversarii, alia Ratione, aliamve ob causam, in
units.tr: Since faith in God is comprised in this persuasion together with obedience, which the Holy Scriptures declare to be how a man is justified before God, it can already be sufficiently established from what has been said what the cause and foundation of this faith is in man himself: namely, a love and zeal for doing what is right and avoiding what is wrong. The same author, De Servatore, part 4, chap. 12: "From these words of Christ (namely John 3:19) it is plain," he says, "that the cause of rejecting the gospel is men's wickedness and malice, and of receiving it their uprightness." He likewise says in the same place: "Faith is the gift of God, because no one to whom the ability to believe in Christ is given (and this ability is given generally to all to whom Christ is proclaimed) had merited beforehand that this ability should be given to him; nor is it because whoever believes in Christ has this from a special gift of the Holy Spirit, which those who do not believe lack, so that it was not in the power of those who do not believe to believe." Seventh: that the preached word of the gospel in no way confers faith, nor is it the effective cause of faith, not even by way of an instrument. So Moscorovius, De Baptismo contra Smiglecium, chap. 6, p. 114, where he affirms that the preaching of the gospel does not simply confer faith, but only, by its work and ministry, stirs the mind to believe; and if that mind is upright, faith arises from the same power of the word. On the contrary, Scripture and experience alike testify that this uprightness of which Moscorovius speaks is not presupposed in the preached gospel (at least in very many cases), but is brought about by it, since very many wicked men are read to have been converted at the sound of the word heard, the grace of Christ which accompanied this preaching softening their hearts. So it is reported of Zacchaeus, and of the three thousand Jews who were pricked in heart at Peter's sermon because of Christ's crucifixion, which they had brought about, and of many others recorded in the Gospel history. Scripture also repeatedly extols this power of the preached word magnificently. For Paul plainly asserts that the gospel of Christ preached by him is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, Rom. 1. 16. Likewise the power or virtue of God to those who are saved, 1 Cor. 1. 18, is compared to a hammer breaking a rock, Jer. 23. 29; to a two-edged and piercing sword, Heb. 4. 12; to a chosen or polished arrow, Isa. 49. 2; to rain and snow which make the earth fruitful, Isa. 55. 10, 11; and to fruitful seed, Luc. 18. 11. Spiritual birth is also attributed to it, Jas. 1. 18; 1 Pet. 1. 23; spiritual life, Jo. 6. 63; spiritual illumination, Psal. 119. 105; 2 Pet. 1. 19; spiritual sanctification, Jo. 17. v. 17; and eternal life, Jo. 6. 68 and 20. 31. Eighth, that sin remains in the justified when the guilt is removed, since in justification sins are covered and not imputed. Smalcius, Err. 157. Ninth, that in Christ (since he is a bare man) one must trust not as in the primary object of our salvation, but only as in an intermediate object, or instrumental cause. So Socinus against Wiekius, chap. 4. These are his own words: "But neither is it so necessary for us to trust in Christ the man as in the author of our happiness, that is, the sole and first cause. Nor will the adversaries ever prove that we ought to trust in

units.la: Christo nobis confidendum esse, quam ut in secunda seu instrumentali efficiente Felicitatis nostrae Causa, & ob id, quod ab illo uno Deo, nobis absolute felicitandis; hac conditione, ut illum pro Tali habeamus, prosatus fuit. Resp. ad Argum. 1um. Imo, neque Christi sanguinem seu mortem volunt esse Causam proximam instrumentalem Justificationis ex parte ipsius; sicut nec fidem ex parte nostri, sed utramque duntaxat causam sine qua non istius effectus; qua sc. confirmavit promissa ista Divina, quae Patris nomine annunciavit, Foedusque, inter Deum & nos confirmavit; ut salutem nostram perfecit, inquit, per Divinam istam Potestatem, quam, morte ipsius interveniente, consecutus est: vid. Socini Miscell. non longe ab Initio. Et part. 3. de servat. cap. 9. Smalc. item de error. Arian. cap: 9. p. 76. At è contra, licet S. Scriptura Christum non statuat solam Justificationis nostrae Causam, aut absolute primam, statuit tamen eum Justificationis nostrae Auctorem, à quo dependeremus, & in quo Fiduciam salutis consequendae collocaremus; seu, ut verbo dicam, non ut causam Instrumentalem proprie sic dictam, sed potius ut causam primariam, à qua caeterae omnes inferiores dependent; ut & Actus, atque effectus ipsius. Siquidem dicitur causa Fidei. Pax, & Charitas, cum fide, optantur à Christo, aeque ac à Deo Patre; ut Ephesiis donentur. Eph. 6. 23. & passim in principiis Epistolarum, Gratia & Pax optantur, in salutatione Fidelium, à Deo Patre, & Domino nostro Jesu Christo. Idem dicitur ἀρχηγὸς[?] καὶ τελειωτὴς[?] Auctor; simul & consummator Fidei nostrae. Heb. 12. 2. Αἴτιος[?], seu causa aeternae salutis, cunctis qui ipsi obsequuntur. Ib. cap. 5. 9. sicut per sanguinem ipsius justificati fuimus, sic multo magis, postquam fuimus reconciliati, salvabimur per vitam ipsius, id est, per ipsum in Cælis nunc viventem. Rom: 5. 9, 10. Creditis in Deum, & in me credite, ait Ipse ad Apostolos. Jo: 14. 1. Hinc dicitur sol Justitiæ[?]. Mal. 4. 2. oriens ex Alto. Luc. 1. 78. Lux vera, quæ illuminat omnem Hominem venientem in hunc Mundum. Jo. 1. 9. Rex Justitiæ. Heb. 7. 2. Justitia nostra. Jer: 23. 6. Justificati sumus, ut & sanctificati, per illius nomen. 1 Cor. 6. 11. Nullumque aliud nomen sub Cœlo datum est inter Homines, per quod oportet nos salvari; neque salus est in aliquo Alio. Act: 4. 12. Comparatur demum cum Adamo, qui fuit principalis causa introducti peccati, ut & Condemnationis atque mortis inde consequentis; unde sequitur, ipsum esse æque principalem causam justificationis ac salutis nostræ, quæ consistit in Remissione istius Peccati, Abolitione mortis, & collatione vitæ æternæ. Alioquin, Antitypus Typo non responderet; neque Remedium morbo æquipolleret. Collationem vero hanc ab Apostolo diligenter & accurate institutam habemus; tum Rom: 5. 12. 21. tum, 1 Cor: 15. 21, 22; & v. 45. 49.
units.tr: Christ for any other reason or on any other ground than that he is the secondary or instrumental efficient cause of our happiness, and for this reason, that he was sent by that one God, who alone is to make us happy, on this condition, that we regard him as such." Reply to the first argument. Indeed, they do not hold that the blood or death of Christ is the proximate instrumental cause of justification on his side, any more than faith is on ours; they hold only that each is a cause without which the effect does not come about. By his death he confirmed these divine promises, which he announced in the Father's name, and confirmed the covenant between God and us, "so that he accomplished our salvation," he says, "through this divine power which he obtained by his intervening death." See Socinus, Miscellanea, not far from the beginning; and part 3 of De Servatore, chap. 9. Also Smalcius, De errore Arianorum, chap. 9, p. 76. On the contrary, although Holy Scripture does not set up Christ as the sole cause of our justification, or absolutely the first, it does set him up as the author of our justification, on whom we depend and in whom we place our trust for obtaining salvation. To put it briefly, he is not the instrumental cause properly so called, but rather the primary cause on which all the inferior causes depend, as also its acts and effects. For he is called the cause of faith. Peace and love, along with faith, are wished for by Christ just as much as by God the Father, that they may be given to the Ephesians, Eph. 6. 23; and throughout the openings of the epistles grace and peace are wished to the faithful from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. The same is called the author [ἀρχηγὸς] and perfecter [τελειωτὴς] of our faith, Heb. 12. 2; and the cause [αἴτιος] of eternal salvation to all who obey him, Heb. 5. 9. "Since we have been justified by his blood, much more, now that we have been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life, that is, by him now living in heaven," Rom. 5. 9, 10. "Believe in God, and believe in me," he himself says to the apostles, Jo. 14. 1. Hence he is called the sun of righteousness, Mal. 4. 2; rising from on high, Luc. 1. 78; the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world, Jo. 1. 9; the king of righteousness, Heb. 7. 2; our righteousness, Jer. 23. 6. We were justified, as well as sanctified, through his name, 1 Cor. 6. 11. And there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved, nor is there salvation in any other, Act. 4. 12. Lastly, he is compared with Adam, who was the principal cause of the sin introduced, and of the condemnation and death following from it. Whence it follows that he is equally the principal cause of our justification and salvation, which consists in the remission of that sin, the abolition of death, and the bestowal of eternal life. Otherwise the antitype would not correspond to the type, nor the remedy equal the disease. This comparison the Apostle has set out carefully and accurately: Rom. 5. 12, 21; 1 Cor. 15. 21, 22; and vv. 45, 49.

units.la: Decimo; Quod credere, nostra Peccata deleta fuisse, per ea quæ Christus passus est, non sit ista Fides, qua justificamur; imo nullo modo esse possit. Ita Socinus, part: 4. de Servat: cap: 9. in ipso Titulo istius Capitis. At S. Scriptura ex adverso passim affirmat, Christum Passione sua [illegible, ~6 letters], id est, Pretium Redemptionis, solvisse pro nostris omnium Peccatis; quod si nobis vera, vivaque fide applicemus, tunc demum Peccata nostra actu deleri. Illud pertinet ad satisfactionem; Hoc, ad satisfactionis Acceptationem. Illud, ad salutis Acquisitionem spectat; Hoc, ad ejusdem Applicationem. Unde sequitur, eam esse veram & salvificam Fidem, quæ meritum Christi, cum omnibus Beneficiis exinde pendentibus, rite apprehendit & applicat. Undecimo ; Quòd natura Fidei justificantis non consistat in Apprehensione Christi, & Applicatione meriti ipsius. Hoc enim Socinus pro humano Commento, & Somnio inanissimo habet—Amen, inquit, dicunt isti (id est, Evangelici) Fidem istam, non quidem propria Dignitate, sed quia ipsum Christum apprehendit, justificare? —At hæc vestra Christi Apprehensio, meritum humanum Commentum, & inanis-simum Somnium est. Sic ille, part. 4. de Servat: cap. 11. Smalcius item asserit, Plane insolens & exoticum quiddam esse, in meritum Christi Fidem requiri At certe S. Scriptura describit Fidem salvificam sub notione accipiendi Christum, & ea quæ per Christum consequimur, sc. Reconciliationem, Gratiam, & Justitiam, Misericordi-am, & promissum Spiritus Sancti. Quotquot receperunt eum, dedit illis potestatem Filios Dei fieri, His, qui credunt in nomen ejus. Jo: 1. 12. Gloriamur in Deo, per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum per quem Reconciliationem accepimus. Rom: 5. 11. Christus nos redemit à maledictione legis—ut Benedictio illa Abrahæ ad Gentes perveniret in Christo Jesu, ut promissum acciperemus per Fidem. Gal: 3. 13, 14. Sicut accepistis Jesum Christum Do-minum, in ipso ambulate. Col: 2. 6. Non habemus pontificem, qui non potest affici sensu Infirmitatum nostrarum, tentatum autem per omnia similiter, absque tamen peccato. Accedamus ergo cum Fiducia ad Thronum Gratiæ, ut misericordiam consequamur [seu accipiamus λάβωμεν [?]] & Gratiam inveniamus, in Auxilium tempestivum. Hebr: 4. 15, 16. Idem Apostolus de Fide Abrahæ differens, qua Promissum Dei juramento firmatum firmiter amplexus est, hortatur nos, ad imitationem hujusce Patris Fidelium, ut validam consolationem habeamus, utpote qui confugimus [κρατῆσαι?] ad apprehendendam ipsam [Nobis] propositam. Ib: cap. 6. 18: ipsam sc. vitæ æternæ in Cœlis, ab illo Jesu nobis comparatam, qui Præcursoris nostri instar illuc ingressus est, factus secundum ordinem Melchisedech Pontifex in æternum; ut postea se explicat. v. 19, 20. monetur item Timotheus, ut Divitibus hujus sæculi denunciaret, ipsam in Deo vivo ponere. ἵνα ἐπιλάβωνται, ut apprehendant vitam illam æternam. 1 Tim. 6. 17, 19. Denique, Deus, per Isaiam Prophetam, sese amplissimis Benedictionibus prosecuturum ístos Alienigenas atque Eunuchos pollicetur, qui apprehenderint Fœdus suum, Isa: 56. 4, 6. nimirum per Fidem in Promissis inibi contentis, & Obedientiam Præceptis adhibitam, ex ista Fide procedentem. Ex quibus satis patet, Fidem justificantem non male describi, cum dicitur consistere in prædicta Apprehensione, & Applicatione. Quid enim est, Christo confidere, & in illo salutis nostræ fiduciam ponere, quam ejusdem Meritum apprehendere, & nobis ipsis applicare? Duodecimo; Quod credere, & non credere dependeant ex probitate, vel malitia Hominum, quibus Christus annunciatur. Ita Socinus--Ex probitate Hominis fit, ut Evangelio Fides adhibeatur & rursus--Imprudentia (sc. non Credentium) malitia causa est & origo; non sensus atque Animi Probitas Fidei causa est & Origo, quam Evangelio alii adjungunt. De Servat: part 4. cap. 12.. At è contra, Scriptura passim attribuit Fidem salvificam (cum remissione Peccatorum & salute æterna exinde consequentibus, non præviis Hominum operibus aut Meritis, aut Probitati innatæ, sed meræ Dei Misericordiæ, & gratuito Ipsius dono. Gratia salvi facti estis per Fidem; & hoc non ex vobis, Dei Donum est; non ex Operibus, ne quis glorietur; inquit Apostolus. Eph. 2. 8, 6. Vobis ἐχαρίσθη[?], gratuito datum est pro Christo, non solum ut in eum credatis, sed ut etiam pro illo patiamini. Phil: 1. 29. Conclusit Scriptura omnia sub Peccato, ut promissio ex fide Jesu Christi daretur Credentibus. Gal: 3. 22. Non ex operibus Justitiæ, quæ fecimus nos, sed secundum Misericordiam suam salvos nos fecit, per lavacrum Regenerationis, & Renovationis Spiritus Sancti; Quem effudit in nos abunde per Jesum Christum salvatorem nostrum; ut justificati Gratia Ipsius, Hæredes simus secundum spem vitæ æternæ. Tit: 3. 5, 6, 7. Præcellimus? nullo modo. Nam Ratione reddita antea ostendimus, Judæos simul omnes & Græcos esse sub peccato: sicut scriptum est, non est justus, ne unus quidem. Scimus autem, quæcunque lex dicit, iis, qui in lege sunt, dicere, ut omne os obstruatur, & totus mundus fiat obnoxius Condemnationi Dei, Rom: 3. 9, 10; 19. Omnes enim peccaverunt, ac deficiuntur Gloria Dei; justificati gratis ipsius Gratia, per Redemptionem quæ est in Christo Jesu. Ib: v. 23, 24. & postea idem Apostolus differens de Abrahamo, dicit enim gratuito justificatum fuisse, non ex bonis operibus quibusdam præcedentibus, vel ex probitate aliqua aut connata, aut morali, per frequentes sc. virtutis Actiones acquisita, & in Habitum adaucta; sed ex mera Dei Gratia, & misericordia, quæ justificat, non operantem, sed credentem in eum qui justificat Impium, & cui fides sua reputatur ad justitiam. Sicut & David dicit Beatificationem illius Hominis cui Deus imputat justitiam sine operibus; Beati, quorum remissæ sunt Iniquitates, & quorum obtecta sunt Peccata. Beatus Vir, cui non imputat Dominus Peccatum. Cap. 4. 1,8. & Cap. sequenti -Si unius lapsu multi mortui sunt, multo magis Gratia Dei, & Donum per Gratiam, quæ est unius illius Hominis Jesu Christi in multos redundavit. v. 15. qui redundantiam illius Gratiæ, & Doni justitiæ accipiunt, in vita regnabunt, per unum Jesum Christum. v. 17. ubi abundavit peccatum, superabundavit Gratia; ut sicut Peccatum regnavit in mortem, ita & Gratia regnaret per justitiam, in vitam æternam, per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum. v. 20, 21. & cap. 6, 23. Stipendia peccati, mors; Donum autem gratuitum, seu Donativum Dei, vita æterna, per Christum Jesum Dominum nostrum. Ex his aliisque S.Scripturæ locis,quæ huc adduci poterant,plus satis apparet, quam gratuita Res sit Fides, cum condonatione peccatorum, & vita sempiterna, quæ Fidem præsupponunt, & ex ea, quantum ad nos, dependent. Siqui autem sunt, vel fuerint, quorum Probitas Animi, Christi notitiam, & Evangelii annunciationem prævenit, Fideque salvificæ viam parat, neque Indoli Naturæ, neque morum probitati nativis viribus acquisitæ deberi censenda est, sed prævenienti Dei Gratiæ, per quam ab eo edocti, & tracti sunt, ut ad Christum veniant, inque ipsum credant; ut ipse Christus loquitur. Jo: 6. 44, 45. [illegible, ~7 letters], apti seu idonei ad Regnum Dei. Luc. 9. ult: τεταγμένοι, parati seu dispositi ad vitam æternam. Act: 13. 48. Decimo tertio; Quod Homo infidelis, & non renatus, bona opera præstare possit. Ita Smalcius -Certum est, etiam Hominem non renatum posse; Natura & Ratione Duce, Bona Opera praestare, licet non ita perfecte, quemadmodum Is qui renatus est; nec ita perfecta, nec Deo etiam ita accepta, quemadmodum ea sunt, qua quis Christi amore facit. Sic ille, cont: Frantz: Disp: 1. De Bonis Operibus. At e contra, licet non prorsus incommode dici possit, Bona opera praestari posse ab Homine infideli, & non renato, in Genere loquendo, & respectu effectuum, qui ad alios inde devenerunt; haud tamen, proprie loquendo, hoc affirmari potest de istius modi operibus, cum destituta sint, requisitis ad opus bonum necessariis, quale sc. Deo acceptum sit, & efficax ad Felicitatem aeternam comparandam. Similidem & bono efficiente, & bono subjecto, & bono Fine destitutum sit; cum neque à Gratia Dei, sive Spiritu Sancto producantur; neque ex Homine per Fidem reconciliato, & regenito procedant; neque in Dei Gloriam tendant. Nemini enim ignotum est, quomodo celeberrimi Gentilium Philosophi, & eorum Discipuli, sibi ipsis tribuerint quicquid eximium, vel in ipsis esset, vel ab ipsis perfectum, nimirum virtutes, virtutumque Opera quomodo item suam ipsorum famam, & Gloriam, nominisque celebritatem apud Posteros, in omnibus quaesiverint; vel ad summum, Patriae suae, eorumque salutem, atque Commodum in hoc seculo; quomodo demum, eo usque abfuerint à Reconciliatione per Fidem, Regeneratione per Spiritum, & supernaturali Dei Gratia, cujus ope virtutum Habitus ad summum usque Gradum perducere possent, & egregia Opera perficere; ut Reconciliationis hujusce & Regenerationis Mysteria, vel palam abnegaverint, vel omnino ignoraverint; Fidem Christianam irriserint; suisque viribus nativis, atque Industriae summae, omnia se debere professi sint, quibus supra vulgus eminebant; imo interdum eo usque elati fuerint, ut se Diis non tantum aquaverint, sed & praetulerint; quia nempe Dii natura [?]Eoni fuerunt, ipsi autem ex instituto, & industria, e spontanea voluntatis in adversa mutabilis electione, constantique liberi Arbitrii, inter tot tantasque Tentationes, quae ad malum assidue solicitarunt, Proposito.
units.tr: Tenthly: That to believe that our sins were blotted out through what Christ suffered is not that faith by which we are justified; indeed, it cannot in any way be so. Thus Socinus, part 4 of De Servatore, ch. 9, in the very title of that chapter. But Holy Scripture, on the contrary, affirms everywhere that Christ, by his Passion [illegible, ~6 letters], that is, the price of redemption, paid for the sins of all of us; and that only when we apply this to ourselves by a true and living faith are our sins actually blotted out. The former pertains to satisfaction; the latter to the acceptance of satisfaction. The former concerns the acquisition of salvation; the latter its application. Hence it follows that that is the true and saving faith which rightly grasps and applies the merit of Christ, together with all the benefits depending on it. Eleventhly; That the nature of justifying faith does not consist in the apprehension of Christ and the application of his merit. For Socinus holds this to be a human invention and a most empty dream: "Do they," he says, "(that is, the Evangelicals) say that this faith justifies, not by its own worth, but because it apprehends Christ himself?" "But this apprehension of Christ by you is a human invention and a most empty dream." Thus he, part 4 of De Servatore, ch. 11. Smalcius likewise asserts that "it is a quite strange and foreign thing to require faith in the merit of Christ." But Holy Scripture certainly describes saving faith under the notion of receiving Christ, and of receiving what we obtain through Christ: namely reconciliation, grace, and righteousness, mercy, and the promise of the Holy Spirit. "As many as received him, to them he gave power to become the sons of God, to those who believe in his name." John 1:12. "We glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have received reconciliation." Rom. 5:11. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law... that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise through faith." Gal. 3:13, 14. "As you have received Jesus Christ the Lord, walk in him." Col. 2:6. "We have not a high priest who cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy [or receive it, λάβωμεν [?]] and find grace to help in time of need." Heb. 4:15, 16. The same Apostol, discussing the faith of Abraham, by which he firmly embraced the promise of God confirmed by an oath, exhorts us to imitate this father of believers, so that we may have a strong comfort, as those who have fled [κρατῆσαι?] to lay hold of the hope set before us. Ib. ch. 6:18; namely of eternal life in heaven, procured for us by that Jesus who, as our forerunner, entered there, made a high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec, as he afterwards explains, vv. 19, 20. Timothy is likewise urged to charge the rich of this age to set their hope on the living God, "that they may lay hold" [ἵνα ἐπιλάβωνται] of that eternal life. 1 Tim. 6:17, 19. Finally, God, through the prophet Isaiah, promises to bestow the greatest blessings on those foreigners and eunuchs who lay hold of his covenant, Isa. 56:4, 6, namely through faith in the promises contained there, and obedience applied to the precepts, proceeding from that faith. From these passages it is sufficiently plain that justifying faith is not badly described when it is said to consist in the aforesaid apprehension and application. For what is it to trust in Christ and to place the hope of our salvation in him, if not to apprehend his merit and apply it to ourselves? Twelfthly; That to believe and not to believe depend on the goodness or the malice of the men to whom Christ is announced. Thus Socinus: "It comes from the goodness of a man that faith is given to the Gospel," and again: "The cause and origin is the imprudence (that is, of those who do not believe) and malice; it is not the sense and probity of mind that is the cause and origin of faith, which others add to the Gospel." De Servatore, part 4, ch. 12. But on the contrary, Scripture everywhere ascribes saving faith (together with the forgiveness of sins and the eternal salvation that follows from it) not to any prior works or merits of men, or to innate probity, but to the sheer mercy of God and his free gift. "By grace you are saved through faith; and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God; not of works, lest anyone should boast," says the Apostle. Eph. 2:8, 9. "To you it has been freely given [ἐχαρίσθη?] for Christ's sake, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for him." Phil. 1:29. "Scripture has concluded all things under sin, that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe." Gal. 3:22. "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour, that being justified by his grace we might be heirs according to the hope of eternal life." Titus 3:5, 6, 7. Do we excel? In no way. For, having given the reason, we showed earlier that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin: as it is written, there is none righteous, no, not one. Now we know that whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world become liable to the condemnation of God. Rom. 3:9, 10, 19. "For all have sinned and come short of the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." Ib. vv. 23, 24. Then the same Apostol, discussing Abraham, says that he was justified freely, not from certain good works going before, or from some probity either innate or moral, acquired through frequent acts of virtue and increased into a habit; but from the mere grace and mercy of God, which justifies not the one who works but the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, and whose faith is reckoned to him for righteousness. So also David speaks of the blessedness of the man to whom God imputes righteousness without works: "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin." Rom. 4:1, 8. And in the following chapter: "If through the fall of one many died, much more the grace of God and the gift by the grace of that one man, Jesus Christ, abounded unto many." v. 15. "Those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life through one, Jesus Christ." v. 17. "Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound; so that as sin reigned unto death, even so grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." vv. 20, 21. And ch. 6:23: "The wages of sin is death; but the free gift of God is eternal life through Christ Jesus our Lord." From these and other passages of Holy Scripture, which could be cited here, it appears more than enough how free a thing faith is, together with the forgiveness of sins and everlasting life, which presuppose faith and depend upon it, so far as we are concerned. But if there are, or have been, any whose probity of mind anticipates the knowledge of Christ and the announcement of the Gospel, and prepares the way to saving faith, this is to be reckoned due neither to the disposition of nature nor to moral probity acquired by native powers, but to the prevenient grace of God, by which they are taught and drawn by him so that they come to Christ and believe in him, as Christ himself speaks. John 6:44, 45. [illegible, ~7 letters], fit or suitable for the kingdom of God. Luke 9, last verse. [τεταγμένοι], prepared or disposed for eternal life. Acts 13:48. Thirteenthly; That an unbelieving man, not born again, can perform good works. Thus Smalcius: "It is certain that even a man not born again can, by nature and with reason as his guide, perform good works, though not so perfectly as one who has been born again; nor are they so perfect, nor so acceptable to God, as those things which a man does out of love for Christ." Thus he, against Frantz, Disp. 1, On Good Works. But on the contrary, although it may not be altogether unfitting to say that good works can be performed by an unbelieving man who is not born again, speaking generally and with respect to the effects that have come from them to others, yet this cannot properly be affirmed of such works, since they lack what is necessary for a good work, such as would be acceptable to God and effective for obtaining eternal happiness. Likewise they are lacking in a good efficient cause, a good subject, and a good end; since they are not produced by the grace of God or the Holy Spirit, nor do they proceed from a man reconciled through faith and regenerated, nor do they tend to the glory of God. For it is known to no one how the most celebrated philosophers of the Gentiles and their disciples ascribed to themselves whatever was excellent in them or perfected by them, namely their virtues and the works of virtue; how likewise they sought in everything their own fame and glory, and the renown of their name among posterity; or at most the welfare, safety, and advantage of their country in this age; how, finally, they were so far removed from reconciliation through faith, regeneration through the Spirit, and supernatural grace of God, by whose help they could have brought the habits of virtue to their highest degree and performed outstanding works, that they either openly denied or wholly ignored the mysteries of this reconciliation and regeneration; mocked the Christian faith; and professed that they owed everything to their native powers and their highest industry, by which they rose above the common people. Indeed, at times they were so lifted up that they not only made themselves equal to the gods but even preferred themselves to them, because, namely, the gods were of nature eternal, but they by design and industry, by a free choice of a changeable will turned towards the bad, and a constant free arbitrament, amid so many and so great temptations which assiduously urged them to evil, had made their purpose.

units.la: §. 74. De Sacramentis in Genere affirmant, tum usum eorum maxime legitimum esse posse inter Aliquos, qui non sunt Christi Populus; ut antea e Smalcio ostendimus: tum fabulosum esse, ut affirmemus, Sacramenta esse Canales quosdam, per quos Divinitatis virtutes ad nos, & in nos diffamant. Sic enim Smalcius Cont: Frantz: Disp: 9. p. 422. & multo arrogantius in Exam: 100. errorum, ubi hanc Propositionem diserte verbis statuit: Per Sacramenta Gratiam Hominibus conferri, tantum non Blasphemia est. Err. 9. At e contra, nihil evidentius est, tum in S. Scriptura, tum in Doctrina atque Praxi veteris Ecclesiae, quam quod Christus Sacramenta, quae sunt Evangelici Foederis sigilla, Ecclesiae suae propria esse voluerit, quodque eadem ipsi insuper donaverit, ut salutis media per Spiritus sui Gratiam efficacia, quoties ex Illius Praescripto administrantur, atque suscipiuntur.
units.tr: §. 74. Concerning the sacraments in general, they affirm both that their most lawful use can be among certain people who are not Christ's people, as we showed earlier from Smalcius; and that it is a fable to say that the sacraments are certain channels through which the powers of the Deity flow to us and into us. Smalcius says so in Cont. Frantz. Disp. 9, p. 422, and, much more arrogantly, in the Examen of 100 errors, where he states this proposition in plain words: "That grace is conferred on men through the sacraments is hardly short of blasphemy." Err. 9. On the contrary, nothing is clearer, both in Holy Scripture and in the doctrine and practice of the ancient Church, than that Christ wished the sacraments, which are the seals of the Gospel covenant, to belong to his own Church, and that he further bestowed on them the power to be means of salvation, effective through the grace of his Spirit, whenever they are administered and received according to his appointment.

units.la: §. 75. De Baptismo haec habent, Primo, Doctrinam de Baptismo non esse Articulum Fidei fundamentalem, sive necessarium; sed Talem, sine quo Pietas Christiana consistere potest, & circa quem unusquisque potest in suo sensu abundare. Hoc enim est quod Socinus in se probandum suscipit. Disp: de Bapt: cap: 17. Smalcius item affirmat, Ipsissimam Falsitatem esse, Christum ad Sacramenta usurpanda, Homines sub sub amissione vitæ æternæ obligasse, Cœna Domini excepta. Atque hoc extendit, non solum ad quinque Sacramenta à Pontificiis superaddi solita, sed & ad ipsum Baptismum. Exam. 100. errorum. Err. 94. At è contra, si Evangelium consulamus, necessitas Baptismi æque urgetur, ac Eucharistiæ à Fidelibus participandæ; imo, ut videtur, verbis paulo disertioribus. Qui crediderit, & Baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit; inquit ipse Christus. Marc. 16. 16. Atque iterum, in suo Responso ad Nicodemum -- Amen, Amen, dico Tibi, nisi quis renatus sive genitus suerit ex Aqua & Spiritu Sancto, non poterit introire in Regnum Dei. Jo: 3. 5. Baptismo item alibi attribuuntur ablutio sive remissio Peccatorum, & stipulatio bonæ Conscientiæ sine quibus ad salutem æternam non pervenitur. Baptizare, & ablue Peccata tua, inquit Ananias ad Paulum. Act: 22. 16. & Petrus ad Judæos --Baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomine Jesu Christi, in remissionem Peccatorum. Ibi c. 2. 38. Atque alibi nos salvos facit Baptismus, non depositio sordium Carnis, sed stipulatio bonæ Conscientiæ apud Deum. 1 Pet: 3. 21. Quem & adeo necessarium putavit, ut in illos etiam conferri debere judicaverit, qui extraordinaria Spiritus Sancti dona prius acceperant. Sic enim ille de Cornelio, ipsiusque cognatis & Amicis, in quos Spiritus Sanctus ceciderat, dum illius Sermoni auscultabant --- Nunquid, ait, Aquam quis prohibere poterit, ut non Baptizentur Hi, qui Spiritum Sanctum acceperunt, sicut & nos? Et jussit eos Baptizari in nomine Domini. Act: 10. 47, 48.
units.tr: §. 75. On baptism they hold the following. First, that the doctrine of baptism is not a fundamental or necessary article of faith, but one without which Christian piety can stand, and on which each person may hold whatever opinion he likes. Socinus undertakes to prove this very thing in himself, Disp. de Bapt. cap. 17. Smalcius likewise asserts that it is the sheerest falsehood that Christ bound men, under pain of losing eternal life, to the use of the sacraments, except the Lord's Supper; and he extends this not only to the five sacraments that the Papists are accustomed to add, but also to baptism itself. Examen of 100 errors, Err. 94. On the contrary, if we consult the Gospel, the necessity of baptism is urged just as strongly as that of believers partaking of the Eucharist; indeed, it seems to be stated in rather plainer words. "He who believes and is baptized will be saved," says Christ himself. Mark 16:16. And again, in his reply to Nicodemus: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless anyone is born again, or born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God." John 3:5. Elsewhere, too, baptism is ascribed the washing away or remission of sins and the pledge of a good conscience, without which eternal salvation is not attained. Ananias says to Paul: "Be baptized, and wash away your sins." Acts 22:16. And Peter to the Jews: "Let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins." Ibid. 2:38. And elsewhere: "Baptism now saves us, not the removal of the filth of the flesh, but the pledge of a good conscience before God." 1 Pet. 3:21. He thought it so necessary that he judged it must be given even to those who had already received the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit. For so he speaks of Cornelius and his relatives and friends, on whom the Holy Spirit had fallen while they were listening to his sermon: "Can anyone," he says, "forbid water, so that these who have received the Holy Spirit, just as we have, should not be baptized?" And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of the Lord. Acts 10:47, 48.

units.la: Paulus quoque dicit, nos per Baptismum induere Christum, & Filios Dei fieri Gal. 3. 26, 26. & per Eundem, commortuos esse, & consepeliri cum Christo;sive complantatos esse in similitudinem mortis ejus, ut Resurrectionis ejusdem Participes reddamur. Ic[?]:Rom.6. 3,4,5. Alibi quoque Baptismum appellat Regenerationis lavacrum. Tit. 3. 5. Haec autem sin-gula requiruntur ad salutem, ac proinde necessitatem Baptismi demonstrant, ut medii divinitus ordinati ad ea comparanda. Secundo; Mandatum Christi, quod Apostolis suis dedit, de cunctis Gentibus baptizandis Matt. 28. 19. non esse intelligendum de Baptismo aque sed de Doctrina Evangelii publicanda, sive initiandis Discipulis per Rudimentorum Fidei Christianae Traditionem. Vid. Soc: disp: de Bapt: cap:2. Tertio; Quod Salutem nostram quaerere in ritu Baptismi, qui initio N. Testamenti usurpatum est, sit imitari Israelitas, qui ex aeneo serpente antiquitus usurpato feceriunt]Idolum; quodque nobis temere persuasimus eo quod Christi Tempore legamus Homines Baptizatos fuisse, idem a nobis etiam requiri, cum tamen Baptismus ille ad nostra Tempora nihil magis pertineat, nec saniori a nobis imitatione usurpetur, quam si quis Arcam Noa, Jugum Jeremiae, aut Regis Joasi Sagittas, sine certo Dei Jussu & mandato, imitari & redintegrare volit. Ita Somoierus[?], Tract: de Bapt: Quarto, Baptismum Aquae a Christo non fuisse praescriptum, sed libere tantum ab Apostolis assumptum. Ita Socinus arguit. Disp. de Bapt: cap. 16. Quinto, Baptismum Aquae Ritum temporarium fuisse, non perpetuum adeoque ad Posteros non pertinere —Praeceptum ablutionis externa, ait Socinus (a Petro datum. Act. 2. 38.) non erat perpetuum, sed ad Tempus datum. Sic Ille, Ib. cap 5. p. 53, &c. Sexto; Baptismum Aquae non requiri ad Christianum Hominem, sive efficiendum, sive etiam declarandum. Soc. lb. cap. 16. Arg 1. Imo neque requisitum tum fuisse in evo Apostolico: Paulo post enim affirmat, Tempore Pauli, quosdam esse non Baptizatos, & tamen vera Ecclesia membra fuisse. Ib. Arg. 3. Septimo; nos in, & per Baptismum, Adoptivos Dei Filios non fieri. Imo Smalcius omnino negat Adoptionem nostram. Homines, inquit, proprie loquendo, non sunt adoptivi Dei Filii. Exam: 157. Errorum. Err. 90. Cujus Assertionis rationem sic alibi reddere conatur, — Fideles & in hoc seculo, ex Deo nati esse dicuntur, & olim Deo atque Christo similes futuri sunt natura. Adoptivus autem proprie sic dictus, nec ex eo natus esse, à quo est adoptatus, nec similis Ipsi natura, dici potest. Ergo, non sunt proprie adoptivi Dei Filii. Sic ille Resp: ad nova Monst: part: 2. cap: 20. p. 165. Quasi adoptati ab Hominibus non sint natura similes Adoptantibus; aut quasi nos, proprie loquendo, vel nunc simus, vel olim futuri simus essentiæ divinæ participes, atque hac ratione Deo Christoque unigenito Ipsius Filio, natura similes. Octavo; Baptismum Aquæ non esse necessarium ad salutem. Soc: de Bapt: cap: 4. p. 45. &c: unde illa Christi verba ad Nicodemum. Jo: 3. 5. non vult intelligi de Sacramento Baptismi, sed vel de ablutione à sordibus Peccatorum, vel de ipsa Pœnitentia, per quam à Peccatis abluimur; vel ea referri vult ad Cognitionem Rerum divinarum; ut à Multis inquit, fit, & fieri debere videtur, nullo vero modo ad Baptismum. Sic enim arguit: Ex eo solo satis constat, hic de Aqua terrena Baptismo Sermonem non esse, quod alioqui Neminem in Dei Regnum ingressurum esse sequeretur; nisi eo Baptismo foret initiatus. At è contra, Veteres tam ex Græca, quam ex Latina Ecclesia, hæc verba de Baptismo Aquæ communiter interpretantur, hujusque Sacramenti necessitatem inde concludunt; non quidem, quod absolute in Dei Potestate non sit, Aliquem sine Hoc salvare (neque enim suam ipsius Misericordiam intra certos limites coercuit, quando libertatem nostram lege sua restrinxit) sed quia hoc Sacramentum instituit ut medium quoddam aeternae salutis comparandae; sive ut januam quandam, per quam Hominibus Aditus patet in Regnum Dei; perque eam solam, si Dei Institutum spectemus, quod Ecclesiae lux dedit: sive per Regnum Dei intelligamus Ecclesiam in hisce Terris militantem, sive illam in Coelis triumphantem. Nono; Baptismum nihil aliud revera esse quam Christi nominis publicam & solennem quandam Professionem. Sic etenim Socinus, dum explicat illa Christi verba, Marc. 16. v. 15, 16. Dico, inquit, in verbis illis [& Baptizatus fuerit] Baptismi nomine comprehendi, vel veram Poenitentiam, vel Christi nominis publicam Prosessionem, vel utramque simul recte intelligi posse. Ib: cap. 3. Quibus haec consona sunt. Cap. 5. ad finem — Cum is Baptismus nihil Aliud sit, quam publica & aperta Jesu Christi nominis Professio, sive ejus Professionis Symbolum. Catechismus Racoviensis pariter Baptismus est Ritus exterior, quo Homines vel a Judaismo, vel e Gentilismo, ad Religionem Christianam accedentes, manifeste profitebantur, se Christum pro suo Domino agnoscere. c. 4. p. 151. Decimo; Baptismum administrari posse in nomine alicujus, qui nec sit vere & natura Deus nec Persona. Nam apud eos Filius Dei est nudus Homo; & Spiritus Sanctus non est Persona, sed Res, nempe virtus seu efficacia Dei Patris. At e contra, cum Baptismus administretur in salutem Baptizati; & Remissionem peccatorum; in Dei solius nomine administrandus est, qui solus Author est istius salutis, & Remissionis Peccatorum. Per hunc Baptismum item conlecramur Deo, & in Illius Fidem atque Religionem initiamur. Est quoque Pars Cultus Deo debiti, fatente ipso Ostorodo inst: cap: 39. §. 4. p. 354. Dicitur item Stipulatio bonae Conscientiae apud Deum. 1, Pet: 3. 21. Denique, solus Deus vim & efficaciam huic Baptismi Ritui conferre valet, sc: in peccatis tollendis, & Regeneratione efficienda; ut de Spiritu nalcatur Spiritualis qui prius fuit Caro de carne natus, uti legimus. Jo: 3. 6. Unde est, quod Paulus à se, tanquam Rem soli Deo propriam removeat hoc, ut aliquis in suiipsius nomen baptizetur. 1 Cor: 1. 13, 15. Quantum vero ad Spiritum Sanctum; modus loquendi neutiquam fert, ut in nomine Rerum varum, quae Personae non sunt, quicquam dicamur facere. Cum item à Christo dicitur, Baptizate εἰς ὄνομα[?], in nomen Patris & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti, notatur Author, sive Institutor, ad cujus mandatum Hoc fieri debet; praecipitur formula, ne Actio ista sit muta; invocatur ille, cui hic effectus debetur; atque editur Confessio, qua persona Baptizata in Deum credere profitetur. Quae omnia soli Personae, non Rei competunt. Praeterea, Baptismus est Caerimonia foederalis, per quam Homo in Foedus cum Deo recipitur; non autem Res nuda, sed persona sola, in cujus nomen Baptizamur, dici proprie poterit, nos secum in Foedus admittere. Denique, in Idiomata sive Attributa Divina Baptismum administrari, nimis absurdum est. Quis enim diceret, Homines Baptizandos esse in nomen Justitiae, Sapientiae, aut Bonitatis & Misericordiae Divinae? Idcirco, nec in Spiritum Sanctum oportuit Baptizare, si modo nuda Dei virtus esset, sive Potentia. Itaque cum Ecclesia Catholica statuamus, Spiritum Sanctum; in Cujus nomen baptizamur, esse personam; sicut in Confesso est apud Omnes, ipsosque etiam Socinianos, Deum Patrem & Filium, esse personas. Undecimo, negant efficaciam Baptismi; & speciatim, istiusmodi effectus ei derogant, quos Catholica Christi Ecclesia Baptismo, rite administrato atque suscepto, semper attribuit; viz: Regenerationem, Remissionem peccatorum, salutem aeternam, & jus ad omnia Christianorum privilegia. Fabula sunt, inquit Smalcius, aliquam internum efficaciam esse in Baptismo. cont: Frantz: disp: 9. p. 289. Et Pisecius asserit —Baptismus non esse unidam[?] salutis, non Causalem Gratiae, non merita Christi in nos derivari; sed Ritum & Ceremoniam esse, per quam Judaei & Gentes se Religione devincirebant, esse Dogma veritati Divinae consonum. Sic ille, Resp: ad 8. Rac. Cam. pag. 95. Smalcius item cont. Frantzium, de Bapt. p. 311. haec affirmat — Aquam Baptismi esse Organum seu Instrumentum Spiritus Sancti, quo in ipso Actu Baptismi Regenerationem operatur, non tantum fa'sum; sed aliquid Idololatricum, omnino condemnandum esse. Idemque alibi, paucis verbis, at rotunde asserit. Per Baptismum Aquae Homines non regenerari; sc. Err. 139. & Catech: Rac: Fallantur vehementer, qui putant se Ritu Baptismi regenerari. p. 152. Contra efficaciam Baptismi ad remissionem peccatorum disserit etiam Socinus. Disp: de Bapt: cap. 7. p. 80. Moscorovius item, de Baptismo. Idemque Socinus negat Baptismum esse medium ordinarium adsciscendi nos in Societatem Ecclesiae, quod est Corpus Christi mysticum, vel induendi Christum, vel ad delenda peccata necessario requisitum, sed hoc respectu tantum quia cum illo conjungitur publica Christi nominis professio, quæ sola sufficit ad hæc Beneficia àDeo consequenda. Sic enim Ille--Non nego quin in Baptismo Aqua, post Christi Resurrectionem institutò, Aliquid sit quod ad Peccatorum remissionem aliquo modo pertineat. Est enim in Ipso, (cum in Jesu Christi nomine ministretur publica & aperta Jesu Christi nominis Professio, quæ nullo pacto omitti debet; Alioquin à Peccatorum reatu liberatio non contingeret. Verum professio ista externa isti Ablutioni non est adeo alligata, ut etiam alio modo fieri non queat; quemcunque sc: vel Ecclesia pro Temporum & locorum ratione elegerit, vel Res ipsa per se necessario tulerit. Itaque si contingat, Aliquem, citra illam ablutionem, publice & aperte Christi Jesu Nomen professum fuisse, & pro eo, qui Ipsi nomen dederit, passim habitum fuisse. quacunque tandem ratione id fieri contigerit, iste omne id habebit, quod in Aqua Baptismo continetur, ad Peccatorum deletionem pertinens nec ullo modo, ut peccata sibi remittantur, aqua prætera ablui necesse habebit. lb:[?]cap:7.p.80 &c. Idem cap.8.dicit,non per Aqua sed perSpiritu Sancti Baptismum,Christianos in unum Corpus coalescere. Quasi Christi Baptismus non comprehendat in se Aquam simul &spiritum,sine quibus una conjunctis consistere nequit, aut compleri. Idem, cap:18. Falsum est inquit, per Aqua Baptismum Christum induí. Et postea-- Non concedendum est, Aqua Baptismum esse ordinariam quandam viam Christum induendi cum nihil per eum Baptismum vel à Deo Hominibus conferatur, vel quavis ratione ipsis accedat, nisi quod per Ipsum Christo publice nomen dant, & ejus familiæ quodammodo adscribuntur. Cum vero Apostolus, ad Hebræos, scribens nos adChristum accedere vnlt[?](Sacerdotem illum magnum super Domum Dei,qui per sanguinem suum nobis Aditum patefecit in Sanctum Sanctorum) storum) cum vero Corde & certa persuasione Fidei. Ad hoc requirens non solum, ut alpersi[?] cordibus purgati simus à Conscientia mala, sed & corpore abluti simus Aqua munda, ut hoc pacto teneamus confessionem Spei minimè vacillantem. quæ verba Antiqui uno consensu, ut & Recentiorum doctissimi, de Baptismo interpretantur, in quo Confessio ista publicè edi solita est; Moscorovius[?] consensum hunc Interpretum, veterum præsertim, scommate excipere aquum putat Prodeant Patres, ait, qui per Aquam mundam (Heb: 10. 22.) Aquam Baptismatis intelligunt, &c. si Rationibus evidentibus instructi fuerint, manus dabimus sibi minus, Idem, quod primi Patres senserunt, faciendum putabimus, nihil esse sine Testimonio Divino, aut evidente Ratione admittendum. Sic ille. De Bapt.: cont. Smigl. cap. 5. p. 103. Quasi hoc Divinum Apostoli Testimonium non sponte ducat nos in hunc sensum, nisi literam sine causa, & contra loci Circumstantias, transferre jubeat in Allegoriam; quasi Patres hunc sensum à primis Fidei Christianæ Magistris non acceperint; quasi hic sensus non optime congruat cum aliis S. Scripturæ locis; aut quasi evidens alia Ratio, vel adducta fuerit à Moscorovio vel adduci possit, quæ sensum adversum aut alienum admittere cogat. Prodeat ergo, si possit, vel Alius quisquam alieni sensus Inventor, istumque Ratione evidenti, aut etiam Divino Testimonio confirmet, manusque dabimus. Duodecimo; Prædobaptismum vel acriter oppugnant, vel saltem negligentui habent, ut Ritum in se nullius, aut exigui admodum momenti, & qui omitti potius deberet, quam administrari. Oppugnatur à [illegible, ~1 letter]erveto, Czechovicio, Smalcio, ministris Transylvanis, & à Moscorovio in Catech. Rac. ubi hæc habet — Infantes ad Ritum Baptismi nullo modo pertinent. Nam nec in Scripturis illum mandatum aut exemplum ea de Re habemus, neque ipsi, ut Res ipsa indicat, Christum pro suo Servatore agnoscere per ætatem possunt. pag. 151, neque hoc sane mirum est, cum alibi, neque voluntatem Dei de nobis servandis, neque Christi Redemptionem in Divinis Literis contestatam, ad Infantes pertinere velit. De Bapt: cont. Smigl. cap. 7. p. 119. Smalcius autem negat, Infantes vel Sanctitatis capaces esse, vel per Baptismum regenerari. Imo, hanc Assertionem Idololatricum quendam sapere dicit. Exam. 157. errorum. Err. 111, 140. Socinus demum, licet paulo moderatior in hac Re videatur, ut unicuique liberum esse velit, Infantes suos Baptizare, ob difficultatem vitandam, & ne plerique omnes (qui adhuc Baptismum aquæ a nemine negligi debere sentiunt) ad Ecclesiam (Sectæ suæ intelligit) aggregari recusarent: Alibi tamen affirmat, Infantes non esse Partem Ecclesiæ. Ad notas Mart. Czechovicii, in lib. de Bapt. Except. 102. Idemque in altero libro, sc. Quod Reg. Pol. Homines &c. errorem vocat, putare Infantium Baptismum esse Divinam Ordinationem, aut certe Rem Divinæ Ordinationi consentaneam. Cap. 4. Err. 6. At è contra, mos Infantes Baptizandi adeo universim, atque adeo antiquus, ab ipsis usque Apostolorum Temporibus, in Ecclesia Christi prævaluit, ut ne Pelagiani quidem, qui negarunt originale aliquod peccatum Infantibus adhærere, ullatenus ausi fuerint huic morî obniti, sed una cum cæteris, Pædobaptismum & approbarunt, & usurparunt; idque juxta formulam Ecclesiæ, in remissionem peccatorum. Quod nunquam fecissent, nisi illum in Scriptura fundarum judicassent, fideique Christianæ apprime consonum, quam tamen in aliis quibusdam lacessere haud verebantur. Decimo, tertio; Idem Socinus negat, vel remissionem peccatorum obsignari nobis in Baptismo, vel Fidem confirmari, vel Spiritus Sancti Gratiam omnibus illum rite suscipientibus conferri. Sic enim ille, lib. Quod Regn: Polon: &c. Alius est error Evangelicorum, cum affirmant Baptismo Divinitus obsignari Peccatorum remissionem; Id quod Cœna Dominica quoque tribuunt; & quemadmodum per Domini Cœnam, sic per Baptismum Adultorum, qui Baptizantur, Fidem confirmari credunt; cum tamen per Baptismum non obsignetur quidem, sed tantum adumbretur Peccatorum remissio. Cap. 4. Err. 6. & paulo post —— Dari hodie Spiritum Sanctum omnibus, qui Baptismum quantumvis rite susceperint, nemo temere affirmare ausus fuerit qui &c. Hoc modo Socinus, illiusque Socii ac Discipuli vilipendunt atque depravant Baptismum, licet ab ipso Christo primitus institutum, & ab ipsius Apostolis constanter usurpatum, ut Ritum solennem quo Deo consecramur, in Ecclesiam Christi admittimur, & ad salutem æternam comparandam habiles reddimur. Unde Ecclesia Catholica jam olim nos jussit credere unum Baptismum in Remissionem peccatorum.
