Atque insuper asseruit, hoc Sacramentum esse medium à Deo institutum, quo omnibus Christianismi Privilegiis initiamur; utpote per quod regeneramur, in Filios adoptamur, membra Christi, Cœlique Hæredes efficimur.
units.tr: Paul also says that by baptism we put on Christ and become sons of God (Gal. 3. 26, 27), and that through it we are buried together with Christ and planted together in the likeness of his death, so that we may be made partakers of his resurrection (Rom. 6. 3, 4, 5). Elsewhere he calls baptism "the washing of regeneration" (Tit. 3. 5). All these things are required for salvation, and so they show the necessity of baptism as a means divinely appointed to obtain them. Second, the command of Christ to his apostles to baptize all nations (Matt. 28. 19) is not to be understood of the baptism of water but of the publishing of the gospel, or of initiating disciples by handing on the rudiments of the Christian faith. See Socinus, De Baptismo, ch. 2. Third, to seek our salvation in the rite of baptism, which was adopted at the beginning of the New Testament, is to imitate the Israelites, who made an idol of the bronze serpent that had been used of old. And because we have rashly persuaded ourselves, since we read that people were baptized in Christ's time, that the same is required of us, although that baptism has nothing more to do with our times, and it is no wiser for us to imitate it than if someone wished to imitate and renew Noah's ark, Jeremiah's yoke, or King Joash's arrows, without a certain command and mandate of God. So Somoierus, in his treatise on baptism. Fourth, water baptism was not prescribed by Christ but only freely adopted by the apostles. So Socinus argues, De Baptismo, ch. 16. Fifth, water baptism was a temporary rite, not a perpetual one, and so does not pertain to posterity. The precept of external washing, says Socinus (given by Peter, Acts 2. 38), was not perpetual but was given for a time. So he, ibid., ch. 5, p. 53, etc. Sixth, water baptism is not required for a man to become a Christian, or even to be declared one. Socinus, ibid., ch. 16, arg. 1. Indeed, it was not even required in the apostolic age, for Paul afterwards affirms that in Paul's time there were some who were not baptized, and yet they were true members of the Church. Ibid., arg. 3. Seventh, we do not become adopted sons of God in and through baptism. Indeed Smalcius flatly denies our adoption: Men, properly speaking, are not adopted sons of God. Examen of errors, 157, err. 90. He tries to give the reason for this assertion elsewhere in this way: Believers are said to be born of God even in this age, and they will one day be like God and Christ in nature. But one who is adopted, properly so called, can be said neither to be born of him by whom he is adopted, nor to be like him in nature. Therefore, they are not properly adopted sons of God. So he, Responsio ad nova monstra, part 2, ch. 20, p. 165. As if those adopted by men were not like their adopters in nature; or as if we, properly speaking, either now are, or will one day be, partakers of the divine essence, and on this ground like God and his only-begotten Son in nature. Eighth, water baptism is not necessary for salvation. Socinus, De Baptismo, ch. 4, p. 45, etc. Hence he wishes those words of Christ to Nicodemus (John 3. 5) not to be understood of the sacrament of baptism, but either of the washing away of the filth of sins, or of repentance itself, through which we are washed from sins; or he wishes them to be referred to the knowledge of divine things, as, he says, many do and ought to do, but in no way to baptism. For he argues thus: From this alone it is quite clear that the discourse here is not about the baptism of earthly water, since otherwise it would follow that no one would enter the kingdom of God unless he had been initiated by that baptism. On the contrary, the ancients, both of the Greek and of the Latin Church, commonly interpret these words of the baptism of water, and from them they conclude the necessity of this sacrament. Not indeed because it is not absolutely in God's power to save anyone without it (for he has not confined his own mercy within fixed limits, when he restrained our liberty by his law), but because he instituted this sacrament as a certain means of obtaining eternal salvation, or as a door through which access into the kingdom of God lies open to men, and through it alone, if we look to God's institution, as the light of the Church has given us to understand; whether we understand by the kingdom of God the Church militant on this earth or the Church triumphant in heaven. Ninth, baptism is in reality nothing other than a public and solemn profession of the name of Christ. For Socinus, explaining those words of Christ (Mark 16. 15, 16), says: I say that in those words [and he who is baptized] the name of baptism is understood either as true repentance, or as the public profession of the name of Christ, or both together may rightly be understood. Ibid., ch. 3. Things consonant with this are found in ch. 5, near the end: Since that baptism is nothing other than the public and open profession of the name of Jesus Christ, or the creed of that profession. The Racovian Catechism likewise says: Baptism is an external rite by which men, coming to the Christian religion from Judaism or from paganism, openly profess that they acknowledge Christ as their Lord. Ch. 4, p. 151. Tenth, baptism can be administered in the name of one who is neither truly and by nature God nor a person. For among them the Son of God is a mere man, and the Holy Spirit is not a person but a thing, namely the power or efficacy of God the Father. On the contrary, since baptism is administered for the salvation of the one baptized and for the remission of sins, it must be administered in the name of him alone who is the sole author of that salvation and remission of sins. Through this baptism we are likewise consecrated to God and initiated into his faith and religion. It is also a part of the worship owed to God, as Ostorodt himself admits (Institutio, ch. 39, §4, p. 354). It is also called the pledge of a good conscience before God (1 Pet. 3. 21). Finally, only God is able to confer power and efficacy on this rite of baptism, namely in taking away sins and effecting regeneration, so that what is born of the Spirit is spirit, having been first flesh born of flesh, as we read (John 3. 6). Hence it is that Paul removes himself, as one who is a matter proper to God alone, from this, that anyone should be baptized in his own name (1 Cor. 1. 13, 15). As for the Holy Spirit, the manner of speaking by no means allows us to say that we do anything in the name of things which are not persons. Likewise, when Christ says, Baptize [into the name, εἰς ὄνομα] of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, he marks the author or institutor, at whose command this must be done; the formula is prescribed so that the action may not be mute; he is invoked to whom this effect is owed; and a confession is made by which the person baptized professes to believe in God. All these things belong to a person alone, not to a thing. Moreover, baptism is a covenant ceremony by which a man is received into covenant with God; but a bare thing, not a person alone, could not properly be said to admit us into covenant with it, in whose name we are baptized. Finally, it is far too absurd to administer baptism in the divine attributes or properties. For who would say that men are to be baptized in the name of the justice, wisdom, or goodness and mercy of God? Therefore, nor ought one to baptize in the Holy Spirit if he were merely the power or might of God. Accordingly, since the Catholic Church holds that the Holy Spirit, in whose name we are baptized, is a person, as is agreed by all, and even by the Socinians themselves, who hold that God the Father and the Son are persons. Eleventh, they deny the efficacy of baptism, and in particular they take away from it those effects which the Catholic Church of Christ has always attributed to baptism rightly administered and received: namely regeneration, remission of sins, eternal salvation, and a right to all the privileges of Christians. They are fables, says Smalcius, that there is any internal efficacy in baptism. Against Frantz, disp. 9, p. 289. And Pisecki asserts that baptism is not the cause of salvation, nor is it the cause of grace, nor are the merits of Christ derived to us by it; it is a rite and ceremony by which Jews and Gentiles bound themselves to a religion, and a dogma consonant with divine truth. So he, Responsio ad 8 Racoviensis Catechismi, p. 95. Smalcius likewise, against Frantz, on baptism, p. 311, affirms this: that the water of baptism is an organ or instrument of the Holy Spirit by which he works regeneration in the very act of baptism is not only false but something idolatrous, altogether to be condemned. And elsewhere he asserts the same thing briefly but bluntly: men are not regenerated through water baptism, Err. 139; and the Racovian Catechism: They are gravely mistaken who think that they are regenerated by the rite of baptism, p. 152. Socinus too argues against the efficacy of baptism for the remission of sins, De Baptismo, ch. 7, p. 80; and Moscorovius likewise, on baptism. Socinus also denies that baptism is the ordinary means of admitting us into fellowship with the Church, which is the mystical body of Christ, or of putting on Christ, or that it is required for the blotting out of sins; but he says this only with respect to the fact that the public profession of the name of Christ is joined with it, and that profession alone is sufficient to obtain these benefits from God. For he says: I do not deny that in water baptism, instituted after Christ's resurrection, there is something which pertains in some way to the remission of sins. For in it (since it is administered in the name of Jesus Christ) there is a public and open profession of the name of Jesus Christ, which must by no means be omitted; otherwise deliverance from the guilt of sins would not come about. But this external profession is not so bound to that washing that it cannot be done in some other way, whatever the Church has chosen according to the circumstances of times and places, or whatever the thing itself of necessity brings with it. And so, if it should happen that someone has publicly and openly professed the name of Jesus Christ without that washing, and has been generally regarded as one who has given his name to him, by whatever means this has happened, he will have all that is contained in the water of baptism that pertains to the blotting out of sins, and he will not need to be washed with water in order that his sins be remitted. Ibid., ch. 7, p. 80, etc. The same, ch. 8, says that Christians are joined into one body not by water but by the Spirit of God. As if the baptism of Christ did not comprehend in itself water and Spirit together, without which it cannot stand or be completed. The same, ch. 18: It is false, he says, that we put on Christ through water baptism. And afterwards: It must not be conceded that water baptism is some ordinary way of putting on Christ, since through that baptism nothing is conferred by God on men, nor does anything come to them in any way, except that through it they give their names publicly to Christ and are in some sense enrolled in his family. But when the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, wishes us to draw near to Christ (that great priest over the house of God, who by his blood opened for us the way into the holy of holies) with a true heart and certain persuasion of faith, requiring of us not only that our hearts be cleansed from an evil conscience, but also that our bodies be washed with pure water, so that in this way we may hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering (Heb. 10. 22), the ancients with one voice, and the most learned of the more recent writers, interpret these words of baptism, in which that confession is customarily made publicly. Moscorovius thinks it fair to mock this agreement of interpreters, especially the ancient ones: Let the Fathers come forward, he says, who understand by "pure water" (Heb. 10. 22) the water of baptism, etc. If they are furnished with evident reasons, we shall give them our hand; we shall think that we should do what the first Fathers thought, since nothing is to be admitted without divine testimony or evident reason. So he, De Baptismo, against Smiglecki, ch. 5, p. 103. As if this divine testimony of the Apostle did not of its own accord lead us to this sense, unless it bade us, without cause and against the circumstances of the passage, turn the letter into an allegory; as if the Fathers had not received this sense from the first teachers of the Christian faith; as if this sense did not agree very well with other passages of Holy Scripture; or as if some other evident reason had been brought forward by Moscorovius, or could be brought forward, that would compel us to admit a contrary or alien sense. Let there then come forward, if he can, some other inventor of an alien sense, and let him confirm it by evident reason or even by divine testimony, and we shall give him our hand. Twelfth, they either fiercely attack infant baptism or at least treat it with neglect, as a rite of no importance or very little, and one that ought rather to be omitted than administered. It is attacked by Ferwet (the name is illegible in the scan), Czechowic, Smalcius, the ministers of Transylvania, and by Moscorovius in the Racovian Catechism, where he has this: Infants do not belong at all to the rite of baptism. For we have neither command nor example of it in the Scriptures, nor can they, as the thing itself shows, acknowledge Christ as their Saviour by reason of their age, p. 151. Nor is this surprising, since elsewhere he will have it that the will of God concerning our salvation, and the redemption of Christ attested in the divine writings, do not pertain to infants, On baptism, against Smiglecki, ch. 7, p. 119. Smalcius, however, denies that infants are capable either of holiness or of being regenerated through baptism. Indeed, he says that this assertion savours somewhat of idolatry. Examen of errors, 157; errors 111, 140. Socinus at last, although he seems somewhat more moderate on this point, wishes it to be free for each person to baptize his own infants, in order to avoid difficulty, and lest almost all (who still hold that water baptism must not be neglected by anyone) should refuse to be joined to the Church (he means the Church of his sect). Yet elsewhere he affirms that infants are not part of the Church. Notes on Martin Czechowic, in his book on baptism, exception 102. And in the other book, namely What the Polish Kingdom, etc., he calls it an error to think that infant baptism is a divine ordinance, or at least something consonant with a divine ordinance. Ch. 4, err. 6. On the contrary, the custom of baptizing infants, so universal and so ancient, prevailed in the Church of Christ from the very times of the apostles, so that not even the Pelagians, who denied that any original sin clings to infants, dared in any way to resist this custom; rather, together with the others, they both approved and practised infant baptism, and did so according to the formula of the Church, for the remission of sins. They would never have done this unless they had judged it to be founded in Scripture and most consonant with the Christian faith, though they did not hesitate to attack it in certain other matters. Tenth, thirteenth: the same Socinus denies that the remission of sins is sealed to us in baptism, or that faith is confirmed, or that the grace of the Holy Spirit is conferred on all who receive it rightly. For thus he says, in the book What the Polish Kingdom, etc.: It is another error of the Evangelicals when they affirm that the remission of sins is divinely sealed in baptism; which they also attribute to the Lord's Supper; and they believe that, just as through the Lord's Supper, so through the baptism of adults who are baptized faith is confirmed; whereas through baptism the remission of sins is not indeed sealed, but only foreshadowed. Ch. 4, err. 6. And a little later: No one would rashly dare to affirm that the Holy Spirit is given today to all who have received baptism, however rightly. In this way Socinus, and his companions and disciples, despise and corrupt baptism, although it was first instituted by Christ himself and was constantly used by his apostles, as the solemn rite by which we are consecrated to God, admitted into the Church of Christ, and made fit to obtain eternal salvation. Whence the Catholic Church long ago bade us believe in one baptism for the remission of sins. And moreover it has asserted that this sacrament is a means instituted by God by which we are initiated into all the privileges of Christianity; for through it we are regenerated, adopted as sons, made members of Christ, and made heirs of heaven.

units.la: §. 76. Quod vero[?] ad alterum Sacramentum, viz. Eucharistiam sive Cœnam Dominicam attinet, hæc docetur. Primo: Smalcius hoc modo exponit[?] verba Christi quando illud[?] primo instituit, scilicet: Hoc est Corpus meum. Id est, inquit ille, hæc Actio frangendi & comededdi[?] Panem, est Commemoratio Christi Corporis pro nobis fracti; sicut Vinum quoque dicitur Sanguis Christi, id est, Repræsentatio effusionis Sanguinis pro nobis post futuræ. Secundo; illa Pauli verba, Panis est Communio Corporis Christi, & Calix est Communio sanguinis Christi; sc. 1 Cor. 10, 16. i-dem Smalcius interpretatur, non de reali aliquam Participatione; sed de professione sola Communionis cum Christo, in participatione Corporis & Sanguinis ipsius, hoc est, eorum omnium, quorum causa Christus mortuus est. Disp. 11. de Cœna. Catechismus item Racoviensis ad eundem modum hæc Apostoli verba accipienda esse vult. Quod sc. ii omnes, qui Calicem hunc benedicunt, id est, eo usu, sancte nomen Domini celebrant; similiter, qui Panem communiter frangunt; aperte testatum faciunt, quod participes sint Corporis & Sanguinis Domini, id est, omnium bonorum, quæ Christus nobis per mortem suam peperit. p. 149.
units.tr: §. 76. As for the other sacrament, namely the Eucharist or the Lord's Supper, the following is taught. First: Smalcius explains the words of Christ when he first instituted it, namely, This is my body. That is, he says, this action of breaking and eating bread is a commemoration of Christ's body broken for us, just as the wine too is called the blood of Christ, that is, a representation of the blood to be poured out for us in the future. Second: Smalcius interprets in the same way those words of Paul, "The bread is the communion of the body of Christ, and the cup is the communion of the blood of Christ" (1 Cor. 10.16). He takes them not of any real participation but only of a profession of communion with Christ, in sharing his body and blood, that is, in all those for whose sake Christ died. Disp. 11 on the Supper. The Racovian Catechism likewise wants these words of the Apostle understood in this way: that all who bless this cup, that is, who by that use celebrate the holy name of the Lord, and likewise those who break the bread in common, openly show that they are partakers of the body and blood of the Lord, that is, of all the good things which Christ won for us by his death. p. 149.

units.la: Tertio; Negant Eucharistiam Sacramenti nomine insigniendam esse, aut aliquid in nobis efficere. Sic enim Smalcius Disput. 12. de Cœna. Thes. 106. vox Sacramenti in hac significatione, barbara, vel saltem S. literis incognita est; ab Hominibus vero otiosis, qui hujusmodi Cæremoniis nescio quid præter S. Scripturam, superstitiosum, aut etiam Idololatricum ex parte, tribuere non sunt veriti, ad tegendum[?] Dolum est usurpata.—Nobis in Cœna Nihil conferri, sed nos esse qui per eam Gratias Deo egimus, ipsissima est Evangelii & purissima veritas. Item.—Dum Christum in ea Actione Corpus suum & Sanguinem nobiscum communicare dicitur, nomine occasio esset Doctrinam hanc, ut anilem, absurdam, & perniciosam exagitandi; & dicendi, ipsos etiam pueros jam intelligere, quantopere delirent, & tantum non insaniant, qui in manducatione panis, & bibitione vini quærunt Christi Corpus & Sanguinem? Similiter Catechismus Racov: Sunt, qui in Cœna Domini, se autumant Corporis & Sanguinis Domini vere participes existere, Spiritualiter tamen, Quæ opinio cum cateris, est fallax & erronea. p. 146. Quarto; Negant hoc Sacramentum ad nostram aliquam utilitatem in salutis negotio pertinere, aut Beneficium aliquod nobis in eo exhiberi. Sic enim Socinus, lib: Quod Regn: Pol: &c: Haud animadvertunt, non ut Aliquid nobis divinitus detur, sed ut nos testificemur Illa, quæ nobis jam data esse agnoscimus, & sentimus; non proprie ad nostram aliquam singularem utilitatem in ipso æterna salutis negotio, sed ad Christi & Dei Gloriam, Summa atque ineffabilis ejus in nos Bonitate & Charitate prædicanda & celebranda, illustrandam atque amplificandam, sacram ceremoniam istam omnino pertinere. Cap: 4. Err: 5. Moicorovius item — Panis Eucharisticus usu tantum ab alio pane secretus est; & ejus usus nihil Aliud est, quam ejus Beneficii Christi, quod carnem suam dederit pro Mundi vita Attmunciato; & eidem pro eodem Beneficio, ac Deo Patri Ipsius Gratiarum Actio. Sic ille, De Bapt: cont: Smigl: cap: 5. p. 98. Smalcius pariter, Disp: 11. de Cœna. Idem hoc Argumento probare contendit, Quia posito eo, quod Finis Cœnæ sit Gratiarum Actio, Alii Fines necessario tollantur — Quemadmodum enim Judæi, inquit, cum Agnum Paschalem comederent, non Beneficium aliquod recens accipiebant, sed pro olim accepto Gratias agebant, & illud commemorabant; sic & Christiani, qui mortem Christi commemorant, & pro ea Gratias agunt, non præsens Beneficium requirunt, sed antiquum memoria repetentes, Illud laudibus extollunt, & religioso, gratissimoque Animo Animo revolvunt, etiam Catech. Racov. — Cum is Finis Cœnæ Domini usurpanda sit, ut pro Beneficiis acceptis Christo Gratias agamus, apparet non eo institutam esse, ut aliquid illic sumamus. p. 154. & postea — Pugnant inter se, reipsa Christi Corporis esse Participem, & illius spiritualiter esse Participem. & Opinionem istam nullo modo certam esse ipsi produnt, cum fatentur modum hunc sumendi Corporis Christi, esse prorsus inexplicabilem; aut qui id fiat, se plane ignorare. p. 148. Quasi multa non occurrant, non solum in Fidei mysteriis, quorum Ratio inexplicabilis sit; sed & in Rebus naturæ, quorum de causis, modoque operandi non tantum incerti simus, sed & plane ignari. Verumtamen, satis nobis constat, tum de iis Fidei Mysteriis, ex Divina Authoritate; tum de effectibus iis naturalibus, ex sensuum nostrorum Testimonio, eoque frequentibus experimentis confirmato. Quinto; negant idem confirmari & augeri in usu hujus Sacramenti. Ita enim Socinus. — Quomodo Christi pro se mortui celebrare memoriam quis poterit, nisi jam sentiat & gustet fructum ipsius Christi mortis? Hunc vero sensum & Gustum habere qua Ratione is poterit, qui firma Fide in ipsum Christum jam non sit præditus? Sic ille. lib. Quod Regn. Pol. cap. 4. Err. 5. ubi & hæc habet — Firma jam Fide cum præditum esse oportet, & Christi pro nobis mortui probe meminisse, qui ad Panem illum comedendum & Calicem illum bibendum digne accedere velit. Est enim sacra hæc Cæremonia in eum Finem à Christo instituta, ut solennis Commemoratio ipsius fiat, quæ erat viz. Corpus suum pro nobis tradidit, & Sanguinem fudit. Smalcius magistro suo suffragatur. — Quomodo tandem verum erit, inquit, Fidem confirmari & augeri per usum Cœnæ Domini, cum fieri posset, ut aliqui s [?]
units.tr: Third: They deny that the Eucharist is to be marked with the name of sacrament, or that it effects anything in us. For so Smalcius, Disp. 12 on the Supper, Thes. 106: the word "sacrament" in this sense is barbarous, or at least unknown to the Holy Scriptures, and was used by idle men, who did not hesitate to attribute to such ceremonies something beyond Scripture, superstitious, or even partly idolatrous, in order to conceal a trick. That nothing is conferred on us in the Supper, but that we are the ones who by it give thanks to God, is the very truth of the Gospel and its purest truth. Likewise: "Since it is said that in that action Christ communicates his body and blood with us, what an occasion this would be for attacking this doctrine as old-womanish, absurd and pernicious, and for saying that even boys now understand how greatly those are deluded, and hardly out of their minds, who seek the body and blood of Christ in eating bread and drinking wine!" Similarly the Racovian Catechism: "There are those who think that in the Lord's Supper they really become partakers of the body and blood of the Lord, but spiritually; this opinion, like the others, is false and erroneous." p. 146. Fourth; they deny that this sacrament pertains to any benefit of ours in the business of salvation, or that any benefit is exhibited to us in it. For so Socinus, in the book Quod Regn. Pol. etc.: "They do not notice that this sacred ceremony pertains wholly not to something being given to us by God, but to our testifying to those things which we acknowledge and feel have already been given to us; not properly to any particular advantage of ours in the very business of eternal salvation, but to the glory of Christ and of God, to be proclaimed and celebrated, illustrated and magnified, for his supreme and ineffable goodness and charity toward us." Chapter 4, Error 5. Moscorovius likewise: "The Eucharistic bread is set apart from other bread only by its use, and its use is nothing other than the thanksgiving to God the Father, for the same benefit, that Christ gave his flesh for the life of the world." Thus he, De Bapt. contra Smiglecius, chap. 5, p. 98. Smalcius equally, Disp. 11 on the Supper. He labours to prove the same by this argument: since it is granted that the end of the Supper is thanksgiving, the other ends are necessarily removed. "For just as the Jews, he says, when they ate the Paschal lamb, did not receive any new benefit but gave thanks for what they had received long before, and recalled it; so too Christians, who remember the death of Christ and give thanks for it, do not seek a present benefit, but, recalling the old one by memory, they extol it with praises and turn it over in a religious and most grateful mind." Also the Racovian Catechism: "Since this is the end for which the Lord's Supper is to be used, namely that we give thanks to Christ for the benefits received, it is clear that it was not instituted so that we should take something there." p. 154. And afterwards: "They are at odds with themselves, since they really are partakers of Christ's body, and spiritually partakers of him; and they themselves show that this opinion is in no way certain, since they confess that this mode of receiving the body of Christ is wholly inexplicable, or that they plainly do not know how it happens." p. 148. As if many things do not occur, not only in the mysteries of faith, whose reason is inexplicable, but also in the things of nature, whose causes and mode of operation we not only are uncertain of, but plainly ignorant of. Nevertheless, it is sufficiently established for us, both concerning those mysteries of faith on the authority of God, and concerning those natural effects on the testimony of our senses, confirmed by frequent experiments. Fifth; they deny that the same is confirmed and increased by the use of this sacrament. For so Socinus: "How can anyone celebrate the memory of Christ, who died for him, unless he already feels and tastes the fruit of Christ's own death? But how can he have this feeling and taste who is not already endowed with firm faith in Christ himself?" Thus he, in the book Quod Regn. Pol., chap. 4, Error 5, where he also has this: "One who wishes to approach worthily to eat that bread and drink that cup must already be endowed with firm faith and rightly remember Christ who died for us. For this sacred ceremony was instituted by Christ for this end, that a solemn commemoration of him be made, that is, of how he handed over his body for us and poured out his blood." Smalcius supports his master: "How, finally, will it be true, he says, that faith is confirmed and increased through the use of the Lord's Supper, since it could happen that some are already most firmly established in faith before they approach the Lord's Supper, as are the Apostles and others like them, who were endowed with the Holy Spirit..."

units.la: [The last word on the page is cut at the foot; the catchword "fit" follows below the last line.] sic in Fide confirmatissimus, antequam ad Coenam Domini accedat; ut de Apostolis, & aliis eorum similibus, qui Spiritu Sancto praediti fuerunt, & sunt, dico potest ac debet? Celebratio autem Coenae Dominicae ad omnes in universum spectat. Adde, inquit, quod omnia, quae nos in Fide confirmare debent, extra Nos posita esse oporteat, nec alium ope nostrum iterum, quo Fidem nostram confirmemus, sed quicquid facimus Fidei nostrae Testificatio est. Sic ille, Disp. 12. De Coena. Thes. 78. Quasi Fides Christianorum in hac vita adeo firma & constans sit, ut nulli vacillationi, etiam inter validissimas Tentationes, obnoxia non sit; quasi ad eum usque Gradum exerceat, ut auctior reddi non possit; aut quasi Paulus aliique Apostoli, in suis Epistolis, non orent simul pro Fidelibus, eosque serio hortentur, ut in Fide, omnique Gratia indies crescant; & sollicite moneant, ne vel Apostasiam ab illa faciant, vel in illa tepescant, aut deficiant. Sexto, Negant hoc Sacramentum a Christo institutum fuisse ad solemnem Recordationem mortis ipsius, sed ad solemnem Celebrationem illius Beneficii, cujus antea meminimus, & quod in animo fixum habemus. Hoc innuit Socinus in verbis paulo supra citatis; & a Smalcio asseritur, Disp. 12. de Coena. Catechismus quoque Racov. negat Coenam Domini ea de causa institutam fuisse, ut mortem Domini Participantibus in mentem revocet. Et Rationem hanc addit - Quod cum, qui vult Coenae Domini participare, ita prorsus animatum esse oportet, ut ex illius animo nunquam mortis Domini excidat memoria. p. 145. At certe Christus satis diserte affirmat, in hujus Sacramenti Institutione, se illud instituisse in suae mortis, & effusi Sanguinis Commemorationem. Hoc est Corpus meum, ait quod pro vobis datur — Hic calix est novum illud Fœdus, sive Testamentum, in Sanguine meo, qui pro Vobis effunditur. — Hoc facite in meam Commemorationem. Luc. 22. 19,20. Apostolus item, ubi de hac Institutione disserit. — Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangitur. Hoc facite in meam Commemorationem. — Hic Calix est Novum Testamentum in sanguine meo. Hoc facite quotiescunque biberitis, in meam Commemorationem. 1 Cor. 11.24,25. Et quo-modo, quaeso, hæc Duo inter se ita connexa non sint, ut alterius sine altero meminisse nequeamus; cum neque mortis Christi, sine isto Beneficio; neque Beneficii istius, sine Christi morte, Recordatio fieri posset à Fidelibus? Certe par est ratio utriusque. Neque magis opus erat, ut ad hujus, quam illius memoriam in perpetuum celebrandam, Sacramentum institueretur; cum utrumque aque aptum sit è memoria Hominum excidere, ac proinde eodem adjumento indigeat, ut illud in memoriam rediga-tur, vel in ea conservetur. Septimo; Negant fideles per legitimum usum hujus Sacramenti, remissionem suorum peccatorum consequi, & Promissorum Divinorum obsignationem. Sic enim Socinus, loco antedicto — Credere se Cœnæ digne colenda suorum Peccatorum remissionem consequi, haud valde diversum est ab eo, quod Papistæ sentiunt, qui illam propterea in Sacrificium pro vivis & mortuis transformarunt, & Idolum ex ea quoddam fecerunt. Et Smalcius — Hos errores graves, inquit, Tempus esset agnoscere; & nec seipsum, nec Populum Christi misere seducere; & efficere, ut confisus his commentitiis Consolationibus, nihil minus cogitet, quam ut Deo obediat. Quis enim de sua Carne cum omnibus concupiscentiis crucifigenda cogitet, si usus[?] Panis & Vini, qui quotidie obvius est, possit remissionem Peccatorum, & obsignationem Divinorum Promissorum, imo stipulationem bonae Conscientiae, & Reconciliationis cum Deo factae, consequi? Sic Ille, Disp. 11 de Coena. Pariter, Catech. Rac. - Aliqui ex usu Coenae Domini, se consequi remissionem Peccatorum, & firmare Fidem sperant - at qui vule [?] digne illius Participem esse, cum de remissione Peccatorum ex parte Dei, certum & confirmatum esse oportet. P. 145. Quasi Panis & Vinum in Coena Dominica, non alios effectus in nobis sortiantur, quam quos cibus communis in corporibus nostris producit, cum Apostolus nos moneat discernere Corpus Domini in hoc Sacramento, ne indigne communicando, Judicium ipsis accersamus. 1 Cor. 11.29. & Dominus ipse, cum Panem Eucharisticum Discipulis traderet, vocaverit Corpus suum, quod pro ipsis datum est; & vinum pariter, sanguinem Novi Testamenti, qui pro ipsis effusus est, & pro multis, in remissionem peccatorum. Matt.26.28. Luc:22.29. Quasi modo dictus Apostolus non affirmet, panem simul, & vinum, in hoc sacramento, esse Communionem, id est, medium communicandi Corpus & Sanguinem Christi. 1, Cor. 10. 16, 17. Quasi mors Christi, cum Beneficiis exinde pendentibus, non vivide repraesententur in illo, nec repraesentantur solum, sed & per Fidem applicentur cunctis digne sumentibus; unde sacrificium frequenter appellatur a Veteribus, & mensa Dominica nomine Altaris insignitur, Apostolo praeeunte. Heb: 13. 10. & 1, Cor: 5. 7. Quasi hoc sacramentum adeo non sit Obstaculo crucifigendae carni, cum suis concupiscentiis, ut ad illud efficiendum sese habeat, instar medii aptissimi atque potentissimi; tum quia Christi Crucifixio in & per illud efficacissime menti repraesentatur, & in memoriam riam reducitur ( quæ ad mortificationis opus peragendum, & validissime obligat, & exemplar exhibet perquam illustre ) tum quia fœdus illud, quod in sanguine suo inter crucifigendum sanxit[?], & in hoc sacramento solenni more commemoratur, à Fidelibus illuc accedentibus solenniter quoque renovatur ; quod non parum facit ad Evangelicam Obedientiam Deo præstandam. Quasi demum, peccata quotidie commissa, quotidiana Remissione non indigeant ; aut fides nostra de remissione peccatorum assidue commissorum, non validius confirmetur sa-cramenti hujus sigillo Diplomati Evangelico anne-xo, quam Indulgentia ista generali, quæ in promis-sis Evangelicis Cunctis offertur. Octavo ; Affirmant cibum & potum in hoc sacramento, esse nudum duntaxat panem & Vinum ; Corpus autem & Sanguinem Christi, negant manducari & bibi in Cœna. Sic Oftorodus Inst: c. 38. p. 232. Socinus item, Opinionem illorum, qui dicunt verum & essentiale Christi Corpus, in Cœna sumi, comedique spiritualiter, risu excipiendum esse autumat. Hæc, inquit, inter se pugnant, revera veram Christi carnem sume-re, & eam spiritualiter sumere. Et postea: Hanc opinionem, ait, cum alii Evangelici, tum Pontificii omnes, cum Risu excipiunt. Quod & ipse probat. & Argumentis firmare nititur. Lib: Quod Regn. &c. At è contra, licet præsentiam Christi corporalem non afferamus in Cœna, neque modum istius præsentiæ definire audeamus, affirmamus tamen, eam esse realem, & Christum Spiritualiter à fidelibus participari. Quod enim realiter non adest, realiter accipi non potest. Neque Corpus & Sanguis Christi, quorum participes reddimur in hoc Sacramento, unquam habebantur in Ecclesia Catholica, pro crasso[?] cræsso & corruptibili Corporis nostri Alimento, sed pro Animæ solus Pabulo; adeoque non nisi spiritualiter accipi possunt. Nono; Sessionem solam probant ad mensam Domini in acceptione hujus sacramenti, Geniculationem autem omnino damnant. Sic enim Ostorodus[?]--Quod Aliqui Symbola geniculando sumunt, habemus nos pro superstitione, quæ haud procul absit ab idolomania pontificia; merito a veris Christianis vitari debeat. Inst. cap. 38. p. 344. At è contra, si aut veteris Ecclesiæ Praxis, aut ipsa hujus Sacramenti Dignitas, cum ratione sumendi, à nobis æstimanda sit, sessio ita ad mensam Domini omnino rejicienda est; cum neque conjona[?] sit isti praxi, quæ cum Adoratione semper conjuncta est, eadem sc. qua in publicis precibus usi sunt; neque naturæ atque Dignitati ipsius Sacramenti, in quo, sicut Symbola precè solenni benedicebantur, universo Populo acclamante, Amen; ita & cum precè Communicantibus distribuebantur, unoquoque Ipsorum pariter dicente, Amen. Hoc innuitur ab Apostolo, cum de hoc more sequitur 1 Cor. 14. 16. Evidentius autem apparet ex antiquis liturgiis tum Græcis, tum Latinis, necnon è Justino M. in Apol: 2. juxta finem; & ex Hieronymo, Comm. 2. in Gal: Atque adeo universim invaluit olim in Ecclesia, ut Augustinus palam testetur ---Nemo Panem istum manducat, nisi prius adoraverit sc. Comm. in Psal. 98. Neque sessio hæc ullo modo probatur ab Ecclesia Christi hodierna, sive orientem, sive Occidentem spectemus. Imo passim ablegatur ab istis Ecclesiis, quæ Protestantium, seu Reformatorum nomine vulgo nuncupantur; & speciatim, à Polon cis, tum Bohemicæ, tum Augustanæ, tum Helveticæ Confessionis quæ non semel in Synodum una congregatæ, huic Sessionis[?] Gestum junctis suffragiis damnarunt, ut in-honestum, & scandalosum, & infidelibus Arianis proprium, qui & Dominum, qui nos redemit, abne-garunt, & se cum illo pari solio collocarunt. vid. Harmon. confess.
units.tr: [The last word on the page is cut at the foot; the catchword "fit" follows below the last line.] so firmly established in the faith before he comes to the Lord's Supper? That is what one may and must say of the Apostles and others like them who were, and are, endowed with the Holy Spirit. But the celebration of the Lord's Supper concerns all people in general. Add, he says, that everything that ought to confirm us in the faith must be placed outside us, and that we need no further aid of our own by which to confirm our faith, but whatever we do is a testimony of our faith. Thus he writes in Disp. 12, On the Supper, Thes. 78. As if the faith of Christians in this life were so firm and constant that it is not liable to any wavering, even amid the most violent temptations; as if it is exercised to such a degree that it cannot be made greater; or as if Paul and the other Apostles, in their Epistles, did not pray together for the faithful, and earnestly exhort them to grow daily in faith and in all grace, and anxiously warn them neither to fall away from it, nor to grow lukewarm or fail in it. Sixth, they deny that this sacrament was instituted by Christ for a solemn remembrance of his death, but for a solemn celebration of that benefit which we mentioned before and which we keep fixed in our minds. Socinus hints at this in the words cited a little above, and Smalcius asserts it, Disp. 12 on the Supper. The Racovian Catechism also denies that the Lord's Supper was instituted for this reason, that it might bring the death of the Lord to the minds of those who take part, and it adds this reason: Since the one who wishes to share in the Lord's Supper must be so disposed that the memory of the Lord's death never falls from his mind. p. 145. But surely Christ states quite plainly, in the institution of this sacrament, that he instituted it in commemoration of his death and of the blood he poured out. "This is my body," he says, "which is given for you." "This cup is the new covenant, or testament, in my blood, which is poured out for you." "Do this in remembrance of me." Luke 22.19, 20. The Apostle likewise, where he discusses this institution: "This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in remembrance of me." "This cup is the New Testament in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me." 1 Cor. 11.24, 25. And how, I ask, are these two things not so connected that we cannot remember the one without the other, since the faithful could not remember the death of Christ apart from this benefit, nor this benefit apart from the death of Christ? Surely the reason is the same for both. Nor was there any more need for a sacrament to be instituted for the perpetual celebration of the one memory than of the other, since each is equally liable to slip out of human memory, and therefore each needs the same aid to be brought back to mind or kept there. Seventh, they deny that the faithful obtain, by the lawful use of this sacrament, the remission of their sins and the sealing of the divine promises. For Socinus, in the place cited above, says: "To believe that one obtains the remission of one's sins by worthily honouring the Supper is not very different from what the Papists think, who for this reason turned it into a sacrifice for the living and the dead, and made a kind of idol of it." And Smalcius: "It is time," he says, "to acknowledge these grave errors, and not to mislead either oneself or the people of Christ wretchedly, and to bring it about that, trusting in these fictitious consolations, one thinks of nothing less than obeying God. For who would think of crucifying his flesh with all its lusts, if the use of bread and wine, which meets us every day, could obtain the remission of sins, the sealing of the divine promises, and indeed the pledge of a good conscience and of reconciliation made with God?" Thus he writes, Disp. 11 on the Supper. Likewise the Racovian Catechism: Some hope that by the use of the Lord's Supper they obtain the remission of their sins and strengthen their faith; but to be a worthy partaker of it, it is necessary to be certain and assured of the remission of sins on God's part. p. 145. As if bread and wine in the Lord's Supper produced in us no effects other than those which ordinary food produces in our bodies, when the Apostle warns us to discern the body of the Lord in this sacrament, lest by communicating unworthily we bring judgment upon ourselves. 1 Cor. 11.29. And the Lord himself, when he handed the Eucharistic bread to the disciples, called it his body, which was given for them; and likewise the wine he called the blood of the New Testament, which was poured out for them, and for many, for the remission of sins. Matt. 26.28; Luke 22.20. As if the Apostle did not just say that the bread and the wine in this sacrament are a communion, that is, the means of partaking of the body and blood of Christ. 1 Cor. 10.16, 17. As if the death of Christ, with the benefits hanging on it, were not vividly represented in it, and not only represented but also applied by faith to all who receive it worthily; for which reason the Fathers often call it a sacrifice, and the Lord's table is named the altar, the Apostle leading the way. Heb. 13.10; 1 Cor. 5.7. As if this sacrament were in no way an obstacle to crucifying the flesh with its lusts, but rather stood as the most fitting and most powerful means of bringing this about; both because the crucifixion of Christ is most effectively presented to the mind in and through it and brought back to memory (which is a very strong obligation to carry out the work of mortification and offers a most illustrious example), and because that covenant which he sealed in his blood while being crucified, and which is solemnly commemorated in this sacrament, is also solemnly renewed by the faithful who come to it; and this contributes not a little to rendering evangelical obedience to God. As if, finally, sins committed daily do not need daily remission; or as if our faith concerning the remission of sins continually committed were not more firmly confirmed by the seal of this sacrament, annexed to the evangelical document, than by that general indulgence which is offered to all in the evangelical promises. Eighth, they affirm that the food and drink in this sacrament are merely bare bread and wine, and they deny that the body and blood of Christ are eaten and drunk in the Supper. Thus Ostorodt, Inst. c. 38, p. 232. Socinus likewise thinks the opinion of those who say that the true and essential body of Christ is taken in the Supper, and eaten spiritually, should be met with laughter. These things, he says, contradict each other: to take the true flesh of Christ really, and to take it spiritually. And afterwards: This opinion, he says, both the other Evangelicals and all the Papists meet with laughter. He also proves this himself and strives to confirm it with arguments, Lib. Quod Regn. etc. On the contrary, although we do not claim a bodily presence of Christ in the Supper, nor dare to define the manner of that presence, we nonetheless affirm that it is real, and that Christ is partaken of spiritually by the faithful. For what is not really present cannot really be received. Nor were the body and blood of Christ, of which we are made partakers in this sacrament, ever regarded in the Catholic Church as the gross and corruptible food of our body, but as the sole food of the soul; and so they can only be received spiritually. Ninth, they approve only sitting at the Lord's table in receiving this sacrament, but altogether condemn kneeling. Thus Ostorodt: That some take the symbols kneeling, we regard as a superstition, which is not far from papal idolatry, and which true Christians ought rightly to avoid. Inst. cap. 38, p. 344. On the contrary, if we are to judge either the practice of the ancient Church or the very dignity of this sacrament and the manner of receiving it, then sitting at the Lord's table must be entirely rejected; for it is not in keeping with that practice, which was always joined with adoration, namely the same posture they used in public prayers, nor with the nature and dignity of the sacrament itself, in which, just as the symbols were blessed with solemn prayer, with the whole people acclaiming "Amen," so also when they were distributed with prayer, each of the communicants likewise said "Amen." The Apostle hints at this custom when he follows up on it, 1 Cor. 14.16. It appears more clearly from the ancient liturgies, both Greek and Latin, and from Justin Martyr, Apology 2, near the end, and from Jerome, Comm. 2 on Galatians. And so it became universally established in the Church of old, as Augustine openly bears witness: "No one eats that bread unless he has first adored it," Comm. on Ps. 98. Nor is this sitting in any way approved by the Church of Christ today, whether we look to the East or the West. Indeed it is commonly rejected by those churches which are generally named after the Protestants or Reformed, and especially by the Poles, and by the Bohemian, the Augsburg, and the Helvetic Confessions, which, having gathered together in synod more than once, condemned this posture with united votes as dishonourable, scandalous, and proper to the unbelieving Arians, who both denied the Lord who redeemed us and placed themselves on the same level as him. See Harmony of the Confessions.

units.la: §. 77. Quod ad statum Animae separatae, dicunt, eam non amplius vivere sed omni sensu carere, nulla voluptate frui, aut dolore torqueri nullam omnino Actionem exercere, aut exercere posse; Deum non videre, sed una cum Corpore dormire usque ad Diem Resurrectionis, quando simul cum eo resuscitabitur. Et, ut hanc Psychopannychiam validius astruant, negant animam humanam esse ex natura sua immortalem. Sic enim Socinus Epist. 5. ad Joan: Vol-kelium ——Tantum id mihi videtur statui posse, post hanc vitam Hominis animam, sive animum, non ita per se subsistere, ut alia Praemia, Poenasve sentiat, vel etiam ista sentiendi sit capax. — In ipso primo Homine, totius Immortalitatis rationem unam Gratiae Dei tribuo; nec in ipsa Creatione quidquam immortalis vitae in Homine agnosco. Quae ejus verba etiam de anima primi Hominis intelligi vult, cujus immortalitatem Pucci-us asseruerat. Idem paulo post differens de istis Christi verbis, quibus Sadducaeos confundebat, Ar-gumento ducto a verbis Dei ad Mosen. Matt. 22. 31, 32. cum Exod. 3. 6. haec habet — Vivere adhuc apud Deum is dici & potest & debet, qui aliquando in vitam, eamque immortalem, ab ipso omnino revocabitur. Tom. 1. p. 145. Huc etiam spectant, quae ad An-dream Dudithium scribit — Nec de Immortalitate animae, neque de altera aliqua vita, ullam in universis veteris Foederis literis mentionem claram atque apertam unquam fieri credo. Agnosco tamen, multa ibi reperiri loca, quae mystice de alia quadam vita fuisse loquantur, eamve immuant. Inter quæ & ille est à Domino Iesu explicatus, Ego Deus Abrahami & Deus Isaaci &c. Sic ille, Epist. 3. ad Dudith. p. 507. Col. 2. Tom. 1. Unde Frantz. non immerito illum sic redarguit. — Non me latet, Te etiam negare immortalitatem Animarum, nisi Christianorum in Resurrectione. Et videbimus infra Te confugere ad impium Dogma Epicureorum, ut eorum Patrocinio Te tegas. Puccii Def. ad Resp. Socini, Præfat: p. 264. col. 2. in fine. Tom. 2. Catech. Rac. in eandem sententiam — Homo natura nihil habet commune cum Immortalitate. pag. 15. Smalcius quidem contra Frantzium, videri vult, contra morem suum, paulo modestior in hoc Dogmate asserendo, dum se credere dicit, Animas vel spiritus Hominum post mortem redire ad Deum, & ita suo modo esse superstites. Disp. de extr. Judic. Sect: 4. Interea tamen, ad ista loca quæ ad immortalitatem animarum asserendam affert Frantzius. Responsa qualiacunque potest, reddit; istaque loca invalida esse affirmat ad probandum illud, cujus gratia afferuntur. Idem Ib. Sect. 3. apertius sensum suum de hac Re profert, cum ait — An Spiritus ille, qui ad Deum redit, & a Corpore separatus est, sensu aliquo præditus sit, & an voluptate aliqua fruatur ante Adventum Christi, & ante conjunctionem illam novam sui cum Corpore glorificato, quod Deus olim daturus est credentibus, valde dubitamus; imo aliter se habere credimus. Nempe quemadmodum Corpus sine Spiritu, Cadaver est: ita vicissim, Spiritus sine Corpore, nullas actiones exercere potest. Idem, Exam. 100. Err. Anima Sanctorum, post mortem, nihil sentiunt, nec aliqua Re perfruuntur, cum sine Corpore nullas operationes exercere possint. Err. 81. & in Exam. 157. Err. Anima Sanctorum, ante Diem Judicii iudicii, Deus[?] non vident. Err. 98. Denique, Idem in Resp. ad nova monstra. part. 1. c. 3. pag. 36. apertissime loquitur, sic inquiens — Sanctos [sc. defunctos] nunc extare, nullo modo praberi posse nobis persuasissimum est. Ino[?], eos omnes, in Christi demum Adventu, novam existentiam consecuturos, certum est ex eo, quod tunc demum ex mortuis resuscitandi esse credantur[?].
units.tr: §. 77. As to the state of the separated soul, they say that it no longer lives but is devoid of all sensation, enjoys no pleasure, suffers no pain, and exercises no action at all, or cannot exercise any. They say it does not see God, but sleeps together with the body until the day of resurrection, when it will be raised up along with it. To support this soul-sleep more strongly, they deny that the human soul is immortal by its nature. For Socinus says thus in Epistle 5 to John Volkelius: ——It seems to me that only this can be affirmed: that after this life the soul, or mind, of man does not subsist of itself in such a way that it perceives other rewards or punishments, or is even capable of perceiving them. — In the first man himself I attribute the whole reason for immortality to the grace of God; nor do I recognise in creation itself any immortal life in man. He wishes these words to be understood also of the soul of the first man, whose immortality Pucci had asserted. The same man, a little later, discussing those words of Christ with which he confounded the Sadducees, and drawing the argument from God's words to Moses (Matt. 22. 31, 32, with Exod. 3. 6), has this: It can and must be said that he lives still with God, who will at some time be wholly recalled by him into life, and an immortal life. Vol. 1, p. 145. To this also belong the things he writes to Andreas Dudith: Nor do I believe that any clear and open mention is ever made, in all the writings of the Old Covenant, of the immortality of the soul or of any other life. I acknowledge, however, that many places are found there which speak mystically of some other life, or hint at it. Among these is also that passage which the Lord Jesus explained: I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac, etc. Thus he, Epist. 3 to Dudith, p. 507, col. 2, vol. 1. Whence Frantz, not undeservedly, refutes him thus: It is not hidden from me that you too deny the immortality of souls, except of Christians at the resurrection. And we shall see below that you take refuge in the impious dogma of the Epicureans, so that you may shelter yourself under their patronage. Pucci, Defence against the reply of Socinus, preface, p. 264, col. 2, near the end, vol. 2. The Racovian Catechism to the same effect: Man by nature has nothing in common with immortality. p. 15. Smalcius, indeed, against Frantz, wishes it to appear that, contrary to his custom, he is somewhat more modest in asserting this dogma, in that he says he believes that the souls or spirits of men return to God after death, and so in their own way survive. Disp. on the last judgment, sect. 4. Meanwhile, however, to the passages which Frantz brings forward to assert the immortality of souls, he gives such replies as he can, and affirms that those passages are invalid for proving the thing for which they are cited. The same man, Ib. sect. 3, states his opinion on this matter more plainly, when he says: Whether that spirit which returns to God, and is separated from the body, is endowed with any sensation, and whether it enjoys any pleasure before the coming of Christ, and before that new conjunction of itself with the glorified body which God will one day give to believers, we very much doubt; indeed we believe the contrary. Namely, just as a body without a spirit is a corpse, so conversely a spirit without a body can exercise no actions. The same, Exam. err. 100: The souls of the saints after death perceive nothing and enjoy nothing, since without the body they can exercise no operations. Err. 81, and in Exam. err. 157: The souls of the saints before the Day of Judgment do not see God. Err. 98. Finally, the same, in Reply to the new monsters, part 1, ch. 3, p. 36, speaks most openly, saying: It is most firmly persuaded to us that the saints [that is, the dead] do not now exist in any way that can be perceived by us. ... It is certain that all of them will attain a new existence at Christ's coming, from the fact that they are believed to be raised from the dead only then.

units.la: §. 78. 16. De Resurrectione, & statu seculi post Resurrectionem futuri, haec opinantur. Primo, eadem numero Corpora Hominum non resurrectura, sed alia spiritualia illis a Deo danda fore. Ita Smalcius in Exam. 100. Err. — Corpora haec, quae nunc circumferimus, resurrectura non credimus, sed alia nobis danda esse, ex Deo, vel ex Coelo, ab Apostolo edocti statuimus. Err. 89. 88. Atque corpora haec a Deo nobis tunc danda, adeo pura & spiritualia esse putat, ut affirmare non vereatur — Post Resurrectionem nos futuros Deo similes, etiam quoad Corpora. Exam: 157. Err: Err: 103, Ostorodus item. Inst. cap. 41. p. 389. haec habet — Paulus, ait, de credentium Corporibus differens, quod post Resurrectionem non sint futura Terrena, sed Spiritualia & caelestia, postquam sc. a Mortuis resurrexerint; & expresse concludit, quod Caro & Sanguis Regnum Dei haereditare non possint, (sc. 1, Cor 15. 5.) nomine Carnis & Sanguinis, Corpora carnalia intelligit. Secundo, Affirmant Impios, cum Diabolis, in aeternum non victuros in Inferno, atque illic variis Cruciatibus, pro diversitate Meritorum, obnoxios futuros, sed potius delendos penitus, & annihilandos esse. Sic acta Manuscripta Colloquii Racoviensis, in quibus haec occurrunt — Animadvertendum est, Christum & Apostolos quodammodo coactos fuisse, Hominum Opinionibus, quæ tunc plerumque vigebant, se accommodare; quemadmodum satis aperte docet parabola Divitis & Lazari.Nam Aliquem in Inferno fuisse, & ibi torqueri aut in sinu Abrahæ decumbere, sunt plane fictitia, & similia Illis, quæ Poetæ de Ixione, Sisypho, Tantalo scribunt. Hac etiam Prudentia hodie apud vulgus Christianorum, in hac materia, utendum est Illis, qui Gloriæ Dei consultum cupiunt. Hæc Illi, plus satis impie. Quasi Christus, & Illius Apostoli, Doctrinam suam accommodaverint falsis & fictitiis Hominum Opinionibus, & pro veritate Evangelii nobis tradiderint Gentilium Poetarum Fabulas, equidem Christus in ista Parabola, Animæ Tormenta in Inferno describit, Similitudinibus à Corporis supplicio desumptis; sicut & alibi, cœlestia gaudia depingit, sub Imagine Cœnæ nuptialis; neque enim aliter à nobis concipi potuerunt, qui omnem fere notitiam nostram per Sensuum Januas intromittimus, & Res Spirituales non nisi Phantasmatibus corporeis velatas contemplamur. At siquis hinc inferat, Res ita repræsentatas esse omnino fictitias atque fabulosas falsisque vulgi Opinionibus accommodatas; summamque prudentiam esse putet, imperitæ plebi imponere, dum eam in Erroribus istis confirmat, quos ex officio detegere tenetur, certè, nec Fidem in Deum tuetur, nec Charitatem erga Homines. Smalcius tamen idem Dogma tuetur, Disp. de Baptis. ubi hæc habet—Solas pios in æternum victuros & nomine petitum est è penetralibus S. Literarum quæ solos vitæ promissione solantur Fideles? Jam, siquis hinc colligat, Impios in æternum non victuros, id non nostra Sententia, sed S. Literis potius adscribendum esset. Cum porro, de Interitu vel Judicio Dæmonum legitur, nonne delendos eos esse, hinc jure colligi potest? Jam, quomodo hoc futurum sit, in eo, unicuique nostro quidem Judicio, licet Sensu suo abundare. Idque idem etiam de Cruciatibus Daemonum & Impiorum esse statuendum. Idem quoque lib. S:2.[?] 5. ad omnia S. Scripturae loca, quae in contrarium adduci solent, ut potest, respondet, ita sc. Sociniani[?] Vitia tollunt, & Homines a peccando abster-ent, dum supplicia peccatoribus impoenitentibus post hanc vitam intentata, e medio tollunt. Ita Gloriae Dei consultum cupiunt, dum S. Scripturas dedecorant, & ludibrio habent. Ita Fidem antiquam restituunt, dum Origenis placita e Platonicis hausta[?], atque olim cum Anathematismis[?] damnata a Theophilo & Epiphanio in synodis Episcoporum, & postea in Concilio quinto Oecumenico, e sepulchro erunt & in lucem collocant. Nemo quidem nescit, vitam sempiternam in S. Literis Piis duntaxat, Fidelibusque promitti atque destinari. At quis nescit, hanc vitam sempiternam esse simul vitam beatam, quae sola vita dicenda est, eoque nomine digna; cum Dolores & Cruciatus, aliaque mala, quae vitae felicitatem vel tollunt, vel imminuunt, non semel nomine mortis, & perditionis insigniantur; Idque non solum in seculo futuro, in quo vocantur mors secunda, & interitus. Apoc. 2. 11. & 20. 6. 14. & 21. 8. 2 Thess.[?] 1. 9.
units.tr: §. 78. 16. On the resurrection, and the state of the age to come after the resurrection, they hold the following. First, that the same numerical bodies of men will not rise, but other spiritual bodies will be given to them by God. So Smalcius in Exam. err. 100: We do not believe that these bodies which we now carry about will rise, but we hold, taught by the Apostle, that other bodies are to be given to us from God, or from heaven. Err. 89, 88. And he thinks these bodies, to be given us by God then, to be so pure and spiritual that he does not hesitate to affirm: After the resurrection we shall be like God, even as to our bodies. Exam. err. 157, err. 103. Ostorodus likewise, Instit. ch. 41, p. 389, has this: Paul, he says, speaking of the bodies of believers, says that after the resurrection they will not be earthly but spiritual and heavenly, after they have risen from the dead; and he expressly concludes that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 15. 5), understanding by the name of flesh and blood carnal bodies. Second, they affirm that the wicked, together with the devils, will not live for ever in hell and be subject there to various tortures according to the diversity of their merits, but rather are to be utterly destroyed and annihilated. So the manuscript Acts of the Racovian Colloquy, in which these things occur: It must be noted that Christ and the Apostles were in some measure compelled to accommodate themselves to the opinions of men, which then for the most part prevailed; as the parable of the rich man and Lazarus shows quite plainly. For that someone was in hell and tormented there, or reclined in Abraham's bosom, are plainly fictitious, and like those things which the poets write about Ixion, Sisyphus and Tantalus. By this same prudence, today among the common people of Christians in this matter, one must deal with those who desire the glory of God to be consulted. Thus they, more than enough impiously. As if Christ and his Apostles had accommodated their doctrine to false and fictitious opinions of men, and had handed down to us, for the truth of the Gospel, the fables of the heathen poets! Indeed, in that parable Christ describes the torments of the soul in hell with similitudes taken from bodily punishment; just as elsewhere he depicts heavenly joys under the image of a wedding feast. For these could not otherwise be conceived by us, who admit almost all our knowledge through the gates of the senses, and contemplate spiritual things only veiled in corporeal phantasms. But if anyone infers from this that things so represented are altogether fictitious and fabulous, and adapted to the false opinions of the crowd, and thinks it the highest prudence to impose on the unskilled common people while he confirms them in those errors which he is bound by his office to expose, he certainly preserves neither faith in God nor charity towards men. Smalcius nevertheless defends the same dogma, in his Disp. on baptism, where he has this: Is it from the innermost parts of Holy Scripture that it has been said that only the pious will live for ever, and that only believers are comforted by the promise of life? Now, if anyone from this gathers that the wicked will not live for ever, this would be ascribed not to our opinion but rather to the Holy Scriptures. Moreover, when it is read concerning the destruction or judgment of the demons, can it not rightly be inferred from this that they are to be destroyed? Now how this will happen is something in which each of us, in his own judgment, may abound in his own sense. And the same is to be determined also concerning the torments of the demons and of the wicked. The same man also, in book 5, answers, as best he can, all the passages of Holy Scripture which are commonly brought against this, namely that the Socinians thus remove vices and keep men from sinning, while they take out of the way the punishments threatened after this life to impenitent sinners. Thus they desire to consult the glory of God, while they dishonour the Holy Scriptures and make them a laughing-stock. Thus they restore the ancient faith, while they bring out of the tomb and into the light the opinions of Origen, drawn from the Platonists and long ago condemned with anathemas by Theophilus and Epiphanius in synods of bishops, and afterwards in the Fifth Ecumenical Council. Indeed, no one does not know that eternal life is promised and destined in Holy Scripture to the pious and to believers only. But who does not know that this eternal life is at the same time blessed life, which alone is to be called life and is worthy of that name, since pains and torments and other evils, which either take away or diminish the happiness of life, have more than once been marked with the name of death and perdition; and this not only in the age to come, in which they are called the second death and destruction (Rev. 2. 11; 20. 6, 14; 21. 8; 2 Thess. 1. 9).

units.la: 1 Tim. 6. 9. Matt. 7. 13. Rom. 9. 22.) sed & in hoc quoque seculo; in quo degimus, vitamque adhuc trahimus? Rogate Dominum, ait Pharao ad Mosem & Aaronem, ut auferat a me mortem istam (locustas intelligens) Exod. 10. 17. Quotidie morior, inquit Paulus, cum disserit de Afflictionibus suis assiduis. 1 Cor. 15. 31. Atque iterum Deus, qui ex tanta morte nos eripuit. 2 Cor. 1. 10. de grandi Periculo loquens. Et rursus in moribus[?] frequenter, sc. [?]ul. 2 Cor. 11. 23. Qui adulterium committit dicitur perdere Animam suam. Prov. 6. 32. non sane eam abolendo, sed a Deo abalienando. Eodem fere sensu, Donum dicitur perdere Cor Ecclesiæ. 7. 7. Paulus denique vult Incestuosum Corinthium Satanæ tradi in Carnis interitum, ut Spiritus salvus fiat in die Domini. 1, Cor. 5. 5. Non certe ut mortem Corporis subiret; sed ut morbo quodam, aliove Cruciatu (instar Iobi) afflictus ac perdomitus, resipiscere disceret, & veniam à domino consequeretur. Quod & postea factum est, ut narratur. 2, Cor. 2. 6 11. vel etiam, ut Paulus ipse, ad quem Angelus Satanæ missus est, ut eum colaphizet, sic excellentia Revelationum supra modum efferretur. 2, Cor. 12. 7. Itaque firma stet fides Catholica, verbis Christi & Apostolorum innixa, quæ Animarum Immortalitatem statuit, & Corporum quoque humanorum post Resurrectionem, cum æternitate Pœnarum Gehennalium. Siquidem Christus, cum ad Judicium venturus est sententiam dicturus in Hœdos æque ac oves, id est, maledictos æque ac Benedictos, eadem plane voce uritur in Amborum merecede assignanda [sc. voce dixit] Hi, inquit, abibunt in Supplicium æternum; justi autem, in vitam æternam. Matt. 25. ult. nempe in supplicium illud æternum, ubi vermis eorum non moritur, & ignis non extinguitur; sed in Gehennam Ignis inextinguibilis, ut alibi loquitur. Marc. 9. 43 48. Quicunque blasphemaverit in Spiritum Sanctum, non habet Remissionem in æternum, sed reus tenebitur æterni Judicii, id est, Condemnationis seu Pœnæ; inquit idem Christus. Cap. 3. 29. Atque iterum: Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam æternam; qui vero non obtempetat Filio, non videbit vitam[?], sed Ira Dei manet super eum. Jo. 3. ait: Apostolus item — Qui ignorant Deum & non obediunt Evangelio, Poenam pendent exitium aeternum, à facie Domini, & à gloriosò ipsius Robore. 2 Thess. 1. 9. Petrus & Judas in eandem sententiam, qui de Gnosticis differentes, aeternas Poenas eis minantur — Quibus, inquiunt, Caligo Tenebrarum in aeternum reservatur.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 6. 9. Matt. 7. 13. Rom. 9. 22.) but also in this present age, in which we live and still drag out our lives? Pharaoh said to Moses and Aaron, "Pray to the Lord that he take away from me this death" (meaning the locusts). Exod. 10. 17. Paul says, "I die daily," when he speaks of his constant afflictions. 1 Cor. 15. 31. And again God is said to have delivered us from so great a death, 2 Cor. 1. 10, speaking of a great danger. And again, often, 2 Cor. 11. 23. He who commits adultery is said to destroy his own soul. Prov. 6. 32. Surely not by annihilating it, but by alienating it from God. In nearly the same sense, a gift is said to destroy the heart of the Church. 7. 7. Finally, Paul wishes the incestuous Corinthian to be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord. 1 Cor. 5. 5. Certainly not that he should undergo the death of the body; but that, afflicted and subdued by some disease or other torment (like Job), he might learn to repent and obtain pardon from the Lord. This indeed happened afterwards, as is related. 2 Cor. 2. 6-11. Or, as with Paul himself, to whom an angel of Satan was sent to buffet him, so that he would not be lifted up above measure by the greatness of the revelations. 2 Cor. 12. 7. Let therefore the Catholic faith stand firm, resting on the words of Christ and the Apostles, which affirms the immortality of souls, and of human bodies also after the resurrection, together with the eternity of the punishments of Gehenna. For when Christ comes to judgment to pronounce sentence upon the goats as well as the sheep, that is, upon the accursed as well as the blessed, he uses the very same word for the reward of both: "These," he says, "shall go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into eternal life." Matt. 25, last verse. Namely, into that eternal punishment, where "their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched," but into Gehenna, the unquenchable fire, as he speaks elsewhere. Mark 9. 43-48. "Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but is liable to eternal judgment," that is, to condemnation or punishment; the same Christ says this. Ch. 3. 29. And again: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him." John 3. The Apostle likewise says: Those who do not know God and do not obey the Gospel shall pay the penalty of eternal destruction, away from the face of the Lord and from his glorious might. 2 Thess. 1. 9. Peter and Jude, speaking to the same effect against the Gnostics, threaten them with eternal punishments: For whom, they say, the darkness of gloom is reserved forever. 2 Pet. 2. 17. Jude v. 13. Finally John, in the Apocalypse, relates in prophetic style how the Devil, who was seducing the nations, is to be cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are also, and they shall be tormented day and night, for ever and ever. Rev. 20. 10.

units.la: 2 Pet. 2. 17. Jud. v. 13. Joannes demum in Apocalypsi prophetice narrat, quomodo Diabolus, qui Gentes seducebat, conjiciendus sit in stagnum ignis & Sulphuris; ubi & Bestia, & Pseudopropheta; & cruciabuntur die ac nocte, in seculà seculorum. Apoc. 20. 10.
units.tr: 2 Pet. 2. 17. Jude v. 13. Finally John, in the Apocalypse, relates in prophetic style how the Devil, who was seducing the nations, is to be cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are also, and they shall be tormented day and night, for ever and ever. Rev. 20. 10.

units.la: §. 79. 17. De magistratu Politico, & potestate illi divinitus concessa multa quoque tenent Heterodoxa. Nam Primo, negant illi fas esse, ut Gladio animadvertat in quosvis Maleficos cujuscunque facinoris rei sint. Etenim Ostorodus affirmat, Praecepta Christi nulli Hominis permittere, ut alteri vitam adimat. Instit. cap. 28. Secundo, Smalcius speciatim excipit Adulteros & fures, ut & Homicidas, à poena capitali subeunda — Quemadmodum Christus, inquit, non praecepit Homicidas capite plectere, sic etiam, & tanto magis, statuendum est, cum non praecepisse, ut Adulteri vel fures capite plectantur; quanto minus est Peccatum reipsa Adulterium, quam Homicidium, vel furtum. Nam Adulterium Honestatem tantum alienam petit; Furtum facultates, Homicidium vero ipsam vitam. Cum autem Frantzius attulerat (Thesi sc. 30*) exempla adulterii, ante legem Mosis, morte puniti; respondet Smalcius: Tam ea quae ante legem, quam quae sub lege, licebant, censeri debere abrogata esse per Christum, quod ad Judicia attinet. Disp. de Rebus civil. Sect. 2. Tertio, Idem Smalcius negat, Sententias Judicum in maleficos, dicendas esse ex legibus Imperatoriis, quae, ut ille affirmat, legalibus Mosis rigidiores multo sunt, & cum Christi sanctissima, ac manfuetissima Religione convenire non possunt. Imo ulterius asserere audet, legem Divinam moralem, & cum illa, legem Naturae, ad legem Christi reformandam esse, limitandam, atque temperandam. lb: Resp: ad Thef. 47. Frantzii. Quarto; Negant Christiano licitum esse, Bellum gerere. Unde sequitur, nec magistratui Christiano fas esse, Bellum indicere, & subditos suos Armis defendere contra Hostium injurias; neque subditis, ad jussum Magistratus, Arma capere. Vid. Smalcium, Disp. 6. de Rebus civil. & Socinum, lib. Quod Reg. Pol. &c. cap. 3. ubi negat, Primo, licere nobis, sive per nos ipsos, sive per Magistratum, injurias ultra ulcisci. Secundo, licere, ita vim vi repellere, ut etiam Hominem interficere liceat, si aliter vis repelli nequeat, cum Bellum injustum nobis infertur. Tertio, Perniciosissimum errorem vocat, purae Religionis, & Divini cultus confervandi Gratia, (si id aliter fieri nequeat) Aliorum Hominum Sanguinem fundere licere, & docere, Christiani Magistratus Officium esse, eos, qui Haereses disseminant, (distertim, si ab Incepto desistere nolunt) non modo vi reprimere, sed etiam interficere. At è contra, Deus cunctis Noae posteris, hoc est, toti humano Generi, hoc Praeceptum dedit — Quicunque effundit san-guinem humanum, per Hominem Sanguis ipsius effunditor, quoniam ad imaginem suam fecit Hominem Deus. Gen: 9. v. 6. Sanguis polluit Terram, (inquit Deus alibi) neque aliter expiari potest, nisi per ejus sanguinem, qui alterius sanguinem fuderit: Num. 35. 33. Quæ Ratio legi huic annexa, etiamsi Israelitis à Deo tunc per Mosem datæ, ubique itemper valet. Christus item ad Petrum, qui Gladium suum distrinxerat injussu Magistratus [?] Converte Gladium tuum in locum suum; omnes enim, qui Gladium acceperint, Gladio peribunt. Matt. 26. 52. Apostolus pariter, de potestate civili, sive Principe differens, Dei, inquit, minister est Tibi in Bonum. Sin malum feceris, Time; non enim frustra Gladium portat. Dei quippe minister est, vindex in iram (id est, ad Poenam infligendam) ei, qui malum fecerit. Rom. 13. 4. Neque cuiquam ignotum est, quomodo piissimi olim Imperatores, aliique Principes Christiani, hanc Gladii potestatem, à Deo sibi datam, exercuerint in maleficos, nemine Episcoporum improbante; & quod Bella gesserint in Christiani nominis Hostes, ut Ecclesiam sibi subditam ab exterorum Injuriis vindicarent. Imo, quod & Gladio animadverterint in quosdam Hæreticos, qui palam Blasphemi erant, aut seditiosi; cujusmodi erant Manichæi in oriente, & Circumcelliones in Africa. Quidni enim hæc eis licerent cum nulla lex Christi vetet, sed potius comprobet? ubi autem non est lex, ibi nec Transgressio est. Rom. 4. 15.
units.tr: §. 79. 17. Many errors are also held by the heterodox concerning the political magistrate and the power divinely granted to him. For first, they deny that it is lawful for him to punish any evildoers, whatever crimes they are guilty of, with the sword. For Ostorodt affirms that the precepts of Christ permit no man to take away the life of another. Institutes, ch. 28. Second, Smalcius specifically excepts adulterers and thieves, as well as murderers, from being subject to capital punishment: Just as Christ, he says, did not command murderers to be beheaded, so likewise, and all the more, it must be held that he did not command that adulterers or thieves be beheaded; the less a sin is in itself adultery than murder or theft. For adultery seeks only another's honour; theft seeks goods; but murder seeks life itself. When Frantzius had cited (in thesis 30) examples of adulterers put to death before the law of Moses, Smalcius replies: Those things which were permitted before the law, as well as those under the law, must be considered abrogated through Christ, so far as judgments are concerned. Disputation on Civil Affairs, sect. 2. Third, the same Smalcius denies that the sentences of judges against evildoers ought to be given according to the imperial laws, which, as he asserts, are much harsher than the laws of Moses, and cannot agree with the most holy and gentle religion of Christ. Indeed he dares to assert further that the moral divine law, and with it the law of nature, must be reformed, limited, and tempered by the law of Christ. Reply to thesis 47 of Frantzius. Fourth: they deny that it is lawful for a Christian to wage war. Hence it follows that it is not lawful for a Christian magistrate to declare war and to defend his subjects by arms against the injuries of enemies; nor for subjects to take up arms at the command of the magistrate. See Smalcius, Disputation 6 on Civil Affairs, and Socinus, the book Quod Regnum Politicum etc., ch. 3, where he denies, first, that we may avenge injuries beyond measure, whether by ourselves or through the magistrate. Second, that we may repel force by force in such a way that it is lawful even to kill a man, if force cannot otherwise be repelled, when an unjust war is waged against us. Third, he calls it a most pernicious error that it is lawful to shed the blood of other men for the sake of preserving pure religion and divine worship (if this cannot otherwise be done), and he teaches that it is the office of a Christian magistrate not only to restrain by force, but even to kill, those who spread heresies (especially if they are unwilling to desist from their undertaking). On the contrary, God gave this precept to all the posterity of Noah, that is, to the whole human race: Whoever sheds human blood, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. Gen. 9. 6. "Blood pollutes the land," God says elsewhere, "and it cannot otherwise be cleansed except by the blood of him who has shed another's blood." Num. 35. 33. This reason attached to this law, although it was then given by God to the Israelites through Moses, holds good everywhere likewise. Christ also said to Peter, who had drawn his sword without the magistrate's command: "Put your sword back into its place; for all who take the sword shall perish by the sword." Matt. 26. 52. The Apostle likewise, speaking of civil power, or of the prince, says: "He is God's minister for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid; for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is God's minister, an avenger for wrath (that is, to inflict punishment) on him who does evil." Rom. 13. 4. It is known to no one how the most pious emperors of old, and other Christian princes, exercised this power of the sword given them by God against evildoers, no bishop disapproving; and that they waged wars against the enemies of the Christian name, so that they might defend the Church subject to them from the injuries of outsiders. Indeed, they also punished with the sword certain heretics who were openly blasphemous or seditious, such as the Manichaeans in the East and the Circumcellions in Africa. For why should these things not be permitted them, since no law of Christ forbids them, but rather approves them? Where there is no law, there is no transgression either. Rom. 4. 15.

units.la: Quid vero Smalcio in mentem venit, cum asserere non vereretur, etiam ipsam legem Divinam moralem, cum lege naturæ ad Christi legem esse reformandam, atque limitandam? Quasi Christus venerit ad hanc quoque legem ex aliqua Parte tollendam, restringendam, aut infirmandam, & non potius, ad eam stabiliendam, explicandam, à Corruptelis vindicandam, atque consummandam sive complendam. Sic enim ipse diserte affirmat, & consentanee se gerit in sermone suo super montem, ubi legis Christianæ Praxin nobis luculenter exponit, & Authoritate legislatoris accurate servandam injungit. Matt. 5. v. 17, &c. Neque ipsi Socitiani hoc alibi negant. Imo, non id solum concedunt, sed & pro eo acriter contendunt; & Theologos istos Evangelicos damnare solent, qui negant Christum Decalogo novas aliquas leges de suo addidisse, sed illum duutaxat explanasse, & à malesanis Scribarum atque Pharisaeorum Glossis vindicasse. Quod vero spectat ad naturam & obligationem legis moralis, ab omnibus Catholicis hactenus pro certo habitum est, eam invariabilem & immotam esse aequi, bonique Regulam, tam in officiis erga Deum, quam erga Homines; Regulam plane indispensabilem Actionum nostrarum; talemque, quae semper & universim obliget Genus humanum. Haec autem lex eadem prorsus est cum lege naturae, quam Gentes etiam intus scriptam habebant in Cordibus suis, & factis demonstrabant, sine litera Tabulis lapideis insculpta; ut Apostolus loquitur. Rom: 2. 14, 15.
units.tr: But what came into Smalcius's mind, when he did not hesitate to assert that even the moral divine law, together with the law of nature, must be reformed and limited by the law of Christ? As if Christ had come to remove, restrict, or weaken this law also in some part, and not rather to establish it, explain it, free it from corruptions, and bring it to completion or fulfilment.
