For he himself affirms this plainly, and consistently conducts himself in his Sermon on the Mount, where he sets out for us the practice of the Christian law with great clarity, and enjoins it to be kept carefully by the authority of the lawgiver. Matt. 5. 17, etc. Nor do the Socinians themselves deny this elsewhere. Indeed they not only concede it but contend for it vigorously, and they are accustomed to condemn those evangelical theologians who deny that Christ added any new laws of his own to the Decalogue, but only explained it and cleared it of the mad glosses of the scribes and Pharisees. As for the nature and obligation of the moral law, it has hitherto been held as certain by all Catholics that it is an invariable and unchanging rule of what is right and good, both in duties towards God and towards men; a rule altogether indispensable for our actions, and such as always and universally binds the human race. This law is altogether the same as the law of nature, which the Gentiles also had written inwardly in their hearts, and demonstrated by their deeds, engraved without the letter on tablets of stone, as the Apostle speaks. Rom. 2. 14, 15.

units.la: §. 80. 18. Negant Diem Dominicum, aliosque Dies Festos, de Jure observandos esse à Christianis; pariterque statos Jejuniorum Dies damnant. Sic enim Catech: Rac: — Nullo modo Christus constituit, ut Diem, quem vocant Dominicum, Sabbati loco obiremus; cum Religio Christi, quemadmodum alias Caeremonias, uti vocantur, ita quoque Deleftum Dierum prorsus tollat; ut aperte scribit Apostolus. Col: 2. 16. Verum, cum Diem Dominicum antiquitus celebrari à Christianis videamus, nos eandem libertatem Christianis omnibus permittimus. pag. 123. Et postea, de jejuniis ita praescribit — Jejunantes certis Diebus astringi nullo pacto debent. Id enim est contra Proprietatem & libertatem Religionis Christianae, quae spiritualis est, nec ullo modo ullis Temporibus astringitur.
units.tr: §. 80. 18. They deny that Christians are bound by right to observe the Lord's Day or other festivals, and they likewise condemn fixed days of fasting. For thus the Catechism of Racow says: In no way did Christ ordain that we should keep the day which they call the Lord's Day in place of the Sabbath, since the religion of Christ, like other ceremonies, as they are called, likewise entirely abolishes the distinction of days, as the Apostle plainly writes. Col. 2. 16. But since we see that the Lord's Day has been celebrated by Christians from ancient times, we grant the same liberty to all Christians. p. 123. And afterwards, concerning fasts, it prescribes as follows: Those who fast must on no account be bound to fixed days. For this is contrary to the nature and liberty of the Christian religion, which is spiritual and is in no way bound to any times.

units.la: At è contra; satis liquet Apostolum isthic loci, sicut de discrimine Cibo um à Judæis ex lege Mosaica observato, ita quoque de Festis Judaicis loqui, sc. Paschæ, Pentecostes, atque Tabernaculorum; una cum neomeniis & sabbatis, quæ fuerunt umbra futurorum; non autem de Festis in Genere. Constat item ex libro Actorum, Apostolos, quamdiu in Judæa degebant, Festa Judaica observasse, una cum Fidelibus ex ista Gente; Templum Hierosolymitanum istis Diebus adiisse; statasque Precum publicarum Horas, simul cum Cæteris, observasse; necnon, cum Judæis provincialibus, per Asiam Græciamque dispersis, sabbata coluisse in Synagogis illorum. Idcirco, multum fallitur Moscorovius in ista sua Catechesi, cum dicit Apostolum in isto loco Delectum Dierum prorsus tollere; neque enim vel Festa Judaica illic abrogat. Tantum docet, fideles è Gentibus, quales erant Colossenses, non obligari ad eorum Observationem: --Nemo, ait, vos judicet, sive damnet, ob Cibum, vel Potum, aut respectu alicujus Festi, aut Novilunii, aut Sabbatorum; Quæ sunt umbra Rerum futurarum. Col: 2. 16, 17. Pariter constat, Diem Dominicum, sive primum Hebdomadæ Diem, à primis usque Temporibus, publicis Ecclesiæ Conventibus, sacrisque officiis peragendis, dicatum fuisse; haud dubie, ex Institutione Apostolica: necnon, quatuor solennia Festa, sc. Passionis Domini, Resurrectionis, Ascensionis, & adventus de Cœlo Spiritus Sancti; quæ Augustinus affirmat anniversaria solennitate celebrata fuisse, ab universa, quacunque se diffundit Ecclesia, ab ipsis Apostolis commendata atque statuta retineri. Epist: 118. Januario. Idem dici potest de Jejunio quadragesimæ anniversario, item Feriæ quartæ & sextæ hebdomadatim, & de vigiliis solemnium Festorum. Quæ omnia veteres referunt ad Traditionem Apostolicam. Neque sane aliam originem habuisse ullo modo verisimile est, cum & tam antiqua sint, & tam universim observata, ut ad alios Authores referri nequeant. Quid? quod cum publicus Dei Cultus sive in Festis, sive Jejuniorum Diebus, sit non solum ex Institutione Divina inter Christianos agnita; sed & pars Religionis naturalis, apud omnes Gentes, ex innato Rationis lumine demonstrata, cunctorumque Praxi ubique stabilita; necesse omnino est, ut ad publicum hunc Cultum celebrandum, sic & certa tempora statuantur. Aliquin, tantum aberit, ut hujusmodi cultus decenter & ordine peragatur, secundum Apostoli mandatum, ut nec omnino peragi possit; cum Populus Christianus plane nesciat, vel ubi, vel quando convenire oporteat, ad sacra publice celebranda.
units.tr: On the contrary, it is quite clear that the Apostle in that passage, just as he speaks of the distinction of foods observed by the Jews under the Mosaic law, so also speaks of the Jewish festivals, namely the Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles, together with the new moons and sabbaths, which were a shadow of things to come, and not of festivals in general. It is also evident from the Book of Acts that the Apostles, as long as they lived in Judea, observed the Jewish festivals together with the believers from that nation; that they went up to the temple at Jerusalem on those days; that they kept the fixed hours of public prayer along with the others; and that, together with the Jews of the provinces scattered through Asia and Greece, they also kept the sabbaths in their synagogues. Therefore Moscorovius is greatly mistaken in his Catechism when he says that the Apostle in that place entirely abolishes the distinction of days; for he does not even abrogate the Jewish festivals there. He only teaches that believers from among the Gentiles, such as the Colossians were, are not bound to observe them: Let no one, he says, judge or condemn you in respect of food or drink, or of a festival, or a new moon, or sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come. Col. 2. 16, 17. Likewise it is established that the Lord's Day, that is, the first day of the week, was set apart from the earliest times for the public assemblies of the Church and for the performance of sacred duties, undoubtedly by apostolic institution; and also four solemn festivals, namely of the Lord's Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, and the coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven, which Augustine affirms were celebrated with an annual solemnity by the whole Church wherever it is spread abroad, and were retained as commended and appointed by the Apostles themselves. Letter 118, to Januarius. The same may be said of the annual fast of Lent, likewise of the Wednesday and Friday fasts of each week, and of the vigils of the solemn festivals. The ancient writers all trace these to apostolic tradition. Nor is it at all likely that they had any other origin, since they are so ancient and so universally observed that they cannot be referred to other authors. Indeed, since public worship of God, whether on festivals or on days of fasting, is not only recognised among Christians from divine institution, but is also part of natural religion, shown among all nations by the innate light of reason and established everywhere by the practice of all; it is absolutely necessary that fixed times be appointed for celebrating this public worship. Otherwise, far from such worship being carried on decently and in order, as the Apostle commands, it could not be carried on at all, since the Christian people would have no idea where or when they ought to assemble to celebrate the sacred rites publicly.

units.la: §. 8. 19. Sed ut in hoc nimis laxi sunt, & licentiæ neutiquam ferendæ Patroni; sic in aliis quibusdam nimis rigidi sunt, ac severi, & morosi libertatis alienæ Censores. Negam enim Christiano fas esse, plus appetere, acquirere, aut habere, quam necessitas vitæ postulat. Plus etenim requirere, ex Ostorodi sententia, est avaritia ista, quæ à Christo, & Apostolo Paulo damnata est. Inst: cap. 31. Verumtamen, cum magistri ipsius, Socini &c.[?] Facultates in Pecuniis consistebant, è Re sua putavit eandem fenori dare, usuras solitas inde exigere, & hisce verbis defendere — Concludo, inquit, illum Fenus per se ullo Divino Præcepto esse prohibitum, nisi illud, quod cum Proximi ipsius, quo exigitur, damno fiat; nec quicquam cavendum praeterea restare, nisi scandalum & offensionem aliorum. Qua tamen tunc demum vitanda est, cum alioqui in nullam aliam majorem necessario sit incurrendum. Mihi, si Pecuniam, quam habeo, Fœnori non darem, multo majus scandalum & offensio praesto esset, quam nunc do. Nam & me, & Filium meam, ad summam inopiam, extremamque egestatem redigerem; ex qua utrique nostrum ingentia salutis ipsius æterna Jactura facienda pericula imminerem. Sic ille causam [?]suam agit contra Scandalum Fœnoris: Epist. 4. ad Christophorum Morstinum, Philippoviæ Capitaneum. Op. Tom. 1. p. 457. col.
units.tr: §. 8. 19. But just as they are too lax in this matter, and their patrons cannot be tolerated in their licence, so in other matters they are too rigid, severe, and fastidious censors of the liberty of others. For they deny that it is lawful for a Christian to desire, acquire, or have more than the necessity of life requires. For, according to Ostorodt's opinion, to seek more than this is that covetousness which has been condemned by Christ and the Apostle Paul. Institutes, ch. 31. Yet when his master Socinus [?] had his resources in money, he thought it fitting for his own affairs to lend the same at interest, to exact the customary usury from it, and to defend this in the following words: I conclude, he says, that lending at interest is not forbidden in itself by any divine precept, except where it is done to the loss of the very neighbour from whom it is exacted; nor does anything further remain to be guarded against, except scandal and offence to others. Yet this is to be avoided only when there is no other greater evil into which one must of necessity fall. If I did not lend the money I have at interest, far greater scandal and offence would be at hand than now when I do lend it. For I would reduce both myself and my son to the utmost want and extreme poverty, from which dangers threaten both of us of enormous loss of our eternal salvation. Thus he argues his case against the scandal of usury. Letter 4 to Christopher Morstin, captain of Philippov. Works, vol. 1, p. 457, col. 2.

units.la: 2. At certe, aliæ viæ Socino suppetebant ad incrementum è Pecunia sua capiendum, in sui & Familiæ suæ sustentationem, quæ nullius offensioni erant obnoxiæ; ita ut illi minime necesse fuerit, cum scandalo cujusquam, ad Fœnus exigendum confugere. Idem Ostorodus Christianis illicitum esse vult, in esu Potu, vestitu, reliquisque illius Generis, voluptatem aliquam quærere; licet olim Judæis permissa fuerit, quibus in Fœdere Mosaico Promissa data sunt de terrena salute atque felicitate. Sic ille, Inst. cap. 30. At ubi, quæso, prohibetur sub novo Fœdere, moderata ista ac tempestiva voluptas, quam Solomon, ut insigne Dei Donum prædicat, & ut eximiam felicitatis humanæ Portionem, quamdiu in his Terris vitam degimus? Eccles: 2. 24. & 3. 22. 8. 15. 6, 7, 8, 9. Christus item in Evangelio nullibi prohibet Epulas, sed eas ita dirigit atque moderatur, ut usui simul nostro commendet, ex ipsius Præscripto celebrandas. Luc: 14. 12, 13, 14. Ipse quoque Convivio excipi dignatus est; adeo frequenter, ut occasionem inde arripuerint Pharisæi eum, pro Guione ac Vini-potore, apud vulgus calumniandi. Quandoque etiam se convivam ultro præbuit, & pia Hospitum officia gratissime semper excepit. Quinimo Pharisæo isti inhumanitatem exprobrat; qui non satis laute & honorifice ipsum excepisset, viz. osculo salutatorio, aqua ad Pedes abluendos, & oleo ad Caput ungendum. Ib. cap. 7. 44, 45, 46. Denique, primum omnium miraculum edidit in epulo nuptiali, ubi aquam in vinum optimæ notæ convertit, ad exhilarandos convivas, cum jam probe bibissent, ut plusquam innuitur. Joh. 2. 10. Et cum jam mundo valediturus esset, dum Bethaniæ epulatus est, in Domo Simonis Leprosi, gratissime accepit unguentum illud pretiosissimum, quo Caput ipsius perfusum est, Opusque istud mulieris pro Bono habuit, & magnopere laudavit; imo, per totum Terrarum Orbem, una cum Evangelio suo, prædicandum esse voluit, in honorificam mulieris istius Memoriam. Et quod observatu dignum est, satis acriter Discipulos quosdam increpuit, qui ad prodigam, ut sibi videbatur, unguenti istius effusionem, indignabantur. Matt. 26. 6-13. Apostolus quoque Corinthiis suis Epulas permittit, etiam in Domibus Idololatrarum, ex ipsis Idolothytis, modo non fiat cum scandalo Infirmorum. 1, Cor. 16. 27, 28, 29. Postremo, tum Christus ipse, tum Joannes in Apocalypsi, cœlestia Gaudia describit, sub Typo epuli magnifici, sive Cœnæ nuptialis. Matt. 22. 2, &c. & 25. 1, &c. Apoc. 19. 9.
units.tr: At any rate, other ways lay open to Socinus for gaining an increase from his money, for the support of himself and his household, which were liable to no one's offence; so that he had no need at all to resort to exacting interest with another's scandal. The same Ostorodt holds that it is unlawful for Christians to seek any pleasure in eating, drinking, clothing, and things of that kind, although it was once permitted to the Jews, to whom under the Mosaic covenant promises of earthly well-being and happiness were given. Thus he writes, Institutes, ch. 30. But where, I ask, is such moderate and seasonable pleasure forbidden under the new covenant, the pleasure which Solomon proclaims as a special gift of God and as an excellent portion of human happiness, as long as we live our life on this earth? Eccles. 2. 24; 3. 22; 8. 15; 6, 7, 8, 9. Likewise Christ nowhere in the Gospel forbids feasts, but so directs and moderates them that he commends them to our use, to be celebrated according to his own precept. Luke 14. 12, 13, 14. He himself also deigned to be entertained at banquets, so often that the Pharisees seized the occasion to slander him before the common people as a glutton and a winebibber. Sometimes he also freely offered himself as a guest, and always most gratefully accepted the kindly services of his hosts. Indeed he rebukes that Pharisee for inhospitality, who had not received him sufficiently lavishly and honourably, namely with the kiss of greeting, water to wash his feet, and oil to anoint his head. Ib. ch. 7. 44, 45, 46. Finally, he performed his very first miracle at a wedding feast, where he turned water into wine of the finest quality, to cheer the guests, who had by then already drunk well, as is more than hinted. John 2. 10. And when he was about to leave the world, while he was feasting at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, he most graciously accepted that very costly ointment with which his head was anointed; he regarded the woman's deed as good and praised it greatly; indeed he wished it to be proclaimed throughout the whole world along with his Gospel, in honourable memory of that woman. And, worth noting, he rebuked fairly sharply certain disciples who were indignant at what seemed to them the wasteful pouring out of that ointment. Matt. 26. 6-13. The Apostle also permits his Corinthians to eat meals, even in the houses of idolaters, and of the very meat offered to idols, provided it does not cause a stumbling-block to the weak. 1 Cor. 10. 27, 28, 29. Lastly, both Christ himself and John in the Apocalypse describe heavenly joys under the figure of a magnificent feast, or wedding banquet. Matt. 22. 2, etc.; 25. 1, etc.; Rev. 19. 9.

units.la: §. 82. 20. His omnibus adjicienda sunt, quæ non incongrue Cæteris anteponi potuerunt; nempe, quæ de primorum Parentum Statu, & conditione tenent tum ante, tum in, tum post lapsum. Nam Primo, De illis in statu Innocentiæ spectatis, hæc asserunt. Nimirum, Primo, Excellentem quandam Dei Creatoris, aut Rerum creatarum notitiam, Neutri concreatam fuisse aut ab origine infusam. Adamum, inquit Smalcius, instar Infantis vel pueri se esse nudum ignoravit. De Ve. Dei Fil. cap. 7. p. 6. Atque iterum, De Conjuge propria, non nisi Sensibus obvia cognovit; sc. quod nominanda foret Eva, quia Mater futura omnium Viventium; & virago, sive vira, quia de viro sumpta est. Socinus item dicit, Adamum Bestiis nomina imposuisse qualia sibi visum est. Putasne, inquit, Bestiarum nomina praestantioris & reconditioris alicujus Significationis fuisse? Annon potius vides Bestiarum nomina non ad Alia respexisse, quam ad ea, quae Sensibus sese prodebant, & unicuique manifesta esse potuissent? De statu primi Hom. cap 4. Haec quoque ibidem habet: Nesciebat Adamus, antequam ex Arbore scientiae boni & Mali comederet, vim illius Fructus (sc. Arboris vitae) aut saltem, quanti vis illa facienda esset, ignorabat, parag. ult. & postea, cap. 6. parag. 2. ita pergit in asserenda Adami Ignorantia: Adamum, quamvis natura mortalis esset, se mortalem esse, nemine indicante, non vere agnovisset; vere autem non agnitum fuisse Adamum, se mortalem esse, nemine indicante, ex eo perspicuum est, quod nos ipsi de nobis Id, non nisi experientia ipsa, & Rationibus, propter experientiam animadversis, nosse potuimus. Haec illi. At e contra, Apostolus diserte affirmat, novum Hominem renovari εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν[?], ad, seu in Agnitionem [Dei sc.] juxta Imaginem Illius, qui Ipsum condidit. Col. 3. 10. unde sequitur: Adamus, qui primum conditus est ad Dei Imaginem, & ad Cujus exemplar exprimendum novus Homo indies renovatur, donec ad integram Ipsius Perfectionem pertigerit, excellentiore quadam Dei Creatoris notitia primitus imbutum fuisse. Quod vero ad Notitiam Creaturarum attinet; illa latis patet ex nominibus, quae iisdem imposuit, priusquam, experientia Magistra, indigenam istam Ingeniorum varietatem, quae in tot Animantium speciebus reperiri didicisse potuerit; quaeque Deus ipse rata habuit, utpote Singulorum naturis apprime Congrua. Gen. 2. 19, 20. Quod & ex Hebræo Sermone liquet, quo Adamus tunc utebatur, cum ista nomina imposuit, ut à viris doctissimis observatum est, quorum Sententia confirmatur Argumentis è Textu sacro petitis. Idcirco, hujusmodi nominum Impositio, luculentum erat tam scientiæ Adamo concreatæ Documentum; quàm Potestatis atque Dominii Ipsius in Creaturas. Ex hac autem una Instantia, si alia Argumenta deessent, non sine Ratione concludi posset, Sapientiam eidem Adamo concreatam fuisse, quæ se ad Cætera omnia simul extenderet, quibus idoneus, plenéque instrutus redderetur, tum ad Cultum Deo rite præstandum, (qui non mediocrem ipsius cognitionem præsupponit) tum ad Dominium in creaturas exercendum; tum, ad suam Ipsius Felicitatem in hisce Terris procurandam, atque perficiendam; tum denique ad instructionem Posterorum, quomodo se gererent, tum erga Deum, tum erga se invicem; quomodo Pietatem erga Illum ut oportet, exercerent, & Societatem inter se mutuo colerent, ex Præscripto legum à se datarum. Atque hanc fuisse sententiam veterum sapientum apud Hebræos, Siracides idoneus Author est, ubi de primis Parentibus ita disserit: Deus Consilium, & linguam, & Oculos, Auresque, & cor dedit Ipsis ad cogitandum; Disciplina Intelligentiæ replevit ipsos; Bona item & mala demonstravit Ipsis. Ecclus. 17. 6, 7. Itaque, cum post lapsum se cognovisse dicuntur, quod nudi fuerint intelligi nequit de nuditate simpliciter[?] accepta, seu privatione vestium (quam ne pueri quidem & infantes hodie ignorant, multo minus primi Parentes nostri in statu Innocentiae) sed de nuditate ignominiosa sive poenali; quae consistebat, partim in privatione istius Gratiae, qua illorum Animae primitus vestitae fuerant a Deo; partim in rebellibus Concupiscentiae motibus quae, freno isto amoto, insurgere coeperunt contra rectae Rationis moderamen. Dicitur etiam de Adamo, quod ad primum Evae conspectum, cum a Deo ad ipsum adduceretur, pro certo noverit, eam fuisse compactam ex Carne & Ossibus Ipsius; quod tamen sensu percipere nequaquam potuit Ipso in somnum profundum demerso. Quod autem Adamus plane nescivisse vim salutarem Fructus Arboris vitae, antequam comedisset ex Fructu vetito, gratis dicitur. Etenim contraria Assertio multo probabilior est; cum haud verisimile sit, Deum celasse Adamum, quod ad vitae felicis Immortalitatem procurandam tantopere conducebat; neque uspiam legamus, Deum hoc demum revelasse Adamo, post esum Fructus vetiti. Cum ergo legimus, Deum ejecisse Adamum de Paradiso, ne forte mitteret Manum suam & sumeret etiam de fructu Arboris vitae, & comederet, & viveret in aeternum; Gen: 3. 22. bene concludi potest Ipsum Fructus istius virtutem salutiferam probe cognovisse a quo Deus collocaverat eum in isto horto Edenis. Denique, Nihil obstat, quo minus Adamus a Principio noverit, se natura mortalem esse, quantum ad Corpus attinet, (quod ex fragili Terrae pulvere compactum erat sicut & Corpora brutorum Animantium) at ex Dono Dei Immortalem permansuturum, quamdiu Innocens. Deinde Mandato obsequens permansurus esset. Neque enim ei metuenda erat Mortis Sententia, nisi ex comminatione Dei, ex hypothesi legis violatae circa eius[?] Fructus vetiti Gen. 2. 17.
units.tr: §. 82. 20. To all these should be added what they hold, not inappropriately, to come after the others: namely, their views on the state and condition of our first parents before, during and after the fall. First, regarding them in the state of innocence, they assert the following. Certainly, they hold that no excellent knowledge of God the Creator, or of created things, was born with either of them or infused from the beginning. "Adam," says Smalcius, "was ignorant that he was naked, like an infant or a boy." On the Divinity of the Son of God, ch. 7, p. 6. And again: "He knew his own wife only through the senses," namely, that she was to be called Eve, because she would be the mother of all living, and "virago," or "vira," because she was taken out of man. Socinus likewise says that "Adam gave the beasts names such as seemed fitting to him. Do you think," he says, "that the names of the beasts had some more excellent and recondite meaning? Do you not rather see that the names of the beasts referred to nothing other than what presented itself to the senses and could be plain to each one?" On the state of the first man, ch. 4. He also has this in the same place: "Adam, before he ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, did not know the power of that fruit (sc. of the tree of life), or at least did not know how great its power was," last paragraph. And afterwards, ch. 6, par. 2, he goes on in asserting Adam's ignorance thus: "Adam, although he was mortal by nature, would not truly have recognised that he was mortal, with no one pointing it out." That Adam did not truly recognise that he was mortal, with no one pointing it out, is clear from the fact that we ourselves could know this about ourselves only through experience itself and reasonings drawn from experience. So he. On the contrary, however, the Apostle plainly affirms that the new man is renewed "into knowledge [εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν]," that is, into the knowledge [of God, namely] according to the image of him who created him. Col. 3. 10. From this it follows that Adam, who was first made in the image of God, and after whose pattern the new man is renewed day by day until he attains to the full perfection of that image, was first imbued with a more excellent knowledge of God the Creator. As for the knowledge of creatures, it is plain enough from the names which he gave them, before, with experience as his teacher, he could have learned that variety of natures native to so many species of living things; names which God himself approved, as being most fitting to the natures of each. Gen. 2. 19, 20. This is also clear from the Hebrew language, which Adam then used when he gave these names, as has been observed by the most learned men, whose opinion is confirmed by arguments drawn from the sacred text. Therefore the giving of such names was a clear proof both of the knowledge born with Adam and of his power and dominion over the creatures. From this single instance, if other arguments were lacking, it could reasonably be concluded that wisdom was born with Adam, extending itself at once to all other things, by which he would be made fit and fully equipped, both to render due worship to God (which presupposes no small knowledge of him), and to exercise dominion over the creatures, and to secure and perfect his own happiness in this earth, and finally to instruct his posterity in how they should conduct themselves, both towards God and towards one another, how they should exercise piety towards him as is fitting, and cultivate fellowship with one another, according to the rule of the laws given by him. That this was the opinion of the wise men of old among the Hebrews is attested by Ben Sira, a reliable author, where he speaks of the first parents thus: "God gave them counsel, and tongue, and eyes, and ears, and a heart to think with; he filled them with the discipline of understanding; he also showed them good and evil." Ecclus. 17. 6, 7. Therefore, when they are said to have known after the fall that they were naked, this cannot be understood of nakedness taken simply, that is, the lack of clothing (which even boys and infants do not fail to know today, much less our first parents in the state of innocence), but of shameful or penal nakedness, which consisted partly in the loss of that grace with which their souls had at first been clothed by God, and partly in the rebellious motions of concupiscence which, once that bridle was removed, began to rise up against the government of right reason. It is also said of Adam that at his first sight of Eve, when she was brought to him by God, he knew for certain that she was made of his flesh and bones, which yet he could by no means perceive by the senses, since he had been plunged into a deep sleep. But to say that Adam knew nothing at all of the saving power of the fruit of the tree of life before he ate of the forbidden fruit is a gratuitous claim. For the opposite assertion is much more probable, since it is hardly likely that God would have hidden from Adam what contributed so greatly to securing the immortality of a happy life, and we nowhere read that God revealed this to Adam only after he ate the forbidden fruit. Therefore, when we read that God drove Adam out of paradise, lest perhaps he should stretch out his hand and take also of the fruit of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever (Gen. 3. 22), it may well be concluded that he had clearly known the saving virtue of that fruit, since God had placed him in that garden of Eden. Finally, nothing stands in the way of Adam's having known from the beginning that he was mortal by nature, as far as his body was concerned (since it had been made from the frail dust of the earth, like the bodies of the brute animals), but that by God's gift he would remain immortal for as long as he remained innocent and obedient to the command. For he had no reason to fear the sentence of death, except from God's threat, given under the supposition that the law concerning the forbidden fruit was violated. Gen. 2. 17.

units.la: Secundo; Imaginem Dei, in qua primi Parentes creati fuerunt, in sanctitate, & justitia quadam peculiari non constitisse. Hanc enim sanctimoniam, quam Frantzius una cum Aliis, tribuit Adamo ante lapsum, Smalcius appellat Ideam quandam in Cerebro Ipsorum natam, de qua ne [illegible, ~3 letters] quidem in S. literis. Disp. 2. cont. Frantz. Atque alibi – Primum Hominem, in sua Creatione, Sanctitatem & Dona supernaturalia accepisse, est vetus, eaque putidissima Fabula. Exam. 157. Err. Err. 704. Eadem quoque habet. Resp. ad nova monst. part. 2. Cap. 24. pag. 215.
units.tr: Secondly, that the image of God in which the first parents were created did not consist in holiness and a certain peculiar righteousness. For this holiness, which Frantzius together with others ascribes to Adam before the fall, Smalcius calls "a certain idea born in their brain, of which not even [illegible, about three letters] is found in the sacred letters." Disp. 2 against Frantz. And elsewhere: "That the first man, in his creation, received holiness and supernatural gifts, is an old and most rotten fable." Examen 157, Errata 704. He has the same also in the Response to the new monsters, part 2, ch. 24, p. 215.

units.la: At e contra, Homo dicitur conditus ad Dei imaginem. Gen: 1.27. cujus Imaginis praecipua Pars est Sanctitas; ad quam proinde repraesentandam, non semel ab eodem Deo admonetur, ubi ait, Sancti estote, sicut & ego Sanctus sum. 1. Pet. 1. 16. Lev: 11. 44. & 19. 2. & 20. 7. unde & Apostolus Paulus Ephesios suos obnixe hortatur, ut vetere Homine deposito, novum induant, qui secundum Deum creatus est in Justitia, & ve a sanctitate. Eph: 4. 24. ea vero sine dubio per Renovationem Evangelicam instaurantur, quae in primis Parentibus ab initio fuerunt, & per lapsum deperdita sunt.
units.tr: On the contrary, man is said to have been made in the image of God. Gen. 1. 27. The chief part of this image is holiness, and to represent this God himself repeatedly admonishes man, saying, "Be holy, for I am holy." 1 Pet. 1. 16; Lev. 11. 44, and 19. 2, and 20. 7. Hence also the Apostle Paul earnestly exhorts his Ephesians to put off the old man and put on the new, who has been created according to God in righteousness and holiness. Eph. 4. 24. Those things indeed are undoubtedly restored through the evangelical renewal which were in the first parents from the beginning and were lost through the fall.

units.la: Solomon quoque affirmat, Deum ab initio fecisse Hominem Rectum [ Hebr: Jashar[?] ] Eccl: 7. ult. hoc est, integri atque sinceri, tum Judicii, tum affectus. Hanc enim vocem 70 Interpretes varie transferunt, sed in eundem fere sensum; viz. δικαιον, ὅσιον, ἀληθὲς[?], ἀγαθὸν[?], καλὸν, ἀρεστὸν[?], εὐθὲς[?] & ὀρθὸν[?], & ἀγαθὸν[?]. Id est, Justum, Sanctum, verum seu veracem, Bonum, Honestum, Acceptum, Rectum & purum Psal: 51. 12. Rom: 12. 2. Eph: 2. 10. Tit: 3. 5. Tertio; Hominem ab initio non creatum fuisse Bonum. Sic enim Socinus Quod ad Hominem attinet, non est intelligendum Deum vidisse ipsum Hominem esse Bonum, sed bonum esse, quod Homo a se creatus fuisset Talis, qualem eum antea descripserat Moses. Praelect: c.
units.tr: Solomon also affirms that God made man upright from the beginning [Hebr. Jashar], Eccl. 7, last verse; that is, whole and sincere, both in judgement and in affection. The Seventy translate this word variously, but to nearly the same sense: just [δικαιον], holy [ὅσιον], true or truthful [ἀληθές], good [ἀγαθόν], honest [καλόν], acceptable [ἀρεστόν], straight [εὐθές] and upright [ὀρθόν], and good [ἀγαθόν]. That is, just, holy, true, good, honourable, acceptable, right and pure. Ps. 51. 12; Rom. 12. 2; Eph. 2. 10; Tit. 3. 5. Thirdly, that man was not made good from the beginning. For so Socinus: "As regards man, it is not to be understood that God saw man himself to be good, but that it was good that man had been made by him such as Moses had earlier described him. Praelect. c. 3. Resp. ad Argum. 2." On the contrary, however, it is established that he was created in the image of God, which was without doubt the best and most perfect pattern. Moses likewise affirms in the same place that all the works of creation were good, and very good. Gen. 1. 31. Therefore, and…

units.la: 3. Resp. ad Argum. 2. At ex adverso, constat eum creatum fuisse ad Dei imaginem, quae sine dubio erat optimum atque perfectissimum exemplar. Moses item ibidem affirmat, omnia Creationis opera fuisse Bona, idque valde Bona. Gen. 1. 31 Ergo, & Homo inter catera, imo, & praecaeteris, quo caeteris excellentior. At Socinus ibidem respondet Non de Animi Bonitate, nec de Justitia, Sermonem illic esse; sed de aptitudine & convenientia ad id, quod Deus antea sibi propositerat. Fatemur quidem, si de Dei Operibus in universum loquamur, quorum Plurima nullatenus capacia sunt Justitiae alicujus internae, aut Bonitatis Animi. At si verba haec ad Hominem referantur, idem ille sensus, quem Socinus iis affingit, probat quod volumus. Siquidem inde sequitur, Hominem ab origine Creationis interna Bonitate praeditum fuisse, & istiusmodi Gratiae dotibus instructum, quibus habilis redderetur ad Deo serviendum, & obsequium legibus ab ipso datis perfecte exhibendum, quae sine tali Auxilio haud praestari potuerunt. Quarto; Adamum & Evam creatos fuisse mortales. At e contra legimus, Mortem Peccati poenam fuisse, quam sc. Deus minatus est Adamo, ex hypothesi Fructus vetiti ab ipso comesti; quae proinde non aliter Ipsum invasisset. Apostolus quoque dilerte affirmat, per peccatum primi Hominis mor-tem tem introiisse in Mundum, atque ita in omnes Homines pertransiisse, five pervaiiffe. Rom. 5. 12. Et ante eum Sapiens Hebræus — Deus, inquit, creavit Hominem in ἀφθαρσίᾳ[?] id est, in statu Incorruptionis, & fecit eum Imaginem τῆς ἰδίας ὑποστάσεως[?] id est, propriiffimæ Natura suæ, [viz. ratione Æternitatis] Invidia autem Diaboli Mors introiit in Mundum, Sap. 2, 23, 24. equidem agnoscimus non inviti, primos humani Generis parentes non habuisse Corpora ex Naturæ suæ Principiis immortalia; (ex fe enim terrena erant, & animalia, ac proinde corruptibilia) sed ex Dono Dei singulari, quod iis ab origine concessum est præ cæteris Animantibus è Terra formatis; ita ut hujus Privilegii virtute potuerint non mori; neque Mortem unquam actu subiissent, fi in primævo Innocentiæ statu permanfiffent. Hæc quoque accessit Fructus Arboris vitæ, cujus virtute non fine ratione putatur Immortalitatem istam terrenæ Corporis, quam ex Dei Dono primitus accepe-ant, promovendam fuisse atque confervandam. Quod & ipsius Dei verba non obscurè innuunt, apud Mosen. Gen. 3. 22. Cum itaque Socinus dicit, peccatum non mortalitatis naturalis, sed necessariæ mortis causa fuit; & cum affirmat, primum Hominem, etiam ante lapsum, naturæ mortalis fuisse; quam Propositionem Argumentis probare laborat. Præleét: cap: 1. Si hoc tantum intelligat, quod modo concessimus, plane nescio quem habeat Adversarium. Quinto; Imaginem Dei, juxta quam Homo creatus est, in Dominio super Creaturas unice consistere; seu ut alii, in eo magis principaliter: minus principaliter autem, in recta Ra- tione. Sic etenim malcius — Non constat, an respectu Animæ Homo conditus dicatur ad Imaginem Dei, cum respectu Rationis, vel potius Potestatis, quam Deus in omnes Res creatas Homini concessit, (quae sine Ratione exerceri non potest) ita appellatum esse legatur. Resp. ad nova Monst. part. 2. Cap. 24. p. 212. At certe Ratio recta fuit olim in Adamo, atque adhuc est in cunctis Illius Posteris, praecipua animae humanae facultas; in qua si Imago Dei consistat, ut Smalcius fatetur, cogitur, sine Causa dubitavit, an respectu Animae conditus dicatur ad Imaginem Dei. At paulo supra ostendimus, Imaginem Dei in Adamo, non solum constitisse in anima, sed & in supernaturalibus Donis sapientiae, Sanctitatis, & Justitiae, quibus Illius Anima à Deo adornata est: Sexto, Mulierem ad Imaginem Dei non fuisse conditam, eo quod Dominium illud in Creaturas ei competere non videatur. At Contrarium plane evincitur, tum de Imagine in Genere, tum de utriusque Dominio in Creaturas. Gen. 1. 26, 27, 28. mulier subdita quidem fuit Marito suo; At Hoc minime impedivit, quo minus Dominium una cum marito suo haberet in caeteras Creaturas. Septimo; Adamum, & Filios ex eo natos, etsi in statu Innocentiae permansisset[?], molestis & onerosis laboribus futuros fuisse obnoxios. Addunt insuper, hujusmodi Onera, quae antea naturalia fuerunt, post lapsum facta fuisse necessaria. Ita enim Socinus——Non est in Concesso, non arandam & vertendam fuisse Terram, si Homo non peccasset; praesertim cum jam Orbis Terrarum Hominibus repletus fuisset, & alibi, quam in Horto illo Plerisque commorandum esset, maxime vero cum non desint, qui velint maledictione in illam Terram nil Aliud mali Illi attulisse, nisi quod ea, quae naturalia erant, necessaria effecerit; ita ut Homo ea non amplius tanquam naturalia, sed tanquam Delicti sui Poenas agnoscere debeat. Sic ille, De statu primi Hom. cap. 6. circa medium. Cæterum ex adverso, nos quidem legimus; Deum poluisse Adamum in Horto Edenis;ad eum colendum atque custodiendum, minime vero ad durum aliquem laborem subeundum. Exercitium itaque Adamo, exercitium iucundum atque salutare, impositum fuisse a Deo lubenter concedimus, at ingrati laboris onus & molestiam non sine Ratione denegamus. Hoc enim ei postea impositum est a Deo, in Poenam peccati, ut in sudore vultus sui Panem comederet. Gen. 3. 19. Qualis autem conditio Adami fuisset, si in statu innocentiæ perseveraßet, eadem sine dubio & Filiorum ipsius futura fuisset, in eodem statu perseverantium; sicut & eundem quoque statum hodie sortiuntur, post ipsius lapsum. Quod vero ipsorum sententiæ favet, qui nihil aliud mali in illa maledictione agnoscere voluit, quam quod ea necessaria effecerit, quæ prius erant Naturalia; in eo naturam calumniatur, Deumque Naturæ Authorem, quasi malorum istorum omnium ab origine causam, quæ peccato originem suam debent; cum Moses diserte testetur, omnia a Deo creata, fuisse ex sua natura Bona; & Felicitatis humanæ, non supplicii instrumenta: quodque labor iste durus ac molestus in quotidiano victu comparando; Herbæ agri in Cibum datæ; pro varietate[?] fructuum in Paradiso nascentium; & sterilitas Terræ maledictæ, quæ Spinas & Tribulos pro Frumento colenti reddebat; non utique naturæ, sed peccati effectus essent, nunquam & nusquam in hoc orbe nostro videndi, nisi peccatum istud hæc mala peperisset. Idcirco naturalia non sunt dicenda, quæ non naturæ primum conditæ, sed Prævaricationi primorum Parentum, originem suam debent: neque hoc duntaxat per peccatum istud effectum fuisse, ut necessaria fierent, quae antehac non erant necessaria, cum sine peccato isto praecedente ne fuissent quidem.
units.tr: 3. Reply to the second argument. On the other side, it is established that man was created in the image of God, which was without doubt the best and most perfect pattern. Moses likewise affirms in the same place that all the works of creation were good, and very good (Gen. 1. 31). Therefore man too was good among the rest, indeed above all the rest, by which he was more excellent than them. But Socinus answers in the same place that the passage does not speak of goodness of soul or of righteousness, but of fitness and suitability for what God had previously planned for himself. We grant indeed that, if we speak of God's works in general, most of them are in no way capable of any inner righteousness or goodness of soul. But if these words are referred to man, the very sense which Socinus attaches to them proves what we want. For it follows from this that man, from the origin of his creation, was endowed with inner goodness and furnished with such gifts of grace as would make him fit to serve God and to perform perfectly the obedience required by the laws given to him, which could not be rendered without such help. Fourth: that Adam and Eve were created mortal. But on the contrary we read that death was the punishment of sin, which God threatened to Adam on the condition of eating the forbidden fruit; and so it would not otherwise have come upon him. The Apostle also clearly affirms that through the sin of the first man death entered into the world, and so passed through, or spread to, all men (Rom. 5. 12). And before him the Hebrew sage says: God created man for incorruption [ἀφθαρσίᾳ], that is, in a state of incorruption, and made him the image of his own substance [ὑποστάσεως], that is, of his own proper nature [viz. by the reason of eternity]; but by the envy of the devil death entered into the world (Wisd. 2. 23, 24). We acknowledge, not unwillingly, that the first parents of the human race did not have bodies immortal from the principles of their own nature (for of themselves they were earthly, and animal, and therefore corruptible), but by a singular gift of God, which was granted to them from the beginning above the other living creatures formed from the earth; so that by virtue of this privilege they could not die, nor would they ever have actually undergone death, if they had remained in the first state of innocence. To this was added the fruit of the tree of life, by whose virtue it is not without reason thought that that immortality of their earthly body, which they had first received by God's gift, was to be promoted and preserved. Which the words of God himself also hint at obscurely, in Moses (Gen. 3. 22). Therefore when Socinus says that sin was the cause not of natural mortality but of necessary death, and when he affirms that the first man, even before the fall, was of a mortal nature, which proposition he labours to prove by arguments (Prelect. ch. 1), if he means only what we have just conceded, I truly do not know what adversary he has. Fifth: that the image of God, according to which man was created, consists solely in dominion over the creatures; or, as others say, chiefly in this, and less principally in right reason. Thus indeed Smalcius: It is not established whether man is said to be made in the image of God with respect to the soul, since it is read that he is so called with respect to reason, or rather to the power which God gave to man over all created things (which cannot be exercised without reason). (Reply to the New Monsters, part 2, ch. 24, p. 212). But surely right reason was once in Adam, and is still in all his posterity, the chief faculty of the human soul; and if the image of God consists in this, as Smalcius concedes, he is wrong to have doubted without cause whether man is said to be made in the image of God with respect to the soul. But a little above we have shown that the image of God in Adam consisted not only in the soul, but also in the supernatural gifts of wisdom, holiness and righteousness, with which his soul was adorned by God. Sixth: that woman was not created in the image of God, because that dominion over the creatures does not seem to belong to her. But the contrary is plainly proved, both concerning the image in general and concerning the dominion of both over the creatures (Gen. 1. 26, 27, 28). The woman was indeed subject to her husband; but this in no way prevented her from having dominion over the other creatures together with her husband. Seventh: that Adam and the sons born of him, even if they had remained in a state of innocence, would have been subject to troublesome and burdensome labours. They add further that such burdens, which were formerly natural, became necessary after the fall. For thus Socinus: It is not granted that the earth would not have had to be ploughed and turned if man had not sinned, especially since the whole world was already filled with men, and most would have had to dwell elsewhere than in that garden; and especially since there are not wanting those who wish that the curse on the earth brought it no other evil except that it made necessary what was natural, so that man ought no longer to acknowledge these things as natural, but as the penalties of his crime. Thus he (On the state of the first man, ch. 6, about the middle). On the other side, however, we read that God placed Adam in the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it, and certainly not to undergo any harsh toil. We therefore gladly concede that the exercise imposed on Adam by God was a pleasant and wholesome exercise, but we deny with good reason that it carried the burden and trouble of irksome labour. For this was afterwards laid upon him by God as a punishment for sin, that he should eat bread in the sweat of his face (Gen. 3. 19). But whatever the condition of Adam would have been had he persevered in the state of innocence, the same without doubt would have been the lot of his sons, persevering in the same state; just as they also now receive the same state after his fall. But as for those who wish to recognise nothing else of evil in that curse except that it made necessary what before were natural things, they calumniate nature in this, and make God the author of nature, as if he were the cause from the beginning of all those evils, which owe their origin to sin; whereas Moses expressly testifies that all things created by God were good in their own nature, and instruments of human happiness, not of punishment; and that this hard and burdensome labour in procuring daily food, the herbs of the field given for food, the variety of fruits growing in Paradise, and the barrenness of the cursed earth, which gave thorns and thistles to the man who tilled it instead of wheat, were effects not of nature but of sin, never and nowhere to be seen in this world of ours, unless that sin had brought forth these evils. Therefore those things are not to be called natural which owe their origin not to nature as first created, but to the transgression of the first parents; nor is it merely the case that through that sin things became necessary which before were not necessary, since without that preceding sin they would not even have existed.

units.la: §. 83. Secundo, De lapsu primorum Parentum, lapsusque istius consequentibus, haec affirmant. Primo; Totum genus humanum in Adamo non peccasse, seu peccati reatum non contraxisse. Ita Socinus, explicans istud D. Pauli Rom. 5. 12. Apostolus, inquit, nequaquam affirmat, in Adamo omnes peccasse. De statu primi Hom. cap. 10. At pace Socini, Apostolus ibidem affirmat, peccatum introiisse in mundum per Adamum, mortemque per istud peccatum, atque ita omnes Homines pertransiisse, in quo, seu eo quod, omnes peccaverunt. Si autem vertamus, [in quo] verba ex se manifesta sunt, quod omnes Adami Posteri in Adamo peccaverint: sin [eo quod] idem sensus exinde colligitur. Nemini enim ignotum est, Infantes quamplurimos quotidie mori, qui in suis ipsorum Personis nihil unquam peccaverunt, neque actu peccare potuerunt; imo (quod plus est, & os ultra obstruit Socino) qui originalis alicujus peccati nulla ex parte rei sunt, ex ipsius sententia. Itaque cum in hos quoque mors pertransierit, eo quod & ipsi, una cum caeteris, peccaverint; necesse omnino est, ut Adami peccatum, de quo Apostolus illic loquitur, illis imputetur in mortem. Hoc vero ex sequentibus clarius innotescet. Siquidem non longe post affirmat, per inobedientiam unius [sc. Adami] multos factos fuisse peccatores, v. 19. ubi loquitur de cunctis Adami posteris. Et paulo prius asserit — Mortem illam, quae introducta fuit per Adami peccatum, vim suam sive Dominium exercuisse in eos etiam, qui non peccaverant ad exemplar Transgressionis[?] Adami. v. 14. in quorum numero, si non soli, ceteræ præcipui sunt illi infantes, qui ante usum Rationis morientes, nullius actualis peccati rei esse potuerant per ætatem; at interim geniti erant, intra Sethi post lapsum, ad imaginem & similitudinem primi Parentis. Quinimo, & experientia quotidiana satis demonstrat, cæteras Pœnas, quæ iunt peccati solitus effectus, in omne Genus humanum exinde redundasse. Neque hinc Injustitiæ, aut nimiæ Rigoris Deus ullo modo argui potest, cum nihil usitatius sit in statu civili, quam ut Perduellio parentum aliudve quovis gravioris notæ flagitium, posteris imputetur, etsi nondum natis, in Dedecus & Damnum totius Familiæ. Legimus item, quod Achanis Sacrilegium, & Davidis Crimen in agendo censu totius Israelis, celeriter in damnum integræ Reipublicæ; & Principis erratum toti populo imputabatur in Pœnam. Cæterum Adamus, non solum totius humani Generis princeps erat, ratione dignitatis & Regiminis, sed & parens Communis ratione naturæ, utpote, in cujus lumbis totum delituit, & ut loquitur Damascenus, [illegible, ~12 letters] virtute quadam seminali continebatur. Unde & Apostolus alibi ait, sicut in Adamo omnes moriuntur, sic & in Christo omnes vivificabuntur. 1 Cor. 15. 22.
units.tr: §. 83. Secondly, concerning the fall of the first parents, and the consequences of that fall, they affirm the following. First: that the whole human race did not sin in Adam, or did not contract the guilt of sin. Thus Socinus, explaining that passage of St Paul (Rom. 5. 12): The Apostle, he says, by no means affirms that all sinned in Adam. (On the state of the first man, ch. 10). But with all respect to Socinus, the Apostle affirms in that same place that sin entered into the world through Adam, and death through that sin, and so passed through to all men, in whom, or because, all have sinned. If we translate the words in whom, the expression is plain in itself, that all Adam's posterity sinned in Adam; but if because, the same sense is drawn from it. For it is known to no one that very many infants die every day who never sinned in their own persons, and were not able to sin actually; indeed (which is more, and stops the mouth of Socinus) who are in no way guilty of any original sin, according to his own opinion. Therefore, since death has passed through to these as well, because they too, together with the others, have sinned, it is entirely necessary that the sin of Adam, of which the Apostle speaks there, be imputed to them for death. This will become clearer from what follows. For not long afterwards he affirms that through the disobedience of one [namely, Adam] many were made sinners (v. 19), where he is speaking of all Adam's posterity. And a little before he asserts that the death which was introduced through Adam's sin exercised its power or dominion even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression (v. 14). Among these, if not only these, are especially those infants who, dying before the use of reason, could not by reason of their age be guilty of any actual sin; yet they were born, after the fall, within the line of Seth, in the image and likeness of the first parent. Indeed, daily experience sufficiently demonstrates that the other punishments, which are the usual effects of sin, have spread from this source over the whole human race. Nor can God be charged with injustice or excessive severity in this, since nothing is more usual in civil society than that the treason of parents, or any other crime of graver note, is imputed to their posterity, even though not yet born, to the shame and loss of the whole family. We likewise read that the sacrilege of Achan and the crime of David in taking the census of all Israel were quickly imputed to the loss of the whole commonwealth; and the error of the prince was imputed to the whole people for punishment. Moreover, Adam was not only the prince of the whole human race, by reason of dignity and government, but also the common parent by reason of nature, inasmuch as the whole race lay hidden in his loins, and, as Damascene puts it, [words illegible in the scan] was contained by a certain seminal virtue. Hence the Apostle also says elsewhere: as in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive (1 Cor. 15. 22).

units.la: Secundo; Imaginem istam Divinam & similitudinem Dei, ad quam Homo primum creatus est, post peccatum in eo remansisse. Soc: Prælect: Cap. 3. Smalc: cont: Frantz: Disp: 7. Ad quod probandum duo potissimum S. Scripturæ loca adducunt, viz. Gen. 9. 6. Jac. 3. 9. in quibus Homo, post lapsum, dicitur factus ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei. Nos è contra, etsi fateamur istam Imaginem Dei in Homine, in qua ab origine conditus est, non penitus • delētam[?] fuisse per peccatum, deformatam tamen asserimus, atque diminutam. Homo quidem adhuc retinet Animam spiritualem, rationalem, immortalem, ac divinorum capacem; liberum item arbitrium in quamplurimis, & aliquale Dominium in Creaturas. At Scriptura simul & experientia testantur, quod humanum Genus, postquam à Deo per peccatum defecit, à primaevo statu multum degeneraverit. Quippe hunc degenerem statum plus satis ostendunt, multiplex Ignorantia mentis nostrae connata, & Pronitas ad errores amplectendos; Perversitas & obstinatio voluntatis qua nata est in voluntatem niti; effrenes Passionum impetus, & exleges Affectuum motus; Torpor, & Ignavia summa, in Bono prosequendo; virésque infirmae ad resistendum malo, ut & ad edomandos rebelles affectus, intraque modum coercendos. Huc accedit Rebellio brutorum Animantium ad extra, quorum pleraque palam abjecisse videntur istud Hominis Dominium, cui primitus subdebantur; reliqua vero, non nisi multo labore, studioque assiduo cicurantur, atque aegre admodum in officio continentur. Hos defectus atque morbos naturae humanae, infelicem primi peccati Sobolem, satis adverterunt ipsi quoque Philosophi atque Poetae Gentilium; qui & de iisdem saepe conquesti sunt, etsi veram illorum Causam ignoraverint. At S. Scriptura, & morbos hos, & morborum originem, crebro clareque indicat; quibus & Remedia suppeditat. Siquidem, pro Dei Imagine, ad quam Adamus primum Creatus fuit, Imaginem Adami post lapsum memorat, secundum quam Sethus genitus est. Gen. 5. 3. Tenebras mentis humanae connatas demonstrat. Item, Φρόνημα σαρκός, seu quod Caro nostra sapit. Rom. 8. 7. [illegible, ~10 letters] quæ Cogitationibus nostris allubescunt. Eph. 2. 3. veterem Hominem. Rom. 6. 6. Concupiscentiam innatam. Jac. 1. 14, 15. Figmentum humani Cordis, malum ab ipla Juventute. Gen. 8. 21. & Carnem Spiritui obluctantem. Gal: 5. 17. Ipsam Conceptionem nostram Iniquitatis labe aspergit. Psal: 51. 5. Onagri pullo Hominem assimilat, cum primum generatur. Job: 11. 12. & Stultitiam in Corde Pueri colligatam esse affirmat, quam virga Correctionis expelli necesse est. Prov: 22. 15. Denique asserit Hominem animalem, (hoc est, Spiritu Dei destitutum) ii.orum omnino incapacem esse, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, quia Stultitia ipsi videntur. 1, Cor: 2. 14. Eadem quoque Scriptura, Illuminationis gratiam, mentisque per Spiritum Dei renovatæ necessitatem passim inculcat, quibus hæc Dei Imago ab origine impressa, & posthac multum deturpata, denuo paulatim instauratur. Tertio; Adamum, per primum illud peccatum, se ipsamque naturam non corrupisse. Ita Socinus, in Prælect: cap: 4. Unum illud Peccatum per se, non modo miversos Posteros, sed ne ipsum quidem Adamum, corrumpendi vim habuit. & Catech. Rac. cap. 10 pag. 195. lapsu Adæ, cum unus Actus fuerit, vim eam, qua depravare ipsam naturam Adami, multo minus vero Posterorum ipsius posset, habere non potuit. At plane contrarium ex Antecedentibus liquet, quæ malignos istius peccati effectus plus satis manifestant, tum in Adami Persona spectandos, tum in ipsius posteris, qui ex illius natura post lapsum participarunt, præcipue vero, in persona ipsius Adami. Per istud enim factus est, ex Recto pravus, e Justo Injustus, e Puro & Sancto Pollutus, e libero Servus peccati, e Dei Filio Satanæ mancipium. Pudor item ex eo facto incuss ei, è conspecta nuditate; Terrorque ex appropinquantis Dei voce, conicii peccatoris Aures feriente, satis ostendunt, quantum in pejus mutatus fuerit, & vel in suo ipsius conspectu Deformis; quamque tristi experimento didicerit istud Boni, malique discrimen, cujus scientiam Diabolus illusorie & fallaciter ipsi promiserat; Boni sc. discrimen, quod paulo antea ex Dei Creatoris Dono possederat; & mali, quod sua ipsius culpa sibi modo conciverat. Idcirco, mirum mihi videtur, quomodo Socinus, ejusque Discipuli asserere possint, per unicum Actum malum, peccantis naturam corrumpi non posse, multoque minus ad alios derivari; cum Contrarium saepe spectetur, tum in natura, tum in moribus, variisque experimentis indubitate probetur. Nam satis constat lepram, Pestem, aliosque morbos contagiosos, unico Contactu vel Afflatu, universam humani Corporis Temperiem corrumpere, & ad alios quoque Tabem suam, virulque derivare. Idem constat de telis veneno tinctis, quae vulnerati Cutim penetrant; de noxiis vaporibus, qui ore, naribusque attrahuntur; & de certorum morborum feminibus, quae in Parentum Corporibus delitescentia, ad Sobolem suam extraduce propagantur. Necnon, Idem constat, sicut in natura, sic etiam in moribus. Unicus enim gravioris illagitii Actus, non solum peccantis Personam flagitiosam reddit ac denominat (viz. adulterum, Homicidam, Furem, Perjurum, Transfugam, Perduellem) sed & habitum vitiosum inchoat, totamque Hominis naturam eo usque depravat, ut multo pronior reddatur ad idem Flagitium denuo perpetrandum. Porro, si unicus Rebellionis actus Angelos Apostatas eo usque corruperit, ut exinde naturam habeant insanabiliter[?]: majam[?] ; quid vetat afferere, unicum primi Hominis peccatum adeo corrupisse ipsius naturam, ut non, nisi Gratia Divina de novo collata, ad primævam Dei imaginem, & pristinæ perfectionis integritatem, instaurari possit. Quarto, Mortem Hominis in posteros ab Adamo derivatam, suisse potius naturæ debitum, quam peccati Pœnam. Vult enim Socinus, Adamum mori quidem potuisse, & suapte natura debuisse, nisi Gratia divina supernaturaliter conservatus fuisset ; non tamen omnino necessarium fuisse ut moreretur, cum Deus ejusmodi Gratia illum omnino privare decrevisset. Sic enim ille, De statu primi hominis — Non aliud malum ex primo illo Delicto ad Posteros omnes necessario manavit, quod moriendi omnimoda necessitas ; non quidem ex ipsius Delicti vi, sed quia, cum jam Homo natura mortalis esset, ob Delictum illud suæ naturali mortalitati relictum essi ; quodque naturale erat, in Delinquentis Pœnam prorsus necessarium est factum. At e contra, Scriptura multa nobis observanda proponit, unde non difficile est concludere, Adamum in statu Immortalitatis creatum fuisse, nec mortem potuisse subire nisi Dei mandatum in esu fructus vetiti violasset ; adeoq; mortem inde consequentem, non fuisse naturæ debitum, proprie loquendo, sed genuinam peccati sobolem. Quæ autem Scriptura in hac Re nobis perpendenda offert, hæc fere sunt. Comminatio mortis Adamo à Deo intentatæ, ex suppositione fructus vetiti ab ipso comesti. Gen. 2. 17. Ubi mors ex conditione peccati istius admittendi denunciatur, non ex conditione naturæ eventura prædicitur. Deinde, mortis decretum peremptorium, non nisi post, & propter peccatum illud admissum — Quia comedisti de arbore, ex qua præcepe[?]ram Tibi, ne comederes in sudore vultus tui vesceris Pane, donec revertaris in Terram, de qua sumptus es; nam pulvis es, & in Pulverem reverteris. Gen. 3. 17, 19. Item, Apostoli duplex Assertio; viz. Per unum Hominem, peccatum in mundum intoivit[?], & per peccatum mors. Rom. 5. 12. & rursus, Stipendium peccati mors. Rom. 6. ult. Denique, primi & secundi Adami Collatio, à quorum primo, lapsus, Reatus, Infirmitas, Ignominia, Condemnatio, mors: à secundo autem; Gratiae Donum, vires firmae, Justitia & obedientia, Absolutio à peccato, Incorruptio & Immortalitas, Gloria, vitaque aeterna, derivatur. vid. Rom. 5. 15. 2[?]. & 1 Cor. 15. 21. 22; 43. 49; 53, 54. Huc adde conditionem Infantium, qui etsi nunquam ad similitudinem Praevaricationis Adami peccarunt, Morti tamen redduntur obnoxii, Illamque actu subeunt, ob reatum originalis istius Peccati, quod Ipsis Adami causa imputatur. Quinto; Mulierem, etiamsi non peccasset, cum Dolore parituram fuisse. Ita Socinus Atque contra, ex Mosis historia patet, hunc Dolorem, post lapsum demum, à Deo Mulieri denunciatum fuisse; idque, in poenam peccati Gen. 3. 16. Sexto; Terram etiam ante lapsum spinas atque tribulos produxisse, & producturam fuisse, si Homo nunquam peccasset. Quod etsi verum sit, indefinite loquendo, certum tamen ex adverso est, horum productionem & incrementum, prout Deus Adamo interminatus est post lapsum, esse partem Maledictionis istius, quam Ipsi, posteriique Ipsius denunciavit. Gen. 3. 17, 18. Sicut & Terrae sterilitatem à Caino colendae, quam ei postea comminatus est, in vindictam Fratricidii. Gen. 4. 12. Utcunque ergo concedamus, spinas & tribulos, ab origine Creationis è Terra productos fuisse, & è Seminibus suis, una cum cæteris vegetabilibus, in perpetuum producendos, (ut certe suos usus habent, hominibus non ignotos ) haud tamen difficultendum est, eos & fuisse & esse, tam maledictionis divinæ diros effectus, quam genuinos Terræ Fructus, si nimiam Illorum copiam Spectemus, variasque noxas Graminibus, Herbis, & Segetibus illatas, quibus obrutis, atque suffocatis, Agricolarum labores irritos reddunt, Tellurique cultissimæ sterilitatem inducunt.
units.tr: Second; that this image of God and likeness of God, in which man was first created, remained in him after the sin. Socinus, Prælectiones, chap. 3; Smalcius, against Franz, disp. 7. To prove this they bring forward chiefly two passages of Holy Scripture, namely Gen. 9. 6 and Jas. 3. 9, in which man, after the fall, is said to have been made in the image and likeness of God. We, on the contrary, though we admit that the image of God in which man was created from the beginning was not wholly blotted out by sin, nevertheless affirm that it was defaced and diminished. Man still retains a spiritual, rational and immortal soul, capable of divine things, and likewise free will in very many matters, and some measure of dominion over the creatures. But Scripture and experience alike testify that the human race, after it fell away from God through sin, has greatly degenerated from its original state. Indeed, this degenerate condition is more than sufficiently shown by the manifold ignorance of our mind, innate to us, and its proneness to embrace errors; by the perversity and obstinacy of the will, which is born to strive against what is willed; by the unbridled onslaughts of the passions and the lawless movements of the affections; by the great torpor and sloth in pursuing the good; and by the feebleness of our strength to resist evil, and to subdue rebellious affections and restrain them within bounds. To this is added the rebellion of the brute animals against us, many of which have plainly cast off that dominion of man to which they were at first subject; while the rest are tamed only with much labour and constant care, and are kept in service with great difficulty. These defects and diseases of human nature, the unhappy offspring of the first sin, have been sufficiently noticed even by the philosophers and poets of the Gentiles, who often complained of them, although they did not know their true cause. But Scripture, both frequently and clearly, indicates these diseases and their origin, and at the same time supplies remedies for them. For in place of God's image, after which Adam was first created, it mentions the image of Adam after the fall, according to which Seth was begotten (Gen. 5. 3); it shows the darkness of the human mind to be innate (cf. Rom. 8. 7, "the mind of the flesh" [Φρόνημα σαρκός], that is, what our flesh savours); [...] which things are pleasing to our thoughts (Eph. 2. 3); it speaks of the old man (Rom. 6. 6); of innate concupiscence (Jas. 1. 14, 15); of the imagination of the human heart being evil from youth (Gen. 8. 21); and of the flesh striving against the Spirit (Gal. 5. 17). It sprinkles even our very conception with the stain of iniquity (Ps. 51. 5); it likens man, when he is first born, to the colt of a wild ass (Job 11. 12); and it affirms that foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child, which must be driven out by the rod of correction (Prov. 22. 15). Lastly, it declares that the natural man (that is, one destitute of the Spirit of God) is wholly incapable of the things of the Spirit of God, because they seem foolish to him (1 Cor. 2. 14). Scripture also repeatedly urges the grace of illumination and the necessity of a mind renewed by the Spirit of God, by which this image of God, impressed from the beginning and afterwards much defaced, is gradually restored anew. Third; that Adam, by that first sin, did not corrupt himself or his nature. Thus Socinus, in the Prælectiones, chap. 4: That one sin, in itself, had the power to corrupt not only all his posterity but not even Adam himself. And in the Racovian Catechism, chap. 10, p. 195: Since the fall of Adam was a single act, it could not have had that power which could deprave the very nature of Adam, much less that of his posterity. But the contrary plainly appears from what has been said above, which shows the baleful effects of this sin more than enough, both as they are to be seen in the person of Adam himself and in his posterity, who after the fall partook of his nature; and especially in the person of Adam himself. For through that sin he was made from upright to crooked, from just to unjust, from pure and holy to polluted, from free to a slave of sin, and from a son of God to a bondslave of Satan. The shame which came upon him from that deed, when he saw his nakedness, and the terror at the voice of the approaching God striking the sinner's ears, sufficiently show how much he had been changed for the worse, and how deformed he was even in his own sight; and how, by bitter experience, he learned that distinction between good and evil whose knowledge the devil had promised him deceptively and falsely: namely, the distinction between good, which he had possessed a little before as the gift of God the Creator, and evil, which he had now brought upon himself by his own fault. Therefore it seems to me strange how Socinus and his disciples can assert that by a single evil act the nature of the one who sins cannot be corrupted, much less passed on to others; when the contrary is often seen, both in nature and in morals, and is proved beyond doubt by various experiences. For it is well known that leprosy, plague and other contagious diseases corrupt the whole temperament of the human body by a single touch or breath, and pass their taint and poison on to others as well. The same is known of weapons smeared with poison, which penetrate the skin of the wounded; of noxious vapours drawn in by the mouth and nostrils; and of the seeds of certain diseases, which, lurking in the bodies of parents, are propagated to their offspring. And the same is likewise known in the moral sphere. For a single act of a more serious crime not only makes the person who commits it wicked and gives him the name (as adulterer, murderer, thief, perjurer, deserter, traitor), but also begins a vicious habit and so depraves the whole nature of the man that he becomes far more prone to commit the same crime again. Further, if a single act of rebellion has so corrupted the apostate angels that they have thenceforth a nature incurably depraved, why should it be forbidden to affirm that the single sin of the first man so corrupted his nature that it cannot be restored to the primal image of God and the integrity of its former perfection except by grace newly bestowed from God? Fourth, that the death of man derived from Adam to his posterity was rather a debt of nature than a punishment of sin. For Socinus wishes that Adam could indeed have died, and by his nature ought to have died, unless he had been preserved supernaturally by divine grace; yet that it was not wholly necessary for him to die, since God had decided to deprive him altogether of such grace. For he says thus, concerning the state of the first man: No other evil necessarily flowed from that first offence to all posterity, namely the absolute necessity of dying; not indeed by the force of the offence itself, but because, since man was already mortal by nature, that natural mortality was left to him on account of that offence; and what was natural has been made wholly necessary as the punishment of the offender. But on the contrary, Scripture sets before us many things to be observed, from which it is not difficult to conclude that Adam was created in a state of immortality and could not have undergone death unless he had violated God's command by eating the forbidden fruit; and therefore the death that followed was not, properly speaking, a debt of nature, but the genuine offspring of sin. The things which Scripture offers us to weigh in this matter are roughly these. First, the threat of death which God uttered to Adam was made on the supposition that he ate the forbidden fruit (Gen. 2. 17). There death is announced as the consequence of the condition of committing that sin, not foretold as the outcome of his nature. Next, the peremptory decree of death came only after, and on account of, that sin committed: "Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life... In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Gen. 3. 17, 19). Likewise there is the Apostle's twofold assertion: by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin (Rom. 5. 12); and again, the wages of sin is death (Rom. 6, last verse). Finally, there is the comparison of the first and second Adam: from the first come guilt, weakness, shame, condemnation, death; but from the second come the gift of grace, firm strength, righteousness and obedience, absolution from sin, incorruption and immortality, glory and eternal life (see Rom. 5. 15, 21; and 1 Cor. 15. 21, 22, 43, 49, 53, 54). Add to this the condition of infants, who, although they have never sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression, are nevertheless made liable to death and actually undergo it, on account of the guilt of that original sin, which is imputed to them through the cause of Adam himself. Fifth; that the woman, even if she had not sinned, would have brought forth with pain. Thus Socinus. But on the contrary, it is clear from the history of Moses that this pain was announced by God to the woman only after the fall, and that it was announced as a punishment of sin (Gen. 3. 16). Sixth; that the earth too, before the fall, had produced thorns and thistles, and would have produced them even if man had never sinned. Although this may be true when spoken indefinitely, it is nevertheless certain, on the contrary, that the production and increase of these, as God threatened Adam after the fall, is part of that curse which he pronounced upon him and upon his posterity (Gen. 3. 17, 18); just as the barrenness of the ground to be tilled by Cain was also threatened to him afterwards, in vengeance for the murder of his brother (Gen. 4. 12). Therefore, however we may grant that thorns and thistles were brought forth from the earth from the beginning of creation, and are to be produced from their seeds in perpetuity along with the other plants (as indeed they have their uses, not unknown to men), it must nevertheless be admitted that they both were and are as dire effects of the divine curse as they are genuine products of the earth, if we consider their excessive abundance and the various harms they inflict on grasses, herbs and crops; by burying and choking these, they render the labours of farmers vain and bring utter barrenness upon the most carefully tilled soil.

units.la: §. 84. Tertio; de peccato Originali, multum adversa docent Fidei Catholicæ. Originale vero dictum est, tum quod à primo Homine suam originem traxerit, tum quod Unicuique nostrum ab ipsa origine connatum sit. Consistit autem, partim in carentia Justitiæ istius Originalis, quæ Adamo concreata est; partim, in pravitate ista morbosa vitiatæ Naturæ, quam ab Ipso derivamus, & qua, tum averti reddimur à Bono, tum ad malum proclives; eaque de Causa, in Satanæ Regno constituti, & æternæ Damnationi obnoxii. At Sociniani hæc Omnia pro Fabulis inanibus habent, atque irritis humani Ingenii Commentis. Nam Primo Socinus dicit, Non fuisse in primo Homine Justitiam illam originalem; ac proinde, originale Peccatum non consistere in ipsius Justitiæ carentia, quæ fiat, ut Homo naturaliter, nisi Dei Gratia superveniente juvetur, nihil nisi errare possit, id est, contra Dei legem committere. Prælect: cap. 4. At è contra, Christus expresse dicit, nos denuo, sive desuper nasci debere, & ex Aqua atque Spiritu regenerari, ut idonei reddamur ad introeundum in Regnum Dei. Item, Quod, quicquid ex Carne natum est, Caro sit; Illud vero solum Spiritus sit, quod ex Spiritu natum est. Jo. 3. 3, 56. Apostolus vero affirmat, nos renovari debere in Spiritu Mentis nostrae, & novum Hominem induere, qui creatus est, secundum Deum, in Justitia & Sanctitate vera. Eph. 4. 23, 24. & cum alibi, dum Collationem instituit inter legem Mosaicam, & Christi Evangelium, appellasset Hoc, Ministerium Spiritus, atque Justitiae, haec subinfert sc. nos in Imaginem Domini transformari; à Gloria in Gloriam, sicut à Spiritu Domini. 2. Cor. 3. ult. Petrus item asserit, nos participes fieri divinae naturae, virtute Promissionum Evangelicarum, cum ex ista Corruptione evasimus, quae est in mundo per concupiscentiam. 2. Pet. 1. 4. Haec autem, & Alia plura, quae prius attulimus, quid Aliud significant, quam privationem originalis Justitiae, nobis omnibus connatam; quam idcirco restaurari oportet per Gratiam Christi in Evangelio oblatam; ut hoc modo capaces efficiamur intrandi in Regnum Coelorum, dum eidem Christo conformes efficimur in Gratia, quem hic idem Petrus, Sancti illius & Justi Titulo, alibi insignire amat, sc. in Concione sua ad Judaeos habita. Act. 3. 14.
units.tr: §. 84. Third, the Socinians hold many views that are strongly opposed to the Catholic faith, namely about original sin. It is called original because it both took its origin from the first man and was born with each of us from our very origin. It consists partly in the lack of that original justice which was created together with Adam, and partly in that diseased corruption of nature which we derive from him, by which we are both turned away from good and inclined to evil, and for that reason are placed under the reign of Satan and liable to eternal damnation. But the Socinians regard all this as empty fables and worthless inventions of the human mind. For first, Socinus says: There was no original justice in the first man, and therefore original sin does not consist in the lack of that justice, so that man, unless he is helped by the grace of God coming upon him, can do nothing but err, that is, commit sin against the law of God. Praelect. ch. 4. On the contrary, Christ expressly says that we must be born again, or from above, and be regenerated of water and the Spirit, so that we may be fit to enter the kingdom of God. Likewise, that whatever is born of the flesh is flesh, but only what is born of the Spirit is spirit. John 3:3, 5-6. The Apostle affirms that we must be renewed in the spirit of our mind and put on the new man, which was created according to God in righteousness and true holiness. Eph. 4:23, 24. And elsewhere, when he compares the law of Moses with the Gospel of Christ, having called the one the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness, he adds that we are transformed into the image of the Lord, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. 2 Cor. 3, last verse. Peter likewise asserts that we become partakers of the divine nature, by the power of the promises of the Gospel, once we have escaped that corruption which is in the world through lust. 2 Pet. 1:4. Now these things, and many others that we have already cited, what else do they signify than the privation of the original justice, born with all of us; which must therefore be restored through the grace of Christ offered in the Gospel, so that in this way we may be made capable of entering the kingdom of heaven, while we are made conformable in grace to that same Christ, whom this same Peter, in his sermon to the Jews, loves to honour with the title of Holy and Just. Acts 3:14.

units.la: Secundo; Naturam humanam, per primum Adami peccatum nullatenus corruptam fuisse atque vitiatam. Vid. Smalc. cont. Frantz. disp. 2. Oftor. Instit. cap. 2. Socinus quoque affirmat—Ex peccato illo primo Parentis, nullam labem aut pravitatem universo humano Generi necessario ingenitam esse, sive insitam quodammodo fuisse. Praeleet. cap. 4. Catech. item Rac. haec habet—Peccatum originis nullum prorsus est; quare nec liberum Arbitrium vitiare potuit—Lapsum vero Adami ipsi Ipsiusve posteris, in Poenam irrogatum fuisse (sc. ad naturam ipsorum depravandam) nec Scriptura docet, uti supra expofuimus[?]; & Deum illum, qui omnis aequitatis Fons est, incredibile prorsus est Id facere voluisse. Cap. 10. p. 195. Et sane minime mirum est, Hoc ab illis negari, qui negant ipsius Adami Naturam per illud suum peccatum ullatenus vitiatam fuisse. At è contra, praeter loca S. Scripturae antehac à nobis allata, quae hunc Morbum, vitiumque Naturae corruptae satis indicant, & Remedii necessitatem simul ostendunt, non abs re erit & alia quaedam afferre, quae in libro Jobi occurrunt; viz. Quomodo potest Homo justificari apud Deum? aut quomodo ille purus esse potest, qui ex muliere natus est? Iob. 25. 4. Quis potest educere mundum ex immundo? ne unus quidem, cap. 14. 4. ubi loquitur Jobus de Homine in Genere, & indefinite, quicunque sc. ex muliere natus est; ut patet v. 1. vet. lat. quae & vulgata versio dicitur, sic explicat — Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine? nonne Tu qui solus es? Sept. vero Interp. sic — Quis purus erit à Sordibus? Ne unus quidem, etsi unus dies sit vita ejus super Terram. Atque iterum in eodem libro legimus — Quid est Homo, ut mundus sit? & natus ex muliere, ut Justus sit? Ecce in Sanctis suis fiduciam non ponit; imo, Coeli non sunt mundi in conspectu ejus. Quanto magis abominabilis, & putidus est Homo, qui imbibit Iniquitatem, ut Aquam? Cap: 15. 14. 16. Quinimo, Hoc idem ab ethnicis agnoscitur, ut quid experientia compertum, etsi quoad Causam ignotum. Quod vel illud Horatii ostendit — Vitiis nemo sine nascitur, optimus ille est, Qui minimis urgetur — Neque hoc naturae humanae vitium ulla ratione Deo imputandum est, ( ut Sociniani invidiose objiciunt ) sed primis Parentibus. Deus enim nullius Mali Author est, sed isti Parentes nostri, ex suo peccato Gratiam Dei perdiderunt, tum pro se, tum pro posteris suis, qua Rectrice Animæ sublata omnes illius Facultates multum debilitatæ sunt, atque confusæ, harmonia pulcherrima in Discordiam versa est, Ordo perturbatus, & Rebellio Affectuum excitata est contra sanæ Rationis dictata, denique Imago Dei Homini primitus impressa, si minus in totum deleta, saltem valde deformata est; adeo ut posthac Adamus Sethum genuisse dicatur (reliquamque proinde sobolem[?]) non juxta Imaginem Dei primævam, sed suam Ipsius, hoc pacto sædatam, mutilamque & primigenia Pulchritudine atque Integritate omnino destitutam. Tertio; Concupiscentiam, sive proclivitatem ad peccandum, ( in qua partim consistit peccatum originis) in omnibus Hominibus naturaliter non esse, neque Hominum istorum, quibus inest peccatum, proprie dici posse. Sic enim Socinus —De mala illa Cupiditate & ad peccandum promitate, licet in plerisque sit, non tamen affirmare possumus, eam in Omnibus prorsus esse. Cum ad Culpam constituendam propria voluntas ejus, qui in Culpa futurus est, omnino requiratur, nullo modo videtur dici posse, in Homine dum nascitur, ullam Culpam locum habere posse, cum Is propria voluntatis tunc nullum usum habeat, nec antea habere potuerit. Cupiditas ista, & ad peccandum Promptitas, cum conjunctam secum Hominis ipsius, in quo est, Culpam non habeat, ejus peccatum proprie dici non potest. Sic ille, Prælect. cap 4.
