At è contra, Apostolus appellat hanc Concupiscentiam, sive proclivitatem ad peccandum, peccatum in se habitans, & legem membrorum militantem adversus legem mentis, & se reddentem Captivum legi peccati. Rom. 7. 17, 18. 18, 23. & agnoscit Eandem, non solum remanere, sed & vires suas in Piis atque Regenitis subinde exerere, contra S. Spiritus motiones, ut agere non possint quod maxime vellent. Gal. 5. 17. Constat item, irregularem hanc Concupiscentiam, qua Genus humanum, ut olim, sic & nunc Dierum, adeo proclive redditur ad peccandum, non fuisse in primis Parentibus ante lapsum (neque enim constiterat cum ista Dei Imagine, juxta quam creati erant) sed per, & post lapsum, originem suam cepisse, & ab eo tempore totum Genus humanum pervasisse, ut fontem quendam sive Fomitem omnis actualis peccati, quod exinde ab Hominibus admissum est. ita Jacobus Unusquisque[?] tentatur, cum a propria Concupiscentia abstrahitur, & inescatur. Deinde Concupiscentia, cum conceperit, parit peccatum; Peccatum vero, cum consummatum fuerit, parit mortem. Cap: 1. 14, 15. Paulus demum affirmat, hanc Concupiscentiam (quam φρόνημα σαρκός[?] vocat. Rom. 8. 7.) esse inimicitiam erga Deum, quia non subjicitur legi Dei, neque subjici potest. Quamvis ergo non imputetur piis atque Regenitis in peccatum, quoties pravis ipsius motibus non consentiunt, ex se tamen, & sua natura peccatum est, in quantum legi Dei adversatur. Peccatum enim nihil aliud est, quam ἀνομία, id est, Aversio seu Discrepantia à lege Dei, Joanne Apostolo definiente. 1 Epist. cap. 3. v. 4. Quarto; Pronitatem ad peccandum, quae in humano Genere hodie conspicitur, non à primo illo Peccato, seu ab illo primi hominis peccandi Actu, statim exortam fuisse, sed continuatis post illud Peccatum peccandi Actibus, peccandi Habitum Homines paulatim contraxisse, Jeque ipsos corrupisse, atque ita Corruptionis femina per Propagationem ad posteros transmisisse. Ita Socinus in lib. Quod Regn. Pol. Cap. 5. & Praelect. Cap. 4. Huic suffragantur Ostor. Instit. Cap. 34. Smalc. cont. Frantz. Disp. 2. & Catech: Rac. Cap. 10. At é contra, praeter loca Scripturae prius adducta, experientia quotidiana testatur, etiam Pueros, ante habitum peccandi repetitis Actibus contractum, esse pronos ad malum, refractarios autem & indociles, ineptos & ignavos, ad Boni Disciplinam atque Praxin; monitis frequentibus, exemplisque pulcherrimis ad imitandum propositis, frustra obstantibus. Constat item, homines non indifferenter se habere ad Bonum & malum, qualiter se primi Parentes habebant in statu Innocentiae, sed ad malum multo proniores esse; quae pronitas in Actum peccati erumpere parata est, quoties à Tentatione congrua extrinsecus solicitatur. Denique, Ratio nobis dictat, vitiosos Animi Habitus, qui morbi quidam spirituales sunt, haud natos esse, instar morborum Corporis, à Parentibus ex traduce derivari. Qui & experientia astipulatur, quae non raro nobis exhibet Filios ad vitium admodum proclives, è spectatissimae virtutis parentibus prognatos; & ex adverso, è Parentibus vitiosissimis Filios probatissimae indolis, bonae Disciplinae capacissimos, & (si ad alios plerosque conferantur) ad omnigenam virtutem comparandam quasi factos, seu potius natos.
units.tr: Second; human nature was in no way corrupted or vitiated by the first sin of Adam. See Smalc. against Frantz, disp. 2; Ostorod, Institutes, ch. 2. Socinus also affirms: From that first sin of the parent, no stain or depravity necessarily inborn in, or in some way implanted in, the whole human race has come. Praelect. ch. 4. The Racovian Catechism likewise says this: Original sin is absolutely nothing; therefore it could not corrupt free will. But the fall of Adam was not imposed as a punishment on Adam himself or on his posterity (namely, to deprave their nature), nor does Scripture teach this, as we have set out above[?]; and it is utterly incredible that God, who is the fount of all equity, wished to do this. Ch. 10, p. 195. And indeed it is no wonder that this is denied by those who deny that the nature of Adam himself was in any way vitiated by his sin. On the contrary, apart from the passages of Holy Scripture cited by us earlier, which sufficiently indicate this disease and vice of corrupted nature and at the same time show the necessity of a remedy, it will not be out of place to bring forward certain other passages which occur in the book of Job, namely: How can a man be justified before God? Or how can he be pure who is born of a woman? Job 25:4. Who can bring the clean out of the unclean? Not one, ch. 14:4, where Job speaks of man in general and indefinitely, whoever, that is, is born of a woman; as is clear from verse 1. The Old Latin version, which is also called the Vulgate, explains it thus: Who can make clean what is conceived from unclean seed? Is it not You, who alone are? But the Septuagint thus: Who will be pure from filth? Not one, even if his life upon the earth were a single day. And again in the same book we read: What is man, that he should be clean? And he who is born of a woman, that he should be just? Behold, He puts no trust in His saints; indeed, the heavens are not clean in His sight. How much more abominable and foul is man, who drinks iniquity like water? Ch. 15:14, 16. Moreover, this same thing is acknowledged by the heathen, as something known from experience, though its cause is unknown. This is shown even by that saying of Horace: No one is born without vices; he is best who is burdened by the fewest. Nor can this vice of human nature be imputed to God in any way, as the Socinians spitefully object, but to the first parents. For God is the author of no evil, but our parents, by their sin, lost the grace of God, both for themselves and for their posterity; with the government of the soul removed, all its faculties were greatly weakened and confused, the most beautiful harmony was turned into discord, order was disturbed, and a rebellion of the affections was stirred up against the dictates of sound reason. Finally, the image of God originally impressed on man, if not wholly blotted out, was at least greatly deformed; so that afterwards Adam is said to have begotten Seth (and the rest of his offspring[?]) not according to the primeval image of God, but according to his own, thus stained and maimed and wholly deprived of the original beauty and integrity. Third; concupiscence, or the inclination to sin (in which original sin partly consists), is not naturally in all men, nor can it properly be said to be in those men in whom sin is present. For thus Socinus: Although that evil desire and readiness to sin is found in most people, we cannot affirm that it is in absolutely all. Since the will of the one who is to be in guilt is wholly required for guilt to be incurred, it seems in no way possible to say that any guilt can have a place in a man at the moment he is born, since at that time he has no use of his own will, nor could he have had one before. That desire and readiness to sin, since it does not have guilt joined with it in the man in whom it is, cannot properly be called his sin. Thus he, Praelect. ch. 4. On the contrary, the Apostle calls this concupiscence, or inclination to sin, sin dwelling in me, and the law of the members warring against the law of the mind, making me a captive to the law of sin. Rom. 7:17, 18, 23. And he acknowledges that it not only remains, but from time to time also exerts its powers in the pious and regenerate, against the motions of the Holy Spirit, so that they cannot do what they would most want. Gal. 5:17. It is also clear that this irregular concupiscence, by which the human race, as of old so also now, is rendered so prone to sin, was not in the first parents before the fall (for it would not have agreed with that image of God according to which they were created), but took its origin through and after the fall, and from that time has pervaded the whole human race, as a kind of fountain or tinder of every actual sin which has since been committed by men. Thus James: each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence. Then concupiscence, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; but sin, when it is full grown, gives birth to death. Ch. 1:14, 15. Paul at last affirms that this concupiscence (which he calls the mind of the flesh [φρόνημα σαρκός]. Rom. 8:7) is enmity toward God, because it is not subject to the law of God, and cannot be subject to it. Although therefore it is not imputed as sin to the pious and regenerate whenever they do not consent to its evil motions, nevertheless in itself and by its nature it is sin, insofar as it is opposed to the law of God. For sin is nothing other than lawlessness [ἀνομία], that is, aversion or discrepancy from the law of God, as the Apostle John defines it. 1 John 3:4. Fourth; the proneness to sin which is seen in the human race today did not arise at once from that first sin, or from that first act of sinning by the first man, but by repeated acts of sinning after that sin, men gradually acquired a habit of sinning, and so corrupted themselves, and thus transmitted the seed of corruption to their posterity by propagation. So Socinus in the book On the Polity of the Kingdom, ch. 5, and in Praelect. ch. 4. Ostorod, Institutes, ch. 34, Smalcius against Frantz, disp. 2, and the Racovian Catechism, ch. 10, agree with this. On the contrary, apart from the passages of Scripture cited earlier, daily experience testifies that even children, before any habit of sinning acquired by repeated acts, are prone to evil, but stubborn and unteachable, unfit and lazy for the discipline and practice of good, although frequent admonitions and most excellent examples set before them for imitation are offered in vain. It is also clear that men are not disposed indifferently to good and evil, as the first parents were in the state of innocence, but are far more prone to evil; and this proneness is ready to break out into the act of sin whenever it is solicited from outside by a suitable temptation. Finally, reason tells us that vicious habits of the mind, which are a kind of spiritual disease, are not born with us, nor are they derived from parents by transmission, like the diseases of the body. Experience also supports this, which not infrequently shows us sons very prone to vice, born of parents of the most distinguished virtue; and conversely, from the most vicious parents, sons of the most upright disposition, most capable of good training, and (when compared with most others) as if made, or rather born, for acquiring every kind of virtue.

units.la: Quinto; Congenitam pravitatem, seu pronitatem ad peccandum in Hominibus, non esse Peccatum; etsi Socinus non simpliciter neget, eam vel nobis inesse, vel in nos propagari. Praelect. cap. 4. Rationem vero suae Assertionis hanc affert, Quod ad Culpam constituendam, propria voluntas ejus, qui in Culpa futurus est, omnino requiratur; at ista congenita pronitas ad peccandum, quæ in Infantibus esse dicitur, de propria illorum voluntate nihil participat, quam in Actum non exerunt, neque exerere possunt. At è contra, licet hæc pronitas seu pravitas, non sit actuale Infantis modo genita[?] peccatum, peccatum tamen sat proprie dici potest, tum quia adversatur legi divinæ; tum quia est quid Deo displicens; tum quia ex natura sua est quid malum; non autem malum Pœnæ, ac proinde malum Culpæ. Quid? quod Sacrificium in lege Mosaica præscribatur etiam pro peccato ignorantiæ, quod tamen involuntarium est. Levit. 5. 2. 6. sed de hoc prius. Sexto, Pœnam peccati Adamitici (sc. mortem) sine peccati ullius Reatu, in posteros transisse. Sic enim Soc. de servat. part. 3. cap. 8.
units.tr: Fifthly, that congenital depravity, or proneness to sin in human beings, is not sin, although Socinus does not flatly deny that it is either in us or propagated into us. Praelect. ch. 4. He gives this reason for his assertion: that to constitute guilt, the own will of the one who is to be guilty is entirely required; but this congenital proneness to sin, which is said to be in infants, has no share in their own will, since they neither put it into act nor can they. On the contrary, although this proneness or depravity is not an actual sin committed by the infant alone, it can nonetheless be called sin quite properly: because it is opposed to the divine law, because it is something displeasing to God, and because by its nature it is an evil; yet it is not an evil of punishment, and therefore not an evil of guilt. What of the fact that the Mosaic law prescribes a sacrifice even for a sin of ignorance, which is nonetheless involuntary? Lev. 5. 2, 6. But of this earlier. Sixthly, that the punishment of Adam's sin (namely death) has passed to his posterity without any guilt of sin. For so Socinus, De servatore, part 3, ch. 8.

units.la: Tametsi omnes ab Adamo progenati, mortis perpetuæ sunt obnoxii, id non ideo fit, quod ipsius Adami Delictum imputetur, sed quia ab eo progeniti sunt, qui mortis perpetuæ divino decreto sunt addicti, atque ita non propter peccati Imputationem, sed propter Generis propagationem id illis contingit. At huic Socini Assertioni refragatur, & Scriptura, & Ratio. Apostolus enim diserte asserit, Mortem in omnes Homines pervasisse per Adami peccatum, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ[?], in quo, seu eo quod, omnes peccaverunt; nam utcunque modo hanc particulam interpretentur, necesse est ut fateantur, ex sensu Apostoli mortem ea de causa irrogatam fuisse Generi humano, eo quod istud Adami peccatum cunctis Hominibus fuerit imputatum. Rom. 5. 12. Ratio quoque astipulatur, quæ docet, neminem Pœnæ subjacere posse, qui non sit reus Culpæ; cum Reatus nihil aliud sit, quam obligatio ad Pœnam. Justitia Dei idem postulat. Septimo, Infantes nondum per Baptismum regenitos, & in Ec[?]ecclesiam admissos (adeoque peccati originalis adhuc reos) regno Dei exclusos non esse. Ita Czechovicius contra Paedobaptistas. Rationem hanc affert, Quod liberi Christianorum vocentur sancti. 1. Cor. 7. 14. At contrarium Christus asserit. Jo. 3. 3, 5, 6. ut modo ostendimus. Apostolus item, cum affirmat, nos esse natura Filios irae. Eph. 2. 3. Cum igitur idem Apostolus dicit, liberos Christianorum esse Sanctos; vel cum Tertulliano dicendum est, eos esse Delignatos Sanctitatis, & per hoc, etiam salutis, ex institutionis disciplina. Vel esse legitimos, non spurios, licet ex altero Parente infideli prognatos. Sic enim Apostolus alibi utitur hac voce sanctificandi, cum de Esculis loquens asserit, omnem Dei Creaturam esse bonam nihilque rejiciendum, si cum Gratiarum actione sumatur, [?] Sanctificatur enim, inquit, per verbum Dei & preces.
units.tr: Although all who are born from Adam are liable to perpetual death, this does not happen because Adam's own offence is imputed to them, but because they are descended from him, and are thereby condemned to perpetual death by divine decree; so that this befalls them not on account of the imputation of sin but on account of the propagation of the race. But both Scripture and reason oppose this assertion of Socinus. For the Apostle plainly asserts that death passed upon all men through the sin of Adam, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, in whom, or because, all sinned; for however they interpret this particle, they must admit that, in the Apostle's sense, death was inflicted on the human race for this reason: that Adam's sin was imputed to all men. Rom. 5. 12. Reason also agrees, which teaches that no one can be subject to punishment who is not liable for guilt, since liability is nothing other than obligation to punishment. The justice of God demands the same. Seventhly, that infants not yet regenerated by baptism and admitted into the Church (and so still liable to original sin) are not excluded from the kingdom of God. So Czechowicz against the paedobaptists. He gives this reason: that the children of Christians are called holy. 1 Cor. 7. 14. But Christ asserts the contrary: John 3. 3, 5, 6, as we have just shown. The Apostle likewise, when he affirms that we are by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2. 3. Since, then, the same Apostle says that the children of Christians are holy, we must either say with Tertullian that they are marked out for holiness, and thereby also for salvation, by the discipline of their upbringing; or that they are legitimate and not illegitimate, although born of one unbelieving parent. For the Apostle uses this word "to sanctify" in this way elsewhere too, when, speaking of foods, he asserts that every creature of God is good and nothing is to be rejected, if it is taken with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified, he says, by the word of God and prayer.

units.la: 1 Tim. 4. 4, 5. ubi per Sanctificari, intelligendum est, fieri esu licitam, sive legitimi usus, nimirum per verbum Dei quod omnium eduliorum usum, Nobis sub Evangelio libere & indifferenter concedit; (comp. Matth. 15. 11.) & per preces ad Deum Creatorem, cui & Gratias agere oportet, quia praebuit; & ab eodem petere, ut quae sic praebuit, sumentibus prosint.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 4. 4, 5. Where "to be sanctified" must be understood as: made lawful to eat, that is, made fit for lawful use; namely by the word of God, which under the Gospel freely and indifferently grants us the use of all foods (compare Matt. 15. 11); and by prayer to God the Creator, to whom we ought also to give thanks, because he has provided them, and to ask of him that what he has so provided may benefit those who partake of it.

units.la: §. 85. Ex hoc Dogmatum Socinianorum Catalogo plus satis patet, quam adversa sint, & Fidei, & moribus Ecclesiae Catholicae; quantamque perniciem afferant Pietati Christianae, adeo ut sufficere jure videatur, ad Fideles contra Illorum virus muniendos vel ea recensuisse. At plura occurrunt, quae merito, nos abterrere possunt ab iisdem amplectendis; Philautia & Arrogantia Defensorum, cum summo Aliorum contemptu conjuncta, qui se Illorum conatibus opponunt; deriso Fidei antiquae Blasphemiis comitata, veterum despectus ac ludibria, non sine Calumniis & mendaciis; Ecclesiae Catholicae Authoritas sede conculcata, & Contumeliis onerata; Contradictiones, & effugia miserrima, cum arctius premerentur ab Adversariis; zelus hypocrisin sapiens, pro Christo, & veritate Evangelii, vitaeque christianae sanctitate, cum interim haec omnia pro viribus corrumpant atque destruant; obstinatio animi & Contumacia summa in erroribus propugnandis, fictae demum excusationes, & Tergiversationes haud ingenuae, in Dogmatibus suis proponendis, cum ad rationem de iis reddendam legitime poscebantur. Haec vitia Socini Sociorumque ipsius latissex antedictis innotescunt; unde initantias quasdam excerpere fas sit; quibus & alias aliquas adjiciam, ad hoc idem plenius, clariusque demonstrandum. Nam primo, Socinus nullum prorsus in vivis Magistrum agnoscere dignatur, qui eum docere potuerit; in tractatu suo de Magistratu, quem contra Palaeologum scripsit; neque aliquem omnino in universa Theologia, (quam fere totam innovando corrupit) praeter Lelium Patrum pridem defunctum, a quo pauculà quaedam conscripta se accepisse fatetur, aliaque plura breviter annotata. Ep. ad Squarcial. Idem Fr. Puccium conterraneum suum, virum nobilem ac doctum, ut ipse fatetur, acriter perstringit, quod multum suis opinionibus fiderit atque tribuerit, novamque quandam Theologiam condiderit. Epist. ad Dudithium. p. 497. Col.
units.tr: §. 85. From this catalogue of the dogmas of the Socinians it is quite plain how hostile they are both to the faith and to the morals of the Catholic Church, and how great a ruin they bring to Christian piety; so that it seems rightly sufficient, to fortify the faithful against their poison, to have listed these alone. But there are further things which may rightly terrify us from embracing them: the self-love and arrogance of their defenders, joined with the greatest contempt for others who oppose their efforts; the mockery of the ancient faith accompanied by blasphemies, the disparagement and ridicule of the Fathers, not without calumnies and lies; the authority of the Catholic Church trampled underfoot and burdened with insults; contradictions and the most wretched evasions when they were pressed too closely by their adversaries; a zeal that savours of hypocrisy, claimed for Christ, the truth of the Gospel and the holiness of Christian life, while all the while they corrupt and destroy these things as far as they can; obstinacy of mind and the utmost stubbornness in defending their errors; and finally feigned excuses and shifty, unfrank evasions in setting out their dogmas, when they were lawfully called upon to give an account of them. These vices of Socinus and his associates are made known to us from what has been said above; from them I may pick out a few examples, and I shall add some others to demonstrate this same point more fully and clearly. For first, Socinus deigns to acknowledge no living teacher who could have taught him anything, in his treatise on the magistrate which he wrote against Palaeologus; nor indeed anyone at all in the whole of theology (which he has corrupted by almost wholly rewriting it), except Lelius, a father long dead, from whom he confesses he received a few short writings, and several other things briefly noted down. Letter to Squarcialupi. The same man sharply censures his fellow countryman Fausto Sozzini's... [note: this is Fr. Pucci] Francesco Pucci, his compatriot, a noble and learned man, as he himself admits, because he trusted too much in his own opinions and relied on them, and founded a certain new theology. Letter to Dudith, p. 497, col.

units.la: 2. Tom. 1. Cum nemo non videat, quam ingeniter ipse istius Criminis reus fuerit, quod Puccio tam fidenter imputat. Idem fatetur, se Scholasticam Theologiam nunquam attigisse, & pleraque sua scripta compositisse, cum nondum Arti Dialecticae ullam operam dedisset; levissime, & omni Praeceptori destitutus [illegible, ~1 letters] tum & bonarum artium litterarumque studiis operam impendisse; & florentissimos aetatis suae Annos, 12. sc. perpetuos, ab Anno viz. 23. ad An. 35. in Patria otio, & partim in Aula; perdidisse; atque adeo haud mirandum esse, si in suis scriptis multa deprehendantur, minus recte tradita & conclusa. Hæc ille, in Ep. ad virum excell. N. N. quam paulo ante obitum conscripsit. Cur ergo tanto zelo & ardore Dogmata sua, ubicunque commoratus est, scripto mandavit, excudi curavit, & scriptorum exemplaria per omnes Terras studio tanto distraxit? Cur ea Discipulis suis tam vehementer inculcavit, & tanquam indubie vera Cun[?]tis persuadere conatus est? Cur non ea ad examen revocavit, quae fatetur se minus recte tradidisse? Cur non correxit? Scilicet fastidivit hoc Socinus, ut tam excelso Ingenio prorsus indignum; veritatem maluit periclitari, quam Palinodiam canere; Fideique potius, quam famæ, facere jacturam. Idem in eadem Epistola, jure metuens ne ob istiusmodi scripta reprehenderetur, hac ratione se purgat, quod vel Jussu eorum, quibus parendum sibi erat; vel Adversariorum provocatione, ad scribendum compulsus fuerit. At pace Socini, hæc excusatio Crimen ipsius auget, cum falsi comperta sit, & illius Hypocrisin aperte manifestet. Eandem tamen antehac reddiderat in Epistola ad Martinum Vadovitam, ubi affirmat, se nunquam, nisi plane provocatum ac lacessitum, vel Amicorum ac fratrum Precibus & Jussis coactum, aliquid hucusque scripsisse, sua autem sponte nihil. Imo, nullum inveniri posse inter omnes, quibuscum familiaritatem habuit, ex quo in Polonia commoratus sit per Annos 19. cum quo vel Disputationem ullam de Rebus Divinis instituerit; nedum egerit cum aliquibus, ut sententiis temiis[?] eorum de Religione abjectis, sua ipsius susciperent. Caeterum, contrarium clare patet ex Epistola Squarcialupi[?] ad ipsum, qui cum eo familiarissime vixit, utpote Concivis, & exilii comes. Hic enim illum ibi unice, at serio redarguit, quod Palaeologum, Hominem gravissimum, ultro lacessiverit, neque secum disputantem, nec contra se, nec de se, nec contra ipsius proximos. Merito igitur, inquit, suspicaris, ne Temeritatis te accusat Graecus, cum, ut fateris, falcem inferas in alienam messem. Ibidem quoque eum reprehendit, quod non solum disputare soleret cum aliter sentientibus, sed & fervide nimis, atque clamose — Scio, ait, non suspicor, immodicum esse Animi tui zelum[?] in Disputatione. Quoties vobis[?] Te admonere disputantem, vel de levi jurgantem, & Clamoribus maximis omnia perturbantem? Quod autem hujusmodi Disputationes fuerint de rebus ad Religionem spectantibus, satis constat ex Socini[?] Responsio ad eandem Epistolam — Immodicum in Disputatione actum meum esse affirmas — sed, cum compertiſsimum habeam, Alios adhuc multis in erroribus versari, ex quibus Deus Bonitate sua me penitus extraxerit; cumque, praeter animi summam quandam Ingenuitatem (fit mihi fas de meipso hoc praedicare) quam mihi natura indidit, Deus Pietatem aliquam Cordi meo infeverit[?], nulla ratione fieri potest, ut saepissime, cum agitur de Religione, a caeteris non aperte dissentiam, sententiamque meam arte retineam, sive in ipsis Dogmatibus, sive in Dogmatum Probationibus, sive in Divinarum literarum Interpretationibus, sive in veritatis patefaciendae via atque ratione, sive quacunque alia de Re, ubi de Dei, Christique Gloria, & animarum salute agitur. In reliquis, enim facile comniveo, & aliis assentiri videor. Sic ille. Et quamvis in eadem sua Apologetica ad Vadovitam Epistola, de pacifico suo Ingenio, moribusque à tumultu[?]ciendo, seditionesve fovenda alienis, multum se jactet, satis tamen apparet, tum ex vitae ipsius historiola, ab equite Polono conscripta; tum ex suis ipsius Epistolis, quod sicut varias Anti-Trinitariorum sectas in unum collegerit, & singularum Opiniones (quotquot in tanta Diversitate poterat) in novum quoddam Systema consarcinaverit (eo facilius, quo plerique ex iis negativae erant, & Fidei receptae eversivae) ita se quoque Cunctorum Patronum, pugilemque strenuum & exercitatum ostentaverit, semper paratum ad Certamen ineundum cum ipsorum Adversariis, cujuscunque Generis aut nominis esset; quod item Quaestiones & Dubia, de quibus crebro interpellabatur, solvere studuerit; haesitantes confirmare, recedentes ad se denuo attrahere, imperitioribus consulere, synodos ipsorum sese consulentes dirigere, iisque instar moderatoris Consilio suo praeesse; denique omnia sectae suae negotia, quae ad Religionem spectabant, pro arbitrio suo administrare. Haec omnia patent ex Polemicis ipsius operibus, & ex Epistolis ipsius & amicorum invicem missis.
units.tr: 2. Tom. 1. Since everyone can see how ingenuous he himself was in the offence for which he so confidently charges Pucci. He admits that he never touched scholastic theology, and wrote most of his works before he had devoted any effort to the art of dialectic; lightly educated and lacking any teacher [illegible]; and that he devoted himself to the study of the liberal arts and letters only late; and that he squandered the flourishing years of his age, twelve whole years, from the twenty-third to the thirty-fifth year, in leisure in his homeland and partly at court; and so it is no wonder if many things are found in his writings which are less rightly handed down and concluded. He says this in a letter to an excellent man, N. N., which he wrote shortly before his death. Why then, wherever he stayed, did he commit his dogmas to writing with such zeal and ardour, have them printed, and scatter copies of his writings through all lands with such eagerness? Why did he press them so vehemently upon his disciples and try to persuade everyone that they were beyond doubt true? Why did he not call back for examination those things which he confesses he had handed down less rightly? Why did he not correct them? Clearly Socinus thought this beneath so lofty a genius; he preferred to risk the truth rather than sing a palinode, and to suffer loss of faith rather than loss of reputation. In the same letter, fearing with good reason that he would be rebuked for such writings, he defends himself on the ground that he was driven to write either by the command of those to whom he had to submit, or by the challenge of his adversaries. But with all respect to Socinus, this excuse adds to his guilt, since it has been proved false and plainly reveals his hypocrisy. He had however already given the same excuse in his letter to Martin Wadowita, where he affirms that he had never written anything hitherto except when he was plainly provoked and attacked, or compelled by the prayers and commands of friends and brothers, and never of his own accord. Indeed, no one can be found among all those with whom he was on intimate terms during the nineteen years he lived in Poland, with whom he conducted any disputation about divine matters, let alone pressed some of them to cast off their opinions about religion and take up his own. Otherwise the contrary is clearly shown by the letter of Squarcialupi to him, who lived with him most intimately, as a fellow citizen and companion in exile. For he there rebukes him solely, but seriously, for having provoked the most grave man Palaeologus unprompted, neither disputing with him, nor against him, nor about him, nor against his associates. Rightly, he says, do you suspect that the Greek may accuse you of rashness, since, as you admit, you put your sickle into another's harvest. He also reproaches him there because he was accustomed not only to dispute with those who thought otherwise, but to do so too fervently and noisily: I know, he says, I do not suspect, that your zeal in disputation is immoderate. How often have I warned you when disputing, or quarrelling over trifles, and throwing everything into confusion with the greatest shouting? That such disputations concerned matters pertaining to religion is quite clear from Socinus's reply to that same letter: You affirm that my conduct in disputation was immoderate; but since I know full well that others are still caught in many errors, from which God in his goodness has entirely drawn me out; and since, apart from a certain great candour of spirit (I may say this of myself) which nature has given me, God has instilled some piety into my heart, it is in no way possible that, when religion is at issue, I should not very often openly dissent from others, and stubbornly keep hold of my opinion, whether on the dogmas themselves, or on the proofs of dogmas, or on the interpretation of the divine letters, or on the way and method of making the truth plain, or on any other matter whatever, where the glory of God and Christ and the salvation of souls is at stake. For in other matters I easily keep silent, and seem to assent to others. So he. And although in that same apologetic letter to Wadowita he boasts a great deal of his peaceable temper and of his avoiding stirring up tumult or fostering sedition among others, it nonetheless appears plainly, both from the brief account of his life written by a Polish knight and from his own letters, that just as he gathered together the various Anti-Trinitarian sects into one, and cobbled the opinions of each (as many as he could, amid such diversity) into a certain new system (all the more easily because most of them were negative and destructive of the received faith), so he also showed himself the champion and vigorous and practised fighter of them all, always ready to enter the contest with their adversaries, of whatever kind or name; that he likewise strove to solve the questions and doubts on which he was constantly consulted; to confirm the wavering, to draw back to himself those who had drifted away, to advise the more unskilled, to direct the synods of his followers who consulted him, and to preside over them with his counsel like a sort of moderator; and finally to manage at his discretion all the affairs of his sect which pertained to religion. All this is evident from his polemical works and from the letters he sent to and exchanged with his friends.

units.la: §. 86. Eandem quoque Philautiam & arrogantiam, quam in scriptis suis demonstrat, Discipulis suis persuadet, dum unumquemque facit S. Scriptura ex suo ipsius sensu Interpretem, Controversiarum judicem, & Dogmatum sibi placentium Cooptatorem; eaque quae sibi sic arridént, pro veris illos admittere vult, ac tenere, licet universus Terrarum orbis in alia omnia ire. Ep. 3. ad Dudith. Atque alibi, minime attendendum vult, quid alii Homines docent, sentiantve, vel antehac docuerint aut senserint, quicunque illi tandem, aut quotcunque sint, aut fuerint. Sic ille, De Ecclesia: p. 344. Eadem vitia in Vorstio illius Discipulo olim notavit Seiten[?]. R. nolter Jacobus, ubi animadvertit, illum novo isto nomine puri putique Evangelici mirifice gloriari; damnare Argumenta, quae vel a Patribus, vel a recentioribus Theologis, pro aeterna Christi generatione afferuntur, ut fallacia aut frivola; & sibi uni arrogare laudem veritatis asserta; his enim verbis utitur, de suis opinionibus loquens — Neque plures uno aliquo semper hic ditiores sunt, nec numero plures, uni alicui singulare quicquam invadeant. Ubi se prorsus eximit a Judicio Synodico Pastorum Ecclesiae, cum dicere paratus sit, quoties ab iis erroris alicujus arguitur, nihil est vobis in me Juris, quia Ego singulare quiddam supra vos omnes habeo. Idem ibidem, cum probe nosset, certas credendi loquendique formulas, de Fidei nostrae mysteriis, per Consequentias e S. literis jam olim fuisse ab Ecclesia stabilitas, Ecclesiam non vult agnoscere eorum, qui ipsi objecti sunt, errorum arbitrandum negat Se Fidem suam ulli humanae Authoritati alligare velle, sequeque, humanas Decisiones a Divinis mysteriis satis scrupulose segregare. Quam procaciter & immodeste Censuram suam fert Socinus, ne dicam impie, de Interdicto sanguinis edendi, quod Deus dedit cunctis Noachi posteris statim a Diluvio, quod item Ecclesiis Gentilium denuo observandum imponitur ab Apostolis, in Synodo Jerosolymitana; & ab eo Tempore obtinuit, per multas Annorum Centurias, in Ecclesia Catholica. Cum enim Christophorus Morstinus, illius affinis objiceret, sibi videri, quod Interdictum istud adhuc valere oporteret, quia Deus prohibuit esum sanguinis sub lege, propter istiusmodi Rationem, quae in perpetuum valebat, viz. quia vita Animalis (de mortuo loquens) esset in sanguine; Socinus ita reponit —Mi Affinis, hoc est quod mihi volui; Deum sui illius Interdicti causam attulisse, quam si quis paulo diligentius consideret, agnosceret illam, aut nullam esse, aut infirmissimam. Id quod sapientissime nihilominus Deus fecit, ut cum ejus Populus ipsumque adeo Genus humanum adultius esset facilius[?], & exercitationes haberet sensus ad cognoscendum, quaenam revera sint Divina, & in perpetuum permansura praecepta; vel ex causa ista interdicendi ejus sanguinis, quae nihil solidi habet, agnosceret interdictum ipsum non debuisse esse perpetuum, utpote, quod non aliunde pendeat, quam a mera & sola Dei voluntate. Sic ille, Epist. 5. ad Chr. Morstinum. p. 458. Col. 1. Quibus in verbis vel sapientiam Divinam plane ludibrio habet, cum eam arguit infirmissimae Rationis allatae ad legem suam stabiliendam, dum interim eam agnoscere & laudare simulat; vel suae saltem Rationis infirmitatem ostendit, dum Contradictoria Deo simul affingit. Porro, haud mirum est, Illum Ecclesiam Dei, ejusque Doctores nihili facere, qui causam interdicti ab ipso Deo legislatore allatam, pro nulla habet, aut nullius valoris; aut si Dogmata Fidei ab iisdem communiter asserta, cavillis & calumniis, convitiis & blasphemiis incessit. Siquidem ille, ejusque Socii hoc modo se gerunt. Cum Socinus urgetur Authoritate Clementis Romani, Dionysii Areopagitae, & Ignatii; respondet, Fabula! Ad Testimo-monium Hieronymi, quod S. Joannes rogatus ab Asiae Episcopis, adversus Ebionis & Cerinthi Dogma consurgens (quod Christum Deum verum esse negabat) suum scripsit Evangelium; sic respondet Hieronymi Testimonio, qui trecentis circiter Annis post scriptum a Joanne Evangelium extitit, nullo modo hac in Re stan-dum dum est; præsertim, cum ejus quodammodo causa agitur. Keip.[?] ad 7. Assert. Posman. Quasi Hieronymus hoc Testimonium non accepisset a majoribus suis, aut quasi Dogma istud, cui Testimonium fert, esset ipsius privata sententia, & non Communis Ecclesiæ Catholicæ. Ibidem fatetur, Eusebium afferere, Joannem, in suo Evangelico, à Christi Divinitate exorsum esse. Ad quod respondet, verum, id ex suo sensu dicit. SS. Trinitatis Dogma, quandoque humanum, quandoque Antichristi Commentum appellat, tempore Justini Martyris inventum; & Symboli Niceni Authoritatem scommate[?] excipit, ut nihil omnino valentem — Egregia, inquit, probatio, cum ad eam (sc. Trinitatem) ex parte confirmandam Nicenum Symbolum afferatur, quod ducentis circiter ac sexaginta, post Apostolorum Christi Tempora, annis compositum fuit. Nempe, cum jam divina veritas, quæ ipsorum Apostolorum Tempore nonnihil contaminari ceperat, magna ex parte, non paucis doctis, piisque viris frustra renitentibus, sedata ac corrupta fuisset. Sic ille, Animadv. in Assert. 10. Posman. Atque alibi, Andr. Dudithius symbolum hoc cum Athanasiano, & Patribus Fidem illic traditam propugnantibus, calamo procaci insectatur, in Epist. ad Jo. Lasicium equitem Polonum — Non sum jocatus, inquit, Lasci, sed serio admodum professus sum Confessionis illius formulam, quæ Athanasii nomine circumfertur (quam non ab Athanasio, sed ab otioso potius aliquo Monacho fuisse scriptam Camerarius noster opinatur) iterumque Nicenum illud Symbolum, non esse S. Literis, & Christiana Pietati consentaneum, sed ex humano Jesu, & Spinosis quibusdam frigidorum Sophistarum argutiis depromptum. Oper: Soc. p. 510. & postea — Audi Augustinum tuum, Trinitatis istius vestræ Architectum.
units.tr: §. 86. He also instils the same self-conceit and arrogance, which he displays in his writings, into his disciples, while he makes each person the interpreter of Holy Scripture by his own judgment, the judge of controversies, and the selector of whatever doctrines please him. Whatever pleases him in this way he wants them to accept and hold as true, even if the whole world goes in a different direction. Ep. 3. ad Dudith. Elsewhere he wants people to pay no attention at all to what other men teach or think, or have taught or thought before, whoever they are, or however many they are or have been. Thus he writes in De Ecclesia, p. 344. Seiten[?]. R. nolter Jacobus earlier noted the same faults in Vorstius, his disciple, where he observes that Vorstius boasts wonderfully of the new title of pure and simple Evangelical, and that he condemns as fallacious or frivolous the arguments that are brought for the eternal generation of Christ either by the Fathers or by more recent theologians, and claims for himself alone the praise of truth. For he uses these words when speaking of his own opinions: Neither are there ever more men richer than one, nor, being more in number, do they lay claim to anything singular against any one man. Here he entirely exempts himself from the synodal judgment of the ministers of the Church, since he is ready to say whenever he is charged with some error by them: You have no right over me, because I have something singular above you all. In the same place, although he knew well that certain set forms of believing and speaking concerning the mysteries of our faith had long before been established by the Church through inferences from Holy Scripture, he refuses to acknowledge the Church as the judge of the errors of those against whom it is directed. He says that he does not wish to bind his faith to any human authority, and that he separates human decisions quite scrupulously from divine mysteries. How insolently and immodestly Socinus, not to say impiously, passes judgment on the prohibition of eating blood, which God gave to all the posterity of Noah immediately after the Flood, and which the Apostles also imposed again upon the Gentile churches in the Council of Jerusalem, and which from that time has held good in the Catholic Church through many centuries of years! For when Christopher Morstin, his relative, objected that it seemed to him that this prohibition ought still to be in force, because God forbade the eating of blood under the law for a reason that held good forever, namely that the life of an animal (speaking of a dead one) is in the blood, Socinus replies thus: My relative, this is what I wanted: God gave as the cause of that prohibition something which, if anyone considers it a little more carefully, he will recognize as either nothing or very weak. Yet God did this most wisely, so that when his people, and indeed the human race itself, had grown more mature, they would have occasion for exercising their senses in recognising what truly are the divine and perpetually lasting precepts; or, from the cause of this prohibition on eating blood, which has nothing solid in it, they would recognise that the prohibition itself ought not to have been perpetual, since it depends on nothing other than the mere and sole will of God. Thus he writes, Ep. 5. ad Chr. Morstinum, p. 458, col. 1. In these words he either makes utter mockery of divine wisdom, when he accuses the very weak reason given for establishing its law, while pretending to acknowledge and praise it, or at least shows the weakness of his own reason, when he ascribes contradictory things to God at the same time. Furthermore, it is no wonder that he makes nothing of the Church of God and its teachers, since he regards the reason for the prohibition given by God himself, the lawgiver, as no reason at all or of no value, or, if the doctrines of faith commonly asserted by them, he assails with quibbles and slanders, insults and blasphemies. For he and his associates behave in this way. When Socinus is pressed with the authority of Clement of Rome, Dionysius the Areopagite, and Ignatius, he replies, A fable! To the testimony of Jerome, that St. John, when asked by the bishops of Asia to rise against the doctrine of Ebion and Cerinthus, who denied that Christ was true God, wrote his Gospel, he replies thus: One must by no means stand by the testimony of Jerome, who appeared some three hundred years after the Gospel was written by John, especially since his cause is somehow being argued. Keip.[?] ad 7. Assert. Posman. As if Jerome had not received this testimony from his elders, or as if that doctrine, to which he bears witness, were his own private opinion and not the common doctrine of the Catholic Church! In the same place he admits that Eusebius asserts that John, in his Gospel, began from the divinity of Christ. To this he replies, True, but he says it from his own sense. The doctrine of the Holy Trinity he sometimes calls a human invention, sometimes a fiction of Antichrist, devised in the time of Justin Martyr; and with a jibe he dismisses the authority of the Nicene Creed as worth nothing at all: A splendid proof, he says, when the Nicene Creed is brought forward to confirm it in part (that is, the Trinity), a creed composed some two hundred and sixty years after the times of the Apostles of Christ. Indeed, when divine truth, which had begun to be somewhat contaminated even in the time of the Apostles themselves, was for the most part settled and corrupted, while many learned and pious men resisted in vain. Thus he writes, Animadv. in Assert. 10. Posman. And elsewhere Andreas Dudithius attacks this creed, together with the Athanasian, and the Fathers who defend the faith handed down there, with a insolent pen, in his letter to John Lasicius, a Polish knight: I was not joking, Lasicius, but I professed quite seriously that the formula of that confession which is circulated under the name of Athanasius (which our Camerarius thinks was written not by Athanasius but rather by some idle monk) and again that Nicene creed are not in accord with Holy Scripture or Christian piety, but are drawn from human and thorny quibbles of cold sophists. Oper. Soc. p. 510, and afterwards: Hear your Augustine, the architect of that Trinity of yours.

units.la: Alia plura non lubet referre, quæ in eadem epistola fastidiose profert contra Authoritatem S. Patrum, Conciliorum, & totius Ecclesiæ Catholicæ. Inter hæc tamen, ne Arrogantiæ argueretur (ut sanè jure merebatur) summum humilitatis ac modestiæ studium ibidem præ se fert, dum ita monet Lacifium suum: Sume in manu sacros libros. Illi Te docebunt, quid sequi, quid fugere debeas. Cave autem, tyrannicum & minus alta sapientem, & humilia omnia contemnentem Animum, ad lectionem adferas. Superbis Deus resistit.
units.tr: I do not care to report the many other things which in the same letter he brings forward with disdain against the authority of the holy Fathers, the Councils, and the whole Catholic Church. Among these, however, so that he might not be charged with arrogance (as he rightly deserved to be), he displays there the highest zeal for humility and modesty, when he advises his Lasicius thus: Take the holy books in your hand. They will teach you what you ought to follow and what to avoid. But beware of bringing to their reading a tyrannical mind, which is of little lofty wisdom and despises all things lowly. God resists the proud.

units.la: At cur ipse respuit Consilium, quod Lacisio suo dat; sensumque suum ab Ecclesia jampridem damnatum Fidei Catholicæ præfert? Cur humiles Fidei Discipulos contemnit, dum suo Ingenio fidit, & se factuose erigit contra Ecclesiæ Tribunal, ab ipso Christo erectum, matrisque veneranda dictata pro nihilo ducit? Nam & alibi, Confessum veteris Ecclesiæ contemptim rejicit, ut nihil omnino valentem; & fidenter negat, Trinitatis mysterium ab Apostolis unquam agnitum fuisse, aut a tota illa orthodoxa Ecclesia. Quasi vetus Ecclesia Fidem suam ab Apostolis non accepisset, infitar sacri Depositi non conservasset, eamque strenuè non propugnasset contra Infideles & Hæreticos. Istiusmodi calumniis Ecclesiam istam primævam, Apostolicam, fidissimamque simplicis Fidei Custodem, atque vindicem, onerare solent; & ut sibi solis arrogent Fidem orthodoxam, Ecclesiam vere Christianam, literarumque S. Interpretationem ad mise rima effugia se conferre coguntur; instar Maleficorum, qui in flagitiis deprehensi, omne legitimum Tribunal aversantur; ut qui probe norunt, se causa casuros, si modo Factorum suorum examen juxta leges receptas instituatur.
units.tr: But why does he himself reject the counsel which he gives to his Lasicius, and prefer his own sense, long since condemned by the Catholic Church? Why does he despise the humble disciples of the faith, while he trusts in his own talent and, with a swelling spirit, raises himself up against the tribunal of the Church, set up by Christ himself, and holds for nothing the venerable dictates of the mother? For elsewhere too he contemptuously rejects the creed of the ancient Church as worth nothing at all, and confidently denies that the mystery of the Trinity was ever acknowledged by the Apostles, or by that whole orthodox Church. As if the ancient Church had not received its faith from the Apostles, had not kept the sacred deposit unimpaired, and had not stoutly defended it against unbelievers and heretics! With calumnies of this kind they are wont to burden that primitive, Apostolic Church, the most faithful guardian and defender of the simple faith; and, in order to claim the orthodox faith and the title of the truly Christian Church for themselves alone, and the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures, they are compelled to take refuge in the most wretched evasions, like criminals caught in their crimes, who shrink from every lawful tribunal, since they know well that they would be lost if an examination of their deeds were conducted according to the accepted laws.

units.la: §. 87. Ita Socinus, ejusque Discipuli se gerunt in hoc Fidei negotio: Symbola omnia antiqua, Apostolici illius Interpretamenta, ut Formulas Fidei adulterinas, & spuria humani Ingenii Commenta, rejiciunt. Imo, decantatum illud Athanasii, haud verentur Satanasii Symbolum nuncupare. Eundem Athanasium, una cum Augustino, Fidei de Trinitate primos Authores sive Architectos appellant; Illum, in Ecclesia Graeca; Hunc, in Latina. Quasi explicare Fidem receptam, sit idem quod de novo condere; aut superstruere, quod fundamenta jacere: aut quasi utraque Ecclesia illos tanti fecisset, & utriusque scripta tam honorifice suscepisset, si modo in Fide innovassent, & Doctrinam ab Apostolis olim receptam Figmentis suis corrupissent. Parum referre dicunt, de Ecclesia, ejusque Signis quaerere, quaenam illa sit, ad quam nos conferre oportet, ad veritatem dijudicandam, salutemque comparandam: & quomodo dignosci possit ab Haereticorum & Schismaticorum Conventibus. Unicuique satis esse, sese ad Scripturas conferre, ex quibus solis veritas salutaris petenda est. Bene quidem, si ad Analogiam Fidei antiquitus receptae eas interpretarentur; caeteraque adjumenta adhibere dignarentur, quibus Pii & modesti uti solent, & quae ad genuinum illarum sensum rite eliciendum valde conducunt. At Hi ex adverso, ad illas legendas accedere solent, sectae suae Dogmatibus non solum prius instructi, sed & penitus imbuti; ita ut sensus genuinos & simplices non eliciant e Scripturis, sed suos illuc afferant, & Scripturis affingant; nec Dogmata sua ad illarum examen referant, sed illarum verba in sententiam suis Dogmatibus faventem pervertant atque detorqueant. Negat Socinus, Ecclesiam aliquam Christi visibilem, in perpetuum existere debere, aut Spiritus veritatis Pastoribus illius à Christo promissum. Eam enim in totum deficere posse existimat, & revera ingentem Eclypsin passam fuisse, proximo post Apostolos seculo. Celeberrimos veteris Ecclesiae Doctores, modo, ut Ignorantiae plusquam puerilis reos arguit; modo sacrilegae perfidiae in veritate per malitiam supprimendae, & Haeresis notam inurendo omnibus iis, qui veritatem ita suppressam in Jus pristinum vindicare studebant. Siquidem, in Praef. ad Solut. 30. Scrup. p. 327. Propositionem hanc expresse negat, Quod necesse sit semper extare aliquam visibilem Ecclesiam, quae puram Doctrinam de Deo, Filioque ejus retineat. & postea, Resp. ad 5um. Non est necessarium, aliquam extitisse isto Tempore (sc. seculo primitivo post Apostolos) veram Ecclesiam faciem neque enim eam perpetuo extituram, usquam revera praedictum, aut absolute promissum est. & Resp. ad 7. Ista Christi verba, Dic Ecclesiae, tunc locum habere censet, cum it de quo loquitur, fuerit in aliqua Ecclesia visibili. Christo voluntas erat, inquit, ut Ecclesia existeret, atque illi cura erat ut Apostolorum opera colligeretur, non tamen sequitur, quin pro Hominum malitia fieri potuerit, ut aliquando, idque per longissimum Tempus, nulla visibilis Ecclesia exiterit. Idem, Resp. ad 2. affirmat, Promissum Christi de Spiritu Sancto, qui instar Ducis nobis praeiret, & doceret omnem veritatem. Jo. 16. 13. non ad alios, praeter Apostolos, spectare; aut si ad alios, solummodo ad veros ipsorum successores, quos necessario extituros fuisse, nusquam scriptum esse arbitratur; neque id de alia veritate accipiendum esse, quam de ea quae prarsu [?] necessaria, est ad salutem.
units.tr: §. 87. This is how Socinus and his disciples conduct themselves in this matter of faith. They reject all the ancient creeds, these interpretations of the Apostolic faith, as adulterate formulas of faith and spurious inventions of human ingenuity. They do not hesitate even to call the famous creed of Athanasius the Creed of Satanasius. They also call this same Athanasius, together with Augustine, the first authors or architects of the faith concerning the Trinity: the former in the Greek Church, the latter in the Latin. As if explaining the received faith were the same as founding a new one, or building upon foundations were the same as laying them; or as if both Churches had held these men in such high esteem and received their writings so honourably, if they had really innovated in the faith and corrupted the doctrine once received from the Apostles with their own fictions. They say that it matters little to inquire about the Church and its marks, which Church it is to which we ought to turn in order to judge the truth and obtain salvation, and how it may be distinguished from the assemblies of heretics and schismatics. Each person is sufficient unto himself to turn to the Scriptures, from which alone saving truth is to be sought. This would indeed be well, if they interpreted the Scriptures according to the analogy of the faith received from antiquity, and condescended to use the other aids which the pious and modest are accustomed to use, and which greatly help to draw out their genuine sense. But these men, on the contrary, come to read them not only instructed beforehand in the dogmas of their sect, but thoroughly steeped in them; so that they do not draw genuine and simple senses from the Scriptures, but bring their own into them and foist them upon the Scriptures; nor do they refer their dogmas to the examination of the Scriptures, but twist and distort the words of Scripture into a meaning favouring their dogmas. Socinus denies that some visible Church of Christ ought to exist forever, or that the Spirit of truth promised by Christ to its ministers exists. For he thinks it can wholly fail, and that in fact it suffered a huge eclipse in the age immediately after the Apostles. He accuses the most celebrated teachers of the ancient Church, now as guilty of more than childish ignorance, now of sacrilegious treachery, in wickedly suppressing the truth, and branding with the mark of heresy all those who sought to restore to its former right the truth so suppressed. Indeed, in the Preface to the Solutions of the 30th Scruple, p. 327, he expressly denies this proposition: That it is necessary that some visible Church always exist, which retains the pure doctrine concerning God and his Son. And afterwards, in the Response to the 5th: It is not necessary that some true Church existed in that time (namely, the primitive age after the Apostles), for it has nowhere really been foretold, or absolutely promised, that it would exist forever. And in the Response to the 7th: He considers those words of Christ, Tell it to the Church, to have force only when that concerning which he speaks is within some visible Church. It was Christ's will, he says, that the Church should exist, and it was his concern that it should be gathered by the work of the Apostles; yet it does not follow that, through the malice of men, it could not happen that at some time, and that for a very long time, no visible Church existed. In the Response to the 2nd, he likewise affirms that Christ's promise concerning the Holy Spirit, who would go before us like a leader and teach us all truth (Jo. 16. 13), does not pertain to others besides the Apostles; or, if it pertains to others, only to their true successors, who he thinks were necessarily to exist, though it is nowhere written that they would; nor is it to be understood of any truth other than that which is absolutely necessary to salvation.

units.la: §. 88. Caeterum, in Ep. ad Squarcialupum. pag. 362. quam petulanti Censura ferit splendidissima illa antiquioris Ecclesiæ lumina, quasi crassis Ignorantiæ tenebris obvoluta fuissent, & propemodum extincta – Quasi non jam reipsa, inquit, compertum sit, in iis quæ ad Christianam Religionem attinent, Homines doctissimos, eosque numero pene infinito, idque per multa jecula, fœdissime lapsos esse; atque penitus ignorasse, quæ hodie Infantes ipsi recte norunt. Atque alibi Apostasiam à Fide Apostolica imputare non veretur Ecclesiæ primitivæ, quod Hæreticos Sui Antecessores sententia sua damnaret – Quamvis, ait, Pauli Samosateni, & Photini ætate, jam contraria sententia ab Ecclesia, hoc est, generatim ab iis, qui Jesu Christo nomen dederant, recepta fuisset; non tamen ea, quæ ab ipsis asseverabatur, nova erat, quippe quam ipsius Christi Apostoli [illegible, ~9 letters] docuissent. Unde etiam dubium non videtur, quin post ipsos Apostolos, aliquamdiu ea ab universali Ecclesia retenta fuerit. Sed neque Historias, nec scripta illius Temporis ulla habemus, nisi eorum, qui contrariam sententiam fuerunt secuti; quibus, quod ad Historiam attinet hac in Re, minime fidendum est; quique, cum tandem Principatum in Ecclesia obtinuerint, facile curare potuerunt, ne Adversariorum scripta in Posterorum manus pervenirent. Hinc perspicuum est, de sententia illorum, qui Hæretici ab ipsis sunt habiti, nihil posse statui, utrum sc. ea ab antiqua Ecclesia, necne, recepta fuerit. Nec mirum, si ea, licet olim passim recepta, iis tanquam Auctoritibus fuerit tributa, qui, postquam Hominum male doctorum culpa quodammodo exolevisset, illam instaurare sine[?] aggressi sunt. Quemadmodum ætate nostra, nonnulla de Christiana Religione sententiæ, quæ jam pene exoleverant, Luthero, Zuinglio, & aliis quibusdam, tanquam auctoribus, attributæ sint, quæ tamen in ipsa universali Ecclesia quondam viguerant. Quod si libri & scripturæ, unde hoc facile faci[?]le intelligi potest, perinde invisi iis fuissent, qui in Ecclesia Dogmatum sunt adepti, atque ii fuerunt, quos amte dixi-mus[?], non minus hoc, quam illud, incertum foret. Perissent enim ipsorum opera omnino ejusmodi quoque scripta. Sed quia plurima in illis sunt, quæ ipsis aperte favent, adeo ut secundum ea scripta sententiam de omnibus Rebus, quæ hodie controversa sunt, ferre non recusent, idcirco ea sunt conservata, & communia ipsorum & Adversariorum arma quodammodo effecta. Verum, quicquid hoc loco adversus Authoritatem sententia nostra à Volano congestum fuerit, satis semper erit nobis, eam Divinis literis non modo non adversari, sed potius consentaneam esse, pro quibus humanam quantamlibet Authoritatem, vel ipso Volano Teste, nihili faciendam esse, satis demonstratum est. Sic ille, Disp. contra Volanum. Tom. 2. p. 421. col. 2. Quæ Socini Apologia pro se, suoque[?] Dogmate, non minus Rationi adversa est, quam Pietati & Charitati Christianæ. Supponit enim, Catholicam Ecclesiam descivisse à Fide, quam Apostoli constanter docuerant, eam autem retentam fuisse tantummodo à Paulo Samosateno, Photino, alisque paucis, ipsorum Discipulis, reliquis omnibus veritatem Evangelicam oppugnantibus, illiusque vindices acerbissime persequentibus; cum tamen post Apostolorum obitum aliquamdiu retenta fuerit ab universali Ecclesia. Quo quid malitiofus aut absurdius fingi potuit contra Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Pastores? Quasi omnes dedita opera, & contra Conscientiam apostatafsent à Fide Apostolica, & Populum Christianum in eandem Apostasiam secum abduxissent, nemine refragante. Quis Christi Discipulus hoc voluisse eos putet? Quis Aristotelis Discipulus, eos hoc potuisse putet, si maxime voluissent? Etenim Religio vetat, ut illud credamus, nec minus Ratio, ut hoc fieri posse credimus. Supponit item, cunctos illius ævi Historicos, veritatem Gestorum suppressisse, & partibus favisse, reliquosque scriptores, celeberrimi nominis in Ecclesia, curasse, ne Adversariorum scripta in Posterorum manus pervenirent. Cum ex adverso satis constet, tum ex Historia Ecclesiastica, tum ex aliis illius ævi monumentis, Acta atque Dogmata Hæreticorum accurate esse relata, singularum Hæresium originem atque progressum; Patronos ac fautores, quinam & quot fuerint; Disputationes habitas cum Catholicis (quarum pleraque adhuc extant) ubi Argumenta illorum cernere est, cum Responsis ad singula. Denique, ex veterum synodorum Actis, quæ unicuique fas est consulere, luculenter apparet, quanta fide atque diligentia, quanta moderatione & æquitate, Novatorum scripta, & sententiæ inde excerptæ, examinabantur, & cum Doctrina Catholica conferebantur; quæ non ante damnatæ sunt, quam deprehensæ fuerint, ex collatione sic instituta, contrariæ Fidei antiquitus receptæ, quam in majorum libris repererant, quamq; ipsi ab Apostolis primitus traditam acceperant. Quam alienum itaque à veritate est, nec minus à modestia, quod Socinus hic affirmat de Hæreticorum Doctrina; eam olim passim receptam fuisse, sed cum Hominum male Doctorum culpa quodammodo exolevisset (sic enim pro insigni sua modestia, appellat eximios Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Doctores) illis tributa fuerit tanquam primis Authoribus, qui tamen ipsam non de novo cuderunt, sed oppressam, & fere abolitam denuo instaurarunt. Cum autem ad hoc probandum, affert Instantiam ex Doctrina Reformatorum, quam Instituto suo valde congruam esse judicat, partim nihil veri in se habet, partim nihil ad Rem. Siquidem Doctrina ista, quæ restituta est ab iis Theologis, & communibus suffragiis Ecclesiarum Reformatarum approbata, viguisse probatur in vetere Ecclesia Catholica, ex indubitatæ fidei scriptoribus, qui prisicis iis Temporibus vigue-runt, quorum Testimonia passim citantur in Har-monia Confessionum, & in Theologorum nostrorum scriptis, tum Dogmaticis, tum Polemicis. Hoc autem de luæ[?] sectæ Dogmatibus Socinus non audet afferere. Providentia enim Divina in hoc eximie elucet, quod, una cum S. Scripturæ voluminibus, scripta Patrum, acta Synodorum, Historicorum Ecclesiasticorum libri, & siqua alia vetustoris ævi monumenta, conservata sint, quibuscum conferri possent Dogmata, Ritusque Ecclesiæ Romanæ, & ad eorum normam emendari, quacunque in re à Recto aberraverint. Et sane æquum est, idem quoque sentire de scriptis veterum, ante Paulum Samosatenum, & Photinum; quæ tamen Socinus favisse vult istis Hæreticis, atque adeo per malitiam suppressa, ne contra ipsorum Adversarios Testimonium ferrent; cum tamen Catholici ex majorum suorum scriptis, Hære-ticorum iltorum[?] Dogmata novitatis arguere solerent, & corruptæ Fidei damnare. Cur non & S. Scripturæ libros ab iisdem quoque oppressos aut depravatos asserit, qui, ut ipse arbitratur, aperte favebant istorum Hæreticorum Doctrinæ & Catholicæ adversabantur? At in confesso est apud omnes, hos neque in seculo isto primævo, neque postea sub Tyrannide Papatus, aut deletos fuisse, aut depravatos, quamvis præcipua Argumenta, quæ contra Ecclesiæ Romanæ errores, & abusus faciunt, illinc deprompta sint. Idcirco, quamvis Pontificii appellent specie tenus ad veterum scripta, ut & ad S. Scripturas, pro Doctri-næ næ[?] suæ vindiciis, haud tamen inde sequitur, Haec magis, quam illas Doctrinae suae patrocinari, quicquid è contra Socino videtur, qui in ipsorum Scriptis parum aut nihil versatus est. Utcunque ergo hic afferat, quamplurima in veterum Scriptis aperte favere Pontificiis, adeo ut secundum ea[?] sententiam de omnibus Rebus, quae hodie controversæ sunt ferre non recusent; atque alibi audacius, sic[?] firmet, ex Pontificiorum Scriptis contra Lutheranos & Calvinianos satis intelligi, quod si præter S. Literas, Istorum Authoritati standum sit, nobis omnibus Causa cadendum esse; sc. Epist. 3. ad Matt: Radecium. summam tamen suam imperitiam in hoc prodit. Pontificii enim Theologi, ut satis notum est, etsi multum deferre videantur Authoritati veterum, cum in genere loquuntur; quoties tamen ad particulares Controversias descenditur, quæ inter illos & nostros agitantur, ubi paulo arctius premuntur illorum Testimoniis, vel tergiversari solent vel ea aperte rejiciunt. Pariter sat liquet, Doctissimos quosque e nostris Theologis, præsertim Anglicanis, fidenter appellare ad veterum Ecclesiæ Doctorum Tribunal, ut Sententiam suam ferant de quæstionibus controversis, cui & acquiescere se velle testantur, quoties concordibus Suffragiis latam comperiunt. Quod vero demum opponit Volano, & Testimoniis ab eo congestis, sibi satis esse, suam[?] Sententiam divinis literis non modo non adversari, sed prorsus consentaneam esse; pra[?] quibus humanam quantamlibet Authoritatem, nihili faciendam esse, miserrimum effugium est, & ineptissima petitio Principii. Sic enim se Judicem constituit in sua ipsius Causa, suæque solius sectæ Sententiam vult esse consentaneam S. Scripturæ; Cunctorum autem aliorum sensus rejicit quotcunque aut qualescunque fuerint, ut alienos & erroneos; & sub praetextu Authoritatis divinae, quae omni humanae praeponenda est, suam occulte ingerit, & in utrinque locum dolore supponit.
units.tr: §. 88. Moreover, in his letter to Squarcialupus (p. 362), he strikes with wanton censure those most splendid lights of the earlier Church, as if they had been wrapped in the thick darkness of ignorance and had been almost extinguished: As if it were not already plainly established, he says, that in matters pertaining to the Christian religion, very learned men, and almost countless in number, have fallen most shamefully over many ages, and have been utterly ignorant of things that infants today know well. And elsewhere he does not hesitate to charge the primitive Church with apostasy from the apostolic faith, because it condemned his own predecessors as heretics: Although, he says, in the time of Paul of Samosata and Photinus a contrary opinion had already been received by the Church, that is, generally by those who had given their name to Jesus Christ; nevertheless the view they asserted was not new, since the apostles of Christ himself had taught it [illegible]. Hence it does not seem doubtful that, after the apostles themselves, this view was retained by the universal Church for some time. But we have no histories or writings of that time except those of men who followed the contrary opinion; and in this matter we can by no means trust their account of history. Once they had gained control in the Church, they could easily take care that the writings of their opponents did not reach the hands of posterity. Hence it is clear that nothing can be decided about the opinion of those who were regarded as heretics by them, namely whether or not it was received by the ancient Church. Nor is it surprising if this view, though once widely received, was attributed to those who undertook to restore it after it had in some measure faded through the fault of poorly taught men, just as in our own age certain opinions about the Christian religion, which had almost faded away, have been attributed to Luther, Zwingli and some others as their authors, although they once flourished in the universal Church itself. But if books and writings, from which this can easily be understood, had been as hateful to those who had obtained the doctrines in the Church as they were to those whom I have just mentioned, it would be no less uncertain in the one case than in the other. For their works of that kind would have perished altogether. But because there are many things in them that openly favour these men, so that they do not refuse to pronounce on all the matters now in dispute according to those writings, they have been preserved, and have in some sense become a common weapon of both them and their adversaries. Yet whatever has been gathered by Volanus against the authority of our view in this place, it will always be enough for us that our view not only does not oppose the divine writings but is rather in agreement with them; for which reason, as Volanus himself bears witness, it has been sufficiently shown that human authority, however great, is to be held as nothing. So he writes, in his disputation against Volanus, vol. 2, p. 421, col. 2. This apology of Socinus for himself and his doctrine is no less opposed to reason than to Christian piety and charity. For he supposes that the Catholic Church had departed from the faith which the apostles had constantly taught, and that this faith was retained only by Paul of Samosata, Photinus and a few others, their disciples, while all the rest attacked the Gospel truth and most bitterly persecuted its defenders; yet it was in fact retained by the universal Church for some time after the death of the apostles. What more malicious or absurd thing could be invented against the pastors of the Catholic Church? As if they all, deliberately and against their conscience, had apostatized from the apostolic faith and had led the Christian people with them into the same apostasy, with no one objecting. What disciple of Christ would think they wished this? What disciple of Aristotle would think they could have done it, even if they had wished to? For religion forbids us to believe the first, and reason no less forbids us to believe the second is possible. He also supposes that all the historians of that age suppressed the truth of events and favoured one party, and that the other writers of famous name in the Church took care that the writings of their adversaries did not reach the hands of posterity. Yet on the other side it is quite certain, both from ecclesiastical history and from other monuments of that age, that the acts and doctrines of the heretics were carefully recorded, the origin and progress of each heresy, who and how many were its patrons and supporters, the disputations held with Catholics (many of which still survive), where their arguments may be seen together with the replies to each. Finally, from the acts of the ancient synods, which anyone may consult, it clearly appears with what faith and diligence, with what moderation and fairness, the writings of the innovators and the opinions excerpted from them were examined and compared with Catholic doctrine. They were not condemned until they had been found, by such a comparison, contrary to the faith received from of old, which they had found in the books of their elders and had received as first handed down by the apostles. How alien, then, from truth, and no less from modesty, is what Socinus here asserts about the doctrine of the heretics: that it was once widely received, but that, since it had in some measure faded through the fault of poorly taught men (for so, with his remarkable modesty, he calls the eminent teachers of the Catholic Church), it was attributed to them as its first authors, though they did not in fact coin it anew, but restored it after it had been suppressed and nearly abolished. Now, to prove this, he brings forward an instance from the doctrine of the Reformed, which he judges to be very suitable to his purpose; but it partly has nothing true in it and partly has nothing to do with the matter. For that doctrine, which was restored by those theologians and approved by the common votes of the Reformed Churches, is shown to have flourished in the ancient Catholic Church, from writers of undoubted faith who lived in those early times; their testimonies are cited on every side in the Harmony of the Confessions and in the writings of our theologians, both dogmatic and polemical. But Socinus does not dare to assert this of the doctrines of his own sect. For the providence of God shines out remarkably in this, that along with the volumes of Holy Scripture there have been preserved the writings of the Fathers, the acts of the synods, the books of ecclesiastical historians and whatever other monuments of more ancient times there are, with which the doctrines and rites of the Roman Church might be compared, and by whose standard they might be corrected wherever they have strayed from the right path. And indeed it is fair to think the same also of the writings of the ancients before Paul of Samosata and Photinus; yet Socinus wishes these to have favoured those heretics, and so to have been suppressed through malice, lest they bear witness against their adversaries; though Catholics were accustomed to use the writings of their elders to prove the novelty of those heretics' doctrines and to condemn their corrupted faith. Why does he not also assert that the books of Holy Scripture were suppressed or corrupted by those same men, who, as he himself thinks, openly favoured the doctrine of these heretics and were opposed to the Catholic faith? But it is admitted by all that these books were neither destroyed nor corrupted, either in that earliest age or later under the tyranny of the Papacy, although the principal arguments against the errors and abuses of the Roman Church are drawn from them. Therefore, although the Papists appeal, in appearance at least, to the writings of the ancients, as well as to Holy Scripture, in defence of their doctrine, it does not follow that these writings favour their doctrine rather than that the Scriptures do, whatever Socinus may think, who has had little or no acquaintance with their writings. However, although he here asserts that very many things in the writings of the ancients openly favour the Papists, so that they do not refuse to pronounce on all the matters now in dispute according to those writings; and although elsewhere he rashly maintains that from the Papists' writings against the Lutherans and Calvinists it is sufficiently clear that, if the authority of these men is to be followed besides Holy Scripture, all of us must give up our cause (Epist. 3 to Matthew Radecius), he shows his great inexperience in this. For Papist theologians, as is well known, although they seem to defer greatly to the authority of the ancients when they speak in general terms, yet whenever one descends to the particular controversies that are debated between them and us, and where they are pressed rather closely by the testimonies of the ancients, they are wont either to evade them or to reject them openly. Likewise it is quite plain that the most learned of our theologians, especially the English, confidently appeal to the tribunal of the ancient teachers of the Church to give judgment on controverted questions, and declare that they are willing to acquiesce in it whenever they find that it has been pronounced by unanimous votes. But as for what he finally objects to Volanus and to the testimonies gathered by him, that it is enough for him that his opinion not only does not oppose the divine writings but is wholly in agreement with them; before which, human authority, however great, is to be held as nothing, this is a most wretched evasion and a most foolish begging of the question. For in this way he makes himself judge in his own cause, and wants the opinion of his own sect alone to be in agreement with Holy Scripture; but he rejects the senses of all others, however many and of whatever kind, as alien and erroneous; and under the pretext of divine authority, which is to be preferred to all human authority, he covertly thrusts in his own, and lays a trap for the reader on either side.

units.la: §. 89. Cumque idem alibi vehementer exagitet Fr. Davidis, & Chr. Franken Discipulos, qui (ipsius Principiis insistentes) negabant Christum invocandum esse (quia Deus solus appellatur exauditor precum, & Cordium inspector) censeatque illos non habendos esse pro Christianis, ut qui reipsa Christum non habeant; & Jesum esse Christum, licet fortasse aperte verbis non audeant, re tamen ipsa omnino negent. Instit. Christianae Rel. pr 656. col. 2. Tom. 1.
units.tr: §. 89. Since he elsewhere vehemently attacks the followers of Francis David and Christopher Franck, who (adhering to his own principles) denied that Christ is to be invoked, because God alone is called the hearer of prayers and the inspector of hearts, he judges that these men are not to be regarded as Christians, since in reality they do not have Christ; and although perhaps they do not dare to say openly that Jesus is the Christ, in fact they utterly deny it. Institutio Christianae Religionis, p. 656, col. 2, vol. 1.

units.la: Cumque in epistola sua ad Synodum Nægroviensem, nullum amplius cum Talibus in Rebus sacris commercium habendum esse arbitretur; atque insuper injungi velit omnibus suae sectae Ministris, ut in publicus precibus, statutis quibusdam Diebus, Christum Jesum Dei Filium nominatim invocarent. Tom. 1. p. 491. col. 1. Alibi tamen hanc Christi Invocationem in eo genere Adiaphororum ponit, quae nec jussa sunt, nec vetita; & diserte affirmat, eam hac ipsa de Causa non esse necessariam. Sic Ille Ep. ad Geo. Eniedinum. Tom. 1. p. 485. col. 2.
units.tr: Since in his letter to the Synod of Nagyvárad he thinks that no further dealings in sacred matters are to be held with such people, and moreover wishes it enjoined on all the ministers of his sect that, on certain set days in public prayers, they should invoke by name Christ Jesus, the Son of God. Vol. 1, p. 491, col. 1. Elsewhere, however, he places this invocation of Christ among those indifferent things which are neither commanded nor forbidden, and he expressly affirms that for this very reason it is not necessary. So he writes in his letter to Georg Enyedi, vol. 1, p. 485, col. 2.

units.la: Affirmat item, ad Christi Invocationem afferendam, nihil opus esse, ut nos sciamus, eum fuisse Servatorem à Patre datum. Sive enim nos hoc sciamus, inquit, sive minus, verissimum id est, & erit semper. De Invoc. Christi Tom. 1. p. 356. col. 1. Quibus verbis inter se collatis, ut Contradictoria videtur afferere, dum hoc Dogma de Christo invocando, & necessarium censet & adiaphorum; ita satis pro Imperio cunctis suae sectae Ministris istam invocandi Christi Praxin imponi curat, etsi à Deo minime jussam, prout Ipsi visum est. Quinetiam, Invocationem hanc Exigit ab iis, qui haud certi sunt, utrum Christus Nobis fuerit in Servatorem à Patre datus, annon? Quasi Oratio accepta esse possit sine Fide; aut Fides non praesupponat cognitionem illius Numinis, ad quod preces nostras dirigimus, aut, denique, quasi salutem ab eo rite poscere quaeamus, de quo dubii sumus, an Talis sit, qui nobis salutem istam conferre possit.
units.tr: He likewise affirms that to bring forward the invocation of Christ, there is no need for us to know that he was given by the Father as Saviour. For whether we know this or not, says he, it is most true and always will be. On the Invocation of Christ, vol. 1, p. 356, col. 1. When these words are set side by side, he seems to assert contradictory things, since he holds this doctrine of invoking Christ to be both necessary and indifferent. Thus he takes care to impose, by his own authority, this practice of invoking Christ on all the ministers of his sect, although it has not been commanded by God, as it seemed good to him. Moreover, he demands this invocation of those who are not sure whether Christ was given to us by the Father as Saviour or not. As if prayer could be acceptable without faith, or faith did not presuppose knowledge of that Divinity to whom we direct our prayers; or, finally, as if one could properly ask salvation from one about whom one is in doubt whether he is such a one as can bestow that salvation upon us.

units.la: §. 90. Ita tergiversatur Socinus, ita Subterfugia quaerit, ita totam Antiquitatem aut calumniatur aut contemnit, dum suo Dogmati patrocinium undiquaque petit. Quod malae Causae maximum Indicium est. Neque hoc ei Proprium fuit. Idem enim factitatum legimus à senioribus Anti-Trinitariis, quorum Socinus, ut in Doctrina, sic in moribus videtur fuisse Discipulus. Siquidem accepimus primarios quosdam ex horum numero, tam Polonos, quam exteros, qui post Servetum Genevae combustum, in partes Transylvaniae & Poloniae certatim confugerant, haeresesque suas illic disseminare caeperant, quamprimum innotuere Ecclesiis Evangelicis & malesanae fuerunt Doctrinae sic ab iis traditae, comperti suerint, haeretica sua Dogmata dissimulasse tamen, fidemque orthodoxam palam professos fuisse, quoties in Synodos citabantur, ad respondendum de suspicione haereseos. Ita Petrus Statorius Thionvilanus, in Synodum Pinczoviensem citatus, hanc suam Confessionem edidit, propriaque manu consignavit. A. D. 1559.—Prophetiam & Apostolicam Doctrinam, quae veram Dei Patris, Filii, & Spiritus Sancti cognitionem continet, Amplector ac veneror, parique religione Deum Patrem, Filium, ac S. Spiritum, distincte secundum sacrarum literarum veritatem, colendam, implorandumque precibus libere profiteor. Denique omnem haereticam de Deo Patre, Filio, & Spiritu Sancto Blasphemiam, plane detestor, sive Ariana illa, sive Servetiana, sive Eunomiana, sive Stancariana fuerint.
