Georgius item Blandrata, postquam Calvinus Ecclesias Polonicas, & Palatinum Vilnensem de ipso tempestive[?] monuisset, in altera synodo Pinczoviensi[?], A. D. 1561. quasi adversus Calvini injurias sese defensurus, his verbis Fidem suam publice testatus est: Fateor me credere in unum Deum Patrem, in unum Dominum Jesum Christum Filium ejus, & in unum Spiritum Sanctum, quocum est essentialiter Deus. Deorum pluralitatem detestor, cum unus nobis sit tantum Deus, essentia indivisibilis. Fateor, tres esse distinctas Hypostases, & aeternam Christi Divinitatem ac Generationem, & Spiritum Sanctum, verum & aeternum Deum, ab utroque procedentem. Sic. Hi Fidem suam ore testati sunt. Hac tamen Professione non obstante, satis constat, illos primos, atque acerrimos haeresis Anti-Trinitariorum Patronos ac Propugnatores extitisse, una cum Franc. Lismanino, qui tamen in altera synodo ejusdem Anni, Se non adeo Rem, atque Doctrinam Fidei, ac verba illa Scholastica Trinitatis, ac similia, accusare profitebatur. Itaque magis magisque indies detecti, cum non amplius sua virulenta Dogmata occultare potuerunt, & sub nomine Evangelicorum latenter obrepere, post unum & alterum Colloquium inter ipsos & Orthodoxos habitum, schismate palam facto, in segreges Coetus abiere: vid. hist. Eccles. Slavonic. lib. 1.[?] Hoc modo dissimulare soliti sunt hujusce Sectae Antesignani, cum primum exorti sunt, & numero pauciores essent; quasi sui Dogmatis ipsos puderet, aut saltem ex impendentis periculi metu illud palam afferere non auderent. Qua in Re jure desideramus, non solum ipsorum Constantiam, sed & sinceritatem, contra quam graviter peccarunt, tam dissimulando, quod revera tenuerunt, quam profitendo illud, quod Corde abnegarunt; utrumque contra animi sui sententiam, & Conscientia refragante, ut eventus paulo post docuit. Ita mendaces deprehensi sunt primi hujus Sectae Authores, non minus in se, quam in Deum & veritatem Catholicam; nec magis infames sunt ob Haeresin, quam ob Hypocrisin.
units.tr: §. 90. Thus Socinus evades, thus he seeks subterfuges, thus he either slanders or despises the whole of antiquity, while everywhere he seeks patronage for his doctrine. This is the greatest sign of a bad cause. Nor was this peculiar to him. For we read that the same thing was practised by the older Anti-Trinitarians, of whom Socinus seems to have been the disciple in morals as well as in doctrine. For we have learned that some of their leading men, both Poles and foreigners, who after Servetus was burned at Geneva had hastened to Transylvania and Poland and had begun to spread their heresies there, as soon as they became known to the Evangelical Churches, and it was discovered what unsound doctrine they taught, nevertheless concealed their heretical opinions, and openly professed the orthodox faith whenever they were summoned to synods to answer on suspicion of heresy. Thus Peter Statorius of Thionville, summoned to the Synod of Pinczów, published this confession of his and signed it with his own hand, in the year 1559: I embrace and revere the prophetic and apostolic doctrine, which contains the true knowledge of God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and I freely profess that God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are to be worshipped and implored in prayer with equal reverence, distinctly, according to the truth of the sacred letters. Finally, I utterly detest every heretical blasphemy concerning God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, whether it be that of the Arians, of Servetus, of Eunomius, or of Stancaro. Likewise Georg Blandrata, after Calvin had in good time warned the Polish churches and the Palatine of Vilnius about him, in another synod at Pinczów, in the year 1561, as if about to defend himself against Calvin's charges, publicly attested his faith in these words: I confess that I believe in one God the Father, in one Lord Jesus Christ his Son, and in one Holy Spirit, who is essentially God with him. I detest the plurality of gods, since for us there is only one God, one indivisible essence. I confess that there are three distinct Hypostases, and the eternal Divinity and Generation of Christ, and the Holy Spirit, the true and eternal God, proceeding from both. Thus these men attested their faith by word of mouth. Yet, notwithstanding this profession, it is well established that these same men became the first and most bitter patrons and champions of the Anti-Trinitarian heresy, together with Francis Lismanino, who nevertheless professed at another synod of the same year that he did not so much accuse the matter and doctrine of faith, nor those Scholastic words of the Trinity, and similar terms. Accordingly, as they were more and more exposed day by day, when they could no longer conceal their virulent doctrines and creep in secretly under the name of Evangelicals, after one or two conferences held between them and the orthodox, the schism being openly made, they departed into separate assemblies: see Ecclesiastical History of Slavonia, book 1. In this way the forerunners of this sect were accustomed to dissemble when they first arose and were still few in number, as if they were ashamed of their doctrine, or at least did not dare to assert it openly for fear of the impending danger. In this matter we justly miss not only their constancy but also their sincerity, in which they sinned grievously, both by dissembling what they really held and by professing what they had in their hearts renounced; both were against the judgement of their own minds, and their conscience protesting, as the outcome shortly afterwards showed. Thus the first authors of this sect were detected as liars, no less against themselves than against God and Catholic truth; and they are no less infamous for hypocrisy than for heresy.

units.la: §. 91. Utcunque igitur Socinus, illiusque Socii ac Discipuli, summam humilitatem ac modestiam simulent, cum sincero veritatis amore, pieque vitae studio; utcunque zelum Gloriae Divinae illustrandae, Fidei verè Christianae ubique propagandae, & salutis animarum promovendae præ se ferant; utcunque vitae sanctitatem præ omnibus magnifacere videantur, dicantque se facile posse dissentiri[?] in opinionibus ferre, modo Christianae vitae Innocentiae, & singulari morum Integritati, studeatur; utcunque demum Amicorum judicium, eruditionem, & auctoritatem, se plurimi facere prætendat Socinus; & ante omnia Divini numinis auxilium, tum pro se, tum pro amicis imploret, quod utrorumque dirigat & adjuvet in via veritatis; ex antedictis tamen satis liquet, hæc omnia simulari tantum, cum facta dictis minime responderint. Cunctos enim præ se contemnunt; Fidem Catholicam non solum ferociter oppugnant, sed & saepissimis Convitiis proscindunt; Ecclesiam Catholicam non solum deserunt, sed & ir[?] partes discindunt, imo quantum in se est, destruunt, & e[?] medio tollunt; partim, dum eam extirpasse[?] per aliquot secula negant; partim, dum Religionis Christianæ fundamentalia subvertunt. Quod pro vero antiquitus habitum esset, rejiciunt; Hæreses olim ab Ecclesia Catholica damnatas denuo resuscitant, & perniciosissimos suos errores, etiam post sententiam à cunctis per orbem Christianum Ecclesiis contra illos latam; & palmaria Catholicorum Argumenta, quibus perfossi & postrati sunt, mordicus tamen retinent, & obstinatissimè propugnant; cum vero Trinitatem habeant pro Cerebri humani Idolo, necesse est ut omnes illius Cultores, hoc est, omnes Catholicæ Ecclesiæ Filios, pro Idololatris habeant, adeoque æternæ salutis incapaces; monitis Amicorum, quantumcunque pii doctique fuerint, cedere recusant; Preces, quas ad Deum dirigunt, ut in via veritatis dirigantur, vel non ex animo offerunt, vel culpa sua inefficaces reddunt; dum præconceptis Opinionibus pertinaciter adhærent, & media ad veritatem inveniendam requisita, quæ Deus & Ecclesia illius, eorum. usui impensius commendarunt, adhibere renuunt; cum autem pro aliis sic orant, hoc solum à Deo petunt, ut Catholicam fidem & Ecclesiam deserentes, sua Dogmata amplectantur, suorumque Cœtibus se adjungant. Post emo[?], cum zelum intensiorem præ se ferant pro sincera Pietate, & integritate vitæ Christianæ; utrăque tamen convellere satagunt per geminum illud dogma de Psychopannychia & totali perditione impiorum in die Judicii, uti antehac observavimus. Itaque sive originem hujus Sectæ, sive fœdos exitus quamplurimum Professorum isti primitus adhærentium, spectemus; sive perniciosissimam Consequentiam, & malignos effectus errorum, quos obstinatè tuentur, istamerito[?] abstterrere possunt unumquemque Pium, qui saluti suæ ferio consulit, quo minus isti se adjungat. Siquidem Anti-Trinitariorum primarii Duces, quorum Copias Socinus tandem in unum, quasi exercitum collegit, ut contra Ecclesiam Catholicam conjunctis viribus militarent; aut sponte profugi erant, & perfidi Desertores Ecclesiarum Evangelicarum, aut inde expulsi; qui exinde in Poloniam, Transylvaniam, Regionesque vicinas confluxerunt; aut Homines ibidem orti & educati, at nullius fere aut mali nominis. Ex primo genere erant Valentinus Gentilis, Geo: Blandrata, Jo: Paulus Alciatus, aliique quidam; quibus etiam accenseri poteit utrumque Socinus. Ex altero autem quam bonæ Indolis, vitæ, famæque fuerint, facile discere possumus ab excellenti quodam viro (sic enim Socinus illum appellat) qui inter cæteros scrupulos, numero 30. quos Socino solvendos proponit, hunc objicit, numero 13ium. — Quod hujusmodi Sectariorum plerique nulla Pietatis commendatione, nullo laudato priorís vitæ exemplo commendati forent. Imo, inquit, ut plerumque vidimus, hæc Doctrina de Christo per Homines vagabundos, & contentionum zeli carnalis plenos; alios ex Lustri[?], Audu[?], Ganeis[?], prolata est. Quibus Principiis quomodo partes exitus responderint, Idem paulo post indicat, Sc.Scrup. 18. ubi de his Sectariis affirmat, quod, postquam præfervidus ipsorum zelus paulatim deferbuit in propagando Christi Regno, (ut ipsi præ se ferebant) in quendam Atheismum prolaberentur, ita ut alii apertè Christum, alii vero etiam Deum & inferos negarent. Quod & Socinus alibi fatetur, uti prius advertimus, neque aliud habet quod reponat, quam illud Joannis Apostoli, é nobis prodierunt, sed ex nobis non erant. At hoc utique parum valet ad Dogma Socinianum, illiusque Patronos ab hoc Apostasiae crimine vindicandum, cum istius Doctrinae soboles genuina sit; quippe quae Fidei, Pietatisque fundamenta subvertit; quibus e medio sublatis, quid amplius restat, quam opinionum incertitudo, discursatio vaga per inextricabiles errorum labyrinthos, vicissitudo Religionum & Cultuum, quos desultoria levitate invicem permutant, tandemque praeceps Ruina in Abyssum Athe-ismi.
units.tr: §. 91. Therefore, however much Socinus and his associates and disciples may pretend the highest humility and modesty, together with a sincere love of truth and a pious zeal for a holy life; however much they may display zeal for illustrating the glory of God, for propagating the truly Christian faith everywhere, and for promoting the salvation of souls; however much they may seem to prize above all the holiness of life, and say that they can easily tolerate differences of opinion, provided that care is taken for the innocence of Christian life and singular integrity of morals; and finally, however much Socinus claims to value greatly the judgement, learning and authority of his friends, and above all implores the help of the divine majesty, both for himself and for his friends, that it may direct and aid both in the way of truth: nevertheless, from what has been said above, it is quite clear that all these things are merely feigned, since their deeds in no way correspond to their words. For they despise everyone else; they not only fiercely attack the Catholic faith, but also tear it apart with the most frequent reproaches; they not only desert the Catholic Church, but also split it into parts, indeed, as far as in them lies, they destroy it and remove it from the midst; partly by denying that it has existed for some centuries, partly by overturning the fundamentals of the Christian religion. What has been held as true from antiquity they reject; heresies long ago condemned by the Catholic Church they raise up again; and their most pernicious errors, even after the sentence pronounced against them by the Churches throughout the Christian world, and the palmary arguments of the Catholics by which they have been pierced and laid low, they nevertheless hold stubbornly and defend most obstinately. Since they regard the Trinity as an idol of the human brain, they must necessarily regard all its worshippers, that is, all the sons of the Catholic Church, as idolaters, and therefore incapable of eternal salvation. They refuse to yield to the admonitions of friends, however pious and learned they may be. The prayers which they direct to God, that they may be guided in the way of truth, they either offer without sincerity or render ineffectual by their own fault, while they cling pertinaciously to preconceived opinions and refuse to use the means required for finding the truth, which God and his Church have most earnestly commended to their use. And when they pray for others in this way, they ask God only for this, that they, deserting the Catholic faith and Church, may embrace their doctrines and join their assemblies. Furthermore, while they display a more intense zeal for sincere piety and integrity of Christian life, they nevertheless labour to overthrow both by that twofold dogma of the soul's sleep and the total destruction of the wicked on the day of judgement, as we observed above. Therefore, whether we look at the origin of this sect or at the foul ends of very many of its professors who at first adhered to it, or at the most pernicious consequences and the baneful effects of the errors which they obstinately defend, these things can justly deter every pious person who is seriously concerned for his own salvation from joining them. For the chief leaders of the Anti-Trinitarians, whose forces Socinus at last gathered together into one body, as an army to fight jointly against the Catholic Church, either fled of their own accord and were treacherous deserters from the Evangelical Churches, or were expelled from them; and from there they flocked into Poland, Transylvania and the neighbouring regions. Others were men born and brought up there, but of almost no good or bad reputation. To the first kind belonged Valentine Gentile, Georg Blandrata, John Paul Alciati, and certain others, to whom Socinus himself may also be reckoned. As to the second kind, what good character, life and reputation they had, we can easily learn from a certain excellent man (for so Socinus calls him), who, among the other scruples, thirty in number, which he proposes for Socinus to solve, objects this to him, the thirteenth: that most of such sectaries were commended by no praise of piety, by no esteemed example of their former life. Indeed, he says, as we have mostly seen, this doctrine concerning Christ has been put forward by vagabond men, full of the zeal of contentions and of carnal passions, some from brothels, some from taverns, some from gambling houses. How the outcome of these principles corresponded to them, the same writer indicates a little later, on Scrup. 18, where he affirms of these sectaries that, after their fervent zeal gradually cooled in propagating the Kingdom of Christ (as they themselves professed), they slid into a certain atheism, so that some openly denied Christ, and others even denied God and hell. This Socinus also admits elsewhere, as we noted before, and he has nothing else to reply except that saying of the Apostle John: They went out from us, but they were not of us. But this avails little to clear the Socinian doctrine and its patrons from this crime of apostasy, since this doctrine is its genuine offspring; for it overturns the foundations of faith and piety. When these are removed, what remains but uncertainty of opinions, a wandering roaming through the inextricable labyrinths of error, a changing of religions and forms of worship, which they exchange with one another in fickle levity, and at last headlong ruin into the abyss of atheism.

units.la: §. 92. Post Catalogum errorum Socinianorum, qui vel ex nuda recitatione falsitatem[?] suam demonstrant, Pii cujusque oculis, animisque Fidelium horrorem incutiunt, fas sit eorundem concessa subjicere, quae vel ab amicis sanioribus moniti vel ab Antagonistis arctius pressi, in scriptis suis exhibent. Haec autem excerpsi praecipue ex ipso Socino, Sectae hujus magistro; quaedam item e Catechismo Racoviensi, e Schlichtingio in Symbolum, e Joachimo Stegmanno de judice & norma Controversiarum Fidei, & ex Andrea Dudithio. Quae vero e Socino exhibeo, fere omnia extant in Tomo 1° oper: ipsius, & sic se habent.
units.tr: §. 92. After the catalogue of Socinian errors, which by bare recital show their falsehood and strike horror into every pious eye and the minds of the faithful, it is permitted to add those concessions which they set out in their writings, either when warned by saner friends or when pressed more closely by their antagonists. I have excerpted these chiefly from Socinus himself, the master of this sect; some also from the Racovian Catechism, from Schlichting on the Creed, from Joachim Stegmann on the judge and norm of controversies of faith, and from Andreas Dudith. Nearly all of what I give from Socinus is found in Tome 1 of his works, and reads thus.

units.la: §. 93. 1. In Solut. 30. scrupulorum ab excellenti quodam viro propositorum, p. 327. Resp. ad Scrup. 23um. haec habet. Lutherum homines adduxit ad ejusmodi Rerum Divinarum cognitionem, quae satis esse poterat ad salutem aeternam consequendam per Lutherum ea fuerunt patefacta, quae ad Hominem fidelem constituendum sunt necessaria. Idem Ep. 3. ad Dudithium. p. 502. neutiquam[?] se dubitare affirmat, quin multi sint, vel saltem esse possint, è numero Calvinianorum, & Lutheranorum, qui Coelestis[?] vitae hereditatem sunt adituri, cum se ad praescriptum Christi gesserint. De Papistis, inquit, idem affirmare nolim, quos omnes hodie die Idololatras esse statuo. Novi vero neminem Idololatrarum salutis aeternae compotem fore. Quibus in vetbis fatetur, Evangelicos utriusque Communionis, habere omnia ad Fidem & salutem aeternam necessaria, & posse, dum tales manent, ad Christi praescriptum se gerere. Cur itaque Schisma fecit in Ecclesiis Evangelicis? Cur Discipulos suos, à publicis ipsorum conventibus, & ab omni Communione in Sacris, semovere voluit? Cur segreges suorum Coetus instituit, ob discrimen in Rebus ad salutem minime necessariis? Cur Dogmata sua, tam nova in se, tam Evangelicorum Doctrinæ adversantia, tanto fervore, tam acri zelo, ubique urget, & quasi necessaria ad salutem, cunctis inculcat? Cur Evangelicorum Dogmata alibi impugnat, ac damnat, ut summe perniciosa, Fidei Christianae adversa, & salutis aeternae destructiva; praesertim, illa de Trinitate, & satisfactione Christi? Cur Ecclesiam unamquamque, quae istud S.S. Trinitatis Dogma asserit, Antichristianam appellat? Cur eandem Trinitatem, habet pro fictitio Idolo, & humani cerebri Commento, quam tamen omnes ubique Catholici & credant, & colunt, ut ipse probe novit; ac proinde, cunctos illius cultores pro Idololatris, habet, quos omnes à regno Coelorum excludit? Si quidem alibi, non pudet eum affirmare, Contra Fidem de uno vero Deo nullum gravius in Christi Ecclesiam ab Antichristi spiritu errorum invectum fuisse, quam in Deo, inque illius simplicissima essentia, plures esse Personas inter se distinctas, quarum qualibet sit verus Deus. Animadv. in 1°. Assert.Coll. Posnan. p. 423. & in Resp. ad librum Jac. Coveti, quem scripserat contra Theses ipsius de Jesu Christo Servatore, ubi totis viribus impugnat Christi Satisfactionem[?], satis innuit, Covetum[?] in Defensione istius Doctrinae, contumeliosum fuisse in Deum, ejusque Filium, dum Evangelium ministravit; Populique sibi commissi damnationem procurasse, dum illius salutem se curare credidit. Unde & illum hortatur, precari Deum, ut sibi veniam benignus daret, suoque Spiritu mentem ipsius perfunderet.
units.tr: §. 93. 1. In the Solution of the 30th scruple proposed by a certain excellent man, p. 327, in the Reply to the 23rd Scruple, he has this: Luther led men to such a knowledge of divine things as could be sufficient for obtaining eternal salvation; those things were revealed through Luther which are necessary for making a faithful man. The same, in Ep. 3 to Dudith, p. 502, he affirms that he by no means doubts that there are, or at least can be, many from the number of the Calvinists and Lutherans who will enter upon the inheritance of heavenly life, when they have conducted themselves according to the precept of Christ. About the Papists, he says, I would not wish to affirm the same, whom I today judge all to be idolaters. But I know of no idolater who will be a partaker of eternal salvation. In these words he confesses that Evangelicals of both communions have all things necessary for faith and eternal salvation, and can, so long as they remain such, conduct themselves according to the precept of Christ. Why then did he make a schism in the Evangelical churches? Why did he wish to remove his disciples from their public assemblies and from all communion in sacred things? Why did he set up separate gatherings of his own people, on account of a difference in matters by no means necessary to salvation? Why does he urge his own doctrines, so new in themselves and so opposed to the doctrine of the Evangelicals, everywhere with such fervour and such keen zeal, and inculcate them on all as if necessary to salvation? Why does he attack and condemn the doctrines of the Evangelicals elsewhere, as most pernicious, adverse to the Christian faith, and destructive of eternal salvation; especially those concerning the Trinity and the satisfaction of Christ? Why does he call every church which asserts this dogma of the most holy Trinity Antichristian? Why does he hold this same Trinity to be a fictitious idol and an invention of the human brain, which yet all Catholics everywhere both believe and worship, as he himself knows well; and consequently does he count all its worshippers as idolaters, all of whom he excludes from the kingdom of heaven? For elsewhere he is not ashamed to affirm: Against the faith concerning the one true God, no more grievous error has been brought into the Church of Christ by the spirit of Antichrist than that in God, and in his most simple essence, there are several Persons distinct from one another, each of whom is true God. Animadversions on the first assertion of the Posnan Colloquy, p. 423; and in the Reply to the book of Jacob Covetus, which he had written against his theses concerning Jesus Christ the Saviour, where with all his might he attacks Christ's satisfaction, he sufficiently hints that Covetus, in defending that doctrine, was insulting toward God and his Son, while he ministered the Gospel, and procured the damnation of the people committed to him, while he believed he was caring for their salvation. Whence he also exhorts him to pray to God that he would graciously grant him pardon and pour his Spirit into his mind.

units.la: §. 94. 2. Idem in Resp. ad Scrupulum 30. qui sic se habuit. Cur tantopere omnes Ritus Caeremoniae, Traditiones à nostris respuuntur, etiam sine delectu, quas à vetustissimis Ecclesiae Patribus commendari videmus & observatas à Multis sine Scandalo, cum tamen Illos Spiritu Sancto egregie imbutos nos ipsi non diffiteamur? Respondet Socinus. Si nostri Homines ab aliis jamdiu separati non essent, ab iisque penitus explosi, & pro Omnium pessimis reputati (quod attinet ad Doctrinam, loquor) facile paucas quasdam Caeremonias, quas & multa vetustas, & Sanctorum Virorum Authoritas commendabat, retinuissent; in quibus viz. quamvis verbo Dei additis, nullius tamen falsus Dei Cultus, nulla evidens superstitio fuisset. Sed quando jam tanta Divisio inter nos & reliquos omnes est facta, satius visum est Ecclesias nostras paulo diligentius reformare, ut ad simplicitatem illam Apostolicam, nobis haud obscure in Apostolorum ipsorum Actis atque Epistolis delineatam, quam proxime accedant, antiquissimarumque illarum Ecclesiarum quam simillimae sint. Sic Ille. At qui separationem hanc fecerunt ab omnibus Ecclesiis Evangelicis, aut Causam isti separationi dederunt? Quomodo factum est, ut tantopere exosi sint, non solum istis, sed & cunctis per totum Orbem Christianorum Ecclesiis, nisi ob Dogmata haeretica atque Blasphema, quae communi omnium Ecclesiarum Suffragio damnantur, etsi in Aliis quibus-dam inter se discrepantium? Qua de Causa renuunt, se veteris ævi Ecclesiis conformes præbere in Doctrina æque ac in Disciplina, Cultusque divini Cæremoniis, cum utrobique par sit Ratio? Cur in materia Agendorum, non admittunt, & in praxin reducunt, quæ Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ ol-im observarunt; quorumque mentio occurrit in novo Testamento, inque veteris Ecclesiæ monumentis, & ad nostra usque Tempora Praxi non interrupta derivata sunt? Cur veteres, ipsique Ritus, (quod & ipsi non diffitentur) à seipsis probatos, ea de Causa rejiciunt, quod in usu sint apud Ecclesias Evangelicas, à quibus ut seperati sunt, ita & damnati? Non sic Evangelici egerunt cum Ecclesia Romana, cum Illius communionem in sacris deserere coacti sunt. Tunc enim æquum putarunt retinere quod antiquitus obtinuerat, quod ad ædificationem spectavit, quodque usui statuique præsentis Ecclesiæ commode inserviit, licet in Ecclesia Romana variis superstitionibus antea corruptum. Sic Abusum tollere prudenter instituerunt, Usumque pristinum denuo restituere: quod veræ Reformationis opus est. At Socinus cum suis, omnia fere è medio sustulerunt, quæ ab Apostolis, piissimisque Ipsorum Successoribus, in Ecclesiam introducta sunt ut, ex antedictis patet, praxique sua reprobarunt, quæ ex Rationis suæ Sententia non potuerunt non probare.
units.tr: §. 94. 2. The same, in the Reply to Scruple 30, which runs thus. Why are all rites, ceremonies, and traditions so indiscriminately rejected by us, which we see commended by the most ancient Fathers of the Church and observed by many without scandal, though we ourselves do not deny that they were eminently imbued with the Holy Spirit? Socinus replies: If our people had not long been separated from others and utterly cast out by them, and regarded as the worst of all (I speak as to doctrine), they would easily have retained a few ceremonies which both much antiquity and the authority of holy men commended, in which, although additions were made to the word of God, there would nevertheless have been no false worship of God, no evident superstition. But since so great a division has been made between us and all the rest, it has seemed better to reform our churches somewhat more carefully, so that they may come as near as possible to that Apostolic simplicity, sketched for us not obscurely in the Acts and Epistles of the Apostles themselves, and may be as much like those most ancient churches as possible. Thus he. But who caused this separation from all the Evangelical churches, or gave the cause for it? How has it come about that they are so hated not only by these but by all the churches of Christians throughout the whole world, except on account of heretical and blasphemous dogmas, which are condemned by the common suffrage of all churches, even though in certain other points they disagree among themselves? For what reason do they refuse to show themselves conformed to the churches of antiquity both in doctrine and in discipline, and in the ceremonies of divine worship, since the reasoning is equal in both? Why, in matters of observance, do they not admit and put into practice what the Apostolic church once observed, whose mention occurs in the New Testament and in the monuments of the ancient church, and which has been handed down without interruption in practice to our own times? Why do they reject the ancient things and rites (which they themselves do not deny) approved by themselves, for this reason, that they are in use among the Evangelical churches, from which, as they are separated, so also they are condemned? The Evangelicals did not act thus with the Roman Church, when they were compelled to forsake its communion in sacred things. For then they judged it fair to retain what had obtained from of old, what pertained to edification, and what served conveniently the use and order of the present church, although in the Roman Church it had previously been corrupted by various superstitions. Thus they prudently resolved to remove the abuse and restore the former use again, which is the work of true Reformation. But Socinus and his followers have removed almost everything that was introduced into the Church by the Apostles and their most pious successors, as is clear from what was said above, and have rejected in practice what, by the judgment of their own reason, they could not but approve.

units.la: §. 95. 3. Idem in Epist. ad Simonem Ronembergium. p. 430. col. 1. in fine, hæc habet Nulli dubium esse potest, quin Christianæ Ecclesiæ in Rebus indifferentibus id faciendum sit, quod major Pars Eorum, qui Christi nomen profitentur, faciunt, (quanto igitur magis, id,quod maxima? ) ut quam vehementissime Concordia & Pax, cum Omnibus Christiani nominis quaeratur, neve exteris Christi nomen ludibrio exponatur, & divina veritati propagandae Aditus praecludatur. Ergo, ex Sententia Socini, ex officio incumbit Christi nomen profitentibus, quicunque sunt, aut cujuscunque sectae, se conformes praebere praxi Ecclesiae Catholicae praesentis aevi, in Rebus adiaphoris; ita ut minor pars in hoc cedere debeat majori; sicut olim decretum est in Concilio Niceno, circa diem Paschatis. Deinde, hoc fieri vult, ratione istius Concordiae atque Pacis, quas omnimode prosequi, summaque Cura confervate oportet, cum Omnibus Christianismum prositentibus, ne sanctissimam istam Fidem, sic a nobis professam, culpa nostra ludibrio exponamus, & ulteriorem Illius progressum intempestiva nostra morositate apud exteros impediamus. col.2.
units.tr: §. 95. 3. The same, in the letter to Simon Ronemberg, p. 430, col. 1, near the end, has this: No doubt can be entertained that in indifferent matters the Christian Church must do what the greater part of those who profess the name of Christ do (how much more, then, that which is the greatest?) so that concord and peace are sought most vehemently with all who bear the Christian name, lest the name of Christ be exposed to mockery among outsiders, and access to the propagation of divine truth be shut off. Therefore, according to Socinus's opinion, it is the duty of those who profess the name of Christ, whoever they are or whatever sect, to show themselves conformed to the practice of the Catholic Church of the present age in matters indifferent; so that the lesser part ought to yield in this to the greater, just as it was once decreed at the Council of Nicaea concerning the day of Easter. Next, he wills this to be done on account of that concord and peace, which ought to be pursued in every way and kept with the greatest care, with all who profess Christianity, lest by our fault we expose that most holy faith, so professed by us, to mockery, and by our untimely obstinacy impede its further progress among outsiders. col. 2.

units.la: §. 96. 4. Idem in Epist. ad Geo. Eniedinum p. 484. Cui, cum dubitaret de invocatione Christi, eo quod non expresse praecipiatur in S. Scriptura, ita respondet Socinus [illegible, ~12 letters], inquit, Deus odit, & frustra se coli humanis Commentis affirmat. Ergo subjicis, nihil est in Cultu Dei pro Bono habendum, nisi quod Ipse jussit ac mandavit. Respondeo, Commenta humana ea non esse, quae ab aliquo divino Decreto atque Operatione, Nobis non modo patefacta & inculcata, sed etiam diligentissime commendata pendent, qualis operatio est exaltatio Jesu Christi; ejus, inquam, absolutum in suam Ecclesiam Regnum, plenissimaque Gubernatio, cum iis omnibus conjuncta &c. & paulo prius — videas multa esse, quae non debent ex Ecclesia explodi, & tamen non sunt omnino necessaria. Ubi advertere possumus; Primo, Socinum multa suo judicio probanda ducere, quæ tamen non sunt diserte mandata in S. Scriptura, quoties ad Rem suam facit. Deinde, quamplurima esse, quæ ipse, cum suis, improbat ac rejicit, cum tamen rite deducantur è S. Scripturæ Principiis, & fundentur in aliqua lege, Operatione, vel Decreto Divino ibidem memorato; nostræ item observationi commendentur, vel ex Regulis parallelis isthic occurrentibus, vel sanctorum exemplis inibi probatis; ut Adoratio & Invocatio Trinitatis, Christi satisfactio, ejusdem Dietas, Spiritus S. Personalitas, necessitas Baptismi & efficacia, necessitas item Ordinationis, & Politiæ Ecclesiasticæ ab Apostolis institutæ, Consecratio Templorum, Dies stati ac solennes tum Festorum, tum Jejuniorum, usus Trisagii in sacris, Ritusque quamplurimi ad Liturgiam, atque Disciplinam Ecclesiasticam pertinentes, quos ipsi tamen nihili faciunt, si minus aperte damnant. Denique multa observatu haud necessaria, neutiquam tamen ejicienda esse ex Ecclesia. Quæ regula, si modo valeat, istorum omnium Adiaphorum usum confirmat, quæ vel ab Ecclesia habemus injuncta, vel Communi Piorum praxi nobis commendata.
units.tr: §. 96. 4. The same, in his letter to Georgius Eniedinus, p. 484. When Eniedinus doubted about invoking Christ, because it is not expressly commanded in Holy Scripture, Socinus replies as follows: [illegible, ~12 letters] said he, God hates it, and vainly claims that He is worshipped by human inventions. Therefore you add that nothing in the worship of God is to be held good except what He Himself has ordered and commanded. I reply that those are not human inventions which depend on some divine decree or operation, not only revealed and impressed upon us but also most diligently commended. Such an operation is the exaltation of Jesus Christ, that is, his absolute kingdom over his Church and his most full government, together with all those things joined to it, etc. And a little earlier: you may see that there are many things which ought not to be cast out of the Church, and yet are not altogether necessary. Here we may notice two things. First, Socinus judges many things to be worthy of approval which are not expressly commanded in Holy Scripture, whenever they serve his purpose. Second, there are very many things which he and his followers disapprove and reject, although they are rightly deduced from the principles of Holy Scripture and founded on some law, operation or divine decree recorded there. Likewise they are commended to our observance, either by parallel rules occurring there or by examples of the saints approved there. Such are the adoration and invocation of the Trinity, Christ's satisfaction, his deity, the personality of the Holy Spirit, the necessity and efficacy of baptism, likewise the necessity of ordination and of the ecclesiastical polity instituted by the apostles, the consecration of temples, the fixed and solemn days both of feasts and of fasts, the use of the Trisagion in sacred services, and very many rites pertaining to the liturgy and ecclesiastical discipline. Yet they make nothing of these, if they do not openly condemn them. Finally, many things that are not necessary to observe are nonetheless by no means to be cast out of the Church. This rule, if it holds good, confirms the use of all these adiaphora, which we have either been enjoined by the Church or which are commended to us by the common practice of the pious.

units.la: §. 79. Idem, In Disp. de Baptismo Aquæ. p. 736. Cap. 17. col. 2.
units.tr: §. 79. The same, In Disputation on Water Baptism, p. 736. Chap. 17, col. 2.

units.la: Censet, ut quicunque è Judæis, Turcis, Aliisque infidelibus, ad fidem Christianam convertuntur, initientur Ecclesiæ per Baptismum; isque Judicii hanc Rationem adfert. Etsi, inquit, ea de Re nullum expressum & perpetuum extat mandatum, Apostolos tamen[?] qui id facere consueverunt, imitari debet, præsertim, cum ab universa Ecclesia eum morem receptum, & perpetuo usu comprobatum fuisse, aut constet[?], aut certè admodum credibile videatur, quæ si aliter aliquando facere instituerent, aliter quoque singulis privatis Ecclesiis esse faciendum. Unde sequitur, nobis non solum fas esse, sed & necesse, ex lege Decori, imitari Apostolos in Rebus ad agenda ipectantibus[?], etiam in iis, de quibus nullum extat mandatum. Deinde, hoc imitandi officium praeci-pue nobis incumbere, quoties aliquid ab Apostolis usurpatum Ecclesia Catholica admisit; seculisque sequentibus universali, constantique Praxi comprobatum est, sive Praxis illa certo cognita fuerit, sive à Testibus fide dignis accepta. Singulas demum privatas, sive particulares Ecclesias, se[?] debere Catholicae conformes praebere.
units.tr: He holds that whoever among the Jews, Turks and other unbelievers are converted to the Christian faith should be initiated into the Church by baptism, and he gives this reason for his judgment: Although, he says, there is no express and perpetual command about this matter, nevertheless we ought to imitate the apostles, who were accustomed to do this, especially since it is either established, or seems very credible, that this custom was received by the whole Church and approved by perpetual use. If the apostles had at some time decided to act otherwise, then individual private churches would also have to act otherwise. Hence it follows that we are not only permitted but also bound, by the law of decency, to imitate the apostles in matters pertaining to conduct, even in those things for which there is no command at all. Next, this duty of imitation lies chiefly upon us whenever the Catholic Church has admitted something used by the apostles, and it has been confirmed by universal and constant practice through the following centuries, whether that practice was known with certainty or received from trustworthy witnesses. Finally, each private or particular church ought to show itself conformable to the Catholic church.

units.la: §. 98. 6. Legitimum Adiaphororum usum qualia sc. in S. literis non praecipiuntur, aut prohibentur, alibi clarius & fortius asserit; viz. in Resp. ad notas Andr. Dudithii ad Disput. Socini de Baptismo. p. 739. col. 2. in fine. ubi sic inquit. Addere Dei Praeceptis, quod Moses fieri vetuit, nihil est aliud, quam aliquid inducere, vel faciendum dicere, tanquam a Deo praeceptum, quod tamen Deus non praecepit; non autem simpliciter id facere, id est, eo nequaquam appositio, quod Deus ita praecepit, Deut. 4. 2. Quod si haec Interpretatio non adhibeatur, sequetur, nihil prorsus fieri posse, quod Deus non praecepit; quod & ipsi semper Communi, & sacra Historia mille in locis advertunt. Ob. At sequeretur hinc, bonam Intentionem, & Pharisaicas [illegible, ~12 letters] stabiliendas esse. Resp. Bona Intentio, nisi in Actum Dei praeceptis adversantem erumpat, culpanda non est. Pharisaica vero [illegible, ~12 letters] nisi interim Dei Praecepta negligantur, per se ipsa non damnantur in S. literis. Haec ille de Adiaphoris, satis Orthodoxe.
units.tr: §. 98. 6. He asserts the lawful use of adiaphora, that is, those things which are not commanded or forbidden in the Sacred Letters, more clearly and strongly elsewhere, namely in his Reply to the notes of Andreas Dudithius on Socinus's Disputation on Baptism, p. 739, col. 2, near the end, where he says as follows: To add to God's precepts what Moses forbade to be done is nothing other than to introduce something, or to say that it must be done, as if commanded by God, when God has not commanded it; but not simply to do that which is not in itself contrary to what God has so commanded, Deut. 4. 2. If this interpretation is not adopted, it will follow that nothing at all can be done which God has not commanded; which the common experience and sacred history notice in a thousand places. Objection: But it would follow from this that good intention and Pharisaic [illegible, ~12 letters] should be established. Reply: A good intention, unless it breaks out into an act contrary to God's precepts, is not to be blamed. But Pharisaic [illegible, ~12 letters], unless meanwhile God's precepts are neglected, are not in themselves condemned in the Sacred Letters. Thus he speaks about adiaphora, quite orthodoxly.

units.la: §. 99. 7. Idem in Tract. de Ecclesia, quem ex variis Epistolis in unum compegit, haec habet de certis, Doctrinae Capitibus stabiliendis, quae a singulis Ecclesiae membris agnoscenda sunt pro veris, sc. [?]
units.tr: §. 99. 7. The same, in a Treatise on the Church, which he compiled into one from various letters, holds the following about the establishing of certain heads of doctrine, which must be acknowledged as true by each member of the Church, namely: [?]

units.la: p. 347. Col. 1. Certa aliqua Doctrinae Capita constituere, sine quibus nemini salus contingere queat; & qui in istis Tecum non sentiunt, in tuam Ecclesiam non recipere, aut eum inde ejicere, ut Apostolicum est, sic & nunc & semper fieri, & potuit & debuit. Videat modo Quis-que, ut Capita ista ea constituat, quae constituenda sunt. Id autem facile fiet, si ut profesto [?] debet, ex solo, eoque aperto Dei verbo, omnia petantur. Quod si nihilominus hac in parte erratum fuerit, quatenus aliqua Capita constituta fuerint, quae ex isto numero vera non sint, non idcirco vera Christi Ecclesia ea, quae hoc fecerit, esse desierit, dummodo nullum eorum praetermiserit, quae ex isto sunt numero. Et quacunque tandem ratione in iis constituendis erraverit, in eo tamen nunquam errare dici poterit, quod eos recipere noluit, qui in illis secum non consentiant. Imo errorem erroris adderet, si eos reciperet. Etenim, contra suam ipsius Conscientiam ageret, & eos fratrum loco haberet, & Christi Fidelium, quos tamen a salutari Christi Doctrina abesse plane sibi persuasisset. Quibus in verbis, non solum unumquemque Ecclesiae particularis Fundatorem, sed & Ecclesiae pridem fundatae Praepositos, Authoritate donat, fundamentales Fidei Christianae Articulos, sine quibus nemo salutem consequi potest, non constituere tantum, sed & aliis imponere pro talibus; eosdemque Judices constituit in hoc negotio, quaenam sint haec fundamentalia, & quae non sint; Deinde, ex hoc Capite Ecclesiarum reformatarum Confessiones suo Calculo probat, ut rite factas & jure impositas unicuique membro istarum Ecclesiarum. Neque enim audet afferere Confessiones istas deficere in aliquo dogmate, quod ad Salutem necessarium sit. Imo contrarium affirmat, ut modo ex Illius Scriptis ostendimus. Comprobat item, Judicium earundem Ecclesiarum, in Censuris contra suam sectam latis, reliquosque Anti-Trinitarios, quos è sua Communione universim excludunt. Imo, ex hoc probare videtur Censuras & Anathemata Ecclesiæ Romanæ, contra cæteras Ecclesias à se dissidentes lata; cum sit Ecclesia sui Juris; & utcunque plurima habeat superflua atque Superstitiosa, quæ Fidei antiquitus receptæ de novo adscivit, non tamen deficere putatur in necessariis. Probat saltem veteris Ecclesiæ Praxin in regula Fidei condenda; in exigendo Confessionem ejusdem à Filiis suis; in Decretis suis Synodicis, quibus eam munivit undique, & contra omnis Generis Hæreticos asseruit; in Censuris item contra eosdem cum Anathemate latis, quibus Socinianorum Antecessores à sua Communione pepulerunt. Isti Patres, Catholica Ecclesia per totum Orbem diffusa, istiusmodi Censuras approbante; Ipsorumque consortium, præsertim in sacris, ut perniciosum atque Pestiferum, abhorrente. Tales Erant Ebion, Cerinthus, Sabellius, Paulus Samosatenus, Arius, Eunomius, Photinus, Macedonius, aliique Anti-Trinitarii.
units.tr: p. 347, col. 1. To establish certain heads of doctrine, without which no one can obtain salvation; and to refuse to receive into your Church, or to expel from it, those who do not agree with you on these points, as is Apostolic, so both now and always it has been and could be and ought to be done. Let each one see only that he establishes those heads which ought to be established. This will be easy to do if, as one ought, everything is sought from the sole and open Word of God. But if nevertheless an error has been made in this respect, in so far as some heads have been established which are not true in that number, the true Church of Christ which has done this does not for that reason cease to be the Church, provided it has omitted none of those which belong to that number. And however it may have erred in establishing them, it can never be said to have erred in this, that it refused to receive those who do not agree with it on these points. Indeed, it would add error to error if it did receive them. For it would act against its own conscience, and would regard them as brothers and faithful of Christ, whom it had nonetheless plainly persuaded itself are far from the saving doctrine of Christ. In these words he grants authority not only to each founder of a particular church but also to the leaders of churches long since founded: they not only establish the fundamental articles of the Christian faith, without which no one can obtain salvation, but also impose them on others as such. He also makes these same men judges in this matter, as to which things are fundamental and which are not. Then, from this head, he approves the Confessions of the reformed Churches by his own reckoning, as rightly made and lawfully imposed on each member of those Churches. For he does not dare to assert that those Confessions are deficient in any dogma that is necessary to salvation. Rather, he affirms the contrary, as we have just shown from his writings. He likewise approves the judgment of the same Churches in the censures passed against his own sect and the other Anti-Trinitarians, whom they exclude universally from their communion. Indeed, from this he seems to approve the censures and anathemas of the Roman Church, passed against the other churches dissenting from it; since it is a church of its own right, and although it has added many superfluous and superstitious things to the faith received from antiquity, it is nonetheless thought not to be lacking in essentials. At least he approves the practice of the ancient Church in framing a rule of faith, in requiring a confession of it from its sons, in its synodical decrees by which it fortified it everywhere and defended it against every kind of heretic, and likewise in the censures with anathema passed against the same heretics, by which they drove the forerunners of the Socinians out of their communion. Those Fathers, the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world approving such censures, and abhorring fellowship with them, especially in sacred matters, as pernicious and deadly. Such were Ebion, Cerinthus, Sabellius, Paul of Samosata, Arius, Eunomius, Photinus, Macedonius, and the other Anti-Trinitarians.

units.la: §. 100. 8. Idem in Epist. ad Synodum Nægrovienfem. p. 491. Col 1.
units.tr: §. 100. 8. The same, in his Letter to the Synod of Nægrovia, p. 491, col. 1.

units.la: Censet omnes Fr. Davidis Discipulos, cæterosque similia sentientes, excommunicandos esse — Non est, inquit, cum Istis amplius, ut mihi quidem videtur, in Rebus sacris Commercium habendum. Deinde vult statas Precum formulas omnibus Verbi Dei Ministris injungi, quas statutis diebus in Publico usurpent. Has denique preces ad Christum nominatim dirigi vult ut hoc modo suæ Partis Homines discriminentur à Francisco Davidianis, aliisque quibuscunque Anti-Trinitariis, qui necessarium hunc Fidei Articulum viz. Christum invocandum atque adorandum esse, ut divinæ Majestatis factum participem, abnegarunt: Ex hac autem Socini Sententia sequitur, si paritas Rationis valeat, Catholicos non esse culpandos ex eo, quod Socinianos è Cœtibus suis excludant, & à Sacris arceant, eo quod Fidei Articulos ad salutem, ut Ipsi judicant, necessarios, palam & obstinate negent. Neque ex hoc etiam, quod certas publicarum precum Formulas Ministris injungant, ex officio usurpandas, ut hac nota dignoscantur ab Hæreticis, Fideque Catholicam aperte profiteantur. E. G. Quibus Trinitas Personarum invocatur, tum conjunctim, tum separatim; potestas Regum à Deo solo derivari agnoscitur, illique soli subdita; satisfactio Christi pro universi Generis humani peccatis, in officio Eucharistico; Necessitas Gratiæ divinæ ad Tentationes superandas omneque opus bonum perficiendum, à Deo indesinenter petendæ; Reatus peccati originalis, statusque damnationis inde consequentis, qui in officio Baptismali exponitur; efficacia utriusque Sacramenti, veraque Christi præsentia in Cœna Dominica; Resurrectio ejusdem numero Corporis, quæ in officio funebri asseritur; Insolubile Conjugii vinculum in officio Matrimonii; ministrorum Evangelicorum, sive cleri triplex ordo, & necessitas ordinationis ad opus ministerii, ab iis solemniter peragendæ, qui ad hoc potestatem habent in Ecclesia à Christo, ejusque Apostolis communicatam[?], in officio ordinationis; Denique, Potestas clavium in excommunicatione Communicatam[?] & readmissione Pœnitentium, sive in ligando & absolvendo; quam Ecclesia exercet, prout opportunum est, non solum in foro Ecclesiastico, sed & erga eos, qui ad Eucharistiam accedunt, & in officio Visitationis infirmorum; prout mos antiquus se habuit, ejusmodi Institutis conformis, quae ipsa jam olim accepit, & pro ratis habuit. Haec aliaque quaedam majoris, momenti Dogmata, Ecclesia nostra Anglicana, (ut & Aliae quaedam publicis precibus interserenda caravit, ut omnibus constaret, quam sincerus & unanimis esset Filiorum suorum Consensus in Doctrina Fidei neque Socinus hanc Praxin damnare potest, cum (ut paulo prius ex eo observari in Tract. de Ecclesia) Potestatem concedat Ecclesiae Praepositis, recipiendi Proselytos in Ecclesiam, & receptos ejiciendi, pro arbitrio suo; atque alibi statuat, ut ad Coenam Domini non accedant, qui peccato aliquo sunt illaqueati, quod eos à vita aeterna arcere possit; & si ipsi hoc non faciunt, debet (inquit) Ecclesia eos arcere. Sic ille, De usu & fine Coenae Domini. p. 775. Col. 2. in fine.
units.tr: He judges that all the disciples of Francis David, and others who think similarly, are to be excommunicated. It is not, he says, as it seems to me, to be held any longer in sacred matters with these men. He then wants fixed forms of prayer enjoined on all ministers of the Word of God, to be used in public on set days. Finally, he wants these prayers addressed to Christ by name, so that in this way the men of his own party may be distinguished from the Francis Davidians and all other Anti-Trinitarians, who have denied that necessary article of faith, namely that Christ is to be invoked and adored as a sharer in the divine majesty. From this opinion of Socinus it follows, if the same reasoning holds, that Catholics are not to be blamed for excluding the Socinians from their assemblies and keeping them from the sacred rites, since the Socinians openly and obstinately deny articles of faith which they themselves judge necessary to salvation. Nor is it blameworthy that Catholics enjoin on their ministers certain set forms of public prayer, to be used by virtue of their office, so that they may be distinguished by this mark from heretics and openly profess the Catholic faith. For example, there are forms in which the Trinity of Persons is invoked, both jointly and severally; in which the power of kings is acknowledged to derive from God alone and to be subject to him alone; in which the satisfaction of Christ for the sins of the whole human race is set forth in the office of the Eucharist; in which the necessity of divine grace to overcome temptations and to accomplish every good work is to be constantly sought from God; in which the guilt of original sin and the state of damnation consequent upon it are set out in the office of Baptism; in which the efficacy of both sacraments and the true presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper are taught; in which the resurrection of the same numerical body is asserted in the funeral office; in which the indissoluble bond of marriage is affirmed in the office of Matrimony; in which the threefold order of evangelical ministers or clergy, and the necessity of ordination to the work of the ministry, are laid down, to be solemnly performed by those who have the power in the Church for this, communicated by Christ to his Apostles, in the office of ordination; and lastly, in which the power of the keys is set out, in the excommunication and readmission of penitents, that is, in binding and loosing, which the Church exercises as occasion requires, not only in the ecclesiastical court but also towards those who approach the Eucharist, and in the office for the visitation of the sick, as the ancient custom had it, in conformity with those institutions which the Church had long since received and held to be valid. These and certain other dogmas of greater weight our English Church thought fit to insert in its public prayers, and certain others too, so that it might be clear to all how sincere and unanimous was the agreement of its sons in the doctrine of faith. Nor can Socinus condemn this practice, since (as was observed a little earlier from his Treatise on the Church) he grants the presiding officers of the Church the power of receiving proselytes into the Church and of expelling those received, at their own discretion; and elsewhere he lays down that those who are entangled in some sin which could shut them out from eternal life should not approach the Lord's Supper; and if they themselves do not do this, the Church (he says) ought to keep them away. Thus he, On the Use and End of the Lord's Supper, p. 775, col. 2, near the end.

units.la: §. 101. 9. Idem, Tract. de Ecclesia. p. 347. col. 2. agnoscit necessitatem officii Ministrorum in Ecclesia, & eorundem Authoritatem in Gregem Christianum. Sic enim inquit. Sine munere ministrorum verbi Dei, sicut nihil unquam in Religione Christiana profectum est, sic Nihil unquam aut proficitur[?], aut proficí potest. Tantum cavendum est, ne dominentur Gregi. Quod tamen ipsius Petri Tempore potius in ipsorum Pastorum voluntate, quam in Freno aliquo Ipsis quodammodo à Populo injiciendo, repositum fuisse, ejus verba non obscure docent, in quibus hac de Re, non quidem Populo, sed ipsis Pastoribus, damnur[?] Praecepta. Similia quaedam in Epistolis Pauli ad Timotheum & Titum scripta extant. Ex quibus nullo negotio intelligi potest, eorum, ipsi [?] Populo docendo praefecti erant, exiguam fuisse Auctoritatem, qua ut bene uterentur, potius Ipsorum voluntatis esset, quam Populi cura. Hinc autem sequitur, necessario requiri, ut Ministri Evangelici habeant Munus istud sibi collatum ab Aliquo, qui Potestatem ad hoc habet in Ecclesia Dei, alioquin, illud legitime nec suscipient, nec administrabunt. Deinde sequitur, illos non suscipere Potestatem suam spiritualem a Populo, cui docendo incumbunt; huic enim praesunt, non subsunt, neque Muneris sui Rationem Illi reddere tenentur, seu bene seu male Illud obierint. Quis autem in Socinianorum Coetibus, ejusmodi potestatem confert pastoribus per solennem Manuum Impositionem, juxta Ritum ab Apostolis introductum & per omnia exinde secula constanter usurpatum? Pastores Illorum, ut puto, non sibi vendicabunt Missionem extraordinariam, qualem Apostoli habuerunt; sin ordinariam non habent, quo jure Munus istud sactum usurpant, sc. docendi publice in Ecclesia, Sacramenta administrandi, & gubernandi populum Dei? cum nec ipsi illud ab alio legitime susceperint, nec sua sponte sibi possint assumere? Iubenter item discere vellem, quam Authoritatem Sociniani Pastoribus suis tribuant; qualem Fidem, obedientiamque illis deberi profiteantur; quibus item Regulis utantur, in judicando de Doctrina a Pastoribus suis praedicata; quibusque signis discriminent veros Doctores a Falsis. Cum enim singuli interpretentur Scripturam in sensu suo; nec Auditores astringantur ad sensum cujusque privati Doctoris admittendum; sed prout sibi visum fuerit, aut consonum menti Dei in Scriptura patefactae, saneque Rationi, aut ab iisdem dissonum, illum vel amplectantur, vel aversentur; plane nescio, quomodo hæc Socini secta, certum Judicium, sibique constans ferre posset, vel de Doctrina, vel de Doctoribus suis.
units.tr: §. 101. 9. The same, in the Treatise on the Church, p. 347, col. 2, acknowledges the necessity of the office of ministers in the Church, and the authority of these men over the Christian flock. For he says: Without the office of the ministers of the Word of God, just as nothing has ever advanced in the Christian religion, so nothing ever is or can be advanced. Only care must be taken that they do not lord it over the flock. Yet that in Peter's own time this power lay rather in the will of the pastors themselves than in any bridle that could in some way be put on them by the people, his words make plain enough, in which precepts on this matter are given not to the people but to the pastors themselves. Similar things are found in Paul's letters to Timothy and Titus. From these it can be understood without difficulty that the authority of those who were set over the people for teaching was slight, and that using it well depended more on their own will than on the care of the people. From this it follows that it is necessarily required that evangelical ministers have their office conferred on them by someone who has the power for this in the Church of God; otherwise they will neither lawfully receive nor lawfully administer it. Further, it follows that they do not receive their spiritual power from the people whom they are charged to teach; for they preside over the people, they are not subject to them, and they are not bound to render an account of their office to them, whether they have discharged it well or badly. But who, in the assemblies of the Socinians, confers such power on their pastors by the solemn imposition of hands, according to the rite introduced by the Apostles and constantly practised through all the ages since? Their pastors, I suppose, will not claim the extraordinary mission which the Apostles had; but if they have no ordinary one, by what right do they take up that office, namely of teaching publicly in the Church, administering the sacraments, and governing the people of God, since they have not lawfully received it from anyone else and cannot assume it of their own accord? I would also gladly learn what authority the Socinians grant their pastors; what faith and obedience they profess are owed to them; what rules they use in judging the doctrine preached by their pastors; and by what signs they distinguish true teachers from false ones. For since each man interprets Scripture in his own sense, and the hearers are not bound to accept the sense of any private teacher, but accept or reject him as it seems to them agreeable to the mind of God revealed in Scripture and to sound reason, or discordant with these, I simply do not know how this Socinian sect could give a firm and consistent judgement either on its doctrine or on its teachers.

units.la: §. 102. 10. Idem hæc asserit de S. Scripturæ libris. 353. col. 1. in eodem Tract. de Ecclesia — Ego quidem sentio, nihil in iis Scriptis, quæ communiter ab iis, qui Christiani sunt dicti, recepta & pro divinis habita sunt, constanter legi, quod non verissimum sit, hocque ad divinam Providentiam prorsus pertinere arbitror, ut ejusmodi Scripta nunquam depravantur, corrumpantur, neque ex toto, neque ex Parte. Et si aliqui Codices aut exemplaria alicubi mendosa sint, ex Aliis emendationibus, vel ex antiquorum Interpretum Auctoritate emendari queunt. Præstat, mi Frater, mihi crede, cum in aliquem Scripturæ locum incidimus, qui nobis falsam Sententiam continere videatur, una cum Augustino, hac in parte Ignorantiam nostram fateri, quam tum, si alioquin indubitatum plane sit, in dubium revocare. Sic Ille. At nonne par ratio valet de summa Fidei in Symbolis antiquis comprehensa, de Sacramentalibus & Ritibus, & de sensibus certorum locorum S. Scripturæ, quos Veteres testantur se accepisse, per Traditionem Apostolicam, una cum ipsis S. Scripturæ libris? Cur etiam existimaremus parilem Dei curam, atque Providentiam Ecclesiæ suæ eo usque per omne Tempus invigilasse, Cujus Fidei atque custodiæ sacros hosce libros credidit, ut non sineret Illam deficere in Dogmatibus ad salutem necessariis, & apostatare à Fide illic tradita; præsertim, cum exemplaria istorum Codicum ubique ad manum essent, quæ consulere in promptu erat; imo publice lecta & expolita in Ecclesiis? Cur igitur alibi dicit, Ecclesiam posse totaliter deficere per multa secula; imo & actu defecisse? Eadem quoque Ratio valet, debita proportione servata, de veterum Synodorum Decretis, quae ad normam Doctrinae ab Apostolis traditae conformata dicuntur. Idem quoque affirmare aequum est, de veterum Patrum scriptis, eadem proportione habita; quod so. ad manus nostras integra & incorrupta pervenerint, quantum saltem ad summam [?] atque substantiam Doctrinae ab iis ibidem traditae; & quod eandem Ecclesia Catholica sui Temporis tenuerit, quomodo a majoribus acceperat, sicut illi quoque ibidem testantur. Quinimo, & mihi aequum videtur, ut Socinus agnoscat veterum interpretum Auctoritatem in aliis etiam majoris momenti rebus, quoties una mente & voce consentiunt in aliquo S. Scripturae loco explicando, vel in certo aliquo Dogmate affirmando, quod ex ea deducunt. In his itaque & similibus, non inique postulatur a Socini Discipulis, ut tantum modestiae, Aequitatis, studiique pro veritate simul & Pace Ecclesiae offenderent, quantum illos inducat ad suspicandum, potius aliquid erroris suis opinionibus inesse, quam ut falsi arguant Doctrinam a veteribus Ecclesiae Doctoribus traditam, & Communiter assertam.
units.tr: §. 102. 10. The same author asserts the following about the books of Holy Scripture, p. 353, col. 1, in the same Treatise on the Church: For my part I think that nothing is consistently read in those writings which are commonly received and regarded as divine by those who are called Christians, which is not entirely true; and I judge that it pertains wholly to divine providence that such writings are never corrupted, neither wholly nor in part. And if some codices or copies are faulty somewhere, they can be corrected from other readings, or by the authority of the ancient interpreters. It is better, my brother, believe me, when we come upon some passage of Scripture which seems to us to contain a false sense, to confess our ignorance in this matter together with Augustine, rather than to call in question what is otherwise plainly beyond doubt. Thus he. But does not the same reasoning hold for the sum of the faith comprehended in the ancient creeds, for the sacramental rites and ceremonies, and for the senses of certain passages of Holy Scripture, which the Fathers testify they received through Apostolic tradition along with the books of Holy Scripture themselves? And why should we think that God's care and providence over his Church have watched so long through all time, to whose faith and keeping he entrusted these holy books, that he did not allow it to fail in dogmas necessary to salvation, or to fall away from the faith handed down there; especially since copies of those codices were everywhere at hand, which anyone could readily consult, and indeed were read publicly and expounded in the churches? Why then does he say elsewhere that the Church can wholly fail for many ages, or indeed has actually failed? The same reasoning holds, with due proportion observed, for the decrees of the ancient synods, which are said to have been framed according to the rule of the doctrine handed down by the Apostles. It is equally fair to affirm the same, with the same proportion observed, of the writings of the ancient Fathers: that they have come down to our hands whole and uncorrupted, at least as far as the sum and substance of the doctrine delivered in them is concerned, and that the Catholic Church of their own time held the same doctrine as it had received from its forebears, as they themselves also testify there. Indeed, it seems fair to me that Socinus should also acknowledge the authority of the ancient interpreters in other matters of greater weight, whenever they agree with one mind and voice in explaining some passage of Holy Scripture, or in affirming some dogma which they draw from it. In such matters and similar ones, it is not unreasonable to require of the disciples of Socinus that they show such modesty, fairness and zeal for truth, and at the same time for the peace of the Church, as to lead them to suspect that there is something of error in their own opinions, rather than to argue that the doctrine handed down by the ancient teachers of the Church, and commonly held, is false.

units.la: §. 103. 11. Similia habet, ubi disserit de libro Apocalypseos, & Testimoniis, quae exinde adversus eos, qui Jesu Christi invocationem prorsus negant, petuntur. Tom. 2. p. 803. Col. 2. Liber Apocalypseos, quamvis Auctor ejus ignoretur, seu potius ignorari a quibusdam asseratur (universalis enim Ecclesia Confessus cum Joanni Apostolo vendicat) est tamen jam a multis seculis, & hodie praesertim, in Ecclesia receptissimus —quinetiam universa Apostolorum & Evangelistarum scripta, nisi quatenus cum scriptis Mosis & Prophetarum apertissime consentiunt, & ab illis evidenter, & literaliter, ut vocant, confirmantur, minimi nobis facienda erunt. Quare cavendum diligenter est, ne vel apicem quidem unum in receptis ab Ecclesia libris, nedum ipsos libros in dubium vocari, illis aliqua per nos occasio praebeatur. Alioquin ad universa novi Foederis scripta subvertenda, eis ampla Fenestra aperietur. Ex qua Socini sententia pariter concludi poterit, unamquamque Doctrinam, vel expositionem S. Textus, quam Ecclesia universalis hujus ævi Christo, ejusque Apostolis acceptam refert & Cui Testimonium praebetur ab antiquis Ecclesiae Catholicae Doctoribus, quod ab iisdem tradita suerit, non esse in dubium vocandam, utpote quae Divinam Authoritatem sibi astipulantem habeat[?].
units.tr: §. 103. 11. He says similar things where he discusses the book of Revelation and the testimonies drawn from it against those who utterly deny the invocation of Jesus Christ. Tom. 2. p. 803. Col. 2. The book of Revelation, although its author is unknown, or rather some say he is unknown (for the consensus of the universal Church claims it for the Apostle John), has nevertheless for many centuries, and especially today, been most widely received in the Church. Indeed, the whole writings of the Apostles and Evangelists, unless insofar as they agree most plainly with the writings of Moses and the Prophets and are evidently and literally, as they say, confirmed by them, must be held in very little regard by us. Therefore we must take great care that we give no occasion for anyone to call into doubt even a single jot in the books received by the Church, much less the books themselves. Otherwise a wide window will be opened for overturning all the writings of the New Covenant. From Socinus's opinion it can equally be concluded that no doctrine or interpretation of holy Scripture which the universal Church of this age holds to have been received from Christ and his Apostles, and which is attested by the ancient teachers of the Catholic Church as having been handed down by them, should be called into doubt, since it has divine authority on its side.

units.la: Deinde, ad hujusmodi Doctrinam acceptandam, non requiri, ut evidenter consentiat cum Mosis & Prophetarum scriptis, aut ex iisdem literaliter confirmetur. Cujusmodi sunt quaedam Fidei mysteria, quae non adeo clare ac plene in libris veteris Testamenti traduntur, ut Dogma Trinitatis, Incarnatio Christi, Opus Redemptionis per sanguinem Christi, cum omnibus eo spectantibus, Resurrectio generalis, abolitio legis Mosaicae, & aliquot alia tum etiam, ne minimum quidem Apicem Doctrinae Christianae immutandum esse, aut de eo ambigendum, ut cum Ariani ὁμοούσιον[?] substituerunt loco ὁμοιούσιον[?]. Denique scripta Patrum, quae hodie extant, & pro genuinis universim agnoscuntur, fidem à nobis mereri in iis, quae testantur de Doctrina atque praxi Ecclesiae Catholicae sui temporis, & quod eosdem à majoribus suis acceperint; æquum item esse, ut quam Authoritatem ac venerationem per tot hucusque secula merito obtinuerunt in Ecclesia Dei, apud nos hodie quoque retineant.
units.tr: Further, to accept such a doctrine it is not required that it agree plainly with the writings of Moses and the Prophets, or be literally confirmed by them. Such are certain mysteries of the faith, which are not set forth so clearly and fully in the books of the Old Testament: the doctrine of the Trinity, the Incarnation of Christ, the work of redemption through the blood of Christ with all that pertains to it, the general resurrection, the abolition of the Mosaic law, and several others. Nor should even the smallest jot of Christian doctrine be altered or called into question, as the Arians did when they put ὁμοούσιον[?] in place of ὁμοιούσιον[?]. Finally, the writings of the Fathers that survive today and are generally acknowledged as genuine deserve our trust in what they bear witness to about the doctrine and practice of the Catholic Church of their time, and that they had received these things from their forebears. It is likewise fair that they should retain today among us the authority and reverence which, by merit, they have held in the Church of God through so many centuries.

units.la: §. 104. 12. Idem, de Ecclesia, p. 357. Tom. 1. arguit, per Christi Jessionem ad dextram Dei Patris intelligi debere, supremam post Deum potestatem atque Gubernationem, donec mors ultimus Hostis aboleatur, duraturam. Atque hoc probat, non solum è Circumstantiis S. Contextus; & ex Pauli, aliorumque Apostolorum expositione; sed etiam ex tota Religionis nostrae Analogia. At quid intelligit per hanc Analogiam? Num fundamentales Christianae Religionis articulos, hic illic per Scripturam dispersos, & per Apostolos in Symbolum collectos, & postea in Synodis Oecumenicis à Patribus explicatos? Sin hos intelligat (ut à Theologis vulgo intelligi solent) nisi æquum putet in sua ipsius Causa Judicem esse, contra Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Testimonium, necesse est ut fateatur, non pauca esse Dogmata pro fundamentalibus ab ea semper habita, quæ tamen ipse & sui pro falsis habent, fideique Christianæ multum adversis.
units.tr: §. 104. 12. In the same work, on the Church, p. 357. Tom. 1, he argues that the session of Christ at the right hand of God the Father must be understood to mean a supreme power and government under God, which will endure until death, the last enemy, is destroyed. And he proves this not only from the circumstances of the holy context and from the exposition of Paul and the other Apostles, but also from the whole analogy of our religion. But what does he mean by this analogy? The fundamental articles of the Christian religion, scattered here and there through Scripture, gathered by the Apostles into a creed, and afterwards explained by the Fathers in the Ecumenical Synods? If he means these (as theologians commonly understand it), then, unless he thinks it fair to be judge in his own cause against the testimony of the Catholic Church, he must admit that there are not a few doctrines which the Church has always held to be fundamental, and which he and his followers regard as false and highly opposed to the Christian faith.

units.la: Eadem fere profitetur Andr:Dudithius in Epist.ad Bez. Op. Soc. Tom. 1. p.526. Nobis Religio esse debet, vel latum unguem à Scriptura discedere, nam scriptum legimus, siquis non acquiescit sanis sermonibus &c.
units.tr: Andreas Dudith professes almost the same in his letter to Beza, Op. Soc. Tom. 1, p. 526. Religion ought to mean to us that we do not depart a finger's breadth from Scripture, for we read what is written: if anyone does not consent to sound words, &c.

units.la: 1 Tim.(?. 3. Non igitur admittimus, neque etiam debemus, novas, atque adeo portentosas Res, quæ cum Analogia fidei, cum totius Scriptura perpetua Harmonia, & consensu pugnant. Bene habet. At quis Interpretabitur hanc Scripturam; & cujus Interpretationi potius adhærescemus? Num veterum Ecclesiæ Doctorum, quorum fidem & authoritatem Ecclesia Catholica semper agnovit; an Socinianorum recentium, quorum Antecessores ob easdem Hæreses, fædafque S. Paginæ corruptelas, jam olim explosi sunt, & Anathemate percussi; utpote qui nova, & monstrosa, & à fide Catholica plane abhorrentia, propalaverint? Quos Judices statuemus in hac Re, an sc. Doctrina tradita sit consona fidei Analogiæ, perpetuæque Scripturæ Harmoniæ, an cum ea discordet? Num existimabimus Patres Catholicos, vel eam prorsus ignorasse vel ex Consilio, & scientes impugnasse? Certe illi Dogmata sua, quæ cum in libris à se contra Hæreticos conscriptis defenderunt; tum Synodicis Decretis contra eosdem firmarunt, non tantum huic Fidei Analogiæ, seu perpetuæ Scripturæ Harmoniæ, in majoris momenti Articulis, omnino conformia judicarunt, sed & ejusdem partem non exiguam. Et ex adverso, omnes Catholici, tum hujus ævi, tum prioris cujusque ab ipsa Christianismi origine, Socinianorum Placita, ut ei adversantia, in totum repudiarunt.
units.tr: 1 Tim.(?. 3. Therefore we neither admit, nor ought we to admit, new and indeed monstrous things, which clash with the analogy of faith and with the constant harmony and agreement of the whole of Scripture. Good. But who will interpret this Scripture, and to whose interpretation shall we rather adhere? That of the ancient teachers of the Church, whose faith and authority the Catholic Church has always acknowledged; or that of the recent Socinians, whose predecessors, for the same heresies and the foul corruptions of holy Scripture, were long ago driven out and struck with anathema, as having put forward new, monstrous doctrines wholly abhorrent from the Catholic faith? By what judges shall we decide in this matter, namely whether the doctrine handed down agrees with the analogy of faith and the constant harmony of Scripture, or whether it disagrees with it? Shall we suppose that the Catholic Fathers either knew nothing of it at all, or attacked it knowingly and on purpose? Certainly they not only judged their doctrines, which they defended in the books they wrote against heretics and confirmed by synodal decrees against the same, to be wholly in conformity with this analogy of faith, or constant harmony of Scripture, in the articles of greatest importance, but also with no small part of it. And on the other side, all Catholics, both of this age and of every earlier age from the very origin of Christianity, have utterly rejected the tenets of the Socinians as opposed to it.

units.la: §. 105. 13. Idem Socinus in Epist. 3. ad Matt. Radecium, & in modo dicto Tract. de Ecclesia, prope finem; plurimum tribuit Authoritati veterum, ut fortius afltruat Invocationem & Adorationem Christi contra Francisco-Davidianos. Verba antehac citavi, in quibus hæc occurrunt observanda. Primo, Christi Deitatem agnoscere cogitur, dum ait, Eum fuisse unum illum Deum, qui omnia ex Nihilo creavit, vel saltem ex illius substantia genitum; juxta Sententiam veterum, qui in hoc errare non potuerunt. Deinde quod pro apertissima veritate habendum sit, & mordicus retinendum, quicquid traditum habemus ab antiquis Ecclesiæ Doctoribus, pietatis & eruditionis nomine celeberrimis, & à sanctissimis Martyribus[?], ab ipso ferme nascentis Christi Ecclesiæ Initio. Tum,quod adeo gravem errorem(qualis alioquin esset Ille de Christi Divinitate) nunquam tenuissent, nisi ipsi animadvertissent, ea evidentissime in S. Scriptura Christo attribui, quæ soli Deo tribui solent; pro Cæteris autem, Adorationem & Invocationem, vel illa, ex quibus necessario inferuntur; illa ut absolute debita, Hæc ut apprime congrua. Denique, illum apertissimæ veritati resistere, qui ejusmodi Patrum Consensui, in Dogmate aliquo sic tradito ab eis, & expositione S. Scripturæ, refragarentur. Siquidem non immerito censet, veritatis evidentiam in litera S. Scripturæ elucescentem, & Conclusiones inde clare deductas effecisse, ut in eadem Sententia convenirent; & Catholicam Traditionem, eos ad istum sensum faciliùs eliciendum, istasque Conclusiones sine dubio amplectentes, quasi manu duxisse. Æquum itaque videtur, ut Illius Discipuli, non solum in hoc Dogmate, sed & in Aliis majoris momenti, pariter acquiescant in Sententia veterum, ubi inter se consentiunt in explicando S. Scripturæ sensu in Conclusionibus ex ea deductis; & in condemnatione Hæresium, quas suis Temporibus exortas, & diligentissimè excussas, tam S. Scripturæ, quam Doctrinæ Ecclesiæ Catholicæ sui seculi, à Majoribus autem acceptas, adversas judicarunt. Non igitur, se opponant hodiernis Christi Ecclesiis, quæ hanc judicandi Regulam profitentur, Patrumque Authoritati, in hujusmodi Dogmatibus asserendis, innituntur. Ne dicant veterem Christi Ecclesiam, quæ Patrem illorum ductum sequebatur, in Doctrina admodum corruptam fuisse, si minus à Fide prorsus apostatasse. Agnoscant Dogmata jam olim recepta, & à Patribus defensa, sc. Trinitatis, Satisfactionis Christi, Justificationis, Peccati Originalis, Necessitatis gratiae, efficaciae Sacramentorum, aliaque permulta, quae passim in illorum Scriptis occurrunt, aeque ac hoc de Christi Deitate, cui Adoratio atque Veneratio debentur. Et cum Socinus, ut hanc fortius astrueret, e re sua putaverit, ad veterum Authoritatem, tanquam ad Asylum confugere, quando acriter oppugnabatur ab Adversariis, in Caula, quam contra eos tuebatur; non iniquum putent illius Discipuli, siqui eadem Authoritate utantur, ad patrocinium Fidei Catholicae, contra haeretica ipsorum Dogmata. Aequum enim est ut quem Testem pro nobis producimus etiam contra nos admitti patiamur; cum illius Testimonium, si modo Fide dignus sit, utrobique pariter valeat, sin fidem non mereatur, neque pro nobis valere debeat.
units.tr: §. 105. 13. The same Socinus, in his third letter to Matthew Radecki, and in the work mentioned, near the end of the treatise on the Church, places great weight on the authority of the ancients, in order to assert more strongly the invocation and adoration of Christ against the Francisco-Davidians. I have quoted the words above; in them the following points are to be noted. First, he is compelled to acknowledge the deity of Christ when he says that he was that one God who created all things out of nothing, or at least begot them from his own substance, according to the opinion of the ancients, who could not have erred in this. Next, that whatever we have received from the ancient teachers of the Church, most celebrated for their name of piety and learning, and from the most holy martyrs, from almost the very beginning of the nascent Church of Christ, must be held as most evident truth and held fast with tooth and nail. Then, that they would never have held so grave an error (such as, indeed, that concerning the divinity of Christ would be) unless they had seen that those things were most clearly attributed to Christ in holy Scripture which are customarily attributed to God alone; and for the rest, adoration and invocation, or those things from which they are necessarily inferred: the former as absolutely due, the latter as especially fitting. Finally, that he resists most evident truth who would contradict such a consensus of the Fathers on any doctrine so handed down by them, and on their exposition of holy Scripture.
