For he not unreasonably holds that the evidence of the truth shining forth in the letter of holy Scripture, and the conclusions clearly drawn from it, brought it about that they agreed in the same opinion; and that Catholic tradition, undoubtedly embracing those conclusions, led them, as if by the hand, to elicit that sense more easily. It seems fair, therefore, that his disciples should likewise acquiesce in the judgment of the ancients, not only on this doctrine but also on others of greater importance, wherever they agree in explaining the sense of holy Scripture and in the conclusions drawn from it, and in the condemnation of the heresies which arose in their own times, were carefully examined, and were judged opposed both to holy Scripture and to the doctrine of the Catholic Church of their age, received from their forebears. Therefore let them not set themselves against the Christian churches of today, which profess this rule of judgment and rest on the authority of the Fathers in asserting such doctrines. Let them not say that the ancient Church of Christ, which their own founder followed, was altogether corrupt in doctrine, if not wholly apostate from the faith. Let them acknowledge the doctrines long since received and defended by the Fathers, namely the Trinity, the satisfaction of Christ, justification, original sin, the necessity of grace, the efficacy of the sacraments, and very many others which occur everywhere in their writings, just as much as this one concerning the deity of Christ, to whom adoration and veneration are due. And since Socinus, in order to strengthen this point, thought it expedient for his cause to take refuge in the authority of the ancients as in a sanctuary, when he was fiercely attacked by his adversaries, in the fold which he defended against them, his disciples should not think it unfair if they use the same authority in defence of the Catholic faith against their own heretical doctrines. For it is only fair that we should allow a witness whom we produce on our side to be admitted even against us; since his testimony, if indeed he deserves belief, holds equally on both sides, but if he does not deserve belief, it ought not to hold for us either.

units.la: §. 106. 14. Idem in Epist. 5. ad Radecium. p. 394. Col. 1. Cum Sententia illius rogaretur de tribus Germanis Fratribus, quorum Ars erat, imagines quasdam metallo insculpere, respondet — Quod ad Ipsorum Artem attinet, nemo meo judicio offendi debet illis Imaginibus, quae ab omni periculo in Idolatriam inducendi penitus absunt. Ex qua Socini Sententia sequitur, Lutheranos non esse culpandos, qui antiquas imagines Papismi tempore erectas adhuc retinent in suis Ecclesiis; imo, cum aliquas de novo condentes, novas pariter imagines in iisdem collocant, sc. Christi crucifixi, B. Virginis, Apostolorum, aliorumque Sanctorum; non autem Cultus, sed Commonefactionis, historiae, memoriae, & ornatus gratia. Ut enim Cultus istiusmodi imaginum prohibetur ex mandato superiorum, ita nec exhibetur à Populo. Multo minus culpanda est Ecclesia Anglicana, quae non solent Imagines extantes Christi & Sanctorum è metallo aut ligno, aut lapide fabrefactas ( cujusmodi in Lutherano-rum Templis cernuntur ) in Ecclesiis suis vel retinere vel de novo erigere, eo quod superstitiosorum Abusui magis pateant; sed vel in parietibus aut fenestris depictas, vel aulaeis intertextas, vel etiam ligno aut metallo insculptas, cum nullo prorsus Idololatriæ periculo. Nemo enim inter nos aut eas veneratur, aut venerandas putat, contra Dei & Ecclesiæ mandatum.
units.tr: §. 106. 14. The same, in Letter 5 to Radecius, p. 394, col. 1. When his opinion was asked about three German brothers whose craft was engraving images in metal, he replied: As for their art itself, in my judgment no one should be offended by those images which are wholly free from any danger of leading to idolatry. From this opinion of Socinus it follows that the Lutherans are not to be blamed for keeping in their churches the old images set up in the time of Popery; indeed, when they build new churches, they likewise place new images in them, namely of the crucified Christ, the Blessed Virgin, the Apostles, and other saints, not for worship but for reminder, history, memory and decoration. For just as the worship of such images is forbidden by the command of the superiors, so it is not offered by the people. Much less is the English Church to be blamed, which does not, in its churches, keep or newly erect images of Christ and the saints carved from metal, wood or stone (such as are seen in the temples of the Lutherans), because these are more open to the abuse of the superstitious; but only images painted on walls or windows, woven into hangings, or even carved in wood or metal, which carry no danger of idolatry at all. For among us no one either worships them or thinks they should be worshipped, contrary to the command of God and the Church.

units.la: Idem in antedicta Epist. ad Sim. Romembergium, seniorem Ecclesiæ Anab. apud Cracoviam. p. 430. col. 1. Pædobaptismum probat, & Illius validitatem asserit. Cum enim ille acrius urgeret necessitatem rebaptizandi omnes eos, qui ad Cœtus suos accederent, ita respondet Socinus. Cum Plerique Omnes eorum, qui hodie Christum profitentur saris esse statuant, siquis in ipsa Infantia Baptismum à Quocunque Christi Ministrum præse ferente, quantumvis mentiente, acceperit, idem vos quoque staruere debetis. Equidem addit, si modo Baptismus Res indifferens est. In quo graviter errat, ponendo hoc Sacramentum inter Adiaphora. At Argumentum hoc ejus à majori valet ex eo, quod Plerique Christiani, quorum Judicio nititur, hujus Sacramenti necessitatem afferant ad salutem consequendam. Idem in Disp. de Bapt. Aquæ. p. 736. col. 1. cap. 17. in princ. improbat reiterationem Baptismi. Quoniam passim, inquit, receptum est, ut qui Ecclesiæ annumerari debeant, Aquæ Baptismo sint tincti, tingantur vero Aquæ Baptismo omnes, qui pro jam Tinctis non habentur. Et paulo Post, sc.[?] 737. col.
units.tr: The same, in the aforesaid Letter to Simon Romemberg, the elder of the Anabaptist congregation at Cracow, p. 430, col. 1. He approves infant baptism and asserts its validity. For when Romemberg pressed hard the necessity of rebaptizing all who came to their assemblies, Socinus replies thus: Since almost all of those who today profess Christ hold that it is enough if anyone has received baptism in infancy from any minister of Christ, however unworthy, you too ought to hold the same. Indeed he adds: if only baptism is a matter of indifference. In this he errs gravely, by placing this sacrament among things indifferent. Yet his argument holds a fortiori, since most Christians, on whose judgment he relies, hold this sacrament to be necessary for obtaining salvation. The same, in the Disputation on Water Baptism, p. 736, col. 1, ch. 17 at the beginning, disapproves of rebaptism. Since it is commonly accepted, he says, that those who ought to be counted in the Church have been washed with water baptism, but all those who are not regarded as already washed are to be washed with water baptism. And a little later, p. 737, col.

units.la: 2. Pædobaptismum probat, ut Rem licitam, etsi Infantes non sint Fidei capaces; argumento à Circumcisione [?] ducto, quæ ad Infantes, etiam ex Dei lege pertinebant, quamvis si Instituti hujus originem, rationemque spectemus, Abrahamo primitus data fuerit, ut sigillum Justitiæ Fidei.
units.tr: 2. He approves infant baptism as a lawful thing, even though infants are not capable of faith, by an argument drawn from circumcision, which also pertained to infants by the law of God; although, if we consider the origin and purpose of this institution, it was first given to Abraham as a seal of the righteousness of faith.

units.la: §. 108. 16. Idem, in Epist. ad Mart. Vadovitam. p. 476. col. 2. concedit, Hæresiarchas, qui Seditionem concitant, aut suo Commodo student, in hæresibus propagandis, severissimè tractandos, ut qui non intellectus, sed voluntatis vitio laborent. Concedit item, & illos Hæresiarchas, qui solius Intellectus vitio laborant instar Furiosorum & mente captorum tractandos esse, qui licet miseratione digni sint, attamen cum Aliis nocivi deprehenduntur, reprimi solent, & Catenis etiam, si opus fuerit, constringi; sic & Hos, miserandos quidem esse, interea tamen, conatus Ipsorum in sua Doctrina propaganda, impedire oportere, idque (si aliter fieri nequeat) Carcere & Vinculis.
units.tr: §. 108. 16. The same, in the letter to Martin Vadovita, p. 476, col. 2, concedes: Heresiarchs who stir up sedition, or seek their own advantage in spreading heresies, are to be treated most severely, as those who suffer from a fault of the will rather than of the intellect. He likewise concedes: and those heresiarchs who suffer only from a fault of the intellect are to be treated like madmen and the insane, who, although they deserve pity, yet when they are found harmful to others, are usually restrained, and even bound with chains if need be; so these too are to be pitied, yet meanwhile their attempts to propagate their doctrine must be hindered, and that (if it cannot be done otherwise) by prison and fetters.

units.la: §. 109. 17. Idem, Epist. 3. ad Dudithium. p. 502. col. 2. sic ait, Videre nequeo, cur dicas, adeo id esse Hominis difficile; ut aliam post hanc restare vitam credat, in os enim Tibi reclamant perpetua tot Seculorum, inde ab omni memoria, experimenta, contra quæ, nec illa, quas Tu allegas, Rationes, nec quotquot unquam allegari poterunt, quicquam virium habent. Ubi Primo, observandum occurrit, quam tristes Socinianismi [?] effectus fuerint, quibus ipsa Christianæ Fidei Principia admodum quassata erant, si minus subversa. Siquidem hic Dudithius, qui de altera vita tantopere ambigebat, imo & Argumentis eam oppugnare ausus est, inter Anti-Trinitarios principem locum tenuit, sive Ingenium, sive eruditionem, sive Dignitatem ejus spectemus. Deinde, quid intelligit Socinus per experimenta perpetua tot seculorum, quibus altera post hanc vita probatur? Num Apparitiones mortuorum? At Illæ infirma valde erant hujus Rei Documenta, cum potuerint esse sensuum nostrorum illusiones, vel malorum Spiritunum[?] ludibria; quod & sæpenumero factum est. Præterea, Ethnici negarunt Resurrectionem Corporis; & ipse Socinus Animarum apparitionem negavit, quippe qui affirmavit eas, post separationem à Corporibus suis somno quodam lethargico obrutas jacere sine omni sensu & motu; ac proinde revisere non posse hunc mundum, in quo degimus, aut si forte intelligat secula Patriarcharum piorum, Judæorum, & Christianorum, sibi ordine succedentium, qui unici veri Dei cognitionem professi sunt, Illumque solum coluerunt; abneget suam Psychopannychiam, & abolitionem totalem Impiorum in Die Judicii, cum multis aliis Dogmatibus, quæ in Scriptis suis tuetur. Agnoscat item Sacrificia piacularia, Dei omnipræsentiam & omniscientiam, corruptionem Naturæ humanæ post lapsum Adami cum Aliis quamplurimis, quæ negat. Postremo, si per tot seculorum experimenta, intelligat concordantia sapientum atque Piorum Judicia istis Seculis degentium, contra quæ nullæ omnino Rationes, quæ à quoquam adduci possunt, quicquam valere poterunt; applicet hanc Regulam ad Dogmata à se asserta, & Argumenta, quibus illa astruere conatur, pro invalidis habeat, &, una cum ipsis Dogmatibus rejiciat.
units.tr: §. 109. 17. The same, Letter 3 to Dudith, p. 502, col. 2, says thus: I cannot see why you say that it is so hard for a man to believe that another life remains after this one; for the constant experiences of so many ages, from all memory, cry out in your face, and against these neither those reasons which you allege, nor any that could ever be alleged, have any force. Here, first, it is to be observed what sad effects Socinianism had, by which the very principles of the Christian faith were badly shaken, if not overthrown. For this Dudith, who doubted so greatly about the other life, and even dared to attack it with arguments, held the chief place among the Anti-Trinitarians, whether we look at his talent, his learning or his dignity. Next, what does Socinus understand by the constant experiences of so many ages, by which the other life is proved? Are they appearances of the dead? But these were very weak proofs of this matter, since they could be illusions of our senses or mockeries of evil spirits, as has often happened. Moreover, the heathens denied the resurrection of the body; and Socinus himself denied the appearance of souls, since he affirmed that after separation from their bodies they lie sunk in a kind of lethargic sleep, without any sense or motion, and therefore cannot revisit this world in which we live. Or if perhaps he means the ages of the pious patriarchs, Jews and Christians, succeeding one another in order, who professed the knowledge of the one true God and worshipped him alone, then let him renounce his psychopannychy and the total annihilation of the wicked at the Day of Judgment, along with many other doctrines which he defends in his writings. Let him likewise acknowledge atoning sacrifices, the omnipresence and omniscience of God, the corruption of human nature after the fall of Adam, along with very many others which he denies. Lastly, if by the experiences of so many ages he means the agreed judgments of the wise and the pious living in those ages, against which no reasons at all that anyone can bring will have any force; let him apply this rule to the doctrines he asserts, hold the arguments by which he tries to establish them to be invalid, and reject them together with the doctrines themselves.

units.la: §. 110. 18. Idem, Catech. fragment. cap. 2. p. 681. Col. 2. ut Christi Adorationem probet, ad Cypriani Authoritatem se confert, in Textu Apocalypseos citando, sc. Cap. 19. 10. & 22. 9. ubi pro Deum adora, (prout hodie legimus) habet, Jesum Dominum adora. Ita enim Cyprianus hoc Angeli Responsum effert, De Bono Patientiæ in fine ubi, inquit, Socinus, (sub nomine Magistri) vox [solum] subintelligenda est. Discipulo autem replicante, Tunc Deus Pater excludendus esset. Respondet Magister, Angelus non exclusisset. Nam de Rebus creatis ejus verba accipienda essent, quemadmodum Ipse erat Res creata. Ac si dixisset, Inter Res creatas, nec me, nec ullum Alium adorare debes praeter Jesum. Namque ille est Dominus, nos autem Omnes Servi, ut Tu es. Sic Ille. Ergo, qui Socini Sententiam in hoc sequuntur, eandem quoque Authoritatem in Aliis agnoscant, & similes S. Textus expositiones admittant, ubi par Ratio valet. Admittant Testimonium ejusdem Cypriani, ubi his verbis citat Illud Joannis. 1. Epist. 5. 7. & hi Tres unum sunt, hoc est, Pater, Verbum, & Spiritus Sanctus. Sic enim Ille, De Unit. Ecclesiæ. Licet hæc Clausula omittatur in permultis Codicibus à Syro item & Vet. Latino necnon à Patribus quamplurimis tam Græcis, quam Latinis. Admittant pariter similem Catholicorum expositionem de sensu particulæ [Solum] in illis Christi verbis ad patrem directis. Hæc est Vita æterna, ut cognoscant Te Illum solum verum Deum. Jo. 17. 3. ita ut hæc Particula non Ipsum Christum excludat à participatione Deitatis, (qui ab eodem Joanne alibi appellatur Filius Dei unigenitus. Cap. 1. 14, 18. & à Paulo, [illegible, ~6 letters] seu proprius Filius, per Antonomasiam. Rom. 8. 32.) sed Creaturas solas. Siquidem, ipse Christus alibi affirmat, se esse unum cum Patre; neque se negat esse talem Dei Filium, qui Patri æqualis sit, quamvis ob hoc Blasphemiæ incusatus à Judæis, nec semel lapidationi expositus, unde & Apostolus affirmat, Illum non rapinam duxisse, se esse æqualem Deo. Denique, ipse nihil moratus accusationem Blasphemiæ, neque periculum à Judæis, qui Illum interficere studebant, palam asserit Patris sui esse Placitum, ut Omnes honorent Filium, sicut honorant Patrem, qui misit Ipsum. Jo. 5. 23. Ita enim & ipse Socinus intelligit hanc Particulam [Sicut ] & hoc Argumento nititur, ut probet Adorationem divinam Christo debitam esse. De Ecclesia. p. 353. col.
units.tr: §. 110. 18. The same, in the Catechism fragment, ch. 2, p. 681, col. 2, to prove the adoration of Christ, appeals to the authority of Cyprian, citing the text of the Apocalypse, namely ch. 19.10 and 22.9, where instead of Worship God (as we read today) it has Worship Jesus the Lord. For Cyprian gives the angel's answer in this form, in On the Good of Patience at the end, where, says Socinus (under the name of his Master), the word only [solum] is to be understood. But when the disciple objected, Then God the Father would have to be excluded, the Master replies: The angel would not have excluded him. For his words would have to be taken of created things, since he himself was a created thing. As if he had said: among created things you ought to worship neither me nor any other except Jesus. For he is the Lord, but we are all servants, as you are. Thus he. Therefore, those who follow Socinus's opinion in this matter should likewise acknowledge the same authority in other places, and admit similar explanations of Holy Scripture wherever the same reasoning holds. Let them admit the testimony of the same Cyprian, where he cites in these words the saying of John, 1 Epistle 5.7: and these three are one, that is, the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit. For thus he, On the Unity of the Church. Although this clause is omitted in very many manuscripts, both the Syriac and the Old Latin, and very many Fathers, both Greek and Latin. Let them likewise admit the similar Catholic explanation of the sense of the particle [Only] in those words of Christ addressed to the Father: This is eternal life, that they may know thee, the only true God. John 17.3. so that this particle does not exclude Christ himself from sharing in the Deity (who is elsewhere called by the same John the only-begotten Son of God, ch. 1.14, 18, and by Paul [illegible] or his own Son, by antonomasia, Rom. 8.32), but only creatures. For Christ himself elsewhere affirms that he is one with the Father; nor does he deny being such a Son of God as is equal to the Father, although for this reason he was accused of blasphemy by the Jews, and more than once exposed to stoning; whence the Apostle also affirms that he did not think it robbery to be equal with God. Finally, he himself, unmoved by the charge of blasphemy or the danger from the Jews who sought to kill him, openly asserts that it is his Father's pleasure that all should honour the Son, just as they honour the Father who sent him. John 5.23. For Socinus himself understands the particle [Sicut] in this way, and relies on this argument to prove that divine worship is due to Christ. On the Church, p. 353, col.

units.la: 2. Æquum est quoque; ut admittant pro veris, alias S. Scripturæ Sententias, prout à patribus in Scriptis suis passim citantur, ubi Codices hodierni inter se discrepant. Denique non inique ab iisdem postulatur, ut istiusmodi S. Textus expositiones non repudient, quas verba proprie sumpta quasi sponte suggerunt, quibus scopus S. Scriptoris favet, & quæ consonæ reperiuntur locis parallelis, ubi eædem Phrases occurrunt observandæ, & eadem Materia tractatur, tales demum, quas Socinus hic loci dat, atque Aliis, ut Rationi consonas, proponit admittendas.
units.tr: 2. It is also fair that they accept as true other sayings of Holy Scripture, as the Fathers cite them everywhere in their writings, where today's manuscripts differ among themselves. Finally, it is not unreasonable to ask them not to reject those interpretations of such a Scripture text which the words, taken in their proper sense, seem to suggest of their own accord, which agree with the author's aim, and which are found consistent with parallel passages where the same phrases occur and the same subject is treated. In short, these are the interpretations which Socinus here offers, and which he proposes to others to be admitted as agreeing with reason.

units.la: §. III. 19. Idem, in Disp. de Baptismo Aquæ. p. 737. Col. 1. hæc habet. Omnia fiant, quæ ad totius Ecclesiæ unitatem atque concordiam, & Singulorum simul ædificationem ac salutem pertinere possint. Illud enim Pauli semper pro Oculis habendum, debemus nos firmiores imbecillitates Infirmorum sustinere. Rom. 14. 1. loquitur quidem de baptizandis infantibus Adultorum, qui antea Baptismum non susceperant, eum tamen petebant. At si hæc Ipsius Regula universim teneat, ut ab illo proponitur, admitti postulat, non solum in Adiaphoris, quæ ad Disciplinam, Ceremonias, Cultusque divini Formulas pertinent, quoties ab Ecclesia Catholica præscribuntur, vel apud plerosque Christianos in usu sunt, sed etiam in Ecclesiæ Decretis, quæ ad Doctrinam spectant, & Opinionibus passim inter Christianos receptis, siquidem consensus in his, & ejusdem Fidei Professio manifeste tendunt ad conservationem Unitatis, Concordiæ, & Ædificationis ad salutem; sicut è contra, Dissensus in Fide, & Opinionum Fidei receptæ adversarum difformis Professio, ex natura sua introducunt in Ecclesiam discordiam, atque Schismata, eademque fovent; quibus ni tempestive occurratur, pro Ædificatione Ruina, pro salute Perditio sequetur.
units.tr: §. III. 19. The same man, in his Disputation on Water Baptism (p. 737, col. 1), says this: Let all things be done which can contribute to the unity and harmony of the whole Church, and to the edification and salvation of each one together. For we must always keep before our eyes that saying of Paul, that we ought to bear with the firmer the weaknesses of the weak. Rom. 14. 1. Indeed, Paul speaks of baptizing the infants of adults who had not received baptism before but were asking for it. But if this rule of his holds generally, as he puts it, it demands to be admitted not only in matters indifferent, which pertain to discipline, ceremonies and the forms of divine worship, whenever they are prescribed by the Catholic Church or are in use among most Christians, but also in the decrees of the Church which concern doctrine, and in opinions commonly received among Christians. For agreement in these matters, and a common profession of the same faith, plainly tend to preserve unity, harmony and edification unto salvation; on the other hand, disagreement in faith, and a profession of opinions opposed to the faith received, by their very nature bring discord and schisms into the Church and foster them. Unless these are promptly checked, ruin will follow in place of edification, and destruction in place of salvation.

units.la: §. 112. 20. In disputatione, quam idem Socinus habuit cum Christiano Franken, & extat inter Opera illius. Tom. 2. p. 767. non unum occurrit observandum; quod ipsius Causæ officere videtur. Nam primo, cum Franken recusaret disputationem inire cum Socino è sacra Scriptura Testimoniis, quæ detorqueri possunt, atque adeo ab Omnibus nunc, etiam absurdissimis sectariis (ut vere inquit) detorquentur ad victoriam; sed Ratione, si modo Illi placeret, secum agere vellet; tandem annuit Socinus, hoc Argumento nixus, quod vera Ratio non sit contraria Theologiæ veræ; quin è contra verum vero tam consentiat, quam Album Albo, aut Pulchrum Pulchro. Unde sequitur Socini Rationem non esse veram, sanamque, quæ contradicit veteris Theologiæ Principiis, quam Catholica Ecclesia pro vera semper agnovit, ut à primis Evangelii Præconibus acceptam, qui Ecclesias,ubique fundarunt. Secundo Franken sic urget Socinum, Non Causam tuam sublevat, quod S. Literæ Christum adorari jubent; nam & ego multa contra Te sacra Testimonia afferre possum, quibus & solus natura Deus adorari jubetur, & hunc Honorem nulli Creaturæ tribuendum esse significatur.
units.tr: §. 112. 20. In the disputation which the same Socinus held with the Christian Franken, and which exists among his Works (Tom. 2, p. 767), more than one point deserves notice, which seems to harm his own cause. For first, when Franken refused to enter into a disputation with Socinus from the testimonies of Holy Scripture, which can be twisted, and therefore are now twisted to victory by all, even the most absurd sectaries (as he truly says), but wished to deal with him by reason, if only it pleased him, Socinus at last agreed, relying on this argument: that true reason is not contrary to true theology; on the contrary, truth agrees with truth as well as white agrees with white, or beautiful with beautiful. From this it follows that the reasoning of Socinus is not true and sound if it contradicts the principles of the old theology, which the Catholic Church has always acknowledged as true, having received them from the first heralds of the Gospel who founded churches everywhere. Second, Franken presses Socinus thus: It does not help your cause that the Holy Letters command that Christ be worshipped; for I too can bring against you many sacred testimonies by which God alone, by nature, is commanded to be worshipped, and it is shown that this honour is to be given to no creature.

units.la: Ad illa omnia Testimonia ego possum respondere. Respondet Socinus, Cui reponit Franken; & ego ad omnes tuos locos, Christi Adorationem urgentes probabilem potero Responsionem afferre. Quis igitur nobis praebebit Regulam, ad quam moderemur hanc diversitatem? Respondet Socinus, Scriptura recte intellecta nobis erit Regula. Cui Franken iterum; Regula debet esse recta & certa, Scriptura autem, quatenus ab hoc vel illo Homine recte intellecta affirmatur, non est recta & certa Regula, quoniam dilatatur, coarctatur, & pro varietate Ingeniorum, in varios sensus distrahitur. Replicat Socinus, satis inepte & ridicule: De veritate mea Sententia (viz. e S. Literis) tam sum certus, quam certo scio, me ipsum Pileum manibus tenere. Cui Franken sic reponit, sane multo gravius, & Rationi congruentius: Tua ista Certitudo non potest mihi & Aliis certa esse veritatis Regula. Nam reperietur Alius quispiam, qui dicat, Sententiam Tuam contrariam e S. Literis, sibi esse perjuasissimam atque certissimam. Cumque in utroque eadem de Re summa sit certitudo, eaque diversa & contraria quomodo hæc[?] esse potest veritatis Regula, Recta & certa veritatis Regula non potest sibi ipsi esse contraria, sed eadem semper sese modo habet, quibuscunque tandem Rebus dimetiendis applicetur. Hæc ille in utramque partem de Regula Controversias dijudicandi, cum ad S. Literas utrinque appellatur. Ex quibus intelligitur, quam difficile, seu potius quam impossibile sit, eandem determinari apud eos, qui sibi fas putant, S. Literas pro arbitrio exponere, suosque sensus illis ad libitum affingere.
units.tr: I can answer all those testimonies. Socinus replies. To this Franken rejoins: And I shall be able to give a plausible answer to all your passages urging the worship of Christ. Who, then, will give us a rule by which we may regulate this disagreement? Socinus replies: Scripture rightly understood will be our rule. To this Franken answers again: A rule ought to be right and certain; but Scripture, insofar as it is affirmed to be rightly understood by this or that man, is not a right and certain rule, since it is stretched, narrowed, and pulled into various senses according to the variety of men's minds. Socinus replies, quite foolishly and absurdly: I am as certain of the truth of my opinion (namely, from the Holy Letters) as I am certain that I hold my own cap in my hands. To this Franken replies in a way that is far more serious and more in keeping with reason: Your certainty cannot be a certain rule of truth for me and for others. For there will be found someone else who says that your opinion, contrary to the Holy Letters, has been most persuasive and most certain to him. And since on both sides there is the same certainty about the same matter, and yet they are different and contrary, how can this be a rule of truth? A right and certain rule of truth cannot be contrary to itself, but always remains the same, whatever matters it is applied to measure. He says this on both sides concerning the rule for judging controversies, when appeal is made on each side to the Holy Letters. From these things it is understood how difficult, or rather how impossible, it is to fix the same rule among those who think it lawful to expound the Holy Letters at their own pleasure and to attach their own senses to them as they wish.

units.la: Tertio.
units.tr: Thirdly.

units.la: Cum Franken urgeret, Christum utpote finitam substantiam (juxta Socinum) non posse esse Objectum divinae Adorationis atque Invocationis, cum talis capax non sit infinitae sapientiae aut Potentiae, quae quæ ad istiusmodi Objectum Cultus divini necessario requirantur. Socinus respondet, Philosophica sunt Ista, & Christi Doctrina iminica. Cui Franken rufsus, Atqui initio huius Disputationis dicebas, verum vero non esse contrarium. Quomodo ergo nunc vera mea Ratio adversatur Christi Doctrinæ. Huic vero Socinus nihil habet quod reponat, quam, non est vera sed sophistica tua Ratiocinatio. At Franken in sequentibus ostendit, hanc suam Ratiocinationem, Socini principiis insistentem, nullatenus esse sophisticam, sed tam Theologiæ, quam Philosophiæ consonam. Quarto, Cum Franken sic arguit, Divina ista Potestas, quam Socinus Christo tribuit, non est Adoratione Religiosa digna, nisi eam ad divinam usque Naturam extendamus, quemadmodum faciunt Trinitarii, existimantes indissolubili nexu colligatam esse Divinam Potestatem, cum essentia & Adoratione Divina; verumque esse Idololatram, qui Adorationem à Deitate sejungit. Respondet Socinus, Decipiuntur isti, Ratione subverten-tes Theologiam. Cum Franken reponit, Dissolve igitur, si potes, istorum Rationes. Sic enim argumentantur, illi veri sunt Idololatræ, qui serviunt, id est, adorant seu invocant eos, qui natura non sunt Dii. Gal. 4. 8. qui Conservos, eosque qui sunt è fratrum numero, nec aliquid amplius, adorant. Apoc. 19. 10. & 22. 9. qui Creaturam aliquam invocant, aut religioso Cultu adorant præter Jehovam solum. Matt. 4. 10. cum Deut. 6. 13. & 10. 20. qui demique fiduciam ponunt in Homine, & statuunt carnem Brachium suum, hi enim Maledicta pronuntiantur Jer. 17. 5. Respondet Socinus, Rationes istæ è S. Literis depromptæ, Ni-hil aliud concludunt, quam Christum non esse adorandum, ut Rerum omnium Auctorem, Parentem, & Architectum, posse autem ac debere adorari, ut quoddam medium, per quod ejusmodi Adoratio tendit in Deum. Replicat Franken, hanc Causam Adorationis, nempe opus Creationis, Christo competere non posse juxta Socini sententiam, qui statuit eum nihil Commune habere cum Deo Patre in isto opere, utpote qui longe post ab eo creatus sit, & in mundum missus. Deinde, cum eximia illa Potestas, quam Socinus asserit Christo a Deo Patre datam, non pertingat ad Divinam illam excellentiam, qua in Patre residet, quomodo ei deberi potest Divina Adoratio atque Invocatio, qua praecipue Partes sunt excellentissimae illius Honoris, quem Deus sibi soli vendicat? Quinto, Cum Franken urgeret illud ipsius Dei Dictum apud Iaiam, Ego sum Jehovah, illud est nomen meum, & Gloriam meam alteri non dabo Isa. 42. 8. Quod iterum quoque repetit cap. 48. 11. Ergo, inquit ille, cum Adoratio & Invocatio Divina sint partes cultus ad Dei Gloriam peculiariter spectantis, Christo, nudo Homini, tribui nullo modo possunt, ut qui a Deo multum diversus sit ac proinde Talis, Cui Gloriam istam se denegaturum profitetur, subdit quidem aliquid Socinus Responsi loco, sed quam infirmum sit, & a Ratione alienum, cuivis serio perpendenti facile patebit; quod & Franken statim advertit. Nam primo, inquit Socinus, Dictum hoc sic interpretandum est, non suam[?] Gloriam meam ab altero accipi, & sibi arrogari, contra voluntatem meam. At, replicat Franken, hoc est, Oppositum, Activum, non Dabo, per Passivum, non patiar accipi; seu potius, non eripi mihi, contra voluntatem meam. Quamvis enim dare quandoque positum sit pro accipere, in S. literis, quia Correlativa sunt; quoties sic. quod sponte datur alicui, ab eo sponte accipitur; nonquam tamen ponitur dabo, sumi contra voluntatem meam, seu mihi per vim eripi. Has enim, cum omnino contraria sint sibi invicem, non se mutuo respiciunt, adeoque alterum in alterius locum substitui non potest. Hic itaque geminus verborum sensus est, nunquam suum, ut alius quicunque sibi assumat Gloriam mihi soli debitam, neque ipse unquam eam alio transferam. Deinde, hoc effugium quærit Socinus --Potest hoc modo illud Isaiæ dictum intelligi, Gloriam meam alteri non dabo, id est, totam meam Gloriam alteri non cedam. Christo autem data est pars tantum hujus Gloriæ. Cui Franken ita replicat. Illud non est interpretari, sed torquere Scripturam. Nam eodem modo quis posset totam in absurdissimos, planeque contrarios sensus trahere. Ut primum illud Præceptum, non habebis Deos alienos præter me (ut hoc unum pro multis E.G. ponam) Te magistro, sic interpretabimur, non habebis Deos alienos præter me, quibus totum Honorem mihi debitum tribuas; habere autem Tibi fas est alios Deos, quibus mea partem Gloriæ impertias. Sed hæc tibi forsan non absurda videntur. Neque Socinus in hoc sibi constat. Nam paulo prius contrarium asseruerat, quando dixit, Non divido Adorationem illam, quæ soli Deo debetur, inter Christum & Deum; sed dico, Deum adorari tanquam Authorem Rerum omnium; Christum autem, ut quoddam medium, per quod ejusmodi Adoratio tendit in Deum. Hæc habuit Socinus, quæ reponeret Adversario, istum Isaiæ locum contra ipsius sententiam alleganti; quam valide, judicent æqui lectores. Oftorodus itaque Responsis hisce diffisus, alia quædam affert, viz. hæc. Primo, inquit, per hujusmodi oppositionem, Adversarii explicant ea, quæ clara per se lucent, per ea quæ obscura sunt, Novum Testamentum per vetus, multa denique loca, per obscurum aliquem. Deinde, per vocem [ Alteri ] neque Christus, neque Piorum quisquam intelligitur. Alioquin lioquin, Propheta sibiipsi contradiceret. Cap. 46. ult. Apostolis item. Rom. 5. 2. 2 Thes. 1. 12. 1 Pet. 5. 10. Apoc. 21. 11. Ipsique Christo. Ib. cap. 3. 21. Ergo, solum intelligit Idola, & Imagines Gentilium. Tertio, non dabo, inquit, Idem sonat, quod non permittam, ut Homines propria Authoritate Gloriam ipsius aliis ascribant, &c. Idolis. Psal. 106. 20. Postremo, inquit, satis liquet, sensum genuinum verborum hæc esse, quod Deus nolit Gloriam suam ad alios transferri, &c. ut per alienationem ipse illa spolietur. Hoc vero ipsum Honorem Christi non attingit; cum ille, testante Scriptura S. à Deo ipso ei sit concessus, nec Deus propterea Gloria sua privetur, sed potius maximo Honori ipsice-dat. At neque hæc argumentum inde petitum solvunt. Nam primo, verba Dei apud Isaiam per se clara sunt, ubi bis repetuntur; atque alibi occurrunt plurima S. Scripturæ Testimonia, quibus hæc Gloria Adorationis atque Invocationis divinæ Deo soli ascribitur & asseritur. Neque ullatenus insolitum est, ut Christus & Apostoli illius Doctrinam suam confirment Testimoniis è lege petitis, & è Prophetis. Deinde, loca, quæ citat ad probandum, Gloriam Dei fuisse aliis communicatam, nihil ad rem faciunt; & si facerent, nimium probarent; nempe, Gloriam Adorationis atque Invocationis divinæ, aliis præterquam Christo, à Deo concessam. Itaque, cum dicit Deus, se positurum in Sione salutem, in Israele Gloriam suam. Isa. 46. ult. hoc tantum vult, se illustraturum justitiæ veritatisque suæ Gloriam in salute Israelis, qui coluit ipsum in Sione. Cum autem Apostoli dicunt, Deum nos facturum suæ Gloriæ participes. 1 Cor. 15. 49. Phil. 3. 21. 1 Jo. 3. 2. Eodem sensu accipiendum est, quo illud Petri, cum affirmat, nos per Promissa Evangelica factos esse participes divinæ naturæ. 2 Pet. 1. 4. non recte, quasi nunc in statu gratiæ sieremus proprie participes essentiæ divinæ, quæ dividi nequit in partes; vel quasi Gloriam Deitati propriam, in altero seculo consecuturi essemus; sed respectu effectuum atque qualitatum à Deo in nos emanantium, quibus inchoatis plenius similes illi reddimur nunc Temporis in Gratia, & postea reddendi sumus in Gloria. Sedere demum in Throno cum Christo, quod ipse victori pollicetur. Apoc. 3. 21. est nihil aliud, quam unumquemque talem, suo modo & gradu Dignitatis atque Gloriæ cœlestis, una cum Christo, consortem esse. Col. 3. 4. Sic alibi Paulus affirmat, Sanctos mundum judicaturos, 1 Cor. 6. 2. Hoc tamen neutiquam æquat illos Christo Judici, neque derogat aliquid supremæ ipsius Potestati, in mundo judicando; ut neque Apostolorum Prærogativæ, de quibus idem Christus affirmat, quod cum ipse sessurus sit in Throno suo glorioso, illi quoque sint sessuri in duodecim Thronis, judicantes duodecim Tribus Israelis. Matt. 19. 28. Tertio, verba ista Dei generaliter efferuntur de omni, quod non est Deus, seu quod est alterum à Deo; neque restringi debent ad idola Gentilium, quamvis Instantiæ ponatur in iis quandoque, eo quod à cunctis fere Gentibus pro Diis colerentur. Neque enim minus prohibet Deus Honorem suum impertiri cuicunque Creaturæ in Cœlo, vel in Terra, quam Idolis & Imaginibus, ut soli, lunæ, stellis, elementis, Principibus Gentium & Heroibus defunctis. Postremo, Deus non solum prohibet, Gloriam sibi debitam, alteri tribui, ita ut ipse simul ea spolietur, sed & nullam illius partem alteri communicari vult. Siquidem Judæi tunc temporis, publice colebant Deum in Templo suo, & sacrificiis, & precibus, & observatione Festorum solennium, ut patet ex eodem Propheta. Isa. 1. sed Idololatriae rei peragebantur, eo quod Deos alienos una cum vero Deo colerent. Imo, quod plus est, & verbis istis multo congruentius, Deus isthic affirmat, se non concessurum alteri cuipiam qualemcunque partem Gloriae suae, utpote quae sit Majestatis Divinae praerogativa, nulli Creaturae communicabilis. Siquidem, non minus in Dei ignominiam cedit, Gloriam sibi propriam alteri tribuere velle, quam ut alter contra suam voluntatem sibi istam arroget. Imo magis dedecorosum Deo videtur, & ab eo alienum, ut quod majestati suae proprium est, alteri sponte cederet, quam ut contra fas ab altero arripi pateretur; vel alteri, contra mandatum suum, ab homine dari. Hoc enim est, Idololatriam permittere duntaxat; istud autem, probare. Hoc itaque saepe factum est, & fere universum: istud vero nunquam. Quod ergo a Christo dictum est Juveni isti, qui cum ipsius Deitatem non agnosceret, humillime tamen eum salutavit, magistri boni Titulo ipsum honorans, quare me dicis Bonum? Nemo est Bonus, praeter unum, qui est Deus. Matt. 19. 17. non incommode adaptari potest Socini affectis[?], qui, cum Christi Deitatem, non solum, cum isto juvene, non agnoscant, sed & omnino negent, cultum tamen Divinum ipsi exhibent, & ab aliis omnibus exhiberi postulant; Quare me ut Deum colitis, cum Deitatem meam prorsus negetis. Ego, ex vestra opinione, nudus Homo sum, & non Deus. Nemo autem Honorem Deo debitum meretur, nisi solus Deus; qui palam professus est, se Gloriam hanc suam alteri non daturum. Ergo, vel me Deum agnoscite, vel nolite ut Deum honorare.
units.tr: When Franken pressed that Christ, as a finite substance (according to Socinus), cannot be the object of divine adoration and invocation, since such a being is not capable of the infinite wisdom or power which are necessarily required for such an object of divine worship, Socinus replied: These are philosophical points, and they are hostile to Christ's doctrine. To this Franken answered again: But at the beginning of this dispute you said that truth is not contrary to truth. How then does my reasoning now oppose the doctrine of Christ? Socinus has nothing to reply except this: your reasoning is not true but sophistical. But Franken shows in what follows that this reasoning of his, which rests on the principles of Socinus, is in no way sophistical, but consonant with theology as much as with philosophy. Fourthly, when Franken argues thus: This divine power which Socinus attributes to Christ is not worthy of religious adoration, unless we extend it to the divine nature itself, as the Trinitarians do, who think that divine power is bound by an indissoluble tie to the divine essence and to divine adoration; and whoever separates adoration from the Deity is truly an idolater. Socinus answers: Those men are deceived, subverting theology by reason. Franken replies: Then dissolve, if you can, their arguments. For they argue thus: those are true idolaters who serve, that is, adore or invoke, those who by nature are not gods. Gal. 4. 8. who adore fellow-servants, and those who are of the number of brethren and nothing more. Apoc. 19. 10. & 22. 9. who invoke some creature, or worship with religious cult anyone besides Jehovah alone. Matt. 4. 10. with Deut. 6. 13. & 10. 20. who finally place their trust in man and make flesh their arm; for these are pronounced accursed. Jer. 17. 5. Socinus answers: these arguments, drawn from Holy Scripture, conclude only that Christ is not to be adored as the Author, Parent and Architect of all things, but that he can and ought to be adored as a certain mediator through whom such adoration tends to God. Franken rejoins: this ground of adoration, namely the work of creation, cannot belong to Christ according to the opinion of Socinus, who holds that he has nothing in common with God the Father in that work, being created long afterwards and sent into the world. Then: since that remarkable power which Socinus asserts was given to Christ by God the Father does not reach that divine excellence which resides in the Father, how can divine adoration and invocation be owed to him, which are the chief parts of that most excellent honour which God claims for himself alone? Fifthly, when Franken pressed that saying of God himself in Isaiah, I am Jehovah, that is my name, and my glory I will not give to another Isa. 42. 8. which he also repeats ch. 48. 11. Therefore, he says, since adoration and divine invocation are parts of the worship that pertains peculiarly to the glory of God, they can in no way be attributed to Christ, a mere man, who is very different from God and so is one to whom God professes he will deny that glory, Socinus does add something by way of reply, but how weak it is and foreign to reason will easily be clear to anyone who weighs it seriously; which Franken also at once notices. For first, says Socinus, this saying must be interpreted thus: my glory is not to be received from another and claimed for himself against my will. But Franken replies: this means that the opposite, the active "I will not give," is taken as the passive "I will not suffer," or rather "it will not be taken from me against my will." For although "to give" is sometimes used in Scripture for "to receive," because they are correlatives, whenever something is freely given to someone, it is freely received by him; yet "I will give" is never taken to mean "it is taken against my will, or torn from me by force." For these, since they are wholly contrary to each other, do not correspond mutually, and so one cannot be substituted for the other. Here, therefore, is the twofold sense of the words: that no one else should ever claim for himself the glory due to me alone, nor will I ever transfer it to another. Then Socinus seeks this escape: In this way that saying of Isaiah can be understood, "my glory I will not give to another," that is, I will not yield my whole glory to another. But only a part of this glory has been given to Christ. To which Franken replies thus: That is not to interpret but to twist Scripture. For in the same way someone could draw the whole of it into the most absurd and plainly contrary senses. For example, let us take the first commandment, "You shall have no other gods before me" (to take this one of many for instance): on your teaching we would interpret it thus, "You shall have no other gods before me, to whom you may give the whole honour due to me; but it is permitted you to have other gods to whom you may impart a part of my glory." But perhaps these things do not seem absurd to you. Nor is Socinus consistent in this. For a little earlier he had asserted the opposite, when he said: I do not divide that adoration which is due to God alone between Christ and God; but I say God is adored as the Author of all things, while Christ is adored as a certain mediator through whom such adoration tends to God. Socinus had these things to set against his opponent, who was citing this passage of Isaiah against his opinion; how strongly, let fair readers judge. Ostorodus, therefore, distrusting these replies, brings forward certain other things, namely these. First, he says, by such opposition our adversaries explain things that shine clear in themselves by things that are obscure, the New Testament by the Old, and in short many passages by some obscure one. Then, through the word [another] neither Christ nor any of the pious is understood. Otherwise the prophet would contradict himself. Ch. 46, last verse. Likewise to the Apostles. Rom. 5. 2. 2 Thes. 1. 12. 1 Pet. 5. 10. Apoc. 21. 11. And to Christ himself. Ibid. ch. 3. 21. Therefore he understands only idols and images of the Gentiles. Thirdly, "I will not give," he says, means the same as "I will not permit" men by their own authority to ascribe his glory to others, etc., to idols. Psal. 106. 20. Lastly, he says, it is sufficiently clear that the genuine sense of the words is this: that God is unwilling for his glory to be transferred to others, etc., so that by alienation he himself should be despoiled of it. But this does not touch the honour of Christ, since he, as Holy Scripture testifies, was granted it by God himself, and God is not on that account deprived of his glory, but rather gives it the greatest honour. But neither do these things resolve the argument drawn from it. For first, the words of God in Isaiah are clear in themselves, where they are repeated twice; and elsewhere many testimonies of Holy Scripture occur, by which this glory of divine adoration and invocation is ascribed and asserted to God alone. Nor is it at all unusual that Christ and his Apostles confirm their doctrine with testimonies taken from the law and the prophets. Next, the passages which he cites to prove that the glory of God has been communicated to others have nothing to do with the matter; and if they did, they would prove too much, namely that the glory of divine adoration and invocation was granted by God to others besides Christ. Thus, when God says that he will set salvation in Zion and his glory in Israel (Isa. 46, last verse), he means only that he will display the glory of his justice and truth in the salvation of Israel, who worshipped him in Zion. But when the Apostles say that God will make us partakers of his glory (1 Cor. 15. 49; Phil. 3. 21; 1 Jo. 3. 2), this must be understood in the same sense as Peter's saying, where he affirms that we have become partakers of the divine nature through the evangelical promises (2 Pet. 1. 4): not in the sense that in the state of grace we are now properly partakers of the divine essence, which cannot be divided into parts, or that in the next age we shall attain the glory proper to the Deity; but with respect to the effects and qualities flowing from God into us, by which, begun in us, we are made more fully like him now in time in grace, and afterwards are to be made like him in glory. Lastly, to sit on the throne with Christ, which he promises to the victor (Apoc. 3. 21), is nothing other than for each such person, in his own way and degree of heavenly dignity and glory, to be a partner with Christ (Col. 3. 4). So elsewhere Paul affirms that the saints will judge the world (1 Cor. 6. 2). Yet this in no way makes them equal to Christ the Judge, nor does it detract anything from his supreme power in judging the world; nor does it take from the prerogative of the Apostles, of whom the same Christ affirms that, as he himself will sit on his glorious throne, they too will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19. 28). Thirdly, these words of God are spoken generally of everything that is not God, or that is other than God, and ought not to be restricted to the idols of the Gentiles, although the instance is sometimes put in them, because they were worshipped as gods by almost all the Gentiles. For God forbids his honour to be imparted to any creature in heaven or on earth no less than to idols and images, such as the sun, moon, stars, elements, princes of the Gentiles and deceased heroes. Lastly, God not only forbids that the glory due to him be given to another, so that he himself is at the same time despoiled of it, but also wills that no part of it be communicated to another. For the Jews of that time publicly worshipped God in his temple, with sacrifices, prayers and observance of the solemn feasts, as is clear from the same prophet (Isa. 1); yet they were guilty of idolatry, because they worshipped alien gods along with the true God. Indeed, what is more, and far more fitting to these words, God there affirms that he will not grant to any other whatever part of his glory, as being a prerogative of divine majesty, communicable to no creature. For it turns no less to God's dishonour to wish to ascribe to another a glory proper to himself, than for another, against his will, to claim it for himself. Indeed it seems more disgraceful to God and foreign to him that what is proper to his majesty should of its own accord yield to another, than that it should be suffered to be seized by another contrary to right, or given by a man to another contrary to his command. For that is to permit idolatry only; but this is to approve it. The former has often happened, and almost universally; the latter never. Therefore what Christ said to that young man, who, not recognising his Deity, yet greeted him most humbly, honouring him with the title of good teacher: "Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, who is God" (Matt. 19. 17), can fittingly be applied to the followers of Socinus, who not only do not acknowledge the Deity of Christ, as that young man did, but altogether deny it, yet still offer him divine worship and demand that all others offer it: "Why do you worship me as God, when you utterly deny my Deity? In your opinion I am a mere man, and not God. But no one deserves the honour due to God except God alone, who has openly professed that he will not give this glory of his to another. Therefore either acknowledge me as God, or do not wish to honour me as God."

units.la: §. 113. 21. Idem in Resp. ad Defens: Fr. Puccii. Tom. 2. p. 273. col. 2. Sentio, inquit, omnia Dogmata, quibuscum Fides in Christum, & Conservatio Præceptorum Dei, consistere non potest, salutem, si retineantur, penitus eripere, & ob eam causam omnino ab omnibus respuenda esse. Quid ergo fiet de permultis Socini Dogmatibus, quae Fidei Christianae adversa comperiuntur; si modo illa habenda sit pro Fide in Christum, quae a Christo & Apostolis Ecclesiae Catholicae tradita fuit, & ab ea semper retenta? Quam bene item convenit Doctrinae Socinianorum de Psychopannychia & totali Impiorum perditione in die Judicii, cum obedientia Fidei, seu Conservatione Præceptorum Dei, cum è contra habenas laxent omnimodæ vitiorum licentiæ?
units.tr: §. 113. 21. The same author, in his Reply to the Defence of Fr. Puccius, vol. 2, p. 273, col. 2: I think that all doctrines with which faith in Christ and the keeping of God's commandments cannot coexist utterly destroy salvation if they are retained, and for that reason must be wholly rejected by everyone. What then will become of very many of Socinus's doctrines, which are found to be contrary to the Christian faith, if that is to be held as faith in Christ which was handed down by Christ and the Apostles to the Catholic Church and always retained by her? How well too does the Socinian doctrine of psychopannychia and of the total destruction of the wicked on the day of judgment agree with obedience to the faith, or the keeping of God's commandments, when on the contrary it loosens the reins to every kind of licence of vice?

units.la: §. 114. 22. Idem agnoscit necessitatem Gratiæ divinæ ad studia nostra dirigenda, mentemque illustrandam in cognitione Rerum divinarum. Sic enim precatur pro Fr. Puccio, in fine Responsi modo dicti —Deus Opt. Max. pro sua Clementia Te nunquam deserat, & studia ac labores tuos ad Ecclesiae suae utilitatem dirigat atque convertat. Pro Coveto pariter — Deum ex animo precor, ut Spiritu suo mentem tuam perfundere, ac sui cognitionis luce collustrare velit. Resp. ad Covetum. Tom. 2. Plura ejusmodi occurrunt in illius Epistolis.
units.tr: §. 114. 22. The same author acknowledges the necessity of divine grace to direct our studies and to illuminate the mind in the knowledge of divine things. For he thus prays for Fr. Puccius at the end of the Reply just mentioned: May God, most good and great, never forsake you in his clemency, but direct and turn your studies and labours to the profit of his Church. Likewise for Covetus: I pray to God from my heart that he may be pleased to pour his Spirit into your mind and illuminate it with the light of his knowledge. Reply to Covetus, vol. 2. Many such things occur in his letters.

units.la: §. 115. Hæc è Socini scriptis habemus, sequuntur alia quædam è Catechismo Racoviensi. 1. De libris Novi Testamenti hæc habet. Quia ab ipsa Christianæ Religionis origine, Christiani omnes, etsi inter se diversi sententiis, in eo tamen concordes & consentientes fuere, Authores scriptorum Novi Testamenti eos fuisse, quos scripta præ se ferunt. Idcirco, qui tam unanimi tot Ætatum & Hominum consensui repugnare vult, hanc justissimam Causam ejus Rei afferre oportet. Recte quidem. At nonne par Ratio valet de iis S. Scripturæ sensibus, & articulis Fidei, & quibuscunque majoris momenti Dogmatibus, in quibus Christiani veteris ævi consenserunt, & hodierni simul consentiunt; præsertim, cum testentur se eadem ab Apostolis accepisse, una cum libris, & Titulis librorum Novi Testamenti ? 2. Inter causas dissidiorum, quæ in eruendo Scripturæ sensu emergunt, hanc postremo adducit, Quod Homines Spiritus S. Donum, quod Deus promisit Dies, noctesque eum invocantibus, non, quo par est, studio, implorent. p. 14.
units.tr: §. 115. These things we have from Socinus's writings; certain other things follow from the Racovian Catechism. 1. On the books of the New Testament it says this: Since from the very origin of the Christian religion all Christians, although they differed among themselves in opinions, agreed and concurred in this, that the authors of the writings of the New Testament were those whom the writings themselves name. Therefore, whoever wishes to oppose such a unanimous consent of so many ages and men must bring forward a most just cause for this. Rightly so, indeed. But does not the same reasoning hold for those senses of Holy Scripture, and articles of faith, and whatever doctrines of greater moment, in which the Christians of the earlier age agreed and in which those of the present day agree as well; especially since they testify that they received the same things from the Apostles, together with the books and the titles of the books of the New Testament? 2. Among the causes of disagreement that arise in drawing out the sense of Scripture, he finally adduces this: that men do not implore the Holy Spirit's gift, which God promised to those invoking him day and night, with the zeal that is fitting. p. 14.

units.la: 3. Cognitio via ad immortalitatem ducentis Rationem humanam longe excedit; uti Apostolus diserte ait, Homo animalis non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. 1 Cor. 2. 14. Per ea vero intelligit, de quibus paulo superius egit, v. 9, 10. Quæ oculus non vidit, nec Auris audivit, nec in Cor Hominis ascenderunt, quæ Deus præparavit diligentibus se, & nobis revelavit per Spiritum suum. Quod & de Immortalitate, & via ad eam tendente accipi, Res ipsa aperte monet. pag. 18.
units.tr: 3. Knowledge that leads to immortality far exceeds human reason; as the Apostle plainly says, the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. 1 Cor. 2. 14. But he understands by those things of which he treated a little above, v. 9, 10: What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him, and has revealed to us through his Spirit. The thing itself plainly warns that this is to be understood also of immortality and of the way leading to it. p. 18.

units.la: 4. Tertiam orationis Dominicæ Petitionem, scil. Fiat voluntas tua, ut in Coelis, sic & in Terra, ita explicat. In hac oratione Deum precamur, ut nobis in obedientia præstanda, quæ ei debetur, & qua vita atque factis exprimenda est, opem afferat. Multum enim opis Homo indiget, ut ea quæ Deus ei, potissimum sub Evangelio mandavit, præstare possit. Sunt enim ea ejusmodi, quæ vires ipsius multis partibus superent. p. 109.
units.tr: 4. He explains the third petition of the Lord's Prayer, namely, Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven, as follows: In this prayer we ask God to bring help to us in rendering the obedience owed to him, which must be expressed in our life and deeds. For man needs much help to be able to perform what God has commanded him, especially under the Gospel. For these are of such a kind that they exceed his strength in many respects. p. 109.

units.la: 5. Eos, qui Christum non invocant, nec adorandum censent, non esse Christianos sentio, cum reipsa Christum non habeant, & licet verbis id negare non audeant, reipsa negent tamen. p. 115. Quid igitur sentiendum de iis, qui ejusdem Christi Deitatem negent, quæ Invocationis & Adorationis istius, qua Christus colitur, fundamentum & causa est? 6. Liberatio nostra per Christum voce Redemptionis exprimitur, quod maxime intervenit similitudo inter eam & Redemptionem proprie sic dictam, viz. Homo captivus; qua Hominem captivum detinent, Peccatum &c.[?] & mundus, Diabolus & mors; Deus & Christus, Captivi Redemptor; Denique Redemptionis Pretium, Ipse Christus, vel anima ipsius à Deo & ipso Christo impensa. Adjicit quidem — Tantum eo differt, quod in nostra hac liberatione, nemo est, qui accipiat aliquid liberationis nomine. Sic ille. p. 185, 186. At nonne hoc sequitur è concessis modo dictis? Num Christus animam suam impendit in Redemptionis pretium, & nemo est qui accipiat hoc pretium sic à Christo impensum? Quomodo ergo tunc Redemptio peragitur? Certè dare & accipere, in hoc Redemptionis negotio, correlativa sunt, & mutuo se inferunt. Sicut ergo nemo proprie accipit, quod non ab aliquo datur; ita nemo proprie & cum effectu dat, quod non ab aliquo accipitur. Ita in hoc opere Redemptionis, pretium illud, quod Christus Dei Filius impendit, Pater accipit. Quod & Scriptura non semel testatur. Redemisti nos Deo per sanguinem. Apoc. 5. 9. Christus semetipsum pro nobis tradidit oblationem & Hostiam Deo, in odorem suaveolentem. Eph. 5. 2. Sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum æternum semetipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo, emundabit conscientiam nostram ab operibus mortuis, ad serviendum Deo viventi. Hebr. 9. 14. Sacrificium & oblationem noluisti, corpus autem adaptasti mihi. Tunc dixi, ecce adsum, ut faciam, O Deus, voluntatem tuam. —Qua voluntate sanctificati sumus, per oblationem corporis Jesu Christi semel factum, Heb. 10. 5,7, 10. Unde sequitur, quod sicut oblationes & sacrificia pro peccato, quæ Deo juxta legem offerebantur, ab eo acceptabantur, ad reatum offerentis tollendum; ita multo magis, corpus istud humanum, quod Deus Pater Filio suo adaptavit, ut offeretur in sacrificium pro peccato, juxta ipsius decretum ac voluntatem ab eo pariter acceptabatur, ad sanctificandum Genus humanum, seu emundandum à Pollutione ista, quam ex peccato contraxerat. Quod & alibi asseritur: Deus fecit, ut is, qui non novit peccatum [id est, Christus?] pro nobis peccatum esset, id est, sacrificium pro peccato. 2 Cor. 5. ult. Christus ipsemet peccata nostra sursum tulit in Corpore suo super lignum. 1 Pet. 2. 24.
units.tr: 5. I do not think those are Christians who do not invoke Christ nor judge him to be worshipped, since in fact they do not have Christ, and although they dare not deny it in words, they nevertheless deny it in fact. p. 115. What then should be thought of those who deny the very Deity of Christ, which is the foundation and cause of that invocation and adoration by which Christ is worshipped? 6. Our liberation through Christ is expressed by the word redemption, in which a likeness especially intervenes between it and redemption properly so called, namely a captive man, whom the captors hold: sin etc. and the world, the Devil and death; God and Christ are the redeemers of captives; and finally the price of redemption is Christ himself, or his soul offered by God and by Christ himself. He does add: It differs only in this, that in our liberation there is no one who receives anything under the name of liberation. Thus he. p. 185, 186. But does not this follow from the concessions just mentioned? Did Christ offer his soul as the price of redemption, and is there no one who receives this price so offered by Christ? How then is redemption accomplished? Surely giving and receiving are correlatives in this business of redemption and imply one another. Just as no one properly receives what is not given by someone, so no one properly and effectively gives what is not received by someone. So in this work of redemption, the Father receives that price which Christ the Son of God offered. Scripture also attests this more than once: You redeemed us to God by your blood. Rev. 5. 9. Christ gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God, as a fragrant odour. Eph. 5. 2. The blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, will cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God. Heb. 9. 14. Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you prepared for me. Then I said, Behold, I come, that I may do your will, O God. By which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ made once for all. Heb. 10. 5, 7, 10. Whence it follows that just as the offerings and sacrifices for sin that were offered to God according to the law were accepted by him, to remove the guilt of the offerer, so much more was that human body, which God the Father prepared for his Son so that it might be offered as a sacrifice for sin, likewise accepted by him according to his own decree and will, to sanctify the human race, or to cleanse it from that pollution which it had contracted through sin. This is also asserted elsewhere: God made him who knew no sin [that is, Christ?] to be sin for us, that is, a sacrifice for sin. 2 Cor. 5, last verse. Christ himself bore our sins up in his body on the tree. 1 Pet. 2. 24.

units.la: 7. Communiter in Hominibus natura, exigua admodum sunt vires, ad ea, quæ Deus ab illis requirit, perficiendum. Nihilominus tamen ea vires non ita prorsus exigua sunt, ut Homo, si vim sibi facere velit, divino auxilio accedente, non posset voluntati Divinæ obsecundare. pag. 197.
units.tr: 7. Commonly in human nature the powers are very small for performing what God requires of them. Nevertheless those powers are not so utterly small that a man, if he is willing to force himself, with divine help coming to him, could not obey the divine will. p. 197.

units.la: 8. Libenter concedimus, neminem esse Hominem, qui voluntate & cursu suo, hoc obtinere potuerit, vel possit, ut Deum ad conferendum aliquod Beneficium in illum moverit. Sic enim Apostolus, non est volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei. Rom. 9. 16. pag. 208.
units.tr: 8. We readily concede that there is no man who, by his will and effort, could have obtained, or could obtain, this, that he moved God to confer some benefit upon him. For so the Apostle says: It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. Rom. 9. 16. p. 208.

units.la: 9. Fateor, Deum interdum quosdam Homines ita à Gratia sua rejicere, ut nec respicere, nec corrigi possint, ut Pharaonem, & Judam. pag. 210.
units.tr: 9. I confess that God sometimes so rejects certain men from his grace that they can neither be regarded nor corrected, as Pharaoh and Judas. p. 210.

units.la: 10. Panca & obscura S. Scripturæ Testimonia, omnino juxta sententiam & plurium & clariorum accipienda sunt. pag. 217.
units.tr: 10. The few and obscure testimonies of Holy Scripture must altogether be taken according to the opinion of the more numerous and clearer ones. p. 217.

units.la: §. 116. Hæc occurrunt in Catechismo Racoviensi. Sequuntur ea, quæ habentur apud Jonam Schlichtingium, in explicatione Symboli. 1. Symbolum, inquit, quod Apostolicum vocatur, antiquissimum esse, ipsamque simplicissimam, qualis ab initio fuit tradita, Apostolicam continere veritatem, à nemine fuit dubitatum. Quae causa nobis fuit, ut cum toti orbi testatum esse vellemus nos ipsi Apostolicæ, & primævæ veritati in omnibus insistere, in edenda hac Ecclesiarum nostrarum confessione, Symboli istius vestigia presso pede sequeremur. Sic ille, Epist. ad lect. p. 3. Bene est, quod extra dubium ponat summam Antiquitatem Symboli hujus, & simplicissimam veritatem ab Apostolis traditam, in ea contineri asserat. Sed oportet praeterea, ut hoc antiquissimum & Apostolicum Symbolum accipiat; non solum quoad verba, sed & sensum eundem, quo vetus Ecclesia illud accepit; alioquin Apostolicæ & primævæ veritati in omnibus neutiquam insistet; cum hæc non in vocibus, sed in rebus consistat. Hunc autem sensum reperire est explicatum in Conciliis antiquis, in Scriptis Patrum, & in iis Fidei Regulis, sive Symbolis isthic occurrentibus, quibus veteres plenius & apertius exposuerunt Fidem ab Apostolis acceptam, contra sui Temporis Hæreticos, & à pravis Ipsorum Glossis, variisque Corruptelis eandem vindicarunt. Equidem Schlichtingius in hoc suo Opusculo, passim citat Testimonia S. Scripturæ, quibus suam Sententiam, in cujusque Articuli explicatione, confirmare nititur. At quam absurdum est, & Rationi absonum, citare Scripturam in suo sensu, vel in sensu veterum Hæreticorum, quos Ecclesia Catholica olim damnavit, contra sensum istum, quem ipsa ab Apostolis, aliisque Ecclesiarum Fundatoribus acceptum, Filiis suis constanter tradidit? Par ratio est de litera S. Scripturæ, quam Hæretici absurdissimi una cum Catholicis, olim retinuerunt, atque adhuc retinent; quorum interim singulae sectae, etiam ipsis Socinianis Judicibus, pro Orthodoxis non habentur.
units.tr: §. 116. These points occur in the Racovian Catechism. What follows is what Jonas Schlichting gives in his explanation of the Creed. 1. The Creed, he says, which is called the Apostles', is very ancient, and no one has ever doubted that its very simple form, as it was handed down from the beginning, contains the Apostolic truth. This was our reason, in publishing this confession of our Churches, for following the footsteps of that Creed closely, since we wished to testify to the whole world that we ourselves hold firmly to the Apostolic and primitive truth in all things. Thus he writes in the Preface to the Reader, p. 3. It is well that he places beyond doubt the great antiquity of this Creed, and asserts that the most simple truth delivered by the Apostles is contained in it. But he ought also to accept this most ancient and Apostolic Creed not only in its words but in the same sense in which the early Church received it. Otherwise he will by no means hold to the Apostolic and primitive truth in all things, since that truth consists not in words but in realities. This sense, however, is to be found explained in the ancient Councils, in the writings of the Fathers, and in those rules of faith, or creeds, that occur there, in which the ancients set out more fully and clearly the faith received from the Apostles, against the heretics of their own time, and defended it against their perverse glosses and various corruptions. Indeed, Schlichting in this little work of his repeatedly cites passages of Holy Scripture by which he tries to confirm his own opinion in the explanation of each article. But how absurd and contrary to reason it is to cite Scripture in his own sense, or in the sense of the old heretics whom the Catholic Church long ago condemned, against that sense which she herself received from the Apostles and the other founders of the Churches and has constantly handed down to her children! The same reasoning applies to the letter of Holy Scripture, which the most absurd heretics have retained along with the Catholics, both formerly and still now; yet individual sects of them are not regarded as orthodox, even by the Socinian judges themselves.

units.la: §. 117. 2. De Spiritu Sancto hæc habet. Primi ipsi Christiani in Spiritum Sanctum tanquam in Divinum Ecclesiæ Doctorem, credendum esse dixerunt; quod rectissime fieri agnoscimus. Ib. p. 6. Adjicit quidem, sed perperam — Eo ipso tamen, dum eum in Rerum, quæ Persona non sunt, Censum referunt, sese de Spiritu Sancto, usitatissima figura, loqui innuerunt. At è contra, ex omni historia Ecclesiastica constat, Spiritum Sanctum habitum fuisse pro tertia S. S. Triadis Persona, à cunctis[?] Catholicis, contrariamque Sententiam, ut hæreticam, in Eunomio, Macedonio, aliisque Pneumatomachis condemnatam fuisse. Et ipsum Doctoris nomen, quem veteres illi tribuerunt, & Schlichtingius approbat, idem denotat, si vox proprie accipiatur. Interdum quidem, S. Scriptura præeunte, de Spiritu Sancto figurative loquuntur, prout accipitur pro Dono, seu effectu Spiritus Sancti, pro Afflatu seu virtute Dei; sed quoties proprie loquuntur (quod apud eos multo usitatius est) Personam semper indigitant. Quod etiam in Symbolis antiquis manifeste cernitur. Cum itaque Schlichtingius hic affirmat, Veteres Spiritum Sanctum retulisse in Censum Rerum, quæ Personæ non sunt, non solum gratis dictum est, sed & gravissima Calumnia, in favorem sectæ suæ conficta. Idem postea licet asserat Spiritum Sanctum esse Nihil Aliud, quam Afflatum Dei, Virtutem Dei & efficaciam, Medium seu Instrumentum divinum, quod à voluntate divina regitur; & virtutem Altissimi, prout ab Angelo Gabriele appellatur. Luc. 1. 35. Cogitur tamen ibidem, istiusmodi Titulis Ipsum adornare, quæ Personæ soli proprie competunt, ut cum eum appellat, veritatis Evangelica, una cum Patre & Filio, cœlestem Authorem, & Magistrum, & Ducem, & Testem. Ideo, inquit, & in Nomen illum, sicut in Patris & Filii, tincti, initiatique sumus. Nam sicut Pater misit Filium de Cœlo, sic Filius in Cœlum prosectus, sui loco misit Spiritum Sanctum, in quo veluti Redux Orbi universo Evangelicam prædicavit veritatem. Illum quoque vocat legatum Christi fidelem, qui Nihil à seipso loquitur, sed quodcunque audit, Id loquitur; Paracletum item, & Advocatum, Ecclesiæ suæ datum. Hæc, aliaque Plura, quæ ex Evangelio ut plurimum collecta una congerit in explicatione Articuli de Spiritu Sancto, non nisi Personæ proprie attribui possunt; neque aliquam Causam isthic loci assignat, quæ cogat nos in locum proprii sensus figurativum supponere.
units.tr: §. 117. 2. On the Holy Spirit he holds this: The first Christians themselves said that the Holy Spirit is to be believed in as the divine Teacher of the Church; and we acknowledge that this is done most rightly. Ibid., p. 6. He does add, but wrongly: Yet by the very fact that they place him among the things which are not persons, they indicate that they are speaking of the Holy Spirit by a very common figure. On the contrary, it is clear from all ecclesiastical history that the Holy Spirit was regarded by all Catholics as the third Person of the Holy Trinity, and that the opposite opinion was condemned as heretical in Eunomius, Macedonius and the other Pneumatomachi. Even the title of Teacher, which the ancients gave him and Schlichting approves, means the same thing, if the word is taken properly. Indeed, sometimes, following Holy Scripture, they speak of the Holy Spirit figuratively, as when it is taken for the gift or effect of the Holy Spirit, for the breath or power of God; but whenever they speak properly (which is much more common among them) they always designate a Person. This is also clearly seen in the ancient creeds. Therefore, when Schlichting here affirms that the ancients counted the Holy Spirit among the things which are not persons, this is not only said without warrant but is also a most grievous calumny, invented in favour of his sect. Afterwards, although he asserts that the Holy Spirit is nothing other than the breath of God, the power and efficacy of God, a divine means or instrument which is governed by the divine will; and the power of the Most High, as the Angel Gabriel calls it, Luke 1. 35, he is nevertheless compelled in the same place to adorn him with titles which belong properly to a Person alone, as when he calls him, together with the Father and the Son, the heavenly Author, Teacher, Leader and Witness of the Evangelical truth. Therefore, he says, we have also been baptized and initiated into his name, as into the name of the Father and the Son. For just as the Father sent the Son from heaven, so the Son, having gone away into heaven, sent the Holy Spirit in his place, and through him, as one returning, proclaimed the Evangelical truth to the whole world. He also calls him the faithful envoy of Christ, who does not speak of himself but says whatever he hears; likewise the Paraclete and the Advocate given to his Church. These and many other things, which he gathers together from the Gospel in his explanation of the article on the Holy Spirit, can only properly be attributed to a Person; nor does he assign any reason in that place which would compel us to suppose a figurative sense in place of the proper one.

units.la: §. 118. 3. De plenitudine Symboli ita differit — Symbolum hoc omnia, quæ ad Christianam Fidem, & sic ad æterna Salutis adeptionem requiruntur, continere, vel inde patet, quod antiquitus ad hæc usque Tempora in omnibus Christianorum Ecclesiis usu receptum fuit, eos qui Ecclesiæ per Baptismum aggregantur, non de aliis quam de Symboli ipsius articulis, interrogare; & si ad Omnia in hoc Symbolo expressa interrogati annuerint, eosdem in Christianum Nomen cooptare. Qui mos nunquam in Ecclesiis invaluisset, nisi jam olim creditum fuisset ipsius Symboli professionem plenam esse & genuinam Christianismi Tesseram.
units.tr: §. 118. 3. On the fullness of the Creed he argues thus: That this Creed contains all that is required for the Christian faith, and so for the attainment of eternal salvation, is evident from this alone: that from ancient times down to the present day it has been the custom in all Christian Churches to question those who are admitted into the Church by baptism about nothing but the articles of this very Creed; and if they assent to being questioned on all that is expressed in this Creed, they are enrolled under the name of Christian. This custom would never have taken hold in the Churches unless it had long been believed that the profession of this Creed was full and the genuine badge of Christianity.

units.la: Sic Ille in præf. p. 7, 8. Recte quidem, contra Pontificios, & siqui sunt alii, qui Articulos Fidei multiplicant, post Fidem hanc ab Apostolis receptam, & ab origine Ecclesiæ traditam. At cum ex. hinc infert Quam cum unicam Ecclesia nostra agnoscant, non ulla Alia magis quam ista Christianum Nomen & Titulum usurpare debent Fraudulenter agit, Conclusionem inferendo contra veritatem, quæ sibi ignota esse non potuit; nimirum, quod illi, cæterique suæ sectæ Homines Verba duntaxat Symboli hujus antiqui admittant, at minime illud interpretentur juxta sensum Antiquorum; quem igitur quamdiu rejiciunt, & suum ex adverso in locum illius substituunt, quo jure expectant, ut in Ecclesiam Catholicam admittantur, & pro genuinis Ipsius Filiis agnoscantur? Ignorare item non potuit, quod vetus Ecclesia coacta fuerit non semel explicare hoc Symbolum in Synodis, sensumque genuinum afferere contra varias Hæreticorum ccrruptelas, quos & in iisdem Synodus damnavit, & à sua Communione prorsus abscidit. Qua fronte igitur postulant Sociniani, ut præ cæteris Ecclesiis Christianum nomen & Titulum sibi vendicent, eo quod Symbolum hoc verbo tenus agnoscant, cum Fidem ipsam Verbis istis contentam, Christique Fidelibus commendatam reapse negent, quantum ad plures Articulos, contra sensum Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, tum veteris tum hodiernæ? Quo jure se Catholicos existimari petunt ab Aliis, vel etiam censeri æquum putant à suis, quamdiu. Tales manent? Non alio sane, quam sectæ cujusque Generis, quæ Christianismum ore tenus profitentur & S. Literas (in quibus hujus Symboli Articuli continentur) pro verbo Dei habent, pro genuinis Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Filiis haberi postulant, cum interea istas literas in sensus malesanos & hæreticos detorqueant, quibus Fidem Catholicam fædissime corrumpunt.
units.tr: Thus he writes in the Preface, pp. 7, 8. Rightly indeed, against the Papists, and any others who multiply the articles of faith beyond this faith received from the Apostles and handed down from the origin of the Church. But when he infers from this, Since our Church acknowledges this as the only one, they ought to claim the Christian name and title on no other ground than this, he acts deceitfully, drawing a conclusion contrary to the truth, which cannot have been unknown to him. Namely, that they and the other men of his sect admit only the words of this ancient Creed, but by no means interpret it according to the sense of the ancients. As long as they reject that sense and put their own in its place, by what right do they expect to be admitted into the Catholic Church and acknowledged as genuine sons of it? Nor can he have failed to know that the ancient Church was compelled more than once to explain this Creed in Synods, and to assert its genuine sense against the various corruptions of the heretics, whom the same Synods condemned and cut off entirely from their communion. With what face, then, do the Socinians demand that they should claim the Christian name and title before all other Churches, on the ground that they acknowledge this Creed in its bare words, when in fact they deny the faith contained in those words and commended to the faithful of Christ, as regards many articles, against the sense of the Catholic Church, both ancient and modern? By what right do they ask to be considered Catholics by others, or think it fair to be counted so by their own people, as long as they remain such as they are? Clearly by no other right than that of any sect whatsoever, which professes Christianity with its lips, holds the Scriptures (in which the articles of this Creed are contained) to be the word of God, and yet twists those writings into mad and heretical senses by which it foully corrupts the Catholic faith, and yet demands to be regarded as genuine sons of the Catholic Church.

units.la: §. 119. 4. S. Scriptura Canonica apud nos haud dubia est Authoritas, p. 9. Verissime quidem. Sed quo certo Judicio Scripturam Canonicam à libris Apocryphis distinguere norunt? Nonne ad hoc Discrimen instituendum, necesse est adhibere Testimonium atque Judicium Ecclesiæ Catholicæ? Cur ergo recusant Ejusdem Testimonio atque Judicio inniti in Canonico S. Scripturæ sensu tradendo, eundemque discriminando à quovis sensu spurio & apocrypho?
units.tr: §. 119. 4. Holy Scripture, the Canon, is among us an undoubted authority, p. 9. Most truly indeed. But by what sure judgement do they know how to distinguish the canonical Scripture from the apocryphal books? Is it not necessary, in order to make this distinction, to employ the testimony and judgement of the Catholic Church? Why, then, do they refuse to rest on the testimony and judgement of that same Church in delivering the canonical sense of Scripture, and in distinguishing it from every spurious and apocryphal sense?

units.la: §. 120. 5. De expiatione nostrorum Peccatorum per Christi sanguinem ita disserit.
