Christus sacratissimum suum sanguinem effudit, tanquam victima piacularis, pro peccatis nostris, ut illa, tam præstanti, & prorsus eximio, Deoque acceptissimo sacto suo interveniente, penitus expiaret & de illorum expiatione at remissione, æternaque salute, nos plane certos redderet; quandoquidem per propriam sanguinis sui effusionem introivit in illa Sancta cælestia, ut sese, tanquam magnum sacerdos coram Dei vultu offerret, coram illo appareat, interpelletque pro nobis. Sic ille, p. 60. & postea. Si Christus posuerit Animam suam peccatum (id est victimam pro peccato) videbit semen &c. Isa. 53. 10. Idem docent omnia Scriptura loca, in quibus sanguini Christi peccatorum nostrorum expiatio & Remissio tribuitur, Christique sanguis cum Victimis expiatoriis confertur, vel Christus per sanguinem suum in cælestie[?] Tabernaculum, ad expianda peccata nostra, ingressus esse dicitur. Sic ille, p. 65. unde bene concludi potest, Christum satisfecisse Deo pro peccatis nostris per sanguinis sui effusionem; sive Christi sanguinem sic effusum ad remissionem peccatorum à Deo impetrandam, fuisse Pretium ab illo acceptatum. Siquidem victimæ piaculares sub lege Mosaica, Deo satisfaciebant, ejusque iram placabant pro peccato contra legem admisso, illius reatum tollendo. Deinde si Factum hoc Christi, in sanguine suo effundendo pro nostris peccatis fuerit Deo acceptissimum, ergo Pretium hujus sanguinis, ut a Christo oblatum fuit, sic & a Deo in hunc finem acceptum fuit. Sin acceptum non fuit ad hunc finem consequendum, quomodo Christus per hanc sanguinis sui effusionem nos certos reddere posset, de peccatorum nostrorum expiatione atque remissione, & de aeterna salute, quas hoc pacto nobis acquisivisse dicitur? Quomodo demum magnus hic sacerdos, per victimam hanc piacularem, & sibi & nobis Aditum patefecit in caelestè Tabernaculum, si minime Deo grata fuerit, & in eum finem accepta quo salutem nostram in Coelo perficeret?
units.tr: §. 120. 5. On the expiation of our sins through the blood of Christ he argues as follows. Christ poured out his most sacred blood as a propitiatory victim for our sins, so that by this act, which is most excellent and altogether remarkable and most acceptable to God, he might completely expiate them, and might make us entirely certain of their expiation and remission and of eternal salvation. For by the outpouring of his own blood he entered into those holy heavenly places, that he might present himself as a great priest before the face of God, appear before him, and intercede for us. Thus he, p. 60, and afterwards. If Christ shall have made his soul a sin offering (that is, a victim for sin), he shall see his seed, etc. Isa. 53. 10. All the passages of Scripture teach the same thing, in which the expiation and remission of our sins are ascribed to the blood of Christ, and the blood of Christ is compared with the expiatory victims, or Christ is said to have entered the heavenly tabernacle through his own blood to expiate our sins. Thus he, p. 65. From this it can well be concluded that Christ satisfied God for our sins by the outpouring of his blood; or that the blood of Christ so shed was accepted by God as a price for obtaining the remission of sins. For under the Mosaic law the propitiatory victims made satisfaction to God and appeased his wrath for a sin committed against the law, removing its guilt. Next, if this deed of Christ, in pouring out his blood for our sins, was most acceptable to God, then the price of this blood, as it was offered by Christ, was also accepted by God for this purpose. But if it was not accepted to achieve this end, how could Christ, by this outpouring of his blood, make us certain of the expiation and remission of our sins and of eternal salvation, which he is said to have acquired for us in this way? Lastly, how could this great priest, through this propitiatory victim, have opened the way for both himself and us into the heavenly tabernacle, if it had not been pleasing to God and accepted to the end that he might bring our salvation to completion in heaven?

units.la: §. 121. 6. Idem sic explicat Articulum Symboli nonum, de Ecclesia Catholica. Credimus Christianos Ecclesiam, id est, congregationem visibilem constituere debere, eamque sanctam, non civilem, credimus eandem debere esse Catholicam seu universalem, id est, non uni alicui populo astrictam, ut sit Judaica, sed omnibus populis communem; nec Doctrina & Fide variam, sed ubique & omni Tempore, initio ab Apostolis facto, unius ejusdemque Doctrinae & Fidei; istius nempe, quae Symbolo hoc comprehensa est; ut qui hanc retineat, vere sit Catholicus; qui vero Contrarii aut alieni quippiam admisceat, hactenus Catholicus esse non possit. In hanc igitur Sanctam Ecclesiam Catholicam credimus, quia haec omnia, quae Christiani, sanctis moribus dediti, semper & ubique professi sunt, pro veris & indubitatis agnoscimus. pag. 113. unde concludimus fuisse, & esse, & semper fore visibilem Christianorum Ecclesiam; nec uni Genti, nec uni alicui sectæ astrictam, quæ sibi soli Ecclesiæ Christianæ nomen arrogare velit; eandem quoque retinere Doctrinam istam atque Fidem Catholicam, quam Apostoli ubique prædicarunt, & Ecclesiis à se fundatis, sacerrimi Depositi loco, tuendam commendarunt; Catholicos esse, qui hanc integram servant & inviolatam; Hæreticos autem, qui adversi quidpiam, aut alieni intermiscent. Denique in Ecclesiam Catholicam eo usque credendum esse, ut pro veris & indubitatis omnia ista habeamus, quæ semper & ubique professa est. Postulamus itaque à Socinianis, ut sua Dogmata ad hanc Regulam per-pendant; tunc enim, vel ea abdicare cogentur, vel haud ægre ferent, si minus in Censum Catholicorum ascribantur.
units.tr: §. 121. 6. He explains in the same way the ninth article of the Creed, on the Catholic Church. We believe that Christians must constitute the Church, that is, a visible congregation, and that it must be holy, not civil. We believe that it must be Catholic or universal, that is, not bound to any one people, so as to be Jewish, but common to all peoples; nor varied in doctrine and faith, but everywhere and at all times, from the beginning made by the Apostles, of one and the same doctrine and faith, namely that which is comprehended in this Creed; so that whoever holds to it is truly Catholic, but whoever mixes in anything contrary or foreign cannot be Catholic so far. We therefore believe in this holy Catholic Church, because we acknowledge as true and indubitable all those things which Christians, devoted to holy morals, have always and everywhere professed. p. 113. From this we conclude that there has been, and is, and always will be a visible Church of Christians; not bound to one nation or to any one sect, which would wish to claim the name of the Christian Church for itself alone; that it also holds that same Catholic doctrine and faith which the Apostles preached everywhere, and which they commended to the churches founded by them, to be guarded as a most sacred deposit; that those are Catholics who keep this whole and inviolate, and those are heretics who mix in anything contrary or foreign. Finally, we must believe in the Catholic Church to such an extent that we hold as true and indubitable all those things which she has always and everywhere professed. We therefore demand of the Socinians that they weigh their dogmas by this rule; for then they will either be compelled to renounce them, or will bear it without much grief if they are not counted among the Catholics.

units.la: §. 122. 7. Idem ad Sanctorum Communionem hæc requirit. Credimus unumquemque, qui salvus esse vult, debere cum Sanctis istis, id est, Discipulis Christi Sanctam habere Conversationem, & Rerum sanctarum, quæ Christianam Pietatem constituunt, communionem. Porro, Res istæ sanctæ sunt, Fides, confessio, pænitentia, Baptismus Aquæ, sacrorum conventuum diligens frequentatio, eucharistiæ celebratio, item Fructus & Opera Fidei ac Pænitentiæ, & Spiritus Sancti, post Fidem ac Pænitentiam, divino munere, in Christianis habitantis, sc. perfecta Charitas, sanctaque, omnemque civilem Honestatem exuperans, vitæ conversatio, veraque Regeneratio, sine quibus Fides est infmilis[?] & mortua. p. 117. ubi agnoscit necefsitatem duorum Sacramentorum, sc. Baptismi, & Eucharistiæ; & opus Regenerationis, una cum Dono Charitatis, gratiæ Spiritus Sancti attribuit.
units.tr: §. 122. 7. He requires the same concerning the communion of the saints. We believe that everyone who wishes to be saved must have holy conversation with those saints, that is, the disciples of Christ, and communion in the holy things which constitute Christian piety. Now these holy things are faith, confession, repentance, the baptism of water, diligent attendance at sacred assemblies, the celebration of the Eucharist; likewise the fruits and works of faith and repentance, and the Spirit of God, dwelling in Christians after faith and repentance by divine gift, namely perfect charity, and a holy way of life which surpasses all civic decency, and true regeneration, without which faith is weak and dead. p. 117. Here he acknowledges the necessity of the two sacraments, namely Baptism and the Eucharist, and ascribes the work of regeneration, together with the gift of charity, to the grace of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: §. 123. 8. Efficaciam Baptismi his Verbis agnoscit — Quicunque salvus esse vult, Baptismum Aqua Jubire debet, ut per eum Christo initietur, & Ecclesiæ inferatur, & per sacrum hoc lavacrum peccata præterita abluat, nec carnis deponat sordes, nudam tantum Ceremoniam Corpore obeundo, sed id quod illa denotat, & cujus causa est instituta, Animo perageudo, & opere deinceps exequendo, bonæ Conscientiæ Interrogationem in Deum obtineat, per Resurrectionem Jesu Christi. p. 118.
units.tr: §. 123. 8. He acknowledges the efficacy of baptism in these words: Whoever wishes to be saved must submit to baptism with water, so that through it he may be initiated into Christ and joined to the Church, and through this holy washing may wash away his past sins; and not put off the filth of the flesh merely by performing the bare ceremony with the body, but by carrying out in his mind what it signifies and for which it was instituted, and by afterwards working it out in deed, he may obtain a good conscience towards God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. p. 118.

units.la: §. 124. 9. Eucharistiæ quoque effectus ita describit, dum ista Apostoli verba exponit. Panis iste, quem frangimus, Communio Corporis Christi est, & Calix Benedictionis, cui benedicimus, Communio Sanguinis Christi est. 1 Cor. 10. 16[?]. h.e. inquit, id, per quod communicamus ipsi Corpori & sanguini Christi. Nam cum ex uno Pane omnes participemus, fit, ut unus Panis, & unum Corpus simus, id est, Communione ac societate inter nos copulemur, (qui alter istius sacri Ritus finis est.) Cum vero hic Panis Corpori Christi, illiusque memoriæ unice sacratus sit, sit, ut ei Communicantes, ipsi Corpori Christi communicemus, tantoque sanctius & arctius inter nos conjungamur; non secus atque illi, qui victimas comedebant, altaris, & qui Idolothyta, Dæmoniis communicabant, quod victima altari consecrata essent. Idolothyta Dæmonii immolarentur. pag. 119.
units.tr: §. 124. 9. He also describes the effect of the Eucharist, while expounding these words of the Apostle. The bread which we break is the communion of the body of Christ, and the cup of blessing which we bless is the communion of the blood of Christ. 1 Cor. 10. 16[?]. That is, he says, that by which we communicate in the very body and blood of Christ. For since we all partake of one bread, it comes about that we are one bread and one body, that is, we are joined together in communion and fellowship among ourselves, which is the other purpose of this sacred rite. But since this bread is consecrated solely to the body of Christ and to its remembrance, it follows that by partaking of it we communicate in the very body of Christ, and are joined together among ourselves all the more holily and closely; just as those who ate the sacrifices were partakers of the altar, and those who ate things offered to idols communicated with demons, because the victims had been consecrated to the altar. The things offered to idols were sacrificed to demons. p. 119.

units.la: §. 125. 10. De Remissione peccatorum hæc asserit. — Credimus omnia præterita, quamvis gravissima, Peccata; omnesque etiam, post agnitam veritatem, intercurrentis humanæ imbecillitatis lapsu, omnibus Sanctorum, quam diximus, Communionem habentibus, per obedientiam, & sanguinem, & Oblationem Jesu Christi, plenissime remisit; eoque hac Ratione non ex legis operibus, propriisque meritis, sed sine illis ex Dei Gratia justificari. Quæ quidem Remissio peccatorum, ac Justificatio, fide & Pœnitentia, ex parte nostra, comparatur, Fidei vero & Pœnitentia fructibus, conservatur. pag. 123, 124.
units.tr: §. 125. 10. On the remission of sins he asserts the following. We believe that God has most fully forgiven all past sins, however grievous, and also all those lapses of human weakness that intervene after the truth has been recognised, to all who have, as we have said, communion with the saints, through the obedience, blood and offering of Jesus Christ; and so we believe that in this way they are justified by the grace of God, not by the works of the law or by their own merits, but without them. This remission of sins and justification indeed is obtained on our part by faith and repentance, but it is preserved by the fruits of faith and repentance. p. 123, 124.

units.la: §. 126. 11. Mihi agnoscere quoque videtur ejusdem numero Corporis Resurrectionem, dum ista Scripturæ loca citat, in confirmationem hujus articuli quæ illud plane demonstrant. viz. Jo. 6. 39, 40. Rom. 8. 11. & 8. 23. 1 Cor. 15. 29, 30, 32, 42, 43, 44. 2 Cor. 5. 1, 4. Phil. 3. 20, 21. Quid enim proprie dicitur resurgere, nisi quod prius cecidit; aut resuscitari, nisi quod antea mortis somno quasi sepultum jacuit? Idem quod seminatur, non autem alterum aliquod semen, exsurgit in segetem. Si Christus surrexit in eodem corpore, & nos pariter, qui habemus eundem Spiritum vivificum, in nobis habitantem, cujus virtute mortalia nostra Corpora vivificabuntur. Christus servator noster, ut ait Apostolus, transformabit Corpus nostrum humile, ut fiat conforme Corpori suo glorioso. Ergo est idem corpus humile quoad substantiam, quod ita transformatur; licet forma seu species externa immutetur. Quod & alibi ab eo clarius asseritur, oportet hoc corruptibile induere Incorruptionem, & hoc mortale induere Immortalitatem. 1 Cor. 15. 53. Ergo corpora hæc nostra de novo vestientur, non illorum loco nova substituentur. Equidem caro & sanguis Regnum Dei hæreditare non possunt, id est, corruptibilis caro & sanguis, ut Apostolus ibidem sensum suum explicat, cum statim adjicit, – Neque corruptio hæreditat Incorruptionem. Et sane, si Corpora istorum, qui vivi deprehendentur in Domini nostri Adventu, immutabuntur folum (ut istic asseritur) remanebunt autem quoad substantiam, par ratio valebit de corporibus mortuorum, ex hypothesi quod Deus potentiæ suæ vires, Justitiæque suæ æquitatem, erga utrosque pariter exercere velit, in suorum corporibus glorificandis; de quo non est, quod ambigamus.
units.tr: §. 126. 11. It seems to me that he also acknowledges the resurrection of the same body, when he cites these passages of Scripture in confirmation of this article, which clearly prove it, namely Jo. 6. 39, 40. Rom. 8. 11. & 8. 23. 1 Cor. 15. 29, 30, 32, 42, 43, 44. 2 Cor. 5. 1, 4. Phil. 3. 20, 21. For what is properly meant by rising again, except that which previously fell; or by being raised, except that which previously lay as if buried in the sleep of death? That which is sown rises up as a crop, and it is the same thing that is sown, not some other seed. If Christ rose in the same body, so too shall we, who have the same life-giving Spirit dwelling in us, by whose power our mortal bodies will be made alive. Christ our Saviour, as the Apostle says, will transform our lowly body so that it becomes conformed to his glorious body. Therefore it is the same lowly body, as to substance, which is so transformed, although its form or outward appearance is changed. This he asserts even more clearly elsewhere: this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. 1 Cor. 15. 53. Therefore these our bodies will be clothed anew; new ones will not be substituted in their place. Indeed, flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, that is, corruptible flesh and blood, as the Apostle explains his own meaning in the same place, when he immediately adds: Neither does corruption inherit incorruption. And certainly, if the bodies of those who are found alive at the coming of our Lord are only changed (as is asserted there), but remain as to substance, the same reasoning will hold for the bodies of the dead, on the hypothesis that God wishes to display equally towards both the powers of his might and the equity of his justice in glorifying the bodies of his people; about which there is no reason for us to doubt.

units.la: §. 127. Hæc è Schlichtingio in Symbolum. Restant adjicienda, quæ reperire est apud Joachimum Stegmannum in libello de Judice & norma Controversiarum Fidei. 1. Appellamus, inquit, ad Judicium omnium, qui sana Ratione utuntur, etiam Adversariorum. Act. 4. 19. 1 Cor. 10. 15. Idcirco, nisi putet alios omnes, qui ipsorum Dogmata, post accuratum examen adhibitum damnarunt, sana ratione omnino destitutos esse, necesse est, ut ipse, suaeque sectae Homines, eadem quoque damnent. At si Rationem sanam ipsorum propriam esse velint, Cæteris omnibus exclusis, nec modestiam certe sapit, nec sanam Rationem.
units.tr: §. 127. These things are taken from Schlichting on the Creed. There remain to be added those things which may be found in Joachim Stegmann's booklet on the Judge and the Norm of Controversies of Faith. 1. "We appeal," he says, "to the judgment of all who use sound reason, even of the adversaries." Acts 4. 19; 1 Cor. 10. 15. Therefore, unless he thinks that all the others who have condemned their doctrines after a careful examination are wholly destitute of sound reason, he must necessarily condemn the same doctrines himself, along with his people. But if they want sound reason to be their own, with all others excluded, this savours neither of modesty nor of sound reason.

units.la: §. 128. 2. Inter principia maxime Generalia, atque certa, ab eo recensetur —Communis illa Fides, quam tum viri graves, tum consentientia Historiarum Monumenta, constansque fama publica, apud omnes merentur. Talia enim inficiari nemo audet, nisi qui ipsum hoc universum velit evertere. Recte quidem. Ergo & ipsi fidem adhibeant iis, quæ veteres Ecclesiæ Doctores, Historici Ecclesiastici, atque synodorum testantur de Ecclesiæ primitivæ Doctrina, de Traditione Apostolica, & de novellis Hæreticorum Dogmatibus, contra Fidem Catholicam tunc temporis exortis, & unanimi Ecclesiæ sententia condemnatis.
units.tr: §. 128. 2. Among the most general and certain principles he counts "that common faith which grave men, the consenting monuments of histories, and constant public report deserve from everyone. For no one dares to deny such things, except one who wishes to overturn this whole universe itself." Rightly so. Therefore let them also give credence to what the ancient Doctors of the Church, the ecclesiastical historians, and the synods bear witness to concerning the doctrine of the primitive Church, the apostolic tradition, and the new doctrines of heretics which arose at that time against the Catholic faith and were condemned by the unanimous judgment of the Church.

units.la: §. 129. 3. Judex est, qui recte explicat Scripturam, & ex ea colligit. Hoc quidem verissime. Sed quis sententiam feret de hoc Judice, an recte explicet hanc Scripturam, & ex ea rite colligat? Num ipsi soli, an orbis Christianus, qui ex adverso stat?
units.tr: §. 129. 3. "The judge is one who rightly explains Scripture and draws conclusions from it." This is most true. But who will pass judgment on this judge, whether he rightly explains this Scripture and rightly draws conclusions from it? Is it he alone, or the Christian world, which stands against him?

units.la: §. 130. 4. Totius Ecclesiae, aut praecipuorum ejus membrorum, sive extra Concilium, sive in Concilio congregatorum; seu id à Papa approbatum sit, seu non sit; tantum abest, ut aspernentur (Socinianī[?] sc.) aut contemnant Judicium, ut facilius & certius multos, quam seorsim singulos; Doctos praesertim, quam simpliciores, quid verum falsumve sit, discernere ac dijudicare posse censeant; modo omnes illi sanam Rationem, & animum ab affectibus, seu Partium, opinionumque praeconceptarum studio liberum, in Judicium adhibeant. Plus enim vident oculi, quam oculus, & quod unum effugit, multorum sedulitatem & industriam fallere vix potest. Hinc sequitur, Socinianos submittere se debere Ecclesiae Catholicae Judicio in rebus ad Fidem spectantibus; necnon, Synodorum decretis, quae ab Ecclesia approbata sunt; Denique, tot Theologorum doctissimorum sententiae, qui illorum Placitis Haeresis notam inusserunt; nisi dicere velint, eos omnes sanae Rationis expertes esse, & à pravis affectibus, insano Partium studio, & opinionibus praeconceptis eo usque in transversum abreptos, ut prorsus inepti sint ad Judicium indifferenter ac libere ferendum. Quod non minus sanae Rationi, quam Christianae Charitati adversatur.
units.tr: §. 130. 4. Of the whole Church, or of its principal members, whether gathered outside a council or within one, and whether or not the judgment has been approved by the Pope, the Socinians (sc.) are so far from scorning or despising it that they think many people can discern and decide what is true or false more easily and more certainly than single individuals, and learned people more than simpler ones, provided all of them bring sound reason to the judgment and a mind free from passions, and from the zeal of parties and preconceived opinions. For eyes see more than an eye, and what escapes one person can hardly deceive the diligence and industry of many. Hence it follows that the Socinians must submit themselves to the judgment of the Catholic Church in matters pertaining to faith; likewise to the decrees of synods which the Church has approved; and finally to the opinions of so many most learned theologians who have branded their tenets with the mark of heresy; unless they wish to say that all of these are without sound reason, and are dragged so far across by depraved passions, insane zeal for parties, and preconceived opinions that they are wholly unfit to pass judgment impartially and freely. This is no less contrary to sound reason than to Christian charity.

units.la: §. 131. 5. An aliquis in Ecclesiae gremium admittendus; aut, si in Ecclesia fuerit, an ejiciendus sit? Ecclesia sive judicio, sive arbitrio subjectum est. p. 35. ubi authoritatem Ecclesiae agnoscit in exercitio Disciplinae suae, quantum ad membrorum suorum admissionem, vel ejectionem, prout illi visum fuerit; & consequenter, in repellendis, vel expellendis Hæreticis, quales Sociniani sunt ex ipsius Judicio. Itaque, nihil est, quod querantur de Ecclesia, cum hanc Disciplinæ suæ Partem erga eos exercet.
units.tr: §. 131. 5. "Is anyone to be admitted into the bosom of the Church, or, if he is already in the Church, is he to be cast out? The Church is subject to judgment or to discretion." p. 35, where he acknowledges the authority of the Church in exercising its discipline, as regards the admission or expulsion of its members, as it sees fit; and consequently in repelling or expelling heretics, such as the Socinians are by his own judgment. Therefore they have no cause to complain of the Church when it exercises this part of its discipline towards them.

units.la: §. 132. 6.Non vult unumquemque esse Judicem in iis, quæ ad Religionem pertinent ut, quidvis pro libitu statuat, sine ulla reverentia Ecclesiæ aut Reipublicæ; aut sine metu Turbarum —Tantum abest, inquit, ut Ecclesia abjicere respectum liceat, ut potius qua Ratione quisque legitimum Ecclesiæ membrum fi-at, vel maneat, acri Judicio inquirendum sit. p. 52. Cur itaque Socinus unumquemque suo arbitrio relinquit in Rebus Theologicis, ut de iis, prout sibi visum fuerit, statuat? Cur ille, una cum Sociis ac Discipulis, Catholicam Ecclesiam adeo vilipendit, & illius Judicium suo postponit, imo contemptim rejicit, perinde ac si nihil omnino valeret? Cur non Schismata passim excitavit in Ecclesiis Polonicis, aliisque vicinis, & Conventicula nescio quot suorum contra leges ubique coegit, quibus necesse erat Rempublicam quoque conturbari; sed & potestatem atque Jura Magistratus Politici diminuere tentavit, in Resp. ad Palæologi librum de magistratu? Qua de Causa cum seditionis postularetur apud Stephanum Batoreum Poloniæ Regem, Cracovia discedere coactus est, & in ædi-bus Christophori Morstinii Paulicovii Domini Refugium quærere? Cur item Socinus neminem solicitum esse vult de hoc, ut exquirat, quænam sit illa vera Christi Ecclesia, ad quam se conferre debeat veritatis inquirendæ, & salutis comparandæ Causa; sed unumquemque privatum Sacræ Scripturæ Interpretem constituit, & genuini sensus arbitrum? Cur demum hic ipse Stegmannus paulo post sibiipsi in hoc contradicit, cum ait ——Non tantum norma nobis (cumprimis autem divina litera) fatis clare & perspicue proposita est, sed & vires seu facultates sufficientes concessa sunt, ut si modo velimus, & animum intendimus) dijudicare possimus, utrum, & quo in errore haereamus; quidque verum atque sequendum; & contra, quid falsum, atque sugiendum, dignoscere. Quod si ita sit, quomodo fit, ut tot Ingeniosi, & eruditi, & industrii veritatis inquisitores, ad eam tamen non pertingant, sed in errorum Devia diversimode abducantur? cujus luculentum Judicium est, Contrarietas illa, quam cernimus in illorum Interpretationibus, & sententiis. Idcirco necesse est, ut hujusce Defectus Cau-sam alibi quaeramus; nempe, in neglectu mediorum istiusmodi, quae Deus nobis utenda proposuit subsidio ad veritatem exquirendam; qualia sunt Traditio Catholica, Consensus Patrum, Judicium praesentis Ecclesiae, externa; & Gratia Spiritus Sancti interius illuminans; quam Oftorodus haud necessariam esse putat, ut nec ipse Stegmannus paulo infra. pag. 89. ubi affirmat, Unumquemque sine peculiari illustratione Spiritus Sancti dijudicare posse tantum, quantum intelligi ad salutem sufficit, quamvis plus intelligere possit, & certius judicare de eo quod novit, accedente ope Spiritus Sancti. & post paulo pag. 91. Multa sunt in S. literis fatemur, ad quae peritius & perfecte intelligenda, Spiritus Sancti Illustratione opus esse credimus. Illa autem talia esse dicimus, sine quorum intellectu peritiore quisque credere, ac porro etiam servari queat. Inde, non nisi jam Credentibus Spiritum Sanctum dari legimus; non certe, ut primum aliquid intelligant, quo credere possint, (id enim seipsum evertit) sed ut plura intelligant, tum que ad Fidei ipsorum confirmationem, tum ad aliorum informationem faciunt. Non mirum est igitur, si ex hoc duplici neglecta factum [?] sit, ut & veritatem non assequantur, & in errores incidant. Neque enim Deus solet Spiritus sui gratiam largiri, nisi humiliter petentibus, & in diligenti usu istorum mediorum aliquae [?] versantibus, quae ad veritatis affectionem, errorumque fugam, summa cura atque Benignitate nobis indulsit.
units.tr: §. 132. 6. He does not want each person to be judge in matters pertaining to religion, so that he may decide whatever he pleases, without any reverence for the Church or the commonwealth, or without fear of disturbances. "So far is it from being permitted to disregard the Church," he says, "that rather, by what standard each person becomes or remains a lawful member of the Church, must be inquired into with keen judgment." p. 52. Why then does Socinus leave each person to his own judgment in theological matters, to decide about them as he sees fit? Why does he, together with his associates and disciples, so despise the Catholic Church and set his own judgment above its judgment, indeed reject it with contempt, as if it were worth nothing at all? Why did he not stir up schisms everywhere in the Polish churches and neighbouring ones, and gather I know not how many conventicles of his followers against the laws everywhere, by which the commonwealth too was bound to be thrown into confusion? He also tried to diminish the power and rights of the civil magistrate, in his reply to Palaeologus' book on the magistracy. For this reason, when he was accused of sedition before Stephen Báthory, King of Poland, he was forced to leave Kraków and seek refuge in the house of Christopher Morstin, Lord of Pawlikowice. Likewise, why does Socinus not want anyone to be concerned to inquire which is the true Church of Christ, to which one should betake oneself for the sake of seeking the truth and obtaining salvation; but instead appoints each private person as interpreter of Holy Scripture and arbiter of its genuine sense? Why, finally, does this same Stegmann contradict himself a little later on this point, when he says: "Not only is the norm (especially the divine letter) set before us clearly and plainly enough, but sufficient powers and faculties have also been granted, so that, if only we wish and apply our minds, we can judge whether and in what error we are, and distinguish what is true and to be followed, and on the contrary what is false and to be shunned." If this is so, how does it come about that so many ingenious, learned and diligent seekers of truth do not reach it, but are led off in different directions into the byways of error? A clear proof of this is the contrariety we see in their interpretations and opinions. Therefore we must look elsewhere for the cause of this defect; namely, in the neglect of those means of this kind which God has set before us to use as aids in seeking the truth: such as the Catholic tradition, the consent of the Fathers, the judgment of the present Church, which are external; and the grace of the Holy Spirit illuminating within. Ostorodt thinks this is not necessary, as Stegmann himself does a little below, p. 89, where he affirms: "Each person can judge, without a special illumination of the Holy Spirit, only so much as suffices to understand for salvation, although he can understand more, and judge more certainly about what he knows, with the help of the Holy Spirit added." And a little after, p. 91: "We grant that there are many things in the Holy Scriptures for whose more skilled and perfect understanding we believe the illumination of the Holy Spirit is needed. But we say that those things are of such a kind that without a more skilled understanding of them each person can nevertheless believe and also be saved. Hence we read that the Holy Spirit is given only to those who already believe; certainly not so that they may first understand something by which they can believe (for that would overturn itself), but so that they may understand more, which serves both the confirmation of their faith and the instruction of others." It is no wonder, then, if from this double neglect it has come about that they neither attain the truth nor fall into errors. For God is wont to bestow the grace of his Spirit only on those who ask humbly and who are diligently engaged in the use of these means, which he has granted us with the greatest care and kindness, for the love of truth and the flight from error.

units.la: §. 133. 7. De Re ignota nemo recte judicat. At credendum est unicuique in sua arte experto. Sic ille, pag. 73. Hinc sequitur, non unumquemque e plebe Christiana, sed eruditos solos admittendos esse pro idoneis Judicibus, in Dogmaticis [?] controversis, quorum sententia inniti oportet eos, qui ad judicandum ex se inepti sunt. Sed quid facient, quoties eruditi in hujusmodi Rebus determinandis, sententiis inter se discrepant? Certe, in Rebus dubiis, tutius est illis adhaerere, quos verisimilius est nos fallere, nec posse nec velle; hoc est, eorum ductum sequi, qui non tantum numero plures sunt, sed & Doctrinae, probitatisque nomine celebriores; seu (quod eodem fere recidit) praepositorum illius Ecclesiae, cujus membra sumus, Decretis acquiescere. Ubicunque sc. manifestos error non apparet, qui oppugnet caeteras Ecclesiae Catholicae partes, vel veteris Ecclesiae fidem atque Praxin, vel S. Scripturam.
units.tr: §. 133. 7. "No one judges rightly about a thing he does not know. But one must believe each person who is experienced in his own art." Thus he, p. 73. Hence it follows that not every person from the Christian people, but only the learned, are to be admitted as suitable judges in dogmatic controversies, and that those who are not fit to judge for themselves must rest upon their opinion. But what will they do whenever learned men disagree among themselves in determining such matters? Certainly, in doubtful matters it is safer to adhere to those whom we are less likely to be deceived by, since they are neither able nor willing to deceive us; that is, to follow the lead of those who are not only more numerous but also more celebrated for learning and integrity; or (which comes to nearly the same thing) to acquiesce in the decrees of the leaders of that Church of which we are members. Wherever, that is, no manifest error appears which attacks the other parts of the Catholic Church, or the faith and practice of the ancient Church, or Holy Scripture.

units.la: §. 134. 8. Si de Divinis judicandum sit, quae Christianam Religionem constituunt, Principia Divina omnino perspecta oportet, habeat. Accedat libertas a praejudicio, & sincerus Amor veritatis. Imprimis autem, Illustratio Spiritus Sancti, cujus ductum Ratio sequatur in judicando. Sic Ille. pag. 77. At haec Divina PrinPrincipia dignosci certo nequeunt, neque Conclusiones ex iis rite colligi, si Adjumenta modo memorata neglectui habeantur. Et sane si Sociniani, cum aliis Hæreticis, immunes essent à Philautia ac Præjudicio, veritatemque sincero Amore colerent, istiusmodi errores tam arctis amplexibus nunquam foverent, & tam obstinate tuerentur; mediis omnibus retegendi eos, interea, aut superbe contemptis aut saltem crasse neglectis. Interim tamen, bene se habet, quod ad hoc opus judicandi imprimis requirat illustrationem Spiritus Sancti, cujus ductum Ratio sequi debeat. Hunc enim qui sequitur, neque in ignorantiæ tenebris ambulabit, neque in devias errorum ambages se abduci patietur. Hoc autem lumen atque hunc Ducem, quicunque de Cœlo sibi dari velit, necesse est, ut (Impedimentis recte judicandi procul amotis) oculos suos aperiat ad hoc Cœleste lumen intromittendum, & Ducem præeuntem sedulo sequatur. Alioquin, hoc Divinum Auxilium vel omnino negabitur ei, vel incassum dabitur. Neque enim Deus hujusmodi Donum aut conferre in invitos solet, aut apud Ingratos & Ignavos conservare.
units.tr: §. 134. 8. If one is to judge concerning divine matters, which make up the Christian religion, one must have thoroughly understood the divine principles. Let freedom from prejudice be added, and a sincere love of truth. Above all, there must be the illumination of the Holy Spirit, whose guidance reason should follow in judging. Thus he writes, p. 77. But these divine principles cannot be recognised with certainty, nor conclusions rightly drawn from them, if the aids just mentioned are neglected. And indeed, if the Socinians, along with other heretics, were free from self-love and prejudice, and cherished truth with a sincere love, they would never have embraced such errors so closely, nor defended them so obstinately. Meanwhile they would have used every means of uncovering them, instead of proudly despising them or at least grossly neglecting them. Still, it is good that for this work of judging he chiefly requires the illumination of the Holy Spirit, whose guidance reason ought to follow. For whoever follows this will neither walk in the darkness of ignorance nor allow himself to be led into the devious windings of error. Whoever wishes to receive this light and this guide from heaven must necessarily, with the hindrances to right judging removed far away, open his eyes to take in this heavenly light and diligently follow the guide who goes before. Otherwise this divine help will either be wholly denied to him or given in vain. For God does not usually bestow such a gift on the unwilling, nor preserve it among the ungrateful and the slothful.

units.la: §. 135. 9. Fides certior est scientia, etiam ea, quæ sensuum Testimonio nititur. Credis tamen haud dubie, Te videre, audire, legere. Imo, propterea credis, quia verum id esse agnoscis. Sicut Thomas. Jo. 20. 28, 29.
units.tr: §. 135. 9. Faith is more certain than knowledge, even that which rests on the testimony of the senses. Yet you undoubtedly believe that you see, hear and read. Indeed, you believe it precisely because you recognise it to be true. Like Thomas. Jo. 20. 28, 29.

units.la: §. 136. 10. Multa credimus vera esse, quorum modum, quo pacto is sese omni ex parte habeat, Ratio perfecte non intelligit. Unde illud Taciti De moribus Germanorum — Sanctius & reverentius visum, decretis Deorum credere, quam scire.
units.tr: §. 136. 10. We believe many things to be true whose manner, that is, how exactly they stand in every respect, reason does not fully understand. Hence that saying of Tacitus in On the Manners of the Germans: "It seemed more holy and more reverent to believe the decrees of the gods than to know them."

units.la: §. 137. Hæc Socini, aliorumque quorundam præcipuæ notæ Socinianorum, Concessa[?] notare, operæ
units.tr: §. 137. These concessions of Socinus and of certain other notable Socinians I have thought worth the effort to note,

units.la: pretium duxi, quo via facilius præstruatur ad Ipsorum Dogmata aggrediënda atque demolienda. Quam discordent enim cum iis, quæ alibi in scriptis suis passim asserunt, ac tuenda suscipiunt; & quantum virium habeant ad ea debellanda, nonæ-gre animadverti potest ab æquo lectore, qui utraque inter se conferre velit. Itaque egregie dictum est à Stegmanno in hoc ipso libello. pag. 128. —
units.tr: so that the way may be made easier for attacking and overthrowing their doctrines. How far they disagree with what they assert everywhere else in their writings and undertake to defend, and how little strength they have to overcome those things, can easily be noticed by a fair reader who wishes to compare the two. Thus Stegmann has excellently said in this same little book, p. 128.

units.la: Ita mira Res est veritas, ut non possint non perpetuo se conficere Contradictionibus, quicunque eam oppug-natum eunt. Qui etiam postea, in Cap. de abusu Rationis, ingenue quidem fatetur vim præjudicii in sententia ferenda; & ad hoc demonstrandum, varias affert instantias; at interim, suæ sectæ Præjudicia, quibus Ratio inter judicandum pervertitur, & à recto aberrare cogitur, vel discerne e nequit, vel non vult agnoscere.
units.tr: "Truth is so wonderful a thing that those who set out to attack it cannot help constantly contradicting themselves." He also later, in the chapter on the abuse of reason, frankly admits the force of prejudice in passing judgement, and to demonstrate this he brings forward various instances. Yet meanwhile he either cannot discern, or does not wish to acknowledge, the prejudices of his own sect, by which reason is perverted in judging and compelled to stray from the right.

units.la: §. 138. Hactenus de Socinianorum Concessis. Reliquum est ut eis proponamus quædam postulata; quæ, ut arbitror, haud iniqua putabunt; cum vel antecedentibus Demonstrationibus, vel ipsorum Concessis, vel evidenti Ratione & Æquitati innitantur. Sunt autem hæc quæ sequuntur:
units.tr: §. 138. So far concerning the Socinians' concessions. It remains to put forward to them certain demands, which, I think, they will not consider unfair, since they rest either on the preceding demonstrations, on their own concessions, or on evident reason and equity. These are as follows:

units.la: 1. S. Scriptura, non obstante illius plenitudine atque Perspicuitate, variis & adversis, falsisque interpretationibus est obnoxia, ita ut moraliter impossibile sit, prout Hominum Ingenia & affectus se habent, ut de vera ejus sententia inter omnes Christianos conveniat, modo licentia unicuique detur in suo ipsius sensu acquiescere. Siquidem experientia cujusque ævi abunde testata est, quam fæde, misereque [?] sensus S. Contextus fuerit corruptus, & in longe alienum transfiguratus; idque in Rebus maximi momenti, tum ad fidem, tum ad mores spectantibus.
units.tr: 1. Scripture, notwithstanding its fullness and perspicuity, is open to various, conflicting and false interpretations, so that, given the way human minds and affections are disposed, it is morally impossible for all Christians to agree on its true meaning, provided everyone is granted the licence to rest in his own sense. For the experience of every age has abundantly shown how foully and wretchedly the sense of the context has been corrupted and twisted into something far alien, and this in matters of the greatest moment, whether concerning faith or morals.

units.la: §. 139. 2. Traditiones rituales, sive consuetudines ab Apostolis, virisque Apostolicis introductæ, & ab Ecclesia Catholica generaliter observatæ per plures annorum Centurias; præsertim, si adhuc retentæ sint ab Ecclesiis, & numero pluribus, & Dignitate insignioribus; si minus observatu sint universim & absolute necessariæ, attamen æstimandæ sunt, & ex sua natura licitæ, & observatu laudabiles, neutiquam vero ab illis damnandæ, qui iis minime uti solent. Idem censendum est de eis, quæ jampridem, certa de Caula, usurpari cessarunt. Necnon de eis, quas Ecclesiæ particulares hic illic observarunt, vel adhuc observant, à Catholica vero non sunt damnatæ, adeoque silentio saltem approbatæ. Illæ vero, quæ semper & ubique invaluerunt, nec damnari possunt sine crimine Hæresis, nec contemptim omitti, sine crimine Schismatis. Cujusmodi sunt Pædobaptismus, observatio Dici Dominici, aliorumque quorundam Festorum, certæ & solennes precum publicarum Formulæ, Impositio manuum in Ordinatione Ministrorum, & Reconciliatione Pœnitentium, Dedicatio Ædium sacrarum, aliaque quædam, de quibus constat, eas receptas fuisse ab Apostolis, ut perpetuo & universaliter observandas. Sic enim Authoritas Apostolica vilipenditur, adeoque Divina, quæ in Apostolis residebat; cujusque virtute hujusmodi instituta primo condebant, & Ecclesiarum usui in posterum commendabant.
units.tr: §. 139. 2. Ritual traditions, or customs introduced by the Apostles and apostolic men and generally observed by the Catholic Church through many centuries, especially if they are still retained by churches both more numerous and more distinguished in dignity, are to be esteemed, even if they are not universally and absolutely necessary. By their nature they are lawful and laudable to observe, and by no means to be condemned by those who are not in the habit of using them. The same is to be judged of those which have long since ceased to be used for a certain cause, and likewise of those which particular churches have observed here and there, or still observe, but which have not been condemned by the Catholic Church, and so have at least been approved by silence. But those which have prevailed always and everywhere cannot be condemned without the crime of heresy, nor contemptuously omitted without the crime of schism. Of this kind are infant baptism, the observance of the Lord's Day and of certain other festivals, fixed and solemn formulas of public prayer, the laying on of hands in the ordination of ministers and in the reconciliation of penitents, the dedication of sacred buildings, and certain other things about which it is established that they were received from the Apostles to be observed perpetually and universally. For thus the apostolic authority is held in contempt, and so the divine authority which resided in the Apostles, by whose power they first established such institutions and commended them to the churches' use in future.

units.la: §. 140. 3. Ubi Ritus atque Consuetudines in diversis Ecclesiis differunt, aut in eadem Ecclesia liberę observationis sunt, nihil dici aut agi debet, quod in contemptum, vel scandalum tendat, aut istorum Rituum, aut Ecclesiarum, quæ iis utuntur, aut quorumcunque ejusdem Ecclesiæ membrorum, quibus in usu sunt. Sic enim praecipit Apostolus: Estote sine offendiculo, & Judaeis, & Graecis, & Ecclesiae Dei. 1 Cor. 10. 32. Qui edit, non edentem ne pro nihil habeat; & qui non edit, edentem ne condemnet; Deus enim assumpsit eum. Rom. 14. 3. Ne amplius alii alios judicemus; sed hoc potius judicate, non esse offendiculum ponendum fratri, aut scandalum. Ib. v. 13. Suum quoque exemplum in hoc nobis imitandum proponit: Factus sum Judaeis, ut Judaeus; exlegibus, ut exlex; infirmis, ut infirmus, omnibus factus sum omnia, ut omnino aliquos servarem. 1 Cor. 9. 20, 21, 22. Ego per omnia omnibus placeo, non quaerens meum ipsius Commodum, sed Commodum multorum, ut salventur. Ib. cap. 10. ult. eandem quoque Regulam ex ore S. Ambrosii exceptam, sibique & Monicae Matri datum[?] oraculi instar habuit Augustinus, & perinde observavit, ut non semel testatus est. Cum enim ab iis consuleretur de Jejunio Sabbati, quod Romae observabatur, Mediolani non item; ita respondit Ambrosius: Quando hic sum, inquit (id est, Mediolani) non jejuno sabbato; quando Romae sum, jejuno sabbato; & ad quamcunque Ecclesiam veneritis, ejus morem servate, si pati scandalum non vultis, aut facere. Aug. Epist. 86. ad Casulanum. Ubi sic pergit, in Regula hac ulterius explicanda: Sed quoniam contingit, ([?]maxime in Africa) ut una Ecclesia, vel unius Regionis Ecclesiae, alios habeant Sabbato prandentes, alios jejunantes, mos eorum mihi sequendus videtur, quibus Populorum eorum Congregatio commissa est. Quapropter, si Consilio meo libenter acquiescis, tuo Episcopo in hac Re noli resistere; & quod facit ipse, sine ullo Scrupulo, vel Disceptatione sectare.
units.tr: §. 140. 3. Where rites and customs differ among churches, or are of free observance within the same church, nothing ought to be said or done that tends to the contempt or scandal either of those rites, or of the churches which use them, or of any members of the same church who practise them. For thus the Apostle instructs: "Be without offence both to Jews and to Greeks and to the church of God." 1 Cor. 10. 32. "Let him who eats not despise him who does not eat; and let him who does not eat not condemn him who eats; for God has received him." Rom. 14. 3. "Let us no longer judge one another; but judge this rather, that no stumbling block or occasion of offence be placed in a brother's way." Ib. v. 13. He also sets his own example before us to imitate in this: "I became to the Jews as a Jew, to those under the law as under the law, to the weak as weak; I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." 1 Cor. 9. 20, 21, 22. "I please all men in all things, not seeking my own advantage but the advantage of many, that they may be saved." Ib. ch. 10, end. Augustine too received this same rule from the mouth of St Ambrose, and held it as an oracle, both for himself and for his mother Monica, and observed it accordingly, as he testified more than once. For when they consulted him about fasting on the Sabbath, which was observed at Rome but not at Milan, Ambrose answered thus: "When I am here, I do not fast on the Sabbath; when I am at Rome, I fast on the Sabbath; and to whatever church you come, observe its custom, if you do not wish to suffer or to cause scandal." Aug. Epist. 86 to Casulanus. Where he goes on to explain this rule further: "But since it happens (especially in Africa) that one church, or the churches of one region, fast on the Sabbath while others feast, I think the custom of those to whom the congregation of their people is entrusted should be followed by me. Therefore, if you willingly acquiesce in my advice, do not resist your bishop in this matter; and what he does, follow without any scruple or dispute."

units.la: §. 141. 4. Si constet de sensu alicujus loci Scripturæ sacræ, quod iste ab Apostolis devenerit, & ab iisdem Ecclesiæ relictus sit, cæteris omnibus præferendus est; & nulla Interpretatio ei adversa, à nobis admittenda est. Utrum vero sensus iste ab Apostolis devenerit, annon, judicandum est à Testimonio veteris Ecclesiæ, quod extat in Scriptis Patrum, qui Tale quid asserunt, communibusque suffragiis, ratum faciunt; & in Synodorum Decretis, ubi Idem accuratius excutitur, solenniusque confirmatur.
units.tr: §. 141. 4. If it is established concerning the sense of some passage of Holy Scripture that it has come down from the Apostles and been left by them to the Church, it is to be preferred to all others, and no interpretation contrary to it is to be admitted by us. Whether that sense has come down from the Apostles or not is to be judged from the testimony of the early Church, which is found in the writings of the Fathers, who assert such a thing and confirm it by common consent, and in the decrees of the Synods, where the same is examined more accurately and confirmed more solemnly.

units.la: §. 142. 5. Apostoli ore Tradiderunt, dum adhuc in vivis erant, & post se reliquerunt, summulam quandam Doctrinæ Christianæ omnibus istis Ecclesiis, quas toto orbe plantarunt, priusquam libri novi Testamenti conscripti fuerint, & per Ecclesias istas dispersi. Hanc enim professi sunt, & in Illius Fidem baptizati, quicunque in Christi Ecclesiam admissi sunt; quorum multa Millia memorantur, etiam ante Matthæi Evangelium in vulgus editum, quod cæteros novi Testamenti libros antecessisse perhibetur. Quicunque item hanc Fidei Apostolicæ Formulam corrupisse deprehensi sunt, vel addendo, vel auferendo, vel sensum ejus genuinum depravando, pro Hæreticis habiti sunt & ex Illius Sententia damnati. Hæc demum pro Regula data est cunctis S. Scripturæ Interpretibus, ut ad Illius Amussim expositiones suas omnes dirigerent; quam si forte neglexerint, & alienum, incongruumque sensum de suo comminiscerentur, expositio ista pro heterodoxa & erronea habebatur, si minus pro hæretica.
units.tr: §. 142. 5. While they were still alive, the Apostles handed down by word of mouth, and left behind them, a brief summary of Christian doctrine for all the churches they planted throughout the world, before the books of the New Testament were written and circulated among these churches. For everyone who was admitted into Christ's Church professed this summary and was baptized into faith in it, and many thousands are recorded to have done so, even before Matthew's Gospel was published among the people, which is said to have preceded the other books of the New Testament. Likewise, whoever was found to have corrupted this Apostolic formula, either by adding to it, taking away from it, or distorting its genuine sense, was regarded as a heretic and condemned by its authority. Finally, this formula was given as a rule to all interpreters of Holy Scripture, so that they would direct all their expositions by its standard. If they happened to neglect it and devised for themselves an alien and incongruous sense, that exposition was regarded as heterodox and erroneous, if not heretical.

units.la: §. 143.6.Quod universa tenet Ecclesia, nec Conciliis institutum, sed semper retentum est, non nisi Authoritate Apostolica traditum rectissime creditur. Hanc Regulam olim tulit Augustinus: De Bapt. cont. Donatistas. Lib. 4. cap: 24. Rationi certe valde congruam. Siquidem hæc Unicuique dictat, unumquemque efsectum necessario habere Causam sibi correspondentem, ac proinde ejusdem latitudinis. Quodcunque ergo antiquitus & universim per totam Ecclesiam obtinuit, necesse est, ut se referat ad Apostolos, ut Authores, qui Ecclesias ubique fundabant, sive ad Fidem, sive ad Praxin spectet; nisi constet de Decreto alicujus Concilii Oecumenici, quod istud Dogma, vel institutum primitus introduxit, & Ecclesiæ Catholicæ commendavit.
units.tr: §. 143. 6. What the whole Church holds, which has not been instituted by councils but has always been retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority. Augustine laid down this rule long ago: On Baptism against the Donatists, Book 4, chapter 24. It is certainly very well suited to reason. For reason dictates to everyone that every effect necessarily has a cause corresponding to it, and therefore of the same extent. Whatever has prevailed from antiquity and universally throughout the whole Church must therefore necessarily refer back to the Apostles as its authors, who founded churches everywhere, whether it concerns faith or practice; unless it is established by a decree of some ecumenical council that first introduced that doctrine or institution and commended it to the Catholic Church.

units.la: §. 144. 7. Istæ Traditiones pro Apostolicis habendæ sunt, quæ ad has Regulas quadrant, viz. Primo, Quando universa Ecclesia cujuscunque ævi Aliquid pro Fidei Dogmate amplectitur, & Oppositum pro hæretico damnat, etsi neque expresse inveniatur in S. Literis, neque Deductio illius ex principiis ibi contentis, Unicuique sit obvia. Ratio est, quia Catholica Ecclesia semper professa est, atque hodie profitetur, se omnia Fidei Dogmata ab Apostolis accepisse, neque novas aliquas de Fide Revelationis post Illorum mortem, vel præ se fert, vel expectat. Tenet hæc Regula simpliciter, ni forte evidenter ostendi possit aliquod Dogma, quod Ecclesia Catholica hujus, vel cujuscunque antecedentis ævi tenet, aut esse tenuit, vel fuisse plane contrarium S. Scripturæ, aut Ecclesiæ veteris Doctrinæ; vel eam damnare, aut damnasse, quod illa de Fide tenuit. Quod certe neutiquam probabile, si modo Possibile sit. Secundo, Quando universa Ecclesia Aliquod observat, probatque quod nulla humana Potestas efficere va-let, let, sed à Dei solius Institutione dependet, quoad efficaciam Gratiamque ei annexam, æquum est dicere, Illud à Christo, & Apostolis ejus suisse traditum. Ratio est, quia non est in Ecclesiæ Potestate, aliquam verborum Formulam, aut quemcunque alium Ritum instituere, cui divina Gratia necessario annexa sit, aut ejusdem vehiculum sit, ex vi suæ Ipsius Institutionis, quæ non nisi humana est; cum Totum hoc pendeat ex Institutione divina, atque adeo ex eadem Authoritate ad Ecclesiam derivari debeat; sicut & ipsa Ecclesia, sic ad eam derivatum fuisse profitetur. Hæc autem Regula eandem in Agendis vim habet, quam Prior habuit Credendis. Tertio, Quando omnes Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Doctores uno ore testantur, se tale Fidei Dogma, talemve Consuetudinem, ab Apostolis accepisse, sive in Conciliis una Congregati, sive seorsim in libris à se conscriptis, certissimum est Catholicæ Traditionis Argumentum. Quis enim dicere audeat, vel eos ignorasse, quid à suis Majoribus acceperint; vel ex industria consensisse Omnes, in Posteris mendacio admodum perniciosò sallendis contra propriam sui Conscientiam? Quarto, Vincentius Lirinensis in suo Commonitorio adversus Hæreses has, aliasque quascunque Regulas huc pertinentes in unam hanc contulit, quæ sola ex omni parte Tuta est, atque completa; nimirum, ut eam Traditionem pro Apostolica habeamus, quæ ubique, semper, & ab omnibus recepta est; seu, quæ pro Testimonio adducit Universitatem, Antiquitatem, & Consensum unanimem; Universitatem receptionis per Ecclesiam Catholicam; Antiquitatem originis, à Sanctis Majoribus, & Patribus nostris, usque ad Apostolos deducta; Consensum item unanimem omnium, vel pene omnium Ecclesiæ Sacerdotum atque Magistrorum. Sic ille. Common. cap. 3.
units.tr: §. 144. 7. Those traditions are to be held as apostolic which accord with these rules, namely: First, when the whole Church of any age embraces something as a dogma of faith and condemns the opposite as heretical, even though it is not expressly found in the Holy Scriptures, nor is its deduction from the principles contained there obvious to everyone. The reason is that the Catholic Church has always professed, and still professes today, that it received all the dogmas of faith from the Apostles, and neither displays nor expects any new revelations of faith after their death. This rule holds simply, unless perhaps it can be clearly shown that some dogma which the Catholic Church of this or of any earlier age holds, or has held, was either plainly contrary to Holy Scripture or to the doctrine of the ancient Church, or that it condemns or has condemned what that Church held as faith. This is certainly by no means probable, if indeed it is possible at all. Second, when the whole Church observes and approves something which no human power can bring about, but which depends solely on the institution of God as to its efficacy and the grace attached to it, it is fair to say that this was handed down by Christ and his Apostles. The reason is that it is not within the power of the Church to institute some formula of words or any other rite to which divine grace is necessarily attached, or which is the vehicle of it by virtue of its own institution, since that institution is merely human; whereas the whole matter depends on divine institution, and must therefore be derived to the Church from the same authority, just as the Church itself professes that it was derived to it. This rule has the same force in matters of practice as the former has in matters of belief. Third, when all the teachers of the Catholic Church bear witness with one voice that they received such a dogma of faith or such a custom from the Apostles, whether gathered together in councils or separately in books written by them, this is the most certain argument of Catholic tradition. For who would dare to say either that they were ignorant of what they had received from their ancestors, or that all of them agreed deliberately to deceive posterity with a lie most pernicious, and contrary to their own conscience? Fourth, Vincent of Lérins, in his Commonitory against these heresies and all other rules pertaining here, brought them together into one, which alone is safe in every respect and complete; namely, that we should hold that tradition as apostolic which has been received everywhere, always, and by all; or which adduces as its witness universality, antiquity, and unanimous consent; universality of reception throughout the Catholic Church; antiquity of origin, traced back from our holy forefathers and fathers to the Apostles; likewise the unanimous consent of all, or nearly all, of the priests and teachers of the Church. So he. Commonitory, chapter 3.

units.la: §. 145. 8. Ecclesia Christiana his notis dignoscitur, & ab omni alia Societate discriminatur; quod sc. sit una, Sancta, Catholica, & Apostolica. Una in fe, & respectu Regiminis; Sancta, respectu Fidei & morum; Catholica, respectu Amplitudinis; ut quæ nulli uni Genti astricta sit; Apostolica denique respectu Originis sive Fundationis. Una, ut excludat Schismaticos; Sancta, ut excludat Atheos & Infideles, Profanos atque Libertinos; Catholica, ut excludat Hæreticos & Perduelles; & Apostolica, ut excludat Enthusiastas, & quoscunque novæ Fidei Præcones. Porro, quicunque non est Membrum Ecclesiæ hisce notis insignitæ, extra quam non est salus, pro vere Christiano seu Fideli non est agnoscendus.
units.tr: §. 145. 8. The Christian Church is recognized by these marks and distinguished from every other society: that it is one, holy, catholic, and apostolic. One in faith and with respect to government; holy with respect to faith and morals; catholic with respect to its extent, as it is not bound to any single nation; and finally apostolic with respect to its origin or foundation. It is one, so as to exclude schismatics; holy, so as to exclude atheists and unbelievers, profane and libertine persons; catholic, so as to exclude heretics and traitors; and apostolic, so as to exclude enthusiasts and all heralds of a new faith. Moreover, whoever is not a member of a Church marked by these notes, outside of which there is no salvation, is not to be acknowledged as a true Christian or believer.

units.la: §. 146. 9. Ecclesia Christi est Cœtus visibilis, semperque fuit, eritque Talis, usque ad secundum ipsius Adventum. Hæc autem Ecclesiæ visibilitas, atque Duratio perpetua, ut divinis Christi Promissis innititur, sic & experientia omnium hucusque Seculorum de facto confirmata est. Eclipsin quidem passa est interdum, & in quibusdam Mundi Partibus, ubi olim inclaruit, multum obscurata est, si minus in totum defecit; at ex hac Eclipsi se paulo post recepit, pristinoque lumine denuo resplenduit; imo, & novas Regiones Tenebris prius obsitas, Evangelicæ veritatis salutari lumine perfudit. Nunquam autem, vel Hæreticorum clandestinis molitionibus, vel aperta Persecutorum vi, vel intestinis Filiorum suorum Dissidiis, vel atrocibus rectæ Fidei Professorum scandalis moribusque flagitiosis eo usque oppressa est, ut non tempestive resurgeret[?]. resurrexerit, Hostes vicerit, Perduelles subegerit; Filios diffidentes inter se tandem conciliaverit, mores emendaverit, disciplinam refarciverit, morbifque abactis, sanitatem, prius laesam, & imminutam recuperaverit. Constat item Coetus hic visibilis, tam ex malis, quam ex Bonis, qui in externa ipsius communione simul degunt; ita ut Mixtio haec non solum Plebem Christianam, sed & Ecclesiae pastores, Comprehendat. Quod satis patet tum ex Historia Ecclesiastica cujusque seculi, quae Rem ipsam demonstrat; tum ex Christi Parabolis, quae futuram praedixerunt; sc. Ex Parabolis de Tritico & Zizaniis, in eodem Agro; de bonis & malis Piscibus, in eodem Reti; necnon, de Ovibus & Haedis, in eadem Caula. Quibus adjici potest illud Apostoli, De vasibus ad Honorem & Contumeliam, in eadem Domo. 2 Tim. 2. 20.
units.tr: §. 146. 9. The Church of Christ is a visible assembly, and always has been, and will be such until his second coming. This visibility and perpetual duration of the Church rests on the divine promises of Christ, and has likewise been confirmed in fact by the experience of all the ages hitherto. It has indeed at times suffered an eclipse, and in some parts of the world where it once flourished it has been greatly obscured, if not wholly extinguished; yet soon after this eclipse it has recovered itself, and has shone forth again with its former light; indeed it has even bathed new regions, previously covered in darkness, in the saving light of evangelical truth. Yet it has never been so overwhelmed, whether by the secret schemes of heretics, or by the open violence of persecutors, or by the internal dissensions of its own sons, or by the atrocious scandals and wicked morals of those who profess the true faith, that it did not rise again in good time, overcome its enemies, subdue its traitors, eventually reconcile its divided children, amend its morals, repair its discipline, and, with the diseases driven out, recover its health, which had been injured and diminished. It is also established that this visible assembly, which dwells together in outward communion, consists of the bad as well as the good; so that this mixture includes not only the Christian people but also the ministers of the Church. This is plain enough both from the ecclesiastical history of every age, which demonstrates the fact itself, and from Christ's parables, which foretold it: namely, the parables of the wheat and the tares in the same field; of the good and bad fish in the same net; and likewise of the sheep and the goats in the same fold. To these may be added the Apostle's words about the vessels to honour and dishonour in the same house. 2 Tim. 2. 20.

units.la: §. 147. 10. Ecclesia Catholica uniuscujusque ævi, & speciatim hujus, in quo degimus, non censenda est errare in Re aliqua majoris momenti, sive ad Credenda, sive ad Agenda spectante. Proinde, singulis illius membris tutissimum est ipsi confidere, in Determinatione Rerum controversarum, & in ipsius Sententia acquiescere, sive Fidem respiciat, sive Praxin, in iis sc. quae ad Cultum divinum, & Politiae Ecclesiasticae administrationem pertinent.
units.tr: §. 147. 10. The Catholic Church of every age, and especially of this in which we live, is not to be judged to err in any matter of greater importance, whether it concerns things to be believed or things to be done. Therefore it is very safe for each of its members to trust in it when controversies are being decided, and to acquiesce in its judgment, whether that judgment concerns faith or practice, namely in those matters which pertain to the worship of God and the administration of ecclesiastical polity.

units.la: §. 148. 11. Ecclesia non Catholica duntaxat, sed & quaevis Particularis, quae sc. Independens est, & sui Juris, habet Authoritatem legislativam circa Adiaphora definienda, quam omnia Ipsius membra agnoscere tenentur, ejusque Decretis obtemperare.
units.tr: §. 148. 11. Not only the Catholic Church but any particular church that is independent and has its own right possesses legislative authority to define matters indifferent, and all its members are bound to acknowledge this authority and obey its decrees.

units.la: §. 149. 12. Discrimen necessario statuere oportet, inter Pastores Ecclesiae, plebemque Christianam ; cum pastores habeant munus sibi proprium, quod nemo usurpare debet, five exercere , fine Missione legitima, hoc est, qui non est ad illud exercendum rite vocatus, ordinatus, & admissus.
units.tr: §. 149. 12. A distinction must necessarily be drawn between the ministers of the Church and the Christian people, since the ministers have a function proper to themselves, which no one ought to assume or exercise without lawful mission, that is, without being duly called, ordained and admitted to it.

units.la: §. 150. 13. Judicium pastoralis Di[?]rectionis valde necessarium est in Ecclesia Christiana, nec temere rejiciendum à Plebe, utpote quod innititur Peritia simul atque Potestate Pastorum, qui à Christo summo Illo Pastore, Gregi ducendo præficiuntur.
units.tr: §. 150. 13. The judgment of pastoral direction is very necessary in the Christian Church and should not be rashly rejected by the people, since it rests on the skill and authority of the ministers, who are set over the flock by Christ, that great Shepherd, to lead it.

units.la: §. 151. 14. Jurisdictio præterea competit primariis Ecclesiæ Pastoribus, qui dicuntur Episcopi; & Judicium coercivum, in Censuris Ecclesiasticis, quas ex Officio, & Potestate sibi à Christo data, tum legibus latis decernunt, tum juxta leges istas infligunt, in immorigeros & obstinatos. Alioquin, ordo, Decorum, atque Pax, conservari nullo modo possent in Ecclesia Dei. Eadem potestas se pariter extendit ad Doctrinam Fidei, Cultusque Divini Praxin, quas eisdem incumbit,non solum proponere, sed & observandas præscribere.Extendit se quoque ad Personas omnium suæ Jurisdictioni subditorum,delitibus inter eos exortis judicium ferendo, errores condemnando, veritatem confirmando, Convictos erroris, & in Contumacia perseverantes, Censuris coercendo, & à Communione Ecclesiæ tandem secludendo.
units.tr: §. 151. 14. Moreover, jurisdiction belongs to the chief pastors of the Church, who are called bishops, and also coercive judgment in ecclesiastical censures, which they impose, by the office and power given them by Christ, both by enacting laws and by inflicting penalties under those laws on the disobedient and obstinate. Otherwise, order, decency and peace could in no way be preserved in the Church of God. This same power extends equally to the doctrine of the faith and the practice of divine worship, which it is their task not only to propose but also to prescribe for observance. It extends also to the persons of all who are subject to its jurisdiction, by passing judgment on disputes arising among them, condemning errors, confirming the truth, restraining with censures those convicted of error and persisting in obstinacy, and finally excluding them from communion with the Church.

units.la: §. 152. 15. Authoritas Conciliorum Generalium est sub Christo suprema in Terris, tum in determinandis Fidei Controversiis, tum in legibus Ecclesiasticis ferendis, quæ omnes Christianos obligent, in Rebus ad mores atque Disciplinam spectantibus.
units.tr: §. 152. 15. The authority of general councils is, under Christ, the highest on earth, both in determining controversies of faith and in enacting ecclesiastical laws, which bind all Christians in matters pertaining to morals and discipline.

units.la: §. 153. 16. Decreta Synodorum legitime procedentium, & ab Ecclesia Catholica approbatarum, (etsi Generales non fuerint) non sunt à quoquam Fideli repudianda; quippe quæ singulos Christianos obligant, tum ad professionem Fidei ibidem decretæ, tum ad praxin Disciplinæ, juxta Canones Illarum Authoritate sancitos. At magis præcipue & peculiari jure Ecclesiarum istarum Membra obligant, quæ Delegatos suos ad Synodum miserunt, quarumque Delegati illuc ita immissi, Ecclesiarum suarum sensum atque Sententiam, in Synodo integre, summaque fide repræsentarunt, & congruenter Suffragia sua una cum Cæteris, tulerunt.
units.tr: §. 153. 16. The decrees of synods lawfully convened and approved by the Catholic Church (even if they were not general) are not to be rejected by any faithful person, since they bind individual Christians both to the profession of faith decreed there and to the practice of discipline according to the canons sanctioned by their authority. Yet the members of those churches are bound in a more especial and peculiar way, whose delegates were sent to the synod, and whose delegates, so sent, faithfully and in full represented the sense and judgment of their churches in the synod and gave their votes in agreement with the others.

units.la: §. 154. 17. Concilia vere Generalia, qualia erant sex Priora, cum ab Ecclesia Catholica jam olim fuerint approbata, merito postulârint, ut Authoritas Illorum universim agnoscatur, qua patet Ecclesia Christiana; & ut Decreta illic facta, præsertim ea quæ ad fidem spectant, admittantur ab omnibus vere Fidelibus.
units.tr: §. 154. 17. Councils truly general, such as the first six, since they were approved long ago by the Catholic Church, have rightly demanded that their authority be acknowledged in general, by which the Christian Church is made manifest, and that the decrees made there, especially those concerning faith, be admitted by all truly faithful persons.

units.la: §. 155. 18. Etsi nullæ Revelationes, post Christum & Apostolos, Ecclesiæ datæ fuerint ad condendum novos Fidei articulos, & substantiam Cultus divini aut Politiæ Ecclesiasticæ immutanda, opus est tamen interiore Spiritu & Illuminatione ad Scripturam rite intelligendam, & Mysteria Fidei, ut oportet, percipienda; qui Spiritus nunc dierum, non est quærendus aut expectandus, nisi in usu istiusmodi mediorum, quæ idem Christus, & Ipsius Apostoli Ecclesiæ commendarunt; quæ item Ipsa in hunc finem olim cum Fructu usurpavit, Nobisque tradidit usurpanda.
units.tr: §. 155. 18. Although no revelations have been given to the Church after Christ and the Apostles for framing new articles of faith or for changing the substance of divine worship or ecclesiastical polity, there is nonetheless need of an inward Spirit and illumination to understand Scripture rightly and to perceive the mysteries of faith as they ought to be perceived. This Spirit is not to be sought or expected in our days except in the use of those means which Christ himself and his Apostles commended to the Church, and which the Church itself formerly used with profit for this end and handed down to us to be used.

units.la: §. 156. Hæc sunt Postulata, quæ Catholici à Socinianis approbari petunt, ut Christianismi principiis sanæque Rationi apprime congrua. Restant Alia quædam, quæ ab iisdem emendari postulant, sive corrigi, ut Christianismo, sanæque Rationi adversa; quippe quæ perperam ab eis, vel omissa, vel admissa sunt, hoc est, asserta, & in praxin redacta. Hæc autem fere sunt.
units.tr: §. 156. These are the demands which Catholics ask the Socinians to approve, as most consonant with the principles of Christianity and with sound reason. There remain certain others, which they ask the same men to amend, or correct, as opposed to Christianity and sound reason, since they have wrongly either omitted or admitted these things, that is, asserted them and put them into practice. These, however, are mostly the following.

units.la: §. 157. 1. Ut Dogmata sua ferant ad S. Scripturæ normam examinanda; non autem eam detorqueant ad sua ista Dogmata confirmanda. Sive, ut sine Præjudicio accedant ad S. Literas consulendas; adeoque cunctis opinionibus suis malesanis valedicere parati sint quamprimum eas verbo Dei adversas comperiunt, prout exponitur juxta AnalogiamFidei sive summamDoctrinæ Christianæ in S. Literis traditæ, & juxta sensumEcclesiæ Catholicæ, qui ut universaliter hodie admissus est, sic & antiquitus acceptus atque approbatus.
units.tr: §. 157. 1. That they subject their dogmas to the test of the rule of Holy Scripture, and not twist Scripture to confirm those dogmas of theirs. Or, that they approach the Holy Letters for consultation without prejudice, and so be ready to bid farewell to all their unsound opinions as soon as they find them opposed to the word of God, when Scripture is explained according to the analogy of faith, that is, the sum of Christian doctrine delivered in the Holy Letters, and according to the sense of the Catholic Church, which, as it is universally admitted today, so too was received and approved from antiquity.

units.la: §. 158. 2. Ut non sibi fas putent sensus novos atque peregrinos, perversos, & hactenus in Ecclesia Christi, aut inauditos, aut damnatos, S. Scripturæ pro libitu affigere, iis neglectis atque contemptis, quos Verba præ se usitate ferunt, & quos denotare solent in cæteris Scripturæ locis, etiam ipsis Socinianis Interpretibus; Tales item, quibus Scopus S. Contextus præcipue favet, locique Circumstantiæ optime congruunt; Quos demum Ecclesia Catholica, ut suo Suffragio approbat, sic & à Majoribus traditos accepit.
units.tr: §. 158. 2. That they do not think it lawful to attach to Holy Scripture at their own pleasure new, strange, perverse senses, hitherto unheard of or condemned in the Church of Christ, neglecting and disregarding those meanings which the words ordinarily bear, and which they usually denote in other passages of Scripture, even by the Socinian interpreters themselves; likewise such senses as the scope and context of Scripture especially favour and the circumstances of the place agree with best; and finally those which the Catholic Church, by its approval, has accepted as handed down by our forefathers.

units.la: §. 159. 3. Ut licentiam, sibi non permittant mutandi ad arbitrium puncta, commata, periodos, apices literarum; ipsaque literas, syllabas, vocesque integras; non solum nulla exemplarium probatorum Authoritate suffulti, sed & contra Fidem Codicum vetorum, eorumque qui vulgo leguntur[?] hodieque recepti sunt ab Ecclesia. Atque hoc, ut sua Ipsorum Dogmata stabiliant, Sensibusque pravis istis, quos Verbo Dei affingunt, fidem faciant, è libris sacris ita corruptis atque interpolatis; & Catholicorum Argumenta inde perita simul elusent. Cum enim non solum infame sit [?] in Actionibus forensibus, quæ circa Res civiles versantur; graveque malæ Causæ Argumentum, publicas Tabulas fallare, Testiumve viciata suffragia in forum producere, sed & gravi multa [?] plectendum; certe multo magis in sacris, ubi summæ injustitiæ accedit summa Impietas, sacrilegium fraudi.
units.tr: §. 159. 3. That they do not permit themselves licence to change at will points, commas, periods, the tittles of letters, and the letters, syllables and whole words themselves, supported not only by no authority of approved copies, but also against the witness of the old manuscripts and of those that are commonly read and still today accepted by the Church. And they do this so that they may establish their own dogmas and lend credence to those perverse senses which they attach to the word of God, using the sacred books so corrupted and interpolated; and by this means they also elude the arguments of Catholics with skill. For just as it is not only disgraceful in legal proceedings concerning civil affairs, and a grave sign of a bad cause, to falsify public records or to bring into court the corrupted testimony of witnesses, but also to be punished with a heavy fine; so much more surely in sacred matters, where great injustice is joined with great impiety, is the crime of sacrilege joined with fraud.

units.la: §. 160. 4. Ut lumen Rationis humanæ non opponant lumini Revelationis divinæ. Hoc nempe debile, & obscurum est, & diversimode fallax, ut unicuique patet, in Rerum quoque naturalium atque moralium examine, quæ nobis multo propiores sunt, & intellectu faciliores. Illud autem, ut in se clarum est, ita & certum; quippe quod in veritatis notitiam ducit, sine cujusvis erroris periculo.
units.tr: §. 160. 4. That they do not set the light of human reason against the light of divine revelation. For reason is weak and obscure, and in many ways deceptive, as is plain to everyone, even in the examination of natural and moral things, which are much closer to us and easier to understand. But revelation, as it is clear in itself, so also is certain, since it leads to the knowledge of truth without danger of any error.

units.la: Neque certum duntaxat, sed & absolute necessarium ad discernendum, riteque dijudicandum ista Fidei Christianæ mysteria, quorum cognitio ad salutem necessaria est. Equidem fatemur, hoc Revelationis divinæ lumen à Socinianis verbotenus agnosci, & quod aliquatenus ab eo se duci patiantur.
units.tr: Revelation is not only certain but absolutely necessary for discerning and rightly judging those mysteries of the Christian faith, the knowledge of which is necessary for salvation. Indeed, we admit that the Socinians acknowledge this light of divine revelation in words, and that they allow themselves to be led by it to some extent.

units.la: At interim sæpius evenit, ut cum aliquod Fidei mysterium mentis ipsorum oculo contemplandum proponitur, quod Hominis ψυχικὸς sive animalis judicio repugnat, aut saltem illius captum excedit; nimirum cui simile quidpiam ab eis reperiri nequit inter Creaturas, aut, quod in Contractibus, aliisve Commerciis inter Homines peragi solitis, sibi haud æquum videtur, rectæque Rationi consonum, hunc suæ mentis oculum aut occludant, aut avertant, ne agnoscere cogantur, quod non possunt non intueri.
units.tr: Yet meanwhile it happens quite often that when some mystery of the faith is set before the eye of their mind to be contemplated, which is repugnant to the judgment of the natural [ψυχικὸς] man, or at least exceeds his grasp (namely, one for which they can find nothing similar among creatures, or among the things that are customarily done in contracts and other dealings between men, and which seems to them unfair and not consonant with right reason), they either close or turn away this eye of their mind, so that they need not be compelled to acknowledge what they cannot but see.

units.la: §. 161. 5. Ut Hæreses antiquas, & Orco jam olim damnatas Ecclesiæ Catholicæ sententia, è sepulchris suis non effoderent, ad pestem de novo spargendam per Orbem Christianum. Quis enim, qui modo æquus sit sanæ Rationis arbiter, non facile concesserit, veterem illam Ecclesiam optime nosse, qualem Doctrinam acceperit ab Apostolis, aliisque viris Apostolicis, qui Ecclesias particulares in diversis Mundi Regionibus primo plantarunt?
