Unde sequitur, nullos Judices magis idoneos desiderari posse qui quascunque Doctrinas de novo exortas, cum ipsi adhuc in vivis essent, ad Fidei Apostolicæ Regulam examinarent. Quomodo factum est igitur, ut quamprimum Hæreses istæ [illegible, ~9 letters] cæperint, non solum arguerentur, ut novæ ac peregrinæ, sed ut adversæ quoque Fidei semel traditæ, & Communiter in Ecclesiis receptæ? Cur illorum Temporum Episcopi adeo conturbabantur ad primam horum Dogmatum famam, si nihil novi aut periculosi illis inesset? Cur invicem literas mittebant, Concilia statim inibant, solicite monebant de hisce novatoribus cavendis & se mutuis exhortationibus studiosissime exacuebant ad hujusmodi Hæreses in ipso exortu supprimendas? Cur tam sedulo festinarunt, & undique coibant in Synodos, quoties aliquantulum otii dabatur, ut junctis Consiliis atque conatibus glisscenti Incendio tempestive occurrerent, si parum aut nihil mali Hæresibus istis inesset? Cur hoc fecerunt, etiam sub ethnicis Imperatoribus, & apertis Ecclesiæ Hostibus, nisi multo majus periculum Christianismo imminere judicarent à Corruptoribus Fidei, quam à Persecutoribus Fidelium? Legimus enim, complures orientis Episcopos, sub Aureliano imp. convenisse ad exturbandum Paulum Samosatenum è sede Antiochena, & illius Hæresin una comprimendam; eandem Hæresin, quam impii isti Hæresiarchæ Ebi-on on & Cerinthus, Joannis Apostoli temporibus, primo divulgaverant; & à Photino Sirmiensi Episcopo postea redintegratam; propter quam & condemnatus est; idque, non solum à Catholicis, in Concilio Sardicensi; sed & ab ipsis Arianis, in Concilio Sirmiensi: à Socinianis demum, aliisque AntiTrinitariis, post tot secula, ex orco resuscitatam.
units.tr: §. 161. 5. That they would not dig up from their graves, by the judgment of the Catholic Church, ancient heresies long since condemned to the underworld, to spread the plague anew throughout the Christian world. For who, if he is a fair judge of sound reason, would not readily grant that the ancient Church knew very well what doctrine it had received from the Apostles and from the apostolic men who first planted particular churches in the various regions of the world? Hence it follows that no more suitable judges could be desired, to examine by the rule of the apostolic faith whatever doctrines arose anew while those men were still alive. How, then, did it come about that as soon as these heresies [illegible] began, they were refuted not only as new and strange, but also as contrary to the faith once delivered and commonly received in the churches? Why were the bishops of those times so greatly disturbed at the first report of these doctrines, if nothing new or dangerous was in them? Why did they send letters to one another, at once hold councils, anxiously warn about these innovators, and most zealously stir one another by mutual exhortations to suppress such heresies at their very birth? Why did they hasten so eagerly, and gather from all sides into synods whenever a little leisure was granted, so that by joining counsels and efforts they might timely meet the spreading fire, if these heresies contained little or no harm? Why did they do this even under heathen emperors and open enemies of the Church, unless they judged that a far greater danger hung over Christianity from the corrupters of the faith than from the persecutors of the faithful? For we read that several bishops of the East gathered under the emperor Aurelian to drive Paul of Samosata from the see of Antioch and to suppress his heresy together; the same heresy which the impious heresiarchs Ebion and Cerinthus had first spread in the times of the Apostle John, and which was afterwards revived by Photinus, bishop of Sirmium, on account of which he was also condemned, and this not only by the Catholics, in the Council of Sardica, but also by the Arians themselves, in the Council of Sirmium; and which the Socinians and other anti-Trinitarians, after so many centuries, have raised again from the underworld.

units.la: §. 162, 6. Ut, si coerceri nolunt intra Catholicismi Terminos, veteresque receptae Fidei limites, quin, iis transcensis aut perruptis, aliena & peregrina Dogmata inter Christianos disseminare velint, à convitiis saltem & calumniis abstinerent. Ne causam suam agant maledictis & mendaciis; neque Catholicam Ecclesiam seculi primitivi, in qua Doctrinae Apostolicae Simplicitas atque Puritas, una cum sanctitate morum, quam maxime viguerunt, infamem reddere conentur, quasi Apostaliam[?] fecisset à Fide Apostolica, aut eam saltem foedissime corrupisset. Cessent item piissimorum Episcoporum, & pro Fide Christiana Martyrum, famam malevolentissimis obtrectationibus incessere, quasi Doctrinam istam quam Apostoli Ecclesiae primitus tradiderant, sacrisque Literis consignarant in usum Posterorum, pro virili sua supprimere studuissent, dum omnibus modis conati sunt sinceros veritatis Evangelicae Professores, non tantum cunctis odiosos reddere, sed & ex orbe Christiano penitus exterminare. Siquidem Haereticos istius aevi, AntiTrinitariorum hodiernorum Patres, primosque Dogmatum Socinianorum Authores pro solis Fidei Apostolicae Professoribus habent, à qua Catholici istorum temporum in universum degeneraverant, eaque de causa Professores hosce sinceros acerrime persecuti sunt. Ita susque deque vertunt omnia, Catholicos in Novatorum, & Novatores in Catholicorum classem, sedem, nomenque transferentes.
units.tr: §. 162, 6. That, if they will not keep within the limits of Catholicism and the old received bounds of the Faith, but wish, having crossed or broken through them, to spread alien and foreign doctrines among Christians, they should at least abstain from insults and calumnies. Let them not conduct their cause with curses and lies. Nor should they try to make infamous the Catholic Church of the first age, in which the simplicity and purity of apostolic doctrine flourished most of all, together with holiness of life, as if it had apostatised from the apostolic faith or at least had most foully corrupted it. Let them likewise cease to assault, with the most malicious slanders, the reputation of the most pious bishops and of the martyrs for the Christian faith, as if they had striven, so far as they could, to suppress that doctrine which the apostles had first delivered to the Church and committed to sacred writings for the use of posterity. For they have tried in every way not only to make sincere professors of the Gospel truth hateful to everyone, but to exterminate them utterly from the Christian world. For they regard the heretics of that age, the present-day fathers of the anti-Trinitarians and the first authors of the Socinian dogmas, as the only professors of the apostolic faith, from which the Catholics of those times had wholly degenerated; and for that reason they have most bitterly persecuted these sincere professors. Thus they turn everything upside down, transferring Catholics into the class, seat and name of innovators, and innovators into that of Catholics.

units.la: §. 163. 7. Ut veterum Patrum insigniumque Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Doctorum Authoritatem non adeo vilipendant; illorumque Testimonia, quæ ab hodiernis Catholicis afferuntur ad asserendam Fidem Praxinque antiquæ Ecclesiæ, contemptim rejiciant, quasi nihil omnino valerent. Siquidem Hi, eximia suorum quoque Temporum Ornamenta simul erant atque Munimenta; luminaria Ecclesiæ in Terris hisce militantis, præfulgida luminaria, sole Justitiæ accensa, & undiquaque veritatis Evangelicæ radios spargentia; strenui imprimis Catholicæ Fidei Assertores, & Pugiles invictissimi, quam, ut ab Apostolis acceperant, ita fidissime conservarunt, studiosissime docuerunt, & constantissime defenderunt, contra unicuiusque generis Adversarios, Gentiles, Judæos, & Hæreticos; quam denique, ut à majoribus susceperant, ita posteris tradiderunt, sanctissimi instar Depositi, neque in Toto, neque in Parte, aut diminutam, aut depravatam. Horum utique Authoritas non parum valebit apud omnes modesti & moderati ingenii Christianos. Utcunque enim fas sit de privatis illorum opinionibus liberius paulo ferè censuram, (quæ eo usque duntaxat à nobis fidem merentur, quousque Argumentorum vires sese porrigunt, è S. Scriptura, vel è Ratione petitorum) attamen se Res aliter habet in iis, quæ de publica Ecclesiæ Fide atque Praxi testantur, quorum [?]inscii esse non poterant. Hic nempe æstimandi sunt, non ut privati Doctores, sed ut publici Testes. Quoties itaque testantur, nemine redarguente, Ecclesam[?] sui Temporis hanc Doctrinam, & universim approbasse & à majoribus accepisse; hanc item Disciplinam in Politia administranda; hunc ordinem, & hos Ritus in cultu Divino peragendo, & suscepisse pariter, & usurpasse, quis temere rejiciat ipsorum Testimonium? Siquidem in his probitas potius, quam Peritia requiritur. Duum[?] autem esset, valde durum, illos ut malæ fidei Testes ablegare, aut saltem suspectos habere, qui pro Fide Catholica tam strenuè decertarunt, imo & mortem oppetierunt; quæ omne genus falsi tantopere[?] aversatur, ut nec pro salute animarum, pro Deo, ejusque veritate tuenda, mendacium quovis ullatenus permittat. Sed & peritia quoque, non probitate sola, eminuerunt antiquiores ævi Doctores; præsertim in Fidei Dogmatibus, in quibus exquirendis, excolendisque diligentissimam operam navarunt. Itaque, sive fidelitatem in Testando, sive peritiam in Fide, de qua testantur, spectemus, haud facile nos in errorem inducere poterunt; adeoque digni censendi sunt, quorum Testimonium in hoc negotio admittamus.
units.tr: §. 163. 7. That they should not so cheapen the authority of the ancient Fathers and the distinguished teachers of the Catholic Church, nor contemptuously reject their testimonies, which present-day Catholics bring forward to establish the faith and practice of the ancient Church, as if they were worth nothing at all. For these men were both the outstanding ornaments and the bulwarks of their own times: lights of the Church militant on earth, shining lights kindled by the Sun of Righteousness and scattering the rays of evangelical truth on every side; vigorous defenders of the Catholic faith and most unconquered champions, who preserved it as faithfully as they had received it from the apostles, taught it most zealously and defended it most steadfastly against adversaries of every kind, Gentiles, Jews and heretics; and who, finally, handed it down to posterity as they had received it from their forebears, like a most holy deposit, neither diminished nor corrupted in whole or in part. Certainly their authority will carry no little weight with all Christians of a modest and moderate disposition. For although it may be somewhat lawful to pass freer judgement on their private opinions (which deserve our assent only so far as the force of the arguments drawn from Holy Scripture or from reason extends), the matter stands otherwise with what they bear witness to concerning the public faith and practice of the Church, of which they could not be ignorant. Here they are to be esteemed not as private teachers but as public witnesses. Whenever, therefore, with no one contradicting, they testify that the Church of their time approved this doctrine in general and had received it from their forebears; likewise this discipline in administering the polity; and this order and these rites in performing divine worship, and that they had both adopted and used them, who would rashly reject their testimony? For in such matters probity rather than skill is required. Moreover, it would be very harsh to dismiss as dishonest witnesses, or at least to hold in suspicion, those who fought so vigorously for the Catholic faith, indeed even died for it; a character that shuns every kind of falsehood so greatly that it does not permit a lie in any way, not even for the salvation of souls, for God, or to defend his truth. But the older teachers excelled not only in probity but also in skill, especially in matters of faith, in investigating and cultivating which they devoted the most diligent effort. Therefore, whether we look to their faithfulness in testifying or to their skill in the faith to which they bear witness, they will hardly be able to lead us into error; and so they are rightly considered worthy to have their testimony admitted in this matter.

units.la: §. 164. 8. Ut sibi licentiam non assumant, decretoriam sententiam ferendi contra omnes Ecclesias Christi Fidem hodie profitentes, quæ longe lateque per orbem dispersæ sunt. Quod certe fieri non potest, sine summa Temeritate, atque Arrogantia. Siquidem has omnes vel crassæ Ignorantiæ, vel affectati erroris reas peragunt, quod falsa adhuc obstinate tueantur, & sinceram Evangelii veritatem summa perversitate rejiciant, etiam postquam & hanc & ista ipsi (ut arbitrantur) evidentissime demonstraverint. Neutiquam enim ipsos latere potest, quomodo cunctæ Ecclesiæ Christianismum profitentes, non hujus ævi duntaxat, sed & omnium retro seculorum, Socinianismi Dogmata damnaverint.
units.tr: §. 164. 8. That they should not assume for themselves the licence of pronouncing a decisive judgement against all the Churches of Christ that profess the faith today, which are dispersed far and wide over the world. This certainly cannot be done without the greatest rashness and arrogance. For they make all of these guilty either of gross ignorance or of deliberate error, in that they obstinately maintain false doctrines and with the utmost perversity reject the sincere truth of the Gospel, even after they themselves have (as they think) most clearly demonstrated both this truth and those doctrines. For it cannot possibly escape them how all the churches professing Christianity have condemned the dogmas of Socinianism, not only of this age but of all past ages.

units.la: Præsertim Ecclesiæ nuperioris seculi, in quo hæc nova Dogmata à Socino divulgata sunt, quamprimum apud ipsas innotescere cæperunt, atque insuper speciosissimis, quæ excogitari poterant, Argumentis studiosissime asserta sunt, ista tamen Communibus suffragiis damnarunt. Quis autem sana Ratione præditus, multoque magis Christiana Charitate vel modice imbutus, animum inducat ut credat, tot millia Catholicorum manifestam veritatis lucem, cum se ultra oculis ingess-sit[?], aut non potuisse discernere, aut contra illius fulgorem oculos sponte occlusisse, ne videre cogerentur, quod agnoscere noluerunt? Quin potius credamus, intra Fines Ecclesiæ Catholicæ quamplurimos reperiri, & semper fuisse repertos, qui Ingenio & perspicacitate Judicii pollent, qui veritatem intimo cordis amant, omnesque industria quærunt; qui Pietate, morumque Integritate inter cæteros excellunt; quibus denique, ante omnia, salus animarum in summo Pretio est, cui nihil magis officit, quam salutare Evangelii lumen affectatæ Ignorantiæ, errorisque Tenebris opprimere, & contra apertam veritatem mendacium perversissime tueri.
units.tr: Especially the churches of the last century, in which these new dogmas were spread by Socinus: as soon as they began to become known to them, and were moreover most diligently asserted with the most specious arguments that could be devised, they nevertheless condemned them by common consent. But who, endowed with sound reason, and still more slightly imbued with Christian charity, would bring himself to believe that so many thousands of Catholics, when the manifest light of truth had been thrust upon their eyes beyond measure, either could not discern it, or of their own accord shut their eyes against its brightness, so that they would not be forced to see what they were unwilling to acknowledge? Rather let us believe that within the bounds of the Catholic Church there are, and always have been, very many who excel in genius and acuteness of judgement, who love the truth from the depths of their heart and seek it with all diligence; who surpass the rest in piety and integrity of life; and to whom, above all, the salvation of souls is of the highest worth, which nothing hinders more than to oppress the saving light of the Gospel with the shadows of affected ignorance and error, and most perversely to defend a lie against the plain truth.

units.la: §. 165. 9. Ut si cohibere se nolunt, quin impugnent fundamentalia Christianismi Principia, saltem à Maledictis & Blasphemiis se abstineant, Ne Deum Christianorum, qui ab ipso Christi & Apostolorum ævo, ad nostra usque Tempora, in Trinitate Personarum agnoscitur & colitur, scommatibus, & opprobriis, fædissimisque convitiis proscindant, quasi monstrosum aliquod Commentum, & cerebri male feriantis Idolum. Ne alia quamplura Christianae Fidei mysteria, quorum supra memini, vilipendant, & insectentur non solum ut falsa & inania, sed & summe perniciosa atque pestifera. Non sic Apostoli se gesserunt in Evangelio praedicando, ne quidem contra Idola Gentilium, Ritusque illos impios, immites, & impuros, quibus Idola illa colebantur. Nam, si Scribae Ephesio fides (qui, ut ipse Idolorum cultor erat, ita Res Pauli, & Sociorum ejus apud Ephesum ignorare non poterat) & ipse Paulus, & qui cum eo erant, etsi Idololatriam acerrimo zelo impeterent, & evertere conarentur, attamen haud soliti sunt falsa ista Idololatrarum numina atrocibus convitiis & maledictis incessere, sed aeque immunes se praestiterunt a Blasphemia in Gentilium Deos, ac a sacrilegio in direptione Templorum. Sic enim ille in oratione ad suos Ephesios Adduxistis Homines istos, neque sacrilegos, neque Blasphemantes Deam vestram. Cum item Athenis esset & conspiceret urbem, ut Idolis refertam, sic & illorum cultui omnino deditam, quamvis ad hoc Spiritus ejus exacerbaretur, a contumeliis tamen abstinuit, tum in Idola ista, tum in ipsos Idololatras; nihil asperius efferens in Athenienses, quam quod adverteret eos quasi superstitiosos esse; & occasione arrepta ex conspectu cujusdam Arae, cui inscriptum erat, Ignoto Deo, veri Dei notitiam, cultumque praedicans Quem, inquit, ignorantes colitis, Hunc ego vobis annuncio. Ita se Paulus gerebat, ita caeteri quoque Apostoli, sobrie & modeste Rem suam agentes; neque atrocia convitia temere jactantes, sed solidis Argumentis Adversarios suos erroris convincentes. Porro, quod ipse Paulus facere assuevit, idem in mandatis dat Timotheo suo: Servum Domini pugnare, non oportet, sed mansuetum esse erga omnes, aptum ad docendum, tolerantem malos, cum lenitate erudientem eos, qui se contra opponunt; experiendo, an Deus forte illis datura[?] sit Resipiscentiam, ad veritatem agnoscendam. 2 Tim. 2. v. 24, 25. Apostolos ergo in hoc, ut in caeteris, Sociniani sibi proponant imitandos; & ante omnia solicite sibi caveant à crimine Blasphemiæ, quam Deus sub lege, diro lapidationis supplicio plectendam voluit; & piissimi Principes sub Evangelio, hanc Dei sententiam comprobantes, eandem vel capitali supplicio, aliove perquam severo, castigandam duxere. Imo, & ante eos Ethnici, naturæ Duce, ultimum supplicium statuerunt in Blasphemiæ Reos; neque aliter Pietatem in Deos suos se satis demonstrare posse arbitrati sunt. Exemplo sint, præ cæteris, Athenienses modo memorati, in iis, quæ decreverunt contra Protagoram, Diagoram, Alcibiadem, ipsumque Socratem, quamvis de hoc crimine per calumniam damnatum.
units.tr: §. 165. 9. That if they will not restrain themselves from attacking the fundamental principles of Christianity, they should at least abstain from abuse and blasphemy, and not tear apart with mockeries, reproaches and most foul insults the God of the Christians, who from the age of Christ and the Apostles down to our own times has been acknowledged and worshipped in the Trinity of Persons, as some monstrous invention and an idol of a badly disordered brain. Nor should they vilify and assail the many other mysteries of the Christian faith mentioned above, not only as false and empty but as most pernicious and deadly. The apostles did not behave thus in preaching the Gospel, not even against the idols of the Gentiles and those impious, unclean and filthy rites by which those idols were worshipped. For when the town clerk of Ephesus (who, being himself a worshipper of idols, could not be ignorant of the affairs of Paul and his companions at Ephesus) ... Paul himself and those with him, though they attacked idolatry with the most ardent zeal and tried to overthrow it, were nevertheless not accustomed to assail those false deities of the idolaters with atrocious insults and curses, but showed themselves as free from blasphemy against the gods of the Gentiles as from sacrilege in plundering their temples. For thus he speaks in his address to the Ephesians: You have brought these men here, who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of your goddess. Again, when he was at Athens and saw the city full of idols, and so wholly given over to their worship, although his spirit was stirred up by this, he nevertheless abstained from insults, both against those idols and against the idolaters themselves, declaring nothing more harshly against the Athenians than that he observed them to be, as it were, superstitious. Seizing the occasion from the sight of a certain altar inscribed To the Unknown God, he proclaimed the knowledge and worship of the true God: Whom you ignorantly worship, this one I announce to you. Thus Paul conducted himself, and thus the other apostles too, carrying on their business soberly and modestly, neither rashly hurling atrocious reproaches but convicting their adversaries of error by solid arguments. Further, what Paul himself was accustomed to do, he also commands in his instructions to Timothy: The servant of the Lord must not strive, but must be gentle towards all, apt to teach, patient with the evil, instructing with gentleness those who set themselves against him; if perhaps God may give them repentance to acknowledge the truth. 2 Tim. 2. v. 24, 25. Let the Socinians therefore set the apostles before themselves as models to imitate in this, as in other things; and above all let them carefully guard against the crime of blasphemy, which God under the law willed to be punished with the dreadful penalty of stoning. The most pious princes under the Gospel, confirming this sentence of God, have judged it to be punished with capital punishment or some other very severe penalty. Indeed, even before them the heathens, guided by nature, decreed the extreme penalty for those guilty of blasphemy, nor did they think they could otherwise sufficiently demonstrate their piety towards their gods. Examples are, above all, the Athenians just mentioned, in what they decreed against Protagoras, Diagoras, Alcibiades and Socrates himself, although the last was condemned for this crime through calumny.

units.la: §. 166. 10. Ut sibi solis non sapiant, aliosque omnes pro insipientibus habeant. Cum enim rectam rationem omnium Controversiarum Judicem statuunt, eandem sibi solis attribuere solent, quasi suæ sectæ propriam. Quod enim Enthusiastæ dant Spiritui privato, Hi Rationi privatæ tribuunt; quod illi lumini extrinsecus infuso, Hi lumini naturæ ingenito. In hoc quidem nimium liberales erga Rationem merè humanam, & desuper non illuminatam; cum experimentis frequentibus constet, quam varia sit & fallax in sua sententia ferenda, non solum in diversis Hominibus, quorum Ingenia & mores plurimum variantur; sed & in eodem, pro diversitate Ætatum atque studiorum. Quomodo igitur tam incerto Duci confidere possunt in Rebus Fidei, quæ non nisi Cælesti lumine discernuntur, & rite agnoscuntur, cum tam sæpe homines fallat, etiam in naturalibus & moralibus, quæ nobis multo propiora sunt, & intellectu faciliora? At certe multo iniquius & arrogantius est, sanam Rationem, præsertim in rebus Theologicis, sibi solis vindicare, quasi peculiarem quandam sectæ suæ Prærogativam; ac si alii omnes Christianismum profitentes sanæ mentis compotes haud essent. De Chinensibus quidem fertur, quod sua Genti soli binos oculos tribuant, Europæis unum, Cateris nentrum. At Sociniani, in hoc paulo arrogantiores, qui neque Europæis, paucis suæ sectæ exceptis, vel unicum concedunt. Illi Europæ incolas, non nisi luscos esse volunt; at Hi, plane Cæcos existimant.
units.tr: §. 166. 10. That they may not be wise to themselves alone and regard all others as fools. For when they set up right reason as the judge of all controversies, they are wont to assign it to themselves alone, as if it were the peculiar property of their sect. What the Enthusiasts give to the private Spirit, these give to private Reason; what those give to an outwardly infused light, these give to the light of nature implanted in us. In this they are far too generous towards reason that is merely human and not enlightened from above, since frequent experience shows how varied and fallacious it is in passing judgment, not only in different men, whose talents and characters differ greatly, but also in the same man, according to the differences of age and study. How, then, can they trust so unsteady a guide in matters of faith, which are discerned only by heavenly light and rightly recognised, when it so often deceives men even in natural and moral matters, which are much closer to us and easier to understand? But surely it is far more unjust and arrogant to claim sound reason for themselves alone, especially in theological matters, as if it were a peculiar prerogative of their sect, as if all others who profess Christianity were not of sound mind. It is said of the Chinese that they grant two eyes to their own people, one to the Europeans, and neither to the rest. But the Socinians, somewhat more arrogant in this, grant not even a single eye to Europeans, apart from a few of their own sect. The Chinese want the inhabitants of Europe to be only one-eyed; these men think them plainly blind.
